shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in acute bleeding: where it saves lives, and where it doesn’t
shelves.question: Does tranexamic acid save lives in acute bleeding — and where does it not?
shelves.mesh: Tranexamic Acid · Antifibrinolytic Agents · Hemorrhage · Wounds and Injuries · Brain Injuries, Traumatic · Postpartum Hemorrhage · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage
shelves.balance: Given early, tranexamic acid saves lives in bleeding trauma, head injury, and childbirth. In acute GI bleeding it saves no one and clots more veins. Timing is the drug.

cards.headline: CRASH-2: tranexamic acid in bleeding trauma (Lancet 2010)
cards.summary: All-cause mortality 14.5% vs 16.0% (RR 0.91 , 95% CI 0.85–0.97) — about 15 fewer deaths per 1,000 treated; 20,211 adults with traumatic bleeding, randomized within 8 hours of injury.
cards.people: 20,211 adults with, or at risk of, significant traumatic bleeding, randomised within 8 hours of injury — 274 hospitals in 40 countries
cards.result: All-cause mortality 14.5% vs 16.0% (RR 0.91 , 95% CI 0.85–0.97; p=0.0035) — about 15 fewer deaths per 1,000 treated. Death due to bleeding 4.9% vs 5.7% (RR 0.85 , 0.76–0.96). Vascular occlusive events were not increased
cards.source: CRASH-2, Lancet 2010; PMID 20554319 · ISRCTN86750102 · NCT00375258 · rxcui 10691

cards.headline: CRASH-3: tranexamic acid in traumatic brain injury (Lancet 2019)
cards.summary: Head-injury death 18.5% vs 19.8% (RR 0.94 , 0.86–1.02); benefit concentrated in mild-to-moderate injury (RR 0.78 ), none in severe injury (RR 0.99 ) — 12,737 adults with traumatic brain injury.
cards.people: 12,737 adults with traumatic brain injury, GCS ≤12 or bleeding on CT, no major extracranial bleeding; the primary analysis covers the 9,202 treated within 3 hours of injury
cards.result: Head-injury death 18.5% vs 19.8% (RR 0.94 , 0.86–1.02). In the prespecified sensitivity analysis excluding GCS 3 and bilateral unreactive pupils: 12.5% vs 14.0% (RR 0.89 , 0.80–1.00). Benefit concentrated in mild-to-moderate injury (RR 0.78 , 0.64–0.95); none in severe injury (RR 0.99 , 0.91–1.07). Vascular occlusive events and seizures were similar

cards.headline: WOMAN: tranexamic acid in post-partum haemorrhage (Lancet 2017)
cards.summary: Death due to bleeding 1.5% vs 1.9% (RR 0.81 , 0.65–1.00); in women treated within 3 hours of giving birth, RR 0.69 — 20,060 women with post-partum haemorrhage.

cards.headline: HALT-IT: tranexamic acid in acute GI bleeding (Lancet 2020)
cards.summary: Death due to bleeding within 5 days: 4% vs 4% (RR 0.99 , 0.82–1.18) — no benefit; venous thromboembolism 0.8% vs 0.4% (RR 1.85 ) — 12,009 adults with acute GI bleeding.
cards.people: 12,009 adults with significant acute upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding — 164 hospitals in 15 countries
cards.result: Death due to bleeding within 5 days: 4% vs 4% (RR 0.99 , 0.82–1.18) — no benefit. Arterial thromboembolic events were similar ( 0.7% vs 0.8% ), but venous thromboembolism was higher with tranexamic acid ( 0.8% vs 0.4% ; RR 1.85 , 1.15–2.98). The trialists’ conclusion: tranexamic acid should not be used for gastrointestinal bleeding outside a randomised trial

shelves.title: The first six hours of septic shock: the EGDT arc
shelves.question: Did early goal-directed therapy save lives in septic shock — and what did the three multicenter trials that followed find?

shelves.title: Epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
shelves.question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does epinephrine help patients survive — and survive well?
shelves.mesh: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest · Epinephrine · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Emergency Medical Services · Double-Blind Method · Survival Rate · Hospital Mortality
shelves.balance: Epinephrine restarts hearts and gets more people to day 30 alive — about 1 extra survivor per 125 treated — but it does not significantly increase good-neurology survival, and more of the extra survivors are severely impaired.

cards.headline: PARAMEDIC2 (Perkins 2018): epinephrine — more survivors at day 30, not more good recoveries.
cards.summary: 30-day survival 3.2% epinephrine vs 2.4% placebo, OR 1.39 (1.06–1.82) — about 1 extra survivor per 125 treated ; favorable neurologic outcome 2.2% vs 1.9% (not significant); among survivors, severe neurologic impairment 31.0% vs 17.8% .
cards.people: 8,014 adults, UK ambulance services
cards.result: 30-day survival 3.2% epinephrine vs 2.4% placebo, OR 1.39 (1.06–1.82) — about 1 extra survivor per 125 treated; favorable neurologic outcome 2.2% vs 1.9% (not significant); among survivors, severe neurologic impairment 31.0% vs 17.8% .
cards.watchOut: the survival gain is real but small, and it is not matched by good-neurology survival — the extra survivors are more often severely impaired; single trial, shelved by developer’s exception.
cards.source: Perkins GD et al., N Engl J Med 2018 (PMID 30021076 · ISRCTN73485024)

shelves.title: Ketamine vs etomidate for emergency intubation
shelves.question: When you intubate a critically ill patient, does the induction drug — ketamine or etomidate — change how they do?
shelves.mesh: Adrenal Insufficiency · Aged · Anesthetics, Intravenous · Critical Illness · Etomidate · Female · France · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Intubation, Intratracheal · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Ketamine · Male · Middle Aged · Morbidity · Multiple Organ Failure · Prospective Studies · Single-Blind Method · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The 2009 trial found organ failure identical between the two, with etomidate's known tax: adrenal suppression in most recipients. The 2022 trial added a wrinkle — survival at day 7 favored ketamine — but by day 28 the difference had washed out. Two trials, no proven mortality difference at a month; the honest answer is that the drug choice matters less than its reputation, with one early signal still unexplained.

cards.headline: KETASED 2009: organ failure identical (SOFA 10.3 vs 9.6) — but adrenal insufficiency far more common after etomidate (OR 6.7).
cards.summary: Maximum SOFA score 10.3 (SD 3.7) on etomidate vs 9.6 (3.9) on ketamine — mean difference 0.7 (95% CI 0.0–1.4; P=0.056), not significant. Intubation conditions did not differ. Adrenal insufficiency was significantly more frequent after etomidate (odds ratio 6.7, 3.5–12.7). No serious adverse events with either drug.
cards.people: 469 patients analyzed for the primary outcome (234 etomidate, 235 ketamine) undergoing rapid-sequence intubation
cards.result: Maximum SOFA score 10.3 (SD 3.7) on etomidate vs 9.6 (3.9) on ketamine — mean difference 0.7 (95% CI 0.0–1.4; P=0.056), not significant. Intubation conditions did not differ. Adrenal insufficiency was significantly more frequent after etomidate (odds ratio 6.7, 3.5–12.7). No serious adverse events with either drug.
cards.watchOut: The trial measured organ failure and a laboratory harm (adrenal suppression), not survival — it can acquit etomidate on SOFA but cannot settle whether the adrenal hit ever costs a life.
cards.source: Jabre P et al., Lancet 2009 (PMID 19573904 · NCT00440102)

shelves.title: Antibiotics vs appendectomy for appendicitis: a real alternative — with an appendicolith exception and a five-year tail
shelves.question: In uncomplicated acute appendicitis, can antibiotics replace appendectomy — and for whom does that trade fail?
shelves.balance: Mostly yes, with two carve-outs. CODA (1,552 adults) found antibiotics noninferior to appendectomy on 30-day health status, and 71% of the antibiotics group had avoided surgery at 90 days — but complications ran higher with antibiotics (8.1 vs 3.5 per 100 patients), driven entirely by patients with an appendicolith (20.2 vs 3.6 per 100; 41% of them came to surgery). APPAC (530 CT-proven uncomplicated cases) missed its strict noninferiority test, yet 72.7% avoided appendectomy at one year with no penalty for having waited; by five years 39.1% of the antibiotics group had had an appendectomy, while overall complications favored antibiotics (6.5% vs 24.4%). The honest offer: antibiotics first is reasonable for uncomplicated appendicitis without an appendicolith, accepting roughly a 3-in-10 chance of surgery within a year and 4-in-10 by five years.

cards.headline: Antibiotics matched surgery on 30-day health status — but 29% were operated on by 90 days, and an appendicolith changed everything
cards.summary: Antibiotics were noninferior on the primary outcome, 30-day health status (EQ-5D mean difference 0.01; 95% CI −0.001 to 0.03, margin 0.05). By 90 days, 29% of the antibiotics group had undergone appendectomy — 41% with an appendicolith vs 25% without.
cards.people: 1,552 adults with appendicitis at 25 US centers (776 antibiotics, 776 appendectomy; 414 had an appendicolith); 47% of the antibiotics group were never hospitalized for the index treatment; 96% of operations were laparoscopic
cards.result: Antibiotics were noninferior on the primary outcome, 30-day health status (EQ-5D mean difference 0.01; 95% CI −0.001 to 0.03, margin 0.05). By 90 days, 29% of the antibiotics group had undergone appendectomy — 41% with an appendicolith vs 25% without. Complications were more common with antibiotics (8.1 vs 3.5 per 100; rate ratio 2.28), attributable to the appendicolith subgroup (20.2 vs 3.6 per 100; rate ratio 5.69) and not to patients without one (3.7 vs 3.5 per 100). Serious adverse events 4.0 vs 3.0 per 100 (not significant).
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is how patients felt at 30 days, not cure — the surgery-avoidance and complication numbers are the real trade, and they split sharply on the appendicolith. Follow-up here is 90 days; APPAC’s five-year report is the long view.
cards.source: CODA Collaborative, N Engl J Med 2020 · PMID 33017106 · NCT02800785

cards.headline: APPAC failed its own noninferiority test — yet 72.7% never needed the operation in year one
cards.summary: Surgery succeeded in 99.6%. In the antibiotics group, 27.3% (70/257) had an appendectomy within one year and 72.7% (186/256) never required surgery — but the efficacy difference (−27.0%) crossed the prespecified 24% noninferiority margin, so noninferiority was NOT demonstrated.
cards.people: 530 patients aged 18–60 with CT-confirmed uncomplicated acute appendicitis in Finland; 273 surgery, 257 antibiotics
cards.result: Surgery succeeded in 99.6%. In the antibiotics group, 27.3% (70/257) had an appendectomy within one year and 72.7% (186/256) never required surgery — but the efficacy difference (−27.0%) crossed the prespecified 24% noninferiority margin, so noninferiority was NOT demonstrated. Of the 70 who came to surgery, 82.9% still had uncomplicated appendicitis, 10.0% had complicated disease, and 7.1% had no appendicitis at all. No abscesses or other major complications were attributed to the delayed operations.
cards.watchOut: “Failed noninferiority” and “most avoided surgery” are both true — the margin demanded antibiotics nearly match a 99.6% operation. The trial excluded complicated appendicitis by CT, and its surgery arm was open appendectomy, not laparoscopic.
cards.source: Salminen P et al., JAMA 2015 · PMID 26080338 · NCT01022567

cards.headline: At five years, 39.1% of the antibiotics group had had an appendectomy — and complications still favored antibiotics
cards.summary: Beyond the 70 first-year appendectomies, 30 more patients (16.1% of those still at risk) had surgery between years 1 and 5; cumulative appendicitis recurrence reached 39.1% (100/256) at five years — 34.0% at year 2, then a slowing climb. Overall complications at five years were 6.5% in the antibiotics group vs 24.4% in the surgery group (P<0.001).
cards.type: Five-year follow-up of a randomized trial
cards.people: The APPAC cohort (530 randomized; 256 in the antibiotics group with follow-up): appendectomy vs the same antibiotic regimen
cards.result: Beyond the 70 first-year appendectomies, 30 more patients (16.1% of those still at risk) had surgery between years 1 and 5; cumulative appendicitis recurrence reached 39.1% (100/256) at five years — 34.0% at year 2, then a slowing climb. Overall complications at five years were 6.5% in the antibiotics group vs 24.4% in the surgery group (P<0.001), a 17.9-point difference; hospital stay did not differ, and sick leave ran 11 days longer after surgery.
cards.watchOut: This is the same trial as Card 2 at a later horizon, not a second trial — count it as one exhibit. Recurrence keeps accruing after year one, so “antibiotics first” buys most patients an avoided operation, not a permanent cure.
cards.source: Salminen P et al., JAMA 2018 · PMID 30264120 · NCT01022567

shelves.title: Epinephrine in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
shelves.question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does epinephrine improve survival — and survival with a good neurologic outcome?
shelves.mesh: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest · Epinephrine · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Emergency Medical Services · Humans
shelves.balance: Epinephrine restarts hearts and raises 30-day survival — 3.2% vs 1.3% in the big trial — but has not been shown to raise survival with a good neurologic outcome, and more of its survivors live with severe impairment. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for survival; the intact-survival claim is unproven.

cards.summary: 30-day survival 3.2% vs 1.3% ; favorable neurologic outcome 2.2% vs 1.9% — not significant — 8,014 adults with out-of-hospital arrest.

cards.result: 30-day survival 3.2% vs 1.3% ; favorable neurologic outcome 2.2% vs 1.9% — not significant.
cards.watchOut: Among survivors, severe neurologic impairment was more common with epinephrine.

shelves.title: Amiodarone and lidocaine in shock-refractory VF / pulseless VT
shelves.question: In shock-refractory ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia, do amiodarone or lidocaine improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Ventricular Fibrillation · Tachycardia, Ventricular · Amiodarone · Lidocaine · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents · Humans
shelves.balance: Neither drug has beaten placebo on survival to discharge overall. Amiodarone improved survival to admission in 1999; in the 2016 three-way trial the only signal was in bystander-witnessed arrests. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE at best, subgroup-bound.

shelves.title: Temperature control after cardiac arrest
shelves.question: After cardiac arrest, does cooling to 33 °C beat 36 °C — or normothermia with fever treated?
shelves.mesh: Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest · Hypothermia, Induced · Body Temperature · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Humans
shelves.balance: Cooling to 33 °C after arrest does not beat 36 °C, and does not beat normothermia with fever treated — two large trials agree. The one dissent is in nonshockable rhythms (HYPERION), a subgroup-sized trial. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY (for the negative claim).

shelves.title: Second-line drugs for established status epilepticus
shelves.question: After benzodiazepines fail in established status epilepticus, which second-line drug stops the seizure?
shelves.mesh: Status Epilepticus · Anticonvulsants · Levetiracetam · Phenytoin · Valproic Acid · Humans
shelves.balance: Levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, and valproate are indistinguishable — each stops seizures in just under half of benzodiazepine-refractory patients. In children, levetiracetam has not beaten phenytoin either, in two trials. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone in bacterial meningitis
shelves.question: Does dexamethasone improve outcomes in bacterial meningitis — and does the answer depend on where the patient is?
shelves.mesh: Meningitis, Bacterial · Dexamethasone · Glucocorticoids · Humans
shelves.balance: Dexamethasone’s answer depends on where the patient is. It cut death and bad outcomes where patients arrive early with susceptible organisms (Europe 2002, Costa Rica 1991); it did nothing in Malawi adults and children, and pointed toward harm in a small Pakistan trial. Setting is part of the result. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE — setting-dependent; no global claim.

shelves.title: Thrombolysis and catheter treatment for intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism
shelves.question: In intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism, do thrombolysis or catheter treatments help more than they harm?
shelves.mesh: Pulmonary Embolism · Fibrinolytic Agents · Tenecteplase · Alteplase · Thrombectomy · Humans
shelves.balance: Full-dose lysis prevents hemodynamic collapse (1.6% vs 5.0%) and buys it with major bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%); it has not been shown to save lives in this group. The alternatives — half-dose lysis, catheter techniques — rest on small trials, surrogate endpoints, or composites driven by ICU use. Developer’s verdict: POSSIBLE for decompensation prevention; the harm figures are part of the claim.

shelves.title: Restrictive transfusion thresholds in acute bleeding

shelves.balance: In acute upper GI bleeding, transfusing at a hemoglobin of 7 rather than 9 g/dL lowered 45-day mortality (5% vs 9%) and rebleeding. The paired question in septic shock — where the restrictive threshold proved equally safe, with half the blood — is answered by TRISS, which lives on Shelf #124 (Reference 3) under the one-home rule and is not re-carded here. Developer’s verdict: LIKELY for GI bleeding; see Shelf #124 for septic shock.

shelves.title: Plasma and platelet ratios in massive transfusion: 1:1:1 stops the bleeding sooner — overall mortality does not significantly move
shelves.question: In severe trauma with major bleeding, does transfusing plasma, platelets and red cells in a 1:1:1 ratio rather than 1:1:2 save lives?
shelves.mesh: Blood Component Transfusion · Blood Platelets · Erythrocytes · Exsanguination · Female · Hemostasis · Humans · Male · Plasma · Shock, Hemorrhagic · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: The only large randomized test missed both of its mortality endpoints — 24-hour mortality 12.7% vs 17.0% (P=.12) and 30-day 22.4% vs 26.1% (P=.26) for 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 — and this shelf prints that null first, because it is the honest headline. What the higher ratio did deliver, in PROPPR itself, was hemostasis (86% vs 78% achieving it) and fewer deaths from exsanguination by 24 hours (9.2% vs 14.6%), at no measured cost across 23 prespecified complications. The observational PROMMTT cohort points the same way — early high ratios associated with lower 6-hour mortality — but it is association, and PROPPR is what the association survived when randomized: a bleeding-control benefit, not a proven overall-survival benefit. POSSIBLE. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PROPPR (Holcomb 2015, JAMA): both mortality primaries missed — 24-hour 12.7% vs 17.0% (P=.12), 30-day 22.4% vs 26.1% (P=.26); deaths from exsanguination fewer (9.2% vs 14.6%, P=.03)
cards.summary: 680 severely injured patients at 12 North American level I trauma centers, predicted to need massive transfusion; plasma, platelets and red cells in a 1:1:1 ratio vs 1:1:2 . Primary outcomes — mortality at 24 hours ( 12.7% vs 17.0% ; difference −4.2% [−9.6 to 1.1]; P=.12) and at 30 days ( 22.4% vs 26.1% ; difference −3.7% [−10.2 to 2.7]; P=.26) — did not differ significantly . What 1:1:1 did change: death from exsanguination by 24 hours 9.2% vs 14.6% (P=.03), and hemostasis achieved in 86% vs 78% (P=.006), with no difference in any of 23 prespecified complications despite more plasma and platelets given.
cards.type: Pragmatic, phase 3, multisite, randomized clinical trial (PROPPR), JAMA 2015. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01545232. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 680 severely injured patients who arrived at 1 of 12 level I trauma centers in North America directly from the scene and were predicted to require massive transfusion (338 assigned 1:1:1; 342 assigned 1:1:2), treated between August 2012 and December 2013.
cards.result: No significant differences were detected in mortality at 24 hours (12.7% in the 1:1:1 group vs 17.0% in the 1:1:2 group; difference, −4.2% [95% CI, −9.6% to 1.1%]; P=.12) or at 30 days (22.4% vs 26.1%, respectively; difference, −3.7% [95% CI, −10.2% to 2.7%]; P=.26). Exsanguination, which was the predominant cause of death within the first 24 hours, was significantly decreased in the 1:1:1 group (9.2% vs 14.6% in the 1:1:2 group; difference, −5.4% [95% CI, −10.4% to −0.5%]; P=.03). More patients in the 1:1:1 group achieved hemostasis than in the 1:1:2 group (86% vs 78%, respectively; P=.006). Despite the 1:1:1 group receiving more plasma (median 7 U vs 5 U, P<.001) and platelets (12 U vs 6 U, P<.001) and similar amounts of red blood cells (9 U) over the first 24 hours, no differences were found for the 23 prespecified complications, including ARDS, multiple organ failure, venous thromboembolism, sepsis, and transfusion-related complications.
cards.watchOut: The mortality null is the headline and prints first. The exsanguination result is a cause-specific outcome, not a primary endpoint — real, and consistent with the hemostasis finding, but it is not a demonstrated overall-survival benefit. In a pragmatic trial the two ratio arms also converge once the opening packs are given, which dilutes the contrast the trial could detect.
cards.source: Holcomb JB et al. Transfusion of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells in a 1:1:1 vs a 1:1:2 ratio and mortality in patients with severe trauma: the PROPPR randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015;313(5):471–482. PMID 25647203 · NCT01545232

cards.headline: PROMMTT (Holcomb 2013, JAMA Surgery): the observational source of the ratio idea — early ratios at or above 1:1 tracked with lower 6-hour mortality (adjusted HR 0.31 for plasma:RBC)
cards.summary: 1,245 trauma patients (905 in the analysis group) at 10 US level I centers, transfused early after admission, followed with minute-by-minute product timing. In time-dependent Cox models, higher early ratios were associated with lower 6-hour mortality: plasma:RBC adjusted HR 0.31 [0.16–0.58], relative ; platelet:RBC adjusted HR 0.55 [0.31–0.98], relative ; patients with ratios below 1:2 in the first 6 hours were 3 to 4 times more likely to die than patients at 1:1 or higher. After 24 hours the ratios carried no association with mortality.
cards.type: Prospective observational cohort study (PROMMTT) with time-varying (time-dependent proportional hazards) analysis, JAMA Surgery 2013. No registry ID — an observational cohort; none on the record. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Adult trauma patients at 10 US level I trauma centers who survived at least 30 minutes after admission and received at least 1 unit of red cells within 6 hours (n=1,245); the analysis group (n=905) received at least 3 total units of blood products within 24 hours.
cards.result: Plasma:RBC and platelet:RBC ratios were not constant during the first 24 hours (P<.001 for both). In a multivariable time-dependent Cox model, increased ratios of plasma:RBCs (adjusted hazard ratio 0.31; 95% CI, 0.16–0.58) and platelets:RBCs (adjusted hazard ratio 0.55; 95% CI, 0.31–0.98) were independently associated with decreased 6-hour mortality, when hemorrhagic death predominated. In the first 6 hours, patients with ratios less than 1:2 were 3 to 4 times more likely to die than patients with ratios of 1:1 or higher. After 24 hours, plasma and platelet ratios were unassociated with mortality, when competing risks from nonhemorrhagic causes prevailed.
cards.watchOut: Observational: the time-dependent design answers the survivor-bias critique of the earlier ratio literature (you cannot receive a high ratio if you die in the first hour), but confounding by indication and by center cannot be removed by modeling. This study is the hypothesis PROPPR (Reference 1) then tested — and PROPPR’s mortality primaries were null. Read the pair together: association first, randomization second, conclusion trimmed accordingly.
cards.source: Holcomb JB et al. The prospective, observational, multicenter, major trauma transfusion (PROMMTT) study: comparative effectiveness of a time-varying treatment with competing risks. JAMA Surg. 2013;148(2):127–136. PMID 23560283. DOI 10.1001/2013.jamasurg.387

shelves.title: Prehospital plasma: why did the helicopter trial win and the city trial lose?
shelves.question: Does plasma given before hospital arrival save lives in bleeding trauma — and does the answer depend on how long the transport takes?
shelves.mesh: Air Ambulances · Blood Component Transfusion · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Humans · Male · Plasma · Resuscitation · Shock, Hemorrhagic · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: The entire randomized record is two trials, and they disagree. PAMPer — plasma during air transport, where journeys are long — cut 30-day mortality from 33.0% to 23.2%. COMBAT — plasma during urban ground transport, median under 20 minutes — found 15% vs 10% against plasma and stopped for futility. Pooled, the pair shows a 24-hour mortality signal (RR 0.69) that dissolves by one month (RR 0.86, not significant). The transport-time explanation is coherent — plasma may need time at risk to pay — but it is an explanation fitted to two points, and by this library’s house rule for one positive against one null it would grade MAYBE (weak evidence) — the developer rules it POSSIBLE. Shelf #241 holds these trials’ home cards; this shelf asks the setting question they raise together. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PAMPer (Sperry 2018, NEJM): plasma in the air cut 30-day mortality — 23.2% vs 33.0% [re-card — home Shelf #241]
cards.summary: 501 injured patients at risk of hemorrhagic shock, cluster-randomized by air-medical base: two units of thawed plasma during air transport vs standard-care resuscitation. Mortality at 30 days was significantly lower with plasma: 23.2% vs 33.0% (difference −9.8 percentage points [−18.6 to −1.0]; P=0.03). Survival curves separated by 3 hours and stayed separated; the prothrombin-time ratio on hospital arrival was lower with plasma (1.2 vs 1.3, P<0.001). No significant differences in multiorgan failure, acute lung injury/ARDS, nosocomial infections, or transfusion reactions.
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicenter, cluster-randomized, phase 3 superiority trial (PAMPer), N Engl J Med 2018. Registry ID verified against the record’s own databank: NCT01818427 (the home card on Shelf #241 predates this check and shows no registry ID; the record carries one). Re-card; home Shelf #241. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 501 patients evaluated during air medical transport at risk for hemorrhagic shock: 230 received plasma and 271 received standard-care resuscitation.
cards.result: Mortality at 30 days was significantly lower in the plasma group than in the standard-care group (23.2% vs 33.0%; difference, −9.8 percentage points; 95% CI, −18.6 to −1.0; P=0.03). A similar treatment effect was observed across nine prespecified subgroups (test for heterogeneity P=0.79). Kaplan–Meier curves showed an early separation beginning 3 hours after randomization and persisting to 30 days (log-rank P=0.02). The median prothrombin-time ratio after arrival at the trauma center was lower in the plasma group (1.2 vs 1.3, P<0.001). No significant differences were noted for multiorgan failure, acute lung injury–acute respiratory distress syndrome, nosocomial infections, or allergic or transfusion-related reactions.
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomized by air base and open-label: crews knew the assignment. The comparison that matters is against Card 2 — the same intervention, tested in the same funding program, in a ground system with short transports, found nothing. PAMPer alone does not tell you whether plasma works; the pair tells you where it might.
cards.source: Sperry JL et al. Prehospital plasma during air medical transport in trauma patients at risk for hemorrhagic shock. N Engl J Med. 2018;379(4):315–326. PMID 30044935 · NCT01818427. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa1802345

cards.headline: COMBAT (Moore 2018, Lancet): plasma on the ground did nothing — 28-day mortality 15% vs 10%, stopped for futility [re-card — home Shelf #241]
cards.summary: 144 trauma patients in hemorrhagic shock during urban ground transport to a single level I center (Denver); two units of plasma in the ambulance vs saline. Transport times were short — median 19 vs 16 minutes . Mortality within 28 days did not differ: 15% on plasma vs 10% on saline (P=0.37, as-treated). No differences in safety outcomes; the trial was stopped for futility after 144 of 150 planned enrollments.
cards.type: Pragmatic, randomized, single-center trial (COMBAT — Control of Major Bleeding After Trauma), Lancet 2018. Registry ID verified against the record’s own databank: NCT01838863 (the home card on Shelf #241 predates this check; the record carries one). Re-card; home Shelf #241.
cards.people: 144 patients randomly assigned at the scene by paramedics (as-treated analysis: 125 eligible patients — 65 plasma, 60 saline). Median age 33 years (IQR 25–47); median New Injury Severity Score 27; 56% required blood transfusion within 6 hours. The record’s abstract does not print a sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: The groups were similar at baseline and had similar transport times (plasma median 19 min [IQR 16–23] vs control 16 min [14–22]). The groups did not differ in mortality at 28 days (15% in the plasma group vs 10% in the control group, P=0.37). In the intention-to-treat analysis there were no significant differences in safety outcomes and adverse events. Due to the consistent lack of differences, the study was stopped for futility after 144 of 150 planned enrollments. The authors concluded that blood products might be beneficial in settings with longer transport times, but the financial burden would not be justified in an urban environment with short distances to mature trauma centers.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-center, and its point estimate leans against plasma — treat the lean as noise around a null, not as evidence of harm. Its real contribution is the contrast: median transport under 20 minutes may simply leave no time for prehospital plasma to matter, which is a claim about settings, not about plasma.
cards.source: Moore HB et al. Plasma-first resuscitation to treat haemorrhagic shock during emergency ground transportation in an urban area: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2018;392(10144):283–291. PMID 30032977 · NCT01838863. DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(18)31553-8
cards.search: combat (moore 2018, lancet): plasma on the ground did nothing — 28-day mortality 15% vs 10%, stopped for futility [re-card — home shelf #241] 144 trauma patients in hemorrhagic shock during urban ground transport to a single level i center (denver); two units of plasma in the ambulance vs saline. transport times were short — median 19 vs 16 minutes . mortality within 28 days did not differ: 15% on plasma vs 10% on saline (p=0.37, as-treated). no differences in safety outcomes; the trial was stopped for futility after 144 of 150 planned enrollments. in trauma patients with hemorrhagic shock transported by ground ambulance in an urban area with short transport times, does plasma-first resuscitation improve survival? pragmatic, randomized, single-center trial (combat — control of major bleeding after trauma), lancet 2018. registry id verified against the record's own databank: nct01838863

cards.headline: The two trials pooled (Coccolini 2019, World Journal of Emergency Surgery): 24-hour mortality favors plasma (RR 0.69); one-month mortality does not reach significance (RR 0.86)
cards.summary: 2 randomized trials, 626 patients (295 plasma, 331 usual care) — PAMPer and COMBAT are the entire randomized record. Pooled: 24-hour mortality lower with prehospital plasma, RR 0.69 [0.48–0.99], relative ; one-month mortality RR 0.86 [0.68–1.11], relative — not significant ; no effect on acute lung injury (OR 1.03) or multiorgan failure (OR 1.30).
cards.type: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, World Journal of Emergency Surgery 2019. (A meta-analysis — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the analysis itself.)
cards.people: Two randomized trials including 626 patients with hemorrhagic shock (295 in the plasma arm and 331 in the usual-care arm) — the PAMPer and COMBAT trials carded above.
cards.result: Twenty-four-hour mortality seems to be reduced in the pre-hospital plasma group (RR=0.69; 95% CI 0.48–0.99). Pre-hospital plasma has no significant effect on 1-month mortality (RR=0.86; 95% CI 0.68–1.11), nor on acute lung injury or multi-organ failure rates (OR=1.03; 95% CI 0.71–1.50, and OR=1.30; 95% CI 0.92–1.86, respectively). The authors concluded that pre-hospital plasma infusion seems to reduce 24-hour mortality in hemorrhagic shock patients, without influencing 1-month mortality, acute lung injury, or multiorgan failure.
cards.watchOut: A meta-analysis of two discordant trials inherits their disagreement: the pooled early benefit is PAMPer’s signal averaged with COMBAT’s null, and the confidence interval for the outcome that matters most — one-month mortality — still includes no effect. Pooling does not manufacture the missing third trial.
cards.source: Coccolini F et al. Pre-hospital plasma in haemorrhagic shock management: current opinion and meta-analysis of randomized trials. World J Emerg Surg. 2019;14:6. PMID 30815028
cards.search: the two trials pooled (coccolini 2019, world journal of emergency surgery): 24-hour mortality favors plasma (rr 0.69); one-month mortality does not reach significance (rr 0.86) 2 randomized trials, 626 patients (295 plasma, 331 usual care) — pamper and combat are the entire randomized record. pooled: 24-hour mortality lower with prehospital plasma, rr 0.69 [0.48–0.99], relative ; one-month mortality rr 0.86 [0.68–1.11], relative — not significant ; no effect on acute lung injury (or 1.03) or multiorgan failure (or 1.30). pooling the randomized trials of prehospital plasma in hemorrhagic shock, what happens to early and one-month mortality? systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials, world journal of emergency surgery 2019. shelves.title: Early cryoprecipitate in major hemorrhage: CRYOSTAT-2 — empiric fibrinogen for everyone saves no one
shelves.question: In bleeding trauma patients activating a major hemorrhage protocol, does adding early, high-dose cryoprecipitate to standard care improve survival?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Component Transfusion · Blood Transfusion · Female · Fibrinogen · Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Wounds, Penetrating
shelves.balance: CRYOSTAT-2 is a large, well-run, international trial with a flat answer: 28-day mortality 25.3% with early high-dose cryoprecipitate vs 26.1% without (OR 0.96 [0.75–1.23]), and identical thrombotic-event rates. Giving fibrinogen empirically to every major-hemorrhage activation — before any test shows a deficiency — does not improve survival, and the confidence interval excludes a large benefit. That earns LIKELY for the null, fenced to what was tested: empiric use in unselected protocol activations. Whether replacing fibrinogen helps at all is a different question — it has its own shelf (Shelf #523); which product to use is Shelf #426. Card 2 is CRYOSTAT-1, the small feasibility pilot that made this trial possible: early cryoprecipitate proved deliverable within 90 minutes, and CRYOSTAT-2 is what that deliverable intervention achieved when tested at scale. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: CRYOSTAT-2 (Davenport 2023, JAMA): early high-dose cryoprecipitate for everyone on the protocol — 28-day mortality 25.3% vs 26.1%, a clean null
cards.summary: 1,604 injured adults activating a major hemorrhage protocol at 26 UK and US major trauma centers; three pools of cryoprecipitate (≈6 g fibrinogen equivalent) within 90 minutes, on top of standard care, vs standard care alone. All-cause mortality at 28 days: 25.3% vs 26.1% — OR 0.96 [0.75–1.23], relative; P=.74 . No difference in safety outcomes; thrombotic events 12.7% vs 12.9% .
cards.type: Interventional, randomized, open-label, parallel-group, international multicenter trial (CRYOSTAT-2), JAMA 2023. Registry IDs as printed in the record’s own registration line: NCT04704869 · ISRCTN14998314.
cards.people: 1,604 eligible patients enrolled (799 cryoprecipitate, 805 standard care); 1,531 (95%) in the primary analysis. Median age 39 years (IQR 26–55); 79% men; median Injury Severity Score 29; 36% penetrating injury; 33% had systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg at hospital arrival.
cards.result: All-cause 28-day mortality in the intention-to-treat population was 26.1% in the standard care group vs 25.3% in the cryoprecipitate group (odds ratio, 0.96 [95% CI, 0.75–1.23]; P=.74). There was no difference in safety outcomes or in the incidence of thrombotic events between the standard care and cryoprecipitate groups (12.9% vs 12.7%). The authors concluded that among patients with trauma and bleeding who required activation of a major hemorrhage protocol, the addition of early and empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate to standard care did not improve all-cause 28-day mortality.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the intervention was empirical — given to every protocol activation, not to patients proven fibrinogen-deficient. The null answers the empirical question; it does not answer whether cryoprecipitate helps the subgroup with demonstrated low fibrinogen, which is the targeted question Shelf #426’s trials circle. Standard care in both arms already included local major hemorrhage protocols, so this is cryoprecipitate added to good care, not instead of it.
cards.source: Davenport R et al. Early and empirical high-dose cryoprecipitate for hemorrhage after traumatic injury: the CRYOSTAT-2 randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2023;330(19):1882–1891. PMID 37824155 · NCT04704869 · ISRCTN14998314

cards.headline: CRYOSTAT-1 (Curry 2015, BJA): the feasibility pilot — early cryoprecipitate reached 85% of patients within 90 minutes [context card]
cards.summary: 43 adult trauma patients at two UK major trauma centres, unblinded: standard major haemorrhage therapy (n=22) vs standard therapy plus two early pools of cryoprecipitate (n=21). 85% of the CRYO arm received cryoprecipitate within 90 minutes (median 60 vs 108 min, P=0.002); fibrinogen was maintained above 1.8 g/L at all time points during active haemorrhage. All-cause mortality at 28 days was not significantly different (P=0.14).
cards.type: Unblinded randomised feasibility trial (CRYOSTAT-1), British Journal of Anaesthesia 2015. Registry ID from the record’s own registration line: ISRCTN55509212. Context card: this is the cryoprecipitate-side pilot that preceded CRYOSTAT-2 (Reference 1) — it is not a fibrinogen-concentrate trial and does not belong on the product shelf (#426).
cards.people: 43 adult trauma patients (age 16 years or older) with active bleeding requiring activation of the major haemorrhage protocol at two civilian UK major trauma centres (standard therapy 22, early cryoprecipitate 21). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: 85% (95% CI: 69–100%) of CRYO participants received cryoprecipitate within 90 min, median time 60 min (IQR: 57–76) compared with 108 min (67–147) in the STANDARD arm (P=0.002). Fibrinogen concentrations were higher in the CRYO arm and were maintained above 1.8 g litre(-1) at all time points during active haemorrhage. All-cause mortality at 28 days was not significantly different (P=0.14). The authors concluded that early fibrinogen supplementation using cryoprecipitate is feasible in trauma patients and that a definitive randomised trial was needed.
cards.watchOut: A feasibility trial answers ‘can it be given early?’ — not ‘does it help?’ Mortality here is a secondary measure in 43 patients. Its definitive successor is Card 1: CRYOSTAT-2 (n=1,604) took the deliverable intervention this pilot proved out and found no survival benefit from giving cryoprecipitate empirically to every protocol activation. Read the pair as question, then answer.
cards.source: Curry N et al. Early cryoprecipitate for major haemorrhage in trauma: a randomised controlled feasibility trial. Br J Anaesth. 2015;115(1):76–83. PMID 25991760 · ISRCTN55509212

shelves.title: Viscoelastic testing (TEG/ROTEM) in trauma: iTACTIC — the assay did not beat the laboratory
shelves.question: In major trauma hemorrhage, does guiding a major hemorrhage protocol with viscoelastic assays (TEG/ROTEM) improve patient outcomes compared with conventional coagulation tests?
shelves.mesh: Blood Coagulation Disorders · Hemorrhage · Hemostasis · Hemostatics · Humans · Multicenter Studies as Topic · Thrombelastography · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: The one purpose-built trauma trial is null on everything: iTACTIC’s primary outcome (alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 hours) was 67% vs 64%, and 28-day mortality 25% vs 28%, viscoelastic guidance vs conventional tests. The counterweight is a Cochrane pool suggesting lower mortality with TEG/ROTEM guidance (RR 0.76) — assembled mostly from elective cardiac surgery and graded very low certainty by its own reviewers. A single mid-sized trauma RCT with confidence intervals that still admit a moderate benefit earns POSSIBLE for the trauma null, not more: in trauma, viscoelastic guidance is unproven, and the burden of proof has not moved. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: iTACTIC (Curry 2021, Intensive Care Medicine): TEG/ROTEM-augmented protocols vs conventional tests — primary outcome 67% vs 64%, mortality 25% vs 28%; null
cards.summary: 396 trauma patients on empiric major hemorrhage protocols at multiple centers, randomized to viscoelastic-assay-augmented (VHA) or conventional-coagulation-test (CCT) guidance. Alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 hours: 67% vs 64% — OR 1.15 [0.76–1.73], relative . Mortality at 28 days: 25% vs 28% — OR 0.84 [0.54–1.31], relative . No differences in other secondary outcomes or serious adverse events.
cards.type: Multicenter randomized controlled trial (iTACTIC), Intensive Care Medicine 2021. The PubMed record carries no registry ID, so none is printed here. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 396 patients in the intention-to-treat analysis (201 allocated to VHA-augmented protocols, 195 to CCT-guided therapy), all receiving empiric major hemorrhage protocols for major trauma hemorrhage; a prespecified subgroup of 74 patients had severe traumatic brain injury.
cards.result: At 24 hours there was no difference in the proportion of patients alive and free of massive transfusion (VHA 67%, CCT 64%; OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.76–1.73). Twenty-eight-day mortality was not different overall (VHA 25%, CCT 28%; OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.54–1.31), nor were there differences in other secondary outcomes or serious adverse events. In the prespecified subgroup of 74 patients with traumatic brain injury, 64% of the VHA group vs 46% of the CCT group were alive and free of massive transfusion at 24 hours (OR 2.12, 95% CI 0.84–5.34) — not significant.
cards.watchOut: The brain-injury subgroup is the shelf’s temptation and its warning: a prespecified subgroup of 74 patients whose confidence interval (0.84–5.34) includes no effect. It generates the next trial; it does not change practice. Note also what the trial could not test — both arms ran full empiric protocols, so iTACTIC compares guidance strategies layered on modern care, not assays versus nothing.
cards.source: Curry N et al. Viscoelastic haemostatic assay augmented protocols for major trauma haemorrhage (iTACTIC): a randomized, controlled trial. Intensive Care Med. 2021;47(1):49–59. PMID 33048195. DOI 10.1007/s00134-020-06266-1

cards.headline: The wider pool (Cochrane 2026): TEG/ROTEM guidance and mortality RR 0.76 — at very low certainty, in trials that are mostly elective cardiac surgery
cards.summary: 35 randomized trials, 3,096 participants comparing TEG- or ROTEM-guided transfusion with usual care in bleeding adults and children — most of them elective cardiac surgery, not trauma. Mortality: RR 0.76 [0.63–0.92], relative (19 trials, 1,865 participants), graded by the reviewers themselves as very low-certainty evidence . Plasma use fell (RR 0.52) and platelet use fell (RR 0.69); red-cell use did not (RR 0.94).
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (CD007871; update of a review first published in 2011), 2026. Searches to January 5, 2025. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the review itself.)
cards.people: 35 randomized trials with 3,096 participants, in adults or children with bleeding; most trials involved patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery. The mortality analysis included 19 trials and 1,865 participants.
cards.result: TEG-/ROTEM-guided transfusion algorithms may be associated with a reduction in mortality (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.92; 19 trials; 1,865 participants; I²=0%), but the evidence is very uncertain (very low-certainty). They may reduce bleeding volume (standardized mean difference −0.31) and the use of fresh frozen plasma (RR 0.52) and platelet transfusions (RR 0.69), all at very low certainty with high heterogeneity for the transfusion outcomes; no effect was seen on the need for packed red blood cells (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.01).
cards.watchOut: Population mismatch is the whole story of this card: a pooled signal assembled mostly from elective cardiac surgery cannot rescue a trauma claim that the one trauma-specific trial (Reference 1) tested directly and found null. The reviewers’ own grade — very low certainty — is printed because it is part of the result.
cards.source: Kvisselgaard AD et al. Thromboelastography (TEG) or thromboelastometry (ROTEM) to monitor haemostatic treatment versus usual care in adults or children with bleeding. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2026;5:CD007871. PMID 42145275

shelves.title: Replacing fibrinogen: concentrate vs cryoprecipitate — interchangeable on everything measured; survival untested either way
shelves.question: When a bleeding patient needs fibrinogen replaced, is fibrinogen concentrate as good as cryoprecipitate?
shelves.mesh: Afibrinogenemia · Blood Coagulation Factors · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Child, Preschool · Cytoreduction Surgical Procedures · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Infant, Newborn · Male · Plasma · Pseudomyxoma Peritonei · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: Eight randomised comparisons now answer the product question, and they answer it the same way in every setting: the two products are interchangeable on everything that has been measured. In cardiac surgery — the deepest evidence — FIBRES proved concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate on 24-hour transfusion (16.3 vs 17.0 units), and the pooled cardiac trials find no difference in mortality (RR 1.25 [0.79–1.96]), blood loss, transfusion or thrombosis. In trauma, FEISTY shows concentrate reaching the patient about twice as fast (29 vs 60 minutes) — a logistics result, not an outcome result — and RETIC supports concentrate-first hemostatic efficiency against plasma. The remaining trials repeat the pattern across abdominal, paediatric, neonatal and mixed surgery: equal hemostasis, occasional speed or cost advantages, no clinical-outcome separation. The fence is explicit: nearly every primary endpoint on this shelf is a process — units transfused, minutes to delivery, millilitres lost, a laboratory trace, a price — and no trial here is powered for mortality. Choosing between the products is therefore a decision about availability, speed, cost and product safety, not about demonstrated efficacy. Whether replacing fibrinogen improves outcomes at all is a different question — Shelf #523 — and empiric replacement in unselected trauma bleeding is answered, negatively, on Shelf #424. POSSIBLE. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: FIBRES (Callum 2019, JAMA): fibrinogen concentrate noninferior to cryoprecipitate after cardiac surgery — 16.3 vs 17.0 units transfused in 24 hours
cards.summary: 827 randomized patients (735 treated and analyzed) with clinically significant bleeding and hypofibrinogenemia after cardiac surgery at 11 Canadian hospitals; fibrinogen concentrate 4 g vs cryoprecipitate 10 units per dose. Mean allogeneic components transfused in the 24 hours after bypass: 16.3 vs 17.0 units — ratio 0.96 (one-sided 97.5% CI up to 1.09), noninferior (P<.001 for noninferiority; P=.50 for superiority). The trial stopped at its interim analysis once the noninferiority criterion was met (827 of 1,200 planned). Thromboembolic events: 7.0% vs 9.6%.
cards.type: Randomized noninferiority trial (FIBRES), JAMA 2019. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03037424. The PubMed record for this trial carries no MeSH headings; none are printed for this card.
cards.people: 827 randomized patients; 735 (372 fibrinogen concentrate, 363 cryoprecipitate) treated and included in the primary analysis. Median age 64 years (IQR 53–72); 30% women; 72% underwent complex operations; 95% had moderate to severe bleeding; pretreatment fibrinogen 1.6 g/L (IQR 1.3–1.9).
cards.result: Mean 24-hour post-bypass allogeneic transfusions were 16.3 (95% CI, 14.9 to 17.8) units in the fibrinogen concentrate group and 17.0 (95% CI, 15.6 to 18.6) units in the cryoprecipitate group (ratio of means, 0.96 [one-sided 97.5% CI, −∞ to 1.09; P<.001 for noninferiority] [two-sided 95% CI, 0.84 to 1.09; P=.50 for superiority]). The trial met the a priori stopping criterion for noninferiority at the interim analysis after 827 of a planned 1,200 patients were randomized. Thromboembolic events occurred in 26 patients (7.0%) in the fibrinogen concentrate group and 35 patients (9.6%) in the cryoprecipitate group.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is units transfused — a process outcome, not survival — and the shelf’s claim is fenced to exactly that: as a way of replacing fibrinogen after cardiac surgery, the vial performs like the blood product. Noninferiority was declared at an interim stop, which is legitimate under the prespecified rule but leaves the estimate less precise than a completed trial’s. Nothing here speaks to mortality, and nothing here is trauma evidence — that is Card 2’s separate, weaker signal.
cards.source: Callum J et al. Effect of fibrinogen concentrate vs cryoprecipitate on blood component transfusion after cardiac surgery: the FIBRES randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2019;322(20):1966–1976. PMID 31634905 · NCT03037424. DOI 10.1001/jama.2019.17312

cards.headline: RETIC (Innerhofer 2017, Lancet Haematology): concentrate-first beat plasma-first on rescue therapy in trauma coagulopathy — and the trial stopped early
cards.summary: 100 coagulopathic major-trauma patients at a single Austrian center, randomized to first-line coagulation factor concentrates (mainly fibrinogen concentrate) vs fresh frozen plasma. The trial was terminated early for futility and safety : rescue therapy was needed by 52% of the plasma group vs 4% of the concentrate group (OR 25.34 [5.47–240.03]); massive transfusion was needed by 30% vs 12% (OR 3.04 [0.95–10.87]). The primary endpoint, multiple organ failure, did not differ significantly: 66% vs 50% (OR 1.92 [0.78–4.86]; P=0.15).
cards.type: Single-center, parallel-group, open-label randomized trial (RETIC), Lancet Haematology 2017. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT01545635. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 100 patients aged 18–80 years with major trauma (Injury Severity Score above 15), bleeding signs, and plasmatic coagulopathy on rotational thromboelastometry, randomized to FFP (n=48) or factor concentrates (n=52); 94 patients (44 FFP, 50 concentrates) were included in the final interim analysis after six discontinued.
cards.result: The study was terminated early for futility and safety reasons because of the high proportion of patients in the FFP group who required rescue therapy compared with the CFC group (23 [52%] in the FFP group vs 2 [4%] in the CFC group; odds ratio 25.34 [95% CI 5.47–240.03], P<0.0001) and the increased need for massive transfusion in the FFP group (13 [30%] vs 6 [12%]; OR 3.04 [0.95–10.87], P=0.042). Multiple organ failure — the primary clinical endpoint — occurred in 29 (66%) patients in the FFP group and 25 (50%) in the CFC group (OR 1.92 [95% CI 0.78–4.86], P=0.15), not significantly different.
cards.watchOut: Read the early stop in both directions: the rescue-therapy gap is enormous, but a trial stopped at 94 analyzed patients for the very outcome that then headlines the report will overstate whatever it found. The primary endpoint was null. RETIC supports the concentrate’s hemostatic efficiency — the same narrow claim FIBRES proves properly in cardiac surgery — and no more than that.
cards.source: Innerhofer P et al. Reversal of trauma-induced coagulopathy using first-line coagulation factor concentrates or fresh frozen plasma: a single-centre, parallel-group, open-label, randomised trial. Lancet Haematol. 2017;4(6):e258–e271. PMID 28457980 · NCT01545635

cards.headline: FEISTY (Winearls 2021): in bleeding trauma, the vial beat the blood-bank clock — replacement in 29 vs 60 minutes (a pilot; its primary outcome is speed)
cards.summary: 100 trauma patients randomised at four Australian centres; 62 were hypofibrinogenaemic and treated (fibrinogen concentrate 37, cryoprecipitate 25), FIBTEM A5–guided. Time to delivery of fibrinogen replacement: median 29 min [IQR 23–40] with concentrate vs 60 min [40–80] with cryoprecipitate (P=0.0001) . Concentrate dose median 3 g; cryoprecipitate median 8 units. Blood product transfusion, fluid resuscitation and thromboembolic complications were similar. Overall mortality was 15.3%, with more deaths in the concentrate arm — the abstract does not print the arm split.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled pilot trial (FEISTY), Critical Care and Resuscitation 2021. Registry ID verified against the trial registry: NCT02745041 (the PubMed record’s databank line is empty). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 100 adult trauma patients with haemorrhage randomly assigned at four Australian trauma centres; 62 were hypofibrinogenaemic and received the intervention (fibrinogen concentrate 37, cryoprecipitate 25). All 62 were hypofibrinogenaemic before treatment (median FIBTEM A5: 8 mm concentrate, 9 mm cryoprecipitate).
cards.result: Median (IQR) time to delivery of fibrinogen concentrate was 29 min (23–40 min) compared with 60 min (40–80 min) for cryoprecipitate (P=0.0001). In the concentrate arm patients received a median of 3 g (IQR 2–4 g), and in the cryoprecipitate arm a median of 8 units (IQR 8–14 units). Restoration of fibrinogen levels was achieved in both arms after the intervention. Blood product transfusion, fluid resuscitation and thromboembolic complications were similar in both arms. Overall mortality was 15.3%, with more deaths in the fibrinogen concentrate arm. The authors concluded that replacement was achieved substantially faster with concentrate and that the results will inform a larger trial powered for patient-centred outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a process — minutes to replacement — not a clinical outcome, and a pilot with 62 treated patients cannot speak to mortality. Its mortality sentence (‘more deaths in the concentrate arm’, overall 15.3%) comes without an arm split in the abstract, so this card prints it unquantified rather than borrowing a split from secondary summaries. FEISTY’s definitive successor, FEISTY II, has not yet reported. What FEISTY proves: concentrate reaches the bedside about twice as fast. What it cannot prove: that faster fibrinogen changes any outcome.
cards.source: Winearls J et al. Fibrinogen Early In Severe Trauma studY (FEISTY): results from an Australian multicentre randomised controlled pilot trial. Crit Care Resusc. 2021;23(1):32–46. PMID 38046391 · NCT02745041

cards.headline: FORMA-05 (Roy 2020): in pseudomyxoma cytoreductive surgery, concentrate matched cryoprecipitate — hemostatic success 100% in both arms, and it reached theatre 46 minutes faster
cards.summary: 43 patients (concentrate 21, cryoprecipitate 22) undergoing cytoreductive surgery for pseudomyxoma peritonei with predicted blood loss of 2 L or more; concentrate 4 g vs cryoprecipitate two pools of 5 units (about 4.0–4.6 g fibrinogen). Hemostatic success: 100% in both arms (concentrate 95% CI 83.9–100.0; cryoprecipitate 84.6–100.0); noninferiority P=.0095 (post hoc). Concentrate arrived in theatre 46 minutes faster ; plasma fibrinogen rise 0.78 vs 0.35 g/L (P<.0001); FIBTEM A20 rise 3.33 vs 0.93 mm (P=.003). Intraoperative red-cell medians: 1.0 vs 0.5 units. Thromboembolic events were detected with cryoprecipitate only.
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, randomised, controlled phase 2 study (FORMA-05), Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis 2020. No registry ID appears on the record, so none is printed here. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 43 patients undergoing cytoreductive surgery with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy for pseudomyxoma peritonei, with predicted intraoperative blood loss of at least 2 L (fibrinogen concentrate 21, cryoprecipitate 22).
cards.result: One hundred percent of patients receiving fibrinogen concentrate (95% CI: 83.9–100.0, n=21) or cryoprecipitate (84.6–100.0, n=22) achieved hemostatic success. Concentrate demonstrated noninferior efficacy (P=.0095; post hoc) and arrived in the operating room 46 minutes faster. There were significantly greater mean increases with concentrate vs cryoprecipitate in plasma fibrinogen (0.78 vs 0.35 g/L; P<.0001) and FIBTEM A20 (3.33 vs 0.93 mm; P=.003). Factor XIII, factor VIII, and von Willebrand factor activity were maintained throughout surgery. Only red blood cells were transfused intraoperatively (median units: concentrate 1.0; cryoprecipitate 0.5). Thromboembolic events were detected with cryoprecipitate only. Safety was otherwise comparable.
cards.watchOut: A very specific operating theatre: pseudomyxoma cytoreduction is hours-long surgery with predictable, dilutional fibrinogen loss — the friendliest possible setting for either product. The efficacy endpoint is an adjudicated hemostasis composite, the noninferiority P value is post hoc, and 43 patients show the products performing alike here — not that either changes survival anywhere.
cards.source: Roy A et al. Efficacy of fibrinogen concentrate in major abdominal surgery — a prospective, randomized, controlled study in cytoreductive surgery for pseudomyxoma peritonei. J Thromb Haemost. 2020;18(2):352–363. PMID 31654548. DOI 10.1111/jth.14665

cards.headline: Galas 2014 (FICCS): in children after heart surgery, concentrate and cryoprecipitate were indistinguishable — 48-hour blood loss 320 vs 410 mL (P=.67)
cards.summary: 63 children at a single São Paulo centre who bled with fibrinogen below 1 g/dL after cardiopulmonary bypass weaning: fibrinogen concentrate 60 mg/kg (n=30) vs cryoprecipitate 10 mL/kg (n=33). Median 48-hour postoperative blood loss: 320 mL [IQR 157–750] vs 410 mL [215–510] — P=.672, no significant difference . Plasma fibrinogen rose similarly after both products, and there was no difference in allogeneic blood transfusion after the intervention .
cards.type: Single-centre randomised pilot trial (FICCS), Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery 2014. No registry ID appears on the record, so none is printed here. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 63 children undergoing cardiac surgery who developed bleeding with fibrinogen levels below 1 g/dL after cardiopulmonary bypass weaning (fibrinogen concentrate 30, cryoprecipitate 33).
cards.result: The median 48-hour blood loss was not significantly different between the groups (320 mL [interquartile range, 157–750] in the fibrinogen concentrate group vs 410 mL [interquartile range, 215–510] in the cryoprecipitate group; P=.672). After treatment, plasma fibrinogen concentration increased similarly following administration of both products. There were no differences in allogeneic blood transfusion after intervention treatment. The authors concluded that a large trial is feasible and that preliminary results showed concentrate was as efficient and safe as cryoprecipitate in bleeding children undergoing cardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: Card the paper, not its conference predecessor: a 2012 conference abstract of this trial reported total transfusion avoidance of 70% vs 18% — a figure the full paper does not support (the paper reports no difference in transfusion after intervention). The paper’s own result is a null on blood loss in 63 children: consistent with equivalence, and far too small to prove it.
cards.source: Galas FR et al. Hemostatic effects of fibrinogen concentrate compared with cryoprecipitate in children after cardiac surgery: a randomized pilot trial. J Thorac Cardiovasc Surg. 2014;148(4):1647–1655. PMID 24951020

cards.headline: Ayaganov 2024: after heart surgery in Kazakhstan, concentrate corrected fibrinogen like cryoprecipitate — and cost less than half as much locally ($632 vs $1,505 per patient)
cards.summary: 88 adults with hypofibrinogenaemia (below 2.0 g/L) and clinically significant bleeding after cardiopulmonary bypass at a single centre in Astana: cryoprecipitate (n=40; mean 9.33 units) vs fibrinogen concentrate (n=48; mean 1.40 g). The primary endpoint was direct treatment cost: concentrate $631.75 ± $223.67 vs cryoprecipitate $1,505.06 ± $152.40 per patient (P<0.0001) . Fibrinogen rise to 24 hours: 96 ± 65 mg/dL (concentrate) vs 125 ± 65 mg/dL (cryoprecipitate); no significant difference at 48 hours.
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, randomised study, Journal of Cardiothoracic and Vascular Anesthesia 2024. No registry ID appears on the record, so none is printed here. The record states the groups’ demographics were similar but prints neither a mean age nor a sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 88 adult patients who underwent cardiopulmonary bypass from 2021 to 2022 and developed clinically significant bleeding and acquired hypofibrinogenaemia (below 2.0 g/L), randomised to cryoprecipitate (40) or fibrinogen concentrate (48).
cards.result: From before administration to 24 hours after, mean plasma fibrinogen increased by 125 ± 65 mg/dL in the cryoprecipitate group and 96 ± 65 mg/dL in the fibrinogen concentrate group. At 48 hours after administration, there was no significant difference in fibrinogen levels between groups. The mean direct cost of treatment was significantly lower with fibrinogen concentrate ($631.75 ± $223.67 per patient) than with cryoprecipitate ($1,505.06 ± $152.40) (P<0.0001). The authors concluded that the two products had comparable effectiveness on plasma fibrinogen concentration, with concentrate advantageous on handling, cost and purity.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is a price, not a patient: costs at one Kazakh centre reflect local acquisition prices for a pooled blood product versus an imported concentrate, and the ranking will differ — and can invert — in health systems priced differently. The clinical content of this card is its secondary endpoint: both products corrected fibrinogen comparably by 48 hours.
cards.source: Ayaganov D et al. Prospective, randomized study of fibrinogen concentrate versus cryoprecipitate for correcting hypofibrinogenemia in cardiac surgery patients. J Cardiothorac Vasc Anesth. 2024;38(1):80–85. PMID 38016817

cards.headline: Downey 2025: in newborns after heart surgery, concentrate restored hemostasis with less transfusion — in a 36-baby trial whose primary endpoint was a laboratory measure
cards.summary: 36 neonates enrolled (intention-to-treat); 30 completed per protocol (cryoprecipitate 13, fibrinogen concentrate 17), products given within a post-bypass transfusion algorithm. The primary endpoint — percent change in ex vivo clot degradation at 24 hours — showed no difference at the two earlier time points and greater degradation with concentrate at 24 hours (826.5% [95% CI 291.1–1361.9] vs −545.9% [−1081.3 to −10.4], P<.001) . Post-bypass transfusions were lower with concentrate: median 27.2 [19.0–36.9] vs 41.6 [29.2–52.4] mL/kg (P=.043, ITT) . No differences in bleeding or thrombotic events.
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, single-centre randomised trial, Anesthesia & Analgesia 2025. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03932240. The record’s abstract does not print a sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 36 neonates undergoing cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass, randomised to cryoprecipitate (control) or fibrinogen concentrate as part of a post-cardiopulmonary-bypass transfusion algorithm; 30 completed the study per protocol (13 cryoprecipitate, 17 concentrate).
cards.result: After normalising to each patient’s presurgery baseline, no significant differences in clot degradation were observed at the post-treatment or ICU-arrival time points. At 24 hours postsurgery, patients in the concentrate group had greater degradation than controls (826.5%, 95% CI 291.1–1361.9 vs −545.9%, 95% CI −1081.3 to −10.4; P<.001). Concentrate patients received significantly less median post-bypass transfusion than controls (ITT 27.2 mL/kg [19.0–36.9] vs 41.6 [29.2–52.4]; P=.043). No differences were observed in bleeding or thrombotic events. The authors concluded that concentrate adequately restored hemostasis and reduced transfusions in neonates after bypass, without increased bleeding or thrombosis.
cards.watchOut: The smallest card on this shelf, with a laboratory primary endpoint — ex vivo clot degradation — whose 24-hour direction (faster degradation after concentrate) is a mechanistic signal, not a clinical verdict. The transfusion difference is real but secondary, and comes from 30 completers. This card completes the cardiac set that the pooled analysis (Reference 9) summarises; it cannot carry weight alone.
cards.source: Downey LA et al. Effect of in vivo administration of fibrinogen concentrate versus cryoprecipitate on ex vivo clot degradation in neonates undergoing cardiac surgery. Anesth Analg. 2025;141(2):240–251. PMID 39116012 · NCT03932240

cards.headline: AdFIrst (Rahe-Meyer 2025): the largest product trial — concentrate noninferior on intraoperative blood loss (−279 mL vs plasma-or-cryoprecipitate), with fewer thromboembolic events (4% vs 12%)
cards.summary: 222 patients randomised at 15 European hospitals (concentrate 110, control 112); 201 in the per-protocol analysis. Intraoperative blood loss (least-squares mean): 1381 mL [1187–1574] with concentrate vs 1660 mL [1461–1860] with control; difference −279 mL [−552 to −6]; noninferiority P<0.0001 (post-hoc superiority P=.0087). Serious adverse events 25% vs 37%; thromboembolic events 4% vs 12% ; no treatment-related deaths. The control was plasma in spinal surgery and cryoprecipitate in cytoreductive surgery — only the second stratum is this shelf’s comparison.
cards.type: Randomised, active-controlled, partially blinded, phase 3 noninferiority trial (AdFIrst), EClinicalMedicine 2025. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT03444324. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age; it prints 59% female and 97% white.
cards.people: 222 adults (18 years or older) with clinically relevant intraoperative blood loss during major spinal surgery or cytoreductive surgery for pseudomyxoma peritonei at 15 hospitals in Europe (fibrinogen concentrate 110, fresh frozen plasma or cryoprecipitate 112); 59% female, 97% white; 201 patients in the per-protocol set.
cards.result: The primary endpoint was met: least-squares mean intraoperative blood loss was 1381 mL (95% CI 1187–1574) in the concentrate group and 1660 mL (95% CI 1461–1860) in the control group, a difference of −279 mL (95% CI −552 to −6; P<0.0001), beyond the 150 mL noninferiority margin; a post-hoc analysis showed superiority (P=.0087). Serious adverse events were reported in 25% of the concentrate group and 37% of controls. Thromboembolic events occurred in 4% (concentrate) vs 12% (control). There were no treatment-related deaths.
cards.watchOut: Read the comparator honestly: AdFIrst is a mixed-comparator trial — spinal-surgery patients received concentrate vs plasma, and only the cytoreductive (pseudomyxoma) stratum is concentrate vs cryoprecipitate, the comparison this shelf is about. Its pooled noninferiority belongs to ‘concentrate vs the usual first-line product’, not to the cryoprecipitate question alone. A 2026 subcohort paper on the pseudomyxoma patients is a sub-analysis of this same trial (NCT03444324), not a second trial, and is not carded separately.
cards.source: Rahe-Meyer N et al. Efficacy and safety of human fibrinogen concentrate (BT524) in patients with major haemorrhage undergoing major orthopaedic or abdominal surgery (AdFIrst): a randomised, active-controlled, multicentre, partially blinded, phase 3 non-inferiority trial. EClinicalMedicine. 2025;85:103264. PMID 40741224 · NCT03444324

cards.headline: The cardiac trials pooled (Chen 2025): mortality RR 1.25 [0.79–1.96] — and no difference in blood loss, transfusion or thrombosis [synthesis card]
cards.summary: 4 randomised trials, 945 participants (823 adults, 122 children) — FIBRES (Reference 1), Galas (Reference 5), Ayaganov (Reference 6) and Downey (Reference 7) on this shelf. Mortality: RR 1.25 [0.79–1.96], relative (moderate GRADE certainty). Blood loss: standardised mean difference −0.14 [−0.46 to 0.18]. No differences in transfusion rates or in postoperative thrombosis (RR 0.76 [0.47–1.22], relative); the certainty for outcomes other than mortality was low.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine 2025, prospectively registered (PROSPERO CRD42023421670). Synthesis card: this library treats meta-analyses as context, not exhibits — this card summarises the cardiac product trials carded above and adds no new patients. Flagged for the developer, who may strike it.
cards.people: 945 cardiac surgery patients (823 adults, 122 children) across the four randomised trials comparing fibrinogen concentrate with cryoprecipitate for acquired hypofibrinogenaemia.
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed no difference in mortality (RR 1.25, 95% CI 0.79–1.96; moderate GRADE), blood loss (SMD −0.14, 95% CI −0.46 to 0.18), transfusion rates (red cells RR 0.98; platelets RR 0.17; plasma RR 0.48; cryoprecipitate RR 1.02), infections, volume overload, transfusion reactions, or postoperative thrombosis (RR 0.76, 95% CI 0.47–1.22). Subgroup analyses showed substantial heterogeneity (I² from 0% to 98%) for most outcomes between adults and children. The reviewers assessed mortality evidence as moderate certainty and the remaining outcomes as low certainty.
cards.watchOut: The pooled mortality point estimate leans against concentrate (RR 1.25) with an interval spanning meaningful benefit and meaningful harm — in plain terms, 945 randomised cardiac patients cannot distinguish the two products on survival. That silence, repeated across every outcome the reviewers pooled, is the synthesis’s real content: interchangeability on process measures, no signal on outcomes.
cards.source: Chen Y et al. Treatment effects of fibrinogen concentrates vs. cryoprecipitate for correcting hypofibrinogenemia in cardiac surgery patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Front Cardiovasc Med. 2025;12:1671405. PMID 41179562

shelves.balance: This shelf was rebuilt because its first claim died: the comparative evidence is no longer entirely observational. Two phase-3 prehospital trials, published back-to-back in the same NEJM issue in June 2026, each gave up to 2 units of whole blood against blood components — TOWAR (cluster-randomised across 44 North American air bases; 30-day mortality 25.9% vs 20.5%) and SWiFT (individually randomised across 10 English air ambulance services; death or massive transfusion at 24 hours, 48.7% vs 47.7%) — and neither found a benefit; pooled across the three randomised trials, the mortality odds ratios are 1.12 at 24 hours and 1.15 at 28–30 days with zero heterogeneity. The observational literature still points the other way — the largest pool (Ibrahim 2026) finds civilian 24-hour mortality OR 0.73 — but it prints its own caution beside the estimate: I² of 89%, a 95% prediction interval of 0.28–1.91, a null military subgroup, and a search that closed a year before the two big trials reported. Confounding by indication remains a standing explanation for the gap. What the trials did not test is dose: both capped whole blood at 2 units, while the observational signal concentrates where whole blood is a large share of everything transfused — the question the in-hospital trials (TROOP in adults, MATIC-2 in children) are now running to answer. Split stamp: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for prehospital whole blood at up to 2 units; MAYBE (weak evidence) for higher-dose and in-hospital use. Proposed split stamp — proposed, pending the developer’s review. Tier C: mortality claims — the developer’s personal ruling governs this shelf.

cards.headline: TOWAR (Sperry 2026, NEJM): prehospital whole blood did not lower 30-day mortality — 25.9% vs 20.5%, adjusted OR 1.24
cards.summary: 44 North American air medical bases , cluster-randomised 2:1 in 1-month blocks to give up to 2 units of whole blood or as-indicated components (plasma, red cells, or both) before hospital arrival. Of 1,020 eligible patients, 993 were in the primary analysis (695 whole blood, 298 components). 30-day mortality: 25.9% whole blood vs 20.5% components (adjusted OR 1.24 [0.87–1.76], P=0.24) . No substantial difference in adverse events. An observational substudy found no effect of whole-blood storage age (30-day mortality 27.1% for blood stored 15–21 days vs 26.4% for 1–14 days; adjusted OR 0.99 [0.74–1.32]).
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicenter, phase 3, cluster-randomized trial, N Engl J Med 2026. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT04684719.
cards.people: 1,020 eligible injured patients with hemorrhagic shock transported by 44 air medical bases (715 assigned to whole blood, 305 to components; 695 and 298 respectively in the primary analysis). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Mortality at 30 days was 25.9% in the whole-blood group and 20.5% in the component group (adjusted odds ratio, 1.24; 95% CI, 0.87 to 1.76; P=0.24) — the point estimate leans against whole blood, with an interval spanning meaningful benefit and meaningful harm. No substantial between-group differences in adverse events were observed. In the observational storage-age substudy, 30-day mortality was 27.1% among 210 patients who received whole blood stored 15–21 days and 26.4% among 443 who received blood stored 1–14 days (adjusted OR 0.99 [0.74–1.32]). The authors concluded that whole blood for prehospital transfusion did not result in lower 30-day mortality than blood components.
cards.watchOut: Cluster allocation is this trial’s soft underbelly: bases, not patients, were randomised, in monthly blocks — so the product a patient received was tied to the base and the month, and the whole-blood arm arrived sicker at baseline (the critique made in the British Journal of Anaesthesia editorial on the two trials, PMID 42791175). That can move a point estimate; it cannot manufacture agreement with Card 2, an individually randomised trial that reached the same null by a clean road. The second fence is dose: the protocol capped whole blood at 2 units — what this trial refutes is 2-unit prehospital whole blood, not whole blood at any dose (Reference 7).
cards.source: Sperry JL et al.; TOWAR Study Group. Prehospital Resuscitation with Type O Whole Blood for Trauma and Hemorrhage. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(23):2317–2328. PMID 42150044 · NCT04684719. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2602167

cards.headline: SWiFT (Smith 2026, NEJM): 2 units of prehospital whole blood were not superior to components — death or massive transfusion at 24 hours, 48.7% vs 47.7%
cards.summary: 10 air ambulance services in England ; patients with major traumatic hemorrhage individually randomised, unblinded, to up to 2 units of whole blood or standard care (up to 2 units each of red cells and plasma) before hospital arrival. 942 patients randomised; 616 in the analysis (314 whole blood, 302 standard care) after exclusion of nontraumatic hemorrhage and traumatic cardiac arrest. Primary composite — death from any cause or massive transfusion (≥10 units) within 24 hours: 48.7% vs 47.7% (RR 1.02 [0.80–1.31], P=0.84) . Death at all time points appeared similar. Prothrombin time was above the normal range more often with whole blood ( 40.7% vs 30.5% ); serious adverse events numbered 31 (whole blood) vs 37 (standard care); thrombotic events appeared similar.
cards.type: Pragmatic, phase 3, multicenter, unblinded, randomized superiority trial, N Engl J Med 2026. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: ISRCTN23657907.
cards.people: Patients with major traumatic hemorrhage attended by 10 air ambulance services in England: 942 underwent randomization and 616 were included in the analysis (314 whole blood, 302 standard care), after exclusion of participants with nontraumatic hemorrhage or traumatic cardiac arrest. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: A primary-outcome event occurred in 48.7% of the whole-blood group and 47.7% of the standard-care group (relative risk, 1.02; 95% CI, 0.80 to 1.31; P=0.84). The incidence of death from any cause at all time points, massive transfusion, and other secondary outcomes appeared similar in the two groups. Prothrombin times were above the normal range in 40.7% of whole-blood vs 30.5% of standard-care participants. More serious adverse events occurred in the standard-care group (37 vs 31); thrombotic events appeared similar. The authors concluded that prehospital transfusion of 2 units of whole blood was not superior to standard care in reducing the risk of death or massive transfusion within 24 hours.
cards.watchOut: Two cautions. First, the primary endpoint is a composite — death OR massive transfusion — so a reader asking only about mortality should go to the pooled mortality analysis on Card 3 (which is also null). Second, roughly a third of randomised patients were excluded from the analysis population after randomisation (nontraumatic hemorrhage, traumatic cardiac arrest); the exclusions are clinically intelligible, but they mean SWiFT’s analysed 616 are a selected subset of its randomised 942, and the pooled analysis on Card 3 inherits that. Unblinded design is a third, lesser caution — unavoidable with blood products, and the endpoint least bendable by it is death.
cards.source: Smith JE et al.; SWiFT Trial Group. Prehospital Whole Blood in Traumatic Hemorrhage — A Randomized Controlled Trial. N Engl J Med. 2026;394(23):2305–2316. PMID 41841706 · ISRCTN23657907. DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2516043
