cards.headline: The randomised evidence, pooled (Khan 2026): three trials, 1,695 patients analysed — no mortality difference at 24 hours or at 28–30 days, heterogeneity zero
cards.summary: Three randomised trials of prehospital whole blood vs standard blood components in adults with traumatic haemorrhagic shock (searched to 20 May 2026; risk of bias by RoB 2, cluster variant where appropriate): 2,048 patients randomised, 1,695 in the trials’ primary-analysis populations . Pooled random-effects odds ratios: 24-hour mortality OR 1.12 [0.81–1.55], P=0.49; 28–30-day mortality OR 1.15 [0.90–1.47], P=0.28 ; massive transfusion within 24 hours OR 1.09 [0.80–1.50]; thromboembolic complications not significantly different. Statistical heterogeneity was absent throughout (I²=0%) — the three randomised answers agree with each other, which the observational literature’s never do.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials only, Am J Emerg Med 2026. No registry ID on the record; none is printed.
cards.people: Adults with traumatic haemorrhagic shock requiring prehospital blood, in the three eligible randomised trials (TOWAR and SWiFT, Cards 1–2, plus one smaller trial): 2,048 randomised, 1,695 in the trials’ primary-analysis populations.
cards.result: Prehospital whole blood did not differ significantly from blood components in 24-hour all-cause mortality (OR 1.12, 95% CI 0.81–1.55; P=0.49) or 28–30-day mortality (OR 1.15, 95% CI 0.90–1.47; P=0.28). Massive transfusion within 24 hours (OR 1.09, 95% CI 0.80–1.50) and thromboembolic complications likewise showed no significant difference, with all confidence intervals crossing the null and statistical heterogeneity absent throughout (I²=0%). The reviewers note that much of the observational evidence compared whole blood with crystalloid or no transfusion rather than with components, so the randomised data refine rather than overturn that signal — and they call for adequately powered trials to confirm the findings.
cards.watchOut: Read the null precisely: with 1,695 analysed patients, the intervals still admit anything from a ~19% relative reduction to a ~50% relative increase in 24-hour mortality odds. ‘No benefit shown’ at this size is not ‘benefit excluded’ — it is, however, a direct contradiction of the large benefit the observational pool on Card 4 reports, from the only design that randomises. A verification note, printed deliberately: a larger prehospital synthesis (Injury 2026, PMID 42815248; six studies mixing three trials with three cohorts, n=4,040, risk ratios 1.00 and 1.09) reaches the same null by a noisier road — it is a different object from this trials-only pool and is not the source of the odds ratios above.
cards.source: Khan YY et al. Efficacy and safety of prehospital whole blood resuscitation in traumatic haemorrhagic shock: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Am J Emerg Med. 2026;109:229–237. PMID 42526297. DOI 10.1016/j.ajem.2026.07.040

cards.headline: The observational pool (Ibrahim 2026, JAMA Surgery): civilians appear to benefit — 24-hour mortality OR 0.73 — under a prediction interval running from 0.28 to 1.91
cards.summary: 40 studies (2 randomised trials, 38 cohort studies), 49,776 adults with traumatic hemorrhage, searched through June 30, 2025. Overall 24-hour mortality: OR 0.76 [0.60–0.95] favouring whole blood — with I²=87% and a 95% prediction interval of 0.30–1.89 . In civilians (24 studies, n=39,028): OR 0.73 [0.57–0.93], I²=89%, 95% prediction interval 0.28–1.91 , an absolute risk reduction of 4.6 percentage points at a median control mortality of 20% (number needed to treat ≈ 22). In military settings (5 studies, n=2,171): OR 0.99 [0.58–1.70] — no benefit . Civilians also showed lower 30-day mortality (OR 0.76 [0.60–0.98]) and lower transfusion requirements (mean difference −2.66 units).
cards.type: Updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials and observational studies, JAMA Surg 2026 (nonrandomised studies assessed with ROBINS-I; randomised trials with RoB 2; random-effects, Hartung–Knapp). No registry ID on the record; none is printed.
cards.people: Adults (aged 16 years and older) with traumatic hemorrhage in 40 studies totalling 49,776 patients — 24 civilian studies (n=39,028) and 5 military studies (n=2,171) in the prespecified setting subgroups.
cards.result: Whole-blood transfusion, compared with component therapy, was associated with reduced 24-hour mortality (OR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60–0.95; τ²=0.27; I²=87%; 95% prediction interval, 0.30–1.89). In civilians the association was significant (OR 0.73; 95% CI, 0.57–0.93; I²=89%; 95% PI, 0.28–1.91), corresponding to an absolute risk reduction of 4.6 percentage points (95% CI, 1.4–8.6) based on a median control mortality of 20%. No benefit was observed in military settings (OR 0.99; 95% CI, 0.58–1.70). Civilians also showed reduced 30-day mortality (OR 0.76; 95% CI, 0.60–0.98) and lower transfusion requirements (mean difference, −2.66 units; 95% CI, −3.96 to −1.35). The authors concluded that the findings support selective whole-blood protocol implementation in civilian centres while highlighting the need for refined patient selection.
cards.watchOut: This card prints its own refutation beside its headline, as the record does. The confidence interval (0.57–0.93) describes the average of a literature; the prediction interval (0.28–1.91) describes what the next setting should expect — anything from a large benefit to near-doubling of the odds of death. With I² near 90%, the studies are not measuring one effect. Thirty-eight of the forty are cohorts, open to the confounding by indication that Cards 5–6 wear on their faces. And the search closed June 30, 2025 — a year before TOWAR and SWiFT (References 1–2) reported, so the randomised evidence that now dominates this question is not in this pool at all; the two trials it does contain are small and old. Cite the civilian OR as an association with a very wide prediction interval attached, or do not cite it.
cards.source: Ibrahim W et al. Whole-Blood vs Component Therapy in Adult Trauma: An Updated Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. JAMA Surg. 2026;161(5):497–506. PMID 41811314. DOI 10.1001/jamasurg.2026.0197

cards.headline: Whole blood vs components, 14 centers (Hazelton 2022, Annals of Surgery): whole blood associated with lower mortality — the patients who got it arrived sicker
cards.summary: 1,623 bleeding trauma patients in a 14-center prospective observational study: 1,180 received cold-stored whole blood as part of resuscitation, 443 received component therapy alone. The whole-blood group was sicker on arrival (shock index 0.98 vs 0.83; more comorbidities). After adjustment for center, age, sex, mechanism and injury severity, whole-blood patients were 48% less likely to die (relative association; P<0.0001) and 9% less likely to have bleeding complications; no differences in acute kidney injury, venous thromboembolism, or pulmonary complications.
cards.type: Prospective observational study at 14 centers, Annals of Surgery 2022. No registry ID — an observational study; none on the record. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 1,623 trauma patients who received blood during initial resuscitation (53% penetrating, 47% blunt injury): 1,180 (74%) received whole blood and 443 (27%) received component therapy alone.
cards.result: After controlling for center, age, sex, mechanism of injury, and injury severity score in a mixed-effects model, there were no differences between the groups in rates of acute kidney injury, deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism, or pulmonary complications. Whole-blood patients were 9% less likely to experience bleeding complications and were 48% less likely to die than component-therapy patients (P<0.0001). The whole-blood group had presented with a higher shock index (0.98 vs 0.83), more comorbidities, and more blunt mechanism (all P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Association, not assignment: centers chose whole blood, eras and protocols differed, and the adjusted estimate (an association of roughly halved odds of death) sits inside the range this library treats as not solid for observational evidence — precisely the size of effect that confounding by indication manufactures. The sicker-on-arrival whole-blood group cuts the other way and is the strongest argument the association is real; only randomization can settle which force wins.
cards.source: Hazelton JP et al. Use of cold-stored whole blood is associated with improved mortality in hemostatic resuscitation of major bleeding: a multicenter study. Ann Surg. 2022;276(4):579–588. PMID 35848743. DOI 10.1097/SLA.0000000000005603

cards.headline: Warm fresh whole blood in combat casualties (Spinella 2009, Journal of Trauma): 30-day survival 95% vs 82% — retrospective, in a wartime system
cards.summary: 354 transfused US combat casualties , retrospectively compared: 100 received warm fresh whole blood (plus red cells and plasma, no apheresis platelets) vs 254 receiving stored component therapy. Survival at 24 hours: 96% vs 88% (P=0.018); at 30 days: 95% vs 82% (P=0.002). On multivariate logistic regression, warm fresh whole blood use and its volume were independently associated with survival.
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study, Journal of Trauma 2009. No registry ID — a retrospective study; none on the record. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 354 US military combat casualty patients transfused with at least 1 unit of red blood cells in Iraq/Afghanistan-era care: 100 in the warm fresh whole blood group and 254 in the component-therapy group, with similar injury severity, Glasgow Coma Scale scores, base deficit, INR, hemoglobin, and systolic blood pressure on admission.
cards.result: Both 24-hour and 30-day survival were higher in the warm fresh whole blood cohort than in component-therapy patients — 96 of 100 (96%) vs 223 of 254 (88%) at 24 hours (P=0.018) and 95% vs 82% at 30 days (P=0.002), respectively. The component-therapy group received 825 mL more additives and anticoagulants (P<0.001). On multivariate logistic regression, the use of warm fresh whole blood and the volume transfused were independently associated with improved survival.
cards.watchOut: Two fences. First, the product: warm fresh whole blood, drawn from walking blood banks in theater, is not the cold-stored low-titer group O whole blood of Card 5 — fresher platelets, different logistics, different risks. Second, the design: retrospective, in a maturing wartime trauma system where whole-blood availability itself tracked with time and place. This is the study that restarted the modern whole-blood era; it is evidence of promise, not of effect.
cards.source: Spinella PC et al. Warm fresh whole blood is independently associated with improved survival for patients with combat-related traumatic injuries. J Trauma. 2009;66(4 Suppl):S69–S76. PMID 19359973

cards.headline: What would settle it: the dose the trials never gave, and the two in-hospital trials still running — TROOP in adults, MATIC-2 in children
cards.summary: TOWAR and SWiFT share one fence: both capped whole blood at 2 units , given before hospital arrival. The observational literature’s apparent benefit lives elsewhere — in hospital, at transfusion volumes where whole blood is a large share of everything given; cohort analyses report a dose–response, mortality falling as the whole-blood share of total transfusion rises (e.g., a 2026 TQIP cohort analysis, PMID 41995184). Two randomised trials are testing the in-hospital question now. TROOP (15 US level I trauma centers; target 1,100 injured adults predicted to require large-volume transfusion; LTOWB vs component therapy; primary outcome 6-hour mortality; NCT05638581 ). MATIC-2 (children under 18 with traumatic life-threatening hemorrhage; LTOWB vs component therapy, factorial with tranexamic acid vs placebo; primary outcome 24-hour all-cause mortality; NCT06070350 ).
cards.type: Synthesis and pending-trials card — no new completed study. TROOP design from its published protocol (Jansen JO et al., Trials 2025;26:266, PMID 40753420); MATIC-2 design from its ClinicalTrials.gov record (NCT06070350).
cards.people: TROOP’s target population: injured adults predicted to require a large-volume transfusion, at 15 US level I trauma centers (planned n=1,100). MATIC-2’s: injured children under 18 years with hemorrhagic shock and confirmed or suspected life-threatening traumatic bleeding (estimated n=1,000).
cards.result: The dose objection, stated fairly: a 2-unit prehospital intervention is a test of whole blood as an opening move, not as a resuscitation strategy. If whole blood’s value is real but dose-dependent — as the observational dose–response reports suggest — TOWAR and SWiFT could both be true nulls and the in-hospital question could still answer yes. TROOP randomises the in-hospital adult comparison directly (LTOWB vs component therapy in patients predicted to need large-volume transfusion; 6-hour mortality primary). MATIC-2 randomises the paediatric comparison in a Bayesian adaptive platform, factorial with tranexamic acid, with 24-hour all-cause mortality as the primary outcome. Until at least TROOP reports, the higher-dose and in-hospital claim on this shelf stays where the evidence leaves it: MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Do not let the pending trials launder the prehospital result: at 1–2 units before arrival, the randomised answer is in and it is null — ‘the real dose is coming’ is a reason to keep the in-hospital question open, not a reason to grade the tested one as unanswered. Equally, do not let the prehospital nulls close the whole file: neither trial showed significant harm, whole blood’s logistics (one bag, fewer lines, less wastage) are real operational properties, and the two trials that match the observational literature’s setting have not reported.
cards.source: TROOP trial protocol: Jansen JO et al. Trauma resuscitation with Low-Titer Group O Whole Blood Or Products: study protocol for a randomized clinical trial (the TROOP trial). shelves.title: REBOA for uncontrolled bleeding: UK-REBOA — the balloon may increase mortality [Tier C]
shelves.question: In trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage, does adding REBOA to standard emergency department care reduce mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aorta · Balloon Occlusion · Emergency Service, Hospital · Exsanguination · Female · Hemorrhage · Humans · Injury Severity Score · Male · Resuscitation · United Kingdom
shelves.balance: One randomized trial exists, and it points the wrong way: in UK-REBOA, 90-day mortality was 54% with a REBOA strategy vs 42% with standard care alone (OR 1.58 [95% credible interval 0.72–3.52]; 86.9% posterior probability of increased odds of death), with every earlier mortality endpoint leaning the same direction and more deaths from bleeding in the REBOA group. The trial is small and its interval includes no effect — a harm signal, stated as a signal. REBOA spread through trauma systems on registry data and mechanism; the first randomized test found no benefit to weigh against the signal. Tier C — mortality/harm claim: developer-approved Nov 7, 2026 (personal ruling).

cards.headline: UK-REBOA (Jansen 2023, JAMA): 90-day mortality 54% with REBOA vs 42% without — the only randomized test leans toward harm
cards.summary: 90 trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage at 16 UK major trauma centers, randomized to a REBOA-plus-standard-care strategy (n=46) or standard care alone (n=44). All-cause mortality at 90 days: 25 of 46 (54%) vs 18 of 43 (42%) — OR 1.58 [95% credible interval 0.72–3.52], relative ; the posterior probability that REBOA increased the odds of death was 86.9% . Every secondary mortality time point (3 hours, 6 hours, 24 hours, in-hospital, 6 months) leaned the same way, more strongly at earlier times. More of the REBOA group’s deaths were due to bleeding: 8 of 25 deaths (32%) vs 3 of 18 (17%) .
cards.type: Pragmatic, Bayesian, randomized clinical trial (UK-REBOA), JAMA 2023. Registry ID from the record’s own registration line: ISRCTN16184981.
cards.people: 90 patients aged 16 years or older with exsanguinating hemorrhage, enrolled October 2017 to March 2022 and followed for 90 days; 89 were included in the primary analysis. Median age 41 years (IQR 31–59); 69% male; median Injury Severity Score 41 (IQR 29–50).
cards.result: At 90 days, 25 of 46 patients (54%) had died in the REBOA and standard care group vs 18 of 43 patients (42%) in the standard care alone group (odds ratio 1.58 [95% credible interval, 0.72–3.52]; posterior probability of an odds ratio greater than 1 — indicating increased odds of death with REBOA — 86.9%). Among the ten secondary outcomes, the odds ratios for 6-month, in-hospital, and 24-, 6-, and 3-hour mortality were all increased in the REBOA group, with larger increases at earlier mortality endpoints. There were more deaths due to bleeding in the REBOA and standard care group (8 of 25 patients [32%]) than in the standard care alone group (3 of 18 patients [17%]), and most occurred within 24 hours. The authors concluded that a strategy of REBOA and standard care in the emergency department does not reduce, and may increase, mortality compared with standard care alone.
cards.watchOut: Small trial, wide credible interval — the interval includes no effect, so this is a harm signal, not proof of harm, and the shelf prints it as exactly that. But the signal is consistent across every time point, the mechanism is plausible (balloon placement delays definitive hemorrhage control and adds ischemic burden), and there is no offsetting benefit signal anywhere in the trial. The burden of proof now sits on REBOA’s advocates, and it can only be discharged by another randomized trial.
cards.source: Jansen JO et al. Emergency department resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta in trauma patients with exsanguinating hemorrhage: the UK-REBOA randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2023;330(19):1862–1871. PMID 37824132 · ISRCTN16184981

shelves.title: Platelet transfusion before procedures: PACER — before a central line at counts of 10–50,000, give the unit
shelves.question: In patients with platelet counts of 10,000–50,000, can prophylactic platelet transfusion be safely withheld before ultrasound-guided central venous catheter placement?
shelves.mesh: Catheterization, Central Venous · Hemorrhage · Humans · Platelet Count · Platelet Transfusion · Thrombocytopenia · Ultrasonography, Interventional
shelves.balance: PACER asked whether the platelet unit could be skipped and got a clear no: withholding prophylaxis before ultrasound-guided CVC placement failed its noninferiority test, with grade 2–4 catheter-related bleeding at 11.9% without transfusion vs 4.8% with it (RR 2.45), and grade 3–4 bleeding at 4.9% vs 2.1%. The absolute rates are modest and the setting is fenced — counts of 10,000–50,000, ultrasound guidance, hematology and ICU patients — but within that fence the answer is as firm as single-trial answers get: LIKELY. The $410 saved per skipped unit is printed on the card, because the trade was real and the trial priced it. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: PACER (van Baarle 2023, NEJM): withholding platelets before a central line caused more bleeding — noninferiority not met (grade 2–4 bleeding 11.9% vs 4.8%)
cards.summary: 373 episodes of CVC placement in 338 patients with platelet counts of 10,000–50,000 per cubic millimeter (hematology ward or ICU), all ultrasound-guided: one unit of prophylactic platelets vs none. Catheter-related bleeding of grade 2–4: 22 of 185 (11.9%) without transfusion vs 9 of 188 (4.8%) with — RR 2.45 [90% CI 1.27–4.70], relative . Withholding did not meet the prespecified noninferiority margin. Grade 3–4 bleeding: 4.9% vs 2.1% (RR 2.43 [95% CI 0.75–7.93]). Withholding saved $410 per placement.
cards.type: Multicenter, randomized, controlled noninferiority trial (PACER), N Engl J Med 2023. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: Dutch Trial Register NL5534. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 373 episodes of CVC placement involving 338 patients with platelet counts of 10,000 to 50,000 per cubic millimeter, treated on the hematology ward or in the intensive care unit, in the per-protocol primary analysis; all placements were ultrasound-guided.
cards.result: Catheter-related bleeding of grade 2 to 4 occurred in 9 of 188 patients (4.8%) in the transfusion group and in 22 of 185 patients (11.9%) in the no-transfusion group (relative risk, 2.45; 90% CI, 1.27 to 4.70) — the relative risk is expressed for the no-transfusion strategy, and the upper boundary of the 90% confidence interval (4.70) exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of 3.5, so withholding did not meet noninferiority. Catheter-related bleeding of grade 3 or 4 occurred in 4 of 188 patients (2.1%) in the transfusion group and in 9 of 185 patients (4.9%) in the no-transfusion group (relative risk, 2.43; 95% CI, 0.75 to 7.93). Of 15 adverse events, 13 were serious grade 3 catheter-related bleeding events (4 transfusion group, 9 no-transfusion group). The net saving from withholding prophylactic transfusion was $410 per catheter placement.
cards.watchOut: Absolute rates keep this honest: serious (grade 3–4) bleeding was uncommon in both arms — 4.9% vs 2.1% — and every line was ultrasound-guided, in hematology/ICU patients with counts between 10,000 and 50,000. PACER does not answer counts below 10,000, non-ultrasound placement, or other procedures; it answers this question, in this setting, against withholding.

cards.headline: Reading PACER with the threshold question: one procedure answered, the rest still open
cards.summary: PACER is, to date, the definitive randomized answer for one common bedside decision: at platelet counts of 10,000–50,000, give the unit before the ultrasound-guided central line — withholding bought more bleeding (grade 2–4: 11.9% vs 4.8%) for a saving of $410 per placement. The neighboring questions — lumbar puncture, major surgery, epidural catheters, counts below 10,000, lines placed without ultrasound — have no trial of this size and remain governed by the conflicting guideline thresholds PACER’s introduction describes.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card states the scope of Card 1’s answer and names the untested neighboring questions.
cards.people: The population of Card 1: patients with platelet counts of 10,000–50,000 per cubic millimeter undergoing ultrasound-guided CVC placement on hematology wards or in intensive care units.
cards.result: PACER’s result (grade 2–4 bleeding 11.9% without vs 4.8% with prophylactic transfusion; noninferiority of withholding not met) applies to ultrasound-guided CVC placement at the studied platelet counts. The trial’s background states that transfusion guidelines offered conflicting threshold recommendations for this procedure because good-quality evidence was lacking; PACER supplies that evidence for CVC placement only.
cards.watchOut: Do not stretch the card: a trial of central lines under ultrasound does not license conclusions about neuraxial procedures, surgery, or counts below 10,000, where bleeding consequences and mechanics differ. Those thresholds remain extrapolations until their own PACERs are run.
cards.source: Synthesis of Card 1 on this shelf (PMID 37224197).

shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in GI bleeding: HALT-IT — the indication that failed
shelves.question: Does tranexamic acid reduce death from acute gastrointestinal bleeding?
shelves.mesh: Antifibrinolytic Agents · Double-Blind Method · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage · Humans · Male · Tranexamic Acid · Venous Thrombosis
shelves.balance: HALT-IT is as definitive as nulls get: 12,009 patients, death due to bleeding within 5 days at 4% in both arms (RR 0.99 [0.82–1.18]), venous thromboembolism nearly doubled on tranexamic acid (0.8% vs 0.4%; RR 1.85), and an authors’ conclusion that the drug should not be used for GI bleeding outside a randomized trial. Before it, the randomized record in the highest-risk population — liver disease — was literally empty (Reference 2). The null earns LIKELY, and its contrast with trauma and childbirth on Shelf #138 is the most instructive comparison in the tranexamic acid literature: same drug, different bleeding biology. This shelf re-cards HALT-IT from its home on Shelf #138 to give the GI question its own hearing. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: HALT-IT (Roberts 2020, Lancet): tranexamic acid in acute GI bleeding — death from bleeding 4% vs 4%; venous clots doubled [re-card — home Shelf #138]
cards.summary: 12,009 adults with significant acute upper or lower GI bleeding at 164 hospitals in 15 countries; tranexamic acid 1 g loading dose then 3 g over 24 hours vs placebo. Death due to bleeding within 5 days: 4% vs 4% — RR 0.99 [0.82–1.18], relative . Venous thromboembolic events: 0.8% vs 0.4% — RR 1.85 [1.15–2.98], relative . Arterial events (MI or stroke) were similar (0.7% vs 0.8%). The authors’ conclusion: tranexamic acid should not be used for GI bleeding outside a randomized trial.
cards.type: International, multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (HALT-IT), Lancet 2020. Registry IDs from the record’s own registration line: ISRCTN11225767 · NCT01658124. Re-card; home Shelf #138. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 12,009 patients (5,994 tranexamic acid; 6,015 placebo) with significant upper or lower gastrointestinal bleeding, enrolled when the responsible clinician was uncertain whether to use tranexamic acid; 11,952 (99.5%) received the first dose of the allocated treatment.
cards.result: Death due to bleeding within 5 days of randomisation occurred in 222 (4%) of 5,956 patients in the tranexamic acid group and in 226 (4%) of 5,981 patients in the placebo group (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.82–1.18). Arterial thromboembolic events (myocardial infarction or stroke) were similar between the groups (42 [0.7%] of 5,952 vs 46 [0.8%] of 5,977; RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.39). Venous thromboembolic events (deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) were higher in the tranexamic acid group (48 [0.8%] of 5,952 vs 26 [0.4%] of 5,977; RR 1.85, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.98). The investigators found that tranexamic acid did not reduce death from gastrointestinal bleeding.
cards.watchOut: Note the regimen before generalizing the null: HALT-IT used a higher, longer dose (1 g load, then 3 g infused over 24 hours) than the trauma trials, given to patients whose bleeding was often variceal, ulcer-related, or malignancy-related rather than the fibrinolysis-driven hemorrhage of trauma — and enrollment required clinician uncertainty, over six years, across 164 hospitals. The null is robust for this population; the venous-thrombosis excess is the price of a drug given without benefit. This trial’s home is Shelf #138, where it stands beside the trauma and childbirth trials that succeeded; here it answers the GI question on its own.
cards.source: HALT-IT trial investigators (Roberts I et al.). cards.headline: Before HALT-IT, the randomized cupboard was bare (Cochrane 2015): in liver disease — the highest-risk GI bleeders — no randomized trial of antifibrinolytics existed at all
cards.summary: A Cochrane review searching to February 2015 for randomized trials of antifibrinolytic amino acids (including tranexamic acid) for upper GI bleeding in people with acute or chronic liver disease found none — zero eligible randomized trials , and no observational studies from which harms could even be assessed. Its conclusion: the benefits and harms needed testing in randomized trials before the treatment could be recommended or refuted. HALT-IT (Reference 1) was that test, in the broader GI-bleeding population.
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (CD006007), 2015 update; searches of the Cochrane Hepato-Biliary register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE and other sources to February 2015. (A systematic review — no single age or sex mix applies; no registry ID applies to the review itself.)
cards.people: The population of interest: people with acute or chronic liver disease and upper gastrointestinal bleeding — a group in whom hyperfibrinolysis is common and was the mechanistic rationale for antifibrinolytic treatment.
cards.result: The reviewers found no randomised clinical trials assessing antifibrinolytic amino acids for treating upper gastrointestinal bleeding in people with acute or chronic liver disease, and identified no quasi-randomised, historically controlled, or observational studies in which harms could be assessed. They concluded that unless randomised clinical trials are conducted to assess the trade-off between benefits and harms, antifibrinolytic amino acids can neither be recommended nor refuted for upper gastrointestinal bleeding in people with acute or chronic liver diseases.
cards.watchOut: Scope fence: this review covers liver disease specifically, not all GI bleeding — small trials in general GI bleeding populations existed and are the meta-analyses HALT-IT’s introduction cites as grounds for hope. The card’s claim is narrower and stranger: in the population with the strongest mechanistic case for the drug, the randomized record before 2020 was empty.
cards.source: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Solà I. Antifibrinolytic amino acids for upper gastrointestinal bleeding in people with acute or chronic liver disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2015;(6):CD006007. PMID 26058965

cards.headline: Reading HALT-IT with Shelf #138: same drug, same mechanism — the bleeding biology is what differs
cards.summary: Tranexamic acid saves lives in bleeding trauma (CRASH-2), in traumatic brain injury (CRASH-3), and in childbirth (WOMAN) — Shelf #138’s cards. In GI bleeding, the largest trial ever run found no mortality benefit and doubled venous thrombosis . The pattern across the four trials is the lesson: TXA pays when death comes from early fibrinolytic exsanguination in a defined time window; most GI-bleeding deaths arrive later, from rebleeding, liver failure, and comorbidity — ground on which an antifibrinolytic has little to offer and its clotting harm still applies.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads HALT-IT (Reference 1) against the trials that live on Shelf #138 and states the timing-and-biology fence the four trials draw together.
cards.people: The populations of the four trials: bleeding trauma, traumatic brain injury, postpartum hemorrhage (Shelf #138), and acute gastrointestinal bleeding (this shelf).
cards.result: HALT-IT’s primary outcome — death due to bleeding within 5 days — was 4% in both arms (RR 0.99 [0.82–1.18]), in 12,009 patients; the trauma and postpartum trials on Shelf #138 found relative reductions in death due to bleeding when TXA was given early. HALT-IT also enrolled over six years with treatment started later in the illness course than the trauma trials’ first-hours window, and used a 24-hour infusion regimen.
cards.watchOut: Do not over-draw the mechanism story: it is an interpretation fitted to four trials, not a measured result of any of them. What is measured is simpler — in GI bleeding, the drug did not reduce bleeding deaths and did increase venous clots, and that is sufficient for practice.
cards.source: Synthesis of Card 1 on this shelf (PMID 32563378) with Shelf #138 (PMIDs 20554319, 31623894, 28456509).

shelves.title: Calcium in cardiac arrest: COCA — no ROSC benefit, a consistent harm lean, stopped early
shelves.question: Does giving calcium during adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest improve return of spontaneous circulation or survival?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Aged · Calcium Chloride · Double-Blind Method · Epinephrine · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intraosseous · Male · Middle Aged · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest · Return of Spontaneous Circulation · Saline Solution
shelves.balance: COCA, the first placebo-controlled trial of calcium in unselected out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, was stopped early at a planned interim analysis because its own steering committee was worried about harm — and the finished numbers justify the worry without proving it: sustained ROSC 19% vs 27% (RR 0.72, P=.09), 30-day survival 5.2% vs 9.1%, favorable neurology 3.6% vs 7.6%, with the same leans at one year. No significant result, and no result in calcium’s favor: the grade is POSSIBLE for the null, fenced to routine administration — COCA says nothing about calcium for its classic specific indications (hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia, calcium-channel-blocker overdose), which were not its question. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: COCA (Vallentin 2021, JAMA): calcium in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — ROSC 19% vs 27%, every outcome leaning the wrong way; the trial stopped early over harm
cards.summary: 397 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in the Central Denmark Region, double-blind: up to two IV/IO doses of calcium chloride 5 mmol vs saline, first dose right after the first epinephrine. Sustained return of spontaneous circulation: 19% vs 27% — RR 0.72 [0.49–1.03], relative; P=.09 . Alive at 30 days: 5.2% vs 9.1% (RR 0.57). Favorable neurological outcome at 30 days: 3.6% vs 7.6% (RR 0.48). A planned interim analysis led the steering committee to stop the trial early over concern about harm . Long-term follow-up (2022): at 1 year, survival 4.7% vs 9.1% (RR 0.51) and favorable neurology 3.6% vs 8.6% (RR 0.42 [0.18–0.97]) — the leans did not fade.
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomized clinical trial (COCA), JAMA 2021; long-term outcomes reported in Resuscitation 2022 (PMID 35917866). Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT04153435.
cards.people: 397 adult patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest in the Central Denmark Region (January 2020 to April 2021); 391 were included in the analyses (193 calcium, 198 saline). Mean age 68 years (SD 14); 29% women. There was no loss to follow-up.
cards.result: Sustained return of spontaneous circulation occurred in 37 patients (19%) in the calcium group compared with 53 patients (27%) in the saline group (risk ratio, 0.72 [95% CI, 0.49 to 1.03]; risk difference, −7.6% [95% CI, −16% to 0.8%]; P=.09). At 30 days, 10 patients (5.2%) in the calcium group and 18 patients (9.1%) in the saline group were alive (risk ratio, 0.57 [95% CI, 0.27 to 1.18]; P=.17). A favorable neurological outcome at 30 days was observed in 7 patients (3.6%) in the calcium group and 15 patients (7.6%) in the saline group (risk ratio, 0.48 [95% CI, 0.20 to 1.12]; P=.12). Among patients with return of spontaneous circulation who had calcium values measured, 26 (74%) in the calcium group and 1 (2%) in the saline group had hypercalcemia. Based on a planned interim analysis of 383 patients, the steering committee stopped the trial early due to concerns about harm in the calcium group. In the prespecified long-term follow-up, effect estimates remained constant over time: at 1 year, 9 patients (4.7%) in the calcium group and 18 (9.1%) in the placebo group were alive (risk ratio 0.51 [95% CI, 0.24 to 1.09]), and favorable neurological outcome at 1 year was 3.6% vs 8.6% (risk ratio 0.42 [95% CI, 0.18 to 0.97]).
cards.watchOut: The trial is small and stopped early, so none of its harm leans is proof — every primary comparison’s interval includes no effect. But there is no endpoint, at any time point out to one year, on which calcium looks better, and the physiological story writes itself: three quarters of the calcium group’s resuscitated patients were hypercalcemic. The specific-arrest indications for calcium that predate this trial (hyperkalemia, calcium-channel-blocker overdose, hypocalcemia) were not what COCA tested — it tested routine administration to unselected arrests, and routine administration is what it answers.

shelves.title: Does replacing fibrinogen help at all? Concentrate vs placebo across cardiac, trauma, obstetric and liver bleeding
shelves.question: In bleeding patients, does replacing fibrinogen with fibrinogen concentrate improve outcomes — or only the fibrinogen level?
shelves.mesh: Blood Transfusion · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Double-Blind Method · Female · Fibrinogen · Hemorrhage · Humans · Liver Transplantation · Male · Postpartum Hemorrhage · Thrombelastography · Wounds and Injuries
shelves.balance: Split the question. As biochemistry, replacement works every time: every trial on this shelf shows concentrate raising fibrinogen and clot firmness within the hour. As transfusion-sparing, it works sometimes, in one setting: two single-centre cardiac trials cut allogeneic transfusion (Rahe-Meyer 2013; Ranucci 2015), but the multicentre phase 3 in the same setting found the opposite (REPLACE: more units transfused, fewer patients avoiding transfusion), and a JAMA trial dosing to a target fibrinogen level found no reduction in blood loss (Bilecen). As patient benefit — survival, organ failure, complications — there is no positive randomised result anywhere on this shelf. In trauma the evidence is feasibility and laboratory studies, and the one large strategy trial (FiiRST-2 — a concentrate combination, not fibrinogen alone) stopped for futility. In obstetrics, three double-blind trials are null, but they treated women whose mean fibrinogen was 4.1–4.5 g/L; the single trigger-based trial randomised only 55 of 663 enrolled women, just 7 of them truly hypofibrinogenaemic. In liver transplantation, preemptive replacement and higher replacement targets are both null. The untested patient is the one the entire idea was built for: the actively bleeding patient whose fibrinogen is genuinely low. Which product to give that patient is Shelf #426; empiric cryoprecipitate for unselected trauma activations is Shelf #424. Grade: POSSIBLE for the narrow claim that replacement moves fibrinogen and, inconsistently, transfusion counts; for any claim of clinical benefit the evidence is MAYBE (weak evidence) at best, and this balance line says so. Developer-approved Nov 7, 2026.

cards.headline: Rahe-Meyer 2013: first-line concentrate in aortic surgery cut 24-hour transfusion from a median of 13 units to 2 — the positive phase 2 the field built on
cards.summary: 61 patients in the efficacy analysis (concentrate 29, placebo 32) undergoing aortic replacement surgery, dosed FIBTEM-guided as first-line therapy for coagulopathic bleeding after bypass. Allogeneic blood components in the first 24 hours: median 2 vs 13 units (P<0.001) . Total transfusion avoidance: 45% (13 of 29) with concentrate vs 0% (0 of 32) with placebo (P<0.001) . No safety concern observed.
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, placebo-controlled, double-blind randomised trial, Anesthesiology 2013. Registry IDs verified against the trial registry: NCT00701142 · EudraCT 2007-004612-31 (the PubMed record’s databank line is empty). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Patients 18 years or older undergoing elective thoracic or thoracoabdominal aortic replacement surgery involving cardiopulmonary bypass at a single centre, who had clinically relevant coagulopathic bleeding after removal from bypass and completion of surgical hemostasis (29 concentrate, 32 placebo in the efficacy analysis).
cards.result: During the first 24 hours after administration of study medication, patients in the fibrinogen concentrate group received fewer allogeneic blood components than patients in the placebo group (median, 2 vs 13 units; P<0.001; primary endpoint). Total avoidance of transfusion was achieved in 13 (45%) of 29 patients in the fibrinogen concentrate group, whereas all 32 (100%) patients in the placebo group received transfusion (P<0.001). There was no observed safety concern with using fibrinogen concentrate during aortic surgery. The authors concluded that larger multicentre studies were necessary to confirm the role of fibrinogen concentrate in perioperative bleeding.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 61 patients, and a process endpoint — units transfused. The companion bleeding-rate paper and the post-hoc analyses of this trial are the same patients and are not carded separately: this card is the whole trial. And its own group then ran the multicentre phase 3 — Card 2 — which found the opposite. Read this card as the hypothesis, and Card 2 as its test.
cards.source: Rahe-Meyer N et al. Effects of fibrinogen concentrate as first-line therapy during major aortic replacement surgery: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Anesthesiology. 2013;118(1):40–50. PMID 23249928 · NCT00701142

cards.headline: REPLACE (Rahe-Meyer 2016): the multicentre phase 3 went the other way — concentrate patients received MORE blood (median 5.0 vs 3.0 units) and fewer avoided transfusion (15.4% vs 28.4%)
cards.summary: 519 patients randomised at 34 centres for elective aortic surgery; only 152 (29%) met the bleeding criteria and were treated . Allogeneic units in the first 24 hours: median 5.0 [2.0–11.0] with concentrate vs 3.0 [0.0–7.0] with placebo (P=0.026) . Transfusion avoidance: 15.4% vs 28.4% (P=0.047) — fewer avoiders on concentrate. Adverse event rates were comparable.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, phase 3 multicentre trial (REPLACE), British Journal of Anaesthesia 2016. Registry IDs from the record: NCT01475669 · EudraCT 2011-002685-20. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: Patients undergoing elective aortic surgery requiring cardiopulmonary bypass at 34 centres; study medication was given to the 152 randomised patients whose 5-minute bleeding mass after separation from bypass and surgical haemostasis was 60–250 g (median pretreatment bleeding mass 107 g concentrate, 91 g placebo).
cards.result: More allogeneic blood product units were administered during the first 24 hours after fibrinogen concentrate, 5.0 (2.0–11.0), compared with placebo, 3.0 (0.0–7.0), P=0.026. Fewer patients avoided transfusion in the concentrate group (15.4%) compared with placebo (28.4%), P=0.047. Concentrate immediately increased plasma fibrinogen concentration and fibrin-based clot strength. Adverse event rates were comparable in each group. The authors concluded that fibrinogen concentrate was associated with increased allogeneic blood product transfusion — an unexpected finding contrary to previous studies — and noted low bleeding rates, normal-range plasma fibrinogen concentrations before study medication, and variability in adherence to the complex transfusion algorithm as possible contributors.
cards.watchOut: Print it whole: the largest trial of the replacement idea in cardiac surgery found harm on its process endpoint. With only 29% of randomised patients ever qualifying for the drug and pretreatment fibrinogen in the normal range, REPLACE may largely have tested replacement in patients who did not need replacing — the same fence that governs the obstetric cards on this shelf (References 10–12). Both readings are on this card because both are true.
cards.source: Rahe-Meyer N et al. Randomized evaluation of fibrinogen vs placebo in complex cardiovascular surgery (REPLACE): a double-blind phase III study of haemostatic therapy. Br J Anaesth. 2016;117(1):41–51. PMID 27317703 · NCT01475669

cards.headline: Bilecen 2017 (JAMA): concentrate dosed to a fibrinogen target of 2.5 g/L did not reduce intraoperative blood loss — median 50 vs 70 mL (P=.19)
cards.summary: 120 patients undergoing elective high-risk cardiac surgery with intraoperative bleeding, randomised to a single dose of concentrate targeted to a plasma fibrinogen of 2.5 g/L, or placebo. Primary outcome — blood loss between intervention and chest closure: median 50 mL [IQR 29–100] vs 70 mL [33–145]; absolute difference 20 mL [95% CI −13 to 35]; P=.19 — no significant difference . Mean age 71 years; 31% women.
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind clinical trial, JAMA 2017. Registry IDs from the record: NCT01124981 · EudraCT 2009-018086-12.
cards.people: 120 patients (mean age 71 [SD 10] years, 37 women [31%]) undergoing elective high-risk cardiac surgery — combined bypass grafting and valve surgery, multiple valve replacement, aortic root or arch reconstruction — with intraoperative bleeding of 60–250 mL suctioned in 5 minutes, at a single Dutch centre; mean bypass time 200 minutes.
cards.result: For the primary outcome, median blood loss in the fibrinogen group was 50 mL (IQR 29–100) compared with 70 mL (IQR 33–145) in the control group (P=.19); the absolute difference was 20 mL (95% CI, −13 to 35). Safety events within 30 days included 6 cases of stroke or transient ischemic attack (4 in the fibrinogen group), 4 myocardial infarctions (3 fibrinogen), 2 deaths (both fibrinogen), 5 cases of renal insufficiency or failure (3 fibrinogen), and 9 reoperative thoracotomies (4 fibrinogen). The authors concluded that administration of fibrinogen concentrate, compared with placebo, resulted in no significant difference in intraoperative blood loss.
cards.watchOut: A clean null from a well-run double-blind trial — and note how small the measured losses were in both arms (medians under 100 mL), which itself asks how much bleeding was left to prevent. The safety counts lean against concentrate and are printed for completeness; at 120 patients they are noise-sized and prove nothing either way.
cards.source: Bilecen S et al. Effect of fibrinogen concentrate on intraoperative blood loss among patients with intraoperative bleeding during high-risk cardiac surgery: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2017;317(7):738–747. PMID 28241354 · NCT01124981

cards.headline: Ranucci 2015 (SCORE): concentrate after protamine reduced transfusion — odds of any allogeneic product OR 0.40 — in one centre’s 116 patients
cards.summary: 116 patients undergoing complex heart surgery at a single centre: fibrinogen concentrate after protamine vs saline. Any allogeneic blood product transfusion: OR 0.40 [95% CI 0.19–0.84], relative; P=0.015 — significantly lower with concentrate. Total red-cell and plasma units were significantly lower; postoperative bleeding was less: median 300 vs 355 mL (P=0.042) . No safety issues were raised.
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, randomised, placebo-controlled, double-blind trial (SCORE), Journal of the American Heart Association 2015. Registry IDs: NCT01471730 · EudraCT 2011-0046-33.
cards.people: 116 patients undergoing heart surgery with an expected cardiopulmonary bypass duration over 90 minutes at a single centre; patients in the treatment arm received fibrinogen concentrate after protamine administration, controls received saline, with prothrombin complex concentrate or saline as protocolised rescue for ongoing bleeding.
cards.result: Patients in the treatment arm had a significantly lower rate of any allogeneic blood products transfusion (odds ratio, 0.40; 95% confidence interval, 0.19 to 0.84, P=0.015). The total amount of packed red cells and plasma units transfused was significantly lower in the treatment arm. Postoperative bleeding was significantly less in the treatment arm (median, 300 mL; interquartile range, 200 to 400 mL) than in the control arm (median, 355 mL; interquartile range, 250 to 600 mL) (P=0.042). The authors concluded that fibrinogen concentrate limits postoperative bleeding after complex heart surgery, leading to a significant reduction in allogeneic blood product transfusions.
cards.watchOut: The OR of 0.40 would clear this library’s two-fold floor if it were observational — but this is a randomised trial of a process outcome (transfusion avoidance), at one centre, and its direction is contradicted by the multicentre REPLACE trial (Reference 2) and unmatched by Bilecen (Reference 3). A process win inside one centre’s protocol is a claim about that protocol as much as about the drug.
cards.source: Ranucci M et al. Randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial of fibrinogen concentrate supplementation after complex cardiac surgery. J Am Heart Assoc. 2015;4(6):e002066. PMID 26037084 · NCT01471730

cards.headline: FIBCON (Siemens 2020): in infants on bypass, ROTEM screening with individualised concentrate dosing was feasible — a dose-finding trial, not an efficacy trial
cards.summary: 111 infants enrolled (monitoring cohort 21; concentrate 60; placebo 30), mean age 6.4 months, screened intraoperatively by FibTEM maximum clot firmness. The co-primary outcomes were dose and laboratory targets, and they were met — 72% of post-dose fibrinogen levels in the desired range; the required dose varied four-fold. Mean 24-hour mediastinal drain loss: 11.6 (SD 5.2) mL/kg with concentrate vs 17.1 (14.3) with placebo (ANOVA P=0.02 across groups). Twelve possible thromboses occurred in 10 patients, none clearly related to concentrate.
cards.type: Single-centre phase 1b/2a randomised controlled trial (FIBCON), Circulation: Cardiovascular Interventions 2020. Registry IDs from the record: ISRCTN50553029 · EudraCT 2013-003532-68.
cards.people: 111 infants weighing 2.5–12 kg undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass surgery for congenital heart disease at a single centre (mean age 6.4 [SD 5.8] months); infants whose FibTEM maximum clot firmness was 6 mm or less were randomised 2:1 to individualised fibrinogen concentrate or placebo, and those at 7 mm or more entered a monitoring cohort.
cards.result: Intraoperative ROTEM screening effectively excluded low-risk patients: none in the monitoring cohort demonstrated clinically significant early postoperative bleeding. Among randomised patients, the median concentrate dose administered was 114 mg/kg (range 51–218). Fibrinogen levels increased from a mean (SD) of 0.91 (0.22) to 1.7 (0.41) g/L; the post-dose range was 1.2–3.3 g/L, with 72% within the desired range. There was an overall difference in mean 24-hour mediastinal drain loss: cohort 12.6 (6.4), concentrate 11.6 (5.2), placebo 17.1 (14.3) mL/kg (ANOVA P=0.02). Ten patients (8 concentrate, 2 placebo) exhibited 12 possible thromboses; none were clearly related to concentrate.
cards.watchOut: Phase 1b/2a answers ‘can this be dosed precisely in a 6-kg infant?’ — yes, and the four-fold dose variation is genuinely useful knowledge. It answers nothing about outcomes: the drain-loss difference is a secondary outcome in a dosing study. Carded to complete the cardiac set, and labelled for exactly what it is.
cards.source: Siemens K et al. Individualized, intraoperative dosing of fibrinogen concentrate for the prevention of bleeding in neonatal and infant cardiac surgery using cardiopulmonary bypass (FIBCON): a phase 1b/2a randomized controlled trial. Circ Cardiovasc Interv. 2020;13(12):e009465. PMID 33213194 · ISRCTN50553029

cards.headline: FiiRST (Nascimento 2016): 6 g of concentrate within an hour of arrival was feasible in hypotensive trauma — 96% received it in time; mortality similar (a feasibility trial)
cards.summary: 50 hypotensive trauma patients randomised , 45 analysed: 6 g fibrinogen concentrate vs placebo at a single tertiary trauma centre. Feasibility primary outcome: 96% (43 of 45) received the intervention within one hour of arrival (95% concentrate vs 96% placebo). Plasma fibrinogen stayed higher with concentrate for 12 hours (largest difference at 3 hours: 2.9 vs 1.8 g/L, P<0.01). 28-day mortality and thromboembolic complications were similar between groups.
cards.type: Randomised feasibility trial (FiiRST), British Journal of Anaesthesia 2016. Registry ID verified against the trial registry: NCT02203968 (the PubMed record’s databank line is empty). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 50 adult hypotensive patients (systolic arterial pressure 100 mm Hg or below) requiring blood transfusion at a tertiary trauma centre, randomly assigned to 6 g of fibrinogen concentrate or placebo; 45 were analysed.
cards.result: Overall, 96% (43/45) [95% CI 86–99%] of patients received the intervention within one hour; 95% and 96% in the concentrate and placebo groups, respectively (P=1.00). Plasma fibrinogen concentrations remained higher in the concentrate group for up to 12 hours after admission, with the largest difference at three hours (2.9 vs 1.8 g/L; P<0.01). The 28-day mortality and thromboembolic complications were similar between groups. The authors concluded that early infusion of fibrinogen concentrate is feasible and increases plasma fibrinogen concentration during trauma resuscitation, and that larger trials are justified.
cards.watchOut: Feasibility is the whole claim: the drug can be given inside the first hour and it raises fibrinogen. Forty-five analysed patients cannot detect outcome effects, and none was seen. FiiRST’s name was reused by its successor strategy trial (Card 9, FiiRST-2) — a different trial, a different question, carded separately.
cards.source: Nascimento B et al. Fibrinogen in the initial resuscitation of severe trauma (FiiRST): a randomized feasibility trial. Br J Anaesth. 2016;117(6):775–782. PMID 27956676 · NCT02203968

cards.headline: FIinTIC (Ziegler 2021): prehospital concentrate protected clot firmness on the way to hospital — FIBTEM rose 13→15 mm on concentrate vs fell 12.5→11 mm on placebo (a laboratory primary outcome)
cards.summary: 53 evaluable trauma patients (concentrate 28, placebo 25) treated by 12 helicopter and emergency-doctor services across Austria, Germany and the Czech Republic. Primary outcome — change in FIBTEM maximum clot firmness before hospital arrival: rose from 13 to 15 mm on concentrate and fell from 12.5 to 11 mm on placebo; between-group difference in change 5 mm [3–7] (P<0.0001) . Plasma fibrinogen in the concentrate group stayed above the 2.0 g/L critical threshold throughout.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised pilot study (FIinTIC), European Journal of Anaesthesiology 2021. Registry IDs from the record: NCT01475344 · EudraCT 2010-022923-31. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 53 evaluable trauma patients 18 years or older with major bleeding and need of volume therapy, treated prehospital at the scene or during transport by helicopter emergency medical services and emergency-doctor vehicles, and admitted to four trauma centres (concentrate 28, placebo 25).
cards.result: Median FIBTEM maximum clot firmness decreased in the placebo group between baseline and admission to the emergency department, from 12.5 [IQR 10.5–14] mm to 11 [9.5–13] mm (P=0.0226), but increased in the concentrate group from 13 [11–15] mm to 15 [13.5–17] mm (P=0.0062). The median between-group difference in the change was 5 [3–7] mm (P<0.0001). Median fibrinogen plasma concentrations in the concentrate group were kept above the recommended critical threshold of 2.0 g/L throughout the observation period. The authors concluded that early concentrate administration is feasible in prehospital trauma care, protects against early fibrinogen depletion, and promotes rapid clot initiation and stability.
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a clot-trace number measured on arrival at hospital. FIinTIC proves prehospital delivery works and that fibrinogen depletion can be blunted; whether patients fare better is untested here — and the one large trauma strategy trial that did test outcomes (Reference 9) was null.
cards.source: Ziegler B et al. Efficacy of prehospital administration of fibrinogen concentrate in trauma patients bleeding or presumed to bleed (FIinTIC): a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomised pilot study. Eur J Anaesthesiol. 2021;38(4):348–357. PMID 33109923 · NCT01475344

cards.headline: E-FIT 1 (Curry 2018): early concentrate in major trauma haemorrhage missed its own feasibility target — only 69% received it within 45 minutes; mortality 35.5% overall, with no difference between arms
cards.summary: 39 trauma patients at five UK major trauma centres, randomised on major haemorrhage protocol activation to standard therapy plus 6 g fibrinogen concentrate or placebo . The feasibility target was not met: 27 of 39 (69% [95% CI 52–83]) received the intervention within 45 minutes of admission . Fibrinogen rose by a mean of 0.9 g/L on concentrate vs fell 0.2 g/L on placebo by 2 hours (P<0.0001). Transfusion use and thromboembolic events were similar; all-cause 28-day mortality was 35.5% overall, with no difference between arms .
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial (E-FIT 1), Critical Care 2018. Registry ID from the record: ISRCTN67540073. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 39 adult trauma patients with active bleeding who required activation of the major haemorrhage protocol at five UK major trauma centres, randomised to standard major haemorrhage therapy plus 6 g of fibrinogen concentrate or placebo.
cards.result: Twenty-seven of 39 participants (69%; 95% CI, 52–83%) across both arms received the study intervention within 45 minutes of admission. Fibrinogen levels in the concentrate arm rose by a mean of 0.9 g/L (SD 0.5) compared with a reduction of 0.2 g/L (SD 0.5) in the placebo arm and were significantly higher in the concentrate arm (P<0.0001) at 2 hours; levels were not different at day 7. Transfusion use and thromboembolic events were similar between arms. All-cause mortality at 28 days was 35.5% (95% CI, 23.8–50.8%) overall, with no difference between arms. The authors concluded that early delivery of fibrinogen concentrate within 45 minutes of admission was not feasible in this trial.
cards.watchOut: The missed target is the finding: in real major trauma centres, the drug could not be delivered as fast as the protocol demanded. That delivery problem shadows every early-replacement strategy — concentrate and cryoprecipitate alike (compare CRYOSTAT-1 on Shelf #424, which just met a 90-minute target). A strategy that cannot be delivered on time cannot be evaluated on outcomes, and E-FIT 1 is honest about which question it answered.
cards.source: Curry N et al. Early fibrinogen concentrate therapy for major haemorrhage in trauma (E-FIT 1): results from a UK multi-centre, randomised, double blind, placebo-controlled pilot trial. Crit Care. 2018;22:164. PMID 29914530 · ISRCTN67540073

cards.headline: FiiRST-2 (da Luz 2025): concentrate + PCC packs vs plasma in major trauma — NOT superior (24-hour units 20.8 vs 23.8; ratio 0.87, P=.20), stopped at interim for futility [combination intervention]
cards.summary: 217 patients enrolled at six Canadian level-1 trauma centres; 137 in the primary analysis (concentrate strategy 66, plasma 71). The intervention was a combination — fibrinogen concentrate 4 g PLUS prothrombin complex concentrate 2000 IU — against 4 units of frozen plasma in the first two massive-haemorrhage packs. Mean allogeneic units in 24 hours: 20.8 [16.7–25.9] vs 23.8 [19.2–29.4]; ratio 0.87, P=.20 for superiority — not superior . The trial was terminated at interim analysis for futility (conditional power below 25%). No differences in thromboembolic complications or 24-hour and 28-day mortality. Median age 38; 81% male.
cards.type: Multicentre, parallel-control, superiority randomised clinical trial (FiiRST-2), JAMA Network Open 2025. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT04534751. COMBINATION INTERVENTION: the experimental arm received two concentrates, so this trial tests a concentrates-first strategy — it is not, and must not be quoted as, a trial of fibrinogen concentrate alone.
cards.people: Patients 16 years or older with massive haemorrhage protocol activation on admission at six Canadian level-1 trauma centres (median age 38 [IQR 29–55] years; 81% male; median Injury Severity Score 29; 69% blunt mechanism); 217 enrolled, 137 included in the primary (modified intention-to-treat) analysis.
cards.result: Mean 24-hour transfusions were 20.8 (95% CI, 16.7–25.9) units in the concentrate-strategy group and 23.8 (95% CI, 19.2–29.4) units in the plasma group; the mean ratio was 0.87 (one-sided 97.5% CI, 0.00–1.19; P=.20 for superiority). No significant differences were found in thromboembolic complications or 24-hour and 28-day mortality. The trial was terminated after the interim analysis showed a conditional power of less than 25%, which would have required an impractically large sample to show superiority. The authors concluded that clotting factor concentrates were not superior to frozen plasma for initial resuscitation of patients with trauma, with similar efficacy and safety outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Two fences, both load-bearing. First, the combination flag: fibrinogen plus PCC cannot be decomposed — nothing here isolates fibrinogen’s contribution. Second, the result: the largest randomised test of the concentrates-first idea in trauma stopped for futility on its transfusion endpoint, the very endpoint the strategy was built to move. Carded because it is the strategy’s definitive test to date; quoted carefully or not at all.
cards.source: da Luz LT et al. Factors in the initial resuscitation of patients with severe trauma: the FiiRST-2 randomized clinical trial. JAMA Netw Open. 2025;8(9):e2532702. PMID 40982282 · NCT04534751

cards.headline: FIB-PPH (Wikkelsø 2015): preemptive concentrate in severe postpartum haemorrhage — transfusion 20% vs 22% (RR 0.95), null — in women whose mean fibrinogen was 4.5 g/L
cards.summary: 249 women randomised , 244 in the intention-to-treat analysis, with severe postpartum haemorrhage: a single 2 g dose of fibrinogen concentrate vs saline, given preemptively regardless of fibrinogen level. Red-cell transfusion up to 6 weeks: 20% vs 22% — RR 0.95 [0.58–1.54], relative; P=0.88 . No difference in any secondary outcome. No thromboembolic events. At inclusion, mean blood loss was 1459 mL and mean fibrinogen was 4.5 (SD 1.2) g/L.
cards.type: Investigator-initiated, multicentre, double-blind, parallel randomised controlled trial (FIB-PPH), British Journal of Anaesthesia 2015. Registry IDs from the record: NCT01359878 · EudraCT 2009-017736-41. The population is women with postpartum haemorrhage; no age mix is printed in the abstract.
cards.people: 249 women with severe postpartum haemorrhage randomised (124 concentrate, 125 placebo); 244 included in the intention-to-treat analysis. At inclusion the subjects had a mean blood loss of 1459 (SD 476) mL and a mean fibrinogen concentration of 4.5 (SD 1.2) g/L. The intervention group received a mean dose of 26 mg/kg, which raised fibrinogen by 0.40 g/L relative to placebo (P=0.002).
cards.result: Postpartum blood transfusion occurred in 25 (20%) of the fibrinogen group and 26 (22%) of the placebo group (relative risk, 0.95; 95% confidence interval, 0.58–1.54; P=0.88). No difference was found in any predefined secondary outcome, per-protocol analysis, or adjusted analysis. No thromboembolic events were detected. The authors concluded that they found no evidence for the use of 2 g fibrinogen concentrate as preemptive treatment for severe postpartum haemorrhage in patients with normofibrinogenaemia.
cards.watchOut: The authors’ own fence is this shelf’s key teaching point: pregnancy raises fibrinogen physiologically, so a postpartum-haemorrhage population averages 4.5 g/L — replacement was tested in women who mostly were not deficient. A null here refutes preemptive dosing of unselected bleeders; it does not test the woman whose fibrinogen is genuinely low, who remains essentially untrialled (Reference 12).
cards.source: Wikkelsø AJ et al. Pre-emptive treatment with fibrinogen concentrate for postpartum haemorrhage: randomized controlled trial. Br J Anaesth. 2015;114(4):623–633. PMID 25586727 · NCT01359878

cards.headline: FIDEL (Ducloy-Bouthors 2021): systematic early concentrate in persistent postpartum haemorrhage — composite failure 40.0% vs 42.4% (adjusted OR 0.99), null
cards.summary: 437 women at 30 French hospitals with persistent postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal delivery, escalating from oxytocin to prostaglandins: 3 g fibrinogen concentrate vs placebo within 30 minutes. Composite failure (haemoglobin fall of at least 4 g/dL and/or transfusion of at least 2 units within 48 hours): 40.0% vs 42.4% — adjusted OR 0.99 [0.66–1.47], relative; P=0.96 . No significant differences in secondary outcomes. Mean fibrinogen at inclusion was 4.1 (SD 0.9) g/L ; mean blood loss 877 mL.
cards.type: Multicentre, double-blind, randomised placebo-controlled trial (FIDEL), BJOG 2021. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT02155725. The population is women with postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal delivery; no age mix is printed in the abstract.
cards.people: 437 patients with persistent postpartum haemorrhage after vaginal delivery requiring a switch from oxytocin to prostaglandins at 30 French hospitals (224 fibrinogen concentrate, 213 placebo). At inclusion, blood loss (877 ± 346 mL) and plasma fibrinogen (4.1 ± 0.9 g/L) were similar in both groups.
cards.result: Failure rates were 40.0% in the fibrinogen group and 42.4% in the placebo group (odds ratio 0.99 after adjustment for centre and baseline plasma fibrinogen; 95% CI 0.66–1.47; P=0.96). No significant differences in secondary efficacy outcomes were observed. Mean plasma fibrinogen was unchanged in the fibrinogen group and decreased by 0.56 g/L in the placebo group. No thromboembolic or other relevant adverse effects were reported in the fibrinogen group, versus two in the placebo group. The authors concluded that early systematic administration of 3 g of fibrinogen concentrate did not reduce blood loss, transfusion needs or postpartum anaemia.
cards.watchOut: The second of the shelf’s three obstetric nulls, and the largest: systematic dosing — every persistent bleeder, regardless of fibrinogen level — in a population averaging 4.1 g/L. Together with FIB-PPH (Reference 10), FIDEL closes the ‘give it to everyone early’ strategy in postpartum haemorrhage. It does not address targeted replacement of documented deficiency.

cards.headline: OBS2 (Collins 2017): viscoelastometric-guided concentrate in postpartum haemorrhage — units transfused IRR 0.72 [0.3–1.7], null — and only 55 of 663 enrolled women were ever randomised
cards.summary: 663 women enrolled with postpartum haemorrhage of 1000–1500 mL; only those whose FIBTEM A5 was 15 mm or less with ongoing bleeding were randomised — 55 women . Allogeneic units transfused: adjusted IRR 0.72 [0.3–1.7], relative; P=0.45 — not significant . One thrombotic event in each group. Only 7 of the 55 randomised women had a fibrinogen of 2 g/L or below.
cards.type: Double-blind randomised controlled trial (OBS2), British Journal of Anaesthesia 2017. Registry IDs from the record’s registration line: ISRCTN46295339 · EudraCT 2012-005511-11. The population is women with postpartum haemorrhage; no age mix is printed in the abstract.
cards.people: 663 women with postpartum haemorrhage of 1000–1500 mL were enrolled; 55, whose FIBTEM A5 was 15 mm or less and who continued to bleed, were randomised to fibrinogen concentrate or placebo, triggered by viscoelastometric testing.
cards.result: The adjusted incidence rate ratio for the number of allogeneic units transfused in the fibrinogen group compared with placebo was 0.72 (95% CI 0.3–1.7), P=0.45. In pre-specified subgroup analyses, subjects with a FIBTEM A5 of 12 mm or less at randomisation who received concentrate received a median of 1 (0–4.5) unit of allogeneic products and had an additional 300 (100–350) mL blood loss, whereas those receiving placebo received 3 (0–6) units and had 700 (200–1550) mL additional loss; these differences were not statistically significant. There was one thrombotic event in each group. The authors concluded that infusion of concentrate triggered by a FIBTEM A5 of 15 mm or less did not improve outcomes in postpartum haemorrhage, that replacement does not appear required above that level, and that an effect below it cannot be excluded.
cards.watchOut: The enrolment funnel is the finding: at a FIBTEM trigger of 15 mm, almost no bleeding postpartum woman qualified — most postpartum haemorrhage is not a fibrinogen-deficiency state at these thresholds, because term fibrinogen is physiologically high. The IRR of 0.72 sits inside this library’s not-solid band and is null besides. Below the trigger, where deficiency is real, the trial randomised 55 women, 7 of them truly hypofibrinogenaemic: the exact patient the replacement idea exists for remains effectively untrialled.

cards.headline: Sabaté 2016: preemptive concentrate in liver transplantation — transfusion 52.9% vs 42.7% (P=.217), null — and the paper’s printed RR contradicts its own percentages
cards.summary: 99 patients allocated (concentrate 51, saline 48); the primary endpoint was assessed in 92. Preemptive concentrate (median 3.54 g) dosed to reach a plasma level of 2.9 g/L vs saline. Percentage of patients transfused with blood: 52.9% [42.5–63.3] on concentrate vs 42.74% [28.3–57.2] on saline (P=0.217) — numerically MORE transfusion on concentrate. The paper prints a relative risk of 0.80 [0.57–1.13] beside those percentages. Thrombotic events: 2.1% vs 11.4%.
cards.type: Multicentre, haemoglobin-stratified, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, American Journal of Transplantation 2016. Registry IDs from the record: NCT01539057 · EudraCT 2010-024584. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 99 patients undergoing liver transplantation allocated to preemptive fibrinogen concentrate (51) or saline (48); the primary endpoint — percentage of patients requiring red blood cells — was assessed in 92 patients after electronic record failures. Nine saline patients (20.9%) required fibrinogen at graft reperfusion, compared with one concentrate patient (2.1%) (P=0.005).
cards.result: Blood was transfused to 52.9% (95% CI 42.5–63.3%) of patients in the fibrinogen group and 42.74% (95% CI 28.3–57.2%) in the saline group (P=0.217). The paper reports a relative risk for blood transfusion of 0.80 (95% CI 0.57–1.13). Thrombotic events occurred in one patient (2.1%) in the fibrinogen group and five patients (11.4%) in the saline group. Seven patients (14.6%) in the fibrinogen group and nine (20.3%) in the saline group required reoperation. The authors concluded that preemptive administration of fibrinogen concentrate did not influence transfusion requirements.
cards.watchOut: An inconsistency inside the paper, flagged rather than smoothed over: the percentages it prints (52.9% transfused on concentrate vs 42.7% on saline) imply a relative risk above 1, yet the paper prints RR 0.80 [0.57–1.13]. One of the two is wrong in print; this card reports both, exactly as printed. Either way the result is null and sits inside this library’s not-solid band — but a reader checking the source will find the discrepancy, and the shelf does not hide it.
cards.source: Sabaté A et al. Impact of preemptive fibrinogen concentrate on transfusion requirements in liver transplantation: a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Am J Transplant. 2016;16(8):2421–2429. PMID 26880105 · NCT01539057

cards.headline: TROMBOFIB (Caballero 2023): two fibrinogen targets in liver transplantation (11 mm vs 8 mm) — red-cell transfusion 74.7% vs 72.9%, null [a dosing-target trial: both arms received concentrate]
cards.summary: 189 patients enrolled , 176 transplanted and analysed (intervention target 91, standard target 85). Both arms received fibrinogen concentrate , dosed to different FIBTEM A10 targets (11 mm vs 8 mm). Proportion requiring red-cell transfusion during transplantation or within 24 hours: 74.7% [65.5–83.3] vs 72.9% [62.2–82.0]; difference 1.8% [−11.1 to 14.78]; P=0.922 . Thrombotic events 4% in both groups; reoperation, retransplantation and mortality did not differ. Nearly 70% of both groups required concentrate to reach their target.
cards.type: Randomised, blinded, multicentre strategy trial (TROMBOFIB), Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis 2023. Registration: EudraCT 2018-002510-13, per the trial’s own reports (the PubMed record’s databank line is empty). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.people: 189 patients scheduled for liver transplantation at three Spanish hospitals, allocated to an intervention target (FIBTEM A10 of 11 mm) or a standard target (8 mm); 176 underwent transplantation with fibrinogen replacement and were analysed by intention to treat (91 intervention, 85 control).
cards.result: The proportion of patients requiring red blood cells did not differ between the groups: intervention 74.7% (95% CI, 65.5%–83.3%); control 72.9% (95% CI, 62.2%–82.0%); absolute difference 1.8% (95% CI, −11.1% to 14.78%) (P=.922). Thrombotic events occurred in 4% of patients in both groups; reoperation and retransplantation rates and mortality did not differ. Nearly 70% of patients in both groups required fibrinogen concentrate to reach the target. Using an 11-mm target increased maximum clot firmness without affecting safety, but provided no clinical benefits. The authors noted that the similar low plasma fibrinogen concentrations in the groups could explain the lack of significant between-group outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Not a replacement trial: both arms got the drug, randomised to different targets — it answers ‘how high a target?’, and the answer is that the higher target bought nothing. Registry caution, printed deliberately: reports from this group have attached NCT01539057 to this trial, but that number belongs to Card 13’s trial (Sabaté 2016); TROMBOFIB’s own registration is the EudraCT number on this card.

cards.headline: Fenger-Eriksen 2009: concentrate reversed starch-dilution coagulopathy on the clot trace — postoperative transfusion 2 of 10 vs 8 of 10 — in a 20-patient cystectomy trial [context card]
cards.summary: 20 patients with sudden excessive bleeding during radical cystectomy, resuscitated 1:1 with hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.4) to a 30% dilution, then randomised to fibrinogen concentrate or placebo. The primary endpoint — maximum clot firmness (a laboratory measure) — fell further on placebo and rose significantly on concentrate . Postoperative red-cell transfusion: 2 of 10 patients on concentrate vs 8 of 10 on placebo (P=0.023) .
cards.type: Prospective, randomised, placebo-controlled clinical trial, Journal of Thrombosis and Haemostasis 2009. No registry ID appears on the record, so none is printed here. Context card: the earliest randomised demonstration on this shelf, included for completeness and labelled for its size and mechanism.
cards.people: 20 patients experiencing sudden excessive bleeding during elective radical cystectomy, whose blood loss was substituted 1:1 with hydroxyethyl starch 130/0.4 to a dilution level of 30% (10 concentrate, 10 placebo). The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: Whole-blood maximum clot firmness was significantly reduced after 30% dilution in vivo with hydroxyethyl starch. Placebo resulted in a further decline of maximum clot firmness, whereas randomised administration of fibrinogen concentrate significantly increased it. Only 2 of 10 patients receiving fibrinogen substitution required postoperative red blood cell transfusions, compared with 8 of 10 in the placebo group (P=0.023). Platelet function and thrombin generation were reduced after 30% hemodilution, and fibrinogen administration caused no significant changes in either.
cards.watchOut: Context, stated plainly: 20 patients, a laboratory primary endpoint, and a coagulopathy manufactured by starch dilution — a resuscitation fluid that has since fallen out of use. This trial shows concentrate restores clot firmness in vivo, which was genuinely unknown in 2009; it is not evidence about bleeding patients generally, and the shelf does not rest on it.
cards.source: Fenger-Eriksen C et al. cards.headline: Reading the replacement trials together: the drug reliably raises fibrinogen and sometimes cuts transfusion — no trial has shown patients do better [synthesis card]
cards.summary: Across fifteen randomised trials on this shelf, one result never varies: concentrate raises fibrinogen and clot firmness within the hour. Everything downstream of that is unsettled. Transfusion fell in two single-centre cardiac trials and rose in the multicentre phase 3 ; trauma evidence is feasibility and laboratory studies plus one futility-stopped strategy trial; three obstetric trials are null in women who were not fibrinogen-deficient ; both liver trials are null. No card on this shelf shows a benefit in mortality, organ failure, or any patient-centred clinical outcome.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1–15 together, states what the shelf can and cannot carry, and names the population no trial has properly tested.
cards.people: The populations of Cards 1–15: bleeding or at-risk patients in cardiac surgery (including infants), trauma, postpartum haemorrhage, liver transplantation, and one small cystectomy cohort.
cards.result: Replacement reliably achieves its biochemical target in every setting tested. Its effect on transfusion is setting- and protocol-dependent: positive in Rahe-Meyer 2013 and Ranucci 2015 (single-centre cardiac), negative in REPLACE (multicentre cardiac), null in Bilecen 2017, the three obstetric trials, and both liver trials, and untested for outcomes in the trauma pilots. The obstetric nulls were obtained at mean fibrinogen levels of 4.1–4.5 g/L; the one trigger-based obstetric trial randomised 55 of 663 women, 7 of them with fibrinogen at or below 2 g/L. No completed trial has randomised a sizeable population selected for documented hypofibrinogenaemia with active bleeding outside cardiac surgery and small trauma pilots.
cards.watchOut: Replacement treats a number, and the number is easy to move — which is exactly why positive laboratory and transfusion results on this shelf should be read with suspicion: transfusion is a clinician-mediated endpoint, several of these trials were unblinded or protocol-bound, and the one trial large and rigorous enough to escape those concerns (REPLACE) found the opposite of benefit. The honest summary is not that replacement fails; it is that replacement is unproven where it matters, in the patient it was designed for.
