shelves.title: Sri Lanka’s antivenom trial: adrenaline before the drip prevents severe reactions — the steroid undoes it (country 43)
shelves.question: In snakebite patients about to receive antivenom, does premedication with adrenaline, promethazine, or hydrocortisone prevent severe acute reactions?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anaphylaxis · Antivenins · Double-Blind Method · Epinephrine · Humans · Hydrocortisone · Promethazine · Snake Bites · Sri Lanka · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: A prevention-of-harm shelf from a single large, rigorous trial: 1,007 Sri Lankan snakebite patients, factorial and double-blind, in a setting where antivenom itself causes reactions in 75% of recipients. Low-dose adrenaline prevented severe reactions — 43% relative reduction at 1 hour, 38% through 48 hours; promethazine and hydrocortisone did nothing; hydrocortisone, added to adrenaline, negated its benefit. Sri Lanka is a not-yet-covered country, so the country exception applies; LIKELY, not the top tier, because one trial — however well built — prices its benefit against one region’s antivenom. Proposed stamp LIKELY — proposed, pending the developer’s review.

cards.headline: Antivenom premedication trial (de Silva 2011, PLoS Medicine): low-dose adrenaline cut severe reactions by 43% (relative) — in a 1,007-patient factorial trial in Sri Lanka
cards.summary: 1,007 snakebite patients at five secondary referral hospitals in Sri Lanka, randomised double-blind in a 2×2×2 factorial design to low-dose adrenaline ( 0.25 mL of 1:1,000, subcutaneously ), promethazine 25 mg IV, and hydrocortisone 200 mg IV — each against matching placebo, all given immediately before antivenom infusion. Reactions were common: 752 patients (75%) reacted, 43% of reactions severe , 89% within the first hour. Compared with placebo, adrenaline reduced severe reactions by 43% (relative) [95% CI 25–67] at 1 hour and by 38% [26–49] up to and including 48 hours — the prespecified primary endpoint. Adrenaline pretreatment was safe in this cohort.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled 2×2×2 factorial trial, PLoS Med 2011. Registry ID from the record’s own databank: NCT00270777.
cards.people: 1,007 patients with snakebite envenoming at five secondary referral hospitals in Sri Lanka, about to receive antivenom of the type used across South Asia — a product class with a notoriously high reaction rate. The record’s abstract does not print a mean age or sex mix, so none is stated here.
cards.result: In total, 752 (75%) patients had acute reactions to antivenom: 9% mild, 48% moderate, and 43% severe; 89% of the reactions occurred within 1 hour, and 40% of all patients received rescue medication during the first hour. Compared with placebo, adrenaline significantly reduced severe reactions by 43% (95% CI, 25 to 67) at 1 hour and by 38% (95% CI, 26 to 49) up to and including 48 hours after antivenom administration. The authors concluded that pretreatment with low-dose adrenaline was safe and reduced the risk of acute severe reactions to snake antivenom.
cards.watchOut: The baseline is the story’s context: a treatment whose standard preparation makes three of four recipients react, nearly half of them severely, is a treatment whose quality is the deeper problem — the record itself closes by saying the need to improve the quality of available antivenom cannot be overemphasised. Premedication results earned against a high-reaction antivenom do not automatically transfer, at the same size, to a cleaner product; the direction (adrenaline first) is the portable part.
cards.source: de Silva HA et al. Low-dose adrenaline, promethazine, and hydrocortisone in the prevention of acute adverse reactions to antivenom following snakebite: a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. cards.headline: The factorial’s second lesson: promethazine did nothing, hydrocortisone did nothing — and hydrocortisone cancelled adrenaline’s benefit
cards.summary: A 2×2×2 factorial design prices every drug and every combination in one experiment, and its verdicts were asymmetric: promethazine — no significant reduction in severe reactions. Hydrocortisone — none either. And in the combination cells, adding hydrocortisone negated the benefit of adrenaline : the two-drug premedication performed like no premedication. At the time of the trial, giving all three was a common ritual; the factorial’s arithmetic says the ritual’s most popular form contained the seeds of its own failure — one working drug, diluted by a partner that undid it.
cards.type: Context card — the factorial contrasts of the de Silva 2011 trial, from its record (PMID 21572992). No new study.
cards.people: The same 1,007 Sri Lankan snakebite patients as Card 1, randomised across all eight combinations of adrenaline, promethazine, hydrocortisone, and their placebos.
cards.result: Adrenaline significantly reduced severe reactions (43% relative at 1 hour; 38% through 48 hours). Hydrocortisone and promethazine did not significantly reduce severe reactions. Adding hydrocortisone negated the benefit of adrenaline. The record’s conclusion names the practice implication directly: pretreatment with low-dose adrenaline was safe and effective — implying the steroid and the antihistamine add cost, delay, and (for hydrocortisone) actual counteraction, without benefit.
cards.watchOut: Factorial interactions rest on thinner numbers than main effects — each combination cell holds about an eighth of the patients — so the hydrocortisone interaction is a strong signal on a smaller base, not a measurement to three decimal places. It is nonetheless the kind of finding factorial designs exist to catch, and it points the same way as the null main effects: hydrocortisone has no supporting role here at all.

cards.headline: Reading the Sri Lanka trial alone: one country, one rigorous design, three verdicts — prevention of harm, priced drug by drug
cards.summary: Sri Lanka enters this library on a single trial the way Zambia and Cambodia did — under the country exception — but this trial is a prevention-of-harm study, the mirror image of the other two: the disease (snakebite) is treated by a drug (antivenom) whose own dangers are the target. The design earns its keep: 1,007 patients, double-blind, placebo-controlled, factorial — large enough and clean enough to return three separate verdicts (adrenaline works; promethazine doesn’t; hydrocortisone doesn’t and interferes) from one experiment. The result later entered WHO snakebite guidance. LIKELY rather than the library’s top tier, for the standing single-trial reason, and because a result measured against South Asian antivenom transfers in direction more safely than in size.
cards.type: Synthesis card — no new study. This card reads Cards 1 and 2 together and states the fence.
cards.people: The population of Cards 1 and 2: 1,007 snakebite patients at five secondary referral hospitals in Sri Lanka receiving antivenom, monitored at least 96 hours for acute reactions.
cards.result: The trial establishes that, before antivenom of the type used in South Asia, low-dose subcutaneous adrenaline prevents roughly two severe reactions in five (relative) that would otherwise occur in the first 48 hours, safely; that promethazine and hydrocortisone premedication are without benefit; and that hydrocortisone co-administration removes adrenaline’s protection. It does not establish adrenaline pretreatment as a substitute for resuscitation readiness — 40% of all patients still needed rescue medication in the first hour — nor does it price the benefit against modern, lower-reaction antivenoms.
cards.watchOut: Cite this shelf when the question is ‘what should precede the antivenom?’ — and keep its own closing warning attached: the durable fix for a 75% reaction rate is a better antivenom, not a better premedication.
cards.source: Synthesis of Cards 1–2 on this shelf (PMID 21572992; NCT00270777).

shelves.title: Incisional negative-pressure wound therapy: open fractures and closed incisions
shelves.question: Does incisional negative-pressure therapy reduce deep surgical-site infection after lower-limb fracture surgery or caesarean delivery versus standard dressings?
shelves.mesh: Bandages · Fracture Fixation, Internal/adverse effects · Fractures, Open/surgery · Injury Severity Score · Lower Extremity/injuries · Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology,prevention & control
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): Two large randomised trials found no significant reduction in surgical-site infection from incisional negative-pressure wound therapy over standard dressings — WHIST (1548 major-trauma lower-limb fracture patients: deep infection 5.84% vs 6.68% at 30 days) and Tuuli 2020 (1624 obese women after caesarean delivery: 3.6% vs 3.4%), with significantly more adverse skin reactions in the caesarean trial (7.0% vs 0.6%). Two large concordant nulls in two different high-risk settings justify LIKELY for the null on routine use in these settings.

cards.headline: WHIST (Costa) 2020: incisional negative-pressure therapy did not reduce deep infection after major-trauma lower-limb fracture surgery (5.84% vs 6.68%)
cards.summary: WHIST (Costa) 2020: incisional negative-pressure therapy did not reduce deep infection after fracture surgery ( 5.84% vs 6.68% ).
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (24 UK major trauma hospitals)
cards.people: 1548 patients aged 16 years or older undergoing surgery for a lower-limb fracture caused by major trauma (785 incisional negative-pressure wound therapy, 763 standard dressing); mean age 49.8 (SD 20.3) years, 38% women, 57% with multiple injuries; 1519 (98%) had primary-outcome data.
cards.result: Deep surgical-site infection at 30 days (CDC criteria) occurred in 5.84% (45 of 770) with negative-pressure therapy vs 6.68% (50 of 749) with standard dressing (odds ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.33; absolute risk difference −0.77%, −3.19% to 1.66%; P=0.52). At 90 days the rates were 11.4% vs 13.2% (odds ratio 0.84, 0.59 to 1.19; P=0.32). None of the five prespecified secondary outcomes (disability, quality of life, scar assessment, chronic pain, other wound complications) differed significantly at any time point. The authors concluded the findings do not support incisional negative-pressure therapy in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The 30-day event rate was lower than expected, so very small effects are not excluded; this is closed incisions after fracture fixation — it says nothing about negative-pressure therapy for open wounds, which is a different intervention and question.

cards.headline: Tuuli 2020: prophylactic negative-pressure therapy after caesarean delivery in obese women did not reduce surgical-site infection (3.6% vs 3.4%) and caused more skin reactions
cards.summary: Tuuli 2020: prophylactic negative-pressure therapy after caesarean delivery in obese women did not reduce infection ( 3.6% vs 3.4% ) and caused more skin reactions.
cards.people: 1624 obese women undergoing caesarean delivery randomly assigned to prophylactic negative-pressure wound therapy applied immediately after incision repair (816) or standard wound dressing (808); mean age 30.4 years, mean body mass index 39.5; 1608 (99%) completed the study.
cards.result: Superficial or deep surgical-site infection (CDC definitions) occurred in 29 (3.6%) in the negative-pressure group vs 27 (3.4%) with standard dressing (difference 0.36%, 95% CI −1.46% to 2.19%; P=0.70). Of 30 prespecified secondary endpoints, 25 showed no significant differences, including other wound complications (2.6% vs 3.1%) and the composite of infections and other wound complications (6.5% vs 6.7%). Adverse skin reactions were significantly more frequent with negative-pressure therapy (7.0% vs 0.6%; difference 6.95%, 1.86% to 12.03%; P<0.001). The authors concluded routine prophylactic use is not supported in this population.
cards.watchOut: Obese caesarean patients at the trial's centres; median device duration was 4 days. The null is about routine prophylaxis in this population, not about therapeutic use on established wound problems.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, two settings, one answer — routine incisional negative-pressure therapy does not prevent infection
cards.summary: Two large trials, two settings, one answer — routine incisional negative-pressure therapy does not prevent infection: LIKELY the null.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: WHIST (1548 trauma fracture patients) and Tuuli 2020 (1624 obese caesarean patients).
cards.result: The point estimates bracket no effect (odds ratio 0.87 in WHIST; a +0.36% absolute difference in Tuuli), confidence intervals exclude any large benefit, and the only significant harm signal runs against the device (skin reactions 7.0% vs 0.6% after caesarean). That is why the null carries LIKELY rather than POSSIBLE: this is not one underpowered trial but two large concordant ones. Diabetic-foot offloading and open-wound negative-pressure therapy live elsewhere (Shelf #291 covers offloading) and are not judged here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial enrolled the very highest-risk incisions (e.g. grossly contaminated or re-operative wounds); absence of benefit in these two large populations should not be stretched into a claim about every wound.

shelves.title: Rapid rule-out pathways for chest pain
shelves.question: Do accelerated diagnostic pathways (high-sensitivity troponin 0/1-h algorithms; the HEART Pathway) safely increase early discharge in suspected ACS?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/blood,complications,diagnosis · Acute Pain/blood,diagnosis,etiology · Biomarkers/blood · Cardiology Service, Hospital · Chest Pain/blood,diagnosis,etiology · Coronary Angiography · Critical Pathways
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY — the HEART Pathway safely increases early discharge · LIKELY the null — implementing a high-sensitivity troponin 99th-centile threshold did not reduce later myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death. The HEART Pathway randomised trial (282 emergency-department patients; primary report Mahler 2015 with 1-year outcomes in Stopyra 2018 — one trial, counted once) cut objective cardiac testing at 30 days (56.7% vs 68.8%), shortened stay by 12 hours and raised early discharge (39.7% vs 18.4%), with no major adverse cardiac events in patients identified for early discharge at 30 days and a 100% negative predictive value among low-risk patients at 1 year (MACE 9.9% vs 11.3% overall). High-STEACS (48,282 patients, stepped-wedge cluster-randomised) reclassified 17% more patients with myocardial injury or infarction using the high-sensitivity assay, yet subsequent myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death at 1 year in reclassified patients did not fall (adjusted odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.75-1.61) — a very large null, stamped LIKELY the null under the library's large-null rule. The High-STEACS endpoint is a null implementation result reported with its mortality component; no benefit claim is made from it.

cards.headline: Mahler 2015 (HEART Pathway RCT): the pathway cut objective testing by 12.1 points, shortened stay by 12 hours, and raised early discharge by 21.3 points — with no missed events in discharged patients
cards.summary: Mahler 2015 (HEART Pathway RCT, pinned at build): the pathway cut objective testing by 12.1 points, shortened stay by 12 hours, and raised early discharge by 21.3 points.
cards.type: Randomized controlled trial (accelerated diagnostic protocol vs usual care)
cards.people: 282 adult emergency department patients with symptoms related to acute coronary syndrome without ST-elevation on ECG, randomized to the HEART Pathway (HEART score plus troponin at 0 and 3 hours) or usual care based on ACC/AHA guidelines; mean age 53 years and 16% had previous myocardial infarction, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: Compared with usual care, use of the HEART Pathway decreased objective cardiac testing at 30 days by 12.1% (68.8% versus 56.7%; P=0.048) and length of stay by 12 hours (9.9 versus 21.9 hours; P=0.013) and increased early discharges by 21.3% (39.7% versus 18.4%; P<0.001). Major adverse cardiac events within 30 days of randomization occurred in 6% (95% CI 3.6%-9.5%) of all participants. No patients identified for early discharge had major adverse cardiac events within 30 days.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 282 patients using troponin measures at 0 and 3 hours: the 'no missed events' claim rests on the patients identified for early discharge, a small denominator for a safety claim — the 1-year report below gives the fuller picture.

cards.summary: Stopyra 2018 (HEART Pathway, 1-year outcomes): low-risk patients had no MACE at 1 year (NPV 100%); overall MACE 9.9% vs 11.3%.

cards.headline: Shah 2018 (High-STEACS): implementing high-sensitivity troponin reclassified 17% more patients but did not reduce MI or cardiovascular death at 1 year (adjusted OR 1.10)
cards.summary: Shah 2018 (High-STEACS, pinned at build): implementing high-sensitivity troponin reclassified 17% more patients but did not reduce MI or cardiovascular death at 1 year.
cards.people: 48,282 consecutive patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome admitted to the emergency departments of ten secondary or tertiary care hospitals in Scotland, with paired cardiac troponin measurements from the standard and trial assays; mean age 61 (SD 17) years, 47% women, as stated in the abstract.
cards.result: The high-sensitivity assay reclassified 1,771 (17%) of 10,360 patients with myocardial injury or infarction who were not identified by the contemporary assay. In those reclassified patients, subsequent myocardial infarction or cardiovascular death within 1 year occurred in 105 (15%) of 720 patients in the validation phase and 131 (12%) of 1,051 patients in the implementation phase (adjusted odds ratio for implementation vs validation phase 1.10, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.61; p=0.620 — a relative measure, non-significant). The authors conclude that their findings question whether the diagnostic threshold for myocardial infarction should be based on the 99th centile derived from a normal reference population.
cards.watchOut: An implementation trial, not a treatment trial: it tests an assay-and-threshold change across whole hospitals, and the outcome comparison is made within the reclassified subgroup across validation and implementation phases.

shelves.title: Diagnostic algorithms for suspected pulmonary embolism
shelves.question: Do the YEARS algorithm and age-adjusted D-dimer cutoffs safely reduce CT imaging in suspected PE (YEARS; ADJUST-PE)?
shelves.mesh: Algorithms · Biomarkers/metabolism · Computed Tomography Angiography/statistics & numerical data · Fibrin Fibrinogen Degradation Products/metabolism · Pulmonary Embolism/diagnosis,therapy · Unnecessary Procedures/statistics & numerical data · Venous Thromboembolism/etiology
shelves.balance: LIKELY: Two large prospective management-outcome studies — labelled honestly as management studies, not blinded randomised trials — show these algorithms safely cut imaging. YEARS (3,465 patients) excluded pulmonary embolism without CT pulmonary angiography in 48% of patients (vs 34% under Wells' rule plus a fixed D-dimer threshold), with a 3-month venous thromboembolism failure rate of 0.61% (95% CI 0.36-0.96) among untreated ruled-out patients. ADJUST-PE (3,346 patients) found a 3-month failure rate of 0.3% (0.1-1.7) in patients left untreated on an age-adjusted cutoff, and in patients aged 75 or older the cutoff raised D-dimer-only exclusion from 6.4% to 29.7% with no additional false-negative findings. Concordant prospective validation at this scale earns LIKELY for safe imaging reduction. Pulmonary embolism treatment after diagnosis is a different question and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: van der Hulle 2017 (YEARS): the algorithm avoided CTPA in 48% vs 34% under Wells plus a fixed cutoff, with a 0.61% 3-month failure rate
cards.summary: van der Hulle 2017 (YEARS): the algorithm avoided CTPA in 48% vs 34% under Wells plus a fixed cutoff, with a 0.61% 3-month failure rate.
cards.type: Prospective, multicentre management-outcome cohort study (not a randomised trial — labelled as such)
cards.people: 3,465 consecutive patients with clinically suspected pulmonary embolism in 12 hospitals in the Netherlands (3,616 screened, 151 excluded), managed by simultaneous assessment of the three-item YEARS clinical decision rule and D-dimer concentrations; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 456 (13%) patients were diagnosed with pulmonary embolism at baseline. Of the 2,946 patients (85%) in whom pulmonary embolism was ruled out at baseline and who remained untreated, 18 patients were diagnosed with symptomatic venous thromboembolism during 3-month follow-up (0.61%, 95% CI 0.36-0.96), of whom six had fatal pulmonary embolism (0.20%, 0.07-0.44). CTPA was not indicated in 1,651 (48%) patients with the YEARS algorithm compared with 1,174 (34%) patients if Wells' rule and a fixed D-dimer threshold of less than 500 ng/mL had been applied, a difference of 14% (95% CI 12-16).
cards.watchOut: A management study without randomisation: safety rests on the observed failure rate in one Dutch cohort, and 6 fatal pulmonary embolisms occurred among ruled-out patients (0.20%) — 'safe' means within the accepted failure benchmark for rule-out strategies, not zero risk.
cards.source: van der Hulle T et al. Simplified diagnostic management of suspected pulmonary embolism (the YEARS study): a prospective, multicentre, cohort study. Lancet. 2017;390(10091):289-297. PMID: 28549662. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the abstract states this trial is registered with the Netherlands Trial Registry, number NTR4193.

cards.headline: Righini 2014 (ADJUST-PE): age-adjusted D-dimer left untreated patients with a 0.3% 3-month failure rate, and raised D-dimer exclusion in over-75s from 6.4% to 29.7%
cards.summary: Righini 2014 (ADJUST-PE): age-adjusted D-dimer left untreated patients with a 0.3% 3-month failure rate, and raised D-dimer exclusion in over-75s.
cards.type: Multicenter, multinational, prospective management outcome study (not a randomised trial — labelled as such)
cards.people: 3,346 consecutive outpatients who presented to the emergency department with clinically suspected pulmonary embolism in 19 centers in Belgium, France, the Netherlands, and Switzerland (prevalence of PE 19%), assessed by clinical probability, highly sensitive D-dimer measurement, and CT pulmonary angiography as the strategy directed; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Among the 2,898 patients with a nonhigh or an unlikely clinical probability, 817 patients (28.2%) had a D-dimer level lower than 500 µg/L and 337 patients (11.6%) had a D-dimer level between 500 µg/L and their age-adjusted cutoff. The 3-month failure rate in patients with a D-dimer level higher than 500 µg/L but below the age-adjusted cutoff (age times 10 in patients 50 years or older), who did not undergo CTPA and were left untreated, was 1 of 331 patients (0.3% [95% CI 0.1%-1.7%]). Among the 766 patients 75 years or older, of whom 673 had a nonhigh clinical probability, using the age-adjusted cutoff instead of the 500 µg/L cutoff increased the proportion of patients in whom PE could be excluded on the basis of D-dimer from 43 of 673 patients (6.4% [95% CI 4.8%-8.5%]) to 200 of 673 patients (29.7% [26.4%-33.3%]), without any additional false-negative findings.
cards.watchOut: The pivotal subgroup — D-dimer between the fixed and age-adjusted cutoffs — is 331 patients with a single failure event; the confidence interval (up to 1.7%) is the honest precision of the safety claim.

cards.summary: Two ways to cut CT imaging in suspected PE, both prospectively validated as safe — LIKELY.

shelves.title: Shorter rabies post-exposure prophylaxis: one-week intradermal regimens
shelves.question: Do abbreviated (one-week) intradermal rabies PEP regimens produce antibody responses non-inferior to standard regimens?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Chlorocebus aethiops · Immunization Schedule · Immunogenicity, Vaccine · Philippines/epidemiology · Post-Exposure Prophylaxis · Rabies/prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The immunogenicity evidence is consistent that one-week regimens seroconvert everyone, and mixed on whether they match standard regimens titre-for-titre. Quiambao 2019 (600 exposed patients, Philippines): the one-week 4-site intradermal regimen, with or without rabies immunoglobulin, was non-inferior to the updated Thai Red Cross 28-day regimen for day-14 seroconversion (100% and 99.4% vs 98.8%), with higher geometric mean titres (11.3 and 9.89 vs 6.15 IU/mL) and better one-year persistence (97.6% and 89% vs 79.8% still ≥0.5 IU/mL). The 2026 Indian equivalence trial (400 healthy volunteers) found the one-week IPC regimen did NOT meet its prespecified day-42 titre-equivalence criterion against the updated Thai Red Cross regimen (geometric mean concentration ratios 0.59 for PCECV and 0.76 for PVRV, against a 0.72–1.04 window) — although every participant in every group was at or above 0.5 IU/mL from day 14 to one year. All of this is surrogate (antibody) evidence: no trial on this shelf measures rabies cases prevented, and none should be read as doing so. Rabies appears elsewhere in the index only inside vaccine-survey material (Shelf #449), which is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Quiambao 2019: the one-week 4-site intradermal regimen was non-inferior to the updated Thai Red Cross regimen for day-14 seroconversion (100% and 99.4% vs 98.8%)
cards.summary: Quiambao 2019: the one-week 4-site intradermal regimen was non-inferior for day-14 seroconversion ( 100% in the lead arm).
cards.type: Phase III, single-centre, open-label, randomised non-inferiority trial in exposed patients
cards.people: 600 participants aged 50 years or younger in the Philippines with WHO category II injuries (allocated to G1) or category III injuries (randomised to G2 or G3), receiving purified Vero cell rabies vaccine (PVRV): G1 (200), one-week 4-site intradermal regimen (4-4-4-0-0) without immunoglobulin; G2 (201), the same regimen with purified equine immunoglobulin; G3 (199), the updated Thai Red Cross 28-day 2-site regimen (2-2-2-0-2) with immunoglobulin.
cards.result: Day-14 seroconversion (rabies virus neutralising antibody ≥0.5 IU/mL) was non-inferior in both comparisons: 100% (G1), 99.4% (G2) and 98.8% (G3). Geometric mean titres at day 14 were 11.3, 9.89 and 6.15 IU/mL, respectively, and by one year the proportions still seroconverted were 97.6%, 89% and 79.8%, with titres of 2.96, 1.37 and 0.97 IU/mL. Safety and tolerability were similar across the three groups.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, open-label immunogenicity trial in real exposed patients — the right population, but the endpoint is an antibody threshold, not rabies prevented (rabies is too rare and too lethal for an efficacy trial), and the vaccine is one product (PVRV).
cards.source: Quiambao BP et al. cards.summary: Thangaraj 2026: the one-week IPC regimen did NOT meet prespecified titre equivalence with the updated Thai Red Cross regimen (GMR 0.59 for PCECV).
cards.type: Phase 4, single-centre, open-label equivalence randomised controlled trial in healthy volunteers
cards.people: 400 healthy adults in India, block-randomised 1:1:1:1 to the one-week Institut Pasteur du Cambodge (IPC) regimen (days 0, 3, 7) or the one-month updated Thai Red Cross (UTRC) regimen (days 0, 3, 7, 28), with either purified chick embryo cell vaccine (PCECV) or PVRV (100 per group); 362 (90.5%) completed the regimen and the day-42 blood draw.
cards.result: The day-42 geometric mean concentration ratio (IPC vs UTRC) was 0.59 (95% CI 0.47 to 0.75) for PCECV and 0.76 (0.61 to 0.95) for PVRV — neither met the prespecified equivalence criterion (the whole 95% CI within 0.72 to 1.04). However, all participants in all four groups had rabies virus neutralising antibody titres ≥0.5 IU/mL at every assessment from day 14 to 1 year. Adverse events were similar between regimens and mostly mild.
cards.watchOut: Two honest caveats in the paper itself: nearly a quarter of participants had baseline titres ≥0.5 IU/mL despite exclusion of reported prior vaccination or dog bite (unrecognised priming may have distorted the ratios), and healthy volunteers are not bitten patients. The trial fails the one-week regimen on titre equivalence while passing it on the seroprotection threshold — which of those should govern policy is a judgement, and the authors say so.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one-week regimens seroconvert everyone; whether their titres 'equal' the standard depends on the yardstick — POSSIBLE, on surrogate evidence only
cards.summary: One-week regimens seroconvert everyone; whether their titres 'equal' the standard depends on the yardstick — POSSIBLE, on a surrogate.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Quiambao 2019 (600 exposed patients, PVRV) and Thangaraj 2026 (400 healthy volunteers, PCECV and PVRV).
cards.result: The apparent disagreement is about endpoints, not patients: on the seroconversion threshold (≥0.5 IU/mL) the one-week regimens pass everywhere (98.8–100% at day 14 in 2019; 100% of all groups from day 14 to a year in 2026, with better one-year persistence for the 4-site regimen in 2019); on the stricter geometric-mean-titre equivalence window, the one-week IPC regimen failed in 2026 (GMR 0.59 and 0.76 vs the 0.72–1.04 criterion). The stamp is POSSIBLE, and it is a stamp about antibody responses — no card on this shelf measures clinical rabies outcomes, and the shelf makes no such claim.
cards.watchOut: Do not convert 'non-inferior seroconversion' into 'equally protective': rabies PEP also depends on wound care, immunoglobulin for category III exposures, and completing whichever regimen is started.

shelves.title: Prehospital airway strategy in cardiac arrest: supraglottic device vs intubation, laryngeal tube vs intubation (AIRWAYS-2, PART)
shelves.question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does an initial supraglottic airway strategy give better functional outcome than tracheal intubation — and does an initial laryngeal-tube strategy give better 72-hour survival than intubation?
shelves.mesh: Airway Management/instrumentation,methods · Allied Health Personnel · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · England · Glottis · Intubation, Intratracheal/instrumentation,methods · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the i-gel question — in AIRWAYS-2 (9,296 patients), a supraglottic-airway-first strategy was no better than tracheal intubation on good functional outcome at 30 days (6.4% vs 6.8%) despite much better initial ventilation success (87.4% vs 79.0%). POSSIBLE for the laryngeal-tube question — in PART (3,004 patients), a laryngeal-tube-first strategy gave higher 72-hour survival than intubation (18.3% vs 15.4%, adjusted difference 2.9%), with hospital survival and good neurological status also higher, but this is a single pragmatic cluster-crossover trial in which first-attempt intubation success was unusually low (51.6%), so the benefit may belong to the setting as much as to the device. The two trials test different supraglottic devices and are not interchangeable evidence. Tier C ruled no at drafting (a resuscitation-strategy question, no drug-benefit claim).

cards.headline: AIRWAYS-2 (Benger 2018): i-gel supraglottic strategy was no better than tracheal intubation on functional outcome at 30 days, despite far better ventilation success
cards.summary: AIRWAYS-2 2018: the i-gel strategy was no better than intubation on good functional outcome at 30 days ( 6.4% vs 6.8% ), despite far better ventilation success.
cards.type: Multicentre, cluster-randomised clinical trial (paramedics randomised; unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 9,296 adults with nontraumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest treated by paramedics from 4 ambulance services in England (4,886 supraglottic airway [i-gel], 4,410 tracheal intubation); median age 73 years; 3,373 (36.3%) were women.
cards.result: Good functional outcome (modified Rankin Scale 0–3 at discharge or 30 days) occurred in 311 of 4,882 patients (6.4%) with the supraglottic strategy vs 300 of 4,407 (6.8%) with intubation (adjusted risk difference −0.6%, 95% CI −1.6% to 0.4%). Initial ventilation was successful in 87.4% vs 79.0% (adjusted risk difference 8.3%, 6.3% to 10.2%), and more supraglottic-strategy patients actually received an advanced airway (85.2% vs 77.6%). Regurgitation (26.1% vs 24.5%) and aspiration (15.1% vs 14.9%) did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Cluster design by paramedic with very different intubation exposure between arms; the trial answers a strategy question (which device first) in one EMS system, not which device is best in expert hands.
cards.source: Benger JR et al. JAMA. 2018;320(8):779-791. PMID: 30167701. Registry ID: ISRCTN08256118, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: PART (Wang 2018): laryngeal-tube-first strategy gave higher 72-hour survival than intubation-first (18.3% vs 15.4%)
cards.summary: PART 2018: a laryngeal-tube-first strategy gave higher 72-hour survival than intubation-first ( 18.3% vs 15.4% ).
cards.type: Multicentre pragmatic cluster-crossover randomised clinical trial (EMS agencies; unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 3,004 adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and anticipated need for advanced airway management, enrolled by 27 EMS agencies in the Resuscitation Outcomes Consortium (1,505 laryngeal tube, 1,499 endotracheal intubation); median age 64 years (IQR 53–76); 1,829 (60.9%) were men.
cards.result: 72-hour survival was 18.3% with the laryngeal-tube strategy vs 15.4% with intubation (adjusted difference 2.9%, 95% CI 0.2% to 5.6%; P=.04). Secondary outcomes also favoured the laryngeal tube: return of spontaneous circulation 27.9% vs 24.3% (adjusted difference 3.6%, 0.3% to 6.8%), hospital survival 10.8% vs 8.1% (2.7%, 0.6% to 4.8%) and favourable neurological status at discharge 7.1% vs 5.0% (2.1%, 0.3% to 3.8%). Initial airway success was 90.3% with the laryngeal tube vs 51.6% with intubation. Oropharyngeal/hypopharyngeal injury, airway swelling and pneumonia did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: Single trial, and its intubation arm performed unusually poorly at first attempt (51.6% success): the comparison may be 'laryngeal tube vs intubation as practised by these agencies', not vs expert intubation. The authors themselves state further research is warranted.
cards.source: Wang HE et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: device-first strategies are at least as good as intubation-first; only the laryngeal tube showed a survival edge, in one trial
cards.summary: Device-first strategies are at least as good as intubation-first; only the laryngeal tube showed a survival edge, in one trial — Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: AIRWAYS-2 (9,296 patients, i-gel vs intubation) and PART (3,004 patients, laryngeal tube vs intubation).
cards.result: Both trials agree that starting with a supraglottic device does not worsen outcomes and secures ventilation far more reliably (first/overall success 87–90% vs 52–79% for intubation). They disagree on benefit: AIRWAYS-2 found no functional-outcome gain (6.4% vs 6.8%), while PART found a 2.9-percentage-point absolute gain in 72-hour survival. Hence the split stamp — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for i-gel on function, POSSIBLE for the laryngeal tube's survival benefit pending replication. In-hospital intubation technique (video laryngoscopy, bougie, preoxygenation) lives on Shelf #758 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not merge the two trials into one 'supraglottic works' claim: different devices, different EMS systems, different primary outcomes.

shelves.title: Defibrillation strategies for refractory ventricular fibrillation: double sequential and vector change (DOSE VF)
shelves.question: In refractory VF after three failed standard shocks, does double sequential external defibrillation or vector-change defibrillation improve survival to discharge and good neurological outcome versus continuing standard defibrillation?
shelves.mesh: Canada · Defibrillators · Electric Countershock/adverse effects,instrumentation,methods · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/mortality,therapy · Ventricular Fibrillation/mortality,therapy · Cross-Over Studies · Cluster Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the headline outcomes are survival to discharge and neurological outcome after cardiac arrest). One cluster-randomised trial with crossover (DOSE VF, 405 patients, stopped early when COVID-19 disrupted the trial) found survival to hospital discharge of 30.4% with double sequential defibrillation and 21.7% with vector-change defibrillation vs 13.3% with standard defibrillation (relative risks 2.21 and 1.71 respectively, printed as relative with the absolute rates beside them), and good neurological outcome higher with double sequential (relative risk 2.21) but not significantly with vector change (1.48, CI crossing 1). A single, small, early-stopped trial caps a survival-benefit claim at POSSIBLE; the currency sweep found no confirmatory randomised trial.

cards.headline: DOSE VF (Cheskes 2022): double sequential defibrillation raised survival to discharge to 30.4% vs 13.3% with standard shocks; vector change gave 21.7%
cards.summary: DOSE VF 2022: double sequential defibrillation raised survival to discharge to 30.4% vs 13.3% with standard shocks (relative risk 2.21); vector change gave 21.7%.
cards.type: Cluster-randomised trial with crossover (six Canadian paramedic services; unblindable by nature), stopped early because of the COVID-19 pandemic
cards.people: 405 adults with refractory ventricular fibrillation during out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (136 standard defibrillation, 144 vector-change, 125 double sequential). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Survival to hospital discharge was 30.4% with double sequential external defibrillation vs 13.3% with standard defibrillation (relative risk 2.21, 95% CI 1.33 to 3.67) and 21.7% with vector-change defibrillation vs 13.3% (relative risk 1.71, 1.01 to 2.88) — relative figures, with the absolute rates (30.4% and 21.7% vs 13.3%) printed beside them. Good neurological outcome (modified Rankin Scale ≤2 at discharge) was more frequent with double sequential (relative risk 2.21, 1.26 to 3.88) but not significantly with vector change (relative risk 1.48, 0.81 to 2.71). Secondary outcomes included termination of VF and return of spontaneous circulation.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 405 patients, terminated early for pandemic logistics rather than for benefit — early stopping plus cluster crossover means the survival ratios (2.21 sits just above the developer's 2.0 observational floor, but this is a randomised estimate from a small stopped trial) should be read as promising, not settled. No second randomised trial exists to confirm either strategy.
cards.source: Cheskes S et al. Defibrillation Strategies for Refractory Ventricular Fibrillation. N Engl J Med. 2022;387(21):1947-1956. PMID: 36342151. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04080986, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a promising single-trial survival signal for double sequential and vector-change defibrillation — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: A promising single-trial survival signal with no confirmatory trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: DOSE VF (405 patients with refractory VF).
cards.result: DOSE VF is the only randomised test of defibrillation strategy in refractory VF: both alternative strategies beat continued standard shocks on survival to discharge in absolute terms (30.4% and 21.7% vs 13.3%), and double sequential also improved good neurological outcome. With one small early-stopped trial and no confirmatory RCT found in the 2024–2026 currency sweep, the stamp is POSSIBLE and the shelf is Tier C — the survival claim awaits the developer's personal verdict. Antiarrhythmic drugs for shock-refractory VF live on Shelf #233 and are not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Extracorporeal CPR for refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (ARREST, Prague OHCA)
shelves.question: Does extracorporeal CPR improve survival with good function in refractory out-of-hospital cardiac arrest — in the single-centre ARREST trial and in the Prague trial of intra-arrest transport to an ECPR/invasive strategy?
shelves.mesh: Advanced Cardiac Life Support/methods,standards · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation/methods · Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation/methods · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/epidemiology,therapy · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Patient Discharge/trends · Reperfusion/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: a survival claim in refractory arrest). The two randomised trials point in different directions. ARREST (30 patients, single centre, stopped at its first interim analysis for superiority) found survival to discharge of 43% with early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation vs 7% with standard ACLS. The larger Prague trial (256 patients) of a bundled invasive strategy (intra-arrest transport, ECPR, immediate invasive assessment) missed its primary outcome — survival with good neurological outcome at 180 days 31.5% vs 22.0% (odds ratio 1.63, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.85; P=.09) — and was stopped for futility, with more bleeding in the invasive group (31% vs 15%). A tiny stopped-early positive trial against a larger neutral-primary trial is the definition of POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ARREST (Yannopoulos 2020): ECMO-facilitated resuscitation gave 43% survival to discharge vs 7% with standard ACLS — in 30 patients, stopped at the first interim look
cards.summary: ARREST 2020: ECMO-facilitated resuscitation gave 43% survival to discharge vs 7% with standard ACLS — in 30 patients, stopped at the first interim look.
cards.type: Phase 2, single-centre, open-label, adaptive randomised controlled trial, terminated early for superiority at a preplanned interim analysis
cards.people: 30 adults aged 18–75 years with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and refractory VF, no ROSC after three shocks, and estimated transfer time under 30 minutes to one US centre (15 standard ACLS, 15 ECMO-facilitated resuscitation, of whom 14 were analysed after one withdrawal); mean age 59 years (range 36–73); 25 (83%) were men.
cards.result: Survival to hospital discharge was 6 of 14 patients (43%, 95% credible interval 21.3–67.7) with early ECMO-facilitated resuscitation vs 1 of 15 (7%, 1.6–30.2) with standard ACLS (risk difference 36.2%, 3.7–59.2; posterior probability of ECMO superiority 0.9861). Cumulative 6-month survival was significantly better in the ECMO group. No unanticipated serious adverse events were observed. The trial was terminated after 30 patients because the posterior probability crossed the prespecified monitoring boundary.
cards.watchOut: Thirty patients at one expert centre with strict eligibility (refractory VF only, short transfer): the 43% vs 7% contrast is the most fragile kind of large effect — stopped at the first interim look, with wide credible intervals. It does not describe what an average system would achieve.
cards.source: Yannopoulos D et al. Lancet. 2020;396(10265):1807-1816. PMID: 33197396. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03880565, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: Prague OHCA (Belohlavek 2022): the invasive ECPR bundle did not significantly improve 180-day survival with good neurological outcome (31.5% vs 22.0%)
cards.summary: Prague OHCA 2022: the invasive ECPR bundle did not significantly improve 180-day survival with good neurological outcome ( 31.5% vs 22.0% ).
cards.type: Single-centre randomised clinical trial, stopped when prespecified futility criteria were met
cards.people: 256 adults with witnessed out-of-hospital cardiac arrest of presumed cardiac origin without ROSC, enrolled in Prague (124 invasive strategy, 132 standard strategy), of a planned 285; median age 58 years; 44 (17%) were women.
cards.result: Survival with good neurological outcome (Cerebral Performance Category 1–2) at 180 days occurred in 39 patients (31.5%) with the invasive strategy vs 29 (22.0%) with standard resuscitation (odds ratio 1.63, 95% CI 0.93 to 2.85; difference 9.5%, −1.3% to 20.1%; P=.09) — a relative measure whose confidence interval crosses no-effect, with absolute rates beside it. Neurological recovery at 30 days was higher with the invasive strategy (30.6% vs 18.2%; odds ratio 1.99, 1.11 to 3.57; P=.02), a secondary outcome. Bleeding occurred more frequently in the invasive group (31% vs 15%).
cards.watchOut: The Prague intervention is a bundle (mechanical compressions, intra-arrest transport, ECPR, immediate catheterisation), so it cannot isolate ECPR's own effect; the trial was possibly underpowered for its 180-day primary, as its authors state. Its odds ratio of 1.63 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band.

cards.headline: Synthesis: ECPR's randomised record is one tiny positive trial and one larger neutral-primary trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: One tiny positive trial and one larger neutral-primary trial — POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: ARREST (30 patients, refractory VF, single centre) and Prague OHCA (256 patients, all-cause witnessed refractory arrest, bundled invasive strategy).
cards.result: The honest summary is discordance: 43% vs 7% survival to discharge in the small stopped-early trial; 31.5% vs 22.0% good-outcome survival at 180 days (not significant) in the larger trial, at the price of twice the bleeding (31% vs 15%). Patient selection differs (refractory VF with short transfer vs broader witnessed arrest), as does the intervention (ECMO on arrival vs a transport-plus-ECPR bundle). POSSIBLE is the ceiling, and the shelf is Tier C for the developer's personal verdict.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote ARREST's 43% vs 7% without Prague beside it, and do not quote either trial as evidence about ECPR in systems without rapid transfer and an established ECPR programme.

shelves.title: Vasopressin plus methylprednisolone for in-hospital cardiac arrest (VAM)
shelves.question: In in-hospital cardiac arrest, does vasopressin plus methylprednisolone added to standard resuscitation improve return of spontaneous circulation — and does any ROSC gain translate into survival or good neurological outcome?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Agents/adverse effects,pharmacology · Confidence Intervals · Denmark · Epinephrine/administration & dosage · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacology · Heart Arrest · Hyperglycemia/epidemiology
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: the shelf carries a survival-to-discharge-with-good-neurology benefit claim from the Mentzelopoulos trial, a mortality-adjacent endpoint in the composite). On the process outcome both randomised trials agree: the vasopressin–steroid combination raises ROSC — VAM: 42% vs 33% (risk ratio 1.30); Mentzelopoulos VSE programme: ROSC ≥20 minutes 83.9% vs 65.9% (odds ratio 2.98) — LIKELY for ROSC. On survival the trials disagree: VAM found 30-day survival numerically lower with the combination (9.7% vs 12%; risk ratio 0.83, not significant) and identical favourable neurological outcome (7.6% vs 7.6%), while the smaller Greek programme found survival to discharge with CPC 1–2 of 13.9% vs 5.1% (odds ratio 3.28) — a single-trial claim, capped at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: VAM (Andersen 2021): vasopressin plus methylprednisolone raised ROSC (42% vs 33%) but 30-day survival was 9.7% vs 12% and neurological outcome identical
cards.summary: VAM 2021: vasopressin plus methylprednisolone raised ROSC ( 42% vs 33% ) but 30-day survival was 9.7% vs 12%.
cards.type: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (10 Danish hospitals)
cards.people: 501 analysed adults with in-hospital cardiac arrest (237 vasopressin + methylprednisolone, 264 placebo), of 512 randomised; mean age 71 years (SD 13); 322 (64%) were men.
cards.result: Return of spontaneous circulation occurred in 100 of 237 patients (42%) in the combination group vs 86 of 264 (33%) with placebo (risk ratio 1.30, 95% CI 1.03–1.63; risk difference 9.6%, 1.1% to 18.0%; P=.03) — a relative figure with absolute rates beside it. At 30 days, 23 patients (9.7%) in the intervention group and 31 (12%) in the placebo group were alive (risk ratio 0.83, 0.50–1.37; P=.48), and favourable neurological outcome (CPC 1–2) was identical at 18 (7.6%) vs 20 (7.6%) (risk ratio 1.00, 0.55–1.83). Among patients with ROSC, hyperglycaemia occurred in 77% vs 73% and hypernatraemia in 28% vs 31%.
cards.watchOut: The ROSC risk ratio of 1.30 sits inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, and the trial's own conclusion is that whether the treatment benefits or harms long-term survival is uncertain. ROSC is a process outcome, not survival.

cards.headline: Mentzelopoulos 2013: the vasopressin–steroid–epinephrine programme raised ROSC (83.9% vs 65.9%) and survival to discharge with good neurology (13.9% vs 5.1%)
cards.summary: Mentzelopoulos 2013: the vasopressin–steroid–epinephrine programme raised ROSC ( 83.9% vs 65.9% ) and survival to discharge with good neurology.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group trial (3 Greek tertiary centres)
cards.people: 268 consecutive patients with in-hospital cardiac arrest requiring epinephrine (130 vasopressin–steroid–epinephrine [VSE], 138 epinephrine + saline placebo). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: ROSC for 20 minutes or longer occurred in 109 of 130 patients (83.9%) in the VSE group vs 91 of 138 (65.9%) in controls (odds ratio 2.98, 95% CI 1.39–6.40; P=.005). Survival to hospital discharge with a CPC score of 1 or 2 occurred in 18 (13.9%) vs 7 (5.1%) (odds ratio 3.28, 1.17–9.20; P=.02) — relative figures with the absolute rates beside them. cards.summary: ROSC improves in both trials; the survival benefit rests on one smaller programme trial and was not reproduced — Split: LIKELY · POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: VAM (501 analysed patients, Denmark) and Mentzelopoulos 2013 (268 patients, Greece).
cards.result: Two double-blind trials agree the combination gets the heart restarted more often (42% vs 33%; 83.9% vs 65.9%). They do not agree that patients live longer or recover better: VAM's 30-day survival was 9.7% vs 12% with identical good-neurology rates, against Mentzelopoulos's 13.9% vs 5.1% discharge-with-good-neurology result from a programme that continued steroids after ROSC. Epinephrine in out-of-hospital arrest lives on Shelves #140 and #232 and is not re-carded here.

shelves.title: Mechanical versus manual chest compressions (PARAMEDIC, LINC)
shelves.question: Does a mechanical piston compression device improve survival or neurological outcome versus high-quality manual CPR in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
shelves.mesh: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation/methods · Cluster Analysis · Emergency Medical Services/methods · Emergency Medical Technicians · England · Heart Massage/methods · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: survival was the primary outcome in both trials, and both were null). PARAMEDIC (4,471 patients, LUCAS-2 vs manual CPR) found 30-day survival of 6% vs 7% (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64–1.15). LINC (2,589 patients, mechanical compressions with simultaneous defibrillation vs guideline manual CPR) found 4-hour survival of 23.6% vs 23.7% and no significant difference in survival with good neurological outcome at any point to 6 months (8.5% vs 7.6%). Two large concordant randomised nulls on survival carry LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): routine mechanical CPR does not improve survival over good manual CPR.

cards.headline: PARAMEDIC (Perkins 2015): LUCAS-2 mechanical CPR did not improve 30-day survival (6% vs 7%; adjusted odds ratio 0.86)
cards.summary: PARAMEDIC 2015: LUCAS-2 mechanical CPR did not improve 30-day survival ( 6% vs 7% ; adjusted odds ratio 0.86).
cards.type: Pragmatic, cluster-randomised, open-label trial (ambulance-station clusters, four UK ambulance services)
cards.people: 4,471 eligible adults with non-traumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (1,652 assigned to LUCAS-2, 2,819 to manual CPR); only 985 (60%) of the LUCAS-2 group actually received mechanical compression. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: 30-day survival was 104 of 1,652 patients (6%) in the LUCAS-2 group vs 193 of 2,819 (7%) with manual CPR (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.64–1.15) — a relative measure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside it, and not significant. No serious adverse events were noted; seven clinical adverse events were reported in the LUCAS-2 group (chest bruising, lacerations, blood in the mouth) and 15 device incidents occurred. The authors conclude that widespread adoption of mechanical CPR devices for routine use does not improve survival.
cards.watchOut: Pragmatic delivery diluted the contrast (40% of the device group never received the device), so the trial tests a deployment strategy; but that is the clinically relevant question for routine use, and its null agrees with LINC's cleaner delivery.
cards.source: Perkins GD et al. Mechanical versus manual chest compression for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (PARAMEDIC): a pragmatic, cluster randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2015;385(9972):947-955. PMID: 25467566. Registry ID: ISRCTN08233942, from the record's databank fields.

cards.headline: LINC (Rubertsson 2014): mechanical compressions with simultaneous defibrillation matched manual CPR on 4-hour survival (23.6% vs 23.7%) and on good-outcome survival to 6 months
cards.summary: LINC 2014: mechanical compressions matched manual CPR on 4-hour survival ( 23.6% vs 23.7% ) and on good-outcome survival.
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (six ambulance services in Sweden, the UK and the Netherlands)
cards.people: 2,589 patients with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (1,300 mechanical CPR, 1,289 manual CPR), followed to 6 months. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Four-hour survival was achieved by 307 patients (23.6%) with mechanical CPR and 305 (23.7%) with manual CPR (risk difference −0.05%, 95% CI −3.3% to 3.2%; P>.99). Among 6-month survivors, 99% in the mechanical group and 94% in the manual group had CPC scores of 1 or 2.
cards.watchOut: LINC tested a specific algorithm (LUCAS compressions plus defibrillation during ongoing compressions), not a device alone; niche uses — transport, cath-lab CPR, prolonged resuscitation — were not the trial's question and are not answered by its null.

cards.headline: Synthesis: two large trials, one answer — mechanical CPR does not beat good manual CPR on survival; LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C
cards.summary: Two large trials, one answer — mechanical CPR does not beat good manual CPR on survival — LIKELY the null, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: PARAMEDIC (4,471 patients) and LINC (2,589 patients) — over 7,000 randomised patients between them.
cards.result: Survival was the primary outcome in both trials and was null in both: 30-day survival 6% vs 7% (PARAMEDIC) and 4-hour survival 23.6% vs 23.7% with good-outcome survival to 6 months of 8.5% vs 7.6% (LINC). That is the pattern the LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) stamp exists for. cards.watchOut: The null covers routine use for survival. It does not rule on mechanical CPR where manual CPR is impossible or unsafe (moving vehicles, few rescuers, catheterisation during CPR).

shelves.title: Vasopressin versus epinephrine for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest
shelves.question: Does vasopressin beat, match, or lose to epinephrine as the first vasopressor in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest?
shelves.mesh: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Drug Therapy, Combination · Emergency Medical Services · Epinephrine/therapeutic use · Heart Arrest/drug therapy,mortality · Hospitalization · Multivariate Analysis
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: the shelf carries a survival-to-discharge benefit claim in the asystole subgroup of the Wenzel trial). Overall equivalence is LIKELY: two randomised head-to-head trials found no significant overall difference in survival to hospital discharge between vasopressin and epinephrine (Wenzel: no difference in VF or PEA admission rates; Ong: discharge survival 2.9% vs 2.3%, relative risk 1.72 with a confidence interval of 0.65–4.51, inside the caution band and not significant). The asystole advantage is MAYBE (weak evidence): it is a subgroup of one trial (admission 29.0% vs 20.3%; discharge 4.7% vs 1.5%), never the primary comparison, and subgroup survival claims in arrest trials have a poor replication record.

cards.headline: Wenzel 2004: vasopressin matched epinephrine overall, with higher admission and discharge rates only in the asystole subgroup (discharge 4.7% vs 1.5%)
cards.summary: Wenzel 2004: vasopressin matched epinephrine overall, with higher admission and discharge rates only in the asystole subgroup (discharge 4.7% vs 1.5% ).
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial (multicentre, European; double-blind drug administration)
cards.people: 1,186 analysed adults with out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (589 vasopressin, 597 epinephrine), of 1,219 randomised; patients received two injections of vasopressin 40 IU or epinephrine 1 mg, then open epinephrine if needed. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in survival to hospital admission in ventricular fibrillation (46.2% vs 43.0%; P=0.48) or pulseless electrical activity (33.7% vs 30.5%; P=0.65). In asystole, vasopressin was associated with higher admission (29.0% vs 20.3%; P=0.02) and discharge (4.7% vs 1.5%; P=0.04) rates. Among 732 patients not resuscitated by the two study injections, additional epinephrine improved admission (25.7% vs 16.4%; P=0.002) and discharge (6.2% vs 1.7%; P=0.002) in the vasopressin group but not the epinephrine group. Cerebral performance was similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: The asystole finding is a subgroup of a trial whose primary comparisons (admission in VF and PEA) were null, from an era of arrest care that predates modern post-ROSC management. Subgroup discharge rates of 4.7% vs 1.5% rest on small absolute numbers of survivors.

cards.headline: Ong 2012: vasopressin vs adrenaline in the emergency department — discharge survival 2.9% vs 2.3%, not significant; adjusted admission favoured vasopressin
cards.summary: Ong 2012: discharge survival 2.9% vs 2.3%, not significant.
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, multicentre, parallel-design trial (four adult hospitals, Singapore)
cards.people: 727 patients with cardiac arrest presenting to or in the emergency department (374 vasopressin, 353 adrenaline), aged over 16 (over 21 at one hospital); traumatic arrests excluded. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Survival to hospital discharge was 11 of 374 (2.9%) with vasopressin vs 8 of 353 (2.3%) with adrenaline (P=0.27; relative risk 1.72, 95% CI 0.65–4.51) — a relative figure inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band with a confidence interval spanning no-effect, printed with the absolute rates beside it. After adjustment, more vasopressin patients survived to admission (22.2% vs 16.7%; P=0.05; relative risk 1.43, 1.02–2.04). Subgroup analysis suggested improved outcomes with vasopressin in prolonged arrests. The authors conclude that combining vasopressin and adrenaline did not improve long-term survival.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen total survivors: the trial is far too small to settle a discharge-survival difference, and its admission outcome is adjustment-dependent. It tests ED-presenting arrests, a different setting from Wenzel's prehospital trial.

shelves.title: Oxygen therapy in suspected acute myocardial infarction (DETO2X)
shelves.question: In normoxaemic patients with suspected MI, does routine supplemental oxygen change death or rehospitalisation with MI at one year — and what did the smaller STEMI trial's infarct-size signal mean beside it?
shelves.mesh: Heart Diseases/diagnosis · Hospitalization · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Myocardial Infarction/diagnosis,mortality,therapy · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/adverse effects · Proportional Hazards Models · Registries
shelves.balance: Split, PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: all-cause mortality was DETO2X's primary outcome). LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) on benefit: DETO2X (6,629 patients, registry-based randomised trial) found 1-year mortality of 5.0% on routine oxygen vs 5.1% on ambient air (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.79–1.21) and no reduction in rehospitalisation with MI (3.8% vs 3.3%; hazard ratio 1.13) — a very large null that excludes a meaningful mortality benefit in normoxaemic suspected MI. POSSIBLE on harm: the smaller AVOID trial in confirmed STEMI found signals of greater myocardial injury with oxygen (higher peak creatine kinase, more recurrent MI, larger infarct size on 6-month MRI) on surrogate and secondary measures — enough to argue against routine oxygen, not enough to prove it harms.

cards.headline: DETO2X (Hofmann 2017): routine oxygen did not reduce 1-year mortality in suspected MI (5.0% vs 5.1%; hazard ratio 0.97)
cards.summary: DETO2X 2017: routine oxygen did not reduce 1-year mortality in suspected MI ( 5.0% vs 5.1% ; hazard ratio 0.97).
cards.type: Registry-based randomised clinical trial (nationwide Swedish registries; open-label oxygen vs ambient air)
cards.people: 6,629 patients with suspected myocardial infarction and oxygen saturation ≥90% (3,311 supplemental oxygen, 3,318 ambient air); oxygen was given at 6 L/min for 6–12 hours (median duration 11.6 hours). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Death from any cause within 1 year occurred in 166 of 3,311 patients (5.0%) assigned to oxygen vs 168 of 3,318 (5.1%) assigned to ambient air (hazard ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.21; P=0.80) — a relative measure, printed with the absolute rates beside it. Results were consistent across all predefined subgroups. Hypoxaemia developed in 1.9% of the oxygen group and 7.7% of the air group.

cards.headline: AVOID (Stub 2015): in confirmed STEMI, oxygen was associated with larger infarct injury — higher peak creatine kinase, more recurrent MI (5.5% vs 0.9%) and larger MRI infarct size at 6 months
cards.summary: AVOID 2015: in confirmed STEMI, oxygen was associated with larger infarct injury and more recurrent MI (5.5% vs 0.9%).
cards.type: Multicentre, prospective, randomised, controlled trial (prehospital, paramedic-diagnosed STEMI; oxygen 8 L/min vs no supplemental oxygen)
cards.people: 638 patients randomised with paramedic-diagnosed STEMI; 441 with confirmed STEMI underwent the primary end-point analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean peak troponin I was similar between oxygen and no-oxygen groups (57.4 vs 48.0 µg/L; ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.92–1.56; P=0.18). cards.headline: Synthesis: no mortality benefit from routine oxygen (LIKELY the null); a smaller trial's injury signals argue the same direction — Tier C
cards.summary: No mortality benefit from routine oxygen; the smaller trial's injury signals argue the same direction — Split: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) · POSSIBLE, Tier C, proposed only.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: DETO2X (6,629 patients, suspected MI, saturation ≥90%) and AVOID (441 analysed patients, confirmed STEMI).
cards.result: The two trials are complementary, not contradictory: the very large one shows routine oxygen does not save lives (mortality 5.0% vs 5.1% at 1 year) or prevent reinfarction admissions; the smaller, sicker one suggests oxygen may add myocardial injury (recurrent MI 5.5% vs 0.9%; larger 6-month MRI infarcts). Together they support treating oxygen as a drug for hypoxaemia, not a routine in normoxaemic MI. The benefit stamp is LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), the harm stamp POSSIBLE — both proposed, Tier C, pending the developer's verdict. Oxygen after stroke is a separate question on Shelf #1019.
cards.watchOut: Quote DETO2X for the mortality answer and AVOID only with its surrogate/secondary caveats attached; merging them into 'oxygen is harmful in MI' overstates AVOID.

shelves.title: A single dose of dexamethasone for acute sore throat (TOAST)
shelves.question: In adults presenting to primary care with acute sore throat not given immediate antibiotics, does one dose of oral dexamethasone speed complete symptom resolution at 24 and 48 hours?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage · Area Under Curve · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Drug Prescriptions/statistics & numerical data · Glucocorticoids/administration & dosage,adverse effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: TOAST (576 adults, double-blind) missed its primary outcome — complete resolution at 24 hours was 22.6% on dexamethasone vs 17.7% on placebo (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 0.92–1.78; P=.14) — but met the 48-hour outcome (35.4% vs 27.1%; relative risk 1.31, 1.02–1.68). The accompanying systematic review of 10 trials (1,426 participants) found single low-dose corticosteroids roughly doubled the chance of pain relief at 24 hours (relative risk 2.2, moderate-quality evidence) and brought complete pain resolution about 11 hours earlier (low-quality evidence). A real but modest, delayed symptom benefit from one trial plus a supportive pooling — with the primary outcome of the best trial null — is POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. This is symptom relief only; no claim about complications is made.

cards.headline: TOAST (Hayward 2017): single-dose dexamethasone did not raise complete resolution at 24 hours (22.6% vs 17.7%) but did at 48 hours (35.4% vs 27.1%)
cards.summary: TOAST 2017: single-dose dexamethasone did not raise complete resolution at 24 hours (22.6% vs 17.7%) but did at 48 hours ( 35.4% vs 27.1% ).
cards.type: Double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised trial (42 family practices in England; single 10 mg oral dose, no immediate antibiotics)
cards.people: 565 eligible randomised adults presenting the same day with acute sore throat not requiring immediate antibiotics (288 dexamethasone, 277 placebo), of 576 enrolled; median age 34 years (IQR 26.0–45.5); 75.2% were women.
cards.result: At 24 hours, complete resolution of symptoms occurred in 65 participants (22.6%) on dexamethasone vs 49 (17.7%) on placebo (risk difference 4.7%, 95% CI −1.8% to 11.2%; relative risk 1.28, 0.92 to 1.78; P=.14) — the primary outcome, not significant. At 48 hours, resolution occurred in 102 (35.4%) vs 75 (27.1%) (risk difference 8.7%, 1.2% to 16.2%; relative risk 1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; P=.03) — relative figures with absolute rates beside them. There were no significant differences in any other secondary outcomes, including duration of moderately bad symptoms, healthcare attendance or days missed from work.
cards.watchOut: A trial that misses its primary outcome and lands a secondary one earns a cautious reading: the honest claim is 'may speed resolution by the second day', not 'works at 24 hours'. Both relative risks sit inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band; the absolute gains are 5–9 percentage points.
cards.source: Hayward GN et al. Effect of Oral Dexamethasone Without Immediate Antibiotics vs Placebo on Acute Sore Throat in Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017;317(15):1535-1543. PMID: 28418482. Registry ID: ISRCTN17435450, as stated in the record's abstract.

cards.headline: Sadeghirad 2017: across 10 trials, single low-dose corticosteroids doubled 24-hour pain relief (relative risk 2.2) and resolved pain about 11 hours sooner
cards.summary: Sadeghirad 2017: across 10 trials, single low-dose corticosteroids doubled 24-hour pain relief (relative risk 2.2) and resolved pain about 11 hours sooner.
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (BMJ Rapid Recommendations)
cards.people: 10 eligible trials enrolling 1,426 individuals aged 5 years or older with acute tonsillitis, pharyngitis or sore throat in emergency-department and primary-care settings; the most common intervention was single-dose oral dexamethasone up to 10 mg. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Patients receiving corticosteroids were twice as likely to experience pain relief at 24 hours (relative risk 2.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 4.3; risk difference 12.4%; moderate-quality evidence) and 1.5 times more likely to have no pain at 48 hours (relative risk 1.5, 1.3 to 1.8; risk difference 18.3%; high-quality evidence) — relative figures with absolute differences beside them. Mean time to onset of pain relief was 4.8 hours earlier and mean time to complete pain resolution 11.1 hours earlier (low-quality evidence). Nine trials sought adverse events; the few reported were mostly disease complications, with similar incidence in both groups.
cards.watchOut: The pooling mixes settings, ages and steroid regimens, its 24-hour relative risk of 2.2 rests on moderate-quality evidence with a wide interval, and TOAST — the largest primary-care trial — was itself null at 24 hours. Risks of repeated dosing in recurrent sore throat were not assessed by the included trials.
cards.source: Sadeghirad B et al. Corticosteroids for treatment of sore throat: systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials. BMJ. 2017;358:j3887. PMID: 28931508. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — this is a systematic review; its PROSPERO registration (CRD42017067808) is stated in its abstract.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one dose of steroid probably shortens a sore throat by hours, with the clearest gain at 48 hours — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: One dose of steroid probably shortens a sore throat by hours, with the clearest gain at 48 hours — POSSIBLE.
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: TOAST (565 analysed adults, primary care) and Sadeghirad 2017 (10 trials, 1,426 participants).
cards.result: The trial and the pooling tell one consistent, modest story: no proven benefit at 24 hours in the best trial (22.6% vs 17.7%, not significant), a significant gain by 48 hours (35.4% vs 27.1%), and pooled estimates of pain resolution brought forward by roughly 11 hours. That is a symptom-relief option for a miserable two days — not an antibiotic substitute proven against complications, and not a claim about any other steroid use. Dexamethasone for croup lives on Shelf #239 and is a different condition and airway question.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the pooled relative risk of 2.2 for 24-hour relief without TOAST's null 24-hour primary beside it.

shelves.title: Drug route in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: intraosseous first vs intravenous first (PARAMEDIC-3, IVIO)
shelves.question: In out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, does an intraosseous-first vascular-access strategy improve survival at 30 days versus an intravenous-first strategy — and how does the Danish IVIO trial read beside it?
shelves.mesh: Emergency Medical Services · Epinephrine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Infusions, Intraosseous/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data · Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest/drug therapy,mortality · Return of Spontaneous Circulation/drug effects · United Kingdom · Injections, Intravenous/adverse effects,statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C ruled YES at build: 30-day survival was PARAMEDIC-3's primary outcome, and both trials were null on survival). Two large randomised trials agree: PARAMEDIC-3 (6,082 patients, UK) found 30-day survival of 4.5% with intraosseous-first vs 5.1% with intravenous-first access (adjusted odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.68–1.32), with return of spontaneous circulation actually lower in the intraosseous group (36.0% vs 39.1%; adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 0.76–0.97); IVIO (1,479 analysed patients, Denmark) found sustained ROSC of 30% vs 29% (risk ratio 1.06) and 30-day survival of 12% vs 10% (risk ratio 1.16, CI crossing 1), and its long-term follow-up found 1-year survival of 11% vs 9% (risk ratio 1.24, CI crossing 1). Faster, easier access (92% vs 80% success within two attempts in IVIO) did not buy survival.

cards.headline: PARAMEDIC-3 (Couper 2025): intraosseous-first access did not improve 30-day survival (4.5% vs 5.1%) and gave less ROSC than intravenous-first
cards.summary: PARAMEDIC-3 2025: intraosseous-first access did not improve 30-day survival ( 4.5% vs 5.1% ) and gave less ROSC than intravenous-first.
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label randomised trial (11 emergency medical systems, UK)
cards.people: 6,082 adults in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest requiring vascular access for drug administration (3,040 intraosseous-first, 3,042 intravenous-first). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At 30 days, 137 of 3,030 patients (4.5%) in the intraosseous group and 155 of 3,034 (5.1%) in the intravenous group were alive (adjusted odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.32; P=0.74). Favourable neurological outcome at hospital discharge occurred in 80 of 2,994 (2.7%) vs 85 of 2,986 (2.8%) (adjusted odds ratio 0.91, 0.57 to 1.47). Return of spontaneous circulation at any time occurred in 1,092 of 3,031 (36.0%) vs 1,186 of 3,035 (39.1%) (adjusted odds ratio 0.86, 0.76 to 0.97) — significantly lower with intraosseous-first. One adverse event, in the intraosseous group, was reported.
cards.watchOut: Open-label strategy trial: it compares 'try IO first' with 'try IV first' as systems actually practise them, including crossovers after failed attempts; it does not test IO access after failed IV, which remains standard rescue practice.

cards.headline: IVIO (Vallentin 2025): intraosseous vs intravenous access — sustained ROSC 30% vs 29%, 30-day survival 12% vs 10%, neither significant, despite faster successful access with IO
cards.summary: IVIO 2025: sustained ROSC 30% vs 29% and 30-day survival 12% vs 10% — neither significant, despite faster access.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (Denmark; unblindable by nature)
cards.people: 1,479 adults with nontraumatic out-of-hospital cardiac arrest included in the primary analysis (731 intraosseous, 748 intravenous), of 1,506 randomised. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Vascular access was established within two attempts in 669 patients (92%) assigned to intraosseous access vs 595 (80%) assigned to intravenous access. Sustained return of spontaneous circulation occurred in 221 (30%) vs 214 (29%) (risk ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.24; P=0.49). At 30 days, 85 (12%) vs 75 (10%) were alive (risk ratio 1.16, 0.87 to 1.56) and a favourable neurological outcome occurred in 67 (9%) vs 59 (8%) (risk ratio 1.16, 0.83 to 1.62) — relative figures inside the 0.5–2.0 caution band, with absolute rates beside them. Prespecified adverse events were uncommon.
cards.watchOut: Smaller than PARAMEDIC-3 and with wider intervals; its survival point estimate leans the opposite way from PARAMEDIC-3's, which is what two trials of a truly null contrast are expected to do. Neither trial shows the access-speed advantage converting into survival.

shelves.title: Routine low-dose oxygen after acute stroke: the Stroke Oxygen Study (SO2S)
shelves.question: In adults with acute stroke who are not hypoxaemic, does routine low-dose oxygen supplementation for the first three days reduce death or disability at 90 days?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Disability Evaluation · Hypoxia/etiology,therapy · Logistic Models · Oxygen/administration & dosage · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy/adverse effects · Stroke/complications,mortality,therapy
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: death or disability at 90 days was the primary outcome). SO2S randomised 8,003 non-hypoxaemic adults with acute stroke to continuous oxygen for 72 hours, nocturnal oxygen for 3 nights, or control (oxygen only if clinically indicated): the common odds ratio for a better 90-day modified Rankin outcome was 0.97 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.05; P=.47) for oxygen vs control and 1.03 (0.93 to 1.13) for continuous vs nocturnal oxygen, and no subgroup benefited. A single trial, but a very large, well-conducted one whose interval excludes the prespecified 1-point clinically important difference in the favourable direction: under the library's rule for very large single null trials, the null carries LIKELY. No confirmatory or contradicting large trial exists; the currency sweep found none.

cards.headline: SO2S (Roffe 2017): routine low-dose oxygen after acute stroke did not reduce death or disability at 90 days (common odds ratio 0.97)
cards.summary: SO2S 2017: routine low-dose oxygen after acute stroke did not reduce death or disability at 90 days (common odds ratio 0.97 ).
cards.type: Single-blind randomised clinical trial (136 UK centres; 1:1:1 continuous oxygen vs nocturnal oxygen vs control)
cards.people: 8,003 adults with acute stroke enrolled within 24 hours of admission who had no clear indication for or against oxygen (2,668 continuous oxygen, 2,667 nocturnal oxygen, 2,668 control); mean age 72 years (SD 13); 4,398 (55%) were men; median NIH Stroke Scale score 5; mean baseline oxygen saturation 96.6%. The primary outcome was available for 7,677 (96%).
cards.result: The unadjusted common odds ratio for a better 90-day modified Rankin Scale outcome was 0.97 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.05; P=.47) for oxygen vs control, and 1.03 (0.93 to 1.13; P=.61) for continuous vs nocturnal oxygen — relative (ordinal) measures; an odds ratio above 1.00 would have indicated improvement, and none was found in any subgroup. At least one serious adverse event occurred in 13.0% of the continuous group, 11.0% of the nocturnal group and 12.1% of controls; no significant harms were identified.
