shelves.title: Defibrillators where the public can reach them: the Public Access Defibrillation trial
shelves.question: Does training and equipping lay community volunteers to use automated external defibrillators, alongside CPR, increase survival to discharge after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest versus CPR alone?
shelves.mesh: Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation · Commerce · Electric Countershock · Emergency Medical Services · Heart Arrest/mortality,therapy · Hospitalization · Housing
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, because the headline outcome is survival after cardiac arrest): In the single pivotal community trial (PAD; 993 community units, more than 19,000 lay volunteers, 24 North American regions), units assigned to CPR-plus-AED volunteers had more survivors to hospital discharge than CPR-only units — 30 survivors among 128 arrests versus 15 among 107 (relative risk 2.0, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.77; P=0.03 — a relative figure at the boundary of the caution band, absolute counts beside it). The effect was concentrated in public locations: only 2 survivors were in residential complexes. No inappropriate shocks were delivered, and functional status at discharge did not differ. One trial with 45 total survivors caps the stamp at POSSIBLE, and no confirmatory randomised trial was pinned at build — searches returned the PAD trial, its design and implementation reports, and reviews only.

cards.headline: PAD Trial (Hallstrom 2004): survival to discharge 30 of 128 arrests with CPR-plus-AED volunteers versus 15 of 107 with CPR alone (relative risk 2.0)
cards.summary: PAD Trial (2004): survival to discharge 30 of 128 arrests with CPR-plus-AED volunteers vs 15 of 107 with CPR alone (RR 2.0 relative).
cards.type: Prospective, community-based, multicentre clinical trial (community units randomised to a structured responder system)
cards.people: 993 community units (such as shopping malls and apartment complexes) in 24 North American regions, with more than 19,000 lay volunteer responders trained in CPR alone or CPR plus automated external defibrillator use; patients with treated out-of-hospital cardiac arrest were similar between groups (mean age 69.8 years; 67% men; 70% arrested in a public location; 72% witnessed).
cards.result: Survivors to hospital discharge numbered 30 among 128 arrests in CPR-plus-AED units versus 15 among 107 in CPR-only units (P=0.03; relative risk 2.0, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.77 — a relative figure, absolute counts beside it; survival proportions 23.4% versus 14.0%). Only 2 survivors were in residential complexes. No inappropriate shocks were delivered, and functional status at hospital discharge did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty-five survivors in total decide this question — the confidence interval (1.07 to 3.77) is wide, the relative risk sits exactly at the 2.0 floor the library sets for solid observational-grade evidence, and the benefit is a public-location benefit; homes, where most arrests occur, contributed almost nothing. 2004-era response systems predate modern dispatcher-assisted CPR. Tier C proposed. No registry ID in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial).

shelves.title: Suicide prevention as an emergency-department system: ED-SAFE 2
shelves.question: Does an emergency-department process-improvement package — universal suicide screening, collaborative safety planning, and structured quality improvement — reduce suicide attempts and deaths in the following months versus care as usual?
shelves.mesh: Suicide · Suicidal Ideation · Suicide Prevention · Emergency Service, Hospital · Emergency Service, Hospital/organization & administration · Feasibility Studies · Interrupted Time Series Analysis
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, ruled at build: the composite outcome includes suicide death, which was rare in the trial — 9 deaths among 2,761 encounters — so no mortality-benefit claim is made beyond what the composite showed): In ED-SAFE 2 (stepped-wedge cluster-randomised trial, 8 US emergency departments), the composite of suicide death or suicide-related acute care visits over 6 months fell from 21% of encounters at baseline to 15.3% in the maintenance phase (adjusted odds ratio 0.57 versus baseline, 0.61 versus implementation — relative figures). The programme predecessor (original ED-SAFE screening study) had already shown universal screening was feasible and nearly doubled risk detection (2.9% to 5.7%). One randomised trial of a system package, with an effect concentrated in the maintenance phase, earns POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: ED-SAFE 2 (Boudreaux 2023): the suicide composite fell from 21% at baseline to 15.3% in the maintenance phase (relative adjusted odds ratio 0.57)
cards.summary: ED-SAFE 2 (2023): the suicide composite fell from 21% at baseline to 15.3% in the maintenance phase (adjusted OR relative) — the composite contains only 9 suicide deaths, printed on the card so it cannot be quoted as a mortality reduction.
cards.type: Stepped-wedge cluster randomised clinical trial (8 US emergency departments; interrupted time series across baseline, implementation and maintenance phases)
cards.people: 2,761 patient encounters in the primary analysis — a random sample of adults (18+) who screened positive on the Patient Safety Screener and were discharged from the ED, drawn from care between January 2014 and April 2018; 50.4% male; mean (SD) age 37.4 (14.5) years. Sites received lean training, built quality-improvement teams, and were coached to increase universal screening and implement collaborative safety planning for discharged at-risk patients.
cards.result: The primary composite (death by suicide or a suicide-related acute health care visit within 6 months) occurred in 546 patients (19.8%) overall — comprising 9 deaths by suicide (0.3%) and 538 (19.5%) with a suicide-related acute visit; some patients had both. By phase: baseline 216 of 1,030 (21%), implementation 213 of 967 (22%), maintenance 117 of 764 (15.3%) (P=.001). Adjusted odds ratios for the maintenance phase were 0.57 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.74) versus baseline and 0.61 (0.46 to 0.79) versus implementation — relative figures, absolute rates beside them. The benefit appeared in maintenance, not during implementation itself.
cards.watchOut: A composite driven almost entirely by return visits (538) rather than deaths (9) — it must never be quoted as a suicide-death reduction. Stepped-wedge phase comparisons carry secular-trend risk, and the implementation phase itself was flat (22%), so the causal story rests on the maintenance contrast. Tier C proposed.
cards.source: Boudreaux ED et al. Effect of an Emergency Department Process Improvement Package on Suicide Prevention: The ED-SAFE 2 Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Psychiatry. 2023;80(7):665-674. PMID: 37195676. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02453243.

cards.summary: Original ED-SAFE screening study (2016): universal screening was feasible and detection rose from 2.9% to 5.7% of ED visits (the predecessor is carded honestly as a non-randomised interrupted time series).
cards.type: Three-phase interrupted time series study (8 emergency departments in seven US states, 2009–2014) — programme predecessor report, not a randomised trial
cards.people: 236,791 ED visit records across three phases (treatment as usual; universal screening; universal screening plus intervention), with chart reviews for documented screening and detection of intentional self-harm ideation or behaviour, and patient interviews to confirm suicidality.
cards.result: Documented screening rose from 26% of visits in phase 1 to 84% in phase 3 (p<0.001), and detection of intentional self-harm rose from 2.9% to 5.7% (p<0.001) — nearly twofold. The majority of detected intentional self-harm was confirmed as recent suicidal ideation or behaviour by patient interview. The authors conclude universal screening in the ED is feasible and that identification is the necessary first step for prevention.
cards.watchOut: A detection study: it shows screening finds risk, not that finding risk prevents attempts — that outcome claim belongs to ED-SAFE 2 alone. Carded as programme background for the shelf's logic chain, labelled as a non-randomised predecessor.

shelves.title: Rewarming is not enough for deep frostbite: iloprost and thrombolysis (the Cauchy trial)
shelves.question: After rapid rewarming of severe frostbite, does adding a prostacyclin (iloprost), thrombolysis, or both reduce amputation compared with older vasodilator-based care?
shelves.mesh: Iloprost · Cohort Studies
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: the primary outcome is amputation, a major-harm outcome). The only randomised trial ever run on medical therapy for severe frostbite, Cauchy 2011, was published by the New England Journal of Medicine as correspondence: its PubMed record (PMID 21226604) carries publication types 'Letter; Randomized Controlled Trial' and contains NO abstract in PubMed or in Europe PMC, so under this library's gate no figure from it can be carded and it is NOT carded here as a trial report — it is fenced in the synthesis, exactly as earlier letter-format records were rejected or fenced rather than silently carded. What can be carded is the 2023 systematic review of 71 reports (978 cases, only one RCT among them), which reports that the single RCT found iloprost beneficial in severe frostbite given within 48 hours and that its meta-analyses of non-randomised data favoured thrombolytics given within 24 hours. That is hypothesis-grade evidence resting on one abstract-less trial report and observational series: MAYBE (weak evidence).

cards.headline: Regli 2023: across 71 frostbite reports (978 cases) there is exactly one randomised trial — and it found iloprost beneficial within 48 hours
cards.summary: Regli (2023): across 71 frostbite reports (978 cases) there is exactly one randomised trial — and its data reach this shelf only through this review.
cards.people: 71 included articles with 978 cases of grade 2 to 4 frostbite, drawn from 1 randomised controlled trial, 20 cohort studies and 51 case reports, from searches of PubMed, Cochrane Trials and Embase, 1900 to 18 June 2022; the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Both meta-analyses the reviewers could run (on non-randomised data) found that patients treated with thrombolytics within 24 hours had better outcomes than patients treated with other modalities. The one randomised controlled trial found that the prostacyclin analogue iloprost was beneficial in severe frostbite if administered within 48 hours. The reviewers conclude iloprost and thrombolysis may be beneficial, that the effectiveness of other commonly used treatments has not been validated, and that more prospective trial or registry data are needed. No pooled amputation rates are given in the abstract, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: A systematic review whose randomised content is a single trial it can only summarise in words: the thrombolysis signal comes from cohort studies and case reports, where treatment-by-indication confounding is expected, and 'better outcomes' in the abstract carries no carded effect size.
cards.source: Regli IB, Oberhammer R, Zafren K et al. Frostbite treatment: a systematic review with meta-analyses. Scand J Trauma Resusc Emerg Med. 2023;31(1):96. PMID: 38072923. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — the review's abstract states PROSPERO registration Nr. 293693.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the Cauchy trial is FENCED, not carded — a letter-format report with no abstract, so no figure from it appears on this shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Cauchy trial is FENCED, not carded — its report is a letter-format record with no abstract in PubMed or Europe PMC, so no figure from it appears on this shelf — MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C: amputation is the primary outcome).
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above and of the fenced record: Cauchy E et al., 'A controlled trial of a prostacyclin and rt-PA in the treatment of severe frostbite', N Engl J Med. 2011;364(2) — PMID 21226604 (publication types: Letter; Randomized Controlled Trial; no abstract in PubMed or Europe PMC, both checked at build).
cards.result: Handling, stated plainly: the Cauchy record is the primary report of the only randomised frostbite-therapy trial (iloprost, rt-PA, both, or buflomedil-based care after rewarming), but the journal published it in correspondence format and neither database carries its abstract, so this library's rule — never card a record whose abstract has not been seen, and never print a figure that is not in the fetched abstract — excludes it as a card. It is therefore fenced here, not rejected as irrelevant and not silently carded: the shelf's only carded evidence is the Regli 2023 review's one-sentence summary that the trial found iloprost beneficial within 48 hours. No amputation rate, risk ratio or subgroup figure from Cauchy is printed anywhere on this shelf. A build-time search for a second randomised frostbite-therapy report found none, so the companion anchor remains unpinned and the shelf stands on the review alone: MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C proposed.

shelves.title: Dexamethasone for mountain sickness when acetazolamide is not enough, or not tolerated (Hackett)
shelves.question: Does dexamethasone prevent and treat acute mountain sickness, and how should a drug that masks the syndrome without acclimatising the traveller be fenced?
shelves.mesh: Altitude Sickness/drug therapy,physiopathology,prevention & control · Dexamethasone/therapeutic use · Hypoxia/drug therapy · Acute Disease · Altitude Sickness/drug therapy,physiopathology · Body Water/metabolism · Brain Edema/diagnostic imaging
shelves.balance: Split: MAYBE (weak evidence) — prevention · POSSIBLE — treatment. The evidence is two small, old reports. In Hackett's Denali field trial, dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 hours did NOT prevent AMS in soldiers flown to 4,400 m (the whole placebo group and 5 of 7 on dexamethasone became ill within 5 hours), so the prevention claim at that dose is MAYBE (weak evidence) and leans null. For treatment, Hackett's open treatment phase (11 men with moderate-to-severe AMS) improved markedly on 4 mg every 6 hours (symptom score 4.5 to 1.0 at 12 hours) with symptoms recurring after abrupt discontinuation (2.4), and Levine's randomised double-blind crossover chamber study (6 men) found dexamethasone reduced symptoms by 63% versus 23% on placebo — real but tiny numbers, capping treatment at POSSIBLE. The fence stands regardless of stamp: dexamethasone suppresses symptoms without acclimatisation, so it is a rescue-and-descent adjunct, never a substitute for going down. Acetazolamide prophylaxis is Shelf #1210; dexamethasone's HAPE-prophylaxis arm sits on Shelf #1211.

cards.headline: Hackett 1988: dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 hours did not prevent AMS on Denali; 4 mg every 6 hours treated it, and symptoms recurred when it stopped
cards.summary: Hackett (1988): dexamethasone 2 mg every 6 hours did not prevent AMS on Denali; 4 mg every 6 hours treated it, and symptoms recurred when it stopped.
cards.type: Field study: randomised, double-blind prevention trial, with an open treatment phase
cards.people: Prevention: 15 subjects flown by helicopter from sea level to 4,400 m on Denali, randomised to placebo (8) or dexamethasone 2 mg orally every 6 hours from 1 hour before take-off (7). Treatment: 11 of those with moderate-to-severe AMS (symptom score 4.5±0.7, range 3 to 11) received dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours, orally or intramuscularly, for 24 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Prevention: the entire placebo group and five of the dexamethasone group developed AMS within 5 hours and became progressively more ill until the trial was terminated at 12 hours — the authors conclude 2 mg every 6 hours did not prevent AMS in this rapid-ascent model. Treatment: all 11 were markedly improved at 12 hours (symptom score 1.0±0.3; P<0.001; range 0 to 3), but symptoms increased after the drug was discontinued at 24 hours (score 2.4±0.5).
cards.watchOut: The treatment phase had no control group — improvement on treatment is confounded by natural history and by the prevention phase's termination; and the prevention null is one dose (2 mg) in 15 subjects under helicopter ascent, an extreme profile few travellers match.
cards.source: Hackett PH, Roach RC, Wood RA et al. Dexamethasone for prevention and treatment of acute mountain sickness. Aviat Space Environ Med. 1988;59(10):950-4. PMID: 3190622. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Levine 1989: in a 6-man chamber crossover, dexamethasone reduced AMS symptoms by 63% versus 23% on placebo
cards.summary: Levine (1989): in a 6-man chamber crossover, dexamethasone reduced AMS symptoms by 63% vs 23% on placebo.
cards.people: 6 men exposed in a hypobaric chamber to a simulated altitude of 3,700 m for 48 hours on two occasions; once AMS was diagnosed by symptoms questionnaire, dexamethasone 4 mg every six hours or placebo was given in randomised crossover fashion. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Dexamethasone reduced the symptoms of acute mountain sickness by 63% (P<0.05), whereas placebo had a minimal effect (reduction by 23%; P not significant). Despite the response, one subject had mild cerebral oedema on brain CT after both placebo and dexamethasone periods.
cards.watchOut: Six subjects in a chamber: this is proof-of-mechanism, not a field trial — and the cerebral-oedema case on both treatments is the standing warning that symptom relief is not the same as the disease being controlled.
cards.source: Levine BD, Yoshimura K, Kobayashi T et al. Dexamethasone in the treatment of acute mountain sickness. N Engl J Med. 1989;321(25):1707-13. PMID: 2687688. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial. Pinned at build by exact-title search (the topic file carried this programme as 'PMID to pin at build').

shelves.title: Blunting the burn's hypermetabolism with propranolol: the Galveston children's programme
shelves.question: Does long-term propranolol reduce cardiac work and preserve lean mass in severely burned children, and did the programme's safety analysis find a cost in inflammation or infection?
shelves.mesh: Adrenergic beta-Antagonists/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Body Composition/drug effects · Burns/drug therapy,mortality · Calorimetry, Indirect · Drug Administration Schedule · Energy Metabolism/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C: mortality is tracked and reported across this single programme's reports in a population where burns kill — 6% control versus 5% propranolol in the safety analysis, printed on its card — and any shelf carrying mortality figures from one centre's programme takes the developer's eye; no survival benefit is claimed). The randomised efficacy report (Herndon 2012, 179 children with >30% TBSA burns, propranolol 4 mg/kg/day for 12 months) found significantly reduced predicted heart rate and resting energy expenditure, less central mass and fat accumulation, prevented bone loss and improved lean-body-mass accretion, with very few adverse effects. The programme's prospective safety analysis (Jeschke 2007, 245 children) found no increase in infection (21% vs 30%), sepsis (7% vs 10%) or mortality, with resting energy expenditure significantly decreased. One centre, one programme, surrogate and body-composition endpoints: POSSIBLE. The opposite pharmacological direction against the same catabolic state — oxandrolone — is Shelf #1227.

cards.headline: Herndon 2012: a year of propranolol reduced cardiac work and resting energy expenditure and improved lean mass in 179 burned children
cards.summary: Herndon (2012): a year of propranolol reduced cardiac work and resting energy expenditure and improved lean mass in 179 burned children.
cards.people: 179 paediatric patients with burns over more than 30% of total body surface area, randomised to control (89) or propranolol 4 mg/kg/day (90) for 12 months postburn, with resting energy expenditure, cardiac function and body composition measured acutely and at 3, 6, 9 and 12 months. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Long-term propranolol significantly reduced the percentage of predicted heart rate and the percentage of predicted resting energy expenditure, decreased accumulation of central mass and central fat, prevented bone loss, and improved lean body mass accretion (analyses adjusted for non-normality and repeated measures; P<0.05 threshold — the abstract reports significance without effect sizes, and none are printed here). There were very few adverse effects at the dose used. The abstract reports no mortality figures; mortality for the programme appears on the safety card below.
cards.watchOut: Significance-without-magnitude reporting: the card cannot say how large the cardiac or lean-mass benefits are, and a single-centre programme that also delivers the burn care cannot separate the drug from the centre's overall results.

cards.result: Mortality — printed because this programme tracks it and the developer reviews mortality figures personally: 6% in the control group and 5% in the propranolol group (no significant difference claimed, and no survival benefit is claimed on this shelf). shelves.title: Oxandrolone to keep the burned child's muscle: the Wolf trial
shelves.question: Does oxandrolone improve net protein balance, lean mass and long-term bone outcomes in severely burned children versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Amino Acids/biosynthesis · Anabolic Agents/pharmacology,therapeutic use · Body Composition/drug effects · Burns/physiopathology,therapy · Food Additives/therapeutic use · Food, Formulated · Gene Expression/drug effects
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: Two randomised reports from the same single-centre programme support benefit on body-composition and bone surrogates, and no carded trial shows a survival or functional benefit. Wolf 2003 (32 severely burned children) found oxandrolone improved net protein balance over one week while placebo did not change, preserved body weight and fat-free mass that placebo lost, and shifted muscle gene expression toward functional muscle proteins. The programme's 5-year randomised trial (Reeves/Herndon 2016; oxandrolone for up to 24 months) found significantly greater whole-body and lumbar-spine bone mineral content, higher adjusted lumbar BMD, fewer children meeting paediatric osteoporosis criteria and greater height velocity, with no attributed adverse effects. Surrogate and growth endpoints from one centre: POSSIBLE. Beta-BLOCKADE against the same catabolic state is Shelf #1226 — the opposite pharmacological direction, cross-referenced, not re-carded.

cards.headline: Wolf 2003: oxandrolone improved net protein balance within a week; placebo children lost weight and fat-free mass, oxandrolone children did not
cards.summary: Wolf (2003): oxandrolone improved net protein balance within a week; placebo children lost weight and fat-free mass, oxandrolone children did not.
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (placebo-controlled, with muscle biopsy gene-expression substudy)
cards.people: 32 severely burned children; after baseline protein-balance studies 5 days after the first excision and grafting procedure, randomised to placebo (18) or oxandrolone 0.1 mg/kg twice daily (14), with repeat balance studies 1 week later; muscle biopsies in the oxandrolone group examined 12,600 genes. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Protein net balance did not change in the placebo group, while oxandrolone-treated subjects had a significant improvement. Body weight and fat-free mass significantly decreased in the placebo group, with no changes in the oxandrolone group. Expression changed in 14 genes versus placebo, including myosin light chain (+2.7-fold), tubulin (+2.3), calmodulin (−2.3) and protein phosphatase I inhibitor (−2.8). The abstract reports significance and fold-changes rather than absolute balance values, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-two children and a 1-week metabolic endpoint: net protein balance is a surrogate, and this trial cannot speak to strength, function, wound outcomes or survival — claims it does not make and this shelf does not borrow.

cards.headline: Reeves/Herndon 2016: oxandrolone for up to 2 years raised bone mineral content and density and height velocity out to 5 years postburn
cards.summary: Reeves/Herndon (2016): oxandrolone for up to 2 years raised bone mineral content and density and height velocity out to 5 years post-burn.
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, single-centre, intention-to-treat, with 5-year prospective follow-up
cards.people: Children aged 0 to 18 years with burns over ≥30% of total body surface area, randomised to placebo (84) or oxandrolone 0.1 mg/kg orally twice daily for 24 months (35), followed annually to 5 years postburn for height, weight, bone mineral content (BMC) and density (BMD). Actual oxandrolone exposure averaged 16±1 months (range 12.1 to 25.2). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Long-term oxandrolone significantly increased whole-body BMC (P<0.02) and lumbar-spine BMC (P<0.05), with effects most pronounced in growth-spurt years (7-18); height-, sex- and age-adjusted lumbar-spine BMD increased significantly (P<0.0009). Fewer oxandrolone patients had lumbar BMD z scores below −2.0 (the paediatric osteoporosis threshold). Height velocity was significantly greater than controls throughout the first 2 years (P<0.05). No adverse side effects were attributed to long-term oxandrolone. Compared with the programme's earlier 12-month administration, 24-month administration gave significantly greater increases in whole-body BMC, whole-body BMD and lumbar BMD (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: Unequal arms (84 placebo vs 35 oxandrolone) and a single centre again: the bone endpoints are densitometry, not fractures prevented — 'reduced risk for future fracture' is the authors' inference from z scores, printed here as inference, not as a fracture outcome.
cards.source: Reeves PT, Herndon DN, Tanksley JD et al. Five-year outcomes after long-term oxandrolone administration in severely burned children: a randomized clinical trial. Shock. 2016;45(4):367-74. PMID: 26506070. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Cutting the burn off early: early excision versus conservative care (Herndon 1989)
shelves.question: Does early tangential excision and grafting beat conservative care with late grafting in severely burned patients — including Herndon 1989's subgroup mortality report, and a 2026 randomised replication of the hospital-stay question?
shelves.mesh: Age Factors · Anti-Infective Agents, Local/therapeutic use · Burns/complications,mortality,surgery · Burns, Inhalation/mortality,therapy · Combined Modality Therapy · Debridement · Infections/etiology
shelves.balance: Split: POSSIBLE — shorter hospital stay · MAYBE (weak evidence) — mortality benefit (subgroup only) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C firm: this shelf carries a mortality report). Herndon 1989 (85 adults with >30% TBSA burns, randomised) found mortality without inhalation injury significantly lower with early excision in patients aged 17 to 30 (9% vs 45%; P<0.025) — a subgroup of a small, old trial, with no mortality difference demonstrable over age 30 or with inhalation injury, and a separate paediatric series in the same report in which mortality rose with burn size and inhalation injury. A subgroup mortality finding from 1989 is MAYBE (weak evidence) by this library's rules and is printed only as a subgroup, on the card and here. The modern, modest claim is better supported: survivors' hospital stay was under one day per percent TBSA in Herndon's series, and the 2026 North India RCT (36 adults) found early excision halved median stay (13.5 vs 28.5 days; P=0.009) with no significant difference in organ dysfunction, transfusion or mortality — POSSIBLE for the stay benefit, and a second randomised 'no mortality difference' datapoint that further fences the 1989 subgroup claim.

cards.headline: Herndon 1989: early excision cut mortality from 45% to 9% — only in the 17-to-30, no-inhalation-injury subgroup (SUBGROUP finding)
cards.summary: Herndon (1989): early excision cut mortality from 45% to 9% — only in the 17-to-30, no-inhalation-injury SUBGROUP , labelled as a subgroup finding on the headline, card and balance.
cards.type: Randomised comparison (early excision versus topical antimicrobial therapy with grafting after spontaneous eschar separation), with a paediatric case series in the same report
cards.people: 85 patients aged 17 to 55 years with burns over more than 30% of total body surface area, randomly assigned to early excision or conservative care. The same report describes 259 children with similar large burns treated by early excision (a series, not a randomised comparison). The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: SUBGROUP RESULT, labelled as such: mortality from burns WITHOUT inhalation injury was significantly decreased by early excision, from 45% to 9%, in patients aged 17 to 30 years (P<0.025). No mortality difference could be demonstrated in patients older than 30 or with concomitant inhalation injury. In the children treated by early excision, mortality increased significantly with increasing burn size and with concomitant inhalation injury (P<0.05). Survivors' mean hospital stay was less than one day per percent TBSA burn in both children and adults. No overall (all-patient) mortality rates are given in the abstract, and none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's Tier C core: a 1989 trial of 85 adults whose survival claim lives entirely inside one age-and-injury subgroup, from an era of burn care (topical antimicrobials, late grafting after eschar separation) that no modern unit replicates — the subgroup's 45%-to-9% contrast must never be quoted as the trial's overall result.
cards.source: Herndon DN, Barrow RE, Rutan RL et al. A comparison of conservative versus early excision. Therapies in severely burned patients. Ann Surg. 1989;209(5):547-52. PMID: 2650643. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields — pre-registration-era trial.

cards.headline: Kakani 2026: early excision halved hospital stay in a North India RCT (13.5 vs 28.5 days) — with no mortality difference
cards.summary: Kakani (2026): early excision halved hospital stay in a North India RCT ( 13.5 vs 28.5 days ) — with no mortality difference (found via Europe PMC after PubMed's dated sweep missed it; disclosed in the sweep field).
cards.type: Prospective, parallel-group, superiority randomised controlled trial (1:1)
cards.people: 36 adults aged 18 to 60 years with 10-40% TBSA deep second- or third-degree burns at a tertiary centre in North India (April 2024 to September 2025), randomised to early excision (≤7 days post-burn; median actual 4.5 days) or delayed excision (median 30.5 days), 18 per group, with follow-up during the same admission.
cards.result: Median hospital stay (primary outcome) was 13.5 days with early excision versus 28.5 days with delayed excision (P=0.009). No significant differences were observed in day-10 SOFA organ-dysfunction score, blood transfusion requirements, or mortality (no rates given in the abstract, and none printed here). Overall wound-culture positivity did not differ significantly (P=0.092), but polymicrobial infections were more frequent in the delayed group (44.4% vs 5.6%; P=0.017). Graft take during the index admission was lower in the early excision group — a result against early excision that the card keeps in view.
cards.watchOut: Thirty-six patients at one centre, with graft take worse in the early arm: the trial supports the stay benefit in a resource-limited setting and simultaneously warns that early excision's benefits are not uniform across outcomes.
cards.source: Kakani A, Rao N, Mago V et al. Impact of early excision in acute burns: A randomized controlled trial from a tertiary centre in North India. Burns. 2026;52(9):108200. PMID: 42868696. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. Pinned at build as the topic file's 'confirmatory early-excision randomised report — PMID to pin at build', via the Europe PMC cross-check.

cards.headline: Synthesis: operate early for stay and wound reasons — POSSIBLE; the mortality legend rests on one 1989 subgroup — MAYBE (weak evidence), Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: operate early for stay and wound reasons — POSSIBLE; the mortality legend rests on one 1989 subgroup — MAYBE (weak evidence) (Tier C).
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Herndon 1989 (85 randomised adults; 259-child series) and Kakani 2026 (36 randomised adults).
cards.result: Thirty-seven years apart, the randomised evidence supports early excision for the outcomes modern trials can measure: hospital stay roughly halved in 2026, survivors out in under a day per percent burned in 1989, fewer polymicrobial wound infections with early excision in 2026. On mortality, the only randomised signals are a 1989 subgroup benefit (ages 17-30, no inhalation injury) and a 2026 null in 36 patients — together, weak evidence, stamped MAYBE (weak evidence) and sent to the developer as Tier C. Modern burn surgery's operate-early doctrine may be right; this shelf records that its trial base is thinner and older than the doctrine's confidence suggests. Burn nutrition (#1049, draft) is a different intervention and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Neither trial resembles a modern high-income burn centre's full protocol (resuscitation, antimicrobials, critical care have all changed since 1989, and the 2026 trial is a single resource-limited centre): transport the direction, not the percentages.

shelves.title: Rocuronium versus succinylcholine for rapid-sequence intubation
shelves.question: In adults undergoing emergency rapid-sequence induction, does rocuronium produce first-pass intubating conditions and safety equivalent to succinylcholine?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Rocuronium · Succinylcholine/adverse effects · Intubation, Intratracheal/methods · Rapid Sequence Induction and Intubation/methods · Neuromuscular Nondepolarizing Agents · Neuromuscular Depolarizing Agents · Aged, 80 and over · Child
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised blinded comparisons in different populations point the same way: in patients aged 80 or over (Vested 2025, 90 patients), excellent intubating conditions at 60 seconds were 73% on rocuronium 1.0 mg/kg versus 75% on suxamethonium 1.0 mg/kg (95% CI for the difference -16 to 20), with first-pass success 98% in both groups and a slower onset for rocuronium (131 vs 99 seconds); in children (Kumar 2023, 200 patients), excellent conditions were 65% on rocuronium 1.2 mg/kg versus 60% on succinylcholine 2 mg/kg. The endpoint is intubating conditions — a surrogate — and neither trial was powered for patient-important harm, so the stamp caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.summary: Vested 2025: in patients 80 or older, excellent intubating conditions were 73% with rocuronium versus 75% with suxamethonium at 60 seconds
cards.type: Randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment (elderly RSI patients)
cards.people: 90 patients aged 80 years or above (ASA I-IV, BMI under 35) randomised to rocuronium 1.0 mg/kg (49) or suxamethonium 1.0 mg/kg (41) during rapid-sequence induction with video laryngoscopy; the abstract does not state mean age beyond the 80-plus entry criterion or the sex mix.
cards.result: Excellent intubating conditions (Fuchs-Buder scale, blinded assessor) occurred in 36 patients (73%) on rocuronium versus 31 (75%) on suxamethonium (95% CI for the difference -16 to 20; P=.82). First-pass success was 48 (98%) versus 40 (98%) (P=.90); intubating difficulty scores did not differ (median 0 in both). Onset time was significantly shorter with suxamethonium (99 vs 131 seconds; P=.01). Postoperative muscle soreness, hoarseness and sore throat did not differ.
cards.watchOut: A 90-patient superiority trial in the very elderly using video laryngoscopy: the confidence interval (-16 to 20 points) is wide, and the trial says nothing about rare succinylcholine harms (hyperkalaemia, malignant hyperthermia) that drive much of the real-world choice.

cards.headline: Synthesis: comparable intubating conditions in both trials, a slower onset for rocuronium — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: comparable intubating conditions in both trials, a slower onset for rocuronium — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Vested 2025 (90 patients aged 80 or over, emergency RSI) and Kumar 2023 (200 children, elective intubation).
cards.result: Across the two blinded comparisons, rocuronium at 1.0-1.2 mg/kg produced intubating conditions and first-pass success statistically indistinguishable from succinylcholine (73% vs 75% excellent conditions in the elderly; 65% vs 60% in children), at the cost of a roughly 30-second slower onset in the elderly trial. shelves.title: Cricoid pressure during rapid-sequence induction (IRIS)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing rapid-sequence induction, does cricoid pressure prevent pulmonary aspiration compared with a sham procedure, without worsening laryngoscopic view?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia/adverse effects,methods · Cricoid Cartilage/physiology · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Laryngoscopy/statistics & numerical data · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Male · Middle Aged · Operative Time · Pneumonia, Aspiration/etiology · Pressure · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one large randomised test (IRIS, 3,472 patients) could not settle the question either way: pulmonary aspiration was rare and nearly identical (0.6% with cricoid pressure versus 0.5% with a sham procedure; risk difference -0.06%, 95% CI -0.57 to 0.42), but the sham procedure FAILED its prespecified noninferiority test (upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI for relative risk 2.00, above the 1.50 margin; P=.14), so omitting cricoid pressure was not proven safe. Cricoid pressure did make intubation harder: Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 views in 10% versus 5% (P<.001) and intubation over 30 seconds in 47% versus 40% (P<.001). A single trial with a failed noninferiority design and a very low event rate caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: IRIS 2019: aspiration was 0.6% with cricoid pressure versus 0.5% with sham — but sham failed noninferiority, and cricoid worsened the view
cards.summary: IRIS 2019: aspiration was 0.6% with cricoid pressure versus 0.5% with sham — but sham failed noninferiority, and cricoid worsened the view
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, noninferiority trial in 10 academic centres
cards.people: 3,472 patients undergoing anaesthesia with rapid-sequence induction, enrolled February 2014 to February 2017 and followed for 28 days or until discharge; mean (SD) age 51 (19) years and 1,777 (51%) were men.
cards.result: The primary end point, pulmonary aspiration, occurred in 10 patients (0.6%) in the Sellick (cricoid pressure) group and 9 patients (0.5%) in the sham group. The upper limit of the one-sided 95% CI of relative risk was 2.00, exceeding the 1.50 noninferiority margin, so noninferiority of the sham procedure was NOT demonstrated (P=.14); the risk difference was -0.06% (two-sided 95% CI -0.57 to 0.42) in both intention-to-treat and per-protocol populations. Pneumonia, length of stay and mortality did not differ significantly, but Cormack-Lehane grade 3-4 views were more frequent with cricoid pressure (10% vs 5%; P<.001) and intubation took over 30 seconds more often (47% vs 40%; P<.001).
cards.watchOut: A failed noninferiority test is not proof that cricoid pressure works: with aspiration under 1%, the trial cannot exclude either a small protective effect or none, and it excluded the highest-risk settings its authors name (pregnancy, outside the operating room).
cards.source: Birenbaum A et al. Effect of Cricoid Pressure Compared With a Sham Procedure in the Rapid Sequence Induction of Anesthesia: The IRIS Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Surg. 2019. PMID: 30347104. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02080754, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: one large trial, an unproven manoeuvre and an unproven omission — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one large trial, an unproven manoeuvre and an unproven omission — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: IRIS 2019 (3,472 patients undergoing rapid-sequence induction).
cards.result: IRIS leaves cricoid pressure where the evidence found it: aspiration rates were 0.6% versus 0.5%, the sham strategy was not shown noninferior, and the manoeuvre measurably worsened laryngoscopic view (grade 3-4 in 10% vs 5%) and intubation time. The honest stamp is POSSIBLE — the trial neither vindicates routine cricoid pressure nor licenses abandoning it on safety grounds.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote IRIS as 'cricoid pressure doesn't work' or as 'stopping it is dangerous': both readings exceed a noninferiority trial whose confidence interval for relative risk reached 2.00 on an outcome occurring in fewer than 1 in 150 patients.
cards.source: Synthesis of Birenbaum A et al. JAMA Surg. 2019. PMID: 30347104. Registry ID as on the individual card.

shelves.title: Prehospital benzodiazepine route for status epilepticus (RAMPART)
shelves.question: In prehospital convulsive status epilepticus, is intramuscular midazolam at least as effective as intravenous lorazepam at stopping seizures before ED arrival?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Child · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Lorazepam/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Male · Midazolam/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Status Epilepticus/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: The one large double-blind randomised test (RAMPART, 893 subjects in the primary analysis) found seizures absent on ED arrival without rescue therapy in 73.4% with intramuscular midazolam versus 63.4% with intravenous lorazepam (absolute difference 10 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 16.1; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority), with similar intubation rates (14.1% vs 14.4%) and seizure recurrence (11.4% vs 10.6%). The win was logistical as much as pharmacological: median time to active treatment was 1.2 minutes intramuscularly versus 4.8 minutes intravenously, partly offset by a slower time from treatment to cessation (3.3 vs 1.6 minutes). One very large blinded trial with a decisive primary result carries LIKELY under the library's large-trial rule.

cards.headline: RAMPART 2012: IM midazolam stopped seizures before ED arrival in 73.4% versus 63.4% for IV lorazepam
cards.summary: RAMPART 2012: IM midazolam stopped seizures before ED arrival in 73.4% versus 63.4% for IV lorazepam
cards.people: Children and adults whose convulsions had persisted for more than 5 minutes and who were still convulsing on paramedic arrival; the primary analysis covers 448 subjects given intramuscular midazolam by autoinjector and 445 given intravenous lorazepam. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: At ED arrival, seizures were absent without rescue therapy in 329 of 448 subjects (73.4%) in the intramuscular-midazolam group and 282 of 445 (63.4%) in the intravenous-lorazepam group (absolute difference 10 percentage points, 95% CI 4.0 to 16.1; P<0.001 for both noninferiority and superiority against a 10-point margin). Endotracheal intubation was needed in 14.1% versus 14.4% and seizure recurrence occurred in 11.4% versus 10.6%. Median time to active treatment was 1.2 minutes (IM) versus 4.8 minutes (IV); median time from treatment to cessation was 3.3 versus 1.6 minutes. Adverse-event rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: The comparison bundles drug, route and speed: midazolam won largely because an autoinjector beats starting an IV in a convulsing patient. The trial's own design paper (PMID 21967361, the topic file's printed anchor) reports no results and is fenced here, not carded; this card is the NEJM results report of the same trial (same registry number).
cards.source: Silbergleit R et al. Intramuscular versus intravenous therapy for prehospital status epilepticus. N Engl J Med. 2012. PMID: 22335736. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00809146, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: the intramuscular route is at least as effective and faster to give — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: the intramuscular route is at least as effective and faster to give — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: RAMPART results report 2012 (893 subjects in the primary analysis, children and adults).
cards.result: RAMPART is the definitive first-line route trial: 73.4% versus 63.4% seizure-free on arrival, no safety penalty on intubation (14.1% vs 14.4%) or recurrence (11.4% vs 10.6%), and a 3.6-minute faster median time to treatment. This shelf answers only the first-line prehospital route question; second-line agents after benzodiazepines are different questions, home on Shelves #144 and #235, and are not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: The result licenses the intramuscular route when IV access is not already in place; it does not show midazolam is the better molecule — given intravenously, lorazepam stopped seizures faster after administration (1.6 vs 3.3 minutes).

shelves.title: Droperidol for sedation of acute behavioural disturbance in the ED
shelves.question: In ED patients with acute behavioural disturbance, is droperidol as effective and safe as other parenteral sedatives (midazolam, olanzapine) for rapid sedation?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Aggression/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Droperidol/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Midazolam/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Procedural Sedation/methods · Treatment Outcome · Violence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The randomised leg is one blinded trial (DORM, 91 patients): median duration of violent behaviour was 20 minutes on intramuscular droperidol 10 mg versus 24 minutes on midazolam 10 mg and 25 minutes on the combination, but additional sedation was needed less often with droperidol (33% vs 62% vs 41%; hazard ratio for midazolam versus droperidol 2.31 relative, 95% credible interval 1.01 to 4.71) and adverse effects were fewer (6% vs 28% vs 7%). The large safety cohort the topic file anchors on (Calver 2015, 1,403 sedated patients) is a prospective OBSERVATIONAL study, not a trial: median time to sedation 20 minutes, abnormal QT in 1.3% of those with an ECG (half attributable to other causes), no torsades. Randomised efficacy from one small trial plus observational safety caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: DORM 2010: IM droperidol and midazolam sedated for a similar duration, but midazolam needed more top-ups and caused more adverse effects
cards.summary: DORM 2010: IM droperidol and midazolam sedated for a similar duration, but midazolam needed more top-ups and caused more adverse effects
cards.type: Blinded randomised controlled trial (intramuscular sedation in the ED)
cards.people: 91 ED patients requiring physical restraint and parenteral sedation for violent, acute behavioural disturbance, from 223 screened; 33 received droperidol 10 mg, 29 midazolam 10 mg and 29 the droperidol/midazolam combination (5 mg each). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Median duration of the violent episode (time security staff were required) was 20 minutes (IQR 11-37) for droperidol, 24 minutes (IQR 13-35) for midazolam and 25 minutes (IQR 15-38) for the combination — no significant difference. Additional sedation was required in 11 (33%) droperidol patients, 18 (62%) midazolam patients and 12 (41%) combination patients (hazard ratio for additional sedation, midazolam versus droperidol, 2.31 relative, 95% credible interval 1.01 to 4.71). Adverse effects occurred in 2 (6%) droperidol, 8 (28%) midazolam and 2 (7%) combination patients, mostly oversedation with midazolam. An abnormal QT occurred in 2 of 31 (6%) droperidol patients, not different from the other groups; injuries and further episodes did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Only 91 of 223 screened patients were randomised, and the primary outcome (security-staff time) is a pragmatic proxy for sedation; the trial was not powered for rare cardiac harm.
cards.source: Isbister GK et al. Randomized controlled trial of intramuscular droperidol versus midazolam for violence and acute behavioral disturbance: the DORM study. Ann Emerg Med. 2010. PMID: 20868907. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Calver 2015: in 1,403 droperidol sedations, abnormal QT was 1.3% and there was no torsades — an observational cohort, not a trial
cards.summary: Calver 2015: in 1,403 droperidol sedations, abnormal QT was 1.3% and there was no torsades — an observational cohort, not a trial
cards.type: Prospective observational study in 6 EDs (NOT randomised — carded as the safety record, labelled as such)
cards.people: 1,403 adult ED patients sedated with droperidol for acute behavioural disturbance (August 2009 to April 2013), median total dose 10 mg (IQR 10-20); 1,009 had an ECG within 2 hours of administration. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: An abnormal QT (by the QT nomogram at-risk line) was found in 13 of 1,009 patients (1.3%, 95% CI 0.7 to 2.3), but 7 of the 13 had another attributed cause (methadone, escitalopram, amiodarone or pre-existing prolongation). Median time to sedation was 20 minutes (IQR 10-30) and 97% were sedated within 120 minutes; additional sedation was required in 435 patients (31.0%). Adverse events occurred in 70 patients (5%) and oversedation without complications in 109 (8%); there were no cases of torsades de pointes. Injuries occurred in 34 staff members and 4 patients.
cards.watchOut: Observational and uncontrolled: sedation times and event rates have no comparator arm, so this cohort supports the safety reading (and the absence of torsades at these doses) but cannot prove droperidol works as well as alternatives — that rests on DORM.
cards.source: Calver L et al. The Safety and Effectiveness of Droperidol for Sedation of Acute Behavioral Disturbance in the Emergency Department. Ann Emerg Med. 2015. PMID: 25890395. shelves.title: Ketamine versus haloperidol for acute agitation in the ED
shelves.question: In adults with severe acute agitation in the ED, does ketamine achieve faster, safer sedation than haloperidol?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: A single small randomised trial (Sadrzadeh 2025, 120 patients) compared intravenous ketamine 2 mg/kg with intravenous haloperidol 5 mg: admission Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) scores were 1.73 on haloperidol and 1.58 on ketamine, falling after treatment to 0.07 (SD 1.25) versus -0.92 (SD 1.19) — deeper sedation with ketamine — and the authors report a faster onset of action for ketamine. The abstract reports no adverse-event counts, intubation rates or time-to-sedation figures, so the safety half of the question is unanswered by this record; one small trial on a sedation-score surrogate caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Sadrzadeh 2025: IV ketamine sedated more deeply than IV haloperidol (post-treatment RASS -0.92 vs 0.07), with faster onset reported
cards.summary: Sadrzadeh 2025: IV ketamine sedated more deeply than IV haloperidol (post-treatment RASS -0.92 vs 0.07), with faster onset reported
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial (two hospitals, Mashhad, Iran)
cards.people: 120 adults aged 18 to 65 years presenting with acute agitation requiring pharmacological intervention (March 2021 to March 2022), randomised to intravenous haloperidol 5 mg or intravenous ketamine 2 mg/kg; mean age was 48.28 (SD 16.75) years in the haloperidol group and 45.42 (SD 16.65) in the ketamine group, and men were 73% and 75% of the groups respectively.
cards.result: Mean admission RASS was 1.73 (SD 0.75) in the haloperidol group and 1.58 (SD 0.61) in the ketamine group. After intervention, mean RASS fell to 0.07 (SD 1.25) on haloperidol and -0.92 (SD 1.19) on ketamine — a deeper level of sedation with ketamine. The authors conclude ketamine had a faster onset of action than haloperidol. The abstract does not report the numerical time to onset, adverse-effect incidences, or intubation rates, although adverse effects and time to onset were prespecified secondary outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre-region, 120-patient trial reported at abstract level with no safety numbers: the deeper RASS (-0.92) can mean better control or oversedation, and this record cannot distinguish the two. The record carries no MeSH terms and no registry ID in its databank fields.

shelves.title: Greater occipital nerve block versus intravenous metoclopramide for ED migraine
shelves.question: In adults presenting to the ED with acute migraine, does greater occipital nerve block with bupivacaine relieve headache as durably as intravenous metoclopramide?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Bupivacaine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Cervical Plexus/drug effects · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Male · Metoclopramide/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Middle Aged · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Nerve Block
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED (favouring metoclopramide): The one direct randomised test (Friedman 2020, 99 patients, double-dummy noninferiority design) found greater occipital nerve block was NOT as efficacious as intravenous metoclopramide: mean 1-hour pain improvement was 5.0 points on a 0-10 scale with the block versus 6.1 with metoclopramide (between-group difference -1.1, 95% CI -2.3 to 0.1 — the lower limit crossed the -1.3 noninferiority margin), sustained 48-hour relief was 22% versus 38%, and rescue medication was needed by 33% versus 17%. A single modest-sized trial caps the verdict at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Friedman 2020: GON block improved pain less than IV metoclopramide at 1 hour (5.0 vs 6.1 points) and gave less sustained relief (22% vs 38%)
cards.summary: Friedman 2020: GON block improved pain less than IV metoclopramide at 1 hour (5.0 vs 6.1 points) and gave less sustained relief (22% vs 38%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-dummy, double-blind, noninferiority trial in 2 EDs
cards.people: 99 adults with migraine of moderate or severe intensity randomised to bilateral greater occipital nerve block with bupivacaine 0.5% (51) or intravenous metoclopramide 10 mg (48); the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean improvement in pain (0-10 scale) at 1 hour was 5.0 (95% CI 4.1 to 5.8) with the nerve block versus 6.1 (95% CI 5.2 to 6.9) with metoclopramide; the between-group difference was -1.1 (95% CI -2.3 to 0.1), failing the prespecified noninferiority criterion (lower limit above -1.3). Sustained headache relief for 48 hours was reported by 11 of 51 (22%) block patients versus 18 of 47 (38%) metoclopramide patients (difference 17%, 95% CI -1 to 35). Rescue medication in the ED was used by 17 of 51 (33%) versus 8 of 48 (17%). An adverse event was reported by 16 of 51 (31%) versus 18 of 48 (38%).
cards.watchOut: Ninety-nine patients is small for a noninferiority question with a 1.3-point margin, and 1-hour pain was the primary endpoint — but every secondary measure (sustained relief, rescue use) pointed the same way, against the block.

shelves.title: Adding ipratropium to salbutamol in acute asthma in the ED
shelves.question: In children and adults with acute asthma in the ED, does adding nebulised ipratropium bromide to salbutamol reduce hospital admission versus salbutamol alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Albuterol/therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Bronchodilator Agents/therapeutic use · Child · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Ipratropium/therapeutic use · Male · Nebulizers and Vaporizers · Peak Expiratory Flow Rate/drug effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two double-blind randomised trials, one in each age group, agree. In children (Qureshi 1998, 434 patients, all also given corticosteroid), hospitalisation was 27.4% with ipratropium added versus 36.5% with salbutamol alone (P=0.05), driven by the severe subgroup (37.5% vs 52.6%; P=0.02), with no benefit in moderate exacerbations (10.1% vs 10.7%). In adults with peak flow under 200 L/min (Lin 1998, 55 patients), airflow improved significantly faster with the combination (P<=.001) and admissions were 3 of 27 versus 10 of 28 (absolute difference 25%, 95% CI 3 to 46; P=.03). Two concordant blinded trials earn LIKELY, scoped to severe exacerbations.

cards.headline: Qureshi 1998: in children, adding ipratropium cut hospitalisation in severe asthma (37.5% vs 52.6%) but not in moderate asthma
cards.summary: Qureshi 1998: in children, adding ipratropium cut hospitalisation in severe asthma (37.5% vs 52.6%) but not in moderate asthma
cards.people: 434 children aged 2 to 18 years with moderate or severe acute asthma exacerbations, all treated with nebulised albuterol every 20 minutes for three doses plus oral corticosteroid; 215 received ipratropium bromide 500 micrograms with the second and third albuterol doses and 219 received saline placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Overall hospitalisation was 59 of 215 (27.4%) in the ipratropium group versus 80 of 219 (36.5%) in the control group (P=0.05). In moderate asthma (peak flow 50-70% predicted or asthma score 8-11), rates were similar: 8 of 79 (10.1%) versus 9 of 84 (10.7%). In severe asthma (peak flow under 50% predicted or score 12-15), ipratropium significantly reduced hospitalisation: 51 of 136 (37.5%) versus 71 of 135 (52.6%) (P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: The overall P value sits exactly at 0.05 and the benefit is a severity subgroup finding — prespecified by severity strata, but the shelf's claim should stay scoped to severe exacerbations, where the absolute gain was about 15 points.
cards.source: Qureshi F et al. Effect of nebulized ipratropium on the hospitalization rates of children with asthma. N Engl J Med. 1998. PMID: 9761804. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Single-dose dexamethasone versus multi-day prednisone after asthma exacerbation
shelves.question: In adults discharged after an acute asthma exacerbation, is a single dose of oral dexamethasone non-inferior to 5 days of prednisone for preventing relapse?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adult · Anti-Asthmatic Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Asthma/drug therapy · Dexamethasone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Prednisone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Recurrence
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised test (Rehrer 2016, 376 patients completing follow-up) came within a whisker of the line and fell the wrong side of it: relapse within 14 days was 12.1% after a single 12 mg dose of dexamethasone plus 4 days of placebo versus 9.8% on 5 days of prednisone 60 mg (difference 2.3%, 95% CI -4.1 to 8.6) — the upper confidence limit exceeded the prespecified 8% noninferiority margin, so noninferiority was NOT demonstrated, by a very small margin (the topic file's summary said it was met; the record says it was not, and the record governs). Hospitalisation at relapse (3.4% vs 2.9%) and adverse effects were similar. One trial with a near-miss noninferiority result caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Rehrer 2016: single-dose dexamethasone missed noninferiority to 5 days of prednisone by a small margin (relapse 12.1% vs 9.8%)
cards.summary: Rehrer 2016: single-dose dexamethasone missed noninferiority to 5 days of prednisone by a small margin (relapse 12.1% vs 9.8%)
cards.people: Adults aged 18 to 55 years with mild to moderate asthma exacerbations randomised to a single oral dose of dexamethasone 12 mg plus 4 days of placebo, or prednisone 60 mg daily for 5 days; 173 dexamethasone and 203 prednisone subjects completed the regimen and 2-week telephone follow-up. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Relapse (unscheduled return visit for additional treatment within 14 days) occurred in 12.1% of the dexamethasone group versus 9.8% of the prednisone group (difference 2.3%, 95% CI -4.1 to 8.6). Because the upper confidence limit (8.6%) surpassed the preset 8% noninferiority margin, noninferiority was not demonstrated — by a very small margin, in the authors' words. Hospitalisation for the relapse visit was 3.4% versus 2.9% (difference 0.5%, 95% CI -4.1 to 3.1), and adverse-effect rates were generally the same in both groups.
cards.watchOut: A near-miss is not equivalence: the data are compatible with single-dose dexamethasone causing up to 8.6 more relapses per 100 patients. The authors note convenience and compliance may still favour dexamethasone, but that is a judgement, not the trial's statistical verdict.
cards.source: Rehrer MW et al. A Randomized Controlled Noninferiority Trial of Single Dose of Oral Dexamethasone Versus 5 Days of Oral Prednisone in Acute Adult Asthma. Ann Emerg Med. 2016. PMID: 27117874. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01241006, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Ketorolac versus morphine for renal colic
shelves.question: In adults with acute renal colic in the ED, does intravenous ketorolac relieve pain as effectively as intravenous morphine, with fewer adverse effects?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised comparisons support comparable analgesia. In the head-to-head trial (Pourafzali 2023, 272 patients), pain scores fell by about 9 points in both groups over 90 minutes with no significant between-group difference, and nausea (5.1%) and reduced oxygen saturation (1.5%) occurred only with morphine, while dizziness was similar (2.9% vs 2.2%). In a double-blind three-arm trial (Safaie 2022, 195 patients), adding ketorolac (or ibuprofen) to morphine beat morphine alone from 15 minutes (120-minute pain scores 2.9 vs 7.0), with the lowest rescue-analgesia use in the ketorolac combination arm. Small single-region trials measuring pain scores cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Pourafzali 2023: ketorolac relieved renal-colic pain as much as morphine over 90 minutes, with fewer opioid-type effects
cards.summary: Pourafzali 2023: ketorolac relieved renal-colic pain as much as morphine over 90 minutes, with fewer opioid-type effects
cards.people: 272 patients with renal colic divided into two groups receiving intravenous morphine or intravenous ketorolac 30 mg; pain and vital signs were recorded before treatment and at 5, 15, 30, 60 and 90 minutes. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix, and its stated morphine dose (1.0 mg/kg) is reproduced nowhere on this card because it is inconsistent with standard dosing and is treated as a probable abstract error.
cards.result: Mean pain scores before and after the intervention did not differ significantly between the two groups (P>0.05), while pain fell significantly over time in both groups (reduction 9.4 points in the morphine group and 9.09 in the ketorolac group; P<0.001). In the morphine group, nausea occurred in 5.1%, dizziness in 2.9% and decreased oxygen saturation in 1.5%; in the ketorolac group the only reported effect was dizziness in 2.2% (between-group differences not significant, P>0.05).
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not describe blinding, and its morphine dose as printed (1.0 mg/kg) would be dangerous if literal — the card therefore reports the comparison, not that dose. Pain-score equivalence in a single trial of 272 patients is a moderate-strength result.
cards.source: Pourafzali SM et al. A Comparative Study of the Effect of Intravenous Morphine and Ketorolac on Pain Control in Patients with Renal Colic. Adv Biomed Res. 2023. PMID: 37057227. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: none in the record.

cards.headline: Safaie 2022: morphine plus ketorolac beat morphine alone for renal-colic pain (2.9 vs 7.0 at 120 minutes)
cards.summary: Safaie 2022: morphine plus ketorolac beat morphine alone for renal-colic pain (2.9 vs 7.0 at 120 minutes)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind clinical trial (three arms, Iran)
cards.people: 195 ED patients aged 18-65 years with acute renal colic and pain score above 6 of 10, randomised to intravenous morphine 5 mg plus ibuprofen 800 mg (65), morphine 5 mg plus ketorolac 30 mg (65), or morphine 5 mg alone (65), with pain scored at 0, 15, 30, 60 and 120 minutes. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: From 15 minutes onward, pain reduction was greater in both combination groups than with morphine alone (P<0.001), with no significant difference between the ibuprofen and ketorolac combinations. At 120 minutes, mean pain scores were 2.9 (95% CI 2.6 to 3.3) in both combination groups versus 7.0 (95% CI 6.7 to 7.4) with morphine alone. Mean rescue-analgesia dose was highest in the morphine-alone group and lowest in the ketorolac combination group (P=0.031). Adverse effects occurred in 18.5% (ibuprofen combination), 20.0% (ketorolac combination) and 13.8% (morphine alone).
cards.watchOut: This trial tests ketorolac as an add-on, not as a morphine replacement — it supports the NSAID's analgesic contribution but cannot by itself show ketorolac alone suffices; that rests on the head-to-head card above.
cards.source: Safaie A et al. shelves.title: Intravenous lidocaine versus ketorolac for renal colic
shelves.question: In adults with suspected renal colic in the ED, does intravenous lidocaine relieve pain as effectively as ketorolac?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one direct head-to-head trial (Shadab 2026, 90 patients) found successful pain relief (at least 3 points on a 10-point scale at 30 minutes) in 68.9% with intravenous lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg versus 60.0% with ketorolac 30 mg (absolute difference 8.9%, 95% CI -10.8 to 28.6; P=0.378), with rescue analgesia in 31.1% versus 40.0% and only mild adverse events. The neighbouring lidocaine trial against fentanyl (Motamed 2017, 90 patients) is a caution: pain severity did not differ overall, but treatment failure at 15 minutes was higher with lidocaine (44.4% vs 17.8%; P=0.006). Two small single-centre trials with wide intervals cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Shadab 2026: IV lidocaine achieved successful pain relief in 68.9% versus 60.0% for ketorolac at 30 minutes (difference not significant)
cards.summary: Shadab 2026: IV lidocaine achieved successful pain relief in 68.9% versus 60.0% for ketorolac at 30 minutes (difference not significant)
cards.type: Prospective, single-centre, randomised controlled trial (POF Hospital, Pakistan)
cards.people: 90 adults presenting to the ED with suspected renal colic and pain score of at least 7 of 10, randomised to intravenous lidocaine 1.5 mg/kg infused over 15 minutes (45) or intravenous ketorolac 30 mg (45). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Successful pain relief (a fall of at least 3 points at 30 minutes) was achieved in 31 patients (68.9%) on lidocaine and 27 (60.0%) on ketorolac (absolute risk difference 8.9%, 95% CI -10.8 to 28.6; chi-square P=0.378). Rescue analgesia was required in 14 (31.1%) on lidocaine and 18 (40.0%) on ketorolac. Adverse events were infrequent and mild — transient dizziness in three lidocaine patients and mild hypersensitivity reactions in two ketorolac patients; no serious adverse events occurred.
cards.watchOut: A 90-patient single-centre trial whose confidence interval (-10.8 to +28.6 points) includes lidocaine being meaningfully worse; 'comparable' here means 'not shown different in a small trial', not proven equivalence.

shelves.title: Regional anaesthesia with propofol versus volatile general anaesthesia for breast-cancer recurrence
shelves.question: In women having potentially curative breast-cancer surgery, does paravertebral regional anaesthesia with propofol reduce cancer recurrence versus sevoflurane general anaesthesia with opioids?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Anesthesia, Conduction/adverse effects,methods · Anesthesia, General/adverse effects,methods · Anesthetics, Inhalation/adverse effects · Breast Neoplasms/pathology,surgery · Female · Humans · Neoplasm Recurrence, Local/etiology,prevention & control · Nerve Block/methods · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control · Sevoflurane/adverse effects
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one large randomised test (Sessler 2019, 2,108 women analysed, 13 hospitals) found breast-cancer recurrence essentially identical between techniques: 102 of 1,043 (10%) with paravertebral regional anaesthesia plus propofol versus 111 of 1,065 (10%) with sevoflurane general anaesthesia and opioids (hazard ratio 0.97 relative, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.28; P=0.84), at a median follow-up of 36 months; the trial was stopped at a prespecified futility boundary. Persistent incisional pain also did not differ (52% vs 52% at 6 months). A single very large trial with a tight result around no effect carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) under the library's large-null rule. Cancer recurrence sits outside this library's Tier C definition (mortality/MI/stroke/CV events), so the stamp is proposed ordinarily.

cards.headline: Sessler 2019: breast-cancer recurrence was 10% versus 10% with regional/propofol versus sevoflurane/opioid anaesthesia (HR 0.97 relative)
cards.summary: Sessler 2019: breast-cancer recurrence was 10% versus 10% with regional/propofol versus sevoflurane/opioid anaesthesia (HR 0.97 relative)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial at 13 hospitals in 8 countries (stopped at a futility boundary)
cards.people: 2,132 women under 85 years having potentially curative primary breast-cancer resection were enrolled; 2,108 underwent surgery and were analysed — 1,043 assigned to regional anaesthesia-analgesia (paravertebral blocks plus propofol) and 1,065 to general anaesthesia (sevoflurane) with opioid analgesia; median follow-up 36 months (IQR 24-49). The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Local or metastatic recurrence occurred in 102 women (10%) assigned regional anaesthesia versus 111 (10%) assigned general anaesthesia (hazard ratio 0.97 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.74 to 1.28; P=0.84). Incisional pain at 6 months was reported by 442 of 856 (52%) versus 456 of 872 (52%), and at 12 months by 28% versus 27% (overall odds ratio 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.17; P=0.99); neuropathic breast pain also did not differ (10% vs 10% at 6 months).
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped early for futility and median follow-up was 3 years — long enough to exclude the hypothesised large protective effect, not late recurrences; the confidence interval (0.74 to 1.28) still admits a modest effect in either direction.
cards.source: Sessler DI et al. Recurrence of breast cancer after regional or general anaesthesia: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2019. PMID: 31645288. shelves.title: Volatile versus total intravenous anaesthesia in cardiac surgery (MYRIAD)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing coronary-artery bypass grafting, does volatile anaesthesia reduce one-year mortality versus total intravenous anaesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Inhalation · Aged · Anesthesia, General · Anesthesia, Intravenous · Anesthetics, General/pharmacology · Anesthetics, Intravenous · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Artery Disease/mortality,physiopathology,surgery · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Single-Blind Method · Stroke Volume
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, one-year mortality primary outcome): The one large randomised test (MYRIAD, 5,400 patients, 36 centres in 13 countries) found death from any cause at 1 year in 2.8% with a volatile-based regimen versus 3.0% with total intravenous anaesthesia (relative risk 0.94 relative, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.29; P=0.71), and at 30 days 1.4% versus 1.3% (relative risk 1.11 relative, 0.70 to 1.76), with no secondary outcome or prespecified adverse event — including myocardial infarction — significantly different. The trial was stopped for futility at the second interim analysis. A very large blinded-assessment trial null on mortality carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, single-blind, controlled trial (36 centres, 13 countries) — stopped for futility
cards.people: 5,400 patients scheduled for elective coronary-artery bypass grafting randomised to an intraoperative regimen including a volatile anaesthetic (desflurane, isoflurane or sevoflurane; 2,709) or total intravenous anaesthesia (2,691); on-pump CABG was performed in 64%, with mean bypass duration 79 minutes. At 30 days mortality was 1.4% versus 1.3% (relative risk 1.11 relative, 95% CI 0.70 to 1.76). shelves.title: Phenylephrine versus ephedrine for spinal hypotension at caesarean delivery
shelves.question: In women having caesarean delivery under spinal anaesthesia, does phenylephrine maintain maternal blood pressure with better fetal acid–base status than ephedrine?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anesthesia, Obstetrical/adverse effects · Anesthesia, Spinal/adverse effects · Blood Pressure/drug effects · Cesarean Section · Double-Blind Method · Ephedrine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Female · Fetal Blood/metabolism · Humans · Hypotension/etiology,prevention & control · Phenylephrine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pregnancy · Vasoconstrictor Agents/administration & dosage,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by outcome: the two blinded trials trade blows. For TREATING established hypotension in non-elective caesarean section (Ngan Kee 2008, 204 women), umbilical arterial and venous pH and base excess were similar between phenylephrine 100-microgram and ephedrine 10-mg boluses, but fetal lactate was higher with ephedrine (umbilical arterial median 2.6 vs 2.4 mmol/L; P=0.002) and maternal nausea/vomiting more frequent (12.7% vs 3.9%; P=0.02). For PREVENTION (Magalhães 2009, 60 women), ephedrine prevented hypotension better (incidence 70% vs 93%; P<0.05) yet umbilical arterial pH and 1-minute Apgar were lower with ephedrine. The consistent thread is a slightly worse fetal acid–base profile with ephedrine; the blood-pressure thread favours whichever drug the protocol used first. Surrogate endpoints (cord pH, lactate) and small trials cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Ngan Kee 2008: treating spinal hypotension, phenylephrine and ephedrine gave similar cord pH, but ephedrine raised fetal lactate and maternal nausea
cards.summary: Ngan Kee 2008: treating spinal hypotension, phenylephrine and ephedrine gave similar cord pH, but ephedrine raised fetal lactate and maternal nausea
cards.people: 204 patients having non-elective caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia, randomised to boluses of phenylephrine 100 micrograms or ephedrine 10 mg for hypotension (systolic pressure under 100 mmHg); 148 were protocol-compliant. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Umbilical arterial and venous pH and base excess were similar between groups. Umbilical arterial lactate was higher in the ephedrine group (median 2.6 [IQR 2.3-3.3] vs 2.4 [1.9-3.0] mmol/L; P=0.002), as was umbilical venous lactate (2.5 [2.2-3.2] vs 2.3 [1.9-2.8]; P=0.016), and more ephedrine patients had nausea or vomiting (12.7% vs 3.9%; P=0.02). Clinical neonatal outcome was similar. Among protocol-compliant patients, umbilical arterial and venous oxygen tensions were lower with phenylephrine although oxygen content was similar.
cards.watchOut: A treatment (not prevention) trial with cord-gas surrogates: pH — the outcome clinicians watch — did not differ, and no clinical neonatal outcome separated the drugs.
cards.source: Ngan Kee WD et al. Randomised double-blinded comparison of phenylephrine vs ephedrine for maintaining blood pressure during spinal anaesthesia for non-elective Caesarean section. Anaesthesia. 2008. PMID: 19032300. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Magalhães 2009: for prevention, ephedrine caused less hypotension (70% vs 93%) but lower cord pH and 1-minute Apgar
cards.summary: Magalhães 2009: for prevention, ephedrine caused less hypotension (70% vs 93%) but lower cord pH and 1-minute Apgar
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind trial (caesarean section under spinal block)
cards.people: 60 patients undergoing caesarean section under spinal block with bupivacaine and sufentanil, randomised to prophylactic ephedrine 10 mg (30) or phenylephrine 80 micrograms (30), with rescue boluses at half the initial dose. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: Hypotension (pressure at or below 80% of baseline) occurred in 70% of the ephedrine group versus 93% of the phenylephrine group (P<0.05); mean doses used were 14.8 (SD 3.8) mg ephedrine and 186.7 (SD 52.9) micrograms phenylephrine. Vomiting, bradycardia and reactive hypertension incidences were similar. Mean umbilical arterial pH and the 1-minute Apgar score were lower in the ephedrine group (P<0.05); 5-minute Apgar did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients and a prophylactic bolus design: the hypotension advantage may reflect dose equivalence choices (80 micrograms phenylephrine) rather than the drugs themselves, and the fetal differences were transient (5-minute Apgar equal).
