shelves.title: Quadratus lumborum block for pain after caesarean delivery
shelves.question: In women after caesarean delivery, does quadratus lumborum block reduce postoperative opioid use and pain versus sham or transversus abdominis plane block?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Muscles · Adult · Analgesia, Obstetrical · Analgesia, Patient-Controlled · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage · Bupivacaine/administration & dosage · Cesarean Section/methods · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Morphine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Nerve Block/methods · Postoperative Pain/etiology,prevention & control · Pregnancy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind trials from the same group support an opioid-sparing effect. Against sham block (Blanco 2015, 50 women), quadratus lumborum block (QLB) with bupivacaine significantly reduced morphine consumption at 6 and 12 hours (not 24-48) and morphine demands through 48 hours (all P<0.001), with lower pain scores at rest and on movement at nearly all time points. Against transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block (Blanco 2016, 76 women), QLB used significantly less morphine at 12, 24 and 48 hours (P<0.05) with similar pain scores. Small, single-group trials with an opioid-consumption surrogate cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.result: Patients receiving local anaesthetic used significantly less morphine than controls at 6 and 12 hours (P<0.001), though not at 24 and 48 hours, and made significantly fewer morphine demands at 6, 12, 24 and 48 hours (P<0.001). shelves.title: Perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusion for postoperative pain and recovery
shelves.question: In adults having abdominal/colorectal surgery, does a perioperative intravenous lidocaine infusion shorten hospital stay and reduce postoperative pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Ileus/epidemiology · Lidocaine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Length of Stay/trends · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology,prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The anchor trial (Herroeder 2007, 60 colorectal patients) found intravenous lidocaine shortened hospital stay by one day and sped return of bowel function, with no difference in daily pain ratings. The Cochrane synthesis (Weibel 2018, 68 trials, 4,525 participants) is much more cautious: it is UNCERTAIN whether lidocaine improves early pain (standardised mean difference -0.50 relative, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.28; very low-quality evidence), it probably has no clinically relevant effect on pain at 24 hours (SMD -0.14 relative) or 48 hours, while estimates for ileus (risk ratio 0.37 relative, 0.15 to 0.87), time to first bowel movement (-7.92 hours) and opioid consumption (-4.52 mg morphine equivalents) were all very low quality. One small positive trial against a very-low-certainty review caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Herroeder 2007: IV lidocaine shortened hospital stay by one day after colorectal surgery, without changing pain ratings
cards.summary: Herroeder 2007: IV lidocaine shortened hospital stay by one day after colorectal surgery, without changing pain ratings
cards.people: 60 patients undergoing colorectal surgery who were unwilling or unable to receive an epidural catheter, randomised to intravenous lidocaine (1.5 mg/kg bolus then 2 mg/min until 4 hours postoperatively) or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Lidocaine significantly accelerated return of bowel function and shortened length of hospital stay by one day; no difference was observed in daily pain ratings. Surgery-induced rises in IL-6, IL-8, complement C3a and IL-1ra and expression of CD11b, L- and P-selectin and platelet-leukocyte aggregates were significantly attenuated by lidocaine. The abstract does not print the absolute stay durations, so none are given here.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients, and the headline outcomes (stay, bowel function) are reported without absolute figures in the abstract; the pain outcome — the one patients feel — was null in this very trial.
cards.source: Herroeder S et al. Systemic lidocaine shortens length of hospital stay after colorectal surgery: a double-blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Ann Surg. 2007. PMID: 17667496. cards.headline: Cochrane 2018: across 68 trials the lidocaine evidence is very low quality; no clinically relevant pain effect after 24 hours
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018: across 68 trials the lidocaine evidence is very low quality; no clinically relevant pain effect after 24 hours
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane)
cards.people: 68 randomised trials with 4,525 participants undergoing elective or urgent surgery under general anaesthesia (open abdominal 22, laparoscopic abdominal 20, other procedures 26), comparing continuous perioperative intravenous lidocaine with placebo/no treatment (66 trials) or thoracic epidural analgesia (2 trials); doses ranged from 1 to 5 mg/kg/hour and infusion durations from the end of surgery to several days.
cards.result: Versus placebo, the reviewers were uncertain whether lidocaine improves early pain (1-4 hours: SMD -0.50 relative, 95% CI -0.72 to -0.28; 29 studies, 1,656 participants; very low-quality evidence) and judged a clinically relevant pain reduction ruled out at 24 hours (SMD -0.14 relative, -0.25 to -0.04) and 48 hours (SMD -0.11 relative, -0.25 to 0.04). Point estimates favoured lidocaine for ileus (risk ratio 0.37 relative, 0.15 to 0.87; 4 studies), time to first defaecation (mean difference -7.92 hours, -12.71 to -3.13; 12 studies), postoperative nausea (risk ratio 0.78 relative, 0.67 to 0.91; 35 studies) and opioid consumption (mean difference -4.52 mg morphine equivalents, -6.25 to -2.79; 40 studies) — all rated very low quality. Comparisons with epidural analgesia (2 trials, 102 participants) were unclear on every outcome.
cards.watchOut: A review card, not a trial: its role is to discipline the anchor trial's optimism. 'Very low quality' in GRADE means the true effects may be substantially different from these estimates in either direction.
cards.source: Weibel S et al. Continuous intravenous perioperative lidocaine infusion for postoperative pain and recovery in adults. Cochrane Database Syst Rev. 2018. PMID: 29864216. cards.headline: Synthesis: faster bowel recovery is plausible, a pain benefit is not established — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: faster bowel recovery is plausible, a pain benefit is not established — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Herroeder 2007 (60 colorectal patients) and Weibel 2018 Cochrane review (68 trials, 4,525 participants).
cards.result: The recovery story (bowel function back sooner, stay about a day shorter in the anchor trial; pooled ileus risk ratio 0.37 relative) is more consistent than the analgesia story: the anchor trial itself found no pain difference, and the Cochrane review rules out a clinically relevant pain effect beyond 24 hours. POSSIBLE for a modest recovery benefit; no stamp is offered for pain relief. Intravenous lidocaine as an ED analgesic is a different question, home on Shelf #1239.
cards.watchOut: Dose and duration varied fivefold across the pooled trials (1-5 mg/kg/hour, hours to days), so 'lidocaine infusion' is not one intervention; toxicity monitoring practice also varied and adverse effects were rarely systematically collected.

shelves.title: Dexmedetomidine to prevent emergence agitation after sevoflurane in children
shelves.question: In children recovering from sevoflurane anaesthesia, does a single dose of dexmedetomidine reduce emergence agitation versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adenoidectomy · Aging · Anesthesia, Inhalation/adverse effects · Anesthetics, Inhalation/adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Dexmedetomidine/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Infant · Male · Psychomotor Agitation/drug therapy,prevention & control · Sevoflurane · Tonsillectomy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind trials agree on direction. Ibacache 2004 (90 children aged 1-10): emergence agitation occurred in 37% on saline versus 17% on dexmedetomidine 0.15 micrograms/kg and 10% on 0.30 micrograms/kg (P<0.05), with no difference in eye-opening time or PACU discharge and no adverse effects. Guler 2005 (60 children aged 3-7, adenotonsillectomy): agitation and pain scores were significantly better with dexmedetomidine 0.5 micrograms/kg (P<0.05), severe agitation and severe pain were significantly less frequent, and severe coughing was reduced — but emergence and extubation times were significantly longer. Consistent small trials on a behaviour-score endpoint, with a real trade-off against recovery time, cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Ibacache 2004: dexmedetomidine 0.3 micrograms/kg cut emergence agitation from 37% to 10% after sevoflurane in children
cards.summary: Ibacache 2004: dexmedetomidine 0.3 micrograms/kg cut emergence agitation from 37% to 10% after sevoflurane in children
cards.people: 90 children aged 1 to 10 years having superficial lower abdominal and genital surgery under sevoflurane, randomised after induction to saline (30), dexmedetomidine 0.15 micrograms/kg (30) or dexmedetomidine 0.30 micrograms/kg (30); all received a caudal block. The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: The incidence of emergence agitation was 37% (95% CI 20 to 54) in the saline group, 17% (4 to 30) with 0.15 micrograms/kg and 10% (0 to 21) with 0.30 micrograms/kg (P<0.05; the saline versus 0.30 dose comparison was significant, 95% CI for the difference 7 to 47). Time to eye opening was 7.5 (SD 5.0) minutes on saline, 8.2 (SD 5.0) on the low dose and 9.8 (SD 4.0) on the higher dose (not significant), and PACU discharge times were similar. No adverse effects attributable to dexmedetomidine were observed.
cards.watchOut: Ninety children having minor surgery with caudal analgesia — pain, a major agitation driver, was already blocked; the dose response (17% at the lower dose, not clearly separated from saline) leaves the minimum effective dose uncertain.
cards.source: Ibacache ME et al. Single-dose dexmedetomidine reduces agitation after sevoflurane anesthesia in children. Anesth Analg. 2004. PMID: 14693585. shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in coronary-artery surgery (ATACAS)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing coronary-artery surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce transfusion and major haemorrhage without increasing death or thrombotic complications?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antifibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aspirin/therapeutic use · Blood Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Coronary Artery Bypass · Coronary Artery Disease/mortality,surgery · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Platelet Aggregation Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Postoperative Complications/chemically induced · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Seizures/chemically induced · Thrombosis/chemically induced · Tranexamic Acid/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, the primary outcome is a death/thrombotic composite): In the one large blinded trial (ATACAS, 4,631 patients analysed), tranexamic acid did not increase the composite of death and thrombotic complications within 30 days (16.7% vs 18.1% on placebo; relative risk 0.92 relative, 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.22), while total blood-product transfusion fell from 7,994 to 4,331 units (P<0.001) and major haemorrhage or tamponade requiring reoperation halved (1.4% vs 2.8%; P=0.001). The price was seizures: 0.7% versus 0.1% (P=0.002). This shelf covers coronary surgery only; the general perioperative TXA question is home on Shelf #138 and POISE-3 on Shelf #1124.

cards.headline: ATACAS 2017: TXA cut transfusion and reoperation for bleeding, did not raise the death/thrombotic composite, but increased seizures (0.7% vs 0.1%)
cards.summary: ATACAS 2017: TXA cut transfusion and reoperation for bleeding, did not raise the death/thrombotic composite, but increased seizures (0.7% vs 0.1%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with a 2-by-2 factorial design (the aspirin comparison is reported separately)
cards.people: 4,662 patients at risk for perioperative complications scheduled for coronary-artery surgery consented; 4,631 underwent surgery with outcome data — 2,311 assigned tranexamic acid and 2,320 placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary outcome (composite of death and thrombotic complications — nonfatal myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism, renal failure or bowel infarction — within 30 days) occurred in 386 patients (16.7%) on tranexamic acid versus 420 (18.1%) on placebo (relative risk 0.92 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.81 to 1.05; P=0.22). Total blood products transfused were 4,331 units versus 7,994 units (P<0.001). Major haemorrhage or cardiac tamponade leading to reoperation occurred in 1.4% versus 2.8% (P=0.001), and seizures in 0.7% versus 0.1% (P=0.002). Heart-failure outcomes are not reported in this record; the composite's mortality component is reported only within the composite, not separately, and no mortality difference is claimed on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The seizure signal is dose-relevant in the wider literature but this record tests one regimen; the composite blends death with softer thrombotic events, and the trial cannot exclude a small thrombotic increase (upper confidence limit 1.05 relative).

shelves.title: Aprotinin versus lysine analogues in high-risk cardiac surgery (BART)
shelves.question: In high-risk cardiac surgery, how do aprotinin, tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid compare on major bleeding and mortality?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Aminocaproates/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Antifibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Aprotinin/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Blood Transfusion/statistics & numerical data · Cardiac Surgical Procedures/mortality · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Lysine/analogs & derivatives · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Hemorrhage/epidemiology,prevention & control · Tranexamic Acid/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (harm) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality harm): The one head-to-head blinded trial (BART, 2,331 high-risk cardiac-surgery patients) was terminated early because of higher mortality with aprotinin. Massive postoperative bleeding was modestly less frequent with aprotinin (9.5% vs 12.1% on tranexamic acid and 12.1% on aminocaproic acid; relative risk 0.79 relative, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.05 for both comparisons), but 30-day death was 6.0% on aprotinin versus 3.9% on tranexamic acid (relative risk 1.55 relative, 0.99 to 2.42) and 4.0% on aminocaproic acid (relative risk 1.52 relative, 0.98 to 2.36); against both lysine analogues combined the relative risk of death was 1.53 relative (1.06 to 2.22). A large blinded trial stopped for a consistent mortality trend carries LIKELY (harm).

cards.headline: BART 2008: aprotinin bled slightly less but died more — 30-day mortality 6.0% versus 3.9% (TXA) and 4.0% (aminocaproic acid); trial stopped early
cards.summary: BART 2008: aprotinin bled slightly less but died more — 30-day mortality 6.0% versus 3.9% (TXA) and 4.0% (aminocaproic acid); trial stopped early
cards.type: Multicentre, blinded, randomised three-arm trial — terminated early for excess mortality in the aprotinin arm
cards.people: 2,331 high-risk cardiac surgical patients randomised to aprotinin (781), tranexamic acid (770) or aminocaproic acid (780). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Massive postoperative bleeding (primary outcome) occurred in 74 patients (9.5%) on aprotinin, 93 (12.1%) on tranexamic acid and 94 (12.1%) on aminocaproic acid (relative risk for aprotinin 0.79 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.59 to 1.05 for both comparisons). Death from any cause at 30 days was 6.0% on aprotinin versus 3.9% on tranexamic acid (relative risk 1.55 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 2.42) and 4.0% on aminocaproic acid (relative risk 1.52 relative, 95% CI 0.98 to 2.36); versus the two lysine-analogue groups combined, the relative risk of death with aprotinin was 1.53 relative (95% CI 1.06 to 2.22). The trial was terminated early because of the higher death rate in the aprotinin group.
cards.watchOut: Early termination can exaggerate an effect, and the pairwise mortality intervals just cross 1.0 — but the direction is identical against both comparators, the combined comparison excludes 1.0, and the bleeding advantage (about 2.6 points) is far smaller than the mortality disadvantage (about 2 points on a lower baseline risk).
cards.source: Fergusson DA et al. A comparison of aprotinin and lysine analogues in high-risk cardiac surgery. N Engl J Med. 2008. PMID: 18480196. shelves.title: Intraoperative methadone versus morphine for postoperative analgesia
shelves.question: In patients having cardiac or major surgery, does a single intraoperative dose of methadone reduce postoperative pain and opioid requirements versus morphine?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analgesia, Patient-Controlled · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Coronary Artery Bypass · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Male · Methadone/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Morphine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/diagnosis,drug therapy,prevention & control · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small double-blind cardiac-surgery trials lean the same way. Udelsmann 2011 (55 patients, three arms including placebo) reports the first rescue analgesic came later, fewer doses were needed, analgesia quality was better and nausea/vomiting less frequent with a single 20 mg induction dose of methadone than 20 mg morphine — but prints no numbers. Carvalho 2018 (100 patients, off-pump CABG) found lower pain scores at 24 hours with methadone (1.9 [SD 2.2] vs 2.9 [SD 2.6]; P=0.029) and fewer patients requiring rescue morphine (29% vs 43%; P=0.002) — yet, inconsistently, a SHORTER time to first analgesic request in the methadone group (145.9 vs 269.4 minutes; P=0.005), an internal contradiction in the record that is flagged on the card. Small trials, an analgesic-consumption surrogate and one inconsistent record cap at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Udelsmann 2011: methadone at induction delayed and reduced rescue analgesia versus morphine or placebo in cardiac surgery (no figures in abstract)
cards.summary: Udelsmann 2011: methadone at induction delayed and reduced rescue analgesia versus morphine or placebo in cardiac surgery (no figures in abstract)

cards.people: 55 patients scheduled for cardiac surgery, divided into three groups receiving 20 mg methadone, 20 mg morphine or placebo at anaesthetic induction. The abstract does not state the per-group numbers, mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Duration of anaesthesia and time to extubation did not differ between groups. The first analgesic dose in the methadone group was administered later than in the other two groups; the need for analgesics was lower, the quality of analgesia (patient-assessed) was better, and the prevalence of nausea and vomiting was lower with methadone. The abstract reports no numerical values, event counts or P values for these outcomes, so none are printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: A 55-patient, three-arm trial reported qualitatively: its role is directional corroboration of the larger trial below, and anyone quoting effect sizes for it is quoting beyond this record.

cards.headline: Carvalho 2018: methadone lowered 24-hour pain scores (1.9 vs 2.9) and rescue-morphine use (29% vs 43%) after off-pump CABG — with one internally inconsistent result
cards.summary: Carvalho 2018: methadone lowered 24-hour pain scores (1.9 vs 2.9) and rescue-morphine use (29% vs 43%) after off-pump CABG — with one internally inconsistent result
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, parallel clinical trial (off-pump coronary bypass)
cards.people: 100 patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting without extracorporeal circulation, randomised to methadone 0.1 mg/kg adjusted body weight (50) or morphine 0.1 mg/kg (50) intravenously at the end of surgery, with pain and analgesic use assessed to 36 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean numerical pain score at 24 hours was 1.9 (SD 2.2) in the methadone group versus 2.9 (SD 2.6) in the morphine group (P=0.029). Fewer methadone patients required rescue morphine (29% vs 43%; P=0.002), and the authors report a number-needed-to-treat of 6 and number-needed-to-harm of 16 for methadone. However, time to first analgesic request was reported as 145.9 (SD 178.5) minutes in the methadone group versus 269.4 (SD 252.9) in the morphine group (P=0.005) — shorter with methadone, which runs against the trial's other findings and its conclusion, and is reproduced here exactly as the record states it.
cards.watchOut: The record contradicts itself: less rescue use and lower pain scores, but a shorter time to first request, in the methadone arm. Whether this is a labelling error in the abstract cannot be resolved from the record — the card prints both figures and the stamp discounts the trial accordingly.

shelves.title: Perioperative gabapentin for postoperative pain and opioid sparing
shelves.question: In adults having surgery, does perioperative gabapentin reduce postoperative opioid requirements and pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Gabapentin/therapeutic use · Analgesics, Opioid · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Oxycodone · Pain Management/methods · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy,etiology,prevention & control · Double-Blind Method
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The two carded records barely test the shelf's question. The topic file's anchor (Guanzon 2026, 114 prolapse-surgery patients) does not compare gabapentin with placebo at all — it compares preoperative-only gabapentin (with postoperative placebo) against pre- plus postoperative gabapentin, and could NOT conclude the shorter course was noninferior for opioid prescription at discharge (27.0% vs 32.0%; absolute difference 5.0%, 95% CI -12 to 21, crossing the 20% margin). The one placebo-controlled trial carded (Lerner 2024, 35 sinus-surgery patients) found no significant difference in pain (P=0.18) or opioid consumption (2.3 vs 4.8 oxycodone tablets; P=0.18) — numerically FEWER tablets on placebo, in an operation where 15 of 35 patients needed no opioid at all. As carded, the placebo-controlled evidence is one tiny null trial: MAYBE (weak evidence). A large older RCT literature exists per the topic file but was not verified for this pack and is not carded.

cards.headline: Guanzon 2026: stopping gabapentin after the preoperative dose was not proven noninferior to continuing it (opioid prescription at discharge 32.0% vs 27.0%)
cards.summary: Guanzon 2026: stopping gabapentin after the preoperative dose was not proven noninferior to continuing it (opioid prescription at discharge 32.0% vs 27.0%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blinded, placebo-controlled noninferiority trial (prolapse surgery) — a DURATION comparison, not gabapentin versus placebo
cards.people: 114 patients undergoing prolapse repair who completed participation: 55 received preoperative and postoperative gabapentin (control) and 59 received preoperative gabapentin with postoperative placebo (experimental); all also received acetaminophen and ibuprofen, with oxycodone as needed. The abstract does not state mean age.
cards.result: An opioid prescription at discharge was required by 27.0% of the control group versus 32.0% of the experimental group (P=0.57; absolute risk difference 5.0%, 95% CI -12 to 21). Refill or new opioid prescriptions within 6 weeks were requested by 10.9% versus 15.3% (P=0.49). Because the upper confidence limit (21%) exceeded the prespecified 20% noninferiority margin, the authors could not conclude that the preoperative-only strategy was noninferior. Secondary outcomes included pain scores, morphine milligram equivalents, nausea and sedation scores; the abstract does not report their values.
cards.watchOut: Every patient received gabapentin preoperatively, so this trial cannot say whether gabapentin itself spares opioids — only that its postoperative continuation was not proven dispensable. The topic file listed it as the shelf's anchor for the placebo question; the record does not support that use, and the card says so.

cards.result: There was no significant difference in mean postoperative pain scores (P=0.18) or postoperative opioid consumption (2.3 oxycodone tablets in the placebo group and 4.8 in the gabapentin group; P=0.18). cards.headline: Synthesis: as carded, the placebo-controlled evidence is one tiny null trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.summary: Synthesis: as carded, the placebo-controlled evidence is one tiny null trial — MAYBE (weak evidence)
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Guanzon 2026 (114 patients, duration comparison) and Lerner 2024 (35 patients, placebo-controlled).
cards.result: Nothing carded here shows perioperative gabapentin reducing pain or opioid use versus placebo: the only placebo-controlled trial is null in 35 low-pain surgical patients, and the larger trial answers a different question (duration) inconclusively. The stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) — the developer's category for 'we don't know' — and the shelf should be rebuilt if the older large RCT literature is verified and carded. Gabapentin for chronic pain is a different question, home on Shelf #345; gabapentin after burn debridement is Shelf #1278.

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): The one randomised test (de Silva 2003, 401 patients in Sri Lanka, single-blind) found death in 5 of 201 patients (2.5%) given multiple-dose activated charcoal versus 16 of 200 (8%) on placebo (percentage difference 5.5%, 95% CI 0.6 to 10.3; P=0.025), with secondary endpoints (life-threatening arrhythmias, atropine dose, pacing, ICU admission) also favouring charcoal. A single single-blind, single-country trial carries POSSIBLE. Note the tension with Shelf #1251: in the much larger unselected self-poisoning trial — over a third of whose patients had taken oleander — multiple-dose charcoal showed no mortality benefit overall; the two shelves answer different questions (oleander-specific protocol versus routine use) and both records stand.

cards.headline: de Silva 2003: multiple-dose charcoal cut oleander-poisoning deaths from 8% to 2.5% (difference 5.5 points; P=0.025)
cards.summary: de Silva 2003: multiple-dose charcoal cut oleander-poisoning deaths from 8% to 2.5% (difference 5.5 points; P=0.025)
cards.people: 401 patients with yellow oleander poisoning: 201 received multiple-dose activated charcoal (50 g every 6 hours for 3 days, after a single admission dose given to all participants) and 200 received sterile water as placebo, alongside a standard treatment protocol. cards.result: Deaths (primary endpoint) were 5 (2.5%) in the treatment group versus 16 (8%) in the placebo group (percentage difference 5.5%, 95% CI 0.6 to 10.3; P=0.025). All secondary endpoints — life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias, dose of atropine used, need for cardiac pacing and intensive-care admission — favoured the treatment group, except number of days in hospital. The treatment was reported as safe and well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (patients, not necessarily assessors, were blinded by the placebo design as described), single-country, and 21 deaths in total: the confidence interval (0.6 to 10.3 points) is wide, and the result predates modern Fab/pacing availability in the study setting.

shelves.title: Activated charcoal dosing strategy in acute self-poisoning
shelves.question: In adults presenting after acute self-poisoning, does single-dose or multiple-dose activated charcoal reduce mortality versus no charcoal?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Antidotes/administration & dosage · Charcoal/administration & dosage · Female · Glasgow Coma Scale · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Organophosphate Poisoning · Pesticides/poisoning · Poisoning/classification,drug therapy,mortality · Rural Population · Sri Lanka · Suicide, Attempted · Thevetia/poisoning · Treatment Failure
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality primary outcome): The one large randomised test (Eddleston 2008, 4,632 patients in three Sri Lankan hospitals, open-label) found mortality of 6.3% with six doses of activated charcoal versus 6.8% with no charcoal (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.70 to 1.33), with no differences in subgroups by poison type, severity on admission or early presentation; the single-dose arm was randomised alongside (1,545 patients) and the report's headline comparison is multiple-dose versus none. The confidence interval still admits a worthwhile benefit or harm, and the design was open-label — so the null is stamped POSSIBLE, not LIKELY. The oleander-specific trial (Shelf #1250) found a benefit in its narrower population; both records stand.

cards.headline: Eddleston 2008: in 4,632 self-poisoning patients, mortality was 6.3% with multiple-dose charcoal versus 6.8% with no charcoal (adjusted OR 0.96 relative)
cards.summary: Eddleston 2008: in 4,632 self-poisoning patients, mortality was 6.3% with multiple-dose charcoal versus 6.8% with no charcoal (adjusted OR 0.96 relative)
cards.type: Open-label, parallel-group, randomised controlled trial in three Sri Lankan hospitals
cards.people: 4,632 patients presenting after acute self-poisoning randomised to no charcoal (1,554), a single 50 g dose of activated charcoal (1,545) or six 50 g doses at 4-hour intervals (1,533); outcomes were available for 4,629. Pesticides accounted for 51% of ingestions and yellow oleander seeds for 36%. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Deaths were 97 of 1,531 (6.3%) in the multiple-dose group versus 105 of 1,554 (6.8%) in the no-charcoal group (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.70 to 1.33). No differences were noted for patients who took particular poisons, were severely ill on admission, or who presented early. The abstract's findings paragraph reports the multiple-dose versus no-charcoal comparison; the single-dose arm's mortality figure is not stated in the abstract and is not printed here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and the interval (0.70 to 1.33 relative) cannot exclude a 30% relative mortality reduction — this is 'no benefit shown', not 'benefit disproven'. Rural Sri Lankan poison mix (pesticides, oleander) also differs from urban Western overdose caseloads.

shelves.title: Shortened acetylcysteine regimens for paracetamol poisoning
shelves.question: In patients treated for paracetamol overdose, can acetylcysteine be stopped early or given in a two-bag regimen without loss of protection, and with fewer adverse reactions, versus the standard three-bag regimen?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/antagonists & inhibitors,poisoning · Acetylcysteine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Adult · Aged · Alanine Transaminase/blood,metabolism · Antiemetics/administration & dosage · Australia · Chemical and Drug Induced Liver Injury/drug therapy · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Drug Overdose/drug therapy · Female · Humans · Liver Failure, Acute/chemically induced,prevention & control · Male · Middle Aged · Ondansetron/administration & dosage · Vomiting/chemically induced,prevention & control
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two randomised trials support shorter, gentler acetylcysteine in selected patients. NACSTOP 2 (Wong 2026, 186 low-risk patients): stopping the two-bag regimen at about 13 hours was non-inferior to the full 20 hours on the prespecified liver-enzyme endpoint (difference in median ALT change -1 IU/L, 95% CI -2 to 1, against a 3 IU/L margin), and no patient in either group developed hepatic injury — but entry required a normal ALT both at presentation and after 12 hours of treatment, so this is a low-risk subgroup result. SNAP (Bateman 2014, 222 patients): a 12-hour modified regimen halved vomiting/retching/rescue-antiemetic use at 2 hours (39 of 108 vs 71 of 109; adjusted odds ratio 0.26 relative, 97.5% CI 0.13 to 0.52) and cut severe anaphylactoid reactions (5 vs 31; adjusted common odds ratio 0.23 relative), with no difference in ALT rise — though SNAP was explicitly not powered to prove the shorter regimen equally protective. Supportive but bounded evidence: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: NACSTOP 2 2026: stopping acetylcysteine at ~13 hours was non-inferior to the full 20-hour two-bag regimen in low-risk patients (ALT difference -1 IU/L)
cards.summary: NACSTOP 2 2026: stopping acetylcysteine at ~13 hours was non-inferior to the full 20-hour two-bag regimen in low-risk patients (ALT difference -1 IU/L)
cards.type: Open-label, non-inferiority randomised controlled trial (six Australian metropolitan EDs)
cards.people: 186 adults randomised (93 stopped early, 93 full regimen) from 860 patients who received acetylcysteine after paracetamol overdose; entry required ALT below 40 IU/L at presentation AND, after 12 hours of treatment, ALT below 40 IU/L with serum paracetamol below 20 mg/L. Median age was 17 years (IQR 16-23) and 162 (87%) were women — a strikingly young cohort, as the record states.
cards.result: Median acetylcysteine infusion time in the early-stop group was 13 hours. The median change in ALT between arrival and 20 hours was -1 IU/L (IQR -4 to 1) with early cessation versus 0 IU/L (IQR -2 to 2) with the full regimen (difference in median change -1 IU/L, 95% CI -2 to 1), meeting the non-inferiority criterion (upper limit below 3 IU/L). No patients in either group developed hepatic injury or hepatotoxicity.
cards.watchOut: Noninferiority on an enzyme surrogate in patients pre-selected for low risk (normal ALT twice over): the trial cannot speak to stopping early in patients with rising enzymes or late presentations, and with zero hepatotoxicity events it was not powered on clinical liver failure.
cards.source: Wong A et al. Early Cessation of Acetylcysteine Treatment After Paracetamol Overdose (NACSTOP 2): A Non-Inferiority Randomised Controlled Trial. Med J Aust. 2026. PMID: 41549406. cards.headline: SNAP 2014: a 12-hour modified regimen caused far less vomiting (36% vs 65%) and fewer severe anaphylactoid reactions (5 vs 31) than the standard regimen
cards.summary: SNAP 2014: a 12-hour modified regimen caused far less vomiting (36% vs 65%) and fewer severe anaphylactoid reactions (5 vs 31) than the standard regimen
cards.type: Double-blind, randomised factorial trial at three UK hospitals (regimen duration × ondansetron pretreatment)
cards.people: 222 patients with acute paracetamol overdose randomised between the standard intravenous acetylcysteine regimen (20.25 hours) and a shorter 12-hour modified protocol, each with or without intravenous ondansetron 4 mg pretreatment; 217 were assessable at 2 hours. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Vomiting, retching or rescue-antiemetic need at 2 hours occurred in 39 of 108 patients on the shorter regimen versus 71 of 109 on the standard regimen (adjusted odds ratio 0.26 — a relative measure — 97.5% CI 0.13 to 0.52; P<0.0001), and in 45 of 109 with ondansetron versus 65 of 108 with placebo (0.41 relative, 0.20 to 0.80; P=0.003). Severe anaphylactoid reactions occurred in 5 patients on the shorter regimen versus 31 on the standard (adjusted common odds ratio 0.23 relative, 97.5% CI 0.12 to 0.43; P<0.0001). A greater-than-50% ALT rise did not differ between regimens (13 of 112 shorter vs 9 of 110 standard) but was more frequent with ondansetron (16 of 111 vs 6 of 111; odds ratio 3.30 relative; P=0.024).
cards.watchOut: SNAP's primary outcome was tolerability at 2 hours, and the authors state plainly that the trial was not powered to detect non-inferiority of protection — the efficacy reassurance comes from the ALT secondary outcome and, for early stopping, from NACSTOP 2.

cards.headline: Synthesis: shorter regimens are gentler and, in low-risk patients, non-inferior on enzyme outcomes — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: shorter regimens are gentler and, in low-risk patients, non-inferior on enzyme outcomes — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: NACSTOP 2 2026 (186 low-risk patients, early cessation) and SNAP 2014 (222 patients, 12-hour modified regimen).
cards.result: The two trials answer complementary halves: SNAP shows a shorter regimen is far better tolerated (vomiting 39/108 vs 71/109; severe anaphylactoid reactions 5 vs 31) without an ALT signal of lost protection, and NACSTOP 2 shows that in patients with normal ALT at presentation and at 12 hours, stopping at ~13 hours is non-inferior to 20 hours on enzyme change with no hepatic injury in either arm. shelves.title: Physostigmine versus lorazepam for anticholinergic toxidrome
shelves.question: In patients with antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) delirium, does physostigmine resolve delirium more effectively than lorazepam?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Akathisia, Drug-Induced/drug therapy · Anti-Anxiety Agents/therapeutic use · Delirium/chemically induced,drug therapy · Diphenhydramine/toxicity · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Lorazepam/therapeutic use · Male · Muscarinic Antagonists/toxicity · Physostigmine/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one blinded randomised trial (Wang 2021) is tiny — 19 adolescents — but the separation is large: delirium persisted after the initial bolus in 44% on physostigmine versus 100% on lorazepam (P=0.01), and at the 4th hour of infusion in 22% versus 100% (P<0.001); agitation scores improved significantly more often after the physostigmine bolus (89% vs 30%; P=0.02), with no seizures, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, intubation or dysrhythmias in either arm. A single very small trial in adolescents (84% diphenhydramine ingestions) caps at POSSIBLE. The older Burns trial named in the topic file could not be verified from the fetched records and is not carded.

cards.headline: Wang 2021: physostigmine cleared antimuscarinic delirium far more often than lorazepam (delirium at 4 hours 22% vs 100%) in 19 adolescents
cards.summary: Wang 2021: physostigmine cleared antimuscarinic delirium far more often than lorazepam (delirium at 4 hours 22% vs 100%) in 19 adolescents
cards.type: Blinded, randomised clinical trial (adolescents with antimuscarinic toxidrome)
cards.people: 19 patients aged 10 to under 18 years with at least one central and two peripheral antimuscarinic symptoms, delirium and moderate agitation: 10 received lorazepam 0.05 mg/kg bolus then saline infusion and 9 received physostigmine 0.02 mg/kg bolus then a 4-hour physostigmine infusion (0.02 mg/kg/hour). Diphenhydramine was the ingested agent in 16 (84%). The abstract does not state the sex mix.
cards.result: Fewer physostigmine patients had delirium after the initial bolus (44% vs 100%; P=0.01) and at the 4th hour of infusion (22% vs 100%; P<0.001). A significant decrease in agitation scores occurred in 89% of the physostigmine arm versus 30% of the lorazepam arm after the bolus (P=0.02), with no difference by the 4th hour (P>0.99). There were no seizures, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, intubations or cardiac dysrhythmias in either arm.
cards.watchOut: Nineteen patients, adolescents only, and mostly one ingested drug (diphenhydramine): percentages like '22% versus 100%' are 2 of 9 versus 10 of 10 — dramatic, but a handful of patients changing group would move them, and adult tricyclic-era toxidromes are untested here.

shelves.title: Octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
shelves.question: In patients with sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia, does adding octreotide to dextrose reduce recurrent hypoglycaemia versus dextrose alone?

shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one verified double-blind randomised trial (Fasano 2008, 40 ED patients) found that a single 75-microgram subcutaneous dose of octreotide added to standard dextrose therapy kept serum glucose consistently higher over the first 8 hours (differences significant from 4 to 8 hours, approaching significance at 1 to 3 hours), with no difference in later hours, and the authors report recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes occurred less frequently with octreotide — without printing the episode counts. A single 40-patient trial on a glucose surrogate caps at POSSIBLE. The older Boyle trial named in the topic file could not be verified from the fetched records and is not carded.

cards.headline: Fasano 2008: octreotide kept glucose higher for 8 hours after sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, with fewer recurrences reported
cards.summary: Fasano 2008: octreotide kept glucose higher for 8 hours after sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, with fewer recurrences reported
cards.people: 40 adults presenting to the ED with hypoglycaemia (serum glucose at or below 60 mg/dL) while taking a sulfonylurea (or insulin plus sulfonylurea), randomised to standard treatment (50% dextrose IV plus oral carbohydrate) with octreotide 75 micrograms subcutaneously (22) or with saline placebo (18). Mean presenting glucose was 39 mg/dL in the octreotide group and 35 mg/dL in the placebo group; the abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mean glucose values were consistently higher in the octreotide group during the first 8 hours — approaching statistical significance from 1 to 3 hours and significant from 4 to 8 hours — with no difference in subsequent hours. The authors state that recurrent hypoglycaemic episodes occurred less frequently in patients who received octreotide than in those who received placebo; the abstract does not give the episode counts or glucose values, so none are printed here.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, a single octreotide dose, and subsequent care left to the inpatient team's discretion: the trial shows a glucose-curve effect, and its recurrence claim is unquantified in the record.

shelves.title: Pralidoxime infusion versus bolus in organophosphate poisoning
shelves.question: In patients with organophosphorus pesticide poisoning, does continuous pralidoxime infusion improve outcomes (mortality, ventilation duration) versus repeated bolus dosing?
shelves.mesh: Acetylcholinesterase/metabolism · Adult · Antidotes/adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use · Atropine/pharmacology · Blood Pressure · Cholinesterase Reactivators/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · India · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · Insecticides/poisoning · Intubation, Intratracheal · Logistic Models · Male · Organophosphate Poisoning · Pesticides/poisoning · Poisoning/mortality · Pralidoxime Compounds/administration & dosage,adverse effects,pharmacokinetics,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, mortality in the outcome set): The balance is genuinely contested. Pawar 2006 (200 patients, open trial, India) found a high-dose constant infusion (1 g/hour for 48 hours after a 2 g load) beat repeated bolus dosing on every reported measure: median atropine need in 24 hours 6 mg versus 30 mg (P<0.0001), intubation 64% versus 88% (relative risk 0.72 relative, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.86), and ventilation 5 versus 10 days (P<0.0001); its abstract asserts a mortality benefit in its interpretation but prints no mortality figures. Eddleston 2009 (235 patients, double-blind, Sri Lanka) asked the prior question — pralidoxime versus NO pralidoxime at a lower infusion dose — and found mortality nonsignificantly HIGHER with pralidoxime (24.8% vs 15.8%; adjusted hazard ratio 1.69 relative, 95% CI 0.88 to 3.26; P=0.12) despite clear acetylcholinesterase reactivation. A positive open regimen trial against a null double-blind placebo trial caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Pawar 2006: high-dose pralidoxime infusion cut intubation (64% vs 88%) and halved ventilation time versus bolus dosing
cards.summary: Pawar 2006: high-dose pralidoxime infusion cut intubation (64% vs 88%) and halved ventilation time versus bolus dosing
cards.type: Single-centre, open randomised controlled trial (moderately severe organophosphorus poisoning, India)
cards.people: 200 patients with moderately severe anticholinesterase pesticide poisoning, all given a 2 g pralidoxime loading dose, then randomised to constant infusion of 1 g/hour for 48 hours (100) or bolus doses of 1 g every 4 hours for 48 hours (100), with pralidoxime continued for all until ventilator weaning. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The high-dose infusion group required less atropine in the first 24 hours (median 6 mg vs 30 mg; difference 24 mg, 95% CI 24 to 26; P<0.0001). Intubation was needed in 64 of 100 infusion patients versus 88 of 100 controls (relative risk 0.72 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.62 to 0.86; P=0.0001), and ventilatory support lasted a median of 5 versus 10 days (difference 5 days, 95% CI 5 to 6; P<0.0001). The abstract's interpretation states the regimen 'reduces morbidity and mortality', but no mortality counts or rates appear in the abstract's findings, so no mortality figure is printed on this card.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with no placebo arm, in one centre's moderately severe caseload: the comparison is dose regimen, not drug versus nothing, and the unprinted mortality claim cannot be weighted. The neighbouring double-blind trial (next card) is the necessary counterweight.
cards.source: Pawar KS et al. Continuous pralidoxime infusion versus repeated bolus injection to treat organophosphorus pesticide poisoning: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2006. PMID: 17174705. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00333944, from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Eddleston 2009: pralidoxime versus placebo — mortality was 24.8% versus 15.8% (adjusted HR 1.69 relative, not significant) despite enzyme reactivation
cards.summary: Eddleston 2009: pralidoxime versus placebo — mortality was 24.8% versus 15.8% (adjusted HR 1.69 relative, not significant) despite enzyme reactivation
cards.type: Double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (organophosphorus insecticide self-poisoning, Sri Lanka)
cards.people: 235 patients with organophosphorus insecticide self-poisoning randomised to pralidoxime chloride (2 g load then 0.5 g/hour infusion for up to 7 days; 121) or saline placebo (114), all with atropine and supportive care. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Mortality (primary outcome) was 30 of 121 (24.8%) with pralidoxime versus 18 of 114 (15.8%) with placebo (adjusted hazard ratio 1.69 — a relative measure — 95% CI 0.88 to 3.26; P=0.12). Intubation was similar (26 of 121 [21.5%] vs 24 of 114 [21.1%]; adjusted hazard ratio 1.27 relative, 0.71 to 2.29). Pralidoxime produced substantial red-cell acetylcholinesterase reactivation in diethyl-compound poisoning and moderate reactivation in dimethyl poisoning, yet adjusting for aged enzyme and plasma insecticide levels moved the mortality estimate further against pralidoxime; the chlorpyrifos/dimethoate subgroup showed no benefit either.
cards.watchOut: A different question from Pawar (drug versus none, at half Pawar's infusion rate, in self-poisoning with mixed compounds): it does not directly refute the high-dose regimen comparison, but it removes any presumption that more pralidoxime exposure is beneficial.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the regimen trial is positive, the placebo trial is null-to-harmful — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.summary: Synthesis: the regimen trial is positive, the placebo trial is null-to-harmful — POSSIBLE, Tier C
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Pawar 2006 (200 patients, infusion versus bolus) and Eddleston 2009 (235 patients, pralidoxime versus placebo).
cards.result: Read together, the oxime evidence cannot carry more than POSSIBLE: if pralidoxime is given, Pawar's high-dose infusion outperformed bolus dosing on atropine need (6 vs 30 mg), intubation (64% vs 88%) and ventilation days (5 vs 10) — but the only double-blind placebo-controlled test found no survival or intubation benefit and a nonsignificant mortality excess (24.8% vs 15.8%). shelves.title: Magnesium sulfate as an adjuvant in organophosphate poisoning
shelves.question: In acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning, does adding intravenous magnesium sulfate to standard atropine/oxime therapy improve outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adolescent · Adult · Atropine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Bangladesh · Cholinesterase Reactivators/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Magnesium/urine · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Muscarinic Antagonists/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Organophosphate Poisoning/drug therapy,physiopathology,urine · Pralidoxime Compounds/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Severity of Illness Index · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The only carded record is a phase II dose-finding safety study (Basher 2013, 50 patients): magnesium was well tolerated with no adverse reactions at total doses of 4 to 16 g, and deaths were distributed 6 of 10 in the small placebo group versus 3 of 16, 2 of 8, 1 of 8 and 0 of 8 across the ascending dose groups. Those mortality counts come from sequential dose-escalation groups of 8-16 patients with a 1-to-4 allocation ratio — the study was designed to test tolerability and magnesium handling, not efficacy, and its own conclusion is that larger studies are required. On this library's scale that is MAYBE (weak evidence): we don't know.

cards.headline: Basher 2013: magnesium up to 16 g was tolerated without adverse reactions in 50 OP-poisoning patients; efficacy untested by design
cards.summary: Basher 2013: magnesium up to 16 g was tolerated without adverse reactions in 50 OP-poisoning patients; efficacy untested by design
cards.type: Phase II dose-escalation study with a small placebo group (Bangladesh)
cards.people: 50 patients with moderate or severe acute organophosphate poisoning, all receiving standard atropinisation and pralidoxime, allocated in four sequential dose groups — 4 g (16 patients), 8 g (8), 12 g (8) and 16 g (8) total magnesium sulfate as intermittent boluses — with 10 placebo controls (one control per four magnesium patients). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: No adverse reactions to magnesium were observed (no significant neuromuscular disturbance or respiratory depression). Twenty-four-hour urinary magnesium at the 16 g dose (234.74 [SD 74.18] mg/dL) differed significantly from control (118.06 [SD 30.76] mg/dL; P=0.019) yet was much lower than 80% of the intravenous load. Deaths were 6 in the control group, 3 in the 4 g group, 2 in the 8 g group, 1 in the 12 g group and none in the 16 g group — counts the authors present descriptively; the study's stated conclusion is that magnesium was well tolerated and larger studies are required to examine efficacy.
cards.watchOut: Sequential dose groups of 8-16 patients are not an efficacy trial: the eye-catching death gradient (6 of 10 controls down to 0 of 8) is exactly the pattern small non-concurrent groups produce by chance and case-mix, and no statistical comparison of mortality is offered in the record.
cards.source: Basher A et al. Phase II study of magnesium sulfate in acute organophosphate pesticide poisoning. Clin Toxicol. 2013. PMID: 23311540. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Antivenom for scorpion envenomation in children (Boyer)
shelves.question: In critically ill children with neurotoxic scorpion envenomation, does scorpion-specific antivenom (F(ab')2) resolve the clinical syndrome faster than placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Animals · Antigens/blood · Antivenins/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Child · Child, Preschool · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Immunoglobulin Fab Fragments/therapeutic use · Infant · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Neuromuscular Diseases/drug therapy,etiology · Prospective Studies · Scorpion Stings/complications,drug therapy · Scorpion Venoms/immunology · Scorpions
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised test (Boyer 2009) is tiny (15 children) but the effect is categorical: the clinical syndrome resolved within 4 hours in all 8 antivenom recipients versus 1 of 7 on placebo (P=0.001), cumulative midazolam sedation was far lower with antivenom (0.07 vs 4.61 mg/kg; P=0.01), and plasma venom was undetectable 1 hour after treatment in all 8 treated children versus 1 on placebo (P=0.001). A double-blind trial with a near-deterministic result earns POSSIBLE despite n=15 — the stamp reflects the sample size, not doubt about direction.

cards.headline: Boyer 2009: scorpion antivenom resolved the syndrome within 4 hours in 8 of 8 children versus 1 of 7 on placebo
cards.summary: Boyer 2009: scorpion antivenom resolved the syndrome within 4 hours in 8 of 8 children versus 1 of 7 on placebo
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial (paediatric intensive care)
cards.people: 15 children aged 6 months to 18 years admitted to a paediatric ICU with clinically significant neurotoxic signs of Centruroides sculpturatus envenomation, randomised to scorpion-specific F(ab')2 antivenom (8) or placebo (7). The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: The primary endpoint — resolution of the clinical syndrome within 4 hours — occurred in all 8 antivenom recipients versus 1 of 7 placebo recipients (P=0.001). Mean cumulative midazolam dose was 0.07 mg/kg with antivenom versus 4.61 mg/kg with placebo (P=0.01). Plasma venom concentrations 1 hour after treatment were undetectable in all 8 antivenom recipients but in only 1 placebo recipient (P=0.001).
cards.watchOut: Fifteen children with one scorpion species in one region: the result is as strong as a trial this size can be, but it says nothing about other species, adults, or antivenom reactions at population scale.
cards.source: Boyer LV et al. Antivenom for critically ill children with neurotoxicity from scorpion stings. N Engl J Med. 2009. PMID: 19439743. shelves.title: Antivenom for redback spider envenomation (RAVE programme)
shelves.question: In patients with latrodectism from redback spider bite, does antivenom (intravenous or intramuscular) relieve pain better than placebo or standard analgesia?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Animals · Antivenins/administration & dosage,pharmacology,therapeutic use · Bayes Theorem · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Pain/drug therapy,etiology · Spider Bites/complications,drug therapy · Spider Venoms/antagonists & inhibitors
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The placebo-controlled test (RAVE-II, 224 patients) found antivenom added to standardised analgesia did NOT significantly improve pain at 2 hours (clinically significant improvement in 34% on antivenom vs 23% on placebo; difference 10.7%, 95% CI -1.1 to 22.6; P=.10) or resolution of systemic effects (26% vs 22%; difference 3.8%, -15 to 23; P=.79), with no secondary outcome significant and acute hypersensitivity reactions in 3.6% of antivenom recipients. The route trial (RAVE, 126 patients, all receiving antivenom) found intravenous barely ahead of intramuscular administration (pain improved 62% vs 53%; +9%, 95% credible interval -8 to +26) — a comparison the authors note is moot if the drug itself adds nothing over placebo. One well-run 224-patient null carries POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): the interval still admits a pain benefit of up to ~23 points.

cards.headline: RAVE-II 2014: redback antivenom did not significantly beat placebo for pain (34% vs 23% improved; P=.10), with hypersensitivity in 3.6%
cards.summary: RAVE-II 2014: redback antivenom did not significantly beat placebo for pain (34% vs 23% improved; P=.10), with hypersensitivity in 3.6%
cards.type: Multicentre randomised placebo-controlled trial (latrodectism, standardised analgesia in both arms)
cards.people: 224 patients over 7 years old with redback spider bite and severe pain, with or without systemic effects, randomised to antivenom (112) or normal saline placebo (112) after standardised analgesia. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: A clinically significant pain reduction at 2 hours (primary outcome) occurred in 38 of 112 antivenom patients (34%) versus 26 of 112 on placebo (23%) (difference in favour of antivenom 10.7%, 95% CI -1.1 to 22.6; P=.10). Resolution of systemic features at 2 hours in the systemic subgroup was 9 of 35 (26%) versus 9 of 41 (22%) (difference 3.8%, 95% CI -15 to 23; P=.79). No secondary outcome (pain at 4 and 24 hours, systemic resolution at 4 hours, opioid or unblinded-antivenom use) differed significantly. Acute systemic hypersensitivity reactions occurred in 4 of 112 antivenom patients (3.6%).
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval (-1.1 to +22.6 points) does not exclude a clinically useful pain benefit — this is 'not shown to work' in 224 patients, and enrolment required severe pain after standard analgesia, the subgroup most likely to be offered antivenom in practice.
cards.source: Isbister GK et al. Randomized controlled trial of intravenous antivenom versus placebo for latrodectism: the second Redback Antivenom Evaluation (RAVE-II) study. Ann Emerg Med. 2014. cards.headline: RAVE 2008: intravenous versus intramuscular antivenom differed by at most a small margin (pain improved 62% vs 53%)
cards.summary: RAVE 2008: intravenous versus intramuscular antivenom differed by at most a small margin (pain improved 62% vs 53%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-dummy, double-blind trial of administration route (all patients received antivenom)
cards.people: 126 patients with latrodectism randomised to intravenous (64) or intramuscular (62) redback antivenom, with a second identical treatment after 2 hours if required; 55 had systemic effects. The abstract does not state mean age or sex mix.
cards.result: Pain improved (clinically significant reduction 2 hours after the last treatment) in 40 of 64 (62%) after intravenous versus 33 of 62 (53%) after intramuscular antivenom (+9%, 95% credible interval -8 to +26); the probability that IV was superior at all was 85%, but the probability of a difference exceeding the prespecified 20% was only 10%. A meta-analysis including a previous trial found no difference in the primary outcome between routes.

shelves.title: Low-dose versus high-dose antivenom for snakebite in India
shelves.question: In patients with haemotoxic/neurotoxic snake envenomation, is a low-dose polyvalent antivenom regimen as effective as high-dose, with fewer reactions and lower cost?
shelves.mesh: Acute Kidney Injury/epidemiology · Adult · Animals · Antivenins/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Clinical Protocols · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · India/epidemiology · Male · Neurotoxicity Syndromes/drug therapy,immunology,physiopathology · Snake Bites/drug therapy,mortality,immunology,physiopathology · Snake Venoms/immunology,toxicity · Whole Blood Coagulation Time
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The randomised record (Sagar 2020, 140 patients with haemotoxic bite, open-label) compared the Indian national protocol (100 mL initial dose, then 100 mL six-hourly, capped at 300 mL) with the local institutional protocol (70 mL, then 30 mL six-hourly): total antivenom required did not differ significantly between protocols, neither did mortality or acute kidney injury reach significance (both numerically higher in the national-protocol group, in patients the authors note were sicker), and no patient in either group relapsed with clotting abnormality. The neurotoxic-bite comparison (Sarin 2017, 51 patients) was NOT randomised — a prospective comparison whose authors call for a randomised trial: the national (lower-dose) protocol used far less antivenom (224 vs 982 mL per patient) with shorter ventilation (24 vs 43.5 hours) and no difference in recovery, reactions or mortality (there were no deaths in either group). Lower-dose regimens look adequate in both records, but the randomised trial is open-label and confounded, and the cleaner dose contrast is observational: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Sagar 2020: national-protocol versus institutional antivenom dosing in haemotoxic bite — no significant difference in dose required, mortality or kidney injury
cards.summary: Sagar 2020: national-protocol versus institutional antivenom dosing in haemotoxic bite — no significant difference in dose required, mortality or kidney injury
cards.people: 140 patients with haemotoxic snakebite randomised to the national protocol (Group A: 100 mL initial dose, then 100 mL every 6 hours until the 20-minute whole-blood clotting time normalised or 300 mL given) or the institutional protocol (Group B: 70 mL, then 30 mL every 6 hours until two consecutive clotting times were negative). The abstract does not state mean age, sex mix or per-group numbers.
cards.result: There was no statistical difference in the total amount of antivenom required between the two groups. Mortality and acute kidney injury were higher in Group A but not statistically significant, which the authors attribute to sicker patients in that group. There was no relapse of clotting-time abnormality in either group; in 12% of patients the clotting time remained prolonged until death. The authors conclude the national protocol did not decrease mortality or morbidity in this comparison.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, with a baseline severity imbalance the authors themselves flag, and no absolute event rates in the abstract: the trial can say 'no significant difference' but cannot certify equivalence of the two dosing strategies.
cards.source: Sagar P et al. Comparison of two Anti Snake Venom protocols in hemotoxic snake bite: A randomized trial. J Forensic Leg Med. 2020. PMID: 32658754. cards.summary: Sarin 2017: in neurotoxic bite, the lower-dose national protocol used 224 mL versus 982 mL with similar recovery — a prospective comparison, not an RCT
cards.type: Prospective comparative study (NOT randomised — labelled as such; authors call for a randomised trial)

cards.result: Progression of neuroparalysis, time to complete resolution of ptosis, ventilator-associated pneumonia and antivenom reactions did not differ between regimens. cards.headline: Synthesis: lower-dose antivenom protocols look adequate; the proof is thin — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: lower-dose antivenom protocols look adequate; the proof is thin — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Sagar 2020 (140 randomised patients, haemotoxic bite) and Sarin 2017 (51 patients, neurotoxic bite, non-randomised).
cards.result: Neither record shows an advantage for giving more antivenom: the randomised haemotoxic comparison found no significant difference in total dose required or outcomes between a higher-initial-dose national protocol and a lower-dose local one, and the neurotoxic comparison achieved the same recovery on roughly a quarter of the antivenom (224 vs 982 mL). Open-label design, severity imbalance and one observational card hold the stamp at POSSIBLE. Single-country (India) data throughout, per the topic file's own flag.
cards.watchOut: Antivenom products and snake species vary by region; an Indian polyvalent-antivenom dosing result does not transfer to other products or species, and neither study was powered for mortality.

shelves.title: Surgical stabilisation of rib fractures (flail chest and displaced fractures)
shelves.question: In patients with flail chest or multiple displaced rib fractures, does operative rib fixation improve pain, ventilation duration and recovery versus conservative management?
shelves.mesh: Flail Chest/diagnostic imaging,etiology,surgery,therapy · Rib Fractures/diagnostic imaging,etiology,surgery,therapy · Fracture Fixation, Internal/methods · Thoracic Injuries/complications,therapy · Intensive Care Units · Length of Stay · Quality of Life · Noninvasive Ventilation · Humans · Adult · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by population: The three randomised trials answer three different versions of the question. In VENTILATED flail chest (Marasco 2013), operative fixation shortened ICU stay after randomisation (285 vs 359 hours; P=0.03) and nearly eliminated post-extubation noninvasive ventilation (3 vs 50 hours; P=0.01), with no difference in 3-month spirometry or 6-month quality of life. In NON-ventilated patients with displaced fractures (Marasco 2022, 124 patients), fixation produced no improvement in pain or quality of life at 3 or 6 months. In the broadest population (SOFRIB 2026, 236 patients), fixation did not reduce ICU stay (mean difference 1.8 days, 95% CI −0.8 to 4.4; P=0.17), lengthened hospital stay (+3.3 days; P=0.01) and raised pneumonia rates (11.4% vs 3.3%; risk ratio 3.45 relative; P=0.02), while improving several quality-of-life and pain-impact scores beyond their minimal clinically important differences. Process gains in the ventilated flail subgroup; null-to-mixed elsewhere: POSSIBLE, and selective rather than routine.

cards.headline: Marasco 2013: in ventilated flail chest, operative fixation shortened ICU stay (285 vs 359 hours) and post-extubation ventilation support
cards.summary: Marasco 2013: in ventilated flail chest, operative fixation shortened ICU stay (285 vs 359 hours) and post-extubation ventilation support
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial (flail chest, ventilator-managed comparator)
cards.people: Adults with traumatic flail chest (a multitrauma cohort) randomised to operative fixation of fractured ribs in the flail segment versus current best-practice mechanical ventilator management; the abstract does not state the number randomised, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Patients in the operative fixation group had significantly shorter ICU stay (hours) postrandomization (285 hours [range 191 to 319 hours] for the surgical group vs 359 hours [range 270 to 581 hours] for the conservative group; P=0.03) and lesser requirement for noninvasive ventilation after extubation (3 hours [range 0 to 25 hours] in the surgical group vs 50 hours [range 17 to 102 hours] in the conservative group; P=0.01). No differences in spirometry at 3 months or quality of life at 6 months were noted.
cards.watchOut: The abstract does not even state how many patients were randomised — a small, single-programme trial whose endpoints are hours of ICU care and ventilation support, not pain, function or survival; it supports a process benefit in the sickest subgroup and nothing broader.
cards.source: Marasco SF et al. Prospective randomized controlled trial of operative rib fixation in traumatic flail chest. J Am Coll Surg. 2013. PMID: 23415550. cards.headline: SOFRIB 2026: in 236 patients, fixation did not shorten ICU stay, increased pneumonia (11.4% vs 3.3%) and hospital stay, but improved quality-of-life and pain scores
cards.summary: SOFRIB 2026: in 236 patients, fixation did not shorten ICU stay, increased pneumonia (11.4% vs 3.3%) and hospital stay, but improved quality-of-life and pain scores
cards.people: 236 adults (18 years or older) with 3 or more displaced rib fractures and pulmonary compromise, severe pain, or deformity, randomised 1:1 at nine American College of Surgeons-verified trauma centers (2014–2024) to surgical stabilization of rib fractures within 5 days (114) or standardized non-operative care (122); analyses were intention to treat. The record carries no MeSH terms and the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: ICU length of stay — the primary outcome — did not differ significantly (mean difference 1.8 days [95% CI −0.8 to 4.4]; P=0.17). Surgical stabilization was associated with longer hospital length of stay (+3.3 days; P=0.01) and higher pneumonia rates (11.4% vs 3.3%; risk ratio 3.45 relative; P=0.02). However, it improved SF-36 general health (+3.3; P=0.04), bodily pain (+4.0; P=0.02), and physical component summary (+3.3; P=0.04), each exceeding the minimal clinically important difference; PIQ-6 scores indicated lower pain impact (−3.9; P=0.02). Return-to-work was more frequent with fixation (62.5% vs 38.7%; P=0.08). The authors conclude the findings support selective rather than routine fixation.
cards.watchOut: A genuinely two-handed trial: the same operation that tripled pneumonia and added hospital days also produced clinically meaningful quality-of-life gains. Quoting either half alone misrepresents it — and a decade-long enrolment window (2014–2024) spans substantial change in non-operative care.

cards.result: The population decides the answer. Ventilated flail chest: shorter ICU and ventilation-support time with fixation (one small trial). Everyone else: no improvement on the primary outcomes in two multicentre trials, a pneumonia excess of 8 percentage points in the largest, offset by better quality-of-life and pain-impact scores. shelves.title: Immediate total-body CT in severe trauma (REACT-2)
shelves.question: In patients with severe trauma, does immediate total-body CT scanning reduce mortality versus conventional imaging with selective CT?
shelves.mesh: Multiple Trauma/diagnostic imaging,mortality · Whole Body Imaging/instrumentation · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Hospital Mortality · Brain Injuries/diagnostic imaging,mortality · Radiation Dosage · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED pending the developer's personal verdict (Tier C, in-hospital mortality primary outcome): The one randomised trial (REACT-2, 1,403 patients randomised at four Dutch hospitals and one in Switzerland) found in-hospital mortality identical between immediate total-body CT and the standard work-up with selective CT: 86 of 541 (16%) versus 85 of 542 (16%) (P=0.92). The prespecified subgroups agreed — polytrauma 22% versus 25% (P=0.46) and traumatic brain injury 38% versus 44% (P=0.31). With no mortality benefit and a higher radiation dose, the trial's own reading is that future work should target patient selection, not routine total-body scanning: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: REACT-2 2016: immediate total-body CT did not reduce in-hospital mortality (16% vs 16%) in severe trauma
cards.summary: REACT-2 2016: immediate total-body CT did not reduce in-hospital mortality (16% vs 16%) in severe trauma
cards.people: 1,403 patients aged 18 years or older with trauma with compromised vital parameters, clinical suspicion of life-threatening injuries, or severe injury, randomly assigned 1:1 at four hospitals in the Netherlands and one in Switzerland to immediate total-body CT scanning (702) or a standard work-up with conventional imaging supplemented with selective CT scanning (701); 541 and 542 patients respectively were included in the primary analysis. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: In-hospital mortality did not differ between groups (total-body CT 86 [16%] of 541 vs standard work-up 85 [16%] of 542; P=0.92). In-hospital mortality also did not differ between groups in subgroup analyses in patients with polytrauma (total-body CT 81 [22%] of 362 vs standard work-up 82 [25%] of 331; P=0.46) and traumatic brain injury (68 [38%] of 178 vs 66 [44%] of 151; P=0.31). Three serious adverse events were reported in patients in the total-body CT group (1%), one in the standard work-up group (<1%), and one in a patient who was excluded after random allocation; all five patients died. Neither doctors nor patients were masked to treatment allocation.
cards.watchOut: An unmasked imaging-strategy trial: the null is on mortality, the outcome that matters, but the trial does not measure diagnostic speed, missed injuries or downstream operations in its abstract — absence of a mortality effect is not absence of any workflow effect, and the radiation dose is a real cost the authors name.
cards.source: Sierink JC et al. Immediate total-body CT scanning versus conventional imaging and selective CT scanning in patients with severe trauma (REACT-2): a randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2016. PMID: 27371185. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01523626, from the record's databank fields. cards.summary: Synthesis: the survival benefit suggested by observational work did not survive randomisation — LIKELY (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: Synthesis of the card above: REACT-2 2016 (1,403 randomised; 1,083 in the primary analysis).
cards.result: REACT-2 exists because published observational work suggested total-body CT saved lives; the randomised test found 16% versus 16% mortality, overall and in the polytrauma and brain-injury subgroups where benefit was most expected. shelves.title: Bromelain-based enzymatic debridement of burns (NexoBrid)
shelves.question: In patients with deep partial- or full-thickness burns, does bromelain-based enzymatic debridement remove eschar faster and reduce surgical excision versus standard care?
shelves.mesh: Bromelains/therapeutic use · Burns/therapy · Burns/surgery,complications · Debridement/methods · Cicatrix · Wound Healing · Humans · Adult · Child · Adolescent · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY — PROPOSED: Two open-label randomised trials, in children and in adults, agree on large effects. In children (Shoham 2025, 145 patients), bromelain-based debridement completed eschar removal in a median of 1 day versus 6 days for standard care (P<0.001) and cut the wound area needing surgical excision from 48.1% to 1.5% (P<0.001), with 12-month scar scores non-inferior (Modified Vancouver Scar Scale 3.8 vs 4.9). In adults (DETECT, 175 patients), complete eschar removal was 93% on NexoBrid versus 4% on gel vehicle (P<.001), surgical excision was 4% versus 72% against standard care (P<.001), median time to removal was 1.0 versus 3.8 days, and debridement blood loss was 14 mL versus 814 mL (P<.0001), again with non-inferior scar scores at 12 and 24 months. The endpoints are process and surgical-burden outcomes rather than survival, and neither trial could be blinded — but the effect sizes are large, mechanistic, and concordant across age groups: LIKELY.

cards.headline: Shoham 2025: in children, NexoBrid removed eschar in 1 day versus 6, and cut surgical excision from 48.1% to 1.5% of wound area
cards.summary: Shoham 2025: in children, NexoBrid removed eschar in 1 day versus 6, and cut surgical excision from 48.1% to 1.5% of wound area
cards.type: Multicentre, open-label, parallel-design randomised controlled trial (children)
cards.people: 145 children aged 0–18 years with deep thermal burns covering 1–30% of total body surface area, enrolled 2015–2020 at 36 burn centers in Europe, the US, Israel and India, and randomised to bromelain-based debridement (72) or standard-of-care eschar removal (73); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: All three primary endpoints were met. The median time to complete eschar removal was significantly lower in the bromelain arm (1 vs 6 days, P<0.001). The mean [SD] percentage of wound area surgically excised was 1.5% [12.1%] versus 48.1% [46.6%] (P<0.001). Mean [SD] 12-month Modified Vancouver Scar Scale scores were 3.8 [2.9] and 4.9 [3.3] in the bromelain and standard-care arms respectively (non-inferiority demonstrated at P<0.001). The incidence of adverse events was similar between the groups, and there were no significant safety issues or deaths during the trial.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: the clinicians deciding how much wound to excise knew the allocation, which can inflate a surgery-sparing endpoint; the scar outcome was assessor-blinded, which is why the non-inferior cosmesis result matters more than the excision gap alone might suggest.

cards.headline: DETECT 2024: in adults, complete eschar removal was 93% with NexoBrid versus 4% with gel vehicle, and surgical excision 4% versus 72% versus standard care
cards.summary: DETECT 2024: in adults, complete eschar removal was 93% with NexoBrid versus 4% with gel vehicle, and surgical excision 4% versus 72% versus standard care
cards.people: 175 adults with deep burns covering 3–30% of total body surface area, randomly assigned in a 3:3:1 ratio to NexoBrid (75), surgical or nonsurgical standard of care (75), or placebo gel vehicle (25); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Complete eschar removal was higher in the NexoBrid versus the gel vehicle group (93% vs 4%; P<.001). Surgical excision was lower in the NexoBrid versus the standard-care group (4% vs 72%; P<.001). Median time to eschar removal was 1.0 and 3.8 days for NexoBrid and standard care respectively (P<.001). Eschar-removal blood loss was lower in the NexoBrid than the standard-care group (14 ± 512 mL vs 814 ± 1020 mL; P<.0001). Modified Vancouver Scar Scale scores at 12 and 24 months were noninferior in the NexoBrid versus standard-care groups (3.7 ± 2.1 vs 5.0 ± 3.1 at 12 months and 3.04 ± 2.2 vs 3.30 ± 2.76 at 24 months). The authors report NexoBrid was safe and well tolerated without deleterious effects on wound closure and scarring.
cards.watchOut: The 93% versus 4% contrast is against an inert gel, the softest comparator in the trial; the standard-care contrasts (excision 4% vs 72%, blood loss) carry the clinical weight, and the trial was open-label like its paediatric sibling.

cards.headline: Synthesis: enzymatic debridement removes eschar faster with far less surgery, and scars no worse — LIKELY
cards.summary: Synthesis: enzymatic debridement removes eschar faster with far less surgery, and scars no worse — LIKELY
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Shoham 2025 (145 children) and DETECT 2024 (175 adults) — two independent randomised trials in different age groups.
cards.result: The programme is consistent at both ends of childhood and adulthood: eschar gone in about a day instead of four to six, surgical excision nearly eliminated as a share of wound area, less blood loss, and blinded scar assessment non-inferior at one and two years. Nothing here speaks to mortality, graft take in the largest burns, or use beyond 30% body surface area — the trials' entry fence — and those limits are part of the shelf.
cards.watchOut: Both trials were run with the manufacturer's programme design across the same investigator network; independent replication outside that programme does not yet exist in randomised form.
