shelves.title: Honey versus silver sulfadiazine for partial-thickness burns
shelves.question: In superficial partial-thickness burns, does honey dressing heal faster than silver sulfadiazine?
shelves.mesh: Honey · Silver Sulfadiazine/therapeutic use · Burns/drug therapy · Wound Healing · Wound Infection/prevention & control · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Young Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Two small randomised comparisons from South Asia, a quarter-century apart, both favour honey. Malik 2010 (150 patients, each contributing two comparable burn sites randomised within-patient) found re-epithelialisation faster with honey (13.47 ± 4.06 versus 15.62 ± 4.40 days; P<0.0001) and fewer Pseudomonas-positive cultures (6 versus 27 patients). Subrahmanyam 1998 (50 patients) found satisfactory epithelialisation by day 7 in 84% of honey-treated wounds versus 72% with silver sulfadiazine, and 100% versus 84% by day 21, with earlier histological reparative activity under honey. Small, single-centre, unblinded dressing trials with a healing-time surrogate: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Malik 2010: honey sites re-epithelialised about 2 days faster than silver sulfadiazine sites in the same patients (13.47 vs 15.62 days)
cards.summary: Malik 2010: honey sites re-epithelialised about 2 days faster than silver sulfadiazine sites in the same patients (13.47 vs 15.62 days)
cards.type: Randomised comparative clinical trial (within-patient, two-site design)
cards.people: 150 patients of all ages with superficial and partial-thickness burns covering less than 40% of body surface area, each having similar burns at two sites on different parts of the body; each patient had one site treated with honey and one with topical silver sulfadiazine, allocated randomly, at a burn centre in Wah Cantt, Pakistan, 2007–2008. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The rate of re-epithelialization and healing of superficial and partial-thickness burns was significantly faster in the sites treated with honey than in the sites treated with silver sulfadiazine (13.47 ± 4.06 versus 15.62 ± 4.40 days; P<0.0001). The site treated with honey healed completely in less than 21 days versus 24 days for the site treated with silver sulfadiazine. Six patients had positive culture for Pseudomonas aeruginosa in the honey-treated site, whereas 27 patients had positive culture in the silver sulfadiazine site.
cards.watchOut: A within-patient design removes between-patient confounding but not assessment bias — healing was judged by clinicians who could see and smell which site had honey — and the culture result counts patients, not sites, in a design where each patient carried both treatments. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.source: Malik KI et al. Honey compared with silver sulphadiazine in the treatment of superficial partial-thickness burns. Int Wound J. 2010. PMID: 20649832. cards.headline: Subrahmanyam 1998: epithelialisation by day 21 in 100% of honey-treated versus 84% of silver sulfadiazine-treated burns (50 patients)
cards.summary: Subrahmanyam 1998: epithelialisation by day 21 in 100% of honey-treated versus 84% of silver sulfadiazine-treated burns (50 patients)
cards.type: Prospective randomised clinical and histological study
cards.people: 50 patients with comparable fresh partial-thickness burns, randomly allocated to honey dressing or silver sulfadiazine (25 in each group); the abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Of the wounds treated with honey, 84 per cent showed satisfactory epithelialization by the 7th day, and 100 per cent by the 21st day. In wounds treated with silver sulfadiazine, epithelialization occurred by the 7th day in 72 per cent of the patients and in 84 per cent by 21 days. Histological evidence of reparative activity was seen in 80 per cent of wounds treated with the honey dressing by the 7th day, with minimal inflammation; 52 per cent of the silver sulfadiazine treated wounds showed reparative activity with inflammatory changes by the 7th day. Reparative activity reached 100 per cent by 21 days with the honey dressing and 84 per cent with silver sulfadiazine.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five patients per arm, percentages without confidence intervals, and a 1998 single-centre record: the direction agrees with the later within-patient trial, but the precision is that of a pilot, and the honey used in these studies is not a standardised medical product. The record names no specific product or brand — products sold today may differ in safety and effectiveness.

cards.summary: Synthesis: two small unblinded trials, one direction — honey heals these burns a few days faster — POSSIBLE

cards.result: Both comparisons favour honey on healing speed (about 2 days faster re-epithelialisation in the larger trial; complete epithelialisation by day 21 in 100% vs 84% in the smaller), and neither shows a harm signal. The evidence is real but thin — two centres, no blinding, no standardised honey preparation, no grafting or scar outcomes — which is exactly the POSSIBLE tier. shelves.title: Biobrane versus silver sulfadiazine in paediatric burns
shelves.question: In children with second-degree burns, does the biosynthetic dressing Biobrane shorten healing time and pain versus 1% silver sulfadiazine?
shelves.mesh: Coated Materials, Biocompatible/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Silver Sulfadiazine/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Bandages, Hydrocolloid/economics · Burns/surgery · Burns/economics,therapy · Wound Healing · Pain Measurement · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool · Adolescent · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The anchor trial (Barret 2000, 20 children with second-degree burns) reports Biobrane superior to 1% silver sulfadiazine on pain, pain-medication requirements, wound healing time and length of hospital stay — but its abstract prints no figures for any of those outcomes, so the size of the advantage cannot be verified from the record. The second trial (Cassidy 2005) compared Biobrane with another modern dressing, Duoderm, and found no significant difference in time to healing or pain scores, with Biobrane statistically more expensive. Biobrane probably beats daily silver-cream tubbing on comfort and speed; against other coverings its edge is unproven: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Barret 2000: Biobrane beat silver sulfadiazine on pain, healing time and hospital stay in 20 children — with no figures printed in the abstract
cards.summary: Barret 2000: Biobrane beat silver sulfadiazine on pain, healing time and hospital stay in 20 children — with no figures printed in the abstract
cards.people: 20 paediatric patients with second-degree (partial-thickness) burns, prospectively randomised to Biobrane or 1% silver sulfadiazine, with the rest of the routine clinical protocols followed in both groups; the abstract does not state the group sizes, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The application of Biobrane to partial-thickness burns proved to be superior to the topical treatment: patients in the biosynthetic temporary cover group presented with less pain and required less pain medication, and length of hospital stay and wound healing time were also significantly shorter in the Biobrane group. None of the patients in either group presented with wound infection or needed skin autografting. The record's abstract states these comparisons without printing the underlying values, so no effect sizes are quoted on this card.
cards.watchOut: Twenty patients and a results-free abstract: this card can support direction, not magnitude. Any source quoting exact healing-day differences for this trial is quoting the full text, not the record carded here.
cards.source: Barret JP et al. Biobrane versus 1% silver sulfadiazine in second-degree pediatric burns. Plast Reconstr Surg. 2000. PMID: 10626971. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: High-dose vitamin C in burn resuscitation
shelves.question: In severely burned patients, does adjuvant high-dose ascorbic acid reduce resuscitation fluid volumes and oedema versus standard resuscitation?
shelves.mesh: Ascorbic Acid/administration & dosage · Burns/therapy · Fluid Therapy/methods · Resuscitation/methods · Edema/therapy · Ringer's Lactate · Lipid Peroxidation/drug effects · Water-Electrolyte Balance/drug effects · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Tanaka 2000, 37 patients with burns over 30% of body surface area at a single Japanese centre) found high-dose ascorbic acid (66 mg/kg per hour for the first 24 hours) roughly halved 24-hour resuscitation fluid requirements (3.0 ± 1.7 versus 5.5 ± 3.1 mL/kg per percentage of burn area; P<.01), reduced first-day weight gain (9.2% ± 8.2% versus 17.8% ± 6.9%) and burned-tissue water content, and shortened mechanical ventilation (12.1 ± 8.8 versus 21.3 ± 15.6 days; P<.05), with haemodynamics and urine output equivalent between groups. A single small trial whose primary measures are fluid volumes and oedema — surrogates — carries POSSIBLE, and no mortality result is reported in its abstract.

cards.headline: Tanaka 2000: high-dose vitamin C cut 24-hour resuscitation fluid needs (3.0 vs 5.5 mL/kg per % burn) and ventilation days in 37 severely burned patients
cards.summary: Tanaka 2000: high-dose vitamin C cut 24-hour resuscitation fluid needs (3.0 vs 5.5 mL/kg per % burn) and ventilation days in 37 severely burned patients
cards.people: 37 patients with burns over more than 30% of total body surface area, hospitalised within 2 hours of injury at a university trauma and critical care centre in Japan, randomly divided into ascorbic acid (19; mean burn size 63% ± 26% TBSA; inhalation injury 15 of 19) and control (18; mean burn size 53% ± 17% TBSA; inhalation injury 12 of 18) groups; fluid resuscitation used Ringer lactate titrated to haemodynamics and urine output of 0.5–1.0 mL/kg per hour, with ascorbic acid 66 mg/kg per hour infused during the initial 24 hours in the treatment group. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Heart rate, mean arterial pressure, central venous pressure, arterial pH, base deficit, and urine outputs were equivalent in both groups. The 24-hour total fluid infusion volumes in the control and ascorbic acid groups were 5.5 ± 3.1 and 3.0 ± 1.7 mL/kg per percentage of burn area, respectively (P<.01). In the first 24 hours, the ascorbic acid group gained 9.2% ± 8.2% of pretreatment weight; controls gained 17.8% ± 6.9%. Burned tissue water content was 6.1 ± 1.8 versus 2.6 ± 1.7 mL/g of dry weight in the control and ascorbic acid groups respectively (P<.01). Fluid retention in the second 24 hours was also significantly reduced with ascorbic acid, the PaO2/FiO2 ratio favoured ascorbic acid at 18–72 hours (P<.01), and the length of mechanical ventilation was 21.3 ± 15.6 days in controls versus 12.1 ± 8.8 days with ascorbic acid (P<.05). Serum malondialdehyde levels were lower in the ascorbic acid group at 18, 24, and 36 hours (P<.05).
cards.watchOut: Thirty-seven patients, unblinded fluid titration by design (volumes were titrated to targets by treating clinicians), and baseline imbalance in burn size (63% vs 53% TBSA) that favours neither group cleanly; the trial reports no mortality or renal outcome in its abstract, and high-dose ascorbate's oxalate and glucose-meter issues sit outside this record.

shelves.title: Hypertonic fluids for burn shock resuscitation
shelves.question: In severely burned patients, does hypertonic (sodium lactate or saline) resuscitation reduce total fluid volume and complications versus isotonic lactated Ringer's?
shelves.mesh: Saline Solution, Hypertonic · Ringer's Lactate · Burns/complications,therapy · Resuscitation · Shock/etiology,therapy · Fluid Therapy · Isotonic Solutions/therapeutic use · Water-Electrolyte Balance · Humans · Adult · Adolescent · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split between the two records: The older randomised trial (Gunn 1989, 51 adults with burns of at least 20% of body surface area) found NO advantage for hypertonic sodium lactate over lactated Ringer's — the authors were not able to demonstrate decreased fluid requirements, improved tolerance of feedings, or decreased weight gain. The larger later comparison (Belba 2009, 110 patients) found higher first-hour fluid and sodium loads with hypertonic lactate saline but lower net fluid accumulation (P=.0025), concluding 24-hour fluid requirements fell — though its abstract describes group allocation loosely and reports P values without the underlying volumes. One null RCT and one positive, loosely reported comparison on a volume surrogate: POSSIBLE, unproven either way.

cards.headline: Gunn 1989: hypertonic sodium lactate showed no advantage over lactated Ringer's for burn resuscitation in 51 adults
cards.summary: Gunn 1989: hypertonic sodium lactate showed no advantage over lactated Ringer's for burn resuscitation in 51 adults
cards.people: 51 adult burned patients with at least 20% total body surface area burns (mean 36.7%, range 20–74%), prospectively randomised on admission to hypertonic saline-lactate (sodium 250 mEq/L, 514 mOsm) or lactated Ringer's solution (sodium 130 mEq/L, 268 mOsm), all admitted within 12 hours of injury; the abstract does not state the group sizes, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Fluid requirements (cc/kg/% BSA), urine output, sodium intake and excretion, serum and urine osmolality, serum creatinine, body weight and enteral intake were compared at 24-hour intervals. The authors state plainly: the data show no advantage of hypertonic sodium lactate over conventional therapy with lactated Ringer's for burn resuscitation; they were not able to demonstrate decreased fluid requirements, improved tolerance of feedings, or decrease in per cent weight gain. The record's abstract is truncated at 250 words in the source journal, and no group-level fluid volumes are printed in it.
cards.watchOut: A 1989 trial with an abstract truncated in the journal itself: the null is stated in words, not numbers, and resuscitation targets of that era predate modern formula-guided practice — it refutes a large benefit, not a modest one.
cards.source: Gunn ML et al. Prospective, randomized trial of hypertonic sodium lactate versus lactated Ringer's solution for burn shock resuscitation. J Trauma. 1989. PMID: 2671402. cards.headline: Belba 2009: hypertonic lactate saline gave lower net fluid accumulation over 24 hours (P=.0025) in 110 severely burned patients
cards.summary: Belba 2009: hypertonic lactate saline gave lower net fluid accumulation over 24 hours (P=.0025) in 110 severely burned patients
cards.type: Prospective comparative study (record publication types include Randomized Controlled Trial; allocation not described in the abstract)
cards.people: 110 patients with severe burns, divided into two groups for comparison: one resuscitated with lactated Ringer's solution according to the Parkland formula for adults and Shriner formula for children, the other with hypertonic lactate saline solution; the abstract does not state the group sizes, mean age or the sex mix, and does not describe the allocation method (the record's publication types include Randomized Controlled Trial).
cards.result: There was a difference between sodium loads (P=.03), fluid load in the first hour (P=.001), sodium load in the first hour (P=.001), and net fluid accumulation (P=.0025). There was a difference regarding plasma sodium and plasma osmolality in the first hour (P=.003, P=.002), and in sodium given (P=.001) and sodium excreted (P=.001) between the two groups. The authors conclude that hypertonic resuscitation gives a higher fluid and sodium load in the first hour, accompanied by a decrease in fluid requirements and fluid accumulation for the first 24 hours of burn shock. The abstract reports P values without the underlying fluid volumes.
cards.watchOut: Adults and children are pooled under two different isotonic formulas, allocation is undescribed, and every result is a bare P value: this record can suggest a volume effect but cannot quantify one, and its design language is weaker than its publication-type label.

cards.headline: Synthesis: one null RCT, one loosely reported positive comparison, a volume surrogate — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: one null RCT, one loosely reported positive comparison, a volume surrogate — POSSIBLE
cards.people: Synthesis of the cards above: Gunn 1989 (51 adults, randomised) and Belba 2009 (110 patients, comparative).
cards.result: The hypertonic idea in burn shock — expand plasma volume with less infused volume — has been tested for three decades without a decisive randomised answer: the cleanest small trial found no advantage, and the larger comparison found less net accumulation without publishing the volumes. Neither record reports mortality or complications as outcomes. POSSIBLE is the ceiling, and the question remains open rather than settled in either direction.
cards.watchOut: Do not import the traumatic-brain-injury hypertonic literature (Shelf #1261) into burn shock: different indication, different fluids, different endpoints.

shelves.title: Early enteral nutrition in major burns
shelves.question: In patients with major burns, does enteral nutrition started within 24 hours improve metabolic response, infection and healing versus delayed feeding?
shelves.mesh: Burns/diet therapy,metabolism · Enteral Nutrition · Energy Metabolism · Time Factors · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — PROPOSED: The one randomised trial (Peck 2004) tested the metabolic claim directly: enteral feeding started within 24 hours did NOT decrease post-burn hypermetabolism — after adjustment for burn size, inhalation injury and age, average daily energy expenditure was if anything higher in the early group (mean difference 0.17 in the REE/BEE ratio; P=0.07). Mortality was similar (early 28%; late 38%) and infections and length of stay were reported as similar between groups, without figures. The trial's record does not state how many patients were randomised, and its measured question is metabolic; the infection and healing outcomes named in this shelf's question were not its endpoints. One small trial, a surrogate primary, an honest null: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: Peck 2004: early enteral feeding did not decrease post-burn hypermetabolism; energy expenditure ran slightly higher (P=0.07)
cards.summary: Peck 2004: early enteral feeding did not decrease post-burn hypermetabolism; energy expenditure ran slightly higher (P=0.07)
cards.people: Burn patients randomised to receive enteral feedings either within 24 hours (early) or 7 days (late) of injury; the record's abstract does not state the number of patients randomised, their mean age or the sex mix — an absence printed here rather than filled from secondary sources. Average age, burn size, infections, and length of stay were similar between groups.
cards.result: Basal energy expenditure was calculated from Harris-Benedict equations and resting energy expenditure obtained from indirect calorimetry, with average daily energy expenditure (DEE) expressed as REE/BEE. Mortality between groups was similar (early, 28%; late, 38%) and not significantly influenced by inhalation injury. When controlled for percentage of total body surface area burn, inhalation injury, and age, the early group had an increased rather than decreased DEE, with a mean DEE 0.17 more than the late group (P=0.07). The authors conclude that early enteral feeding does not decrease the average energy expenditure associated with burn injury.
cards.watchOut: A null on a metabolic ratio in a record that withholds its own sample size: the mortality figures (28% vs 38%) come without a significance test or denominators in the abstract, and must not be quoted as a mortality comparison — feeding-timing practice also rests on gut-function and tolerance grounds this trial did not measure.
cards.source: Peck MD et al. Early enteral nutrition does not decrease hypermetabolism associated with burn injury. J Trauma. 2004. PMID: 15625442. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Silver foam and biosynthetic dressings for partial-thickness burns and scalds
shelves.question: In children and adults with partial-thickness burns/scalds, do modern silver-foam or biosynthetic (Suprathel) dressings heal as fast as standard care with less pain and fewer dressing changes?
shelves.mesh: Bandages · Burns/therapy · Silver Compounds/therapeutic use · Biological Dressings · Polyesters/therapeutic use · Wound Healing · Re-Epithelialization · Procedural Pain · Humans · Child · Child, Preschool · Adolescent · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED, split by comparison: Suprathel versus Mepilex Ag (Hundeshagen 2018, 62 outpatients with partial-thickness burns): healing time identical (12 days in both groups; P=0.75), but pain ratings were significantly lower with Suprathel over the first 5 days (P=0.03; paediatric subgroup P<0.001) and patients reported better overall scar quality (2 versus 4.5; P<0.001) — at considerably higher cost per cm² than Mepilex Ag. Silver foam versus porcine xenograft (Karlsson 2019, 58 children with scalds): silver foam healed significantly faster (median time to 97% healing 9 versus 15 days; P=0.004) with fewer and quicker dressing changes, and similar pain, infection and hospital stay. Modern dressings trade blows by endpoint: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Hundeshagen 2018: Suprathel and Mepilex Ag healed partial-thickness burns in the same 12 days; Suprathel hurt less in the first 5 days
cards.summary: Hundeshagen 2018: Suprathel and Mepilex Ag healed partial-thickness burns in the same 12 days; Suprathel hurt less in the first 5 days
cards.type: Prospective, randomized, controlled trial (outpatient, children and adults)
cards.people: 62 paediatric and adult outpatients with partial-thickness burns, enrolled in a randomised controlled trial (Suprathel 32; Mepilex Ag 30); age, sex, and burn size were comparable between the groups. The abstract does not state mean age or the overall sex mix.
cards.result: Time to reepithelialization was not different between the groups (12 days; P=0.75). Pain ratings were significantly reduced during the first 5 days after burn in the Suprathel group in all patients (P=0.03) and in a pediatric subgroup (P<0.001). Viscoelasticity of burned skin was elevated compared with unburned skin in the Mepilex Ag group at 1 month post burn. Patients treated with Suprathel reported better overall scar quality (Suprathel 2; Mepilex Ag 4.5; P<0.001). The cost of treatment per square centimeter for Mepilex Ag was considerably lower than that of Suprathel. The authors conclude both dressings are feasible and efficacious for outpatient treatment of minor and selected moderate partial-thickness burns, with reduced pain under Suprathel advantageous despite increased cost.
cards.watchOut: The pain advantage is confined to the first 5 days and the scar result is a patient-reported scale at 1 month; the healing endpoint — the outcome the products are sold on — was a dead heat, and the trial's cost finding runs against the less painful dressing.
cards.source: Hundeshagen G et al. A Prospective, Randomized, Controlled Trial Comparing the Outpatient Treatment of Pediatric and Adult Partial-Thickness Burns with Suprathel or Mepilex Ag. J Burn Care Res. 2018. PMID: 28557869. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Karlsson 2019: silver foam healed children's scalds faster than porcine xenograft (97% healing at a median of 9 vs 15 days)
cards.summary: Karlsson 2019: silver foam healed children's scalds faster than porcine xenograft (97% healing at a median of 9 vs 15 days)
cards.type: Prospective randomised controlled trial (single centre, children with scalds)
cards.people: 58 children admitted between May 2015 and May 2018 with partial-thickness scalds to a single burn centre in Linköping, Sweden, treated with a silver-foam dressing (Mepilex Ag) or a porcine xenograft (EZderm); the abstract does not state the group sizes, mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The patients treated with silver-foam dressing had a significantly shorter healing time: the median time to 97% healing was 9 (range 7–23) days compared to 15 (9–29) days in the porcine xenograft group (P=0.004). The median time to complete healing was 15 (9–29) days for silver foam and 20.5 (11–42) days for xenograft (P=0.010). Pain, wound infection, duration of hospital stay, and the proportion of operations were similar between the groups. The number of dressing changes and the time for dressing changes were lower in the silver-foam group (P=0.03 for both variables).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a porcine xenograft, not a biosynthetic dressing: this card shows silver foam beating a biological cover on speed, while the other card shows a biosynthetic matching silver foam on speed and beating it on early pain. Both products in this trial come from the same manufacturer (Mölnlycke), as the record itself states.
cards.source: Karlsson M et al. Superiority of silver-foam over porcine xenograft dressings for treatment of scalds in children: A prospective randomised controlled trial. Burns. 2019. PMID: 31230798. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. cards.headline: Synthesis: healing speed separates silver foam from xenograft, not Suprathel from silver foam; pain favours Suprathel early — POSSIBLE
cards.summary: Synthesis: healing speed separates silver foam from xenograft, not Suprathel from silver foam; pain favours Suprathel early — POSSIBLE

shelves.title: Negative-pressure therapy over skin grafts in burns
shelves.question: In burn patients treated with (Meek) skin grafting, does negative-pressure wound therapy improve graft take/survival versus conventional dressing?
shelves.mesh: Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy/methods · Burns/therapy,surgery,mortality · Skin Transplantation/methods · Graft Survival · Wound Healing · Bandages · Humans · Adult · Middle Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — PROPOSED: The entire randomised record for this question is one single-centre study of 13 burn patients (Zhang 2026), using each patient's two limbs as the comparison — Meek grafting under negative-pressure wound therapy on one side, traditional dressing on the other — and its abstract reports the direction of the results only: polyamide gauze adherence rate and skin survival rate were higher with negative pressure. No rates, no differences and no P values appear in the record, so the size of any benefit cannot be stated, let alone weighed. Thirteen patients, within-patient allocation, and a results-free abstract define weak evidence on this library's scale: MAYBE (weak evidence). Negative-pressure therapy for open wounds generally is home elsewhere (Shelf #1225) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Zhang 2026: negative pressure over Meek grafts gave higher gauze adherence and skin survival rates in 13 patients — no figures in the record
cards.summary: Zhang 2026: negative pressure over Meek grafts gave higher gauze adherence and skin survival rates in 13 patients — no figures in the record
cards.type: Prospective randomized controlled study (single centre, within-patient limb comparison)
cards.people: 13 patients with burn injuries of similar depths on both limbs at a single centre; the limbs were divided into a negative-pressure wound therapy plus Meek grafting group and a Meek grafting (traditional dressing) group, so each patient contributed both treatments. The abstract does not state ages or the sex mix.
cards.result: The polyamide gauze adherence rate and the skin survival rate in the negative-pressure plus Meek group were higher than those in the Meek group, and wound secretion culture results were compared between the groups. The record's abstract prints no numerical values for any of these outcomes — no survival percentages, no differences, no statistical tests — so none are quoted on this card. The authors conclude that replacing traditional dressing with negative-pressure therapy for bandaging after Meek skin grafting can improve the skin survival rate.
cards.watchOut: Thirteen patients and an abstract with no numbers: this is a feasibility-grade signal wearing a definitive title ('Improves the Survival Rate'). The direction is plausible and consistent with negative-pressure experience elsewhere, but plausibility is not measurement.
cards.source: Zhang P et al. Negative Pressure Wound Therapy Improves the Survival Rate of Meek Skin Grafting in Burn Patients: A Prospective Randomized Controlled Study in a Single Center. shelves.title: Gabapentin for pain after burn-wound debridement
shelves.question: In patients undergoing surgical debridement of burn wounds, does perioperative gabapentin reduce morphine consumption and pain versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: none in the record
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: The one double-blind trial (Rimaz 2012, 50 burn patients undergoing surgical debridement/resection of burn wounds) found a single oral dose of gabapentin 1200 mg, given 2 hours before surgery, significantly reduced 24-hour patient-controlled morphine consumption and visual analogue pain scores at rest and on movement at every measured time point (1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20 and 24 hours after the operation; P<0.05), with sedation scores similar and no differences in adverse effects. The abstract reports significance without effect sizes, so the saving cannot be quantified from the record. A single small trial on an opioid-consumption surrogate: POSSIBLE. Perioperative gabapentin across surgery generally is a different, larger question (Shelf #1249) and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Rimaz 2012: a single preoperative gabapentin dose reduced morphine consumption and pain scores after burn debridement (50 patients)
cards.summary: Rimaz 2012: a single preoperative gabapentin dose reduced morphine consumption and pain scores after burn debridement (50 patients)
cards.type: Randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial (single centre)
cards.people: 50 burn patients undergoing resection/debridement of burn wounds, randomised in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study to a single oral dose of gabapentin 1200 mg or placebo 2 hours before surgery; anaesthesia was propofol/fentanyl induction with propofol, remifentanil and nitrous oxide maintenance, and all patients received patient-controlled morphine analgesia (2.5 mg bolus, 10-minute lockout) for 24 hours. All 50 enrolled patients completed the study. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The visual analogue scale scores at rest and during movement at 1, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, and 24 hours after the operation were significantly lower in the gabapentin group than in the placebo group (P<0.05). Morphine consumption was significantly less in the gabapentin group than in the placebo group (P<0.05). Sedation scores were similar in the two groups at all measured times, and there were no differences in adverse effects between the groups. The abstract prints no numerical pain scores or morphine totals, so the size of the reduction cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: One centre, 50 patients, one preoperative dose, and P values without magnitudes: the result supports 'some opioid sparing' and nothing more precise — and a record carrying neither MeSH terms nor a registry ID is harder for agents to verify, which is itself noted here.
cards.source: Rimaz S et al. Effect of gabapentin on morphine consumption and pain after surgical debridement of burn wounds: a double-blind randomized clinical trial study. Arch Trauma Res. 2012. PMID: 24719841. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. MeSH: none in the record.

shelves.title: Dermal regeneration templates versus split-thickness grafts for full-thickness burns
shelves.question: In acute full-thickness burns, do dermal regeneration templates (e.g. Integra) improve scar quality and function versus split-thickness skin grafting alone?
shelves.mesh: Artificial Organs/mortality · Burns/mortality,surgery · Skin Transplantation · Silicone Elastomers · Occlusive Dressings · Random Allocation · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Middle Aged
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — PROPOSED: Disclosure first: the anchor pinned in the topic file for this shelf (PMID 38313591) is, on verification, a systematic review and meta-analysis — not the comparative primary study the topic file described — so it is fenced in the synthesis, and the shelf's randomised anchor is the programme's founding trial pinned by title search instead. That trial (Heimbach 1988, 11 centres, 106 patients with life-threatening burns, 139 sites randomised within-patient) found median artificial-dermis take of 80% versus 95% for all comparative sites — equivalent to non-autograft control materials, below autograft-containing controls — while donor grafts for template sites were half as thick (.006 vs .013 inches; P<.0001) and donor sites healed 4 days sooner (10 ± 6 vs 14 ± 8 days; P<.0001); as wounds matured over a year there was less hypertrophic scarring at template sites and more patients preferred them. One old within-patient trial, take slightly worse, donor and scar outcomes better: POSSIBLE. A later randomised report in this field (PMID 33124156) is a retracted publication and is not evidence; it is named in the synthesis so no agent mistakes it for support.

cards.headline: Heimbach 1988: artificial dermis took slightly less well than control sites (median 80% vs 95%) but used thinner donor grafts, healed donor sites 4 days sooner, and scarred less at one year
cards.summary: Heimbach 1988: artificial dermis took slightly less well than control sites (median 80% vs 95%) but used thinner donor grafts, healed donor sites 4 days sooner, and scarred less at one year
cards.type: Multicentre prospective randomized clinical trial (within-patient site randomisation) — the programme's RCT, pinned at build after the topic file's anchor failed verification
cards.people: 106 patients with life-threatening burns undergoing primary excision and grafting within 7 days of injury at 11 centres; 139 sites were studied, with comparable sites on each patient randomised to the artificial dermis (Burke–Yannas, the template that became Integra) or the investigator's usual skin grafting material (autograft, allograft, xenograft, or a synthetic dressing). Mean burn size was 46.5 ± 15% total body surface area; overall mortality was 13% and mean hospital stay 68 ± 45 days. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Median artificial dermis take was 80% compared with 95% for all comparative sites, but the take was equivalent to that of all nonautograft control materials, and results improved slightly as investigators became more familiar with the material. Donor site thickness for the study site averaged .006'' ± .002'' compared to .013'' ± .018'' for control (P<.0001), and the epidermal donor site healed an average of 4 days sooner (10 ± 6 vs 14 ± 8 days) (P<.0001). As the wounds matured during the first year, both patients and surgeons felt the sites became more comparable in appearance and function; at the completion of the study, there was less hypertrophic scarring of the artificial dermis, and more patients preferred the artificial dermis to the control graft. The authors conclude the artificial dermis with an epidermal graft provides permanent cover at least as satisfactory as available grafting techniques, using thinner donor grafts whose sites heal faster.
cards.watchOut: A 1988 trial of a first-generation template against a mixed bag of controls (including autograft, the strongest comparator): the take deficit is against that mixture, equivalence is against non-autograft materials only, and the scar and preference outcomes are unblinded judgements by patients and surgeons who knew which site was which.
cards.source: Heimbach D et al. Artificial dermis for major burns. A multi-center randomized clinical trial. Ann Surg. 1988. PMID: 3048216. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (pre-registration-era trial). cards.result: The randomised base for dermal regeneration templates in acute burns is essentially this one trial: cover at least as satisfactory as the era's alternatives, bought with a two-stage operation and a take rate below autograft, repaid in donor-site economy and less hypertrophic scarring at a year. Two records are fenced here rather than carded: the 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 28 randomised trials (PMID 38313591), which the topic file mislabelled as a comparative study — it is a synthesis, and this library cards trials, not reviews of them; and a 2021 prospective randomised report on artificial dermis (PMID 33124156) whose record is typed Retracted Publication — it must never be cited as supporting evidence. Modern template-versus-graft RCTs at scale remain scarce, which holds the stamp at POSSIBLE.
cards.watchOut: If an agent offers the retracted 2021 trial or the 2024 review as this shelf's proof, both are category errors — one is withdrawn, the other is secondary literature; the primary randomised record is the 1988 trial carded above.

shelves.title: Conservative versus interventional treatment of primary spontaneous pneumothorax
shelves.question: In haemodynamically stable patients with moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, is conservative management non-inferior to chest-drain intervention for lung re-expansion?
shelves.mesh: Pneumothorax/diagnostic imaging,therapy · Conservative Treatment · Watchful Waiting · Chest Tubes · Drainage/methods · Humans · Adolescent · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One open-label non-inferiority trial (PSP, 316 patients aged 14–50 with a first moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax) found lung re-expansion within 8 weeks in 94.4% with conservative management versus 98.5% with intervention in the complete-case analysis (risk difference −4.1 percentage points, 95% CI −8.6 to 0.5; P=0.02 for non-inferiority against a −9-point margin) — but in the sensitivity analysis treating all missing data as failure, the difference was −11.0 points (−18.4 to −3.5), OUTSIDE the margin, so the authors themselves call the evidence 'modest'. Conservative care (which still intervened in 15.4% of patients under protocol rules) carried a lower risk of serious adverse events and recurrence. A single trial whose primary result is not robust to missing-data assumptions caps at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: PSP trial 2020: conservative management was non-inferior for re-expansion in the complete-case analysis (94.4% vs 98.5%) — but not when missing data counted as failure
cards.summary: PSP trial 2020: conservative management was non-inferior for re-expansion in the complete-case analysis (94.4% vs 98.5%) — but not when missing data counted as failure
cards.type: Open-label, multicentre, non-inferiority trial (Australia and New Zealand)
cards.people: 316 patients aged 14 to 50 years with a first-known, unilateral, moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax, randomly assigned to immediate interventional management (154) or a conservative observational approach (162) and followed for 12 months; 25 patients (15.4%) in the conservative group underwent interventions for protocol-prespecified reasons, and 137 (84.6%) did not. Data were unavailable for 23 intervention and 37 conservative patients in the complete-case analysis.
cards.result: Re-expansion within 8 weeks occurred in 129 of 131 patients (98.5%) with interventional management and 118 of 125 (94.4%) with conservative management (risk difference −4.1 percentage points, 95% CI −8.6 to 0.5; P=0.02 for non-inferiority; the lower boundary lay within the prespecified −9-point margin). In the sensitivity analysis imputing all missing data after 56 days as treatment failure, re-expansion was 129 of 138 (93.5%) versus 118 of 143 (82.5%), a risk difference of −11.0 points (−18.4 to −3.5) — outside the non-inferiority margin. Conservative management resulted in a lower risk of serious adverse events or pneumothorax recurrence than interventional management. The authors conclude the trial provides modest evidence of non-inferiority.
cards.watchOut: Differential missing data (37 conservative versus 23 intervention patients) is the trial's soft spot, and the authors disclose it plainly: under the harsher assumption the non-inferiority claim fails. 'Conservative' also did not mean 'never a drain' — 15.4% crossed over by protocol.
cards.source: Brown SGA et al. Conservative versus Interventional Treatment for Spontaneous Pneumothorax. N Engl J Med. 2020. PMID: 31995686. Registry ID: ANZCTR ACTRN12611000184976, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Ambulatory management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax (RAMPP)
shelves.question: In stable primary spontaneous pneumothorax needing intervention, does ambulatory management with a pleural vent reduce total hospital stay versus standard chest-drain care?
shelves.mesh: Pneumothorax/therapy · Ambulatory Care/statistics & numerical data · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Standard of Care · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The single randomised trial (RAMPP, 236 patients aged 16–55 with symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax) found ambulatory management with a pleural vent significantly shortened total hospital stay to day 30 — median 0 days (IQR 0–3) versus 4 days (0–8) on standard care (P<0.0001; median difference 2 days, 95% CI 1 to 3) — at the cost of more adverse events: 55% of the ambulatory group versus 39% of standard care had adverse events, and all 14 serious adverse events occurred in the ambulatory arm, eight of them related to the intervention (enlarging pneumothorax, asymptomatic pulmonary oedema, device malfunction, leak or dislodgement). One open-label trial with a clear stay benefit and a clear adverse-event price supports POSSIBLE. (Anchor pins, as flagged at drafting: the results report is pinned here as Hallifax et al., Lancet 2020, PMID 32622394 — the topic draft cited the journal as Lancet Respiratory Medicine, which the record corrects to The Lancet; the draft's verified programme record, PMID 31179004, is the trial PROTOCOL and is not carded.)

cards.headline: RAMPP 2020: ambulatory pleural-vent management cut median hospital stay to 0 versus 4 days — but all 14 serious adverse events were in the ambulatory arm
cards.summary: RAMPP 2020: ambulatory pleural-vent management cut median hospital stay to 0 versus 4 days — but all 14 serious adverse events were in the ambulatory arm
cards.type: Open-label, randomised controlled trial (24 UK hospitals)
cards.people: 236 adults (aged 16–55 years) with symptomatic primary spontaneous pneumothorax recruited from 24 UK hospitals between July 2015 and March 2019, randomly assigned to an ambulatory device (117) or standard guideline-based management — aspiration, standard chest tube insertion, or both (119); 114 ambulatory and 113 standard-care patients had data for the primary analysis.
cards.result: At day 30, median total hospitalisation (including readmissions) was significantly shorter with ambulatory treatment (0 days [IQR 0–3]) than with standard care (4 days [0–8]) (P<0.0001; median difference 2 days, 95% CI 1 to 3). Overall, 110 (47%) of 236 patients had adverse events, including 64 (55%) of 117 in the ambulatory arm and 46 (39%) of 119 in the standard-care arm. All 14 serious adverse events occurred in patients who received ambulatory care, eight (57%) of which were related to the intervention, including an enlarging pneumothorax, asymptomatic pulmonary oedema, and the device malfunctioning, leaking, or dislodging. The authors conclude ambulatory management significantly reduced hospitalisation but at the expense of increased adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Open-label with a length-of-stay endpoint — discharge decisions were made by clinicians who knew the allocation; and the serious-adverse-event asymmetry (14 versus 0) is the standing caution: the stay saving is real, and so is the device-event burden.
cards.source: Hallifax RJ et al. Ambulatory management of primary spontaneous pneumothorax: an open-label, randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32622394. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields (the report states prospective registration as ISRCTN79151659). shelves.title: Pigtail catheter versus chest tube for traumatic pneumothorax
shelves.question: In injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax, is a small-bore pigtail catheter as effective as a chest tube, with less pain?
shelves.mesh: Pneumothorax/therapy · Thoracic Injuries/therapy · Chest Tubes/adverse effects · Catheterization/adverse effects · Pain Measurement · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One small single-centre randomised trial (40 injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax; 20 per arm) found 14-Fr pigtail catheters resolved the pneumothorax as successfully as 28-Fr chest tubes, with similar duration of tube placement and insertion-related complications, while tube-site pain was substantially lower with the pigtail at every measurement — after insertion 3.2 versus 7.7, day 1 1.9 versus 6.2, day 2 2.1 versus 5.5 (all significant) — although total pain-medication use did not differ significantly and chest-wall trauma pain was similar in both groups. Forty patients and a pain-score primary endpoint cap the stamp at POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: Kulvatunyou 2014: pigtail catheters matched chest tubes for resolution and complications, with far less tube-site pain (3.2 vs 7.7 after insertion)
cards.summary: Kulvatunyou 2014: pigtail catheters matched chest tubes for resolution and complications, with far less tube-site pain (3.2 vs 7.7 after insertion)
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial (single level I trauma centre)
cards.people: 40 injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax presenting to a level I trauma centre between July 2010 and February 2012, randomised to a 14-Fr pigtail catheter (20) or a 28-Fr chest tube (20); patients requiring emergency tube placement, those who refused, and those unable to respond to pain assessment were excluded. No patient had a flail chest or haemothorax. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: Pain scores related to chest-wall trauma were similar in the two groups. Patients with a pigtail catheter had significantly lower mean (SD) tube-site pain scores than those with a chest tube: at baseline after tube insertion 3.2 (0.6) versus 7.7 (0.6) (P<0.001), on day 1 1.9 (0.5) versus 6.2 (0.7) (P<0.001), and on day 2 2.1 (1.1) versus 5.5 (1.0) (P=0.040). The decreased use of pain medication associated with pigtail catheter was not significantly different. Duration of tube insertion, success rate of pneumothorax resolution and insertion-related complications were all similar in the two groups.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients, all with simple pneumothorax and none with haemothorax or flail chest: 'similar success' in 20 patients per arm cannot exclude meaningful failure-rate differences, and the result does not extend to haemothorax, where tube calibre may matter.
cards.source: Kulvatunyou N et al. Randomized clinical trial of pigtail catheter versus chest tube in injured patients with uncomplicated traumatic pneumothorax. Br J Surg. 2014. PMID: 24375295. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01537289, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Epidural analgesia for traumatic rib fractures
shelves.question: In patients with multiple traumatic rib fractures, does thoracic epidural analgesia improve pain, pulmonary complications and mortality versus systemic/parenteral analgesia?
shelves.mesh: Rib Fractures/complications,physiopathology,therapy · Analgesia, Epidural · Pneumonia/prevention & control · Respiration, Artificial · Pain Management · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: The largest primary randomised trial pinned at build (Bulger 2004) enrolled only 46 patients — of 408 admitted with more than three rib fractures, 282 met exclusion criteria and 80 could not be consented — and found, despite the epidural group having MORE direct pulmonary injury (more flail segments, contusions and chest tubes), a pneumonia rate of 18% on epidural versus 38% on intravenous opioids (adjusted odds ratio 6.0 relative for pneumonia with opioids, 95% CI 1.0 to 35; P=0.05) and, in patients with pulmonary contusion, twice the ventilator days on opioids (incidence rate ratio 2.0 relative, 1.6 to 2.6). A 46-patient trial from 2004 with a barely-significant adjusted estimate is POSSIBLE and no more — this is the weakest pack in its slate, and the shelf says so. (Anchor note: the topic draft anchored this shelf to a systematic review/meta-analysis, PMID 25683770; per build rules the meta-analysis is fenced and the largest primary RCT — Bulger 2004, PMID 15300210 — is carded instead.)

cards.headline: Bulger 2004: epidural analgesia halved pneumonia after multiple rib fractures (18% vs 38%) in a 46-patient trial — despite worse lung injury in the epidural group
cards.summary: Bulger 2004: epidural analgesia halved pneumonia after multiple rib fractures (18% vs 38%) in a 46-patient trial — despite worse lung injury in the epidural group
cards.people: 46 adults (over 18 years) with more than three rib fractures and no contraindication to epidural catheter placement, enrolled between March 2000 and December 2003 from 408 patients admitted with more than three rib fractures (282 met exclusion criteria, 80 could not be consented), randomised to epidural analgesia (22) or intravenous opioids (24). The groups were comparable for mean age, injury severity score, sex, chest Abbreviated Injury Scale and number of rib fractures, but the epidural group had more flail segments (38% vs 21%), pulmonary contusions (59% vs 38%) and chest tubes (95% vs 71%).
cards.result: The rate of pneumonia was 18% in the epidural group versus 38% in the intravenous opioid group. Adjusted for direct pulmonary injury, the risk of pneumonia was greater in the opioid group (odds ratio 6.0 relative, 95% CI 1.0 to 35; P=0.05). Stratified for pulmonary contusion, the opioid group had a 2.0-fold increase in ventilator days (incidence rate ratio 2.0 relative, 1.6 to 2.6; P<0.001). The authors note that epidural analgesia use is limited in the trauma population by numerous exclusion criteria, but that when feasible it was associated with less nosocomial pneumonia and shorter mechanical ventilation.
cards.watchOut: Forty-six patients — barely a tenth of those admitted — with the headline adjusted odds ratio's confidence interval touching 1.0 (1.0 to 35): the result is fragile, the eligible population is highly selected (282 excluded), and pain scores themselves are not reported in the abstract.
cards.source: Bulger EM et al. Epidural analgesia improves outcome after multiple rib fractures. Surgery. 2004. PMID: 15300210. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Ketamine versus morphine for traumatic pain (prehospital and ED)
shelves.question: In patients with acute traumatic pain, does (low-dose) ketamine provide analgesia non-inferior to morphine, with an acceptable adverse-effect profile?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain · Analgesia · Ketamine/therapeutic use · Morphine/therapeutic use · Analgesics, Opioid/therapeutic use · Single-Blind Method · Humans · Adult · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One multicentre single-blind non-inferiority trial (KETAMORPH, 251 patients with out-of-hospital traumatic pain and a verbal pain score of at least 5) found intravenous ketamine non-inferior to morphine for pain reduction at 30 minutes — mean pain-score change −3.7 versus −3.8 (difference 0.1 points, 95% CI −0.7 to 0.9, against a non-inferiority margin of 1.3) — with no clinically meaningful vital-sign differences, but with adverse effects in 40.8% on ketamine versus 16.8% on morphine, most commonly emergence phenomena (20.0% of ketamine patients) versus nausea (10.6% of morphine patients); no adverse event required intervention. A single trial on a pain-score endpoint supports POSSIBLE: ketamine is a legitimate morphine alternative prehospital, with a different and busier minor-adverse-effect profile.

cards.headline: KETAMORPH 2024: prehospital ketamine was non-inferior to morphine for traumatic pain (change −3.7 vs −3.8) with more minor adverse effects (40.8% vs 16.8%)
cards.summary: KETAMORPH 2024: prehospital ketamine was non-inferior to morphine for traumatic pain (change −3.7 vs −3.8) with more minor adverse effects (40.8% vs 16.8%)
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blind, non-inferiority randomised clinical trial (KETAMORPH; 11 French prehospital units)
cards.people: 251 adults with out-of-hospital trauma and a verbal pain score of at least 5, enrolled between November 2017 and November 2022 in 11 French out-of-hospital emergency medical units, randomised to intravenous ketamine (128; 20 mg then 10 mg every 5 minutes) or morphine sulfate (123; 2 or 3 mg every 5 minutes); median age 51 years (IQR 34–69); 111 women (44.9%) among the 247 with data available.
cards.result: The mean pain-score change at 30 minutes was −3.7 (95% CI −4.2 to −3.2) in the ketamine group versus −3.8 (−4.2 to −3.4) in the morphine group (difference 0.1 points, −0.7 to 0.9), meeting the prespecified non-inferiority margin of 1.3. There were no clinically meaningful differences in vital signs. Adverse effects were reported in 49 of 120 patients (40.8%) on ketamine (most commonly emergence phenomenon, 24 of 120 [20.0%]) versus 19 of 113 (16.8%) on morphine (most commonly nausea, 12 of 113 [10.6%]). No adverse events required intervention.
cards.watchOut: Single-blind (patients blinded, clinicians not) with a subjective endpoint, and the adverse-effect comparison cuts both ways: ketamine's emergence phenomena (one in five) against morphine's nausea. Non-inferiority at a 1.3-point margin on a pain scale is adequacy, not equality of experience.
cards.source: Le Cornec C et al. Ketamine Compared With Morphine for Out-of-Hospital Analgesia for Patients With Traumatic Pain: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Network Open. 2024. PMID: 38285446. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03236805, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Intranasal ketamine versus intranasal fentanyl for children's limb-injury pain (PICHFORK)
shelves.question: In children with moderate-to-severe limb-injury pain, is intranasal ketamine non-inferior to intranasal fentanyl for pain relief?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal · Ketamine/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Fentanyl/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Extremities/injuries · Pain Measurement · Double-Blind Method · Humans · Child · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE: One double-blind randomised trial (PICHFORK, 80 children enrolled, 73 analysed, aged 3–13 with isolated limb injury and pain above 6 of 10, all co-administered oral ibuprofen) found intranasal ketamine 1 mg/kg and intranasal fentanyl 1.5 μg/kg produced similar pain reduction at 30 minutes — median reductions of 45 mm versus 40 mm (difference 5 mm, 95% CI −10 to 20 mm) — maintained to 60 minutes, with reductions above 20 mm in 82% versus 79% and satisfaction in 83% versus 72%. Adverse events, mainly mild, were more frequent with ketamine (78% versus 40%), including moderate sedation in three ketamine patients. A single small trial supports POSSIBLE: comparable analgesia, more minor ketamine effects.

cards.headline: PICHFORK 2015: intranasal ketamine matched intranasal fentanyl for children's limb-injury pain at 30 minutes (median reduction 45 vs 40 mm)
cards.summary: PICHFORK 2015: intranasal ketamine matched intranasal fentanyl for children's limb-injury pain at 30 minutes (median reduction 45 vs 40 mm)
cards.people: 80 children aged 3 to 13 years and weighing less than 50 kg with isolated limb injury and pain of more than 6 of 10 at triage, randomised to intranasal fentanyl 1.5 μg/kg (37 analysed) or intranasal ketamine 1 mg/kg (36 analysed); all were co-administered oral ibuprofen 10 mg/kg. Median age was 8 years; 63% were boys; median baseline pain rating was 80 mm.
cards.result: At 30 minutes, median pain-rating reductions were 45 mm for ketamine and 40 mm for fentanyl (difference 5 mm, 95% CI −10 to 20 mm). Reductions exceeded 20 mm in 82% (ketamine) and 79% (fentanyl) of patients (difference 3%, 95% CI −22% to 16%). Pain reduction was maintained to 60 minutes in both groups. Satisfaction was reported by 83% (ketamine) and 72% (fentanyl) of patients (difference 11%, −9% to 30%). Adverse events, mainly mild, were reported by 78% on ketamine and 40% on fentanyl (difference 38% as printed in the record); three ketamine patients had a moderate degree of sedation.
cards.watchOut: Seventy-three analysed children and a confidence interval for the pain difference (−10 to 20 mm) wide enough to include a clinically meaningful advantage either way: 'similar' here means 'no difference detected at this size', and every child also received ibuprofen, so the comparison is of add-on intranasal agents.
cards.source: Graudins A et al. The PICHFORK (Pain in Children Fentanyl or Ketamine) trial: a randomized controlled trial comparing intranasal fentanyl and fentanyl for the relief of moderate to severe pain in children with limb injuries. Ann Emerg Med. 2015. PMID: 25447557. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Perioperative rosuvastatin in cardiac surgery (STICS)
shelves.question: In patients undergoing elective cardiac surgery, does perioperative rosuvastatin prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation or acute kidney injury?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation/prevention & control · Rosuvastatin Calcium/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Acute Kidney Injury/chemically induced · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Perioperative Care · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference, with kidney harm): One large randomised trial (STICS, 1,922 patients in sinus rhythm scheduled for elective cardiac surgery in China) found perioperative rosuvastatin 20 mg daily did NOT prevent postoperative atrial fibrillation (21.1% versus 20.5% on placebo; odds ratio 1.04 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.30; P=0.72) and did not reduce perioperative myocardial injury (troponin I release area under the curve essentially identical; between-group difference 1%, −9 to 13; P=0.80), with no benefit in any subgroup or secondary outcome — while significantly increasing postoperative acute kidney injury by an absolute 5.4 (SE 1.9) percentage points (P=0.005), despite lower LDL cholesterol and C-reactive protein after surgery. A large, internally consistent null with a harm signal carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: STICS 2016: perioperative rosuvastatin did not prevent postoperative AF (21.1% vs 20.5%) or myocardial injury — and increased acute kidney injury by 5.4 points
cards.summary: STICS 2016: perioperative rosuvastatin did not prevent postoperative AF (21.1% vs 20.5%) or myocardial injury — and increased acute kidney injury by 5.4 points
cards.type: Randomised, placebo-controlled trial (elective cardiac surgery, China)
cards.people: 1,922 patients in sinus rhythm scheduled for elective cardiac surgery, randomly assigned to perioperative rosuvastatin 20 mg daily or placebo. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: LDL cholesterol and C-reactive protein concentrations after surgery were lower on rosuvastatin (P<0.001). Postoperative atrial fibrillation did not differ significantly (21.1% rosuvastatin versus 20.5% placebo; odds ratio 1.04 relative, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.30; P=0.72), nor did the area under the troponin I-release curve (102 versus 100 ng×hour per millilitre; between-group difference 1%, −9 to 13; P=0.80). Subgroup analyses indicated no benefit in any category of patient, and rosuvastatin produced no beneficial effects on any secondary outcome, but was associated with a significant absolute excess of 5.4 (SE 1.9) percentage points in postoperative acute kidney injury (P=0.005).
cards.watchOut: STICS tested starting rosuvastatin perioperatively in a largely statin-naive elective population in one country; it does not address continuing long-term statins (a different question), and its biomarker effects (lower LDL and CRP) conspicuously failed to translate into outcome benefit.
cards.source: Zheng Z et al. Perioperative Rosuvastatin in Cardiac Surgery. N Engl J Med. 2016. PMID: 27144849. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01573143, from the record's databank fields. shelves.title: Opioid-free anaesthesia (POFA)
shelves.question: In patients having major or intermediate noncardiac surgery, does dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anaesthesia reduce postoperative opioid-related adverse events versus remifentanil-based anaesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Balanced Anesthesia/methods · Dexmedetomidine/therapeutic use · Remifentanil/therapeutic use · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Humans · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm-leaning; the treatment made no difference): The single randomised test (POFA, 312 patients analysed having major or intermediate noncardiac surgery) REFUTED its hypothesis: the composite of postoperative opioid-related adverse events (hypoxaemia, ileus or cognitive dysfunction within 48 hours) occurred MORE often with dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free anaesthesia than with remifentanil-based anaesthesia — 78% versus 67% (relative risk 1.16 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.33; P=0.031) — driven by hypoxaemia (72% vs 61%; relative risk 1.19 relative, 1.02 to 1.40), and the trial was stopped prematurely because of five cases of severe bradycardia in the dexmedetomidine group. Opioid-free patients did use less postoperative morphine and had less nausea and vomiting, with similar analgesia, but had more delayed extubation and longer recovery-room stays. A stopped-early single trial supports POSSIBLE against the opioid-free strategy as tested. (Journal correction: the topic draft cited this trial as JAMA 2021; the verified record is Beloeil et al., Anesthesiology 2021.)

cards.headline: POFA 2021: opioid-free anaesthesia increased the opioid-related adverse-event composite (78% vs 67%) and the trial stopped early for severe bradycardia
cards.summary: POFA 2021: opioid-free anaesthesia increased the opioid-related adverse-event composite (78% vs 67%) and the trial stopped early for severe bradycardia
cards.type: Randomised trial (POFA) — stopped prematurely for severe bradycardia
cards.people: Patients having major or intermediate noncardiac surgery, randomised to a standard balanced anaesthetic with intraoperative remifentanil plus morphine or to dexmedetomidine-based opioid-free balanced anaesthesia; 312 patients were analysed for the primary outcome (156 per group). All patients received propofol, desflurane, dexamethasone, lidocaine and ketamine infusions, neuromuscular blockade, and postoperative lidocaine infusion, paracetamol, nefopam and patient-controlled morphine. The abstract does not state mean age or the sex mix.
cards.result: The study was stopped prematurely because of five cases of severe bradycardia in the dexmedetomidine group. The primary composite outcome (postoperative hypoxaemia, ileus or cognitive dysfunction within 48 hours of extubation) occurred in 122 of 156 (78%) dexmedetomidine-group patients versus 105 of 156 (67%) in the remifentanil group (relative risk 1.16 relative, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.33; P=0.031). Hypoxaemia occurred in 110 of 152 (72%) versus 94 of 155 (61%) (relative risk 1.19 relative, 1.02 to 1.40; P=0.030); ileus and cognitive dysfunction did not differ. Cumulative 0–48 hour postoperative morphine consumption was lower with dexmedetomidine (median 11 mg [IQR 5–21] versus 6 mg [0–17] as printed in the record's group order) — the record states consumption and postoperative nausea and vomiting (58 of 157 [37%] versus 37 of 157 [24%]; relative risk 0.64 relative, 0.45 to 0.90) were both less in the dexmedetomidine group — while measures of analgesia were similar. Dexmedetomidine patients had more delayed extubation and prolonged post-anaesthesia care unit stay. The authors conclude the trial refuted the hypothesis.
cards.watchOut: One specific opioid-free recipe (dexmedetomidine replacing remifentanil, on a shared multimodal background) in one trial stopped early: the verdict convicts this recipe as tested, not every opioid-sparing technique — and note the record's own morphine-consumption medians are printed in an order that sits awkwardly with its 'less in the dexmedetomidine group' statement, which is why this card quotes the statement as the record gives it rather than re-deriving a direction.

shelves.title: Desflurane versus sevoflurane for recovery from anaesthesia
shelves.question: In ambulatory/minor-to-moderate surgery, does desflurane produce faster emergence and recovery than sevoflurane, and at what cost in adverse respiratory events?
shelves.mesh: Desflurane/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Sevoflurane/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Anesthetics, Inhalation/administration & dosage,adverse effects · Anesthesia Recovery Period · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting/epidemiology,prevention & control · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): The carded randomised test in the population where the question matters most (Taschner 2024, 190 patients aged 65 or older having minor-to-moderate-risk noncardiac surgery with same-day discharge intent) found NO significant difference in postoperative recovery time between desflurane and sevoflurane: median time from PACU arrival to reaching discharge criteria (modified Aldrete score at least 12) was 0 minutes in both groups (P=0.245), because most patients already met criteria on arrival (81.1% desflurane versus 88.4% sevoflurane; P=0.277). Postoperative nausea and vomiting, PACU bispectral index values and maximum S100B concentrations also did not differ. One single-centre trial with a ceiling-limited endpoint supports POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): in older day-case patients, the classic 'desflurane wakes you faster' claim did not survive measurement.

cards.headline: Taschner 2024: in older adults, desflurane did not speed recovery versus sevoflurane — median time to discharge criteria was 0 minutes in both groups
cards.summary: Taschner 2024: in older adults, desflurane did not speed recovery versus sevoflurane — median time to discharge criteria was 0 minutes in both groups
cards.type: Single-centre, prospective, observer-blinded randomised clinical trial
cards.people: 190 patients aged 65 years or older scheduled for minor- to moderate-risk noncardiac surgery, randomised at a single centre to goal-directed desflurane (95) or sevoflurane (95) maintenance anaesthesia with a bispectral index target of 50 (SD 5); all were eligible for same-day discharge.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in median duration of postoperative recovery between groups (desflurane 0 min [IQR 0–0]; sevoflurane 0 min [0–0]; P=0.245). On arrival at the post-anaesthesia care unit, 77 patients (81.1%) in the desflurane group and 84 (88.4%) in the sevoflurane group already had modified Aldrete scores of at least 12 points (P=0.277). There were no significant differences in the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (P=0.606), postoperative bispectral index values (P=0.197), or postoperative maximum S100B concentrations (P=0.821). The authors conclude that, despite previous reports, they did not observe significantly faster recovery times after desflurane anaesthesia.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint hit its ceiling: with four-fifths of patients already discharge-ready on PACU arrival, the trial could not detect small emergence differences in minutes — its null is about clinically meaningful recovery advantage in older day-case patients, not about pharmacokinetic emergence times measured in seconds.
cards.source: Taschner A et al. shelves.title: Total intravenous versus volatile anaesthesia for major noncardiac surgery
shelves.question: In adults having major noncardiac surgery, does total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol improve postoperative outcomes versus volatile inhalational anaesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia, Intravenous/adverse effects,methods · Anesthesia, Inhalation/adverse effects,methods · Propofol/adverse effects,administration & dosage · Elective Surgical Procedures/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Humans · Aged · Female · Male
shelves.balance: LIKELY (the treatment made no difference): One large pragmatic randomised trial (2,508 patients aged 50 or older having elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK hospitals) found total intravenous anaesthesia with propofol and volatile inhalational anaesthesia produced essentially identical recovery: days alive and at home at 30 days were 22.5 (SD 6.8) versus 22.4 (SD 6.6) (incidence rate ratio 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.02; adjusted P=0.68), with no differences in days alive and at home at 90 days, mortality at 30 days, 90 days or 6 months, Quality of Recovery-15 score at day 3, delirium, or major complications (12.4% overall). TIVA patients reported less thirst, hoarseness and nausea/vomiting; the trial's only two cases of certain or probable unintentional awareness both occurred in the TIVA group. A 2,508-patient trial with a dead-centre primary estimate carries LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the recovery claim.

cards.headline: Jhanji 2026: TIVA and volatile anaesthesia gave identical days alive and at home at 30 days (22.5 vs 22.4) in 2,508 older adults having major noncardiac surgery
cards.summary: Jhanji 2026: TIVA and volatile anaesthesia gave identical days alive and at home at 30 days (22.5 vs 22.4) in 2,508 older adults having major noncardiac surgery
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, open-label randomised clinical trial (49 UK NHS hospitals)
cards.people: 2,508 patients aged 50 years or older scheduled for elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK NHS hospitals, randomised 1:1 between January 2022 and April 2024 to maintenance of general anaesthesia with total intravenous anaesthesia (propofol infusion; 1,254) or volatile-based inhalational agents (1,254), with all other perioperative care at clinician discretion; mean age 67 years (SD 8.9); 55% were male.
cards.result: Days alive and at home at 30 days were similar between groups (mean 22.5 [SD 6.8] days TIVA versus 22.4 [SD 6.6] volatile; incidence rate ratio 1.00 relative, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.02; adjusted P=0.68). There were no differences in days alive and at home at 90 days; mortality at 30 days, 90 days, or 6 months; or Quality of Recovery-15 score at day 3. Lower rates of thirst, hoarseness, and nausea and vomiting were reported in the TIVA group. Delirium levels were similar (87.6% had no delirium at day 3). Major complications occurred in 12.4% of patients overall, with no significant between-group differences. Two cases of certain or probable unintentional awareness under anaesthesia were reported, both in the TIVA group.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and pragmatic — depth of anaesthesia, adjuncts and recovery care were clinicians' choice, which is the point for a comparative-effectiveness question but limits mechanistic reading; the two awareness cases are a signal to note (2 of 1,254), not a powered endpoint.
cards.source: Jhanji S et al. Total Intravenous vs Volatile Inhalational Anesthesia for Major Noncardiac Surgery: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2026. PMID: 42584898. Registry ID: none in the record's databank fields. shelves.title: High perioperative oxygen fraction and surgical-site infection (PROXI vs Belda)
shelves.question: In patients having abdominal surgery, does 80% inspired oxygen during and shortly after surgery reduce surgical-site infection versus 30% oxygen?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Humans · Intraoperative Period · Laparotomy · Male · Middle Aged · Oxygen · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy · Perioperative Care · Pneumonia · Postoperative Complications · Postoperative Period · Pulmonary Atelectasis · Respiratory Insufficiency · Risk · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials of the same contrast disagree, and the larger one is null. Belda (2005, 300 colorectal patients, double-blind) found fewer infections with 80% oxygen — 14.9% versus 24.4% (relative risk 0.61, 95% CI 0.38–0.98). PROXI (2009, 1,400 laparotomy patients, blinded) found no difference — 19.1% versus 20.1% (odds ratio 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22) — and no difference in pneumonia, atelectasis, or respiratory failure; 30-day mortality was numerically higher with high oxygen (4.4% vs 2.9%; OR 1.56, CI 0.88–2.77, not significant). A third trial in an open-lung ventilation strategy (iPROVE-O2, 2020) also found no infection benefit (8.9% vs 9.4%). Two of three trials, including by far the largest, show no effect, and Belda's confidence interval only just excludes 1.0 — so the disagreement caps the stamp at POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): on current evidence, 80% oxygen should not be given to prevent wound infection. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PROXI 2009: 80% oxygen did not reduce surgical-site infection — 19.1% vs 20.1% (OR 0.94, CI 0.72–1.22)
cards.summary: PROXI 2009: 80% oxygen did not reduce surgical-site infection — 19.1% vs 20.1% (OR 0.94, CI 0.72–1.22)
cards.people: 1,400 patients undergoing acute or elective laparotomy at 14 Danish hospitals, randomised to 80% or 30% oxygen during and for 2 hours after surgery. The primary outcome was surgical-site infection within 14 days by CDC criteria; secondary outcomes included atelectasis, pneumonia, respiratory failure, and 30-day mortality.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection occurred in 131 of 685 patients (19.1%) on 80% oxygen versus 141 of 701 (20.1%) on 30% oxygen (OR 0.94, 95% CI 0.72–1.22; P=.64) — an absolute difference of about 1 percentage point. Atelectasis (7.9% vs 7.1%), pneumonia (6.0% vs 6.3%), and respiratory failure (5.5% vs 4.4%) did not differ. Thirty-day mortality was 4.4% versus 2.9% (OR 1.56, 95% CI 0.88–2.77; P=.13) — numerically higher with high oxygen but with a confidence interval crossing 1.0, so this trial alone does not establish harm.
cards.watchOut: PROXI mixed acute and elective laparotomy across many procedure types; a benefit confined to elective colorectal surgery (Belda's population) cannot be excluded by this trial, though PROXI's size makes a large general effect unlikely. The mortality point estimate leans against high oxygen but is not significant and should not be carded as proven harm.
cards.source: Meyhoff CS et al. Effect of high perioperative oxygen fraction on surgical site infection and pulmonary complications after abdominal surgery: the PROXI randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2009. PMID: 19826023. Registry ID: NCT00364741, from the record. cards.headline: Belda 2005: in colorectal surgery, 80% oxygen cut wound infection — 14.9% vs 24.4% (RR 0.61, CI 0.38–0.98)
cards.summary: Belda 2005: in colorectal surgery, 80% oxygen cut wound infection — 14.9% vs 24.4% (RR 0.61, CI 0.38–0.98)
cards.people: 300 patients aged 18–80 undergoing elective colorectal surgery at 14 Spanish hospitals, randomised to 80% or 30% inspired oxygen intraoperatively and for 6 hours afterwards, with standardised anaesthesia and antibiotics. Wound infection was diagnosed by blinded investigators using CDC criteria.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection occurred in 22 of 148 patients (14.9%) on 80% oxygen versus 35 of 143 (24.4%) on 30% oxygen — a relative risk of 0.61 (95% CI 0.38–0.98; P=.04), i.e. a 39% relative reduction and an absolute reduction of about 9.5 percentage points. After covariate adjustment the relative risk was 0.46 (95% CI 0.22–0.95). No secondary outcome (bowel function, ambulation, suture removal, hospital stay) differed.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval only just excludes 1.0, and the trial predates PROXI: the same contrast in a population nearly five times larger found nothing. Belda's higher baseline infection rate (24.4% in controls vs PROXI's 20.1%) and colorectal-only, elective population are the candidate explanations for the discrepancy — but the burden of proof sits with the smaller, earlier trial.
