shelves.title: Continuing versus stopping renin–angiotensin inhibitors before major surgery (STOP-or-NOT; SPACE)
shelves.question: In patients on renin–angiotensin system inhibitors having major noncardiac surgery, does continuing the drug through surgery versus stopping it 48 hours before change postoperative complications?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Angiotensin Receptor Antagonists · Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors · Hypotension · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications · Preoperative Care · Renin-Angiotensin System · Surgical Procedures, Operative · Time Factors · Hospital Mortality · Intraoperative Complications
shelves.balance: Two randomised trials agree that the continue-versus-stop decision does not move hard outcomes. STOP-or-NOT (2024, 2,222 patients, major noncardiac surgery) found the composite of death and major postoperative complications identical at 22% in both strategies (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19); continuing caused more intraoperative hypotension (54% vs 41%; RR 1.31, CI 1.19–1.44) without any downstream outcome penalty. The smaller UK SPACE trial (262 patients) found myocardial injury no less frequent when the drug was stopped (48.3% vs 41.3% continuing; OR for continuing 0.77, CI 0.45–1.31, crossing 1.0) and more acute hypertensive episodes when it was stopped. The physiological trade-off is real in both directions — more hypotension if you continue, more hypertension if you stop — but neither trial shows a difference in complications, myocardial injury, or death. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C (the composite includes mortality — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: STOP-or-NOT 2024: continuing RAS inhibitors gave the same 22% rate of death or major complications as stopping (RR 1.02, CI 0.87–1.19) — but more intraoperative hypotension
cards.summary: STOP-or-NOT 2024: continuing RAS inhibitors gave the same 22% rate of death or major complications as stopping (RR 1.02, CI 0.87–1.19) — but more intraoperative hypotension
cards.people: 2,222 patients treated with a renin–angiotensin system inhibitor (46% ACE inhibitor, 54% ARB) for at least 3 months, scheduled for major noncardiac surgery at 40 French hospitals. Patients were randomised to continue the drug until the day of surgery (n=1,107) or to stop it 48 hours before (last dose 3 days pre-operatively, n=1,115). The primary outcome was all-cause mortality or major postoperative complications within 28 days.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 22% in both groups — 247 of 1,107 continuing versus 245 of 1,115 stopping (risk ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.87–1.19; P=.85), an absolute difference of zero. Intraoperative hypotension was more common with continuation (54% vs 41%; RR 1.31, 95% CI 1.19–1.44), but acute kidney injury, organ failure, and hospital and ICU stay did not differ.
cards.watchOut: The trial shows the strategy choice does not change outcomes at 28 days; it does not say the intraoperative hypotension is harmless in every individual — anaesthetists still have to manage a roughly 13-percentage-point absolute excess of hypotensive episodes when the drug is continued. Patients having cardiac surgery and those with severe heart failure were not the studied population.

shelves.title: Liberal versus restrictive transfusion after hip fracture surgery (FOCUS)
shelves.question: In older patients with cardiovascular risk after hip fracture surgery, does a liberal transfusion threshold (haemoglobin 100 g/L) improve death or functional recovery versus a restrictive threshold (80 g/L or symptoms)?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anemia · Blood Transfusion · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Hemoglobins · Hip Fractures · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Mortality · Postoperative Complications · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome · Wound Infection
shelves.balance: One large definitive trial: FOCUS randomised 2,016 patients aged 50+ with cardiovascular disease or risk factors whose haemoglobin fell below 10 g/dL after hip fracture surgery, to transfusion at a 10 g/dL threshold (median 2 units given) or a restrictive strategy (symptoms, or haemoglobin below 8 g/dL; median 0 units). The primary outcome — death or inability to walk across a room unaided at 60 days — was 35.2% liberal versus 34.7% restrictive (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84–1.22; absolute difference 0.5 points, CI −3.7 to 4.7), and 60-day mortality was 7.6% versus 6.6%. Restrictive transfusion was as safe as liberal in exactly the population clinicians most feared under-transfusing, while using far less blood. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference), Tier C (mortality is in the primary composite — the developer rules personally). The general threshold question across critical care is homed on Shelf #124; this shelf is the hip-fracture surgical anchor, with a functional endpoint that shelf does not carry.

cards.headline: FOCUS 2011: a 10 g/dL transfusion threshold did not beat a restrictive strategy — death or inability to walk at 60 days 35.2% vs 34.7% (OR 1.01, CI 0.84–1.22)
cards.summary: FOCUS 2011: a 10 g/dL transfusion threshold did not beat a restrictive strategy — death or inability to walk at 60 days 35.2% vs 34.7% (OR 1.01, CI 0.84–1.22)
cards.people: 2,016 patients aged 50 or older with a history of or risk factors for cardiovascular disease, whose haemoglobin fell below 10 g/dL after hip fracture surgery. Patients were randomised to a liberal strategy (transfuse to keep haemoglobin at or above 10 g/dL) or a restrictive strategy (transfuse for symptoms of anaemia, or at physician discretion for haemoglobin below 8 g/dL). The primary outcome was death or inability to walk across a room without human assistance at 60-day follow-up.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 35.2% of the liberal group versus 34.7% of the restrictive group (OR 1.01, 95% CI 0.84–1.22; absolute risk difference 0.5 percentage points, 95% CI −3.7 to 4.7). Death at 60 days was 7.6% versus 6.6% (absolute difference 1.0 point, 99% CI −1.9 to 4.0), and in-hospital acute coronary syndrome or death was 4.3% versus 5.2%. The liberal group received a median of 2 units of red cells; the restrictive group a median of none. Other complication rates were similar.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval excludes a large benefit of liberal transfusion but not a small one (up to about 4–5 points on the primary composite). FOCUS enrolled patients after surgery whose haemoglobin had already fallen below 10 g/dL — it does not address transfusion during resuscitation from acute bleeding (Shelf #240), nor the myocardial-infarction population, where restriction remains questioned (Shelf #368).

shelves.title: Nitrous oxide in major noncardiac surgery (ENIGMA-II)
shelves.question: In at-risk patients having major noncardiac surgery, does adding nitrous oxide to general anaesthesia increase death or cardiovascular complications versus nitrous-free anaesthesia?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anesthesia, General · Anesthetics, Combined · Anesthetics, Inhalation · Cardiovascular Diseases · Coronary Artery Disease · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nitrous Oxide · Postoperative Complications · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Single-Blind Method · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: One very large trial settles the safety question that the smaller ENIGMA-I era left open. ENIGMA-II randomised 7,112 patients aged 45+ with known or suspected coronary disease having major noncardiac surgery to anaesthesia with or without nitrous oxide. The composite of death and cardiovascular complications at 30 days occurred in 8% in both groups (283 vs 296 patients; relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.83–1.12), and surgical-site infection did not differ (9% vs 9%). The one clear penalty was emetogenic: severe nausea and vomiting in 15% versus 11%, manageable with antiemetic prophylaxis. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference) for the harm question asked — nitrous oxide did not increase death or cardiovascular complications. Tier C (mortality/cardiovascular composite — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: ENIGMA-II 2014: nitrous oxide did not increase death or cardiovascular complications — 8% vs 8% (RR 0.96, CI 0.83–1.12) in 7,112 at-risk patients
cards.summary: ENIGMA-II 2014: nitrous oxide did not increase death or cardiovascular complications — 8% vs 8% (RR 0.96, CI 0.83–1.12) in 7,112 at-risk patients
cards.people: 7,112 patients aged at least 45 years with known or suspected coronary artery disease undergoing major noncardiac surgery internationally, randomised to general anaesthesia with or without nitrous oxide (attending anaesthetists unblinded; patients and assessors blinded). The primary outcome was a composite of death and cardiovascular complications (non-fatal myocardial infarction, stroke, pulmonary embolism, or cardiac arrest) within 30 days; 6,992 patients were assessed for it.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 283 of 3,483 patients (8%) given nitrous oxide versus 296 of 3,509 (8%) not given it (relative risk 0.96, 95% CI 0.83–1.12; P=.64) — an absolute difference of about zero. Surgical-site infection was 9% in both groups (P=.61). Severe nausea and vomiting was more common with nitrous oxide (15% vs 11%; P<0.0001), an absolute excess of about 4 percentage points. Nitrous oxide also reduced volatile-agent requirements.
cards.watchOut: The confidence interval excludes a large cardiovascular hazard but not a small one (up to a relative 12% increase). ENIGMA-II studied major noncardiac surgery in older at-risk patients; it does not speak to nitrous oxide in obstetric, paediatric, or ambulatory practice, and it was not designed to detect effects on rare outcomes such as homocysteine-mediated events over years.

shelves.title: Epidural anaesthesia and analgesia for major abdominal surgery (MASTER)
shelves.question: In high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery, does adding epidural anaesthesia and analgesia to general anaesthesia improve survival or major complications versus general anaesthesia with systemic opioids?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Aged · Analgesia, Epidural · Anesthesia, Epidural · Anesthesia, General · Comorbidity · Endpoint Determination · Humans · Mortality · Obesity, Morbid · Postoperative Pain · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: The MASTER trial (915 high-risk patients having major abdominal surgery) found that adding intraoperative epidural anaesthesia and 72 hours of postoperative epidural analgesia to general anaesthesia did not reduce its primary endpoint: death at 30 days or major morbidity occurred in 57.1% with epidural versus 60.7% with control (P=0.29), and 30-day mortality was 5.1% versus 4.3% (P=0.67). Of eight morbidity categories, only respiratory failure was less frequent with epidural (23% vs 30%; P=0.02), and pain scores were lower over the first 3 days. Catheter insertion caused no major adverse consequences in the trial. So the split is the story: epidurals buy better analgesia and fewer respiratory failures in this population, not survival. PROPOSED SPLIT stamp as above, Tier C (mortality in the primary endpoint — the developer rules personally).

cards.headline: MASTER 2002: epidural did not reduce death or major morbidity (57.1% vs 60.7%; mortality 5.1% vs 4.3%) but cut respiratory failure (23% vs 30%) and improved pain relief
cards.summary: MASTER 2002: epidural did not reduce death or major morbidity (57.1% vs 60.7%; mortality 5.1% vs 4.3%) but cut respiratory failure (23% vs 30%) and improved pain relief
cards.people: 915 high-risk patients (each with at least one of nine defined comorbid states) undergoing major abdominal surgery, randomised to general anaesthesia plus intraoperative epidural anaesthesia and postoperative epidural analgesia for 72 hours (n=447 analysed) or general anaesthesia with systemic opioid analgesia (n=441 analysed). The primary endpoint was death at 30 days or major postsurgical morbidity.
cards.result: At least one morbidity endpoint or death occurred in 255 patients (57.1%) in the epidural group versus 268 (60.7%) in the control group (P=0.29) — an absolute difference of about 3.6 points favouring epidural, not significant. Thirty-day mortality was 5.1% (23 patients) versus 4.3% (19 patients) (P=0.67). Of eight individual morbidity categories, only respiratory failure occurred less often with epidural (23% vs 30%; P=0.02). Postoperative epidural analgesia gave lower pain scores during the first 3 days, and there were no major adverse consequences of epidural catheter insertion.
cards.watchOut: One positive category out of eight tested invites multiplicity caution — the respiratory-failure finding (P=0.02) would not survive strict adjustment for eight comparisons, which is why that half of the split is graded POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. MASTER predates modern enhanced-recovery practice, laparoscopic predominance, and contemporary thromboprophylaxis, all of which may have shrunk any epidural advantage since 2002. No registry ID exists for this pre-registration-era trial.
cards.source: Rigg JR et al. Epidural anaesthesia and analgesia and outcome of major surgery: a randomised trial. Lancet. 2002. PMID: 11965272. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial. shelves.title: Preoperative oral carbohydrate loading
shelves.question: In patients having elective surgery, does a preoperative carbohydrate drink (versus fasting or placebo) reduce preoperative discomfort and postoperative insulin resistance, nausea, and length of stay?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Cholecystectomy, Laparoscopic · Dietary Carbohydrates · Double-Blind Method · Elective Surgical Procedures · Fasting · Female · Gastric Acid · Gastric Mucosa · Humans · Hydrogen-Ion Concentration · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Placebos · Preoperative Care
shelves.balance: Two small double-blind trials from the group that pioneered preoperative carbohydrate loading support a comfort benefit, not a hard-outcome one. Hausel 2001 (252 elective abdominal surgery patients) found a 12.5% carbohydrate drink (800 mL the evening before, 400 mL on the morning of surgery) left patients less hungry and less anxious than both placebo (flavoured water) and overnight fasting while waiting for surgery, and reduced thirst as effectively as placebo — without increasing gastric fluid volumes or acidity and with no adverse events. Hausel 2005 (172 laparoscopic cholecystectomy patients) found less postoperative nausea and vomiting with carbohydrate than with fasting in the 12–24-hour window (P=0.039), with no difference in pain scores. Neither trial measured length of stay or insulin resistance as a clinical endpoint, and both are small, single-group-of-investigators studies of surrogate and symptom outcomes — hence POSSIBLE, and the shelf makes no claim on complications or stay. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (THIN — symptom endpoints only).

cards.headline: Hausel 2001: a carbohydrate drink before surgery reduced hunger, anxiety, and thirst versus fasting — with no increase in gastric contents
cards.summary: Hausel 2001: a carbohydrate drink before surgery reduced hunger, anxiety, and thirst versus fasting — with no increase in gastric contents
cards.people: 252 elective abdominal surgery patients (ASA I–II) randomised to a 12.5% carbohydrate drink, placebo (flavoured water), or overnight fasting. The drink and placebo groups (double-blinded) took 800 mL the evening before and 400 mL on the morning of surgery. Eleven discomfort variables were scored on visual analogue scales while patients waited for surgery; gastric fluid volume and acidity were measured.
cards.result: The carbohydrate group was less hungry and less anxious than both the placebo and fasted groups (P≤0.05), and trend analysis showed consistently decreasing thirst, hunger, anxiety, malaise, and unfitness in the carbohydrate group (P<0.05), while thirst in the fasted group rose. Carbohydrate reduced thirst as effectively as placebo (P<0.0001 versus fasted). The drink did not increase residual gastric fluid volumes or affect acidity, and there were no adverse events.
cards.watchOut: Outcomes are self-rated comfort scores, not complications; the placebo comparison shows part of the benefit is simply drinking something (thirst), though hunger and anxiety favoured carbohydrate over placebo too. A 2001 single-centre study from the intervention's own pioneers, with no registry ID (pre-registration era) — independent replication of the comfort effect is thin.
cards.source: Hausel J et al. A carbohydrate-rich drink reduces preoperative discomfort in elective surgery patients. Anesth Analg. 2001. PMID: 11682427. Registry ID: none — pre-registration-era trial. cards.headline: Hausel 2005: carbohydrate loading reduced nausea and vomiting 12–24 h after laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus fasting (P=0.039)
cards.summary: Hausel 2005: carbohydrate loading reduced nausea and vomiting 12–24 h after laparoscopic cholecystectomy versus fasting (P=0.039)
cards.people: 172 patients (127 women, 45 men) undergoing elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under inhalational anaesthesia, randomised to preoperative fasting, carbohydrate drink (50 kcal/100 mL; 800 mL the evening before and 400 mL two hours before anaesthesia), or placebo; the non-fasting groups were double-blinded. Nausea and pain were scored on visual analogue scales and PONV episodes recorded for 24 hours.
cards.result: The incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting was lower in the carbohydrate group than in the fasted group between 12 and 24 hours after surgery (P=0.039). Nausea scores rose after operation in the fasted and placebo groups but did not change significantly in the carbohydrate group. There were no intergroup differences in pain scores, and anaesthetic, opioid, antiemetic, and fluid use were similar in all groups.

shelves.title: Dexmedetomidine after cardiac surgery (DECADE)
shelves.question: In patients having cardiac surgery, does prophylactic dexmedetomidine reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation and delirium versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Atrial Fibrillation · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Delirium · Dexmedetomidine · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Hypnotics and Sedatives · Infusions, Intravenous · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: One well-blinded placebo-controlled trial says no — with a lean toward harm on one coprimary outcome. DECADE randomised 798 cardiac surgery patients (with cardiopulmonary bypass) to dexmedetomidine infusion from before incision through 24 hours postoperatively or saline placebo. Atrial fibrillation occurred in 30% on dexmedetomidine versus 34% on placebo (relative risk 0.90, 97.8% CI 0.72–1.15; P=.34), and delirium in 17% versus 12% (RR 1.48, 97.8% CI 0.99–2.23) — a non-significant increase whose interval starts at 0.99. Serious adverse events were more frequent with dexmedetomidine (5% vs 2%), with hypotension the recognised mechanism. The trial's own conclusion is that dexmedetomidine should not be infused to prevent atrial fibrillation or delirium after cardiac surgery. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — a single trial, and the delirium point estimate points the wrong way, so this is not a reassurance shelf. Distinct from Shelf #791, which homes low-dose dexmedetomidine for delirium prevention after non-cardiac surgery (Su 2016) — a different population and dose strategy.

cards.headline: DECADE 2020: dexmedetomidine did not reduce atrial fibrillation (30% vs 34%; RR 0.90) and delirium was numerically higher (17% vs 12%; RR 1.48, CI 0.99–2.23)
cards.summary: DECADE 2020: dexmedetomidine did not reduce atrial fibrillation (30% vs 34%; RR 0.90) and delirium was numerically higher (17% vs 12%; RR 1.48, CI 0.99–2.23)
cards.people: 798 patients who had cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass at six US academic hospitals, randomised to dexmedetomidine infusion (0.1 µg/kg/h from before incision, titrated to 0.4 µg/kg/h until 24 h postoperatively) or saline placebo, with patients, caregivers, and evaluators all masked. Coprimary outcomes were new-onset atrial fibrillation and delirium between ICU admission and postoperative day 5 or discharge; 794 patients were analysed.
cards.result: Atrial fibrillation occurred in 121 of 397 patients (30%) on dexmedetomidine versus 134 of 395 (34%) on placebo (relative risk 0.90, 97.8% CI 0.72–1.15; P=.34) — an absolute difference of about 4 points, not significant. Delirium occurred in 17% versus 12% (RR 1.48, 97.8% CI 0.99–2.23) — a non-significant increase. Serious adverse events occurred in 5% versus 2%; death was under 1% in both groups (1 patient each).
cards.watchOut: The delirium interval (0.99–2.23) sits almost entirely above 1.0: the honest reading is 'no benefit, possible harm', and the authors say the drug should not be used for this purpose. The trial was stopped per protocol after its last planned interim analysis rather than for futility. Findings apply to this dosing strategy in cardiac surgery; they do not overturn the different regimen and population of Su 2016 (Shelf #791), nor dexmedetomidine's separate role as an ICU sedative.
cards.source: Turan A et al. Dexmedetomidine for reduction of atrial fibrillation and delirium after cardiac surgery (DECADE): a randomised placebo-controlled trial. Lancet. 2020. PMID: 32682483. shelves.title: High versus low PEEP during open abdominal surgery (PROVHILO; iPROVE)
shelves.question: In patients having open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia, does a high-PEEP, recruitment-manoeuvre ventilation strategy reduce postoperative pulmonary complications versus low PEEP without recruitment?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Aged · Anesthesia, General · Double-Blind Method · Europe · Female · Humans · Lung Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · North America · Positive-Pressure Respiration · Postoperative Complications · Risk Factors · South America · Surgical Procedures, Operative · Tidal Volume · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two multicentre randomised trials agree that aggressive open-lung ventilation does not protect the lungs after abdominal surgery. PROVHILO (900 patients at risk, open abdominal surgery) compared PEEP 12 cmH2O with recruitment manoeuvres against PEEP ≤2 without: postoperative pulmonary complications were 40% versus 39% (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.86–1.20), and the high-PEEP group needed more vasoactive drugs for intraoperative hypotension. iPROVE (1,012 patients, four arms) tested individualised PEEP after recruitment, with or without postoperative CPAP, against standard protective ventilation: the composite of pulmonary and systemic complications was 46–48% in the three intervention arms versus 51% on standard care, every relative risk crossing 1.0. Simpler ventilation — low tidal volume, low PEEP, no routine recruitment — is the strategy the evidence leaves standing. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference).

cards.headline: PROVHILO 2014: high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvres did not reduce pulmonary complications (40% vs 39%; RR 1.01, CI 0.86–1.20) and caused more hypotension
cards.summary: PROVHILO 2014: high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvres did not reduce pulmonary complications (40% vs 39%; RR 1.01, CI 0.86–1.20) and caused more hypotension
cards.people: 900 patients at risk of postoperative pulmonary complications undergoing open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia with tidal volumes of 8 mL/kg at 30 centres, randomised to high PEEP (12 cmH2O) with recruitment manoeuvres (447 allocated) or low PEEP (≤2 cmH2O) without (453 allocated); patients and outcome assessors were masked. The primary endpoint was a composite of postoperative pulmonary complications by day 5; 894 patients were analysed.
cards.result: Postoperative pulmonary complications occurred in 174 of 445 patients (40%) in the high-PEEP group versus 172 of 449 (39%) in the low-PEEP group (relative risk 1.01, 95% CI 0.86–1.20; P=.86) — an absolute difference of about 1 point. Patients in the high-PEEP group developed more intraoperative hypotension and needed more vasoactive drugs.
cards.watchOut: PROVHILO bundled high PEEP with recruitment manoeuvres, so it cannot separate the two — but iPROVE's individualised strategy (next card) points the same way, so the bundle objection does not rescue the approach. The trial used tidal volumes of 8 mL/kg; it does not argue against low-tidal-volume ventilation itself, which both arms shared in iPROVE.
cards.source: Hemmes SN et al. High versus low positive end-expiratory pressure during general anaesthesia for open abdominal surgery (PROVHILO trial): a multicentre randomised controlled trial. Lancet. 2014. PMID: 24894577. Registry ID: ISRCTN70332574, from the record. cards.headline: iPROVE 2018: individualised open-lung ventilation (with or without postoperative CPAP) did not reduce complications versus standard protective ventilation
cards.summary: iPROVE 2018: individualised open-lung ventilation (with or without postoperative CPAP) did not reduce complications versus standard protective ventilation
cards.people: 1,012 patients at intermediate-to-high risk of pulmonary complications undergoing abdominal surgery expected to last over 2 hours at 21 Spanish teaching hospitals, randomised to one of four low-tidal-volume strategies: individualised intraoperative open-lung ventilation plus individualised postoperative CPAP; individualised ventilation plus standard CPAP; standard ventilation plus CPAP; or standard ventilation plus standard oxygen (control). The primary outcome was a composite of pulmonary and systemic complications in the first 7 days; 967 patients were analysed.
cards.result: The composite occurred in 46% (individualised + individualised CPAP; RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.74–1.07), 47% (individualised + CPAP; RR 0.91, 0.76–1.09), and 48% (standard + CPAP; RR 0.95, 0.80–1.14), versus 51% on standard care — every interval crossing 1.0, none significant. No open-lung group needed rescue manoeuvres for hypoxaemia, but that physiological tidiness did not convert into fewer complications.
cards.watchOut: Four-arm design means each comparison rests on roughly 240 patients per arm; the trial excludes a large benefit of the individualised approach but not a small one. Its control arm already used protective low tidal volumes — the null is about adding individualised PEEP, recruitment, and CPAP on top of good standard ventilation, not about ventilation care in general.

shelves.title: P6 wristbands for nausea: about 30% fewer episodes than sham after surgery in relative terms — an adjunct, not a drug substitute
shelves.question: Do wristbands that stimulate the P6 acupoint on the wrist (acupressure or acustimulation bands) reduce nausea and vomiting — after surgery, or during chemotherapy and radiotherapy?
shelves.mesh: Acupuncture Points · Antiemetics · Humans · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Wrist
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — stimulating the P6 point on the wrist reduces postoperative nausea (RR 0.71) and vomiting (RR 0.70) versus sham across 40 randomised trials, with no detectable difference from antiemetic drugs; the direct wristband trials in chemotherapy and radiotherapy point the same way but are smaller and expectancy plays a measurable part. A cheap, safe adjunct — not a replacement for antiemetic drugs where those are indicated.

cards.summary: Cochrane: P6 stimulation cut postoperative nausea and vomiting by about 30% in relative terms versus sham — and matched antiemetic drugs

cards.result: Versus sham: nausea RR 0.71 (95% CI 0.61–0.83), vomiting RR 0.70 (0.59–0.83), rescue antiemetics RR 0.69 (0.57–0.83). Versus antiemetic drugs there was no evidence of difference for nausea (RR 0.82, 0.60–1.13), vomiting (RR 1.01, 0.77–1.31) or rescue treatment. Side effects were minor.
cards.watchOut: Only four of the 40 trials reported adequate allocation concealment, and the pooled techniques range from needles to bands — the wristband-specific estimate is thinner than the headline.

cards.headline: In 739 chemotherapy patients, acupressure bands reduced nausea on the treatment day — but not delayed nausea or vomiting
cards.summary: In 739 chemotherapy patients, acupressure bands reduced nausea on the treatment day — but not delayed nausea or vomiting

cards.result: Patients in the acupressure condition experienced less nausea on the day of treatment than controls (P < 0.05). There were no significant differences in delayed nausea or vomiting. shelves.title: Oral versus intravenous steroids in acute asthma: every head-to-head trial found the drip added nothing for patients who can swallow
shelves.question: In acute asthma exacerbations, are oral corticosteroids as effective as intravenous corticosteroids?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adult · Asthma/drug therapy · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Methylprednisolone/administration & dosage · Middle Aged · Random Allocation · Spirometry · Status Asthmaticus/complications/drug therapy
shelves.balance: Three small head-to-head randomised trials spanning 25 years, in genuinely sick patients, all point the same way. Ratto 1988 randomised 77 patients with status asthmaticus (mean presenting FEV1 26% of predicted) to oral or intravenous methylprednisolone and found no difference in respiratory failure, FEV1, hospital days, speed of improvement or side effects (PMID: 3385910). Harrison 1986 asked the additive version — intravenous hydrocortisone on top of high-dose oral prednisolone in 52 admitted patients — and peak flow at 24 hours was identical (PMID: 2868207). Dembla 2011 randomised 65 admitted adults to oral prednisolone 100 mg daily or intravenous hydrocortisone for 72 hours: peak flow reached 53.2% versus 55.9% of predicted (p = 0.28) (PMID: 22479740). The neighbouring relapse question tells the same story: Rowe's 2017 network meta-analysis of steroids given at emergency-department discharge found no route clearly superior, with intramuscular ranking first only on a probability analysis with wide credible intervals (PMID: 27664401). The pharmacology agrees — oral prednisolone is almost completely absorbed — so the intravenous route's real indications are the patient who cannot swallow, is vomiting, or is ventilated, none of whom populated these trials. None of the three trials was a formal noninferiority study and all are small, so a modest difference cannot be excluded; but in four decades no trial has ever shown the drip to be better. PROPOSED LIKELY (the treatment made no difference — oral corticosteroids are as effective as intravenous in acute asthma) (not Tier C: three concordant RCTs plus a network meta-analysis, though the trials are small and old). Magnesium as an adjunct in acute asthma is a different question, homed at shelf #238.

cards.headline: Ratto 1988: in 77 patients with status asthmaticus, oral methylprednisolone matched intravenous on lung function, respiratory failure and hospital days
cards.summary: Ratto 1988: in 77 patients with status asthmaticus, oral methylprednisolone matched intravenous on lung function, respiratory failure and hospital days
cards.people: 77 patients with status asthmaticus (mean presenting FEV1 26% of predicted) randomly assigned to methylprednisolone 160 or 320 mg orally or 500 or 1000 mg intravenously, daily in divided doses. Spirometry was performed within 1 hour of the first dose, every 6 hours for 24 hours, then every 8–12 hours until discharge or 72 hours.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the oral and intravenous groups in the incidence of respiratory failure, FEV1, days of hospitalisation, rate of improvement in pulmonary function, or side effects. No patient who developed respiratory failure did so more than 3 hours after the initial dose. The authors conclude that oral methylprednisolone is safe and effective in the treatment of status asthmaticus.
cards.watchOut: Small and old: 'no significant difference' in 77 patients is not a formal noninferiority proof, and a modest advantage either way cannot be excluded. But it remains the most direct test in the sickest patients — a presenting FEV1 of 26% predicted is not a mild attack — and nothing since has contradicted it.
cards.source: Ratto D et al. Are intravenous corticosteroids required in status asthmaticus? JAMA. 1988. PMID: 3385910. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Harrison 1986: adding intravenous hydrocortisone to high-dose oral prednisolone did not speed recovery in 52 patients admitted with severe asthma
cards.summary: Harrison 1986: adding intravenous hydrocortisone to high-dose oral prednisolone did not speed recovery in 52 patients admitted with severe asthma
cards.people: 52 severely ill asthmatic patients requiring acute hospital admission without ventilatory failure, all receiving high-dose oral prednisolone and standard bronchodilator therapy, in a double-blind placebo-controlled trial of additional intravenous hydrocortisone.
cards.result: As judged by peak flow measurements 24 hours after admission, intravenous hydrocortisone had no effect on outcome. Parenteral steroids given before admission also conferred no advantage: patients who had received them had been deteriorating for a shorter period and had higher admission peak flows, yet recovered no faster. The authors found no evidence for the continued use of intravenous hydrocortisone in addition to oral prednisolone and bronchodilator therapy in this population.
cards.watchOut: This tests intravenous steroid added to oral, not instead of it: the cleanest reading is that once a full oral dose is in, the drip adds nothing. The instead-of comparison is carried by Ratto 1988 and Dembla 2011.
cards.source: Harrison BD et al. Need for intravenous hydrocortisone in addition to oral prednisolone in patients admitted to hospital with severe asthma without ventilatory failure. Lancet (London, England). 1986. PMID: 2868207. Registry ID: none — pre-registration era. cards.headline: Dembla 2011: oral prednisolone 100 mg daily matched intravenous hydrocortisone over 72 hours in 65 adults admitted with acute asthma
cards.summary: Dembla 2011: oral prednisolone 100 mg daily matched intravenous hydrocortisone over 72 hours in 65 adults admitted with acute asthma
cards.people: 65 adults admitted with an acute exacerbation of bronchial asthma, randomised to oral prednisolone 100 mg once daily (n = 34) or intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg every 6 hours (n = 31) for 72 hours, all concurrently receiving inhaled corticosteroids and bronchodilators. Groups were matched at baseline (peak flow about 20% of predicted before bronchodilator).
cards.result: After 72 hours, peak expiratory flow had improved to 53.23% ± 9.54 of predicted in the oral group versus 55.87% ± 10.34 in the intravenous group (p = 0.28), with no significant difference at any measured point. The authors conclude the two routes had similar efficacy in adults hospitalised with acute exacerbation of asthma.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 65 patients with a surrogate endpoint (peak flow at 72 hours), not relapse or ventilation. The compared doses were not milligram-equivalent — the intravenous arm received the larger glucocorticoid load and still did not win.
cards.source: Dembla G et al. Oral versus intravenous steroids in acute exacerbation of asthma--randomized controlled study. The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2011. PMID: 22479740. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rowe 2017: for preventing relapse after emergency-department discharge, no steroid route proved clearly best — intramuscular ranked first on probability, oral long-course also beat placebo
cards.summary: Rowe 2017: for preventing relapse after emergency-department discharge, no steroid route proved clearly best — intramuscular ranked first on probability, oral long-course also beat placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 13 RCTs (Rowe 2017)
cards.people: Systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 13 randomised trials of systemic corticosteroids — intramuscular, oral short-course or oral long-course — in adults with acute asthma discharged from the emergency department; the outcome was relapse, mostly within 10 days.
cards.result: Corticosteroids overall reduced relapse versus placebo (risk ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.74). In the network analysis, intramuscular steroids (odds ratio 0.21, 95% credible interval 0.05 to 0.73) and oral long-course steroids (OR 0.31, 0.09 to 0.95) significantly reduced relapse within 10 days versus placebo; oral short-course did not reach significance (OR 0.37, 0.04 to 3.38), which the authors attribute to a paucity of research. Probability-of-best analysis favoured intramuscular (62%) over oral short-course (20.3%) and oral long-course (14.1%), with wide credible intervals throughout.
cards.watchOut: This answers a neighbouring question — which route and course best prevent relapse after discharge — not which route treats the acute attack. Its route rankings rest on indirect comparisons with wide intervals, and the intramuscular signal is most plausibly about a guaranteed completed course (a depot injection cannot be left untaken at home), not faster lung recovery.
cards.source: Rowe BH et al. Prioritizing Systemic Corticosteroid Treatments to Mitigate Relapse in Adults With Acute Asthma: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis. Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. 2017. PMID: 27664401. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: give the steroid early and by mouth — the intravenous route has never beaten tablets in a patient who can swallow
cards.summary: Synthesis: give the steroid early and by mouth — the intravenous route has never beaten tablets in a patient who can swallow
cards.people: Three head-to-head randomised trials of route in acute asthma (Ratto 1988, n = 77, status asthmaticus; Harrison 1986, n = 52, intravenous added to oral; Dembla 2011, n = 65) and a 13-trial network meta-analysis of route for relapse prevention after discharge (Rowe 2017).
cards.result: Acute treatment: no significant difference between oral and intravenous steroids in FEV1 or peak-flow recovery, respiratory failure, or hospital days in any trial; peak flow at 72 hours 53.2% (oral) versus 55.9% (intravenous) predicted in the most recent trial. Relapse prevention: steroids beat placebo (RR 0.43); no oral course was shown inferior to an injection, and the intramuscular advantage is a ranking probability, not a demonstrated difference. The defensible residual role for the intravenous route is the patient who cannot swallow, is vomiting, or is ventilated.
cards.watchOut: The trials are small (52–77 patients) and none was designed as a noninferiority study, so the LIKELY stamp rests on concordance — three null trials, a null network analysis, and near-complete oral bioavailability — rather than on any single decisive experiment. Children were barely studied for route (the paediatric trials are small and older); this shelf's claim is for adults and adolescents who can take tablets.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ratto D et al. JAMA. 1988 (PMID: 3385910); Harrison BD et al. Lancet. 1986 (PMID: 2868207); Dembla G et al. The Journal of the Association of Physicians of India. 2011 (PMID: 22479740); Rowe BH et al. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 27664401).

shelves.title: The green-whistle question: methoxyflurane cut pain 17.4 mm more than placebo within 20 minutes and worked at a median 5 minutes — relief first, dizziness second
shelves.question: In adults with moderate-to-severe trauma pain in the emergency department, does low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane relieve pain compared with placebo or standard analgesics?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain*/diagnosis · Acute Pain*/drug therapy · Acute Pain*/etiology · Adolescent · Adult · Analgesia/methods · Anesthetics, Inhalation/administration & dosage · Anesthetics, Inhalation/adverse effects · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Monitoring/methods · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Male · Methoxyflurane*/administration & dosage · Methoxyflurane*/adverse effects · Middle Aged · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement/methods · Treatment Outcome · Wounds and Injuries/complications
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — for rapid short-term pain relief, the randomised record is consistent and the effect is fast. In the STOP! trial's adult subgroup (Coffey F et al., PMID: 27567918), 204 emergency-department patients with minor-trauma pain randomised to inhaled methoxyflurane (up to 6 mL via the Penthrox inhaler — Medical Developments International Limited, named in the publication) or placebo inhaler had a mean pain reduction across 5–20 minutes that was 17.4 mm greater on a visual analogue scale (95% CI −22.3 to −12.5 as a treatment effect favouring methoxyflurane; p<0.0001), a median time to first relief of 5 versus 20 minutes (hazard ratio 2.32), and rescue medication requested within 20 minutes by 2.0% versus 22.8% — at the price of more mostly mild, transient treatment-related adverse events, chiefly dizziness and headache (42.2% vs 14.9%). A systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled randomised data against standard-of-care analgesics (Fabbri A et al., PMID: 33505170) found the pain-intensity difference significantly superior for methoxyflurane (overall estimated treatment effect 11.88, 95% CI 9.75 to 14.00; P<0.0001), superior from 5 minutes onward, with more patients reaching pain at or below 30 mm and relative reductions of at least 30% and 50% — those responder outcomes are reported without absolute rates in the record, so they are not dressed up with invented percentages here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane is an effective, rapid, non-opioid analgesic for acute trauma pain in the emergency setting; the evidence is about the first minutes-to-hour of pain, not about downstream outcomes.

cards.headline: STOP! 2016 (adult subgroup, 204 patients): methoxyflurane inhaler vs placebo for minor-trauma pain — pain fell 17.4 mm more on the VAS, relief at a median 5 vs 20 minutes, rescue drugs 2.0% vs 22.8%
cards.summary: STOP! 2016 (adult subgroup, 204 patients): methoxyflurane inhaler vs placebo for minor-trauma pain — pain fell 17.4 mm more on the VAS, relief at a median 5 vs 20 minutes, rescue drugs 2.0% vs 22.8%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, adult subgroup analysis (STOP!, Coffey 2016)
cards.people: 204 adults from the STOP! trial (300 adults and adolescents randomised) presenting to UK emergency departments with acute pain (numerical rating scale 4–7) from minor trauma, randomised double-blind to low-dose methoxyflurane (up to 6 mL) or placebo (normal saline), both via a Penthrox inhaler (Medical Developments International Limited, Scoresby, Australia — the tested product and company as named in the publication); rescue paracetamol or opioids were available on request. Mean baseline VAS pain was about 66 mm in both groups.
cards.result: Mean change in VAS pain from baseline at 5, 10, 15, and 20 minutes was −20.7, −27.4, −33.3, and −34.8 mm on methoxyflurane versus −8.0, −11.1, −12.3, and −15.2 mm on placebo, an overall treatment effect of −17.4 mm (95% confidence interval −22.3 to −12.5; p<0.0001). Median time to first pain relief was 5 minutes versus 20 minutes (hazard ratio 2.32, 95% CI 1.63 to 3.30; p<0.0001), and 79.4% of methoxyflurane patients felt relief within 1–10 inhalations. Rescue medication within 20 minutes was requested by 2.0% versus 22.8% (p=0.0003). Treatment was rated excellent, very good, or good by 77.6% of patients. Treatment-related adverse events (mostly dizziness and headache) occurred in 42.2% versus 14.9%, none causing withdrawal and most mild and transient.
cards.watchOut: This card is the adult subgroup of a trial that also enrolled adolescents, against a placebo inhaler — not against an active analgesic; the standard-care comparison is the meta-analysis card's job. Pain was moderate (baseline about 66 mm) minor-trauma pain; severe pain and major trauma are outside the tested envelope, and follow-up here is minutes, not days.
cards.source: Coffey F et al. Methoxyflurane Analgesia in Adult Patients in the Emergency Department: A Subgroup Analysis of a Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-controlled Study (STOP!). Advances in Therapy. 2016. PMID: 27567918. Registry ID: NCT01420159. cards.headline: Fabbri 2021 (systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled RCTs): methoxyflurane vs standard-of-care analgesics — pain-intensity difference superior by 11.88 points (95% CI 9.75 to 14.00), from 5 minutes onward
cards.summary: Fabbri 2021 (systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled RCTs): methoxyflurane vs standard-of-care analgesics — pain-intensity difference superior by 11.88 points (95% CI 9.75 to 14.00), from 5 minutes onward
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled RCT data (Fabbri 2021)
cards.people: Pooled data from randomised controlled trials identified by systematic review, comparing low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane with standard-of-care analgesics in adults with trauma-related pain in pre-hospital and hospital settings; the primary endpoint was pain intensity difference from baseline at 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 minutes. A subgroup of elderly patients (65 or older) was analysed separately.
cards.result: The pain intensity difference was statistically superior with methoxyflurane versus standard-of-care analgesics (overall estimated treatment effect 11.88, 95% CI 9.75 to 14.00; P<0.0001), with superiority demonstrated at 5 minutes and maintained across all timepoints. Significantly more methoxyflurane patients achieved pain intensity at or below 30 mm on the visual analogue scale and relative reductions in pain intensity of at least 30% and at least 50%, and median time to pain relief was shorter; findings were consistent in the elderly subgroup. The record does not print absolute responder rates or the pooled trial count, so none are claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Standard of care is a bundle of different drugs and routes across trials, and the review's record carries no MeSH terms, so its source line says so plainly. Industry involvement is common in this literature; the effect is consistent with the placebo-controlled trial, which is why the shelf credits it, but the comparison cannot name a single beaten drug.

systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled rct data (fabbri 2021) pooled data from randomised controlled trials identified by systematic review, comparing low-dose inhaled methoxyflurane with standard-of-care analgesics in adults with trauma-related pain in pre-hospital and hospital settings; the primary endpoint was pain intensity difference from baseline at 5, 10, 15, 20, and 30 minutes. a subgroup of elderly patients (65 or older) was analysed separately. the pain intensity difference was statistically superior with methoxyflurane versus standard-of-care analgesics (overall estimated treatment effect 11.88, 95% ci 9.75 to 14.00; p<0.0001), with superiority demonstrated at 5 minutes and maintained across all timepoints. significantly more methoxyflurane patients achieved pain intensity at or below 30 mm on the visual analogue scale and relative reductions in pain intensity of at least 30% and at least 50%, and median time to pain relief was shorter; findings were consistent in the elderly subgroup. the record does not print absolute responder rates or the pooled trial count, so none are claimed here. standard of care is a bundle of different drugs and routes across trials, and the review's record carries no mesh terms, so its source line says so plainly. industry involvement is common in this literature; the effect is consistent with the placebo-controlled trial, which is why the shelf credits it, but the comparison cannot name a single beaten drug. fabbri a et al. low-dose methoxyflurane versus standard of care analgesics for emergency trauma pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled data. journal of pain research. 2021. pmid: 33505170. registry id: none in the record. mesh: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: against placebo and against standard analgesics alike, methoxyflurane relieves trauma pain faster and deeper in the first half hour — with more dizziness and headache
cards.summary: Synthesis: against placebo and against standard analgesics alike, methoxyflurane relieves trauma pain faster and deeper in the first half hour — with more dizziness and headache
cards.people: One double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (204 adults in the reported subgroup, STOP!) plus a systematic review and meta-analysis of pooled RCTs versus standard-of-care analgesics.
cards.result: Pain reduction versus placebo: −17.4 mm overall across 5–20 minutes (95% CI −22.3 to −12.5); median time to relief 5 vs 20 minutes; rescue medication 2.0% vs 22.8%. Versus standard care (pooled): pain-intensity difference 11.88 points favouring methoxyflurane (95% CI 9.75 to 14.00), superior from 5 minutes. Adverse events versus placebo: 42.2% vs 14.9%, mostly mild and transient dizziness and headache, none causing withdrawal. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Everything on this shelf is short-horizon analgesia for moderate trauma pain in adults able to self-administer an inhaler. It says nothing about repeated dosing, renal or hepatic safety in susceptible patients (the historical high-dose anaesthetic toxicity is a different exposure, but susceptible-patient data here are thin), or use in children.
cards.source: Synthesis of Coffey F et al. Advances in Therapy. 2016 (PMID: 27567918); Fabbri A et al. Journal of Pain Research. 2021 (PMID: 33505170).

shelves.title: A block on arrival for the broken hip: pain beaten at every measurement and median morphine of 0 mg vs 6 mg — in the patients least able to tolerate opioids
shelves.question: In adults with hip fracture, does a preoperative fascia iliaca compartment block reduce pain and opioid use compared with systemic analgesia or placebo block?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Hip Fractures/physiopathology · Humans · Male · Morphine/therapeutic use · Nerve Block/methods · Pain Management*
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a small founding trial with an unusually clean design, backed by a consistent pooled literature. Foss (Foss NB et al., PMID: 17413915) randomised 48 hip-fracture patients on arrival — before X-ray confirmation — double-blind to a fascia iliaca compartment block with 1.0% mepivacaine plus a placebo intramuscular injection, or a placebo block plus intramuscular morphine 0.1 mg/kg: maximum pain relief was superior with the block at rest (P<0.01) and on movement (P=0.02), pain relief was superior at all times and all measurements, median total morphine consumption was 0 mg versus 6 mg (P<0.01), and more morphine-group patients were sedated at 180 minutes (P=0.05). A meta-analysis of eleven trials and 937 hip-fracture patients (Hong HK et al., PMID: 31305398) found the block significantly reduced pain intensity at 1–8, 12, 24, and 48 hours (standardised mean differences from −0.96 to −1.14) and reduced total morphine consumption and nausea, with no difference by 72 hours. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a fascia iliaca block on arrival gives better early pain control than systemic morphine alone in hip fracture and spares opioids in exactly the fragile elderly population that tolerates them worst — the grade stops at likely because the founding trial is 48 patients and the pooled trials vary in technique and timing.

cards.headline: Foss 2007: fascia iliaca block vs intramuscular morphine in 48 hip-fracture patients — pain relief superior at every measurement, median morphine used 0 mg vs 6 mg, less sedation
cards.summary: Foss 2007: fascia iliaca block vs intramuscular morphine in 48 hip-fracture patients — pain relief superior at every measurement, median morphine used 0 mg vs 6 mg, less sedation
cards.people: 48 patients with suspected hip fracture enrolled in the emergency department immediately on arrival, before X-ray confirmation, randomised double-blind to fascia iliaca compartment blockade with 1.0% mepivacaine plus a placebo intramuscular saline injection (n=24), or a placebo block with 0.9% saline plus intramuscular morphine 0.1 mg/kg (n=24); intravenous rescue morphine was available when necessary.
cards.result: Maximum pain relief was superior in the block group both at rest (P<0.01) and on movement (P=0.02), and pain relief was superior at all times and at all measurements in the block group. Median total morphine consumption was 0 mg (interquartile range 0–0) in the block group versus 6 mg (5–7) in the morphine group (P<0.01). More patients in the morphine group were sedated at 180 minutes after block placement (P=0.05). The authors conclude the block is an effective, easily learned procedure that may reduce opioid side effects in this fragile, elderly group.
cards.watchOut: Forty-eight patients and P values without printed effect sizes in the record — the direction and the morphine-sparing are clear, the exact size of the pain-score advantage is not quantified here. The comparison is block versus a single intramuscular morphine strategy, not versus a modern titrated intravenous opioid protocol.
cards.source: Foss NB et al. Fascia iliaca compartment blockade for acute pain control in hip fracture patients: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Anesthesiology. 2007. PMID: 17413915. cards.headline: Hong 2019 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 937 patients): fascia iliaca block in hip fracture — pain lower at 1–48 hours (SMD about −1.0), morphine consumption and nausea reduced, no difference at 72 hours
cards.summary: Hong 2019 (meta-analysis, 11 RCTs, 937 patients): fascia iliaca block in hip fracture — pain lower at 1–48 hours (SMD about −1.0), morphine consumption and nausea reduced, no difference at 72 hours
cards.people: Eleven randomised trials (937 patients) of fascia iliaca compartment block versus placebo for pain control in hip-fracture patients (searches to September 12, 2018), pooling pain intensity, morphine consumption, and nausea.
cards.result: The block significantly decreased pain intensity at 1–8 hours (standardised mean difference −1.03, 95% CI −1.48 to −0.58; P=0.000 as printed), 12 hours (−1.06, −1.36 to −0.75), 24 hours (−1.14, −1.66 to −0.62), and 48 hours (−0.96, −1.33 to −0.60), but not at 72 hours (0.11, −0.12 to 0.34; P=0.355). The block also reduced total morphine consumption and the occurrence of nausea (P<0.05). The reviewers conclude the block has a beneficial role in reducing pain intensity and morphine consumption after hip fracture, while calling for more high-quality trials to identify optimal technique and injectate volume.
cards.watchOut: Standardised mean differences near −1.0 are large, but the pooled trials mix preoperative and postoperative timing and different local anaesthetics and volumes — the average effect is dependable in direction, less so as a promise for any one protocol. The record's framing is pain after hip fracture, which overlaps but is not identical to Foss's on-arrival question.
cards.source: Hong HK et al. The efficacy of fascia iliaca compartment block for pain control after hip fracture: A meta-analysis. Medicine. 2019. PMID: 31305398. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Hip Fractures/surgery · Humans · Nerve Block/methods · Pain Management · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy

cards.headline: Synthesis: better pain scores from the first hours, essentially no morphine needed in the founding trial, and less nausea — an early-hours win that fades by 72 hours, as a single-shot block should
cards.summary: Synthesis: better pain scores from the first hours, essentially no morphine needed in the founding trial, and less nausea — an early-hours win that fades by 72 hours, as a single-shot block should
cards.people: One 48-patient double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (Foss 2007) plus an eleven-trial meta-analysis (937 patients) of fascia iliaca block in hip fracture.
cards.result: Pain: superior at rest and on movement at all measured times in Foss; pooled standardised mean differences −0.96 to −1.14 across 1–48 hours, null at 72 hours. Morphine: median total 0 mg vs 6 mg in Foss (P<0.01); reduced consumption pooled. Nausea: reduced pooled; sedation at 180 minutes: more frequent with morphine in Foss (P=0.05). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here shows an effect on delirium, mobilisation, length of stay, or mortality — the outcomes hip-fracture care ultimately answers to. The shelf supports the block as analgesia on arrival, as one part of hip-fracture care, not as a substitute for timely surgery or geriatric co-management.

shelves.title: Extra MRSA cover for plain cellulitis: cure 83.5% vs 85.5% in the big trial and 85% vs 82% in the small one — an unproven habit, kept honest by one wide interval
shelves.question: In adults with uncomplicated cellulitis, does adding trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to cephalexin improve clinical cure compared with cephalexin alone?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents/adverse effects · Anti-Bacterial Agents/therapeutic use · Cellulitis/drug therapy · Cephalexin/adverse effects · Cephalexin/therapeutic use · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus · Middle Aged · Staphylococcal Infections/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination/adverse effects · Trimethoprim, Sulfamethoxazole Drug Combination/therapeutic use · Young Adult
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — two randomised trials asked whether adding MRSA cover to cephalexin helps non-purulent cellulitis, and neither found it. Moran (Moran GJ et al., PMID: 28535235) randomised 496 analysed outpatients with uncomplicated cellulitis (ultrasound used to exclude abscess) to cephalexin plus trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or cephalexin plus placebo: in the prespecified per-protocol primary analysis, cure was 83.5% versus 85.5% (difference −2.0%, 95% CI −9.7% to 5.7%; P=0.50), while the modified intention-to-treat analysis leaned the other way without significance (76.2% vs 69.0%; difference 7.3%, 95% CI −1.0% to 15.5%; P=0.07) — the authors note that imprecision leaves a clinically important difference possible. Pallin's earlier trial (Pallin DJ et al., PMID: 23457080), 146 analysed patients without abscess, diabetes, or immunosuppression, found cure in 85% versus 82% (risk difference 2.7%, 95% CI −9.3% to 15%; P=0.66), with no subgroup — including nasal MRSA colonisation or purulence — predicting response. A network meta-analysis of ten trials and 1,936 cellulitis or erysipelas patients (Shu Z et al., PMID: 39240378) likewise found no significant differences in cure rates among the antibiotics analysed, including the cephalexin-plus-trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole combination. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): for uncomplicated non-purulent cellulitis, routine added MRSA cover is unproven — the trials cannot exclude a moderate benefit (Moran's intention-to-treat interval reaches +15.5%), but two nulls and a null network are what a prescriber actually has.

cards.headline: Moran 2017: adding TMP-SMX to cephalexin for cellulitis — per-protocol cure 83.5% vs 85.5% (difference −2.0%, P=0.50); intention-to-treat leaned the other way (76.2% vs 69.0%, P=0.07)
cards.summary: Moran 2017: adding TMP-SMX to cephalexin for cellulitis — per-protocol cure 83.5% vs 85.5% (difference −2.0%, P=0.50); intention-to-treat leaned the other way (76.2% vs 69.0%, P=0.07)
cards.people: 500 outpatients older than 12 years with uncomplicated cellulitis and no wound, purulent drainage, or abscess at five US emergency departments (496 in the modified intention-to-treat analysis, 411 per protocol; median age 40, 58.4% men, 10.9% with diabetes; median erythema 13.0 by 10.0 cm), all with ultrasound at enrolment to exclude abscess, randomised double-blind to cephalexin 500 mg four times daily plus trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole 320/1600 mg twice daily (n=248) or cephalexin plus placebo (n=248) for 7 days, enrolled April 2009 to June 2012.
cards.result: In the per-protocol population — the prespecified primary analysis — clinical cure occurred in 182 of 218 (83.5%) on the combination versus 165 of 193 (85.5%) on cephalexin alone (difference −2.0%, 95% CI −9.7% to 5.7%; P=0.50), against a prespecified clinically significant difference of more than 10%. In the modified intention-to-treat population, cure was 189 of 248 (76.2%) versus 171 of 248 (69.0%) (difference 7.3%, 95% CI −1.0% to 15.5%; P=0.07). Adverse event rates and secondary outcomes through 7–9 weeks — overnight hospitalisation, recurrent skin infections, similar infections in household contacts — did not differ significantly. The authors conclude the combination did not yield higher cure in the per-protocol analysis, while noting the intention-to-treat imprecision leaves further research warranted.
cards.watchOut: Read both analyses or read neither: the per-protocol null and the intention-to-treat lean disagree because of who dropped out, and the honest summary is 'no benefit shown, moderate benefit not excluded'. Ultrasound exclusion of abscess makes this a genuinely non-purulent population — purulent cellulitis is a different shelf's question.
cards.source: Moran GJ et al. Effect of Cephalexin Plus Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole vs Cephalexin Alone on Clinical Cure of Uncomplicated Cellulitis: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28535235. Registry ID: NCT00729937. cards.headline: Pallin 2013: cephalexin plus TMP-SMX vs cephalexin alone — cure 85% vs 82% (risk difference 2.7%, 95% CI −9.3% to 15%; P=0.66), no subgroup benefited, including MRSA carriers
cards.summary: Pallin 2013: cephalexin plus TMP-SMX vs cephalexin alone — cure 85% vs 82% (risk difference 2.7%, 95% CI −9.3% to 15%; P=0.66), no subgroup benefited, including MRSA carriers
cards.people: 153 patients with cellulitis, no abscess, symptoms under 1 week, and no diabetes, immunosuppression, peripheral vascular disease, or hospitalisation, in a multicentre double-blind placebo-controlled trial (2007–2011); 146 had outcome data for intention-to-treat analysis (median age 29, range 3–74). All received cephalexin and were randomised to added trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole or placebo for a planned 14 days, with instructions to continue at least 1 week and stop 3 days after they felt cured.
cards.result: Of intervention participants, 62 of 73 (85%) were cured versus 60 of 73 controls (82%), a risk difference of 2.7% (95% confidence interval −9.3% to 15%; P=0.66). No covariates predicted treatment response, including nasal MRSA colonisation and purulence at enrolment. The authors conclude that among patients diagnosed with cellulitis without abscess, adding trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to cephalexin did not improve outcomes overall or by subgroup.
cards.watchOut: Smaller and lower-risk than Moran (diabetes and immunosuppression were exclusions, and children were included), with a confidence interval wide enough to hide a 15-point benefit — it corroborates the null without tightening it. Its flexible stop-when-cured dosing also differs from Moran's fixed 7 days.
cards.source: Pallin DJ et al. Clinical trial: comparative effectiveness of cephalexin plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole versus cephalexin alone for treatment of uncomplicated cellulitis: a randomized controlled trial. Clinical Infectious Diseases. 2013. PMID: 23457080. Registry ID: NCT00676130. p=0.66). no covariates predicted treatment response, including nasal mrsa colonisation and purulence at enrolment. the authors conclude that among patients diagnosed with cellulitis without abscess, adding trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole to cephalexin did not improve outcomes overall or by subgroup. smaller and lower-risk than moran (diabetes and immunosuppression were exclusions, and children were included), with a confidence interval wide enough to hide a 15-point benefit — it corroborates the null without tightening it. its flexible stop-when-cured dosing also differs from moran's fixed 7 days. pallin dj et al. clinical trial: comparative effectiveness of cephalexin plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole versus cephalexin alone for treatment of uncomplicated cellulitis: a randomized controlled trial. clinical infectious diseases. 2013. pmid: 23457080. registry id: nct00676130. mesh: adolescent · adult · aged · anti-bacterial agents/administration & dosage · anti-bacterial agents/adverse effects · cellulitis/drug therapy · cellulitis/microbiology · cephalexin/administration & dosage · cephalexin/adverse effects · child · child, preschool · double-blind method · drug therapy, combination · humans · methicillin-resistant staphylococcus aureus/isolation & purification · middle aged · staphylococcal skin infections/drug therapy · staphylococcal skin infections/microbiology · treatment outcome · trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole drug combination/administration & dosage · trimethoprim, sulfamethoxazole drug combination/adverse effects · young adult

cards.headline: Shu 2024 (network meta-analysis, 10 RCTs, 1,936 patients): no significant cure-rate differences among cellulitis antibiotics — including cephalexin plus TMP-SMX versus cephalexin plus placebo
cards.summary: Shu 2024 (network meta-analysis, 10 RCTs, 1,936 patients): no significant cure-rate differences among cellulitis antibiotics — including cephalexin plus TMP-SMX versus cephalexin plus placebo
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 10 RCTs (Shu 2024)
cards.people: Ten randomised trials (1,936 patients with cellulitis or erysipelas) comparing first- and second-line antibiotics — including cephalexin, cephalexin plus trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, and cephalexin plus placebo among thirteen regimens — on cure rate, pathogen eradication, diarrhoea or vomiting, and rash (searches to July 4, 2024).
cards.result: There were no significant differences in cure rates for cellulitis among the antibiotics analysed, with cefaclor demonstrating the most favourable (but not significantly different) profile for curative outcomes; ceftriaxone was least likely to induce diarrhoea or vomiting. For erysipelas, pristinamycin showed the most promising cure results but the highest rash risk among the compared options, with no significant rash differences among the three antibiotics formally compared. The authors conclude cure rates do not significantly differ among antibiotics for cellulitis.
cards.watchOut: A network ranking across mostly indirect comparisons — 'most favourable profile' language for cefaclor is ranking noise under a null, not a finding. The pool mixes cellulitis with erysipelas and children-era regimens with modern MRSA-era ones; its value here is that it finds no hidden combination-therapy advantage the two direct trials missed.
cards.source: Shu Z et al. Efficacy and safety of first- and second-line antibiotics for cellulitis and erysipelas: a network meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. cards.headline: Synthesis: two direct trials and a network analysis, three nulls — added MRSA cover for non-purulent cellulitis remains an unproven habit, with one wide interval keeping the question technically open
cards.summary: Synthesis: two direct trials and a network analysis, three nulls — added MRSA cover for non-purulent cellulitis remains an unproven habit, with one wide interval keeping the question technically open
cards.people: Two double-blind RCTs of cephalexin plus trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole versus cephalexin alone (496 and 146 analysed patients) plus a ten-trial network meta-analysis (1,936 patients).
cards.result: Cure, combination versus cephalexin alone: 83.5% vs 85.5% per protocol (difference −2.0%, 95% CI −9.7% to 5.7%) and 76.2% vs 69.0% modified intention-to-treat (difference 7.3%, 95% CI −1.0% to 15.5%) in Moran; 85% vs 82% (risk difference 2.7%, 95% CI −9.3% to 15%) in Pallin. Network analysis: no significant cure-rate differences among regimens. Adverse events and secondary outcomes: no significant differences in Moran. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: Contrast shelf #3007: after drainage of an abscess, the same drug did show benefit — purulence and a drained collection change the microbiology and the answer. Nothing here addresses severe cellulitis, periorbital or hand involvement, or patients failing initial therapy, where broader cover is a different decision.

shelves.title: Glue vs stitches for a cut: the scar ties at 3 months and at 1 year, glue is faster and hurts less — and reopens about once in every 25 closures
shelves.question: In children and adults with traumatic lacerations, does octylcyanoacrylate tissue adhesive give equivalent closure, cosmesis, and infection outcomes compared with sutures?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Bandages · Child · Cyanoacrylates/therapeutic use · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lacerations/drug therapy · Lacerations/surgery · Middle Aged · Postoperative Care* · Surgical Procedures, Operative* · Sutures · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the outcomes split cleanly, and the split is the answer. On appearance, the methods tie: Singer's multicentre trial (Singer AJ et al., PMID: 11894031) of 814 patients with 924 lacerations and incisions found no difference at 3 months in optimal appearance (82% vs 83%; P=0.67) or dehiscence (1.6% vs 0.9%; P=0.35), and Quinn's trial (Quinn J et al., PMID: 9832658) found no difference at 1 year in optimal wound scores (73% vs 68%; P=0.60) or cosmetic visual-analogue scores (69 vs 69 mm; P=0.95). On process, adhesive wins: closure was faster (2.9 vs 5.2 minutes; P<0.001) and fewer adhesive wounds were erythematous at 1 week (18% vs 36%; P<0.001), though infection rates were similar (2.1% vs 0.7%; P=0.09). The Cochrane review (Farion K et al., PMID: 12137689), eight trials of adhesive versus standard closure for traumatic lacerations, found no cosmesis difference at any time point, pain scores favouring adhesives (parent visual-analogue weighted mean difference −15.7 mm, 95% CI −21.9 to −9.5) and procedure time favouring adhesives (−5.6 minutes, 95% CI −8.2 to −3.1) — against a small but significant increase in dehiscence favouring standard closure (number needed to harm 25, 95% CI 14 to 100) and less erythema with adhesives (number needed to harm 8 for standard closure, as printed). PROPOSED SPLIT: for suitable low-tension lacerations, tissue adhesive matches sutures on the scar, beats them on speed and pain, and loses slightly on wound reopening — the choice turns on the wound and the patient, not on a winner.

cards.headline: Singer 2002 (814 patients, 924 wounds): octylcyanoacrylate vs standard closure — optimal appearance at 3 months 82% vs 83%, closure faster (2.9 vs 5.2 minutes), infection 2.1% vs 0.7% (P=0.09)
cards.summary: Singer 2002 (814 patients, 924 wounds): octylcyanoacrylate vs standard closure — optimal appearance at 3 months 82% vs 83%, closure faster (2.9 vs 5.2 minutes), infection 2.1% vs 0.7% (P=0.09)
cards.people: 814 patients with 924 wounds (383 traumatic lacerations, 235 excisions of skin lesions or scar revisions, 208 minimally invasive surgeries, and 98 general surgical procedures) at 10 clinical sites, randomised to octylcyanoacrylate tissue adhesive or standard wound closure (sutures or staples), with follow-up at 1 week and 3 months for infection and cosmetic outcome.
cards.result: Groups were similar at baseline. Closure with adhesive was faster than standard closure (2.9 vs 5.2 minutes; P<0.001). At 1 week, infection rates were similar (adhesive 2.1% vs standard 0.7%; P=0.09) and fewer adhesive wounds were erythematous (18% vs 36%; P<0.001). Wound dehiscence did not differ (1.6% vs 0.9%; P=0.35). At 3 months there was no difference in the percent of wounds with optimal appearance (82% vs 83%; P=0.67).
cards.watchOut: Only 383 of the 924 wounds were traumatic lacerations — the rest were surgical incisions and excisions, which are cleaner and lower-tension than the emergency-department wounds this shelf is asked about. The infection point estimate (2.1% vs 0.7%) leans against adhesive without reaching significance; neither this trial nor any other was powered for so rare an outcome.
cards.source: Singer AJ et al. Closure of lacerations and incisions with octylcyanoacrylate: a multicenter randomized controlled trial. Surgery. 2002. PMID: 11894031. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Quinn 1998: adhesive vs suture at 1 year — optimal wound scores 73% vs 68% (P=0.60), cosmetic scores identical (69 vs 69 mm); the 3-month assessment predicted the 1-year result
cards.summary: Quinn 1998: adhesive vs suture at 1 year — optimal wound scores 73% vs 68% (P=0.60), cosmetic scores identical (69 vs 69 mm); the 3-month assessment predicted the 1-year result
cards.people: 136 cases of traumatic laceration randomised prospectively to octylcyanoacrylate tissue adhesive or monofilament suture (5-0 or smaller), with wound scores by a research nurse (validated by a second, blinded nurse) at 5–10 days, 3 months, and 1 year, and standardised photographs rated by a blinded cosmetic surgeon; 77 lacerations were examined at 1 year.
cards.result: No differences in demographic or clinical characteristics were found between groups. At 1 year there was no difference in optimal wound scores (73% adhesive vs 68% suture; P=0.60) or visual analogue cosmesis scores (69 vs 69 mm; P=0.95). Agreement between early and 3-month wound scores was poor (kappa 0.34, 95% CI 0.10 to 0.58), but 3-month and 1-year scores were strongly associated (kappa 0.71, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.90), with a moderate correlation on the cosmesis scale (intraclass correlation 0.48, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.63). The authors conclude that 3-month assessment provides a good measure of long-term cosmetic outcome.
cards.watchOut: Attrition is the weakness: only 77 of 136 lacerations were examined at 1 year, so the long-term equivalence rests on just over half the randomised wounds. This is the traumatic-laceration population the question asks about — cleaner evidence for the scar question than Singer's mixed wounds, at a smaller size.
cards.source: Quinn J et al. Tissue adhesive versus suture wound repair at 1 year: randomized clinical trial correlating early, 3-month, and 1-year cosmetic outcome. cards.headline: Farion 2002 (Cochrane, 8 trials vs standard closure): no cosmesis difference at any time; pain −15.7 mm and time −5.6 minutes favouring adhesive; dehiscence increased (NNH 25)
cards.summary: Farion 2002 (Cochrane, 8 trials vs standard closure): no cosmesis difference at any time; pain −15.7 mm and time −5.6 minutes favouring adhesive; dehiscence increased (NNH 25)
cards.people: Eight randomised trials comparing a tissue adhesive with standard wound closure for acute, linear, low-tension traumatic lacerations in emergency or primary care settings in children and adults (searches to late 2001), plus one trial comparing two adhesives; outcomes included cosmesis, pain, procedure time, and complications. No study was adequately powered for complications, which are rare.
cards.result: No significant difference was found for cosmesis at any time point, by cosmetic visual analogue scale or wound evaluation score, and no age-subgroup differences were found. Pain scores (parent visual analogue weighted mean difference −15.7 mm, 95% CI −21.9 to −9.5) and procedure time (weighted mean difference −5.6 minutes, 95% CI −8.2 to −3.1) significantly favoured tissue adhesives. Small but statistically significant risk differences were found for dehiscence (favouring standard wound care; number needed to harm 25, 95% CI 14 to 100) and erythema (favouring tissue adhesive; number needed to harm 8, 95% CI 4 to 100, as printed). Other complications were not significantly different. The one head-to-head adhesive trial (butylcyanoacrylate vs octylcyanoacrylate, paediatric facial lacerations) found no differences in cosmesis, pain, procedure time, or complications.
cards.watchOut: The review's searches end in 2001 — it pools the founding trials (including Quinn's) rather than adding modern ones, and Singer's large trial appeared the same year. Its dehiscence signal (one extra reopening per 25 closures) is the one harm estimate in this literature with statistical support, and it should be quoted whenever the speed-and-pain advantages are.
cards.source: Farion K et al. Tissue adhesives for traumatic lacerations in children and adults. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2002. PMID: 12137689. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: the scar ties at 3 months and at 1 year; adhesive is faster and less painful; standard closure reopens less often — a genuine trade, not a verdict for either side
cards.summary: Synthesis: the scar ties at 3 months and at 1 year; adhesive is faster and less painful; standard closure reopens less often — a genuine trade, not a verdict for either side
cards.people: Two anchor RCTs (Singer 2002, 924 wounds including surgical incisions; Quinn 1998, 136 traumatic lacerations with 1-year follow-up) plus a Cochrane review of eight adhesive-versus-standard-closure trials in traumatic lacerations.
cards.result: Cosmesis: optimal appearance 82% vs 83% at 3 months (Singer); optimal scores 73% vs 68% and cosmesis 69 vs 69 mm at 1 year (Quinn); no difference at any time point pooled (Cochrane). Speed and pain: closure 2.9 vs 5.2 minutes (Singer); pooled procedure time −5.6 minutes and pain −15.7 mm favouring adhesive. Dehiscence: 1.6% vs 0.9% in Singer (P=0.35); pooled increase with adhesive, number needed to harm 25. Infection: 2.1% vs 0.7% (P=0.09) in Singer; no significant pooled difference. PROPOSED SPLIT — equivalent cosmesis, faster and less painful closure, slightly more dehiscence.
cards.watchOut: Suitability is the boundary: these trials concern simple, linear, low-tension lacerations (the Cochrane eligibility explicitly). High-tension, contaminated, joint-crossing, or deep wounds needing layered closure are outside the evidence, and adhesive there is extrapolation. In children the pain advantage carries extra weight because it can avoid sedation and restraint; the trials support that reasoning but did not measure it as an outcome.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singer AJ et al. Surgery. 2002 (PMID: 11894031); Quinn J et al. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 1998 (PMID: 9832658); Farion K et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2002 (PMID: 12137689).
