shelves.title: Adductor canal block after knee replacement: less morphine and faster walking than placebo in the founding trial — and against femoral block, the same pain relief with a stronger quadriceps
shelves.question: In adults after total knee arthroplasty, does an adductor canal block reduce postoperative pain and opioid use while preserving quadriceps strength, compared with placebo or femoral nerve block?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Amides · Analgesia, Patient-Controlled · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Anesthetics, Local · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee* · Double-Blind Method · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Leg/innervation · Male · Middle Aged · Morphine/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use · Nerve Block* · Pain Measurement/drug effects · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy, epidemiology* · Patient Satisfaction · Preanesthetic Medication · Prospective Studies · Ropivacaine · Treatment Outcome · Walking/physiology*
shelves.balance: The placebo-controlled record is two small double-blind trials from one Danish group. In primary total knee arthroplasty (Jenstrup MT et al., PMID: 22221014), a continuous adductor canal block with ropivacaine cut 24-hour morphine consumption from 56 ± 26 mg to 40 ± 21 mg (P = 0.006), reduced pain during 45-degree knee flexion (P = 0.01, though not at rest, P = 0.06), and patients walked the Timed-Up-and-Go test faster at 24 hours (36 ± 17 vs 50 ± 29 seconds, P = 0.03). In the harder revision-arthroplasty population (Jæger P et al., PMID: 25386752) the block won only its primary endpoint — pain on flexion at 4 hours, 52 ± 22 vs 71 ± 25 mm (mean difference 19, 95% CI 1 to 37) — with area-under-curve pain and morphine use not significantly different, in a trial the authors call underpowered. Against the older femoral nerve block, a 33-study meta-analysis (Hasabo EA et al., PMID: 36042669) found no difference in pain (MD 0.06, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.17) or opioid consumption (SMD 0.08, −0.06 to 0.22), but better preserved quadriceps strength (MD 0.28, 0.11 to 0.46) and better mobilisation to day 2. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the block is a real analgesic against placebo and a strength-sparing equal against femoral block — but the placebo trials are small and single-group, so the stamp stops short of likely.

cards.headline: Jenstrup 2012: adductor canal block cut 24-hour morphine from 56 mg to 40 mg and sped up the walking test after primary knee replacement
cards.summary: Jenstrup 2012: adductor canal block cut 24-hour morphine from 56 mg to 40 mg and sped up the walking test after primary knee replacement
cards.people: 71 analysed patients aged 50–85 years having primary total knee arthroplasty, randomised double-blind to a continuous adductor canal catheter with intermittent ropivacaine 0.75% boluses or placebo (saline), with patient-controlled morphine available to both groups.
cards.result: Morphine consumption 0–24 hours was 40 ± 21 mg with ropivacaine versus 56 ± 26 mg with placebo (P = 0.006). Pain during 45-degree knee flexion was significantly lower with the block (P = 0.01) but pain at rest was not (P = 0.06). The Timed-Up-and-Go ambulation test at 24 hours was significantly faster in the ropivacaine group (36 ± 17 vs 50 ± 29 seconds, P = 0.03).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 71 analysed patients from the group that developed the technique; the pain-at-rest result was null, and the block was a catheter technique with repeated boluses — a single-shot block may not reproduce the 24-hour morphine saving.
cards.source: Jenstrup MT et al. Effects of adductor-canal-blockade on pain and ambulation after total knee arthroplasty: a randomized study. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2012. PMID: 22221014. Registry ID: NCT01104883. cards.headline: Jæger 2014 (revision knee arthroplasty): pain on flexion at 4 hours was 19 mm lower with the block — every other endpoint, including morphine use, was null in an underpowered trial
cards.summary: Jæger 2014 (revision knee arthroplasty): pain on flexion at 4 hours was 19 mm lower with the block — every other endpoint, including morphine use, was null in an underpowered trial
cards.people: 30 analysed patients (36 enrolled) having revision total knee arthroplasty under general anaesthesia, randomised blinded to an adductor canal catheter with ropivacaine (0.75% bolus then 0.2% infusion) or placebo saline, in a population with more chronic pain than primary arthroplasty patients.
cards.result: The primary endpoint, pain during knee flexion at 4 hours, was 52 ± 22 mm with ropivacaine versus 71 ± 25 mm with placebo (mean difference 19, 95% CI 1 to 37, P = 0.04). Pain area-under-curve over 1–8 hours was not significant during flexion (55 ± 21 vs 69 ± 21 mm, P = 0.11) or at rest (39 ± 18 vs 45 ± 23 mm, P = 0.43), and morphine consumption and morphine-related side effects did not differ (P > 0.05). The authors state the study was underpowered after a larger-than-anticipated dropout rate.
cards.watchOut: Only 30 analysed patients in the most painful, chronic-pain-heavy version of the operation; one significant time-point among many comparisons is weak evidence on its own — this card tempers, rather than extends, the primary-arthroplasty result.
cards.source: Jæger P et al. Adductor canal block for postoperative pain treatment after revision knee arthroplasty: a blinded, randomized, placebo-controlled study. PLoS One. 2014. PMID: 25386752. cards.headline: Hasabo 2022 (33 studies, adductor canal vs femoral nerve block): identical pain and opioid results — the canal block's win is quadriceps strength (MD 0.28) and earlier mobilisation
cards.summary: Hasabo 2022 (33 studies, adductor canal vs femoral nerve block): identical pain and opioid results — the canal block's win is quadriceps strength (MD 0.28) and earlier mobilisation
cards.people: 33 studies comparing adductor canal block with femoral nerve block after total knee arthroplasty, pooled for pain control, opioid consumption, quadriceps strength, mobilisation, falls, satisfaction, and length of stay over the first two postoperative days.
cards.result: No significant difference between the blocks for pain control (MD 0.06, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.17, P = 0.33) or opioid consumption (SMD 0.08, 95% CI −0.06 to 0.22, P = 0.28) up to 2 days. Adductor canal block better preserved quadriceps muscle strength (MD 0.28, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.46, P = 0.002) and gave better mobilisation up to 2 days, with a shorter mean hospital stay; the mobilisation advantage did not translate into a significant difference in falls or patient satisfaction.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies mix single-shot and catheter techniques and varied local-anaesthetic regimens; strength was measured on differing scales across trials, and the length-of-stay advantage is reported without a pooled number in the record — treat it as directional, not sized.
cards.source: Hasabo EA et al. Adductor canal block versus femoral nerve block for pain control after total knee arthroplasty: A systematic review and Meta-analysis. Medicine. 2022. PMID: 36042669. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but modest analgesic that earns its place by sparing the quadriceps — not by beating other blocks on pain
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but modest analgesic that earns its place by sparing the quadriceps — not by beating other blocks on pain
cards.people: Two small placebo-controlled trials (71 primary and 30 revision arthroplasty patients) plus a 33-study meta-analysis of adductor canal versus femoral nerve block after total knee arthroplasty.
cards.result: Versus placebo: 24-hour morphine 40 vs 56 mg and faster Timed-Up-and-Go (Jenstrup 2012); in revision surgery only the 4-hour flexion pain endpoint was positive (difference 19 mm), with morphine use unchanged (Jæger 2014). Versus femoral nerve block: pain MD 0.06 and opioid SMD 0.08, both null, but quadriceps strength better preserved (MD 0.28, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.46) with better early mobilisation (Hasabo 2022). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Nothing here compares the block with modern multimodal analgesia alone at scale, and no trial was powered for falls, readmission, or chronic post-surgical pain. The honest claim is narrower than the enthusiasm: early movement hurts less and the leg stays stronger — outcomes that matter for same-week recovery, not yet shown to change anything beyond it.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jenstrup MT et al. Acta Anaesthesiologica Scandinavica. 2012 (PMID: 22221014); Jæger P et al. PLoS One. 2014 (PMID: 25386752); Hasabo EA et al. Medicine. 2022 (PMID: 36042669).

shelves.title: Erector spinae plane block after breast cancer surgery: one small trial cut 24-hour morphine from 16.6 mg to 5.5 mg — in the network ranking of eleven techniques it sits mid-table, not at the top
shelves.question: In adults after breast cancer surgery, does an erector spinae plane block reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption compared with placebo block or no block?
shelves.mesh: Analgesia*/methods · Anesthesia, Conduction*/adverse effects · Bayes Theorem · Humans · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy, prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: The direct placebo-controlled evidence is a single small double-blind trial (Ben Amor M et al., PMID: 38372553): in 50 women having elective breast cancer surgery, an ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block with ropivacaine lowered visual analogue pain scores at almost every time point over 24 hours and cut 24-hour morphine consumption to 5.5 ± 0.9 mg from 16.6 ± 2.8 mg on placebo (p < 0.001), with intraoperative fentanyl also far lower (9.1 ± 4.2 vs 50 ± 9.1 mcg). The wider comparative picture is less triumphant: in a network meta-analysis of 79 randomised trials and 5,686 patients across 11 regional techniques (Singh NP et al., PMID: 35102494), the erector spinae plane block's ranking for 24-hour resting pain (SUCRA 0.59) sat below continuous paravertebral block (0.83), serratus anterior plane block (0.76), and single-level paravertebral block (0.68), on evidence the reviewers graded moderate to very low certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the block works against placebo and is simple and safe in the trial record, but nothing yet shows it is the best of the fascial-plane and paravertebral options, and its one placebo trial enrolled 50 patients at one centre.

cards.headline: Singh 2022 (network meta-analysis, 79 trials, 5,686 patients): erector spinae plane block ranked mid-table (SUCRA 0.59) of eleven techniques for 24-hour pain after major breast surgery
cards.summary: Singh 2022 (network meta-analysis, 79 trials, 5,686 patients): erector spinae plane block ranked mid-table (SUCRA 0.59) of eleven techniques for 24-hour pain after major breast surgery
cards.type: Systematic review and network meta-analysis, 79 RCTs (Singh 2022)
cards.people: 79 randomised controlled trials in 5,686 patients undergoing major oncologic breast surgery, comparing 11 regional anaesthesia techniques (including continuous and single-level paravertebral block, serratus anterior plane block, erector spinae plane block, pectoral blocks, wound infiltration/infusion, and placebo or no intervention) in a Bayesian network meta-analysis; primary outcome 24-hour resting pain score (0–10).
cards.result: SUCRA rankings for 24-hour resting pain were: continuous paravertebral block 0.83, serratus anterior plane block 0.76, continuous wound infusion 0.76, single-level paravertebral block 0.68, erector spinae plane block 0.59, modified pectoral block 0.49, intercostal block 0.45, multilevel paravertebral block 0.41, wound infiltration 0.33, no intervention 0.12, placebo 0.08. Against placebo, the largest estimated pain reductions were for continuous paravertebral block (mean difference 1.26, 95% credible interval 0.43 to 2.12) and serratus anterior plane block (1.12, 0.32 to 1.9). Cluster ranking combining pain and opioid use placed most regional techniques above no intervention or placebo. The certainty of evidence was moderate to very low.
cards.watchOut: Most comparisons in the network are indirect, and a SUCRA rank is a probability of ranking highly, not an effect size — the record gives no erector-spinae-specific effect estimate against placebo, so this card can place the block in the field but cannot size its benefit. Certainty was moderate to very low throughout.
cards.source: Singh NP et al. cards.headline: Ben Amor 2023: erector spinae block with ropivacaine cut 24-hour morphine to 5.5 mg versus 16.6 mg on placebo, with lower pain scores at nearly every time point
cards.summary: Ben Amor 2023: erector spinae block with ropivacaine cut 24-hour morphine to 5.5 mg versus 16.6 mg on placebo, with lower pain scores at nearly every time point
cards.people: 50 ASA I–II women scheduled for elective breast cancer surgery at a single Tunisian centre, randomised double-blind to an ultrasound-guided erector spinae plane block with ropivacaine (n = 25) or placebo (n = 25), with patient-controlled morphine after surgery.
cards.result: Mean visual analogue pain scores were significantly lower in the ropivacaine group at every measured point over 24 hours except the 1st and 16th hours. Twenty-four-hour morphine consumption was 5.5 ± 0.9 mg versus 16.6 ± 2.8 mg (p < 0.001), intraoperative fentanyl consumption was 9.1 ± 4.2 mcg versus 50 ± 9.1 mcg (p < 0.001), and total morphine demand was significantly lower in the block group. The authors conclude the block is effective and safe for post-breast-surgery pain with a morphine-sparing effect.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients at one centre, with effect sizes (a threefold morphine reduction) larger than single small trials usually sustain on replication; the abstract reports no complication counts, so 'safe' here means no signal in 25 blocked patients, not a measured harm rate.
cards.source: Ben Amor M et al. Postoperative Analgesia in Breast Cancer Surgery: Efficiency and Safety of Ultrasound Guided Erector Spinae Plane Block, a randomized controlled double blinded trial. La Tunisie Medicale. 2023. PMID: 38372553. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: effective against placebo in one small trial, mid-ranking among eleven techniques in the network — a reasonable block, not a proven best
cards.summary: Synthesis: effective against placebo in one small trial, mid-ranking among eleven techniques in the network — a reasonable block, not a proven best
cards.people: One 50-patient placebo-controlled trial of erector spinae plane block for breast cancer surgery, set inside a 79-trial, 5,686-patient network meta-analysis of all regional techniques for major oncologic breast surgery.
cards.result: Direct evidence: 24-hour morphine 5.5 vs 16.6 mg and lower pain scores at nearly all time points (Ben Amor 2023). Comparative evidence: erector spinae SUCRA 0.59 for 24-hour resting pain, behind continuous paravertebral (0.83) and serratus anterior plane (0.76) blocks, on moderate-to-very-low certainty evidence (Singh 2022). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The two cards answer different questions — 'does it beat nothing?' (yes, in one small trial) and 'is it the best block?' (no signal that it is). Quoting the morphine figures without the ranking, or the ranking without the certainty grade, would each mislead in opposite directions. Head-to-head trials against paravertebral and serratus blocks, in larger samples, are what is missing.
cards.source: Synthesis of Singh NP et al. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. 2022 (PMID: 35102494); Ben Amor M et al. La Tunisie Medicale. 2023 (PMID: 38372553).

shelves.title: A single phenobarbital load for alcohol withdrawal: ICU admissions 8% versus 25% in the one placebo trial — but pooled against benzodiazepines alone, the admission advantage disappears
shelves.question: In adults with acute alcohol withdrawal in the emergency department, does a single loading dose of phenobarbital reduce ICU admission and withdrawal severity compared with placebo added to benzodiazepine-based care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Alcohol-Induced Disorders, Nervous System/drug therapy* · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage* · Double-Blind Method · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Lorazepam/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Phenobarbital/administration & dosage* · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: The only placebo-controlled test of the exact question is Rosenson J et al. (PMID: 22999778): 102 analysed emergency-department patients with acute alcohol withdrawal all received a symptom-guided lorazepam protocol, and those randomised to a single intravenous phenobarbital load (10 mg/kg) were admitted to intensive care far less often than those given placebo saline — 8% versus 25% (95% CI for the difference 4 to 32) — with no difference in adverse events. The wider literature asks a neighbouring question, phenobarbital instead of or against benzodiazepines, and there the advantage vanishes: a systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies and 1,507 patients (Lee CM et al., PMID: 37923363) found a pooled relative risk of ICU admission of 0.92 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.55), hospital admission 0.98 (0.89 to 1.07), and adverse events 1.1 (0.78 to 1.57), on low-to-moderate quality evidence with moderate-to-high risk of bias and only two randomised trials among the eight. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): the add-on loading-dose strategy is promising and was safe in its one trial, but a single 102-patient study whose headline outcome is a disposition decision — made by clinicians who may not have stayed blind to a sedated patient — cannot carry a stronger stamp against a null pooled record.

cards.headline: Rosenson 2013: one intravenous phenobarbital load (10 mg/kg) on top of a lorazepam protocol cut ICU admissions from 25% to 8%, with no increase in adverse events
cards.summary: Rosenson 2013: one intravenous phenobarbital load (10 mg/kg) on top of a lorazepam protocol cut ICU admissions from 25% to 8%, with no increase in adverse events
cards.people: 102 analysed patients (198 enrolled) presenting to an emergency department with acute alcohol withdrawal, randomised double-blind to a single intravenous dose of phenobarbital 10 mg/kg in saline or placebo saline, with every patient also placed on the institutional symptom-guided lorazepam-based withdrawal protocol; primary outcome was initial level of hospital admission (ICU vs telemetry vs floor).
cards.result: Baseline characteristics and withdrawal severity were similar between groups. Patients who received phenobarbital had fewer ICU admissions than placebo patients (8% vs 25%, 95% CI 4 to 32 for the difference). There were no differences in adverse events between the groups. The authors conclude a single phenobarbital dose combined with a symptom-guided lorazepam protocol decreased ICU admission without increasing adverse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Nearly half of enrolled patients (96 of 198) were excluded from the analysis, and ICU admission is a clinician decision, not a hard outcome — in a trial of a visibly sedating drug, disposition decisions are exactly where imperfect blinding bites. Withdrawal-severity scores themselves are not reported in the record, so the claim is about where patients were sent, not directly about how severe their withdrawal became.
cards.source: Rosenson J et al. Phenobarbital for acute alcohol withdrawal: a prospective randomized double-blind placebo-controlled study. The Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2013. PMID: 22999778. cards.headline: Lee 2024 (meta-analysis, 1,507 patients): phenobarbital versus benzodiazepines in the ED — ICU admission relative risk 0.92, hospital admission 0.98, adverse events 1.1, all null
cards.summary: Lee 2024 (meta-analysis, 1,507 patients): phenobarbital versus benzodiazepines in the ED — ICU admission relative risk 0.92, hospital admission 0.98, adverse events 1.1, all null
cards.people: Eight studies (two randomised trials and six retrospective cohorts) covering 1,507 patients in 2,012 emergency-department treatment encounters for alcohol withdrawal syndrome, comparing phenobarbital with benzodiazepine controls, searched to May 2022.
cards.result: The pooled relative risk with phenobarbital versus benzodiazepines was 0.92 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.55) for ICU admission, 0.98 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.07) for hospital admission, and 1.1 (95% CI 0.78 to 1.57) for any adverse event; heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis of ED readmission. Overall methodological quality was low to moderate, risk of bias moderate to high, and statistical heterogeneity moderate. The authors conclude the literature does not show phenobarbital significantly reduces ICU admissions, hospital admissions, ED readmissions, or adverse events compared with benzodiazepines alone.
cards.watchOut: Six of the eight studies are retrospective cohorts, where phenobarbital is typically given to the sickest patients — confounding by indication pushes this pooled estimate toward null or harm, so it does not cleanly refute the randomised add-on result; equally, its regimens (phenobarbital as replacement therapy, varied doses) are not Rosenson's single loading dose added to lorazepam.
cards.source: Lee CM et al. Phenobarbital treatment of alcohol withdrawal in the emergency department: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2024. PMID: 37923363. cards.headline: Synthesis: the randomised add-on trial says ICU admissions fall; the mostly observational replacement-therapy pool says nothing changes — the question is still open
cards.summary: Synthesis: the randomised add-on trial says ICU admissions fall; the mostly observational replacement-therapy pool says nothing changes — the question is still open
cards.people: One 102-patient placebo-controlled trial of a single phenobarbital load added to lorazepam-based care, plus an eight-study meta-analysis (1,507 patients, six of them retrospective) of phenobarbital against benzodiazepines in ED alcohol withdrawal.
cards.result: ICU admission: 8% vs 25% favouring phenobarbital in the randomised add-on trial (Rosenson 2013); pooled relative risk 0.92 (95% CI 0.54 to 1.55), null, in the meta-analysis (Lee 2024). Hospital admission: pooled RR 0.98, null. Adverse events: no difference in the trial; pooled RR 1.1, null. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence).
cards.watchOut: The two cards are not measuring the same intervention: a protocolised single load on top of benzodiazepines versus phenobarbital used as the main agent, often in sicker patients. A multicentre randomised trial of the loading-dose strategy, with blinded disposition or hard outcomes (intubation, seizures, delirium), is the study that would settle this — until then both 'it works' and 'it doesn't' overstate one half of the record. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rosenson J et al. The Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2013 (PMID: 22999778); Lee CM et al. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2024 (PMID: 37923363).

shelves.title: Prochlorperazine versus metoclopramide for ED migraine: dead even in the head-to-head trial (pain fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points) — a meta-analysis favouring prochlorperazine rests on other, older comparisons
shelves.question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with acute migraine, does intravenous prochlorperazine relieve headache more effectively than intravenous metoclopramide?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Diphenhydramine/administration & dosage · Dopamine Antagonists/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Metoclopramide/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Migraine Disorders/classification, drug therapy* · Patient Satisfaction · Prochlorperazine/administration & dosage, adverse effects, therapeutic use* · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors
shelves.balance: Asked head-to-head, the question has one direct answer. In the randomised double-blind trial by Friedman BW et al. (PMID: 18006188), 77 emergency-department migraine patients received prochlorperazine 10 mg or metoclopramide 20 mg intravenously, both with diphenhydramine 25 mg, and pain relief at one hour was indistinguishable: numeric rating scale scores fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points (difference 0.3, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.6), with similar results at 2 and 24 hours, adverse events in 46% versus 32%, and about three quarters of each group wanting the same drug next time. A systematic review and meta-analysis (Golikhatir I et al., PMID: 30990883) pooling 11 studies and 771 patients reached a friendlier verdict for prochlorperazine — odds ratio 2.89 (95% CI 1.42 to 5.86) for headache relief against metoclopramide among its comparison arms — but that estimate leans on older and smaller trials at differing doses and co-treatments, and the same review found prochlorperazine raised akathisia/dystonia odds against active comparators (OR 2.55, 1.03 to 6.31). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence): either drug is a reasonable first choice and the direct trial says they tie; the claim that prochlorperazine is the stronger of the two rests on indirect pooling the head-to-head does not confirm.

cards.headline: Friedman 2008: prochlorperazine 10 mg versus metoclopramide 20 mg — pain fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points at one hour, a difference of 0.3 with a confidence interval spanning zero
cards.summary: Friedman 2008: prochlorperazine 10 mg versus metoclopramide 20 mg — pain fell 5.5 versus 5.2 points at one hour, a difference of 0.3 with a confidence interval spanning zero
cards.people: 77 randomised emergency-department patients with acute migraine (97 eligible of 152 screened), treated double-blind with intravenous prochlorperazine 10 mg (n = 39) or metoclopramide 20 mg (n = 38), each infused over 15 minutes with diphenhydramine 25 mg; pain scored at baseline, every 30 minutes for 2 hours, and by telephone at 24 hours.
cards.result: The mean change in numeric rating scale pain score at 1 hour (primary endpoint) was 5.5 with prochlorperazine and 5.2 with metoclopramide (difference 0.3, 95% CI −1.0 to 1.6); findings were similar at 2 hours and 24 hours. Adverse events were reported by 46% (18/39) on prochlorperazine and 32% (12/38) on metoclopramide (difference 15%, 95% CI −6% to 36%). Seventy-seven percent (26/34) of prochlorperazine and 73% (27/37) of metoclopramide patients wanted the same medication for a future migraine. The authors conclude either drug, combined with diphenhydramine, is efficacious for ED migraine.
cards.watchOut: Only 77 randomised patients, so the confidence interval (−1.0 to 1.6 points) cannot exclude a clinically meaningful edge for either drug — 'no difference found' is not 'proven equal'. Both arms received diphenhydramine, which may have blunted akathisia differences and is not universal practice; and the metoclopramide dose (20 mg) is one of several in use, so the tie applies to these doses, not to every regimen.
cards.source: Friedman BW et al. A randomized controlled trial of prochlorperazine versus metoclopramide for treatment of acute migraine. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 2008. PMID: 18006188. cards.headline: Golikhatir 2019 (11 trials, 771 patients): prochlorperazine beat metoclopramide for headache relief (OR 2.89) across pooled arms — at a higher akathisia/dystonia risk (OR 2.55)
cards.summary: Golikhatir 2019 (11 trials, 771 patients): prochlorperazine beat metoclopramide for headache relief (OR 2.89) across pooled arms — at a higher akathisia/dystonia risk (OR 2.55)
cards.people: 11 randomised trials (n = 771) with 15 comparison arms of prochlorperazine for acute migraine in the emergency department, against placebo, metoclopramide, and other active comparators, pooled for headache relief, adverse events, and rescue-analgesia requests.
cards.result: Prochlorperazine was more effective than metoclopramide for headache relief (OR 2.89, 95% CI 1.42 to 5.86) and more effective than placebo and other active comparators in the pooled arms. Against placebo, adverse-event odds were higher (OR 5.79, 95% CI 2.43 to 13.79); against other active comparators there was no significant difference in overall adverse events (OR 1.88, 95% CI 0.99 to 3.59), but akathisia/dystonia odds were significantly increased (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.03 to 6.31). Requests for rescue analgesia were significantly lower with prochlorperazine than in other groups.
cards.watchOut: The metoclopramide comparison pools a small number of older arms with varying doses and co-medications, and its verdict conflicts with the largest direct head-to-head trial — pooled odds ratios across heterogeneous small trials are exactly where small-study effects inflate a winner. Some confidence intervals in the record's abstract are internally inconsistent and are not quoted on this card.
cards.source: Golikhatir I et al. The Efficacy and Safety of Prochlorperazine in Patients With Acute Migraine: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Headache. 2019. PMID: 30990883. cards.headline: Synthesis: pick either — the direct trial ties them, the indirect pool prefers prochlorperazine, and the harm that separates them is akathisia
cards.summary: Synthesis: pick either — the direct trial ties them, the indirect pool prefers prochlorperazine, and the harm that separates them is akathisia
cards.people: One 77-patient randomised head-to-head trial of prochlorperazine 10 mg versus metoclopramide 20 mg (both with diphenhydramine), plus an 11-trial, 771-patient meta-analysis of prochlorperazine against all comparators.
cards.result: Head-to-head: 1-hour pain reduction 5.5 vs 5.2 points, difference 0.3 (95% CI −1.0 to 1.6); adverse events 46% vs 32%; desire to repeat the drug 77% vs 73% (Friedman 2008). Pooled: headache-relief OR 2.89 (1.42 to 5.86) favouring prochlorperazine over metoclopramide, akathisia/dystonia OR 2.55 (1.03 to 6.31) against it (Golikhatir 2019). PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) for any superiority of prochlorperazine.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the meta-analysis odds ratio as if it were a head-to-head result — the one trial that randomised the exact comparison found a tie, and guidelines that rank these drugs are leaning on the pooled, older literature. What would change the answer is an adequately powered direct trial at modern doses without routine diphenhydramine. Tier C is set because the direct evidence is a single small trial.
cards.source: Synthesis of Friedman BW et al. Annals of Emergency Medicine. 2008 (PMID: 18006188); Golikhatir I et al. Headache. 2019 (PMID: 30990883).

shelves.title: For acute extremity pain in the ED, one dose of ibuprofen plus acetaminophen matched three opioid combinations — pain down 4.3 points versus 3.5 to 4.4 at two hours
shelves.question: In adults with acute extremity pain in the emergency department, does a single oral dose of a non-opioid combination (ibuprofen plus acetaminophen) relieve pain as well as opioid combinations?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/administration & dosage · Acute Pain/drug therapy · Administration, Oral · Adult · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage · Codeine/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Drug Combinations · Emergency Service, Hospital · Extremities · Female · Humans · Hydrocodone/administration & dosage · Ibuprofen/administration & dosage · Male · Middle Aged · Oxycodone/administration & dosage · Pain Measurement · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in a double-blind trial of 416 adults (aged 21–64) with moderate to severe acute extremity pain at two Bronx emergency departments, a single oral dose of ibuprofen 400 mg plus acetaminophen 1,000 mg reduced pain at 2 hours by 4.3 points on an 11-point scale (95% CI 3.6–4.9), statistically and clinically indistinguishable from oxycodone/acetaminophen (4.4 points), hydrocodone/acetaminophen (3.5 points) and codeine/acetaminophen (3.9 points). The largest between-group difference, 0.9 points, was below the prespecified minimum clinically important difference of 1.3. Adverse events were not assessed in the trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): for a single dose in acute extremity pain, the non-opioid combination relieves pain as well as standard opioid combinations — the opioid adds nothing measurable at two hours.

cards.headline: Chang 2017: pain fell 4.3 points on ibuprofen–acetaminophen versus 4.4, 3.5 and 3.9 on the three opioid combinations (overall p=0.053)
cards.summary: Chang 2017: pain fell 4.3 points on ibuprofen–acetaminophen versus 4.4, 3.5 and 3.9 on the three opioid combinations (overall p=0.053)
cards.people: 416 patients aged 21 to 64 years (411 analysed; mean age 37, 48% women) with moderate to severe acute extremity pain (baseline mean pain score 8.7 of 10) at two urban EDs in the Bronx, New York, randomised (104 per group) to a single oral dose of ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1,000 mg; oxycodone 5 mg + acetaminophen 325 mg; hydrocodone 5 mg + acetaminophen 300 mg; or codeine 30 mg + acetaminophen 300 mg. Primary outcome: decline in pain at 2 hours; minimum clinically important difference prespecified as 1.3 points.
cards.result: Mean pain reduction at 2 hours was 4.3 (95% CI 3.6–4.9) for ibuprofen–acetaminophen, 4.4 (95% CI 3.7–5.0) for oxycodone–acetaminophen, 3.5 (95% CI 2.9–4.2) for hydrocodone–acetaminophen and 3.9 (95% CI 3.2–4.5) for codeine–acetaminophen (p=0.053). The largest pairwise difference (0.9 points, 99.2% CI −0.1 to 1.8) was smaller than the 1.3-point minimum clinically important difference. Adverse events were not assessed.
cards.watchOut: Single-dose, two-hour horizon, extremity pain only, in relatively young patients: the trial does not address repeated dosing, other pain types, or the adverse-event balance that is the real argument for the non-opioid route — that argument is plausible but unmeasured here.
cards.source: Chang AK et al. Effect of a Single Dose of Oral Opioid and Nonopioid Analgesics on Acute Extremity Pain in the Emergency Department: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 29114833. Registry ID: NCT02455518. randomised double-blind clinical trial (chang 2017) 416 patients aged 21 to 64 years (411 analysed; mean age 37, 48% women) with moderate to severe acute extremity pain (baseline mean pain score 8.7 of 10) at two urban eds in the bronx, new york, randomised (104 per group) to a single oral dose of ibuprofen 400 mg + acetaminophen 1,000 mg; oxycodone 5 mg + acetaminophen 325 mg; hydrocodone 5 mg + acetaminophen 300 mg; or codeine 30 mg + acetaminophen 300 mg. primary outcome: decline in pain at 2 hours; minimum clinically important difference prespecified as 1.3 points. mean pain reduction at 2 hours was 4.3 (95% ci 3.6–4.9) for ibuprofen–acetaminophen, 4.4 (95% ci 3.7–5.0) for oxycodone–acetaminophen, 3.5 (95% ci 2.9–4.2) for hydrocodone–acetaminophen and 3.9 (95% ci 3.2–4.5) for codeine–acetaminophen (p=0.053). the largest pairwise difference (0.9 points, 99.2% ci −0.1 to 1.8) was smaller than the 1.3-point minimum clinically important difference. adverse events were not assessed. single-dose, two-hour horizon, extremity pain only, in relatively young patients: the trial does not address repeated dosing, other pain types, or the adverse-event balance that is the real argument for the non-opioid route — that argument is plausible but unmeasured here. chang ak et al. effect of a single dose of oral opioid and nonopioid analgesics on acute extremity pain in the emergency department: a randomized clinical trial. jama. 2017. pmid: 29114833. registry id: nct02455518. mesh: acetaminophen/administration & dosage · acute pain/drug therapy · administration, oral · adult · analgesics, non-narcotic/administration & dosage · analgesics, opioid/administration & dosage · codeine/administration & dosage · double-blind method · drug combinations · emergency service, hospital · extremities · female · humans · hydrocodone/administration & dosage · ibuprofen/administration & dosage · male · middle aged · oxycodone/administration & dosage · pain measurement · young adult

shelves.title: Low-dose ketamine added to morphine deepens early pain relief — an extra 0.76 points at 60 minutes in the pooled trials, below the clinically important line, with less rescue analgesia
shelves.question: In adults with acute pain in the emergency department, does low-dose ketamine added to morphine improve pain relief compared with morphine alone, and at what cost in adverse effects?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/diagnosis/drug therapy · Adult · Analgesia/methods · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · Ketamine/administration & dosage · Male · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Pilot Projects · Retrospective Studies · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — modest and time-limited. In the Beaudoin double-blind trial (60 ED patients with moderate to severe acute pain), summed pain-intensity difference over 2 hours was 4.0 with morphine alone versus 7.0 with morphine plus ketamine 0.15 mg/kg and 7.8 with 0.3 mg/kg (p<0.02), with rescue analgesia needed by 35% of controls versus 20% in each ketamine group and more dysphoria and dizziness on ketamine. The 2023 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (903 patients) found pain scores significantly lower only at 60 minutes (mean difference −0.76, 95% CI −1.19 to −0.33) — a reduction the reviewers themselves note was not clinically significant — with no difference at other time points, less rescue analgesia, no excess of serious side effects, and higher patient satisfaction. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): adjunctive low-dose ketamine buys a small, brief analgesic edge and some opioid sparing, paid for in minor dissociative effects.

cards.headline: Beaudoin 2014: summed 2-hour pain relief 7.0–7.8 with ketamine added versus 4.0 with morphine alone; rescue analgesia 20% versus 35%; more dysphoria and dizziness
cards.summary: Beaudoin 2014: summed 2-hour pain relief 7.0–7.8 with ketamine added versus 4.0 with morphine alone; rescue analgesia 20% versus 35%; more dysphoria and dizziness
cards.people: 60 ED patients aged 18–65 with acute moderate to severe pain (score at least 5 of 10, duration under 7 days) judged to need intravenous opioids at a large urban academic ED, randomised to morphine plus saline placebo, morphine plus ketamine 0.15 mg/kg, or morphine plus ketamine 0.3 mg/kg (20 per group), assessed to 120 minutes with rescue analgesia as needed.
cards.result: Summed pain-intensity difference over 2 hours was higher (more relief) in both ketamine groups than control: 4.0 (IQR 1.8–6.5) for standard care, 7.0 (IQR 4.3–10.8) for 0.15 mg/kg and 7.8 (IQR 4.8–12.8) for 0.3 mg/kg (p<0.02); the two ketamine doses did not differ from each other (p=0.46). The 0.3 mg/kg effect was sustained to 2 hours; the 0.15 mg/kg effect was not. Rescue analgesia was received by 7 of 20 (35%) controls versus 4 of 20 (20%) in each ketamine group (p=0.48), and controls who needed rescue received it sooner. More ketamine patients reported dysphoria and dizziness.
cards.watchOut: A 60-patient pilot-scale trial: the rescue-analgesia difference is not significant, follow-up ends at 2 hours, and the trial cannot characterise rarer ketamine harms (emergence reactions, laryngospasm) at these doses.
cards.source: Beaudoin FL et al. Low-dose ketamine improves pain relief in patients receiving intravenous opioids for acute pain in the emergency department: results of a randomized, double-blind, clinical trial. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2014. PMID: 25377395. cards.headline: Fjendbo Galili 2023: across 8 RCTs (n=903), adjunctive ketamine lowered pain only at 60 minutes (−0.76 points, not clinically significant); rescue analgesia fell, serious side effects did not rise
cards.summary: Fjendbo Galili 2023: across 8 RCTs (n=903), adjunctive ketamine lowered pain only at 60 minutes (−0.76 points, not clinically significant); rescue analgesia fell, serious side effects did not rise
cards.people: 8 randomised trials (903 adults) of a single subanaesthetic dose of ketamine added to opioid analgesia for any painful condition in ED settings, searched to March 2022; included studies were judged at moderate to high risk of bias.
cards.result: Mean pain intensity was significantly lower with adjunctive ketamine at 60 minutes only (mean difference −0.76, 95% CI −1.19 to −0.33); no significant differences at 15, 30, 45, 90 or 120 minutes. Patients receiving adjunctive ketamine were less likely to require rescue analgesia, were no more likely to experience serious side effects, and reported higher satisfaction scores. The reviewers conclude the pain-score reduction was not clinically significant, though combined with reduced opioid requirements the results could still be clinically important.
cards.watchOut: Moderate-to-high risk of bias in the underlying trials and a single significant time point among six tested — multiplicity alone could manufacture the 60-minute signal. Doses and opioids varied across trials.
cards.source: Fjendbo Galili S et al. Subanaesthetic single-dose ketamine as an adjunct to opioid analgesics for acute pain management in the emergency department: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ Open. 2023. PMID: 36972961. cards.headline: Synthesis: a real but small and brief effect — the honest case for ketamine is opioid sparing, not superior analgesia
cards.summary: Synthesis: a real but small and brief effect — the honest case for ketamine is opioid sparing, not superior analgesia
cards.people: One double-blind RCT (60 patients) and one meta-analysis of 8 RCTs (903 patients) of single-dose subanaesthetic ketamine added to opioids for acute ED pain.
cards.result: Pain: SPID advantage for ketamine in the single trial (7.0–7.8 versus 4.0); pooled mean difference −0.76 points at 60 minutes only (95% CI −1.19 to −0.33). Rescue analgesia: less with ketamine in both. Harms: more dysphoria and dizziness; no excess serious side effects in the pooled data. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Neither source supports ketamine as a morphine replacement at these doses, and neither follows patients beyond the ED episode; the benefit window is the first hour or two.

shelves.title: Shoulder dislocation: injecting lidocaine into the joint reduces as successfully as intravenous sedation — with a sixth of the adverse events and a shorter ED stay
shelves.question: In adults undergoing closed reduction of a dislocated shoulder, does intra-articular lidocaine give equivalent reduction success with fewer complications than intravenous analgesia and sedation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adolescent · Lidocaine · Shoulder Dislocation/therapy · Anesthetics, Local · Pain · Emergency Service, Hospital
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of 12 randomised trials (630 patients; 327 intra-articular lidocaine, 303 intravenous sedation) for closed reduction of acute anterior shoulder dislocation in the ED found no difference in reduction success (risk ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.86–1.01), no difference in pain scores after analgesia or in ease of reduction — but significantly fewer adverse events with intra-articular lidocaine (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07–0.33) and a shorter ED length of stay (mean difference −1.48, units as reported in the review; 95% CI −2.48 to −0.47). Heterogeneity was substantial for success (I²=69%) and length of stay (I²=93%), nil for adverse events (I²=0%). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intra-articular lidocaine is an equally effective, safer, faster-throughput alternative to IV sedation for anterior shoulder reduction, particularly when sedation is contraindicated or unavailable.

cards.headline: Sithamparapillai 2022: success RR 0.93 (no difference), adverse events RR 0.16, ED stay shorter by a mean 1.48 (as reported) with intra-articular lidocaine
cards.summary: Sithamparapillai 2022: success RR 0.93 (no difference), adverse events RR 0.16, ED stay shorter by a mean 1.48 (as reported) with intra-articular lidocaine
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Sithamparapillai 2022)
cards.people: 12 randomised trials, 630 patients aged 15 or older (intra-articular lidocaine 327; intravenous sedation 303) undergoing closed reduction of acute anterior shoulder dislocation in the emergency department; searches of MEDLINE and EMBASE to September 2021.
cards.result: No difference in successful reduction (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.86–1.01; I²=69%). Adverse events were significantly fewer with intra-articular lidocaine (RR 0.16, 95% CI 0.07–0.33; I²=0%). ED length of stay was shorter with lidocaine (mean difference −1.48, 95% CI −2.48 to −0.47; I²=93%). No differences in post-analgesia pain scores or ease of reduction.
cards.watchOut: The pooled success estimate's confidence interval (0.86–1.01) cannot exclude a modest success penalty for lidocaine, and heterogeneity is high for the success and stay outcomes; sedation agents and lidocaine techniques varied across the small constituent trials. The review reports the stay difference without its unit in the abstract — read as reported, not converted.

shelves.title: Distal radius fracture reduction: haematoma block achieves the same radiographic result as sedation — dexmedetomidine relieved pain faster at 10 minutes in the one head-to-head trial
shelves.question: In patients with a distal radius fracture, does a haematoma block provide adequate analgesia for reduction compared with procedural sedation or other regional techniques?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Male · Female · Radius Fractures/therapy/surgery · Prospective Studies · Adult · Emergency Service, Hospital · Dexmedetomidine/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Hematoma · Middle Aged · Child · Young Adult · Pain Measurement · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/therapeutic use/administration & dosage · Adolescent · Wrist Fractures
shelves.balance: SPLIT — adequacy splits by outcome. The direct randomised comparison (60 ED patients with distal radius fractures) found no difference between haematoma block and dexmedetomidine conscious sedation in post-reduction radiographic quality (Sarmiento criteria, p=0.89) or physician satisfaction (p=0.512), and no adverse effects in either group — but pain scores 10 minutes after the intervention were significantly lower with dexmedetomidine (p=0.009). A 2026 best-evidence review of haematoma block versus procedural sedation (7 studies, including 4 RCTs) likewise found no consistent difference in procedural success, with the highest-quality RCTs showing no difference in radiographic outcome. PROPOSED SPLIT: for getting the fracture reduced as well, the block is adequate; for how the first minutes feel, sedation acted faster in the single direct trial.

cards.headline: Vişneci 2025: no difference in reduction quality (p=0.89) or physician satisfaction (p=0.512); VAS at 10 minutes significantly lower with dexmedetomidine (p=0.009); no adverse effects
cards.summary: Vişneci 2025: no difference in reduction quality (p=0.89) or physician satisfaction (p=0.512); VAS at 10 minutes significantly lower with dexmedetomidine (p=0.009); no adverse effects
cards.people: 60 patients presenting to an ED with distal radius fractures (28 women, 19 men, 13 children under 12; mean age about 33–35 years per group), randomised to haematoma block or conscious sedation with dexmedetomidine. Pain (VAS) was measured before the procedure, 10 minutes after the intervention, and after reduction; reduction quality was graded on control radiographs by Sarmiento criteria, and physician satisfaction on a 5-point Likert scale.
cards.result: Pre-procedure VAS scores were comparable (p=0.883). VAS 10 minutes after the intervention was significantly lower in the dexmedetomidine group (p=0.009, t=−2.773). Post-reduction quality by Sarmiento criteria did not differ (p=0.89), nor did physician satisfaction (p=0.512). No adverse effects related to either method were observed in any patient.
cards.watchOut: Sixty patients including 13 children — a mixed adult-paediatric sample answering an adult-framed question — and the abstract reports p-values without the actual VAS means, so the size of the early pain advantage cannot be judged from the record. Single centre, single trial.
cards.source: Vişneci EF et al. Comparison of hematoma block and dexmedetomidine for reduction of distal radius fractures in the emergency department: a prospective randomized controlled study. Ulusal Travma ve Acil Cerrahi Dergisi (Turkish Journal of Trauma & Emergency Surgery). 2025. PMID: 40910713. cards.headline: Fox 2026 (best-evidence review): across 7 studies, no consistent difference in procedural success between haematoma block and procedural sedation
cards.summary: Fox 2026 (best-evidence review): across 7 studies, no consistent difference in procedural success between haematoma block and procedural sedation
cards.people: 7 studies (4 randomised trials, 3 observational; two reports from one dataset combined) comparing haematoma block with procedural sedation for manipulation of distal radius fractures in adults in the ED, from structured MEDLINE and Embase searches; outcomes were procedural success and adverse events.
cards.result: Across the included studies there was no consistent evidence of a difference in procedural success between haematoma block and procedural sedation; the highest-quality evidence, from two randomised trials, found no difference in radiographic outcome. For adverse events, one study found less pain in the haematoma block group; no other study detected a statistically significant difference.
cards.watchOut: A Best Evidence Topic is a structured short review, not a full systematic review with meta-analysis — no pooled estimate exists, and the constituent trials are small and old in part.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the block reduces the fracture as well as sedation does; whether it hurts more in the first minutes is unsettled
cards.summary: Synthesis: the block reduces the fracture as well as sedation does; whether it hurts more in the first minutes is unsettled
cards.people: One small RCT (60 patients, mixed ages) against dexmedetomidine sedation, and one best-evidence review (7 studies) against procedural sedation generally.
cards.result: Reduction quality: no difference (p=0.89 in the trial; concordant review). Physician satisfaction: no difference (p=0.512). Early pain: VAS lower at 10 minutes with dexmedetomidine (p=0.009, magnitude not reported); the review's one pain-reporting study favoured the block. Adverse effects: none observed in the trial. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C set: the direct evidence is one small trial plus a short-format review.
cards.watchOut: Haematoma block's practical advantages — no sedation monitoring, no fasting, faster departmental flow — are asserted in practice but are not outcomes either record measured.

shelves.title: Antibiotics after mammal bites: the old Cochrane evidence supports prophylaxis for human bites and hand bites (OR 0.10) — and finds no benefit for ordinary dog or cat bites
shelves.question: In patients presenting after mammalian bites, does prophylactic antibiotic treatment prevent wound infection compared with no prophylaxis, and does the answer differ for dog, cat, and human bites?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Bites and Stings/complications/drug therapy · Cats · Confidence Intervals · Dogs · Humans · Odds Ratio · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Wound Infection/etiology/prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by bite type and site, on old and thin evidence. The 2001 Cochrane review pooled 8 randomised trials of prophylactic antibiotics after mammalian bites. Antibiotics were associated with a statistically significant reduction in infection after human bites (the reviewers note this rests on one trial and needs confirmation). For bites by cats or dogs, prophylaxis did not appear to reduce infection rates. Site mattered independently: prophylaxis after hand bites significantly reduced infection (odds ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.01–0.86; number needed to treat 4, 95% CI 2–50). Wound type (laceration versus puncture) did not appear to modify the effect. PROPOSED SPLIT: prophylaxis — supported for human bites and for hand bites of any species; not supported by trial evidence for uncomplicated dog or cat bites elsewhere on the body.

cards.headline: Medeiros & Saconato 2001 (Cochrane): human bites and hand bites benefit (hand OR 0.10, NNT 4); dog and cat bites do not
cards.summary: Medeiros & Saconato 2001 (Cochrane): human bites and hand bites benefit (hand OR 0.10, NNT 4); dog and cat bites do not
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials (Medeiros & Saconato 2001, Cochrane)
cards.people: 8 randomised controlled trials of prophylactic antibiotics versus placebo or no intervention in patients with bites from any mammal, identified from MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS and the Cochrane Controlled Trials Register to November 2000; the outcome was infection at the bite site, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Prophylactic antibiotics were associated with a statistically significant reduction in infection after bites by humans, and with a significant reduction after bites to the hand (odds ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.86; NNT 4, 95% CI 2 to 50). Prophylaxis did not appear to reduce infection after bites by cats or dogs. Wound type (laceration or puncture) did not appear to influence effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: A 2001 review of small old trials: the human-bite conclusion rests on one trial and the hand-bite estimate's interval runs from 0.01 to 0.86 — the direction is consistent, the size is not pinned down. Modern bite care (irrigation standards, resistant organisms, immunocompromised hosts) postdates this evidence, and no update was carded.
cards.source: Medeiros I et al. Antibiotic prophylaxis for mammalian bites. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2001. PMID: 11406003. shelves.title: Packing a drained perianal abscess cavity bought nothing but pain: 38.2 versus 28.2 on a 100-point pain scale, with fistula and recurrence no lower
shelves.question: After surgical drainage of a perianal abscess, does prolonged packing of the cavity improve healing or reduce recurrence compared with no packing — or mainly add pain?
shelves.mesh: Abscess/surgery · Adult · Anus Diseases/surgery · Bandages · Drainage · Humans · Pain · Rectal Fistula/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — for the packing, not the patient outcomes it was meant to protect. In PPAC2, 433 adults admitted for incision and drainage of a primary perianal abscess across 50 NHS sites were randomised to continued postoperative cavity packing or no packing. Packing hurt more: mean maximum pain scores were 38.2 with packing versus 28.2 without (mean difference 9.9 points on a 100-point scale; p<0.0001). In return, packing bought no significant protection — fistula-in-ano occurred in 15% (32/213) with packing versus 11% (24/220) without (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39–1.22; p=0.20), and abscess recurrence in 3% (7/213) with packing versus 6% (13/223) without (OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.72–4.73; p=0.20), both intervals wide and compatible with small effects either way. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): routine packing of perianal abscess cavities adds significant pain without demonstrated benefit on healing complications.

cards.headline: Newton 2022 (PPAC2): pain 38.2 versus 28.2 with packing (p<0.0001); fistula 15% versus 11% and recurrence 3% versus 6%, both non-significant
cards.summary: Newton 2022 (PPAC2): pain 38.2 versus 28.2 with packing (p<0.0001); fistula 15% versus 11% and recurrence 3% versus 6%, both non-significant
cards.people: 433 adults (mean age 42 years) admitted to NHS hospitals for incision and drainage of a primary perianal abscess, randomised 1:1 at 50 sites to continued postoperative wound packing (n=213) or non-packing (n=220), followed for 6 months with blinded data collection via symptom diaries, telephone and clinics. Primary outcome: mean maximum pain on a 100-point visual analogue scale.
cards.result: Participants allocated to packing reported higher pain than non-packing (38.2 versus 28.2; mean difference 9.9; p<0.0001). Fistula-in-ano was low in both groups: 32/213 (15%) with packing and 24/220 (11%) without (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.22; p=0.20). Abscess recurrence: 13/223 (6%) in the non-packing group and 7/213 (3%) in the packing group (OR 1.85, 95% CI 0.72 to 4.73; p=0.20). The authors conclude avoiding packing is less painful without a negative morbidity risk.
cards.watchOut: A single trial, unblinded by necessity — pain is subjective and patients knew whether their cavity was being repacked, which could inflate the pain gap; conversely the fistula and recurrence intervals are too wide to exclude modest effects of packing in either direction.
cards.source: Newton K et al. Postoperative Packing of Perianal Abscess Cavities (PPAC2): randomized clinical trial. The British Journal of Surgery. 2022. PMID: 35929816. Registry ID: NCT03315169. shelves.title: Absorbable sutures close traumatic lacerations as cosmetically as non-absorbable ones — 79 versus 66 in children, 54.1 versus 54.5 mm in the adult-inclusive trial — with no removal visit
shelves.question: In traumatic lacerations closed in the emergency department, do absorbable sutures give equivalent long-term cosmetic outcomes to non-absorbable sutures that require removal?
shelves.mesh: Absorbable Implants · Catgut · Child · Cosmetic Techniques/adverse effects/instrumentation · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Lacerations/surgery · Male · Nylons · Pain Measurement · Surgical Wound Dehiscence/etiology · Suture Techniques · Sutures/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Wound Infection/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — two randomised trials agree. In children (95 enrolled), plain-gut absorbable versus nylon sutures gave similar short-term optimal wound scores (63% versus 49%; RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.45–1.17) and, at four months in the 63 children followed, blinded plastic-surgeon cosmesis scores of 79 (95% CI 73–85) versus 66 (95% CI 55–76), with no differences in infection or dehiscence. In the second trial (115 enrolled, children and adults, trunk and extremity lacerations), absorbable Vicryl Rapide versus non-absorbable Prolene gave mean cosmesis scores of 54.1 mm versus 54.5 mm on a 100-mm scale (mean difference 0.5 mm, 95% CI −12.1 to 17.2), meeting the trial's 13-mm noninferiority margin, with no significant complication differences. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): absorbable sutures match non-absorbable ones for long-term cosmesis in simple traumatic lacerations, and spare the removal visit.

cards.headline: Karounis 2004 (children): four-month cosmesis 79 versus 66 favouring absorbable numerically; optimal-score rates and complications not significantly different
cards.summary: Karounis 2004 (children): four-month cosmesis 79 versus 66 favouring absorbable numerically; optimal-score rates and complications not significantly different
cards.people: 95 children aged 1–18 years with traumatic lacerations under 12 hours old in a paediatric ED (50 absorbable plain gut, 45 non-absorbable nylon), excluding bites, contaminated, puncture/crush and joint-crossing wounds and scalp lacerations. Wounds were scored at up to 10 days (wound evaluation score) and at 4–5 months by a single blinded plastic surgeon (visual analogue cosmesis scale and repeat score); 63 children completed long-term follow-up.
cards.result: Short-term optimal wound scores: 63% absorbable versus 49% non-absorbable (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.17), with no difference in infection or dehiscence. At four months, mean visual analogue cosmesis was 79 (95% CI 73 to 85) for absorbable versus 66 (95% CI 55 to 76) for non-absorbable; optimal-score proportions were 36% versus 28% (RR 0.88, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.26). Dehiscence 2% versus 11% (p=0.07); infection 0 versus 2 cases (p=0.3). Scar revision was recommended for 3 patients; none proceeded.
cards.watchOut: A third of enrolled children were lost before the long-term cosmetic assessment, and the trial was powered for equivalence of scores, not for the small complication differences it reports — the dehiscence trend (2% versus 11%) is intriguing but fragile at these numbers.
cards.source: Karounis H et al. A randomized, controlled trial comparing long-term cosmetic outcomes of traumatic pediatric lacerations repaired with absorbable plain gut versus nonabsorbable nylon sutures. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2004. PMID: 15231459. cards.headline: Tejani 2014: cosmesis 54.1 versus 54.5 mm (difference 0.5 mm) — noninferiority of absorbable sutures established for trunk and extremity lacerations
cards.summary: Tejani 2014: cosmesis 54.1 versus 54.5 mm (difference 0.5 mm) — noninferiority of absorbable sutures established for trunk and extremity lacerations
cards.people: 115 paediatric and adult patients with traumatic lacerations of the trunk or extremities, randomised to absorbable Vicryl Rapide or non-absorbable Prolene; 73 completed the study (35 absorbable, 38 non-absorbable; mean age 22.1 years). Wounds were checked at 10 days for infection and dehiscence and photographed at 3 months for blinded rating by two plastic surgeons on a 100-mm visual analogue scale; a difference of 13 mm or more was prespecified as clinically significant.
cards.result: Mean observer cosmesis scores were 54.1 mm (95% CI 44.5 to 67.0) for absorbable and 54.5 mm (95% CI 45.7 to 66.3) for non-absorbable (mean difference 0.5 mm, 95% CI −12.1 to 17.2; p=0.9), establishing noninferiority. Complication rates did not differ significantly, though a higher percentage of absorbable-suture wounds developed complications.
cards.watchOut: Only 73 of 115 enrolled patients completed follow-up, and the noninferiority margin (13 mm on a 100-mm scale) is generous — equivalence is claimed within a fairly wide tolerance. Face and hand lacerations were not studied.
cards.source: Tejani C et al. A comparison of cosmetic outcomes of lacerations on the extremities and trunk using absorbable versus nonabsorbable sutures. Academic Emergency Medicine. 2014. shelves.title: Staples versus sutures for skin closure: infection and dehiscence are a wash (OR 0.98) — staples are faster, sutures look better and satisfy patients more; after hip replacement, staples carried more superficial infection
shelves.question: For skin closure, do staples close wounds faster than sutures, and do they differ in infection and cosmetic outcomes?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Digestive System Surgical Procedures/methods · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Skin · Surgical Stapling/methods · Surgical Wound Infection/etiology/prevention & control · Suture Techniques · Sutures
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by outcome and by operation. In abdominal surgery (7 RCTs, 3,705 patients), staples and subcuticular sutures did not differ in surgical-site infection (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.79–1.22) or dehiscence; staple closure was faster, while sutures gave better cosmesis and patient satisfaction. In hip arthroplasty (5 RCTs and 1 cohort), the balance tilted: superficial infection and prolonged wound discharge were more frequent with staples than with sutures, with no significant differences in dehiscence, abscess, wound-score or satisfaction outcomes — and suturing again took longer. PROPOSED SPLIT: staples win on speed everywhere; on infection they tie in abdominal surgery and lose after hip replacement; on appearance and satisfaction, sutures lead where they were measured.

cards.headline: Feng 2021 (abdominal surgery): SSI odds ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.79–1.22) — no difference; staples faster, sutures better cosmesis and satisfaction
cards.summary: Feng 2021 (abdominal surgery): SSI odds ratio 0.98 (95% CI 0.79–1.22) — no difference; staples faster, sutures better cosmesis and satisfaction
cards.people: 7 randomised trials, 3,705 patients undergoing abdominal surgery, comparing subcuticular sutures with skin staples; primary outcome surgical-site infection, with dehiscence, closure time, cosmesis and patient satisfaction as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: No significant difference in surgical-site infection between sutures and staples overall (OR 0.98, 95% CI 0.79–1.22; I²=44%) or in the gastrointestinal-surgery subgroup (OR 0.85, 95% CI 0.66–1.09). Dehiscence incidence was comparable. Staple closure was associated with shorter surgery duration; sutures appeared to provide better cosmesis and patient satisfaction. No significant publication bias was detected.
cards.watchOut: The pooled OR is reported for sutures versus staples as the review frames it; the abstract gives no absolute infection rates, so the absolute stakes of the tie cannot be read from the record. Cosmesis and satisfaction findings are qualitative summaries of heterogeneous secondary outcomes.
cards.source: Feng J et al. Subcuticular sutures versus staples for skin closure in patients undergoing abdominal surgery: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. PLoS ONE. 2021. cards.headline: Liu 2021 (hip arthroplasty): superficial infection and prolonged discharge higher with staples; dehiscence, wound scores and satisfaction not significantly different; sutures slower
cards.summary: Liu 2021 (hip arthroplasty): superficial infection and prolonged discharge higher with staples; dehiscence, wound scores and satisfaction not significantly different; sutures slower
cards.people: 5 randomised trials and 1 retrospective cohort study of skin closure with staples versus sutures after hip arthroplasty, identified from EMBASE, PubMed, Medline, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library.
cards.result: The risks of superficial infection and prolonged discharge were higher with staples than with sutures after hip arthroplasty. There was no significant difference between groups in allergic reaction, dehiscence, inflammation, abscess formation, Hollander Wound Evaluation Scale scores, or patient satisfaction with the closure method. Suturing required a longer operating time.
cards.watchOut: The record reports directions without pooled effect sizes, so the size of the infection penalty cannot be quantified from the abstract — a declared gap for this card. One included study was a retrospective cohort, not a trial.

shelves.title: Canadian Syncope Risk Score: superb in its Canadian validation (area under the curve 0.91; very-low-risk patients had a 0.3% event rate) — but in its first validation abroad it matched clinical judgement overall and its low-risk group still had a 6.7% event rate
shelves.question: In adults presenting to the emergency department with syncope, does the Canadian Syncope Risk Score accurately identify patients at low risk of serious adverse events within 30 days who can be safely discharged?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Arrhythmias, Cardiac/complications · Canada · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/complications · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism/complications · Risk Assessment · Syncope/diagnosis/etiology · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by where it was validated. In the Canadian multicentre validation (3,819 ED patients with syncope, 3.6% with 30-day serious outcomes), the score discriminated excellently (area under the receiver operating curve 0.91, 95% CI 0.88–0.93), calibration was near-perfect (slope 1.0), event rates rose from 0.3% (3 of 1,631) in the very-low-risk group to 51.3% (40 of 78) in the very-high-risk group, no very-low- or low-risk patient died or had a ventricular arrhythmia, and at a threshold of −1 the sensitivity was 97.8% (95% CI 93.8–99.6) with specificity 44.3%. In the first validation outside Canada (345 Italian ED patients, 12% with serious adverse events), discrimination fell to 0.75 (95% CI 0.68–0.81) — similar to clinical judgement at 0.68 — and patients labelled low risk by the score still had a 6.7% event rate, versus 2% for clinician-judged low risk; score sensitivity was 70% (95% CI 54–83) versus 95% (95% CI 84–99) for judgement. PROPOSED SPLIT: the score stratifies beautifully in its home system; abroad, it did not beat — and at the discharge threshold did not match — clinician judgement.

cards.headline: Thiruganasambandamoorthy 2020 (Canadian validation): AUC 0.91, calibration slope 1.0, very-low-risk event rate 0.3%, sensitivity 97.8% at threshold −1
cards.summary: Thiruganasambandamoorthy 2020 (Canadian validation): AUC 0.91, calibration slope 1.0, very-low-risk event rate 0.3%, sensitivity 97.8% at threshold −1
cards.people: 3,819 patients aged 16 or older presenting within 24 hours of syncope to 9 EDs across Canada (mean age 53.9 years, 54.7% women), enrolled March 2014 to April 2018; 139 (3.6%) had adjudicated 30-day serious outcomes (arrhythmic and non-arrhythmic), including 13 deaths (0.3%).
cards.result: Predicted and observed risks did not differ (empirical 3.64% versus model-predicted 3.17%; p=0.26); calibration slope was 1.0 and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.91 (95% CI 0.88–0.93). Serious outcomes rose from 3 of 1,631 (0.3%) in the very-low-risk group to 40 of 78 (51.3%) in the very-high-risk group. No very-low-risk or low-risk patient died or experienced ventricular arrhythmia. At a threshold score of −1 (2,145 of 3,819 patients), sensitivity was 97.8% (95% CI 93.8%–99.6%) and specificity 44.3% (95% CI 42.7%–45.9%).
cards.watchOut: Validation in the score's home country and research network, in a cohort with a low 3.6% event rate — spectrum and setting effects flatter discrimination, and a 44.3% specificity means most patients still score above the discharge threshold.
cards.source: Thiruganasambandamoorthy V et al. Multicenter Emergency Department Validation of the Canadian Syncope Risk Score. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2020. PMID: 32202605. cards.headline: Solbiati 2021 (Italian external validation): AUC 0.75 versus 0.68 for clinical judgement; score-defined low-risk patients had a 6.7% event rate and sensitivity was 70% versus 95%
cards.summary: Solbiati 2021 (Italian external validation): AUC 0.75 versus 0.68 for clinical judgement; score-defined low-risk patients had a 6.7% event rate and sensitivity was 70% versus 95%
cards.people: 345 patients older than 18 presenting with syncope to Italian EDs (from the SyMoNE database; median age 71 years, 50% men, 29% hospitalised), enrolled September 2015 to February 2017, with the score and the treating physician's risk judgement both recorded and 30-day follow-up; 43 patients (12%) had serious adverse events.
cards.result: The area under the curve was 0.75 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.81) for the Canadian Syncope Risk Score and 0.68 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.74) for clinical judgement. The risk of adverse events among patients at low risk was 6.7% by the score versus 2% by clinical judgement, with sensitivity 70% (95% CI 54% to 83%) for the score and 95% (95% CI 84% to 99%) for judgement. The authors conclude that studies showing the score improves outcomes are warranted before widespread implementation.
cards.watchOut: A much older, higher-event-rate cohort (12% versus 3.6%) in a different health system — some performance loss is expected on transport, and 345 patients give wide intervals. But the discharge-relevant number (6.7% events in score-defined low risk) is the one a clinician acts on, and it was not low.
cards.source: Solbiati M et al. Multicentre external validation of the Canadian Syncope Risk Score to predict adverse events and comparison with clinical judgement. Emergency Medicine Journal. 2021. cards.headline: Synthesis: a score that travels imperfectly — trust its strata at home, distrust its discharge threshold abroad until local validation exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: a score that travels imperfectly — trust its strata at home, distrust its discharge threshold abroad until local validation exists
cards.people: Two prospective validation cohorts of the Canadian Syncope Risk Score in ED syncope (3,819 patients in Canada; 345 in Italy).
cards.result: Discrimination: AUC 0.91 (Canada) versus 0.75 (Italy; clinical judgement 0.68). Low-risk safety: 0.3% events in Canadian very-low-risk patients and no deaths or ventricular arrhythmias in the low strata; 6.7% events in Italian score-defined low-risk patients versus 2% for judgement-defined low risk. Sensitivity at working thresholds: 97.8% (Canada, threshold −1) versus 70% (Italy). PROPOSED SPLIT by validation setting, Tier C set: observational cohort evidence carrying a discharge-safety claim.
cards.watchOut: Neither study randomised management by the score, so no record here shows that using it improves outcomes — only that it ranks risk, unevenly by setting.
cards.source: Synthesis of Thiruganasambandamoorthy V et al. JAMA Internal Medicine. 2020 (PMID: 32202605); Solbiati M et al. Emergency Medicine Journal. 2021 (PMID: 34039646).

shelves.title: Implementing the Canadian C-Spine Rule cut cervical imaging by about an eighth in a 12-hospital cluster trial — no fractures missed, and the rule itself beat NEXUS head-to-head
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with possible cervical spine injury, does implementing the Canadian C-Spine Rule reduce imaging rates without missing clinically important injuries?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Canada · Cervical Vertebrae/injuries · Cluster Analysis · Craniocerebral Trauma/diagnosis · Decision Support Systems, Clinical/standards/statistics & numerical data · Diagnostic Imaging/statistics & numerical data · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Injury Severity Score · Male · Middle Aged · Spinal Fractures/diagnosis · Wounds, Nonpenetrating/diagnosis · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for imaging use, with the safety record the trial could show. In a 12-centre matched-pair cluster randomised trial of 11,824 alert, stable adults with blunt head or neck trauma, an active implementation strategy (education, policy, real-time requisition reminders) produced a 12.8% relative reduction in cervical spine imaging (61.7% before to 53.3% after), while control hospitals rose 12.5% relative (52.8% to 58.9%); no fractures were missed and no adverse outcomes occurred (Stiell IG et al., PMID: 19875425). The rule being implemented had itself beaten the NEXUS low-risk criteria head-to-head in 8,283 patients: sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7% and specificity 45.1% versus 36.8%, missing 1 important injury versus 16 (PMID: 14695411). The catch is reach: even after active implementation, 53.3% of these alert, stable patients were still imaged, so the rule trims imaging rather than transforming it. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): implementation measurably reduces cervical imaging with no missed fractures in the trial, on a rule independently shown more accurate than NEXUS.

cards.headline: Stiell 2009: implementation cut imaging from 61.7% to 53.3% (12.8% relative reduction) while controls rose — no fractures missed
cards.summary: Stiell 2009: implementation cut imaging from 61.7% to 53.3% (12.8% relative reduction) while controls rose — no fractures missed
cards.people: 11,824 alert and stable adults presenting with blunt trauma to the head or neck at 12 Canadian university and community emergency departments; six hospitals received active implementation of the Canadian C-Spine Rule (education, policy, real-time reminders on radiology requisitions) and six continued usual practice, over 12-month before and after periods.
cards.result: Cervical spine imaging in the intervention group fell from 61.7% to 53.3% — a 12.8% relative reduction (95% CI 9% to 16%; P=0.01) — while the control group rose from 52.8% to 58.9%, a 12.5% relative increase (P=0.03); the between-group contrast was significant (P<0.001). No fractures were missed and no adverse outcomes occurred.
cards.watchOut: A before–after cluster design in Canadian departments whose baseline imaging rates (52.8–61.7%) were already far below typical US rates; the absolute gain was 8.4 percentage points, and more than half of eligible patients were still imaged after implementation.
cards.source: Stiell et al. Implementation of the Canadian C-Spine Rule: prospective 12 centre cluster randomised trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2009. PMID: 19875425. Registry ID: NCT00290875. cards.headline: Stiell 2003: the rule itself beat NEXUS — sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7%, specificity 45.1% versus 36.8%, 1 injury missed versus 16
cards.summary: Stiell 2003: the rule itself beat NEXUS — sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7%, specificity 45.1% versus 36.8%, 1 injury missed versus 16
cards.people: 8,283 alert, stable trauma patients in nine Canadian emergency departments, in whom 394 physicians applied both the Canadian C-Spine Rule and the NEXUS low-risk criteria before radiography; 169 patients (2.0%) had clinically important cervical spine injuries.
cards.result: Excluding indeterminate cases, the Canadian C-Spine Rule was more sensitive than NEXUS (99.4% vs 90.7%, P<0.001) and more specific (45.1% vs 36.8%, P<0.001), and would have produced lower radiography rates (55.9% vs 66.6%, P<0.001). The rule would have missed 1 patient with an important injury; NEXUS would have missed 16.
cards.watchOut: In 845 patients (10.2%) physicians did not assess range of motion as the rule requires, making those cases indeterminate; sensitivity estimates depend on how those cases are counted (95.3% if all are assumed rule-negative).
cards.source: Stiell et al. The Canadian C-spine rule versus the NEXUS low-risk criteria in patients with trauma. The New England journal of medicine. 2003. PMID: 14695411. cards.headline: Synthesis: a more accurate rule, and proof that pushing it into practice cuts imaging modestly with no missed fractures seen
cards.summary: Synthesis: a more accurate rule, and proof that pushing it into practice cuts imaging modestly with no missed fractures seen
cards.people: One 12-centre cluster randomised implementation trial (11,824 patients) and one 9-centre prospective head-to-head accuracy cohort (8,283 patients), both in Canadian emergency departments.
cards.result: Implementation: imaging 61.7% to 53.3% (12.8% relative reduction) versus a rise at control sites; no missed fractures. Accuracy: sensitivity 99.4% versus 90.7% and specificity 45.1% versus 36.8% against NEXUS, with 1 versus 16 important injuries missed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C because the practice-change claim rests on a single implementation trial.
