shelves.title: Ottawa ankle rules in practice: ankle X-rays down 28% relative, no fractures missed, shorter waits and lower costs — and a systematic review puts the post-test fracture risk below 1.4%
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with acute ankle injury, does implementing the Ottawa ankle rules reduce radiography without increasing missed fractures?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Ankle Injuries/diagnostic imaging/economics · Emergency Service, Hospital/economics/standards/statistics & numerical data · Female · Guidelines as Topic · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Ontario · Patient Satisfaction · Practice Patterns, Physicians'/economics/standards/statistics & numerical data · Radiography/economics/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — less radiation and waiting, with sensitivity at or near 100% in the studies that measured it. In the original controlled implementation study of 2,342 adults, introducing the Ottawa ankle rules produced a 28% relative reduction in ankle radiography at the intervention hospital against a 2% increase at the control hospital (P<0.001), foot radiography fell 14% relative, patients discharged without radiography spent 80 versus 116 minutes in the department, and no fractures were missed — sensitivity was 1.0 for both malleolar (74 fractures) and midfoot (19 fractures) injuries (Stiell IG et al., PMID: 8114236). A systematic review of 27 studies and 15,581 patients found pooled negative likelihood ratios of 0.08 for ankle and mid-foot, which at a 15% fracture prevalence leaves under a 1.4% probability of fracture after a negative rule (PMID: 12595378). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the rules safely cut ankle and foot radiography by roughly a quarter to a third wherever they have been implemented and measured.

cards.headline: Stiell 1994: ankle radiography fell 28% relative at the intervention hospital versus a 2% rise at the control — sensitivity 1.0, no missed fractures
cards.summary: Stiell 1994: ankle radiography fell 28% relative at the intervention hospital versus a 2% rise at the control — sensitivity 1.0, no missed fractures
cards.people: 2,342 adults with acute ankle injuries seen during 5-month periods before and after implementation at a university (intervention) and a community (control) emergency department in Ontario.
cards.result: Ankle radiography fell by a relative 28% at the intervention hospital and rose 2% at the control (P<0.001); foot radiography fell 14% relative versus a 13% rise (P<0.05). Non-fracture patients discharged without radiography spent less time in the department (80 vs 116 minutes, P<0.0001) and cost less ($62 vs $173, P<0.001), with no difference in satisfaction (95% vs 96%) or later radiography (5% vs 5%). Sensitivity was 1.0 (95% CI 0.95 to 1.0) for 74 malleolar fractures and 1.0 (0.82 to 1.0) for 19 midfoot fractures, and radiography use did not rebound over the following 12 months.
cards.watchOut: A non-randomised before–after study with one intervention and one control hospital from the early 1990s; the midfoot sensitivity confidence interval (down to 0.82) reflects only 19 fractures.
cards.source: Stiell et al. Implementation of the Ottawa ankle rules. JAMA. 1994. PMID: 8114236. cards.headline: Bachmann 2003: across 27 studies and 15,581 patients, a negative Ottawa rule leaves under a 1.4% fracture probability at typical prevalence
cards.summary: Bachmann 2003: across 27 studies and 15,581 patients, a negative Ottawa rule leaves under a 1.4% fracture probability at typical prevalence
cards.people: 27 studies reporting on 15,581 patients with ankle or mid-foot injury assessed with the Ottawa ankle rules (32 studies met inclusion criteria).
cards.result: Pooled negative likelihood ratios were 0.08 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.18) for the ankle and 0.08 (0.03 to 0.20) for the mid-foot, and 0.07 (0.03 to 0.18) for both regions in children. Applied to a 15% fracture prevalence, these ratios give a probability of actual fracture below 1.4% after a negative rule. Sensitivity was almost 100% with modest specificity, supporting an expected 30–40% reduction in unnecessary radiographs.
cards.watchOut: Specificity is only modest, so the rules exclude fracture rather than diagnose it; accuracy varied with study methods, and four main methodological threats to validity had to be corrected for in the pooling.
cards.source: Bachmann et al. Accuracy of Ottawa ankle rules to exclude fractures of the ankle and mid-foot: systematic review. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2003. PMID: 12595378. shelves.title: PECARN head-injury rules: in 42,412 children the low-risk groups carried a 100% and 99.95% negative predictive value for clinically important brain injury — and an external validation in 20,137 more children agreed
shelves.question: In children with head injury, does the PECARN decision rule safely identify those at very low risk of clinically important traumatic brain injury in whom CT can be avoided?
shelves.mesh: Algorithms · Biomechanical Phenomena · Brain Injuries/diagnostic imaging/etiology/mortality · Child · Child, Preschool · Craniocerebral Trauma/complications/diagnosis · Decision Support Techniques · Decision Trees · Emergency Medicine/methods · Humans · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Patient Admission/statistics & numerical data · Patient Selection · Pediatrics/methods · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment/methods/standards · Risk Factors · Severity of Illness Index · Tomography, X-Ray Computed/adverse effects/statistics & numerical data
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as a rule-out instrument, this is about as well validated as decision rules get. In the derivation-and-validation cohort of 42,412 children with Glasgow Coma Scale scores of 14–15 presenting within 24 hours of head trauma, clinically important traumatic brain injury (ciTBI) occurred in 0.9% and neurosurgery in 0.1%; in validation, the under-2 rule had a negative predictive value of 100.0% (1176/1176) and sensitivity of 100% (25/25), and the age-2-and-older rule a negative predictive value of 99.95% (3798/3800) and sensitivity of 96.8% (61/63), with neither rule missing a child who needed neurosurgery (Kuppermann N et al., PMID: 19758692). External validation in 20,137 Australian and New Zealand children again found PECARN sensitivities of 100.0% (under 2 years, 38/38) and 99.0% (2 years and older, 97/98) (PMID: 28410792). About a fifth to a quarter of CT-imaged children fell in the low-risk groups — that is the imaging the rule can obviate. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): two very large prospective cohorts agree the low-risk strata can safely forgo CT.

cards.headline: Kuppermann 2009 (PECARN): validation negative predictive value 100.0% (under 2) and 99.95% (age 2+) — neither rule missed neurosurgery
cards.summary: Kuppermann 2009 (PECARN): validation negative predictive value 100.0% (under 2) and 99.95% (age 2+) — neither rule missed neurosurgery
cards.type: Prospective derivation and validation cohort (Kuppermann 2009, PECARN)
cards.people: 42,412 children younger than 18 years presenting within 24 hours of head trauma with Glasgow Coma Scale scores of 14–15 in 25 North American emergency departments (derivation and validation: 8,502 and 2,216 children under 2 years; 25,283 and 6,411 aged 2 years and older). CT was obtained in 14,969 (35.3%); ciTBI occurred in 376 (0.9%) and neurosurgery in 60 (0.1%).
cards.result: In validation, the under-2 rule (normal mental status, no scalp haematoma except frontal, no or brief loss of consciousness, non-severe mechanism, no palpable skull fracture, acting normally) had a negative predictive value for ciTBI of 1176/1176 (100.0%, 95% CI 99.7–100.0) and sensitivity 25/25 (100%, 86.3–100.0); 24.1% of CT-imaged under-2s were in this low-risk group. The age-2+ rule had a negative predictive value of 3798/3800 (99.95%, 99.81–99.99) and sensitivity 61/63 (96.8%, 89.0–99.6); 20.1% of CT-imaged older children were low-risk. Neither rule missed neurosurgery in the validation populations.
cards.watchOut: The rule applies only to children with GCS 14–15 presenting within 24 hours; the under-2 sensitivity confidence interval extends to 86.3% because only 25 validation ciTBIs occurred in that age group, and the intermediate-risk group still needs clinician judgement or observation rather than automatic CT or discharge.
cards.source: Kuppermann et al. Identification of children at very low risk of clinically-important brain injuries after head trauma: a prospective cohort study. Lancet (London, England). 2009. PMID: 19758692. cards.summary: Babl 2017 (PREDICT): external validation in 20,137 children — PECARN sensitivities 100.0% (under 2) and 99.0% (age 2+), ahead of CATCH and CHALICE
cards.people: 20,137 children and adolescents with head injuries of any severity presenting to ten Australian and New Zealand emergency departments; CT was obtained in 2,106 (10%), 83 (<1%) underwent neurosurgery and 15 (<1%) died. PECARN was applicable to 4,011 (75%) of children under 2 and 11,152 (76%) of those 2 and older.
cards.result: PECARN validation sensitivity for clinically important traumatic brain injury was 100.0% (95% CI 90.7–100.0; 38/38) in children under 2 years and 99.0% (94.4–100.0; 97/98) in children 2 years and older — the highest point sensitivities of the three rules tested, ahead of CATCH (95.2% for high-risk predictors) and CHALICE (92.3%).

shelves.title: Ultrasound-first for suspected kidney stones: in 2,759 randomised patients, high-risk missed diagnoses were 0.4% on every strategy — the only clear winner was the radiation bill, lower with ultrasound
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with suspected kidney stones, does an ultrasound-first imaging strategy give equivalent outcomes to CT-first, with less cumulative radiation?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Age Distribution · Aged · Comparative Effectiveness Research · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Hospitalization/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nephrolithiasis/diagnostic imaging · Radiation Dosage · Tomography, X-Ray Computed · Ultrasonography · Young Adult
shelves.balance: SPLIT — clinical outcomes drawn, radiation not. In a multicentre pragmatic randomised trial of 2,759 emergency-department patients aged 18–76 with suspected nephrolithiasis, initial point-of-care ultrasonography, radiology ultrasonography, or CT produced the same low rate of high-risk diagnoses with complications at 30 days (0.4% overall, no difference by strategy), the same serious adverse event rates (12.4%, 10.8% and 11.2%; P=0.50), the same pain scores at 7 days (2.0 in each group), and no significant differences in return visits, hospitalisations, or diagnostic accuracy — but mean 6-month cumulative radiation exposure was significantly lower in both ultrasonography groups (P<0.001) (Smith-Bindman R et al., PMID: 25229916). A systematic review tempers the enthusiasm: pooled point-of-care ultrasound sensitivity for nephrolithiasis was only 70.2% and specificity 75.4%, though moderate-or-greater hydronephrosis was 94.4% specific (PMID: 29427476). PROPOSED SPLIT: ultrasound-first is as safe on patient outcomes and kinder on radiation, but it is the weaker test stone-by-stone, and many ultrasound-first patients still end up scanned.

cards.headline: Smith-Bindman 2014: 30-day high-risk diagnoses 0.4% on all three strategies; serious adverse events 12.4% / 10.8% / 11.2% — radiation significantly lower with ultrasound first
cards.summary: Smith-Bindman 2014: 30-day high-risk diagnoses 0.4% on all three strategies; serious adverse events 12.4% / 10.8% / 11.2% — radiation significantly lower with ultrasound first
cards.people: 2,759 patients aged 18–76 presenting to emergency departments with suspected nephrolithiasis, randomised to initial point-of-care ultrasonography by an emergency physician (908), radiology ultrasonography (893), or abdominal CT (958); subsequent imaging and management were at the treating physician's discretion.
cards.result: High-risk diagnoses with complications within 30 days occurred in 0.4% overall and did not vary by imaging method. Mean 6-month cumulative radiation exposure was significantly lower in the ultrasonography groups than the CT group (P<0.001). Serious adverse events: 12.4% (point-of-care ultrasound), 10.8% (radiology ultrasound), 11.2% (CT) (P=0.50); study-related adverse events 0.4% and similar across groups. Average pain score at 7 days was 2.0 in each group (P=0.84); return visits, hospitalisations, and diagnostic accuracy did not differ significantly.
cards.watchOut: A strategy trial, not a test-accuracy trial: clinicians could and did order CT after ultrasound, so the result endorses ultrasound as the first step of a pathway, not ultrasound instead of CT for every patient; patients with a clear alternative emergency diagnosis were not the study population.
cards.source: Smith-Bindman et al. Ultrasonography versus computed tomography for suspected nephrolithiasis. The New England journal of medicine. 2014. PMID: 25229916. cards.headline: Wong 2018: point-of-care ultrasound for stones is only modestly accurate — sensitivity 70.2%, specificity 75.4%; moderate hydronephrosis is the specific sign (94.4%)
cards.summary: Wong 2018: point-of-care ultrasound for stones is only modestly accurate — sensitivity 70.2%, specificity 75.4%; moderate hydronephrosis is the specific sign (94.4%)
cards.people: Five high-quality studies (1,773 emergency-department patients with renal colic) in the diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis, from nine included articles; any hydronephrosis counted as a positive point-of-care ultrasound, against CT evidence of stone or hydronephrosis, direct stone visualisation, or surgical findings.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 70.2% (95% CI 67.1–73.2%) and specificity 75.4% (72.5–78.2%), with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 2.85 and 0.39. Two studies found moderate-or-greater hydronephrosis had a specificity of 94.4% (92.7–95.8%). Positive findings were also associated with larger stones (>5 mm) in the prognostic studies.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy this modest means a negative point-of-care ultrasound cannot exclude a stone; the review's reference standards varied, and accuracy figures come from a different (smaller, selected) evidence base than the randomised strategy trial.
cards.source: Wong et al. The Accuracy and Prognostic Value of Point-of-care Ultrasound for Nephrolithiasis in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. 2018. PMID: 29427476. cards.headline: Synthesis: start with ultrasound for outcomes and radiation — expect CT to finish a fair share of the work
cards.summary: Synthesis: start with ultrasound for outcomes and radiation — expect CT to finish a fair share of the work
cards.people: One pragmatic randomised strategy trial (2,759 patients) and one diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis (5 studies, 1,773 patients).
cards.result: Outcomes: high-risk diagnoses with complications 0.4% on every strategy; serious adverse events 10.8–12.4% with no significant difference; radiation significantly lower with ultrasound-first. Accuracy: sensitivity 70.2%, specificity 75.4%, rising to 94.4% specificity for moderate-or-greater hydronephrosis. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C because the outcome claim rests on a single trial.
cards.watchOut: The radiation saving shrinks wherever ultrasound-first routinely converts to CT anyway; obese patients and atypical presentations were the hardest for ultrasound in the underlying studies.
cards.source: Synthesis of Smith-Bindman R et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2014 (PMID: 25229916); Wong C et al. Academic emergency medicine. 2018 (PMID: 29427476).

shelves.title: FAST in stable children with blunt torso trauma: a 975-child randomised trial found no gain — CT use 52.4% versus 54.6%, stays and charges the same, and pooled sensitivity in children is only 0.63
shelves.question: In children with blunt abdominal trauma, does the FAST examination improve outcomes — time to surgery, CT use, length of stay, and mortality — compared with usual care without FAST?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Injuries/diagnostic imaging/economics/etiology/surgery · Adolescent · California · Child · Child, Preschool · Emergency Service, Hospital/economics · False Negative Reactions · Female · Health Resources/economics/statistics & numerical data · Hospital Charges · Humans · Laparotomy · Length of Stay/economics/statistics & numerical data · Male · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Tomography, X-Ray Computed/economics/statistics & numerical data · Trauma Centers/economics · Treatment Outcome · Ultrasonography/economics/statistics & numerical data · Wounds, Nonpenetrating/diagnostic imaging
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the population where it was actually tested. Among 925 randomised haemodynamically stable children with blunt torso trauma, adding a FAST examination to standard evaluation changed nothing measured: abdominal CT in 52.4% versus 54.6% (difference −2.2%, 95% CI −8.7% to 4.2%), emergency-department stay 6.03 versus 6.07 hours, median hospital charges $46,415 versus $47,759, and one missed intra-abdominal injury in the FAST group versus none without (difference 0.2%, −0.6% to 1.2%) (Holmes JF et al., PMID: 28609532). The accuracy literature explains why expectations should stay modest: in the Cochrane review, pooled sensitivity of point-of-care sonography in children was 0.63 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.77) against 0.78 in adults, at specificities of 0.91 and 0.97 (PMID: 30548249). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): routine FAST in stable injured children did not improve care, resource use, or outcomes in the only randomised trial.

cards.headline: Holmes 2017: CT 52.4% with FAST versus 54.6% without; stay 6.03 versus 6.07 hours; one missed injury with FAST, none without
cards.summary: Holmes 2017: CT 52.4% with FAST versus 54.6% without; stay 6.03 versus 6.07 hours; one missed injury with FAST, none without
cards.people: 925 haemodynamically stable children and adolescents younger than 18 years (mean age 9.7 years; 62% male) treated for blunt torso trauma at a single US level I trauma centre, randomised to standard trauma evaluation with FAST by the treating emergency physician or standard evaluation alone (April 2012–May 2015). Intra-abdominal injuries were diagnosed in 50 patients (5.4%) and 9 (0.97%) underwent laparotomy.
cards.result: Abdominal CT: 241/460 (52.4%) with FAST versus 254/465 (54.6%) without (difference −2.2%, 95% CI −8.7% to 4.2%). Missed intra-abdominal injury: one case in the FAST group, none in the control group (difference 0.2%, −0.6% to 1.2%). Mean emergency-department stay 6.03 versus 6.07 hours (difference −0.04 hours, −0.47 to 0.40). Median hospital charges $46,415 versus $47,759 (difference −$1,180, −$6,651 to $4,291).
cards.watchOut: One centre, stable children only, and injury prevalence of just 5.4% — the trial cannot speak to unstable children, where FAST is used to triage to theatre rather than to trim CT use; with only nine laparotomies, surgical-timing outcomes were far too rare to judge.
cards.source: Holmes et al. Effect of Abdominal Ultrasound on Clinical Care, Outcomes, and Resource Use Among Children With Blunt Torso Trauma: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28609532. Registry ID: NCT01540318. cards.headline: Stengel 2018 (Cochrane): pooled sensitivity in children 0.63 versus 0.78 in adults — a negative FAST misses more than a third of injuries in children
cards.summary: Stengel 2018 (Cochrane): pooled sensitivity in children 0.63 versus 0.78 in adults — a negative FAST misses more than a third of injuries in children
cards.people: 34 studies with 8,635 participants with blunt thoracoabdominal trauma assessed with point-of-care sonography (including FAST) against CT, surgery, autopsy, or combined reference standards.
cards.result: Overall summary sensitivity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.65 to 0.81) and specificity 0.96 (0.94 to 0.98), with positive and negative likelihood ratios of 18.5 and 0.27. In children, pooled sensitivity was 0.63 (0.46 to 0.77) and specificity 0.91 (0.81 to 0.96), compared with sensitivity 0.78 (0.69 to 0.84) and specificity 0.97 (0.96 to 0.99) in adult or mixed populations.
cards.watchOut: Substantial heterogeneity across studies, and accuracy depended heavily on population and body region; these are test-accuracy data, mostly in broader trauma populations, not evidence that performing FAST changes management or outcomes.
cards.source: Stengel et al. Point-of-care ultrasonography for diagnosing thoracoabdominal injuries in patients with blunt trauma. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30548249. shelves.title: Fomepizole for toxic-alcohol poisoning: acidosis resolved and no survivor lost vision in the two prospective series — 19 ethylene-glycol and 11 methanol patients, and never a comparison group
shelves.question: In patients with toxic alcohol (methanol or ethylene glycol) poisoning, does fomepizole prevent visual loss, acidosis complications, and death, and can it avert dialysis in early presenters?
shelves.mesh: Acidosis/drug therapy/etiology · Adolescent · Adult · Alcohol Dehydrogenase/antagonists & inhibitors · Antidotes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Enzyme Inhibitors/therapeutic use · Female · Fomepizole · Formates/blood · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Methanol/blood/poisoning · Middle Aged · Poisoning/drug therapy · Prospective Studies · Pyrazoles/adverse effects/blood/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the pharmacology is proven in patients; the outcomes are not, because nobody has ever run the comparison. In the prospective ethylene-glycol series, 19 patients received intravenous fomepizole: acid–base status normalised within hours, glycolate and oxalate fell uniformly, one patient with extreme acidosis died, and none of the 10 patients with normal creatinine at enrolment developed renal injury — every case of renal deterioration occurred in patients who arrived with high creatinine and markedly elevated glycolate (Brent J et al., PMID: 10080845). In the methanol series of 11 patients, formic acid fell and metabolic abnormalities resolved in all, nine survived (the two deaths had anoxic brain injury present at enrolment), and none of the seven patients with initial visual abnormalities had detectable visual deficits at the end (PMID: 11172179). Whether fomepizole averts dialysis in early presenters is asserted from mechanism and these series, not tested — dialysis decisions in both studies followed preset criteria alongside the antidote. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): consistent, mechanism-concordant case-series results in 30 patients total, with no comparator arm anywhere in the literature.

cards.headline: Brent 1999 (ethylene glycol): acidosis normalised within hours in 19 patients; renal injury only in those who arrived with high creatinine and glycolate
cards.summary: Brent 1999 (ethylene glycol): acidosis normalised within hours in 19 patients; renal injury only in those who arrived with high creatinine and glycolate
cards.type: Prospective case series (Brent 1999, Methylpyrazole for Toxic Alcohols Study Group)
cards.people: 19 patients with ethylene glycol poisoning (plasma ethylene glycol ≥20 mg/dL) given intravenous fomepizole, continued until plasma ethylene glycol fell below 20 mg/dL; patients meeting specific criteria also underwent haemodialysis. Fifteen patients had acidosis at enrolment (mean serum bicarbonate 12.9 mmol/L).
cards.result: Acid–base status tended to normalise within hours of starting fomepizole; plasma glycolate and urinary oxalate fell uniformly. One patient with extreme acidosis died. Renal function decreased in nine patients — all nine had high serum creatinine and plasma glycolate ≥97.7 mg/dL at enrolment; none of the 10 patients with normal creatinine at enrolment (glycolate ≤76.8 mg/dL) had renal injury during treatment. Few adverse effects were attributable to fomepizole.
cards.watchOut: No comparison group: patients also received dialysis by preset criteria, so the series cannot separate fomepizole's effect from dialysis or from early presentation itself — the renal split by enrolment glycolate is exactly the confounding a control arm would have resolved.
cards.source: Brent et al. Fomepizole for the treatment of ethylene glycol poisoning. Methylpyrazole for Toxic Alcohols Study Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1999. PMID: 10080845. cards.headline: Brent 2001 (methanol): formic acid fell in all 11 patients, nine survived, and no survivor had detectable visual deficits
cards.summary: Brent 2001 (methanol): formic acid fell in all 11 patients, nine survived, and no survivor had detectable visual deficits
cards.type: Prospective case series (Brent 2001, Methylpyrazole for Toxic Alcohols Study Group)
cards.people: 11 consecutive patients with methanol poisoning at participating centres given intravenous fomepizole, with serial measurements of plasma formic acid and fomepizole; formic acid was detectable in eight patients and correlated closely with initial arterial pH (r=0.92, P<0.001).
cards.result: In response to fomepizole, plasma formic acid concentrations fell and metabolic abnormalities resolved in all patients. Nine patients survived; the two who died had anoxic brain injury present at enrolment. Seven patients initially had visual abnormalities, but at the end of the study no surviving patient had any detectable visual deficits related to methanol poisoning. Methanol elimination half-life during treatment was 54 hours. Fomepizole had few adverse effects.
cards.watchOut: Eleven patients, no comparator, and the two deaths were pre-determined by injury present before treatment — the series shows fomepizole blocks formate production in humans, not that it outperforms ethanol or dialysis on vision or survival.
cards.source: Brent et al. Fomepizole for the treatment of methanol poisoning. The New England journal of medicine. 2001. PMID: 11172179. cards.headline: Synthesis: the antidote does its biochemical job in every patient studied — and the clinical questions remain formally untested
cards.summary: Synthesis: the antidote does its biochemical job in every patient studied — and the clinical questions remain formally untested
cards.people: Two prospective multicentre case series totalling 30 patients (19 ethylene glycol, 11 methanol), conducted by the Methylpyrazole for Toxic Alcohols Study Group.
cards.result: Acidosis resolved in all methanol patients and tended to normalise within hours in ethylene-glycol patients; toxic metabolite levels (formate, glycolate, oxalate) fell uniformly; deaths were 1/19 and 2/11, each with catastrophic injury present at enrolment; no survivor had residual visual deficits. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: uncontrolled series only.
cards.watchOut: Withholding an alcohol-dehydrogenase blocker for a randomised trial is widely considered unethical, so this evidence ceiling is probably permanent; the open practical question — who still needs dialysis when fomepizole is given early — is not answered by either series.
cards.source: Synthesis of Brent J et al. The New England journal of medicine. 1999 (PMID: 10080845); Brent J et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2001 (PMID: 11172179).

shelves.title: Lipid emulsion for local anaesthetic toxicity: 81 of 83 reported human cases survived — but the only controlled human study was in volunteers with subclinical toxicity, and it showed no difference
shelves.question: In local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, does intravenous lipid emulsion improve resuscitation success compared with standard advanced life support alone?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Local/adverse effects/toxicity · Fat Emulsions, Intravenous/therapeutic use · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a treatment carried by case reports, graded 'very low quality' by the reviewers who collected them. The collaborative systematic review found 76 human studies: one randomised crossover trial in 16 healthy volunteers with subclinical toxicity, which showed no difference between lipid emulsion and saline, and 73 case reports plus a case series covering 83 patients with real toxicity — 45 (54%) with CNS features, 49 (59%) with seizures, 39 (47%) with cardiovascular features, and 18 (22%) in cardiac arrest — of whom 81 (98%) survived and 63 (76%) had no reported sequelae (Hoegberg LC et al., PMID: 26853119). The companion evidence-based recommendations endorse lipid emulsion for bupivacaine cardiac arrest and, if other therapies fail, for life-threatening toxicity from other local anaesthetics — every recommendation explicitly based on very low quality evidence (PMID: 27608281). Publication bias hangs over the 98% survival figure: failed rescues are far less likely to be written up. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): plausible, widely endorsed, and unproven against standard resuscitation in any controlled human study.

cards.headline: Hoegberg 2016: 83 real-toxicity patients in case reports, 81 (98%) survived — and the single controlled human trial (16 volunteers) showed no difference from saline
cards.summary: Hoegberg 2016: 83 real-toxicity patients in case reports, 81 (98%) survived — and the single controlled human trial (16 volunteers) showed no difference from saline
cards.people: 113 studies and reports of intravenous lipid emulsion for local anaesthetic toxicity published to December 2014: 76 human (one randomised crossover trial in 16 healthy volunteers with subclinical toxicity, one case series, and 73 case reports covering 83 patients) and 38 animal studies.
cards.result: In the 83 case-report patients, presentations included CNS depression or agitation (45, 54%), seizures (49, 59%), hypotension, ECG changes or arrhythmias (39, 47%), cardiac arrest (18, 22%), and CPR or intubation (35, 42%). Eighty-one (98%) survived, including 63 (76%) with no reported sequelae, though sequelae reporting was absent in 15 (18%). The one controlled human study — the volunteer crossover trial — did not show a difference between lipid emulsion and saline in subclinical toxicity. The reviewers concluded the evidence was very low quality and that there is no convincing evidence lipid emulsion beats vasopressors or should be first-line in severe toxicity.
cards.watchOut: Case reports are a publication-biased denominator: dramatic successes get published, failures mostly do not, so 98% survival cannot be read as a treatment effect; animal controlled experiments were themselves split (eight positive, five no benefit, of 14).
cards.source: Hoegberg et al. Systematic review of the effect of intravenous lipid emulsion therapy for local anesthetic toxicity. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2016. PMID: 26853119. cards.headline: Gosselin 2016: expert recommendations endorse lipid emulsion for bupivacaine arrest and as rescue therapy — all on very low quality evidence
cards.summary: Gosselin 2016: expert recommendations endorse lipid emulsion for bupivacaine arrest and as rescue therapy — all on very low quality evidence
cards.people: A collaborative international workgroup appraisal of the lipid-emulsion literature across 22 toxins or toxin categories and three clinical situations, using a two-round modified Delphi process.
cards.result: For cardiac arrest, the workgroup recommended lipid emulsion with bupivacaine toxicity and was neutral for all other toxins. For life-threatening toxicity, it suggested lipid emulsion in bupivacaine toxicity if other therapies fail, and suggested it for toxicity from other local anaesthetics if other therapies fail; as first-line therapy it suggested against lipid emulsion for several non-local-anaesthetic toxins and was neutral for others. All recommendations were based on very low quality of evidence.
cards.watchOut: Consensus recommendations built on case reports formalise practice without adding evidence; the panel was neutral on dosing and infusion duration for non-local-anaesthetic poisoning because the data do not exist.
cards.source: Gosselin et al. Evidence-based recommendations on the use of intravenous lipid emulsion therapy in poisoning. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2016. PMID: 27608281. cards.headline: Synthesis: standard practice on a case-report foundation — survival figures describe reporting, not efficacy
cards.summary: Synthesis: standard practice on a case-report foundation — survival figures describe reporting, not efficacy
cards.people: One systematic review of 113 reports (83 human toxicity cases) and the same workgroup's Delphi recommendations.
cards.result: Human data: 81/83 (98%) case-report survival; one 16-volunteer controlled trial with no difference from saline; recommendations support use in bupivacaine arrest and as rescue in other local-anaesthetic toxicity, all graded very low quality. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: no controlled human efficacy data.
cards.watchOut: Nothing here argues against giving lipid emulsion in a LAST arrest — the shelf grades the evidence, not the bedside decision; it does argue against quoting the 98% figure as if it were a trial result.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hoegberg LC et al. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2016 (PMID: 26853119); Gosselin S et al. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2016 (PMID: 27608281).

shelves.title: Digoxin antibody fragments: in life-threatening intoxication, 80% of 150 patients had complete resolution in an uncontrolled series — in chronic poisoning, the only comparative study found Fab no better than observation
shelves.question: In patients with life-threatening digoxin poisoning, does early treatment with digoxin-specific antibody fragments improve survival and arrhythmia resolution compared with supportive care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Arrhythmia Agents/administration & dosage/poisoning · Chronic Disease · Digoxin/administration & dosage/poisoning · Female · Heart Rate/drug effects · Humans · Immunoglobulin Fab Fragments/administration & dosage · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Potassium/metabolism · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by poisoning type, because the two halves of the evidence answer different questions. In life-threatening digitalis intoxication, the classic multicentre series treated 150 patients with digoxin-specific Fab: of 148 evaluable patients, 119 (80%) had resolution of all signs and symptoms, 14 (10%) improved, and 15 (10%) showed no response, with a median time to initial response of 19 minutes; 54% of patients who had suffered cardiac arrest survived to hospital discharge — but there was no comparison group (Antman EM et al., PMID: 2188752). In chronic digoxin poisoning, the prospective ATOM-4 comparison of 78 patients given initial Fab versus 50 managed supportively found mortality of 12% versus 14% (risk difference −2.5%, 95% CI −14% to 9%), identical median stays of six days, and no difference in heart-rate or potassium change at 4 hours (PMID: 30585517). ATOM-4 excluded patients presenting with ventricular arrhythmias, so the life-threatening question itself has still never had a comparative study. PROPOSED SPLIT: dramatic uncontrolled responses in acute life-threatening poisoning; no measurable benefit over observation in chronic poisoning.

cards.headline: Antman 1990: 119 of 148 evaluable patients (80%) had complete resolution after Fab; median time to first response 19 minutes; 54% of arrest patients survived
cards.summary: Antman 1990: 119 of 148 evaluable patients (80%) had complete resolution after Fab; median time to first response 19 minutes; 54% of arrest patients survived
cards.people: 150 patients with potentially life-threatening digitalis toxicity treated with sheep digoxin-specific Fab fragments dosed to the estimated body load: 50% were on long-term digitalis therapy, 10% had accidental large overdoses, and 39% had suicidal overdoses; ages ranged from several hours after birth to 94 years.
cards.result: Of 148 evaluable patients, 119 (80%) had resolution of all signs and symptoms of digitalis toxicity, 14 (10%) improved, and 15 (10%) showed no response. After the Fab infusion, the median time to initial response was 19 minutes, and 75% of patients had some response by 60 minutes. Fourteen patients had adverse events possibly or probably caused by Fab, most commonly rapid hypokalaemia and exacerbation of congestive heart failure; no allergic reactions were identified. Of patients whose toxicity presented as cardiac arrest, 54% survived hospitalisation.
cards.watchOut: No control group and a 1990 treatment era: how many of these patients supportive care alone would have saved is unknowable from this design, and dosing was generous by modern standards (full estimated body load).
cards.source: Antman et al. Treatment of 150 cases of life-threatening digitalis intoxication with digoxin-specific Fab antibody fragments. Final report of a multicenter study. Circulation. 1990. PMID: 2188752. cards.headline: Chan 2019 (ATOM-4): in chronic poisoning, Fab versus observation — deaths 12% versus 14%, stay six days in both, heart rate and potassium changes identical
cards.summary: Chan 2019 (ATOM-4): in chronic poisoning, Fab versus observation — deaths 12% versus 14%, stay six days in both, heart rate and potassium changes identical
cards.people: 128 prospectively recruited patients with elevated digoxin concentrations and signs or symptoms attributed to digoxin (September 2013–January 2018): 78 initially treated with digoxin-Fab (median dose 1.5 vials) and 50 initially managed supportively. Patients presenting with ventricular arrhythmias before assessment were excluded. Median digoxin concentrations were 4.4 versus 4.2 nmol/L and potassium 5.4 versus 5.1 mmol/L.
cards.result: Deaths: 9 (12%) with Fab versus 7 (14%) with supportive care (risk difference −2.5%, 95% CI −14% to 9%; P=0.68). Median length of stay was six days in both groups. Mean potassium change (−0.5 vs −0.4 mmol/L; P=0.70) and heart-rate change within 4 hours (8 vs 7 bpm; P=0.74) did not differ.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised — clinicians chose who received Fab, and the Fab group arrived sicker (median heart rate 46 vs 52 bpm; systolic pressure 110 vs 125 mmHg) — and, crucially, this is chronic poisoning in comorbid patients, not the acute life-threatening presentations of the Antman series; it cannot refute Fab there.
cards.source: Chan et al. Clinical outcomes from early use of digoxin-specific antibodies versus observation in chronic digoxin poisoning (ATOM-4). Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2019. PMID: 30585517. cards.headline: Synthesis: the sicker the poisoning, the stronger the anecdote and the weaker the design — the comparative null belongs to chronic poisoning only
cards.summary: Synthesis: the sicker the poisoning, the stronger the anecdote and the weaker the design — the comparative null belongs to chronic poisoning only
cards.people: One uncontrolled multicentre series in life-threatening intoxication (150 patients, 1990) and one prospective observational comparison in chronic poisoning (128 patients, 2013–2018).
cards.result: Life-threatening: 80% complete resolution, median response 19 minutes, no comparator. Chronic: mortality 12% versus 14% (risk difference −2.5%, −14% to 9%), identical stays and physiological changes. PROPOSED SPLIT, Tier C: observational evidence throughout, with the acute question untested comparatively.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: no study has compared Fab with supportive care in acute life-threatening digoxin poisoning — ATOM-4's exclusion of ventricular arrhythmias keeps the two evidence halves from meeting.
cards.source: Synthesis of Antman EM et al. Circulation. 1990 (PMID: 2188752); Chan BS et al. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2019 (PMID: 30585517).

shelves.title: Hydroxocobalamin for smoke-inhalation cyanide poisoning: 72% of a prospective treated series survived — and the one comparative study found mortality identical (29% versus 28%)
shelves.question: In suspected cyanide poisoning from smoke inhalation, does hydroxocobalamin improve survival and neurological outcome compared with other antidotes or supportive care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Antidotes/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Emergency Medical Services · Female · Fires · Humans · Hydrogen Cyanide/blood/poisoning · Hydroxocobalamin/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Smoke Inhalation Injury/blood/drug therapy/mortality · Survival Rate · Vitamin B Complex/adverse effects/therapeutic use
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — an antidote whose reputation rests on a case series, with the only comparative data showing no survival difference. In the prospective Paris series, 69 adult smoke-inhalation victims with suspected cyanide poisoning received hydroxocobalamin 5 g (up to 15 g) at the fire scene or in intensive care; 50 (72%) survived, and among the 42 patients with cyanide poisoning confirmed afterwards, 28 (67%) survived; adverse events were mostly chromaturia and skin discolouration, with no serious event attributed to the drug (Borron SW et al., PMID: 17481777). In a burn-centre comparison with historical controls, mortality was 29% with hydroxocobalamin versus 28% without (P=0.90), though the treated group had less pneumonia (23% vs 49%), fewer ventilator days (4 vs 7), and shorter ICU stays (6 vs 10 days) — differences wide open to era effects, since controls were treated in 2002–2008 and the treated group in 2008–2014 (PMID: 27554631). Neurological outcome, the outcome families care about most, was not comparatively measured in either study. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): safe and mechanistically direct, but a survival or neurological benefit over supportive care has never been shown.

cards.headline: Borron 2007: 50 of 69 treated patients (72%) survived; among 42 with confirmed cyanide poisoning, 28 (67%) survived; no serious adverse event attributed
cards.summary: Borron 2007: 50 of 69 treated patients (72%) survived; among 42 with confirmed cyanide poisoning, 28 (67%) survived; no serious adverse event attributed
cards.people: 69 adult smoke-inhalation victims (mean age 49.6 years; 39 comatose) with suspected cyanide poisoning — soot in the face, mouth or nose or expectorations, plus neurological impairment — given intravenous hydroxocobalamin 5 g (maximum 15 g) at the fire scene or in intensive care, 1987–1994; out-of-hospital deaths were excluded and blood cyanide was sampled before treatment (toxicity threshold ≥39 micromol/L).
cards.result: Fifty of 69 patients (72%) admitted to intensive care survived after hydroxocobalamin; in the subgroup with cyanide poisoning confirmed afterwards (n=42), 67% (28/42) survived. The most common adverse events were chromaturia (n=6), pink or red skin discolouration (n=4), hypertension (n=3), erythema (n=2), and increased blood pressure (n=2); no serious adverse events were attributed to hydroxocobalamin.
cards.watchOut: No comparison group, and excluding out-of-hospital deaths builds survivorship into the denominator; 27 of the 69 treated patients never had confirmed cyanide poisoning, so the series mixes antidote effect with the natural history of smoke inhalation.
cards.source: Borron et al. Prospective study of hydroxocobalamin for acute cyanide poisoning in smoke inhalation. Annals of emergency medicine. 2007. PMID: 17481777. cards.headline: Nguyen 2017: mortality 29% with hydroxocobalamin versus 28% in historical controls (P=0.90) — pneumonia and ventilator days lower, in a different treatment era
cards.summary: Nguyen 2017: mortality 29% with hydroxocobalamin versus 28% in historical controls (P=0.90) — pneumonia and ventilator days lower, in a different treatment era
cards.people: 273 adults with suspected smoke-inhalation injury at a burn centre: 138 given hydroxocobalamin (2008–2014) and 135 historical controls who did not receive it (2002–2008); patients under 18, those given an alternate antidote, and those without suspected smoke inhalation were excluded.
cards.result: Mortality was similar: 29% with hydroxocobalamin versus 28% in controls (P=0.90). The hydroxocobalamin group had a lower pneumonia rate (23% vs 49%, P<0.01), fewer ventilator days (4 vs 7 days, P<0.01), more ventilator-free days (20 vs 11, P=0.01), shorter ICU stay (6 vs 10 days, P=0.03), and a trend to shorter hospital stay (7 vs 11 days, P=0.06).
cards.watchOut: Historical controls from an earlier six-year era: every secondary-outcome advantage is confounded by secular improvements in burn and ventilator care, and the primary outcome — mortality — was flat; the study cannot separate the antidote from its decade.
cards.source: Nguyen et al. Utility and outcomes of hydroxocobalamin use in smoke inhalation patients. Burns : journal of the International Society for Burn Injuries. 2017. PMID: 27554631. cards.headline: Synthesis: tolerability is documented, survival benefit is not — the comparative mortality line reads 29% versus 28%
cards.summary: Synthesis: tolerability is documented, survival benefit is not — the comparative mortality line reads 29% versus 28%
cards.people: One prospective treated case series (69 patients) and one retrospective historical-control comparison (273 patients), both in smoke-inhalation victims with suspected cyanide poisoning.
cards.result: Series survival: 72% overall, 67% in confirmed poisoning. Comparative mortality: 29% versus 28% (P=0.90). Secondary outcomes favoured the treated group only against historical controls. Neurological outcome: not comparatively reported in either study. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: observational evidence only, with a null comparative mortality result.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: no randomised or contemporaneously controlled study of hydroxocobalamin in smoke inhalation exists; smoke-inhalation deaths are driven heavily by burns and carbon monoxide, which no cyanide antidote can affect.
cards.source: Synthesis of Borron SW et al. Annals of emergency medicine. 2007 (PMID: 17481777); Nguyen L et al. Burns. 2017 (PMID: 27554631).

shelves.title: High-dose insulin for calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker shock: success rates of 80–100% in published case series — and not one comparative human study behind them
shelves.question: In calcium-channel-blocker or beta-blocker poisoning with shock, does high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy improve haemodynamics and survival compared with conventional vasopressor therapy?
shelves.mesh: Animals · Calcium Channel Blockers/blood/poisoning · Disease Models, Animal · Dose-Response Relationship, Drug · Drug Overdose/mortality/therapy · Guidelines as Topic · Hospitalization · Humans · Insulin/therapeutic use · Length of Stay · Observational Studies as Topic · Treatment Outcome · Vasoconstrictor Agents/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — a mainstay therapy whose entire human evidence base is case reports, case series, and one observational study. The systematic review of treatments for calcium-channel-blocker poisoning screened 15,577 citations and analysed 216 studies, of which 117 were case reports; for high-dose insulin (bolus 1 unit/kg, infusion 0.5–2.0 units/kg/h) it found an association with improved haemodynamic parameters and lower mortality at low quality of evidence, with hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia as the costs — and noted that the only observational human study in the whole review examined high-dose insulin and extracorporeal life support (St-Onge M et al., PMID: 25283255). A focused review of high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy in calcium-channel-blocker and beta-blocker overdose reports success rates of 80.4–100% across published case series, with regular insulin typically bolused at 1 unit/kg then infused at 0.5–1 unit/kg/h alongside dextrose (PMID: 30141827). No study has compared the therapy with vasopressors head-to-head, so 'improves survival compared with conventional therapy' remains an unasked experimental question. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): physiologically coherent and consistently reported, formally untested.

cards.headline: St-Onge 2014: of 216 studies of calcium-channel-blocker poisoning treatments, 117 were case reports — high-dose insulin 'associated with' better haemodynamics and lower mortality, low-quality evidence
cards.summary: St-Onge 2014: of 216 studies of calcium-channel-blocker poisoning treatments, 117 were case reports — high-dose insulin 'associated with' better haemodynamics and lower mortality, low-quality evidence
cards.people: 216 selected studies of treatments for calcium channel blocker poisoning (from 15,577 citations to December 2013), including 117 case reports; the only observational study in humans examined high-dose insulin and extracorporeal life support. Risk of bias was high for all interventions.
cards.result: High-dose insulin (bolus of 1 unit/kg followed by an infusion of 0.5–2.0 units/kg/h) was associated with improved haemodynamic parameters and lower mortality, at the risks of hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia — rated low quality of evidence. Calcium, dopamine, and norepinephrine also improved haemodynamic parameters and survival without documented severe side effects, at very low quality of evidence. No randomised or controlled comparative human study of any treatment was found.
cards.watchOut: 'Associated with' here summarises uncontrolled reports: patients who receive high-dose insulin also receive vasopressors, calcium, and intensive care, and publication bias favours survivors; the review's own bias ratings were high across every intervention.
cards.source: St-Onge et al. Treatment for calcium channel blocker poisoning: a systematic review. Clinical toxicology (Philadelphia, Pa.). 2014. PMID: 25283255. cards.headline: Krenz 2018: published case-series success rates of 80.4–100% for high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy, with a promising safety profile under close monitoring
cards.summary: Krenz 2018: published case-series success rates of 80.4–100% for high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy, with a promising safety profile under close monitoring
cards.people: Published literature 1997–2018 on hyperinsulinaemic–euglycaemic therapy for calcium channel blocker and beta-blocker overdose, limited — in the authors' words — to case reports, case series, retrospective chart reviews, and small prospective studies.
cards.result: The success rate observed in published case series ranged from 80.4% to 100%. Regular insulin was most commonly dosed as an initial bolus of 1 unit/kg followed by an infusion of 0.5–1 unit/kg/hour, with euglycaemia maintained using dextrose-containing intravenous fluids. The therapy exhibited a promising safety profile provided close monitoring is conducted; the authors call for more research on euglycaemia strategies, monitoring, and consistent efficacy goals.
cards.watchOut: A success-rate range across case series has no denominator of all treated patients and no untreated comparator; 'success' was defined differently across the underlying reports.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the therapy is routine, the evidence is anecdote-grade — both reviews say so in nearly the same words
cards.summary: Synthesis: the therapy is routine, the evidence is anecdote-grade — both reviews say so in nearly the same words
cards.people: One systematic review of all calcium-channel-blocker poisoning treatments (216 studies) and one focused review of high-dose insulin euglycaemia therapy (literature 1997–2018).
cards.result: Comparative human studies found: none. Case-series success: 80.4–100%. Systematic-review verdict: improved haemodynamics and lower mortality 'associated', low quality of evidence, high risk of bias. Harms named in the record: hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C: no controlled human evidence.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: whether high-dose insulin adds anything to modern vasopressor care — or merely accompanies it — cannot be answered from the existing literature; dosing in practice (0.5–2.0 units/kg/h) spans a fourfold range for the same reason.

shelves.title: Ketofol versus propofol alone for emergency-department sedation: five trials, 1,250 patients — fewer respiratory adverse effects with the mixture, sedation quality a draw
shelves.question: For adult emergency-department procedural sedation, does a ketamine–propofol combination (ketofol) cause fewer adverse events than propofol alone, with equally effective sedation?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a modest safety edge, not a better sedation. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials in adult emergency-department procedural sedation pooled five eligible trials totalling 1,250 patients (615 ketofol, 635 propofol): two of the five studies found better sedation quality with ketofol and three found no significant difference, while the review found a lower incidence of respiratory adverse effects in the ketofol group than with propofol alone (Ghojazadeh M et al., PMID: 31011553). The theoretical logic — lower doses of each agent trimming both drugs' adverse effects — is thus half confirmed: the respiratory side improved, the sedation itself did not clearly. The record reports the respiratory advantage without a pooled effect size, so its size cannot be stated from this record. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): fewer respiratory adverse events across five small trials, with equivalent sedation quality in most.

cards.headline: Ghojazadeh 2019: 1,250 patients across five trials — respiratory adverse effects lower with ketofol; sedation quality better in two trials, indistinguishable in three
cards.summary: Ghojazadeh 2019: 1,250 patients across five trials — respiratory adverse effects lower with ketofol; sedation quality better in two trials, indistinguishable in three
cards.people: Five randomised trials of adults (≥18 years) undergoing emergency-department procedural sedation, totalling 1,250 subjects: 615 treated with ketamine–propofol (ketofol) and 635 with propofol alone; trials published in English to August 2017 were eligible.
cards.result: Two of the five studies showed a better quality of sedation with ketofol; the other three found no significant difference between ketofol and propofol. The review found a lower incidence of respiratory adverse effects in the ketofol group than in the propofol group. The record reports this direction of effect without a pooled numerical effect estimate.
cards.watchOut: Only five trials with differing ketofol ratios, procedures, and adverse-event definitions; the absence of a pooled effect size in the record means the size of the respiratory advantage — the shelf's whole claim — cannot be quantified from this source, and hypotension and recovery outcomes are not summarised numerically.
cards.source: Ghojazadeh et al. Using Ketamine and Propofol for Procedural Sedation of Adults in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Advanced pharmaceutical bulletin. 2019. PMID: 31011553. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: one meta-analysis, one direction — respiratory events down, everything else about equal
cards.summary: Synthesis: one meta-analysis, one direction — respiratory events down, everything else about equal
cards.people: A single systematic review and meta-analysis of five randomised trials (1,250 adults) in emergency-department procedural sedation; no second independent synthesis was carded.
cards.result: Respiratory adverse effects: lower with ketofol (direction reported, no pooled estimate in the record). Sedation quality: better with ketofol in 2 of 5 trials, no significant difference in 3 of 5. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) on the respiratory outcome, Tier C not set: the base is a meta-analysis of randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: the record's missing pooled effect size is the key number a clinician needs; a future synthesis with full quantitative pooling could move this stamp in either direction.
cards.source: Synthesis of Ghojazadeh M et al. Advanced pharmaceutical bulletin. 2019 (PMID: 31011553).

shelves.title: Nitrous oxide for children's painful procedures: 30 trials say it works for needles and lacerations, matches ketamine-based regimens for fractures — nausea 4.4%, vomiting 3.6%, and worse when combined with other sedatives
shelves.question: In children undergoing painful procedures, does nitrous oxide provide effective and safe procedural analgesia and sedation compared with other agents?
shelves.mesh: Child · Adolescent · Humans · Nitrous Oxide/adverse effects · Midazolam · Ketamine · Lacerations · Pain · Anesthetics, Local · Lidocaine, Prilocaine Drug Combination · Oxygen
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — real analgesia for short, mildly-to-moderately painful procedures, with the indication mattering more than the gas. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 30 trials in children and youth found 70% nitrous oxide beat topical anaesthetic cream (EMLA) for intravenous-insertion pain by 16.5 points on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −28.6 to −4.4; P=0.008), nitrous oxide was 'favourable' against subcutaneous lidocaine, oxygen, and oral midazolam for laceration repair, and 'neutral' — no winner — against intravenous ketamine regimens for fracture reduction (Poonai N et al., PMID: 37171705). Common adverse effects were nausea (4.4%), agitation (3.7%), and vomiting (3.6%), and adverse effects were far commoner when nitrous oxide was combined with midazolam (92.3%) or fentanyl (61.2%) than used alone (24.2%). An earlier systematic review put serious adverse events at under 0.5% and minor events at 4–8% for brief procedures (PMID: 23743110). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): effective and acceptably safe as a single agent for brief procedures; not a substitute for deeper sedation in fracture reduction.

cards.headline: Poonai 2023: 70% nitrous oxide beat EMLA cream by 16.5 pain points for IV insertion; 'neutral' against ketamine regimens for fracture reduction
cards.summary: Poonai 2023: 70% nitrous oxide beat EMLA cream by 16.5 pain points for IV insertion; 'neutral' against ketamine regimens for fracture reduction
cards.people: 30 trials of nitrous oxide in participants aged 0–21 years undergoing emergency-department procedures, reporting procedural distress or pain; comparisons varied by indication (topical anaesthetic, lidocaine, oxygen, oral midazolam, ketamine-based regimens, regional anaesthesia).
cards.result: For IV insertion, 70% nitrous oxide was superior to EMLA cream on a 0–100 visual analogue pain scale (difference −16.5; 95% CI −28.6 to −4.4; P=0.008; three trials), and 50% nitrous oxide plus EMLA beat EMLA alone (−1.2; −2.1 to −0.3; P=0.007), while 50% nitrous oxide alone was not superior to EMLA (−0.4; −1.2 to 0.3; P=0.26). For laceration repair, nitrous oxide was favourable versus subcutaneous lidocaine, oxygen, and oral midazolam, and neutral versus IV ketamine (five trials). For fracture reduction it was neutral versus intramuscular meperidine–promethazine, regional anaesthesia, and IV ketamine–midazolam (three trials). Adverse effects: nausea 4.4%, agitation 3.7%, vomiting 3.6%; total adverse effects 24.2% (278/1147) for nitrous oxide alone versus 92.3% (48/52) with added midazolam and 61.2% (123/201) with added fentanyl.
cards.watchOut: Much of the synthesis is indication-by-indication vote classification ('favourable'/'neutral') rather than pooled effects, concentrations varied (50% vs 70%), and the fracture-reduction neutrality cuts both ways — nitrous oxide neither beat nor clearly matched deeper regimens on every outcome.
cards.source: Poonai et al. Inhaled nitrous oxide for painful procedures in children and youth: a systematic review and meta-analysis. CJEM. 2023. PMID: 37171705. cards.headline: Pedersen 2013: serious adverse events under 0.5%, minor events 4–8% — effective for mildly to moderately painful procedures under 15 minutes
cards.summary: Pedersen 2013: serious adverse events under 0.5%, minor events 4–8% — effective for mildly to moderately painful procedures under 15 minutes
cards.people: Published evidence (English, after 1980) on nitrous oxide for brief painful paediatric procedures, compared with commonly used pharmacological and non-pharmacological alternatives in Danish practice.
cards.result: Nitrous oxide was an effective sedative/analgesic for mildly to moderately painful paediatric procedures and could be administered safely, particularly for short procedures (under 15 minutes). Serious and potentially serious adverse events were rare, occurring in less than 0.5% of cases, while minor events typically occurred in 4–8% of patients.
cards.watchOut: A narrative systematic review without meta-analysis, from a single-country practice perspective; its safety percentages pool heterogeneous procedures and concentrations.
cards.source: Pedersen et al. Nitrous oxide provides safe and effective analgesia for minor paediatric procedures--a systematic review. Danish medical journal. 2013. PMID: 23743110. cards.headline: Synthesis: a good single-agent answer for needles and stitches; a holding measure, not a winner, for fractures
cards.summary: Synthesis: a good single-agent answer for needles and stitches; a holding measure, not a winner, for fractures
cards.people: Two systematic reviews: a 30-trial meta-analytic review (2023) and an earlier safety-focused review (2013).
cards.result: Efficacy: IV-insertion pain −16.5 points (70% nitrous oxide vs EMLA); favourable for laceration repair; neutral against ketamine-based regimens for fracture reduction. shelves.title: Intranasal dexmedetomidine versus nitrous oxide for children's procedural sedation: worst pain scores identical (median FLACC 4 in both) in a 148-child non-inferiority trial
shelves.question: In children needing procedural sedation in the emergency department, does intranasal dexmedetomidine achieve adequate sedation as reliably as nitrous oxide or other standard agents?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Dexmedetomidine/administration & dosage · Nitrous Oxide/administration & dosage · Administration, Intranasal · Child · Female · Male · Child, Preschool · Adolescent · Prospective Studies · Hypnotics and Sedatives/administration & dosage · Procedural Sedation/methods · Pain Measurement · Pain Management/methods · Administration, Inhalation · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the one head-to-head trial, the spray matched the gas on pain. In an open-label randomised non-inferiority trial in a paediatric emergency department, 148 previously healthy children aged 3–15 years with an extremity fracture or luxation or a burn were randomised to intranasal dexmedetomidine or inhaled 50% nitrous oxide; the highest pain score during the procedure (FLACC) was a median of 4 in both groups (IQR 3–6 versus 2–6), and the median between-group difference was 0 (95% CI 0 to 1), meeting non-inferiority (Nikula A et al., PMID: 39568028). Acceptance was a touch lower for the spray: 82.5% of children and 91.5% of parents would accept the same method again, versus 88.1% and 94.6% with nitrous oxide. No serious adverse events were reported in either group. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): equivalent procedural pain control in a single trial — a genuine alternative where nitrous oxide is impractical, not an improvement on it.

cards.summary: Nikula 2024: median worst FLACC 4 (IQR 3–6) on intranasal dexmedetomidine versus 4 (IQR 2–6) on nitrous oxide — difference 0 (95% CI 0 to 1), non-inferior
cards.people: 148 previously healthy children aged 3–15 years with an extremity fracture or luxation or a burn requiring procedural sedation and analgesia in a paediatric emergency department, randomised equally to intranasal dexmedetomidine or inhaled 50% nitrous oxide; the trial was prospective and open-label.
cards.result: The primary outcome — highest pain level during the procedure on the FLACC scale — was median 4 (IQR 3–6) with intranasal dexmedetomidine and median 4 (IQR 2–6) with nitrous oxide; the median of the difference was 0 (95% CI 0 to 1), so dexmedetomidine was not inferior to nitrous oxide. The same method would be accepted again by 82.5% of children and 91.5% of parents in the dexmedetomidine group, versus 88.1% and 94.6% in the nitrous oxide group. No serious adverse events were reported.
cards.watchOut: A single open-label trial: children and staff knew which agent was given, FLACC scoring is observer-rated, and the record does not report onset time or procedure duration — the practical trade-offs (a spray that takes time to work versus gas that needs cooperation) are invisible in the primary result.
cards.source: Nikula et al. A randomized clinical trial of intranasal dexmedetomidine versus inhaled nitrous oxide for procedural sedation and analgesia in children. Scandinavian journal of trauma, resuscitation and emergency medicine. 2024. PMID: 39568028. shelves.title: Intravenous magnesium for acute migraine in the emergency department: seven trials, 545 patients — pain better at 60–120 minutes, not earlier, and the 50%-relief results point in three directions at once
shelves.question: In adults with acute migraine in the emergency department, does intravenous magnesium sulfate relieve headache compared with placebo or standard therapy?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Analgesics, Non-Narcotic/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Emergency Service, Hospital · Headache/drug therapy · Humans · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit) — the reviewers themselves declined to draw a firm conclusion, and the shelf follows them. A systematic review of randomised trials of intravenous magnesium sulfate for non-traumatic headache in the emergency department found seven eligible trials with 545 participants (six in migraine): pain intensity was improved with magnesium versus comparators at 60–120 minutes but not at earlier time points; for the endpoint of pain reduction by 50%, three studies variously reported headache improved, unchanged, and worse with magnesium; complete pain relief was improved in one study and in the migraine-with-aura subgroup of another; rescue-analgesia need and 24-hour recurrence each improved in one study and were unchanged in another (Miller AC et al., PMID: 31566727). Heterogeneity prevented any meta-analysis. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit): a late, inconsistent pain signal across small trials — a reasonable adjunct candidate, not a proven abortive.

cards.headline: Miller 2019: pain improved at 60–120 minutes but not before; 50%-relief results were improved, unchanged, and worse across studies
cards.summary: Miller 2019: pain improved at 60–120 minutes but not before; 50%-relief results were improved, unchanged, and worse across studies
cards.people: Seven randomised trials (545 participants) of intravenous magnesium sulfate in adults (≥18 years) with non-traumatic headache treated in emergency or acute-care settings — six trials in migraine and one in benign non-traumatic headache — against placebo, conventional therapy, dopamine antagonists, NSAIDs, corticosteroids, ergot alkaloids, or triptans.
cards.result: Pain intensity was improved with magnesium sulfate versus comparators at 60–120 minutes, but not at earlier time points. For pain reduction by 50%, three studies reported headache improved, unchanged, and less with magnesium respectively. Complete pain relief was improved with magnesium in one study, and in the migraine-with-aura subgroup in another. Need for rescue analgesia was improved in one study and in the aura subgroup of another; 24-hour recurrence was improved in one study and unchanged in a second. The intended meta-analysis was not performed because of clinical heterogeneity, and the authors state no firm conclusion on efficacy can be drawn, while noting potential benefit for pain control beyond one hour, aura duration, and rescue-analgesia need.
cards.watchOut: Seven small trials with different comparators, doses, and endpoints; the aura-subgroup signals come from single studies, and 'improved at 60–120 minutes' may partly reflect the natural history and co-treatments of an emergency-department visit rather than the magnesium.
cards.source: Miller et al. Intravenous Magnesium Sulfate to Treat Acute Headaches in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review. Headache. 2019. PMID: 31566727. cards.headline: Synthesis: the honest summary is the reviewers' own — potential benefit after an hour, nothing firmer
cards.summary: Synthesis: the honest summary is the reviewers' own — potential benefit after an hour, nothing firmer
cards.people: One systematic review of seven randomised trials (545 participants) in emergency-department headache, six of them in migraine.
cards.result: Pain intensity: improved at 60–120 minutes, not earlier. Fifty-percent relief: one study improved, one unchanged, one worse. Complete relief, rescue need, recurrence: single-study positives against single-study nulls. No pooled estimate exists. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (benefit), Tier C not set: the base is randomised trials, but small and mutually inconsistent ones.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: no adequately powered trial of intravenous magnesium against a single standard comparator (such as metoclopramide) with a prespecified early endpoint exists in this record — that trial would settle the question the review could not.

shelves.title: Intravenous valproate for acute migraine: a seven-trial meta-analysis found it worse than the standard drugs it was compared with — less relief (odds ratio 0.51) and nearly four times the odds of needing rescue therapy
shelves.question: In adults with acute migraine in the emergency department, does intravenous valproate relieve headache as effectively as standard therapies such as metoclopramide or ketorolac?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intravenous · Adult · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Migraine Disorders/drug therapy · Treatment Outcome · Valproic Acid/administration & dosage
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — 'harm' here in the comparative sense this library uses: patients given intravenous valproate did worse than patients given the standard alternatives. A meta-analysis of seven double-blind randomised trials involving 682 emergency-department patients with acute migraine found those receiving intravenous valproate had less improvement in headache intensity than those receiving other active treatments (standardised mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.06; P=0.02), a lower rate of headache relief (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; P=0.002), and higher odds of needing rescue therapy (odds ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.96 to 7.20; P<0.0001) (Wang F et al., PMID: 32740903). The exceptions are narrow: valproate was comparable to dexamethasone, and in migraine without aura there was no significant difference in headache-intensity improvement (standardised mean difference −0.00, −0.54 to 0.54). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): as a first-choice abortive it underperforms the comparators studied; the authors leave it a salvage role, particularly floated for migraine with aura and status migrainosus, on thinner data.

cards.headline: Wang 2020: headache relief odds ratio 0.51 and rescue-therapy odds ratio 3.76 against intravenous valproate versus active comparators
cards.summary: Wang 2020: headache relief odds ratio 0.51 and rescue-therapy odds ratio 3.76 against intravenous valproate versus active comparators
cards.people: Seven double-blinded randomised trials involving 682 patients with acute migraine treated in the emergency department, comparing intravenous sodium valproate with other active treatments (including dopamine antagonists, NSAIDs, and dexamethasone across trials).
cards.result: Patients receiving intravenous valproate had less improvement of headache intensity (standardised mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.73 to −0.06; P=0.02) and a lower rate of headache relief (odds ratio 0.51, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.77; P=0.002) than those receiving other active comparators, and higher odds of rescue therapy (odds ratio 3.76, 95% CI 1.96 to 7.20; P<0.0001). Subgroup analysis showed valproate comparable to dexamethasone for headache-intensity improvement and headache recurrence; in migraine without aura, headache-intensity improvement did not differ significantly (standardised mean difference −0.00, 95% CI −0.54 to 0.54; P=1.00).
cards.watchOut: The comparator is a bundle of different active drugs pooled together, so the result says valproate trails the field, not that it trails each drug individually; most trials were small, and the floated niches (migraine with aura, status migrainosus) rest on subgroup reasoning rather than dedicated trials.
cards.source: Wang et al. Intravenous sodium valproate for acute migraine in the emergency department: A meta-analysis. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2020. PMID: 32740903. cards.headline: Synthesis: against placebo the question is open; against the drugs clinicians actually use, valproate loses
cards.summary: Synthesis: against placebo the question is open; against the drugs clinicians actually use, valproate loses
cards.people: One meta-analysis of seven double-blind randomised trials (682 emergency-department patients with acute migraine).
cards.result: Versus active comparators: headache-intensity improvement −0.39 standardised mean difference; relief odds ratio 0.51; rescue-therapy odds ratio 3.76 — all statistically significant against valproate. Versus dexamethasone alone: comparable. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm) in the comparative sense, Tier C because this is a harm-direction claim resting on one meta-analysis of small trials.
cards.watchOut: Inferiority to active treatment is not toxicity: the record's adverse-event data do not show valproate to be dangerous in this setting, and patients who have failed or cannot take standard agents are exactly the population the pooled trials least represent.
cards.source: Synthesis of Wang F et al. Acta neurologica Scandinavica. 2020 (PMID: 32740903).

shelves.title: Corticosteroids for vestibular neuritis: vestibular function recovered better in the one factorial trial (62.4 versus 39.6 percentage points of improvement) — whether patients feel better is, in the guideline synthesis's words, very uncertain
shelves.question: In patients with acute vestibular neuritis, do corticosteroids improve recovery of vestibular function and symptoms compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acyclovir/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Antiviral Agents/therapeutic use · Caloric Tests · Double-Blind Method · Drug Therapy, Combination · Factor Analysis, Statistical · Female · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans · Male · Methylprednisolone/therapeutic use · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Treatment Outcome · Valacyclovir · Valine/analogs & derivatives/therapeutic use · Vestibular Neuronitis/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the caloric test, with the symptom question honestly open. In a randomised double-blind two-by-two factorial trial of 141 patients with acute vestibular neuritis, mean improvement in peripheral vestibular function at 12 months was 62.4 percentage points with methylprednisolone versus 39.6 with placebo (valacyclovir made no difference, P=0.43; the methylprednisolone effect was significant at P<0.001) (Strupp M et al., PMID: 15269315). The emergency-medicine guideline evidence synthesis, an umbrella review of the systematic reviews (12 studies, 660 patients), found corticosteroids associated with higher complete caloric recovery in a meta-analysis of two trials totalling only 50 patients (risk ratio 2.81, 95% CI 1.32 to 6.00; low certainty), while patient-reported vertigo and dizziness-disability estimates were so imprecise that translation into clinical improvement is 'very uncertain' (PMID: 35975654). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): steroids speed the laboratory recovery of the vestibular organ; a patient-felt benefit has never been shown with comparable rigour.

cards.headline: Strupp 2004: methylprednisolone improved vestibular recovery by about 23 percentage points over placebo at 12 months; valacyclovir added nothing
cards.summary: Strupp 2004: methylprednisolone improved vestibular recovery by about 23 percentage points over placebo at 12 months; valacyclovir added nothing
cards.people: 141 patients with acute vestibular neuritis randomised to placebo (38), methylprednisolone (35), valacyclovir (33), or methylprednisolone plus valacyclovir (35); vestibular function was measured by caloric irrigation (vestibular paresis formula) within 3 days of symptom onset and at 12 months.
cards.result: Mean improvement in peripheral vestibular function at 12 months was 39.6±28.1 percentage points with placebo, 62.4±16.9 with methylprednisolone, 36.0±26.7 with valacyclovir, and 59.2±24.1 with the combination. Analysis of variance showed a significant effect of methylprednisolone (P<0.001) but not of valacyclovir (P=0.43), and the combination was not superior to methylprednisolone alone.
cards.watchOut: The endpoint is a laboratory measure (caloric paresis), not how dizzy patients felt or functioned; a single trial of 141 patients from one research group carries the entire randomised claim, and treatment began within 3 days of onset — later presenters are outside the evidence.
cards.source: Strupp et al. Methylprednisolone, valacyclovir, or the combination for vestibular neuritis. The New England journal of medicine. 2004. PMID: 15269315.
