cards.headline: Oliveira J E Silva 2023 (GRACE synthesis): complete caloric recovery risk ratio 2.81 on 50 patients, low certainty — dizziness-handicap difference +5.1 points with a confidence interval from −8.09 to +18.29
cards.summary: Oliveira J E Silva 2023 (GRACE synthesis): complete caloric recovery risk ratio 2.81 on 50 patients, low certainty — dizziness-handicap difference +5.1 points with a confidence interval from −8.09 to +18.29
cards.type: Umbrella evidence synthesis (Oliveira J E Silva 2023)
cards.people: Two higher-quality systematic reviews selected from five, covering 12 individual studies and 660 patients with acute vestibular neuritis treated with corticosteroids versus placebo or usual care; quality assessed with AMSTAR-2 and certainty with GRADE.
cards.result: In a meta-analysis of two randomised trials totalling 50 patients, corticosteroids were associated with higher complete caloric recovery (risk ratio 2.81, 95% CI 1.32 to 6.00; low certainty). For patient-centred outcomes the estimates were imprecise: one study of 30 patients found a dizziness handicap score of 20.9 points in the corticosteroid group versus 15.8 with placebo (mean difference +5.1, 95% CI −8.09 to +18.29; very low certainty). Minor adverse effects were reported at higher rates with corticosteroids, also at very low certainty. The authors conclude there is limited evidence to support corticosteroid use for vestibular neuritis in the emergency department.
cards.watchOut: An umbrella review inherits the weaknesses of its reviews: the headline risk ratio rests on 50 patients, and the dizziness-handicap point estimate, taken at face value, numerically favours placebo — the honest reading is that symptom benefit is unknown, not disproven.
cards.source: Oliveira J E Silva et al. Corticosteroids for patients with vestibular neuritis: An evidence synthesis for guidelines for reasonable and appropriate care in the emergency department. Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. 2023. PMID: 35975654. cards.headline: Synthesis: the organ recovers faster on steroids; whether the person does is the unanswered half of the question
cards.summary: Synthesis: the organ recovers faster on steroids; whether the person does is the unanswered half of the question
cards.people: One randomised factorial trial (141 patients) and one umbrella review of systematic reviews (12 studies, 660 patients).
cards.result: Caloric recovery: +22.8 percentage points of improvement with methylprednisolone over placebo at 12 months; complete-recovery risk ratio 2.81 (1.32 to 6.00) in pooled small trials. Symptoms: dizziness-handicap difference +5.1 (−8.09 to +18.29), very low certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: the benefit claim rests essentially on a single trial and a surrogate endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Vestibular rehabilitation — the other mainstay — is a separate question not covered by these cards; steroids plus rehabilitation together have not been tested in the records carded here.

shelves.title: Steroids and antihistamines in anaphylaxis: the Cochrane review found zero eligible randomised trials — these routine adjuncts rest on no controlled evidence at all
shelves.question: In anaphylaxis, do corticosteroids or antihistamines added to adrenaline improve outcomes or prevent biphasic reactions — or is the evidence for these routine adjuncts absent?
shelves.mesh: Anaphylaxis/drug therapy · Glucocorticoids/therapeutic use · Humans
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference) — read precisely: no difference has ever been demonstrated, because the trials have never been done; that is an absence of evidence, not a proven absence of effect. The Cochrane review of glucocorticoids for anaphylaxis, searching to September 2011, found no randomised or quasi-randomised study that satisfied its inclusion criteria, and concluded it was unable to make any recommendations for or against glucocorticoids in anaphylaxis (Choo KJ et al., PMID: 22513951). A later systematic review found 30 original papers (22 human studies) in which corticosteroids were used in an average of 68% of anaphylaxis treatments (range 48–100%); steroids appeared to reduce length of hospital stay but not emergency-department revisits, there was no consensus on whether they reduce biphasic reactions, and none of the human studies had data capable of comparing outcomes between treatment groups (PMID: 28884986). Adrenaline remains the only treatment in anaphylaxis with a claim on the outcome evidence — such as it is. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference): the adjuncts are unproven, widely given, and not shown harmful in these reviews; the stamp records the missing evidence, not a demonstrated null effect.

cards.summary: Choo 2012 (Cochrane): zero studies met the inclusion criteria — no recommendations for glucocorticoids in anaphylaxis can be made
cards.people: Planned population: people experiencing anaphylaxis, in randomised or quasi-randomised trials comparing glucocorticoids with placebo, adrenaline, antihistamine, or combinations; searches covered CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL to September 2011, plus trial registries and international experts.
cards.result: No studies satisfied the inclusion criteria. The reviewers state plainly that, based on the review, they are unable to make any recommendations for the use of glucocorticoids in the treatment of anaphylaxis — despite guidelines of the era recommending them.
cards.watchOut: An empty review proves the trials do not exist, not that the treatment fails; anaphylaxis is rare, unpredictable, and ethically awkward to randomise, which explains — without excusing — the permanent evidence gap this shelf records.

cards.headline: Liyanage 2017: steroids used in 68% of treatments across 22 human studies, yet no study could compare outcomes between treated and untreated patients
cards.summary: Liyanage 2017: steroids used in 68% of treatments across 22 human studies, yet no study could compare outcomes between treated and untreated patients
cards.people: 30 original research papers on corticosteroids in emergency management of anaphylaxis: 22 human studies and eight animal or laboratory studies.
cards.result: The average rate of corticosteroid use in emergency treatment was 67.99% (range 48% to 100%). Corticosteroids appeared to reduce length of hospital stay but did not reduce revisits to the emergency department. There was no consensus on whether corticosteroids reduce biphasic anaphylactic reactions. None of the human studies had sufficient data to compare the response to treatment in different treatment groups (corticosteroids, epinephrine, antihistamines). The authors conclude there is no compelling evidence to support or oppose corticosteroid use in emergency anaphylaxis treatment, with no evidence of adverse outcomes from their use.
cards.watchOut: The hospital-stay signal comes from observational data where sicker patients both receive steroids and stay longer (or are kept for observation because steroids were given); animal data in the same review showed genomic steroid effects taking 4–24 hours — slower than anaphylaxis itself runs.
cards.source: Liyanage et al. Corticosteroids in management of anaphylaxis; a systematic review of evidence. European annals of allergy and clinical immunology. 2017. PMID: 28884986. cards.headline: Synthesis: two reviews, one finding — the adjunct cupboard is bare of controlled evidence
cards.summary: Synthesis: two reviews, one finding — the adjunct cupboard is bare of controlled evidence
cards.people: One Cochrane review (zero eligible trials) and one systematic review of 30 papers (22 human studies) on corticosteroids as anaphylaxis adjuncts.
cards.result: Randomised evidence for corticosteroids in anaphylaxis: none. Comparative human outcome data: none sufficient. Usage despite this: 48–100% of treatments across studies. Biphasic-reaction prevention: no consensus. PROPOSED MAYBE (weak evidence) (the treatment made no difference), Tier C: an evidence-absence shelf — the stamp means undemonstrated, and the balance says so explicitly.
cards.watchOut: Antihistamines fare no better evidentially — neither review found comparative outcome data for them either; nothing on this shelf should be read as a reason to delay adrenaline, the one intervention every guideline puts first.

shelves.title: Intramuscular beats subcutaneous adrenaline: peak levels at 8 minutes versus 34 in children, and the thigh beats the arm — two small randomised pharmacokinetic studies settled the route
shelves.question: For anaphylaxis, is intramuscular adrenaline absorbed faster and more reliably than subcutaneous adrenaline?
shelves.mesh: Absorption · Adrenergic Agonists/administration & dosage/blood/therapeutic use · Adult · Anaphylaxis/drug therapy · Arm · Cross-Over Studies · Epinephrine/administration & dosage/blood/therapeutic use · Humans · Injections, Intramuscular · Injections, Subcutaneous · Kinetics · Male · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method · Thigh
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — faster and higher peaks by the intramuscular route, in both age groups studied, on pharmacokinetic rather than outcome evidence. In children with a history of anaphylaxis randomised to a single dose, intramuscular adrenaline from an autoinjector reached a mean maximum plasma concentration of 2,136±351 pg/mL at a mean of 8±2 minutes, while subcutaneous injection reached 1,802±214 pg/mL at 34±14 minutes (range 5–120) — and only two of nine subcutaneous children had peaked by 5 minutes, versus six of eight intramuscular (Simons FE et al., PMID: 9449498). In adults, a randomised blinded six-way crossover study found peak plasma concentrations significantly higher after intramuscular injection into the thigh than after intramuscular or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm (P<0.01) (PMID: 11692118). No serious adverse effects occurred in the children's study. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): intramuscular-into-thigh is the reliably faster route — the finding behind every modern autoinjector instruction — proven on blood levels in small studies, not on anaphylaxis outcomes.

cards.headline: Simons 1998: in children, intramuscular peaked at 8±2 minutes versus 34±14 subcutaneous — and two of nine subcutaneous children took up to 120 minutes
cards.summary: Simons 1998: in children, intramuscular peaked at 8±2 minutes versus 34±14 subcutaneous — and two of nine subcutaneous children took up to 120 minutes
cards.people: 17 children with a history of anaphylaxis to food, Hymenoptera venom, or other substances, in a prospective randomised blinded parallel-group study: nine received subcutaneous epinephrine solution 0.01 mL/kg (maximum 0.3 mg) and eight received 0.3 mg intramuscularly from an autoinjector, with plasma concentrations, heart rate, blood pressure, and adverse effects monitored.
cards.result: Subcutaneous: mean maximum plasma epinephrine concentration 1,802±214 pg/mL at a mean time of 34±14 minutes (range 5 to 120); only two of nine children achieved maximum concentrations by 5 minutes. Intramuscular: 2,136±351 pg/mL at 8±2 minutes — significantly faster (P<0.05) — with six of eight children at maximum by 5 minutes. The terminal elimination half-life was 43±15 minutes. No serious adverse effects were noted in any child.
cards.watchOut: Seventeen children, none of them in anaphylaxis at the time — absorption during actual shock, with peripheral vasoconstriction, could differ; the comparison also pairs route with device (autoinjector intramuscular versus syringe subcutaneous), so needle and formulation effects are bundled in.
cards.source: Simons et al. Epinephrine absorption in children with a history of anaphylaxis. The Journal of allergy and clinical immunology. 1998. PMID: 9449498. cards.headline: Simons 2001: in adults, intramuscular thigh injection gave significantly higher peaks than intramuscular or subcutaneous upper-arm injection (P<0.01)
cards.summary: Simons 2001: in adults, intramuscular thigh injection gave significantly higher peaks than intramuscular or subcutaneous upper-arm injection (P<0.01)
cards.people: Young men in a prospective, randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled six-way crossover study comparing intramuscular and subcutaneous epinephrine injection sites and routes, with peak plasma epinephrine concentration as the outcome.
cards.result: Peak plasma epinephrine concentrations were significantly higher (P<0.01) after epinephrine was injected intramuscularly into the thigh than after intramuscular or subcutaneous injection into the upper arm. The authors recommend intramuscular injection into the thigh as the preferred route and site for initial anaphylaxis treatment.
cards.watchOut: The record reports the direction and significance but not the absolute peak values or times for each arm, and the volunteers were healthy young men — lean thighs absorb differently from the thighs of older or heavier patients in real anaphylaxis.

shelves.title: Take-home ondansetron after a gastroenteritis visit: moderate-to-severe illness over the next week in 5.1% versus 12.5% on placebo — but return visits and IV fluids did not fall
shelves.question: In children discharged after an emergency visit for gastroenteritis, does a multidose ondansetron course at home reduce return visits and intravenous rehydration compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Antiemetics/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Double-Blind Method · Emergency Service, Hospital · Gastroenteritis/complications/diagnosis/drug therapy · Ondansetron/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Vomiting/drug therapy/etiology · Severity of Illness Index · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the illness ran milder at home, even though the utilisation outcomes the question names did not move. In a double-blind randomised trial in six paediatric emergency departments, 1,030 children aged 6 months to under 18 years with gastroenteritis-associated vomiting were given six doses of oral ondansetron or placebo to use against ongoing vomiting over 48 hours: moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis over the following 7 days (modified Vesikari score ≥9) occurred in 5.1% (23/452) on ondansetron versus 12.5% (55/441) on placebo — an absolute difference of −7.4 percentage points (95% CI −11.2 to −3.7) and an adjusted odds ratio of 0.50 (0.40 to 0.60) (Freedman SB et al., PMID: 40673584). Vomiting episodes within 48 hours were fewer (adjusted rate ratio 0.76, 0.67 to 0.87), but the presence and duration of vomiting, unscheduled physician visits, and receipt of intravenous fluids did not differ substantially, and adverse events were similar (odds ratio 0.99, 0.61 to 1.61). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a take-home course softens the week's illness — roughly one moderate-to-severe course avoided for every 14 children treated — without demonstrably keeping children out of the clinic or off the drip.

cards.headline: Freedman 2025: moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis 5.1% versus 12.5% (adjusted odds ratio 0.50) — return visits and IV fluids unchanged
cards.summary: Freedman 2025: moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis 5.1% versus 12.5% (adjusted odds ratio 0.50) — return visits and IV fluids unchanged
cards.people: 1,030 children aged 6 months to less than 18 years with acute gastroenteritis-associated vomiting in six paediatric emergency departments, randomised to six caregiver-administered doses of oral ondansetron or placebo for ongoing vomiting during the first 48 hours after enrolment; the primary outcome was moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis (modified Vesikari score ≥9 of 20) during the 7 days after enrolment.
cards.result: Moderate-to-severe gastroenteritis occurred in 5.1% (23/452) with ondansetron versus 12.5% (55/441) with placebo (unadjusted risk difference −7.4 percentage points, 95% CI −11.2 to −3.7; adjusted odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.60). Vomiting episodes within 48 hours were fewer (adjusted rate ratio 0.76, 0.67 to 0.87), but the presence and median duration of vomiting did not differ meaningfully, and the percentages with unscheduled health-care visits and with intravenous fluids after enrolment did not differ substantially. Adverse events did not differ meaningfully (odds ratio 0.99, 0.61 to 1.61).
cards.watchOut: The primary outcome is a composite severity score driven substantially by vomiting and diarrhoea counts reported by caregivers; the harder service outcomes in the shelf's question — return visits and intravenous rehydration — were null, and outcome data were available for 893 of 1,030 randomised children.

shelves.title: Oral prednisone for acute sciatica: function improved modestly at 3 weeks and a year, pain did not improve at all — and adverse events doubled (49.2% versus 23.9%)
shelves.question: In adults with acute radiculopathy (sciatica) from a herniated lumbar disc, does a short course of oral prednisone improve function and pain compared with placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Oral · Adult · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Glucocorticoids/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Humans · Intervertebral Disc Displacement/complications · Lumbar Vertebrae · Male · Middle Aged · Pain Measurement · Prednisone/adverse effects/therapeutic use · Radiculopathy/drug therapy/etiology
shelves.balance: SPLIT — function yes (a little), pain no. In a randomised double-blind trial of 269 adults with radicular pain for 3 months or less, an Oswestry Disability Index score of at least 30, and an MRI-confirmed herniated disc, a tapering 15-day course of prednisone (60/40/20 mg, 600 mg total) produced a 6.4-point greater improvement in disability at 3 weeks than placebo (95% CI 1.9 to 10.9; P=0.006) and 7.4 points at 52 weeks (2.2 to 12.5; P=0.005) — but leg-pain reduction differed by only 0.3 points at 3 weeks (P=0.34) and 0.6 at a year (P=0.15), surgery rates were the same, and one or more adverse events occurred in 49.2% on prednisone versus 23.9% on placebo (P<0.001) (Goldberg H et al., PMID: 25988461). The broader drug review for sciatica found pooled corticosteroid trials showing a short-term mean pain advantage of −12.2 points on a 0–100 scale (−20.9 to −3.4) across two trials, on evidence it graded low quality overall (PMID: 22331277). PROPOSED SPLIT: a real but modest functional gain that patients may or may not notice, bought with a doubled adverse-event rate, and no analgesia in the best-powered trial.

cards.headline: Goldberg 2015: disability improved 6.4 points more on prednisone at 3 weeks — pain 0.3 points (P=0.34), surgery unchanged, adverse events 49.2% versus 23.9%
cards.summary: Goldberg 2015: disability improved 6.4 points more on prednisone at 3 weeks — pain 0.3 points (P=0.34), surgery unchanged, adverse events 49.2% versus 23.9%
cards.people: 269 adults with radicular pain for 3 months or less, Oswestry Disability Index ≥30 (0–100), and a herniated disc confirmed by MRI, in a large integrated health system in Northern California (2008–2013), randomised 2:1 to a tapering 15-day course of oral prednisone (5 days each of 60, 40, and 20 mg; cumulative 600 mg; n=181) or matching placebo (n=88).
cards.result: Adjusted mean improvement in Oswestry scores was 6.4 points greater on prednisone at 3 weeks (95% CI 1.9 to 10.9; P=0.006) and 7.4 points greater at 52 weeks (2.2 to 12.5; P=0.005). Pain reduction differed by 0.3 points at 3 weeks (−0.4 to 1.0; P=0.34) and 0.6 points at 52 weeks (−0.2 to 1.3; P=0.15) on a 0–10 scale. SF-36 physical component improved 3.3 points more at 3 weeks (P=0.001) but not significantly at 52 weeks. Surgery rates at 52 weeks did not differ. One or more adverse events at 3 weeks: 49.2% prednisone versus 23.9% placebo (P<0.001).
cards.watchOut: A 6–7 point Oswestry difference sits near the border of what patients perceive as meaningful, the 2:1 randomisation leaves a small placebo arm (n=88), and the trial's population — MRI-confirmed herniation with substantial disability — is narrower than the everyday 'sciatica' label.
cards.source: Goldberg et al. Oral steroids for acute radiculopathy due to a herniated lumbar disk: a randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2015. PMID: 25988461. Registry ID: NCT00668434. cards.headline: Pinto 2012: pooled corticosteroid trials showed a short-term pain advantage (−12.2 points, −20.9 to −3.4) — on evidence the reviewers graded low quality
cards.summary: Pinto 2012: pooled corticosteroid trials showed a short-term pain advantage (−12.2 points, −20.9 to −3.4) — on evidence the reviewers graded low quality
cards.people: 23 published reports of randomised trials of analgesic and adjuvant drugs for sciatica in primary care, including two trials of corticosteroids pooled for pain outcomes.
cards.result: The pooled results of two corticosteroid trials showed a mean difference in overall and leg pain of −12.2 points on a 0–100 scale (95% CI −20.9 to −3.4) favouring corticosteroids, in the short term only. Across drug classes, most pooled estimates did not favour active treatment over placebo; the median adverse-event rate was 17% (interquartile range 10–30%) for active drugs versus 11% (3–23%) for placebo. The reviewers judged the evidence for drugs commonly prescribed for sciatica to range from moderate to low quality, limited by small samples, lack of validated outcome measures, and little long-term follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The pooled pain signal comes from two small older trials using mixed steroid routes and regimens, and it conflicts with the larger, later, placebo-controlled oral-prednisone trial on the same shelf — the review's own quality grading says how much weight it can bear.
cards.source: Pinto et al. Drugs for relief of pain in patients with sciatica: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2012. PMID: 22331277. shelves.title: Endoscopy within 6 hours for high-risk upper GI bleeding: mortality 8.9% versus 6.6% with endoscopy at 6–24 hours — rushing found more bleeding lesions and treated more of them, and helped no one measurably
shelves.question: In acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, does endoscopy within 6 hours improve mortality or further bleeding compared with endoscopy within 24 hours?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Aged · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Esophageal and Gastric Varices/diagnosis/therapy · Female · Gastrointestinal Hemorrhage/diagnosis/mortality/therapy · Hospitalization · Humans · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Male · Middle Aged · Peptic Ulcer Hemorrhage/diagnosis/mortality/therapy · Risk Assessment · Time Factors · Time-to-Treatment
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — in the highest-risk patients, where the case for rushing was strongest. In a randomised trial of 516 patients with overt acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding and a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 12 or higher, endoscopy within 6 hours of gastroenterology consultation gave 30-day mortality of 8.9% (23/258) versus 6.6% (17/258) with endoscopy between 6 and 24 hours (difference 2.3 percentage points, 95% CI −2.3 to 6.9), and further bleeding in 10.9% versus 7.8% (difference 3.1 points, −1.9 to 8.1) (Lau JYW et al., PMID: 32242355). The urgent group did get more endoscopic treatment (60.1% vs 48.4%), because ulcers found earlier were more often actively bleeding or showed visible vessels (66.4% vs 47.8%) — earlier scopes find more to treat without changing what happens to patients. A meta-analysis of five randomised trials (926 patients) likewise found no significant benefit of very early over early endoscopy for rebleeding, mortality, ICU admission, transfusion, surgery, or stay, with a higher need for haemostatic treatment when scoping very early (risk ratio 1.23, 1.06 to 1.42) (PMID: 33570742). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): within-24-hours endoscopy is the evidence-based deadline; within-6-hours adds procedures, not survival.

cards.headline: Lau 2020: 30-day mortality 8.9% urgent versus 6.6% early (difference 2.3 points, −2.3 to 6.9); further bleeding 10.9% versus 7.8%
cards.summary: Lau 2020: 30-day mortality 8.9% urgent versus 6.6% early (difference 2.3 points, −2.3 to 6.9); further bleeding 10.9% versus 7.8%
cards.people: 516 patients with overt signs of acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding and a Glasgow-Blatchford score of 12 or higher (scores 0–23, higher indicating greater risk), randomised to endoscopy within 6 hours (258) or between 6 and 24 hours (258) after gastroenterologic consultation.
cards.result: Thirty-day mortality was 8.9% (23/258) in the urgent-endoscopy group and 6.6% (17/258) in the early-endoscopy group (difference 2.3 percentage points, 95% CI −2.3 to 6.9). Further bleeding within 30 days occurred in 28 patients (10.9%) versus 20 (7.8%) (difference 3.1 points, −1.9 to 8.1). Ulcers with active bleeding or visible vessels were found in 105/158 (66.4%) urgent-group patients with peptic ulcers versus 76/159 (47.8%) early, and endoscopic haemostatic treatment was given at the initial endoscopy to 155 patients (60.1%) versus 125 (48.4%).
cards.watchOut: The trial enrolled only high-risk patients (Glasgow-Blatchford ≥12) stable enough to randomise after consultation — it says nothing about exsanguinating or unstable bleeding, where immediate endoscopy (or surgery/interventional radiology) remains a clinical judgement; the point estimates numerically favour the 6–24 hour arm, but the confidence intervals include meaningful effects in both directions.
cards.source: Lau et al. Timing of Endoscopy for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding. The New England journal of medicine. 2020. PMID: 32242355. Registry ID: NCT01675856. cards.headline: Merola 2021: five trials, 926 patients — no benefit of very early endoscopy on any outcome, and a higher need for haemostatic treatment (risk ratio 1.23)
cards.summary: Merola 2021: five trials, 926 patients — no benefit of very early endoscopy on any outcome, and a higher need for haemostatic treatment (risk ratio 1.23)
cards.people: Five randomised trials (926 patients: 468 very early endoscopy, 458 early endoscopy) in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding, comparing very early versus early endoscopy timing.
cards.result: The meta-analysis showed no statistically significant benefit for very early endoscopy compared with early endoscopy in risk of rebleeding, mortality, ICU admission, blood transfusion, surgery, or length of hospital stay. The need for haemostatic treatment was significantly higher with very early endoscopy (risk ratio 1.23, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.42; P<0.01).
cards.watchOut: Timing definitions ('very early' versus 'early') differed across the five trials, and the pooled population mixes risk strata; the meta-analysis corroborates the big trial rather than replacing its high-risk focus.
cards.source: Merola et al. Optimal timing of endoscopy for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Internal and emergency medicine. 2021. PMID: 33570742. shelves.title: Offering families the chance to witness CPR: relatives in the control group had 1.7 times the odds of PTSD symptoms at 90 days — and resuscitation, survival, team stress, and legal claims were all unaffected
shelves.question: Should family members be offered the chance to witness cardiopulmonary resuscitation, and does witnessing reduce their post-traumatic stress compared with not being offered?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Anxiety/etiology · Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation/psychology · Comorbidity · Depression/etiology · Emergency Medical Services · Family/psychology · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Heart Arrest/therapy · Humans · Intention to Treat Analysis · Male · Middle Aged · Single-Blind Method · Stress Disorders, Post-Traumatic/diagnosis/epidemiology/etiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for the relatives, with no cost detected for the patient or the team. In a cluster-randomised trial across 15 French prehospital emergency units, 570 relatives of patients in cardiac arrest were in units assigned either to systematically offer the opportunity to observe CPR or to follow standard practice: 79% of offered relatives witnessed CPR versus 43% under standard practice, and PTSD-related symptoms at day 90 were significantly commoner in the control group (adjusted odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5; P=0.004) and among relatives who did not witness CPR versus those who did (adjusted odds ratio 1.6, 1.1 to 2.5; P=0.02) (Jabre P et al., PMID: 23484827). Witnessing did not affect resuscitation characteristics, patient survival, or the medical team's emotional stress, and produced no medicolegal claims; non-witnessing relatives also had more anxiety and depression symptoms. A 2022 systematic review of 31 studies (including two randomised trials) found the wider evidence low or very low certainty, with family outcomes mixed across studies (PMID: 36087636). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the offer itself appears protective for relatives' mental health; the trial supports offering, not compelling, presence.

cards.headline: Jabre 2013: PTSD symptoms at day 90 — adjusted odds ratio 1.7 (1.2 to 2.5) against the control group; 79% witnessed when offered versus 43% under standard practice
cards.summary: Jabre 2013: PTSD symptoms at day 90 — adjusted odds ratio 1.7 (1.2 to 2.5) against the control group; 79% witnessed when offered versus 43% under standard practice
cards.people: 570 relatives of patients in cardiac arrest receiving CPR from 15 prehospital emergency medical service units in France, with units randomised to systematically offer relatives the opportunity to observe CPR (intervention) or to follow standard practice regarding family presence (control); the primary endpoint was PTSD-related symptoms on day 90.
cards.result: In the intervention group, 211/266 relatives (79%) witnessed CPR, versus 131/304 (43%) in the control group. In intention-to-treat analysis, PTSD-related symptoms were significantly more frequent in the control group than the intervention group (adjusted odds ratio 1.7, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.5; P=0.004) and among relatives who did not witness CPR than among those who did (adjusted odds ratio 1.6, 1.1 to 2.5; P=0.02). Relatives who did not witness CPR also had anxiety and depression symptoms more frequently. Family-witnessed CPR did not affect resuscitation characteristics, patient survival, or the health-care team's emotional stress, and resulted in no medicolegal claims.
cards.watchOut: A prehospital, single-country trial from a physician-staffed EMS system; 43% of control relatives witnessed CPR anyway, diluting the contrast, and the endpoint is symptom scores at 90 days rather than diagnosed PTSD — the trial tests the systematic offer, which is the policy a service can actually adopt.
cards.source: Jabre et al. Family presence during cardiopulmonary resuscitation. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23484827. Registry ID: NCT01009606. cards.headline: Considine 2022: across 31 studies the evidence is low or very low certainty, with family outcomes mixed — Jabre remains the load-bearing trial
cards.summary: Considine 2022: across 31 studies the evidence is low or very low certainty, with family outcomes mixed — Jabre remains the load-bearing trial
cards.people: 31 studies of family presence during adult resuscitation from cardiac arrest (18 quantitative, including two randomised trials; 12 qualitative; one mixed-methods), from 9,459 citations to May 2022.
cards.result: The evidence was of very low or low certainty. High-certainty evidence on patient outcomes is lacking; family members had mixed outcomes for depression, anxiety, PTSD symptoms, and the experience of witnessing resuscitation; provider experience was variable, influenced by setting, education, and experience. Providers reported that a designated family support person and organisational guidelines were important for facilitating family presence.
cards.watchOut: A narrative synthesis without meta-analysis across heterogeneous designs and settings (prehospital, emergency department, ICU); 'mixed outcomes' across mostly observational studies cannot overturn the randomised result, but it does cap how far one French prehospital trial generalises.
cards.source: Considine et al. Family presence during adult resuscitation from cardiac arrest: A systematic review. Resuscitation. 2022. PMID: 36087636. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: offer the choice — the randomised evidence says relatives fare better, and nothing measurable gets worse
cards.summary: Synthesis: offer the choice — the randomised evidence says relatives fare better, and nothing measurable gets worse
cards.people: One cluster randomised trial (570 relatives, 15 EMS units) and one 31-study systematic review.
cards.result: PTSD-related symptoms at 90 days: adjusted odds ratio 1.7 (1.2 to 2.5) against standard practice; witnessing itself: odds ratio 1.6 (1.1 to 2.5) against non-witnessing. Resuscitation characteristics, patient survival, team stress, medicolegal claims: no effect in the trial. Wider literature: low certainty, mixed. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a single randomised trial carries the claim.
cards.watchOut: The intervention is an offer with support, not mere physical presence; services adopting it need the family-support role the review identifies, and relatives who decline should lose nothing — the trial's control arm shows decliners and the unoffered fare similarly worse, which is about the offer, not about forcing attendance.
cards.source: Synthesis of Jabre P et al. The New England journal of medicine. 2013 (PMID: 23484827); Considine J et al. Resuscitation. 2022 (PMID: 36087636).

shelves.title: Hypotensive resuscitation in bleeding trauma: pooled odds ratio for death 0.70 across five randomised trials (1,158 patients) — a real signal built from small, mostly underpowered trials
shelves.question: In bleeding trauma patients, does a hypotensive (restricted) resuscitation strategy targeting a lower systolic pressure before bleeding control improve survival compared with conventional resuscitation?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Blood Pressure/physiology · Fluid Therapy/methods · Humans · Hypotension/etiology/physiopathology/therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Resuscitation/methods · Shock, Hemorrhagic/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Wounds, Penetrating/complications/therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a mortality signal the reviewers themselves call underpowered. A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials comparing permissive hypotension with conventional resuscitation after traumatic injury pooled five trials and 1,158 patients: the pooled odds ratio for 30-day or in-hospital mortality was 0.70 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.92) favouring hypotensive resuscitation, and the hypotensive groups received fewer blood products and had less estimated blood loss (Tran A et al., PMID: 29370058). Intervention targets ranged from systolic 50–70 mmHg or mean arterial pressure ≥50, against control targets of systolic 65–100 or MAP ≥65. Four of the five trials suggested a survival benefit but three were insufficiently powered to show it individually, and study quality was poor to moderate. The largest component experience, a randomised trial targeting MAP 50 versus 65 mmHg during operative resuscitation in 90 patients in haemorrhagic shock, found significantly less blood product and intravenous fluid use, significantly lower early postoperative mortality, less postoperative coagulopathy, and a non-significant trend to lower 30-day mortality in the low-MAP group (PMID: 21610356). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the direction is consistent and the mechanism (less clot disruption, dilution, and hypothermia) coherent — the definitive large trial still does not exist.

cards.headline: Tran 2018: pooled mortality odds ratio 0.70 (0.53 to 0.92) across five trials and 1,158 patients; fewer blood products, less blood loss
cards.summary: Tran 2018: pooled mortality odds ratio 0.70 (0.53 to 0.92) across five trials and 1,158 patients; fewer blood products, less blood loss
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Tran 2018)
cards.people: Five randomised trials (1,158 adult trauma patients with haemorrhagic shock) comparing permissive hypotension with conventional resuscitation, covering preoperative and intraoperative strategies; two trials enrolled penetrating injury only and three also included blunt injury. Intervention targets ranged from systolic blood pressure 50–70 mmHg or mean arterial pressure ≥50 mmHg, versus control targets of systolic 65–100 mmHg or MAP ≥65 mmHg.
cards.result: The pooled odds ratio for 30-day or in-hospital mortality was 0.70 (95% CI 0.53 to 0.92), suggesting a survival benefit for permissive hypotension. Four trials suggested a survival benefit individually, although three were insufficiently powered to find statistical significance. Hypotensive-strategy patients received fewer blood products and had lesser estimated blood loss. Study quality was poor to moderate, owing to poor protocol reporting and lack of blinding.
cards.watchOut: The pooled estimate leans on small trials with varying pressure targets and mixed blunt/penetrating populations; traumatic brain injury — where hypotension is dangerous — is the population these strategies must exclude, and the trials' handling of head injury limits bedside generalisation.
cards.source: Tran et al. cards.headline: Morrison 2011: targeting MAP 50 versus 65 mmHg in 90 operative trauma patients — significantly less transfusion and fluid, lower early postoperative death, less coagulopathy
cards.summary: Morrison 2011: targeting MAP 50 versus 65 mmHg in 90 operative trauma patients — significantly less transfusion and fluid, lower early postoperative death, less coagulopathy
cards.people: The first 90 patients enrolled in a prospective randomised trial of hypotensive resuscitation: trauma patients in haemorrhagic shock requiring emergent surgery, randomised intraoperatively to a target mean arterial pressure of 50 mmHg (low-MAP) or 65 mmHg (high-MAP) and followed for 30 days.
cards.result: The low-MAP group received significantly fewer blood products and less total intravenous fluid during intraoperative resuscitation. Mortality was significantly lower in the early postoperative period in the low-MAP group, with a non-significant trend to lower 30-day mortality. Low-MAP patients were significantly less likely to develop immediate postoperative coagulopathy, less likely to die from postoperative bleeding associated with coagulopathy, and — among those who developed coagulopathy — had significantly lower international normalised ratios, indicating less severe coagulopathy.
cards.watchOut: Preliminary results from the first 90 patients of an ongoing trial, reported without the absolute mortality figures in the record's abstract; a single-centre operative population whose pressures were managed by protocolised anaesthesia care — the prehospital and emergency-department phases are outside this trial.
cards.source: Morrison et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: consistent direction, thin trials — a 30% relative odds reduction for death that one large trial could still overturn
cards.summary: Synthesis: consistent direction, thin trials — a 30% relative odds reduction for death that one large trial could still overturn
cards.people: One meta-analysis of five randomised trials (1,158 patients) and its largest described component trial experience (90 patients, MAP 50 vs 65 mmHg).
cards.result: Mortality: pooled odds ratio 0.70 (0.53 to 0.92) favouring hypotensive resuscitation — a 30% relative reduction in the odds of death, with absolute rates varying across the small component trials. Blood products and estimated blood loss: lower with hypotensive strategies. Coagulopathy: significantly less frequent and less severe in the MAP-50 arm of the component trial. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit), Tier C: a mortality-benefit claim resting on small trials.
cards.watchOut: Declared gap: no adequately powered multicentre trial of hypotensive resuscitation before bleeding control exists in this record; patients with traumatic brain injury need a different (higher) pressure strategy, and this shelf must never be read across to them.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tran A et al. The journal of trauma and acute care surgery. 2018 (PMID: 29370058); Morrison CA et al. The Journal of trauma. 2011 (PMID: 21610356).

shelves.title: Lung ultrasound for pneumonia: pooled sensitivity 0.95 against chest X-ray's 0.77 in head-to-head meta-analysis, with similar specificity — the better bedside test where the expertise exists
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with suspected pneumonia, is lung ultrasound more accurate than chest X-ray for diagnosis when compared with CT or clinical follow-up?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Pneumonia/diagnostic imaging · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — as a diagnostic test, judged against the reference standards the studies used. A systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 studies (2,359 participants) found lung ultrasonography highly accurate for pneumonia in adults, with an area under the summary receiver-operating curve of 0.93 and a diagnostic odds ratio at the optimal cutpoint of 50 (95% CI 21 to 120) (Llamas-Álvarez AM et al., PMID: 27818332). The head-to-head meta-analysis is the sharper result: across five studies comparing both tests, lung ultrasound had pooled sensitivity 0.95 (0.93–0.97) and specificity 0.90 (0.86–0.94), while chest radiography had sensitivity 0.77 (0.73–0.80) and specificity 0.91 (0.87–0.94); against CT as the reference (138 patients), the area under the curve was 0.901 for ultrasound versus 0.590 for radiography (P=0.002) (PMID: 26107512). The catch is operator dependence: these accuracies come from studies where ultrasound was performed and interpreted by enthusiasts, and both reviews found significant heterogeneity. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): more pneumonias found at the bedside at no cost in false positives — in trained hands.

cards.headline: Llamas-Álvarez 2017: 16 studies, 2,359 participants — area under the curve 0.93, diagnostic odds ratio 50 (21 to 120) for lung ultrasound in pneumonia
cards.summary: Llamas-Álvarez 2017: 16 studies, 2,359 participants — area under the curve 0.93, diagnostic odds ratio 50 (21 to 120) for lung ultrasound in pneumonia
cards.people: 16 studies (2,359 participants) of bedside lung ultrasonography for diagnosing pneumonia in adults, with study quality assessed by QUADAS-2 and accuracy pooled with a bivariate random-effects model.
cards.result: The area under the summary receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.93, with a diagnostic odds ratio at the optimal cutpoint of 50 (95% CI 21 to 120). There was significant heterogeneity in both sensitivity and specificity without clear evidence of a threshold effect; a tendency to higher accuracy in high-quality studies was not significant after bivariate meta-regression.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy against mixed reference standards (CT, discharge diagnosis, follow-up) in studies largely performed by experienced sonographers; heterogeneity was significant, and the review does not show that ultrasound-first diagnosis changes antibiotics, admissions, or outcomes.
cards.source: Llamas-Álvarez et al. Accuracy of Lung Ultrasonography in the Diagnosis of Pneumonia in Adults: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Chest. 2017. PMID: 27818332. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Pneumonia/diagnostic imaging · ROC Curve · Sensitivity and Specificity · Ultrasonography

cards.headline: Ye 2015: head-to-head, lung ultrasound sensitivity 0.95 versus chest X-ray 0.77, specificity 0.90 versus 0.91 — against CT, areas under the curve 0.901 versus 0.590
cards.summary: Ye 2015: head-to-head, lung ultrasound sensitivity 0.95 versus chest X-ray 0.77, specificity 0.90 versus 0.91 — against CT, areas under the curve 0.901 versus 0.590
cards.people: Five studies directly comparing lung ultrasonography and chest radiography for adult community-acquired pneumonia, against hospital discharge diagnosis or chest CT as the reference standard (138 patients in the CT-referenced comparison).
cards.result: Using discharge diagnosis as the reference, lung ultrasound had pooled sensitivity 0.95 (0.93–0.97) and specificity 0.90 (0.86–0.94), while chest radiography had sensitivity 0.77 (0.73–0.80) and specificity 0.91 (0.87–0.94). Against CT in 138 patients, the areas under the summary receiver operating curves were 0.901 for ultrasound and 0.590 for radiography (Z statistic 3.093, P=0.002).
cards.watchOut: Only five studies, and the CT-referenced subset is just 138 patients; discharge diagnosis as a reference standard can incorporate the ultrasound result itself, flattering its accuracy (incorporation bias).
cards.source: Ye et al. Accuracy of Lung Ultrasonography versus Chest Radiography for the Diagnosis of Adult Community-Acquired Pneumonia: Review of the Literature and Meta-Analysis. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 26107512. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one conclusion — ultrasound finds roughly a fifth more pneumonias than the chest film, at the same false-positive rate
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses, one conclusion — ultrasound finds roughly a fifth more pneumonias than the chest film, at the same false-positive rate
cards.people: Two systematic reviews and meta-analyses (16 studies, 2,359 participants; and five head-to-head studies) of lung ultrasound for adult pneumonia.
cards.result: Overall accuracy: area under the curve 0.93, diagnostic odds ratio 50 (21 to 120). Head-to-head: sensitivity 0.95 versus 0.77 and specificity 0.90 versus 0.91 for ultrasound versus chest radiography — an 18-percentage-point absolute sensitivity advantage. Against CT: areas 0.901 versus 0.590 (P=0.002). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), Tier C not set: two concordant meta-analyses carry the diagnostic claim.
cards.watchOut: Operator dependence is the standing caveat for every ultrasound shelf: these numbers describe trained study sonographers, and a department adopting ultrasound-first pneumonia diagnosis is buying the training as much as the test.
cards.source: Synthesis of Llamas-Álvarez AM et al. Chest. 2017 (PMID: 27818332); Ye X et al. PloS one. 2015 (PMID: 26107512).

shelves.title: PERC rule in low-risk ED patients: the PROPER randomised trial found no excess missed clots (0.1% vs 0%) and 10 percentage points fewer CT pulmonary angiograms — pooled sensitivity 0.97, specificity only 0.23
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, can a negative PERC rule safely exclude the diagnosis without D-dimer testing or imaging?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Clinical Protocols · Cross-Over Studies · Decision Support Techniques · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Embolism/diagnosis · Risk · Thromboembolism/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — a PERC-negative result in a patient already judged low-risk can end the workup safely, and the one randomised test of that strategy found no safety cost. In the PROPER crossover cluster-randomised trial (Freund Y et al., PMID: 29450523), a thromboembolic event missed at presentation occurred in 0.1% of the PERC group versus 0% of controls over 3 months, while CT pulmonary angiography fell from 23% to 13% (difference −10%, 95% CI −13% to −6%), median ED stay fell by a mean of 36 minutes, and hospital admission fell by 3.3 percentage points. The pooled diagnostic accuracy behind the rule (Singh B et al., PMID: 22177109) is sensitivity 0.97 (95% CI 0.96 to 0.98) with specificity only 0.23 — PERC rules out; it never rules in. Both records apply only after a clinician has already judged the pretest probability low: PERC was never tested as a stand-alone screen in unselected chest-pain patients. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): in gestalt low-risk patients, PERC-negative safely avoids D-dimer and imaging, on one randomised strategy trial plus a concordant accuracy meta-analysis.

cards.headline: PROPER 2018: missed thromboembolism at 3 months 0.1% on PERC strategy vs 0% on conventional — CTPA 13% vs 23%, ED stay 36 minutes shorter
cards.summary: PROPER 2018: missed thromboembolism at 3 months 0.1% on PERC strategy vs 0% on conventional — CTPA 13% vs 23%, ED stay 36 minutes shorter
cards.people: 1,916 patients (mean age 44 years, 51% women) with a low gestalt clinical probability of pulmonary embolism in 14 French emergency departments, August 2015 to September 2016; centres crossed over between a PERC period (PE excluded with no further testing if all 8 PERC items were negative) and a conventional-strategy period; 1,749 patients completed follow-up to 3 months.
cards.result: A PE was diagnosed at initial presentation in 1.5% of the PERC group versus 2.7% of controls (difference 1.3%, 95% CI −0.1% to 2.7%). One PE (0.1%) was diagnosed during follow-up in the PERC group versus none in controls (difference 0.1%, 95% CI −∞ to 0.8%), inside the 1.5% noninferiority margin. CT pulmonary angiography was performed in 13% versus 23% (difference −10%, 95% CI −13% to −6%; P<.001); median ED stay fell by a mean of 36 minutes (95% CI 4 to 68) and hospital admission by 3.3 percentage points (95% CI 0.1% to 6.6%).
cards.watchOut: Cluster-randomised by centre-period, not by patient, and run only in patients a clinician had already judged low-risk — the trial validates PERC as the second step after gestalt, not as a replacement for it. The single missed event means the upper confidence bound, not the point estimate, is the honest safety figure.
cards.source: Freund Y et al. Effect of the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-Out Criteria on Subsequent Thromboembolic Events Among Low-Risk Emergency Department Patients: The PROPER Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2018. PMID: 29450523. cards.headline: Singh 2012 meta-analysis: pooled PERC sensitivity 0.97 (0.96–0.98), specificity 0.23, negative likelihood ratio 0.17 across 13,885 ED patients
cards.summary: Singh 2012 meta-analysis: pooled PERC sensitivity 0.97 (0.96–0.98), specificity 0.23, negative likelihood ratio 0.17 across 13,885 ED patients
cards.people: 12 cohorts (10 prospective, 2 retrospective) from 6 countries, studying 13,885 emergency-department patients with suspected pulmonary embolism, among whom 1,391 PEs were diagnosed; studies reporting PERC diagnostic performance against standard PE workup.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96 to 0.98), specificity 0.23 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.24), positive likelihood ratio 1.24 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.30) and negative likelihood ratio 0.17 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.23). Heterogeneity was significant for specificity (I²=97.2%) and positive likelihood ratio (I²=84.2%). The authors concluded PERC has consistently high sensitivity and low but acceptable specificity for ruling out PE in patients with low pretest probability.

shelves.title: Droperidol and the heart: mean QTc barely moved (424 to 428 ms) in the largest ED series and torsades occurred once in 16,546 patients (0.006%) — a real but very small risk at usual doses
shelves.question: In patients sedated with droperidol in the emergency department, how large is the risk of QT prolongation and torsades at usual doses?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Critical Illness/epidemiology/therapy · Droperidol/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Electrocardiography/methods · Emergency Service, Hospital/statistics & numerical data · Female · Humans · Incidence · Long QT Syndrome/chemically induced/diagnosis/epidemiology · Male · Risk Assessment · Torsades de Pointes/chemically induced/diagnosis/epidemiology · United States/epidemiology
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (harm) — the harm is real but, at usual emergency-department doses, very small, and both large series agree on that scale. In the largest record (Cole JB et al., PMID: 32726229), 15,374 non-critical patients received 18,020 droperidol doses; among patients with ECGs before and after, mean QTc was 424.3 ms before and 427.6 ms after droperidol, and a single case of torsades occurred in a patient with multiple risk factors who tolerated rechallenge — an incidence of 1 in 16,546 (0.006%, 95% CI 0.00015 to 0.03367%). In critically ill patients the mean QTc was 435.7 ms before and 435.8 ms after. A later series (Alshehri AM et al., PMID: 39695417) found a composite of QTc prolongation, torsades, ventricular arrhythmia or hypotension in 9.1% of 327 administrations, with no episode of torsades or serious ventricular arrhythmia and no event rated probable or definite on the Naranjo scale; higher cumulative dose was associated with QTc prolongation (OR 1.27). All of this evidence is observational — there is no randomised cardiac-safety trial — so the shelf is Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (harm): droperidol prolongs QTc slightly on average and torsades is documented but rarer than 1 in 16,000 at usual ED doses; dose and patient risk factors, not the drug name alone, drive the risk.

cards.headline: Cole 2020: torsades 1 in 16,546 patients (0.006%); mean QTc 424.3 ms before vs 427.6 ms after droperidol in non-critical patients, unchanged (435.7 vs 435.8 ms) in the critically ill
cards.summary: Cole 2020: torsades 1 in 16,546 patients (0.006%); mean QTc 424.3 ms before vs 427.6 ms after droperidol in non-critical patients, unchanged (435.7 vs 435.8 ms) in the critically ill
cards.people: All patients receiving droperidol at a US urban Level I trauma centre, 1997–2001: 15,374 non-critical patients receiving 18,020 doses (2,431 with an ECG; 170 with ECGs before and after) and 1,172 critically ill patients (396 with an ECG; 114 with ECGs before and after; 337 ECGs suitable for QT-nomogram plotting).
cards.result: In non-critical patients with paired ECGs, mean QTc was 424.3 ms (95% CI 419.7 to 428.9) before and 427.6 ms (95% CI 424.3 to 430.9) after droperidol. In critically ill patients, mean QTc was 435.7 ms (95% CI 426.7 to 444.7) before and 435.8 ms (95% CI 427.5 to 444.1) after. Of 337 nomogram-plottable ECGs, 13 (3.8%) lay above the at-risk line — 2.2% before versus 4.9% after droperidol. A single case of torsades occurred, in a patient with multiple risk factors, and did not recur on rechallenge: incidence 1/16,546 (0.006%, 95% CI 0.00015 to 0.03367%).
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, single-centre, and from 1997–2001 prescribing: ECGs existed for only a minority of recipients, so QTc data come from a selected subset, and doses and co-medications of that era may differ from current practice. A 0.006% point estimate with a confidence interval reaching 0.034% cannot exclude a risk several times larger in high-risk patients.
cards.source: Cole JB et al. The Incidence of QT Prolongation and Torsades des Pointes in Patients Receiving Droperidol in an Urban Emergency Department. The western journal of emergency medicine. 2020. PMID: 32726229. cards.headline: Alshehri 2024: composite cardiac/hypotension endpoint in 9.1% of 327 administrations, but zero torsades, zero serious ventricular arrhythmia, and no event rated probable or definite
cards.summary: Alshehri 2024: composite cardiac/hypotension endpoint in 9.1% of 327 administrations, but zero torsades, zero serious ventricular arrhythmia, and no event rated probable or definite
cards.people: 327 droperidol administrations in 245 patients in the emergency department of a US academic Level I trauma centre, from droperidol's reintroduction to the formulary on July 1, 2019 through January 31, 2023; major endpoint a composite of QTc prolongation, torsades, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension, with causality rated on the Naranjo scale.
cards.result: The composite safety endpoint occurred in 30 (9.1%) administrations; none of these events was classified as probable or definite on the Naranjo adverse-drug-reaction probability scale. No episodes of torsades or serious ventricular arrhythmia were reported. Higher cumulative droperidol dose was associated with increased odds of QTc prolongation (OR 1.27, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.56), as was creatinine clearance below 60 mL/min (OR 1.01, 95% CI 1.0 to 1.02). The authors concluded the study supports low-dose droperidol use in the ED, with a dose-dependent effect on QTc to consider.
cards.watchOut: Small and retrospective: 327 administrations cannot detect an event that occurs once in 16,000, and the 9.1% composite is dominated by QTc measurements and hypotension rather than arrhythmia. The dose association (OR 1.27) is the actionable signal; the zero numerator for torsades is not proof of zero risk.
cards.source: Alshehri AM et al. Evaluation of droperidol use in the emergency department: a retrospective analysis of QTc prolongation and adverse events. BMC emergency medicine. 2024. PMID: 39695417. cards.people: Two retrospective ED series totalling over 16,500 droperidol recipients (1997–2001 and 2019–2023, both US Level I trauma centres).
cards.result: Mean QTc change: +3.3 ms (non-critical) and +0.1 ms (critically ill) in paired ECGs. shelves.title: Buccal midazolam stopped children's seizures in 56% versus 27% on rectal diazepam in the one head-to-head hospital trial — with no extra respiratory depression
shelves.question: In children with seizures in the emergency department, is buccal midazolam more effective than rectal diazepam at stopping seizures?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Administration, Buccal · Administration, Rectal · Adolescent · Anticonvulsants/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Child · Child, Preschool · Diazepam/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Infant · Male · Midazolam/administration & dosage/adverse effects · Respiratory Insufficiency/chemically induced/etiology · Seizures/complications/drug therapy
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — when there is no intravenous access, the cheek beats the rectum. In the multicentre randomised trial (McIntyre J et al., PMID: 16023510), therapeutic success — seizure cessation within 10 minutes lasting at least 1 hour without respiratory depression requiring intervention — was 56% (61 of 109) on buccal midazolam versus 27% (30 of 110) on rectal diazepam (difference 29%, 95% CI 16 to 41), and the rate of respiratory depression did not differ between groups. The Cochrane review (McTague A et al., PMID: 29320603) pooled the comparison at a risk ratio for seizure cessation of 1.25 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.38) across 4 trials and 690 children, but rated that evidence low to very low quality — smaller than the single big trial's own estimate, and the reason this shelf is POSSIBLE rather than LIKELY. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): buccal midazolam stops acute seizures in children more often than rectal diazepam, with no demonstrated increase in respiratory depression.

cards.headline: McIntyre 2005: therapeutic success 56% (61/109) on buccal midazolam vs 27% (30/110) on rectal diazepam — difference 29% (95% CI 16–41), respiratory depression no different
cards.summary: McIntyre 2005: therapeutic success 56% (61/109) on buccal midazolam vs 27% (30/110) on rectal diazepam — difference 29% (95% CI 16–41), respiratory depression no different
cards.people: 219 seizure episodes in 177 children aged 6 months and older (median age 3 years) presenting to UK hospital emergency departments with active febrile or afebrile seizures and no intravenous access; buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam, dosed 2.5 to 10 mg by age; analysis per protocol.
cards.result: Therapeutic success (cessation within 10 minutes, sustained at least 1 hour, without respiratory depression requiring intervention) was 56% (61 of 109) for buccal midazolam and 27% (30 of 110) for rectal diazepam (percentage difference 29%, 95% CI 16 to 41). Analysis of initial episodes only gave a similar result, the rate of respiratory depression did not differ between groups, and after adjustment for centre, age, epilepsy diagnosis, antiepileptic drug use, prior treatment and seizure length, buccal midazolam remained more effective.
cards.watchOut: Per-protocol analysis and an unblinded route comparison (a cheek dose and a rectal dose cannot be masked from the treating team), in episodes rather than strictly in children — some children contribute more than one episode. Success still failed in 44% on the winning treatment: neither drug is reliable enough to end the escalation plan.
cards.source: McIntyre J et al. Safety and efficacy of buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam for emergency treatment of seizures in children: a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Cochrane 2018: buccal midazolam vs rectal diazepam seizure cessation RR 1.25 (1.13–1.38), 4 trials, 690 children — rated low- to very-low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane 2018: buccal midazolam vs rectal diazepam seizure cessation RR 1.25 (1.13–1.38), 4 trials, 690 children — rated low- to very-low-quality evidence
cards.people: 18 randomised trials with 2,199 children treated for acute tonic-clonic convulsions including convulsive status epilepticus in hospital or emergency settings, across intravenous, intramuscular, buccal, nasal and rectal routes; the buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam comparison drew on 4 trials with 690 children.
cards.result: For buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam, the risk ratio for seizure cessation was 1.25 (95% CI 1.13 to 1.38; 4 trials; 690 children), graded low- to very-low-quality evidence with uncertainty about the effect. Respiratory depression, the most clinically relevant adverse event, occurred in 0% to up to 18% of children across the review's studies, with no individual study showing a difference between anticonvulsants or routes. The review found no new high-quality evidence that would change practice for this comparison.
cards.watchOut: The pooled RR of 1.25 is much smaller than the largest trial's own 56% versus 27% — smaller, older trials dilute it, and the low quality grade reflects imprecision, inconsistency and applicability limits. The review's headline is therefore a floor, not a contradiction, but it caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: Early tracheostomy after severe stroke (SETPOINT2): survival without severe disability at 6 months was 43.5% early versus 47.1% standard — no significant difference, with confidence intervals too wide to exclude real benefit or harm
shelves.question: In patients with severe stroke requiring prolonged ventilation, does early tracheostomy improve long-term functional outcome compared with a standard (later) tracheostomy strategy?
shelves.mesh: Airway Management · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Recovery of Function · Reflex, Abnormal · Respiration, Artificial/adverse effects/methods · Respiratory Tract Diseases/etiology/physiopathology/therapy · Stroke/complications/physiopathology/therapy · Time Factors · Tracheostomy/adverse effects · Treatment Outcome · Ventilator Weaning/methods
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference) — on the outcome that matters, timing did not deliver. In SETPOINT2 (Bösel J et al., PMID: 35506515), 382 ventilated patients with severe ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke were randomised to tracheostomy within 5 days or to continued weaning with tracheostomy if needed from day 10; a tracheostomy was performed in 95.2% of the early group (median day 4) and 67% of the standard group (median day 11). Survival without severe disability at 6 months (modified Rankin Scale 0–4) was 43.5% early versus 47.1% standard (difference −3.6%, 95% CI −14.3% to 7.2%; adjusted OR 0.93, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.42; P=.73). Tracheostomy-related serious adverse events were 5.0% of reported serious events in the early group versus 3.4% in the standard group. The confidence interval is wide enough to include a clinically important difference in either direction, so this is a single-trial null, not proof of equivalence — Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (the treatment made no difference): early tracheostomy did not significantly improve 6-month functional outcome in the one large stroke-specific trial.

cards.headline: SETPOINT2 2022: modified Rankin 0–4 at 6 months in 43.5% (early) vs 47.1% (standard); adjusted OR 0.93 (0.60–1.42), P=.73
cards.summary: SETPOINT2 2022: modified Rankin 0–4 at 6 months in 43.5% (early) vs 47.1% (standard); adjusted OR 0.93 (0.60–1.42), P=.73
cards.people: 382 patients (median age 59 years, 49.8% women) with severe acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke receiving invasive ventilation at 26 US and German neurocritical care centres, randomised July 2015 to January 2020 to early tracheostomy (within 5 days of intubation; n=188) or a standard strategy of ongoing weaning with tracheostomy if needed from day 10 (n=194); 366 patients (95.8%) had primary-outcome data.
cards.result: Tracheostomy (predominantly percutaneous) was performed in 95.2% of the early group at a median of 4 days and in 67% of the standard group at a median of 11 days. The proportion without severe disability (modified Rankin Scale 0–4) at 6 months was 43.5% in the early group versus 47.1% in the standard group (difference −3.6%, 95% CI −14.3% to 7.2%; adjusted odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.42; P=.73). Of the serious adverse events, 5.0% (6 of 121) in the early group versus 3.4% (4 of 118) in the standard group were related to tracheostomy.
cards.watchOut: One trial, and an imprecise one: the 95% CI for the difference runs from 14.3 points of harm to 7.2 points of benefit, so a clinically relevant effect either way cannot be excluded — the authors say so themselves. A third of the standard group never needed a tracheostomy at all, which is itself an argument the early strategy cannot answer.

shelves.title: GFAP/UCH-L1 blood test after head injury: sensitivity 0.976 and negative predictive value 0.996 for CT injury in ALERT-TBI — but no trial has yet shown it actually reduces CT scanning
shelves.question: In adults with mild traumatic brain injury, does a blood biomarker test (GFAP and UCH-L1) safely reduce head CT scanning compared with usual clinical decision-making?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Brain Injuries, Traumatic/blood/diagnostic imaging · Female · Glasgow Coma Scale · Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein/blood · Head/diagnostic imaging · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Retrospective Studies · Tomography Scanners, X-Ray Computed · Ubiquitin Thiolesterase/blood · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the test is an accurate rule-out; the scanning reduction the question asks about has never been randomised. In ALERT-TBI (Bazarian JJ et al., PMID: 30054151), 1,959 adults with Glasgow Coma Scale 9–15 who had a head CT as standard care had serum GFAP and UCH-L1 measured at prespecified cutoffs: 125 (6%) had CT-detected intracranial injury, the combined test was negative in 671 (34%), and for detection of injury it had sensitivity 0.976 (95% CI 0.931 to 0.995) and negative predictive value 0.996 (0.987 to 0.999), with 3 patients CT-positive despite a negative test. The rapid point-of-care version, tested on banked plasma from the same cohort (Bazarian JJ et al., PMID: 34358399), performed similarly in the 1,901 patients with GCS 13–15: sensitivity 0.958 (95% CI 0.906 to 0.982), specificity 0.404, negative predictive value 0.993, positive predictive value 0.098. Because every patient in both records was scanned anyway, the records show who could have avoided a CT, not that using the test safely reduces scanning in practice — that gap, and the single-cohort base, make this Tier C. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a negative GFAP/UCH-L1 test identifies a group at very low risk of CT injury; a management trial proving safe CT reduction is still missing.

cards.headline: ALERT-TBI 2018: sensitivity 0.976 (0.931–0.995), NPV 0.996 (0.987–0.999); test negative in 34% — 3 of 1,959 patients were CT-positive despite a negative test
cards.summary: ALERT-TBI 2018: sensitivity 0.976 (0.931–0.995), NPV 0.996 (0.987–0.999); test negative in 34% — 3 of 1,959 patients were CT-positive despite a negative test
cards.people: 1,959 analysable adults (of 1,977 recruited) presenting to emergency departments with suspected non-penetrating traumatic brain injury, Glasgow Coma Scale 9–15, who underwent head CT as part of standard care and had blood collected within 12 hours of injury, December 2012 to March 2014; serum UCH-L1 (cutoff 327 pg/mL) and GFAP (cutoff 22 pg/mL) combined into a single test result.
cards.result: 125 patients (6%) had CT-detected intracranial injuries and 8 (under 1%) had neurosurgically manageable injuries. The test was positive in 1,288 patients (66%) and negative in 671 (34%). For detection of intracranial injury, sensitivity was 0.976 (95% CI 0.931 to 0.995) and negative predictive value 0.996 (0.987 to 0.999). In 3 patients (under 1% of 1,959) the CT was positive when the test was negative.
cards.watchOut: Everyone was scanned, so this is accuracy, not impact: the 34% test-negative rate is the ceiling of avoidable scans, before clinicians override, patients deteriorate, or the 12-hour sampling window excludes late presenters. The cohort's 6% injury prevalence is higher than in many mild-TBI ED populations, which flatters the negative predictive value. The study was funded by the test's manufacturer and the US Army.
cards.source: Bazarian JJ et al. Serum GFAP and UCH-L1 for prediction of absence of intracranial injuries on head CT (ALERT-TBI): a multicentre observational study. The Lancet. Neurology. 2018. PMID: 30054151. cards.headline: Rapid i-STAT version 2021: sensitivity 0.958, specificity 0.404, NPV 0.993, PPV 0.098 in 1,901 patients with GCS 13–15 — same ALERT-TBI cohort, banked samples
cards.summary: Rapid i-STAT version 2021: sensitivity 0.958, specificity 0.404, NPV 0.993, PPV 0.098 in 1,901 patients with GCS 13–15 — same ALERT-TBI cohort, banked samples
cards.type: Diagnostic accuracy analysis of banked samples (Bazarian 2021)
cards.people: 1,901 patients with Glasgow Coma Scale 13–15 (the population the rapid test is intended for), drawn from 1,918 patients with valid CT scans and plasma specimens among the 2,011 enrolled in ALERT-TBI at 22 US and European sites, 2012–2014; plasma GFAP and UCH-L1 measured on the i-STAT Alinity TBI cartridge and compared with acute traumatic intracranial injury on head CT.
cards.result: The rapid test had sensitivity 0.958 (95% CI 0.906 to 0.982), specificity 0.404 (95% CI 0.382 to 0.427), negative predictive value 0.993 (95% CI 0.985 to 0.997) and positive predictive value 0.098 (95% CI 0.082 to 0.116) for acute traumatic intracranial injury on CT.
cards.watchOut: Not an independent validation — the same patients as the laboratory-test record, re-measured on a faster platform. A positive predictive value of 0.098 means nine of ten positive results have a normal CT: the test can only ever subtract scans, never add diagnostic certainty, and its specificity of 0.404 caps the subtraction at roughly a third of patients.

shelves.title: Hyperbaric oxygen for carbon monoxide poisoning: one positive trial (cognitive sequelae 25.0% versus 46.1%) against two that found nothing — and harm signals when treatment was pushed harder
shelves.question: In patients with acute carbon monoxide poisoning, does hyperbaric oxygen reduce delayed cognitive sequelae compared with normobaric oxygen?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adult · Carbon Monoxide Poisoning/complications/therapy · Cognition Disorders/etiology/prevention & control · Depression/etiology/prevention & control · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hyperbaric Oxygenation/methods · Logistic Models · Male · Memory Disorders/etiology/prevention & control · Neuropsychological Tests · Oxygen Inhalation Therapy
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the three randomised trials point in three directions. Weaver 2002 (PMID: 12362006), the only double-blind trial stopped early for benefit, found cognitive sequelae at six weeks in 25.0% on three hyperbaric sessions versus 46.1% on normobaric oxygen (P=0.007). Scheinkestel 1999 (PMID: 10092916) found no outcome measure worse on normobaric oxygen, more additional treatments on hyperbaric oxygen (28% versus 15%, P=0.01), and delayed neurological sequelae restricted to the hyperbaric group (P=0.03). Annane 2011 (PMID: 21125215) found one-month complete recovery of 58% with one hyperbaric session versus 61% on normobaric oxygen alone in patients with transient loss of consciousness, and significantly worse recovery with two hyperbaric sessions than one in comatose patients (47% versus 68%). PROPOSED SPLIT: benefit shown in one early-stopped trial, no benefit in two others, and worse outcomes when hyperbaric treatment was intensified — the question remains genuinely unsettled.

cards.headline: Weaver 2002: cognitive sequelae at six weeks in 25.0% after three hyperbaric sessions versus 46.1% on normobaric oxygen (P=0.007) — the trial was stopped early
cards.summary: Weaver 2002: cognitive sequelae at six weeks in 25.0% after three hyperbaric sessions versus 46.1% on normobaric oxygen (P=0.007) — the trial was stopped early
cards.people: 152 patients with symptomatic acute carbon monoxide poisoning (76 per group), randomised within 24 hours to three chamber sessions of hyperbaric oxygen or one normobaric-oxygen session plus two normobaric room-air sessions, with neuropsychological testing to 12 months.
cards.result: Cognitive sequelae at six weeks occurred in 19 of 76 (25.0%) in the hyperbaric group versus 35 of 76 (46.1%) in the normobaric group (P=0.007); adjusted odds ratio 0.45 (95% CI 0.22 to 0.92; P=0.03). Cognitive sequelae remained less frequent in the hyperbaric group at 12 months in the intention-to-treat analysis (P=0.04).
cards.watchOut: The trial was stopped after the third of four scheduled interim analyses, which inflates effect estimates; cerebellar dysfunction before treatment — a strong predictor of sequelae (odds ratio 5.71) — was also imbalanced at baseline (4% hyperbaric versus 15% normobaric, P=0.03), favouring the hyperbaric arm before treatment began.
cards.source: Weaver LK et al. Hyperbaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002. PMID: 12362006. cards.headline: Scheinkestel 1999: no outcome measure worse on normobaric oxygen — hyperbaric patients needed more extra treatments (28% versus 15%) and delayed sequelae occurred only in the hyperbaric group
cards.summary: Scheinkestel 1999: no outcome measure worse on normobaric oxygen — hyperbaric patients needed more extra treatments (28% versus 15%) and delayed sequelae occurred only in the hyperbaric group
cards.people: Patients of all grades of carbon monoxide poisoning referred to the Alfred Hospital hyperbaric service, Melbourne, September 1993 to December 1995 (pregnant women, children and burns victims excluded), randomised to daily 100-minute chamber treatments at 2.8 atmospheres (hyperbaric) or 1.0 atmosphere (normobaric sham) for three days, extended to six days if still abnormal, with continuous high-flow oxygen between treatments in both groups.
cards.result: More hyperbaric patients required additional treatments (28% versus 15%, P=0.01; in severely poisoned patients 35% versus 13%, P=0.001). Hyperbaric patients performed worse on the learning test at completion of treatment (P=0.01) and had more abnormal test results (P=0.02). Delayed neurological sequelae were restricted to hyperbaric patients (P=0.03). No outcome measure was worse in the normobaric group.
cards.watchOut: Both groups received high-dose oxygen throughout, so this trial tests the added value of pressure, not of oxygen; follow-up neuropsychology at one month was incomplete ('where possible'), and the record's abstract does not print the total number randomised.
cards.source: Scheinkestel CD et al. Hyperbaric or normobaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning: a randomised controlled clinical trial. The Medical Journal of Australia. 1999. randomised double-blind trial (scheinkestel 1999) patients of all grades of carbon monoxide poisoning referred to the alfred hospital hyperbaric service, melbourne, september 1993 to december 1995 (pregnant women, children and burns victims excluded), randomised to daily 100-minute chamber treatments at 2.8 atmospheres (hyperbaric) or 1.0 atmosphere (normobaric sham) for three days, extended to six days if still abnormal, with continuous high-flow oxygen between treatments in both groups. more hyperbaric patients required additional treatments (28% versus 15%, p=0.01; in severely poisoned patients 35% versus 13%, p=0.001). hyperbaric patients performed worse on the learning test at completion of treatment (p=0.01) and had more abnormal test results (p=0.02). delayed neurological sequelae were restricted to hyperbaric patients (p=0.03). no outcome measure was worse in the normobaric group. both groups received high-dose oxygen throughout, so this trial tests the added value of pressure, not of oxygen; follow-up neuropsychology at one month was incomplete ('where possible'), and the record's abstract does not print the total number randomised. scheinkestel cd et al. hyperbaric or normobaric oxygen for acute carbon monoxide poisoning: a randomised controlled clinical trial. the medical journal of australia. 1999. pmid: 10092916. mesh: adult · animals · carbon monoxide poisoning/complications/physiopathology/therapy · double-blind method · female · humans · hyperbaric oxygenation/adverse effects/methods · male · neuropsychological tests · oxygen inhalation therapy · severity of illness index · suicide, attempted · treatment outcome · victoria

cards.headline: Annane 2011: one hyperbaric session no better than normobaric oxygen (recovery 58% versus 61%), and two sessions worse than one in comatose patients (47% versus 68%)
cards.summary: Annane 2011: one hyperbaric session no better than normobaric oxygen (recovery 58% versus 61%), and two sessions worse than one in comatose patients (47% versus 68%)
cards.people: 385 patients with acute domestic carbon monoxide poisoning at a French critical care unit: trial A (transient loss of consciousness, n=179) randomised to 6 hours of normobaric oxygen or 4 hours of normobaric oxygen plus one hyperbaric session; trial B (initial coma, n=206) randomised to one versus two hyperbaric sessions on a normobaric background.
cards.result: Trial A: complete recovery at one month in 58% with one hyperbaric session versus 61% on normobaric oxygen alone (unadjusted odds ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.71) — no evidence of superiority. Trial B: complete recovery was significantly lower with two hyperbaric sessions than with one (47% versus 68%; unadjusted odds ratio 0.42, 95% CI 0.23 to 0.79).
cards.watchOut: Neither Annane trial compares hyperbaric oxygen with a sham chamber treatment, and trial B has no normobaric-only arm, so its harm signal is about dose (two sessions versus one), not about hyperbaric treatment versus none. The trials were not blinded.
cards.source: Annane D et al. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy for acute domestic carbon monoxide poisoning: two randomized controlled trials. Intensive Care Medicine. 2011. PMID: 21125215.
