cards.headline: Synthesis: one early-stopped positive trial, two null trials, and a dose-related harm signal — SPLIT
cards.summary: Synthesis: one early-stopped positive trial, two null trials, and a dose-related harm signal — SPLIT
cards.people: Three randomised trials (five randomised comparisons) of hyperbaric versus normobaric oxygen in acute carbon monoxide poisoning: Weaver 2002 (n=152), Scheinkestel 1999 (all-grade referrals), Annane 2011 (n=385).
cards.result: Cognitive sequelae at six weeks: 25.0% hyperbaric versus 46.1% normobaric in Weaver. Complete recovery at one month: 58% versus 61% (one session versus none, Annane A) and 47% versus 68% (two sessions versus one, Annane B). Delayed neurological sequelae restricted to the hyperbaric group in Scheinkestel. PROPOSED SPLIT: the evidence does not settle whether hyperbaric oxygen helps, and intensifying it may harm.
cards.watchOut: Single-trial flag does not apply, but the positive trial was stopped early with a baseline imbalance in a key prognostic sign, while the null trials were unblinded or sham-controlled with incomplete follow-up — every arm of this split carries a methodological catch, which is why the stamp is SPLIT rather than a verdict for either side. Tier C: held for the developer's personal verdict under the relaxed 4,000–5,000 intake tier.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weaver LK et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2002 (PMID: 12362006); Scheinkestel CD et al. The Medical Journal of Australia. 1999 (PMID: 10092916); Annane D et al. Intensive Care Medicine. 2011 (PMID: 21125215).

shelves.title: Rapid troponin pathways discharge more chest-pain patients within hours — 0/1-hour protocol freed 45.1% from the ED versus 32.3%, and a single undetectable troponin freed 46% within 4 hours, with no excess 30-day death or infarction in either randomised trial
shelves.question: In patients with chest pain, does a high-sensitivity troponin 0/1-hour pathway discharge safely compared with standard serial testing?
shelves.mesh: Acute Coronary Syndrome/blood,diagnosis,mortality,therapy · Aged · Australia · Biomarkers/blood · Cardiology Service, Hospital · Cause of Death · Emergency Service, Hospital · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Infarction/blood,diagnosis,mortality,therapy · Predictive Value of Tests · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Time Factors · Troponin T/blood · Workflow
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — for flow, with safety shown only to a non-inferiority standard over 30 days. In RAPID-TnT (Chew DP et al., PMID: 31478763), 3,288 patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome randomised to a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin T protocol versus a masked 0/3-hour protocol were discharged from the ED in 45.1% versus 32.3% of cases (p<0.001), with median ED stay 4.6 versus 5.6 hours and less functional testing (7.5% versus 11.0%); 30-day death or myocardial infarction was 1.0% in both arms (incidence rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.53–2.11; non-inferiority p=0.006), and negative predictive value among those discharged was 99.6%. In LoDED (Carlton EW et al., PMID: 32371401), a single undetectable troponin plus a non-ischaemic ECG discharged 46% within 4 hours without a 30-day major adverse cardiac event versus 37% on usual care (adjusted OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.84–2.98), and no patient with an undetectable first troponin had an event within 30 days. Neither trial was powered for rare missed events beyond its non-inferiority margin, and RAPID-TnT saw more myocardial injury recognised in the rapid arm. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): rapid troponin pathways safely speed discharge in two randomised trials; the benefit is hours and avoided tests, not lives.

cards.headline: RAPID-TnT 2019: 0/1-hour protocol discharged 45.1% from the ED versus 32.3% on 0/3-hour standard care — 30-day death or MI 1.0% in both arms, non-inferior
cards.summary: RAPID-TnT 2019: 0/1-hour protocol discharged 45.1% from the ED versus 32.3% on 0/3-hour standard care — 30-day death or MI 1.0% in both arms, non-inferior
cards.people: 3,378 patients presenting to emergency departments in Australia with suspected acute coronary syndrome (3,288 analysed; median age 59 years, 47% female), randomised August 2015–April 2019 to a 0/1-hour high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T protocol reported to the limit of detection (<5 ng/L) or to a masked 0/3-hour protocol reported to ≤29 ng/L, followed for 30 days.
cards.result: Discharge from the ED: 45.1% on the 0/1-hour protocol versus 32.3% on standard care (p<0.001); median ED length of stay 4.6 hours (IQR 3.4–6.4) versus 5.6 hours (4.0–7.1) (p<0.001); functional cardiac testing 7.5% versus 11.0% (p<0.001). The 30-day primary endpoint of all-cause death or myocardial infarction occurred in 17/1,646 (1.0%) versus 16/1,642 (1.0%) (incidence rate ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.53–2.11; non-inferiority p=0.006 against a 0.5% absolute margin; superiority p=0.867). Negative predictive value among discharged patients was 99.6% (95% CI 99.0–99.9%). More myocardial injury was recognised in the 0/1-hour arm.
cards.watchOut: Non-inferiority was declared against a 0.5% absolute margin in a population whose event rate was only 1.0% — the trial cannot exclude a small absolute excess of missed events, and the extra myocardial injury it unmasked has no agreed management pathway yet.
cards.source: Chew DP et al. A Randomized Trial of a 1-Hour Troponin T Protocol in Suspected Acute Coronary Syndromes: The Rapid Assessment of Possible Acute Coronary Syndrome in the Emergency Department With High-Sensitivity Troponin T Study (RAPID-TnT). Circulation. 2019. PMID: 31478763. Registry ID: ACTRN12615001379505 (stated in the record's abstract). cards.headline: LoDED 2020: single undetectable troponin plus normal ECG discharged 46% within 4 hours with no 30-day event, versus 37% on usual care (adjusted OR 1.58, CI crossing 1)
cards.summary: LoDED 2020: single undetectable troponin plus normal ECG discharged 46% within 4 hours with no 30-day event, versus 37% on usual care (adjusted OR 1.58, CI crossing 1)
cards.people: 632 adults (629 analysed; mean age 53.8 years, 41% women) presenting to eight UK hospitals with chest pain, a non-ischaemic ECG, peak symptoms <6 hours earlier, and a clinician intending ACS rule-out investigations, randomised June 2018–March 2019 to the LoDED strategy (discharge if the presentation high-sensitivity troponin was undetectable) or the usual rule-out strategy.
cards.result: The primary outcome — discharge within 4 hours of arrival without a major adverse cardiac event within 30 days — occurred in 141/309 (46%) on LoDED versus 114/311 (37%) on usual care (pooled adjusted OR 1.58, 95% CI 0.84–2.98). Overall 7% of patients had a major adverse cardiac event within 30 days; no patient with an initial undetectable troponin had one within 30 days.
cards.watchOut: The adjusted odds ratio's confidence interval crosses 1 and the authors note effectiveness varied between hospitals and depended on how good each site's usual pathway already was — the strategy adds most where baseline practice is slowest.
cards.source: Carlton EW et al. Limit of detection of troponin discharge strategy versus usual care: randomised controlled trial. Heart. 2020. PMID: 32371401. Registry ID: ISRCTN86184521. cards.headline: Synthesis: two randomised pathway trials agree — hours saved and tests avoided, safety to a 30-day non-inferiority standard, no outcome benefit beyond flow
cards.summary: Synthesis: two randomised pathway trials agree — hours saved and tests avoided, safety to a 30-day non-inferiority standard, no outcome benefit beyond flow
cards.people: Two randomised trials totalling about 3,900 emergency-department patients with suspected acute coronary syndrome (RAPID-TnT, Australia, n=3,288 analysed; LoDED, UK, n=629 analysed), each testing a rapid high-sensitivity troponin discharge strategy against standard serial testing.
cards.result: Early discharge rose from 32.3% to 45.1% (ED discharge, RAPID-TnT) and from 37% to 46% (discharge within 4 hours without a 30-day event, LoDED). Thirty-day death or myocardial infarction was 1.0% in both RAPID-TnT arms (non-inferiority p=0.006); no LoDED patient with an undetectable first troponin had a 30-day event. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): the proven gain is speed and avoided downstream testing, at a safety standard of non-inferiority over 30 days.
cards.watchOut: Both trials predate widespread 0/1-hour adoption as usual care, so the incremental gain over a modern standard pathway is smaller than the gain over the comparators tested; neither trial addresses the management of the extra myocardial injury rapid reporting detects. Single-programme strategy evidence in a relaxed-intake band — Tier C set.
cards.source: Synthesis of Chew DP et al. Circulation. 2019 (PMID: 31478763); Carlton EW et al. Heart. 2020 (PMID: 32371401).

shelves.title: Broken finger or thumb: buddy taping matched splinting for children's reduced finger fractures, splint choice changed mallet-finger failure rates, and one small trial favoured a wire over a splint patients kept removing
shelves.question: I've broken my finger or thumb — should it be buddy-taped, splinted, or fixed with an operation, and does the choice change how well it heals?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Athletic Tape · Child · Child, Preschool · Female · Finger Injuries/surgery · Finger Injuries/therapy · Finger Phalanges/injuries · Fractures, Bone/surgery · Fractures, Bone/therapy · Humans · Male · Range of Motion, Articular · Splints
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer depends on which finger injury is being treated, because the comparative evidence is injury-specific. For displaced extra-articular finger fractures in children that have been put back into place (closed reduction), one randomised trial (Weber 2025, PMID: 39487748; 81 children) found buddy taping non-inferior to splinting for keeping the fracture aligned, and more comfortable; a systematic review of children's Salter-Harris II finger fractures (Sohail 2026, PMID: 40304136) found every fracture healed without complications whichever method was used. For mallet finger (the fingertip droops because the extensor tendon is injured, with or without a small fracture), a multicentre randomised trial (O'Brien 2011, PMID: 21272714; 64 patients) found no difference in the final droop between three splint types, but treatment failure was 23.8% with a Stack splint and 23.8% with a dorsal aluminium splint versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint. And in one small randomised comparison (Mendoza 2022, PMID: 35572082; 41 patients), a Kirschner wire outperformed a Stack splint for mallet finger — but mainly because most splint patients did not keep the splint on. BOUNDARY: this shelf cards only the comparative immobilisation and wire-versus-splint evidence actually found. Fractures needing surgery for other reasons (open fractures, joint involvement, rotation that cannot be corrected) and thumb fractures specifically have no comparative trial carded here — no randomised comparison for thumb fractures was found. PROPOSED SPLIT: taping and splinting look equivalent for children's reduced finger fractures; for mallet finger the splint must fit and be worn, and a wire beat a poorly worn splint in one small study.

cards.headline: Weber 2025 (children's finger fractures): buddy taping was non-inferior to splinting after closed reduction — displacement 3 versus 5 — and significantly more comfortable
cards.summary: Weber 2025 (children's finger fractures): buddy taping was non-inferior to splinting after closed reduction — displacement 3 versus 5 — and significantly more comfortable
cards.people: 81 children aged 4–16 years with displaced extra-articular fractures of the proximal or middle phalanx, treated with closed reduction and then randomised to buddy taping (43 children) or splinting (38 children).
cards.result: Secondary displacement occurred in 3 children in the taping group and 5 in the splinting group; the risk difference fell below the predefined 10% non-inferiority margin, so taping was non-inferior to splinting for maintaining alignment. Comfort was significantly higher with taping. There were no differences between the groups in analgesic use or in total active motion at 6 months.
cards.watchOut: One trial, 81 children, one fracture pattern (displaced extra-articular proximal/middle phalangeal fractures that had already been successfully reduced). It does not cover fractures that could not be reduced, fractures into the joint, thumb fractures, or adults. Non-inferiority within a 10% margin is not proof of exact equality — it rules out taping being worse by more than that margin on this outcome.
cards.source: Weber et al. Buddy taping versus splinting for displaced extra-articular phalangeal fractures in children. J Hand Surg Eur Vol. 2025. PMID: 39487748. Registry ID: NCT04068935. cards.headline: Sohail 2026 (systematic review, children's Salter-Harris II finger fractures): every fracture healed with no complications under nonsurgical care; the included RCT found less displacement, better comfort and lower cost with taping
cards.summary: Sohail 2026 (systematic review, children's Salter-Harris II finger fractures): every fracture healed with no complications under nonsurgical care; the included RCT found less displacement, better comfort and lower cost with taping
cards.people: 5 studies (1 randomised trial, 3 prospective, 1 retrospective) of nonsurgical treatment of Salter-Harris II fractures of the proximal or middle phalanx in children, comparing taping and splinting approaches.
cards.result: Across the included studies all fractures healed, there were no complications, and range of motion was full or near-full. The included randomised trial (Weber 2019, 99 children) found secondary displacement in 1 of 52 taped children versus 3 of 47 splinted children, near-identical total active motion (259 degrees versus 262 degrees, P=.51), better early comfort with taping (visual analogue score 0.9 versus 2.0 at 5 days, P=.01), and lower cost (38 euros versus 160 euros). The review's authors concluded that small samples and heterogeneity prevented a conclusive recommendation between taping and splinting.
cards.watchOut: This review overlaps the Weber 2025 card above (a related trial from the same research area) — it is corroboration, not a wholly independent body of evidence. The review's abstract reports the Weber 2019 displacement comparison in percentage terms that differ from the counts in the full text; the counts (1/52 versus 3/47) are what is printed on this card. Growth-plate (Salter-Harris) fractures in children only — nothing here transfers directly to adult finger fractures.
cards.source: Sohail et al. Nonsurgical treatment of Salter-Harris II fractures of the proximal and middle phalanx in children: a systematic review. Hand (N Y). 2026. PMID: 40304136. systematic review of nonsurgical treatment (sohail 2026) 5 studies (1 randomised trial, 3 prospective, 1 retrospective) of nonsurgical treatment of salter-harris ii fractures of the proximal or middle phalanx in children, comparing taping and splinting approaches. across the included studies all fractures healed, there were no complications, and range of motion was full or near-full. the included randomised trial (weber 2019, 99 children) found secondary displacement in 1 of 52 taped children versus 3 of 47 splinted children, near-identical total active motion (259 degrees versus 262 degrees, p=.51), better early comfort with taping (visual analogue score 0.9 versus 2.0 at 5 days, p=.01), and lower cost (38 euros versus 160 euros). the review's authors concluded that small samples and heterogeneity prevented a conclusive recommendation between taping and splinting. this review overlaps the weber 2025 card above (a related trial from the same research area) — it is corroboration, not a wholly independent body of evidence. the review's abstract reports the weber 2019 displacement comparison in percentage terms that differ from the counts in the full text; the counts (1/52 versus 3/47) are what is printed on this card. growth-plate (salter-harris) fractures in children only — nothing here transfers directly to adult finger fractures. sohail et al. nonsurgical treatment of salter-harris ii fractures of the proximal and middle phalanx in children: a systematic review. hand (n y). 2026. pmid: 40304136. registry id: none in the record (systematic review). mesh: athletic tape · child · finger injuries/therapy · finger phalanges/injuries · fractures, bone/therapy · humans · salter-harris fractures/therapy · splints

cards.headline: O'Brien 2011 (mallet finger splints): no difference in final droop between three splints — but failure was 23.8% with Stack and dorsal splints versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint
cards.summary: O'Brien 2011 (mallet finger splints): no difference in final droop between three splints — but failure was 23.8% with Stack and dorsal splints versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint
cards.people: 64 patients with acute type 1a/1b mallet finger, randomised to a Stack splint, a dorsal padded aluminium splint, or a custom-made thermoplastic thimble splint; all splints were worn continuously for 8 weeks followed by a 4-week graduated withdrawal.
cards.result: There was no difference between the splints in extensor lag (the residual fingertip droop) at 12 or 20 weeks. Treatment failure, however, occurred in 23.8% of the Stack group and 23.8% of the dorsal aluminium group versus 0% of the custom thermoplastic group (P=.04). There was a medium negative correlation between compliance and extensor lag — patients who wore their splint more had less droop. There were no differences in satisfaction or pain between the groups.
cards.watchOut: 64 patients across three arms means roughly 21 per splint — the 0% failure figure for the custom splint rests on a small denominator and could shift with a few events. The trial compares splint designs, all worn for the same 8 weeks; it does not test shorter wear, night-only wear, or surgery. Mallet finger here is the tendon injury pattern (type 1a/1b); large fracture fragments with joint subluxation are a different problem.
cards.source: O'Brien et al. A randomised trial of splinting for mallet finger. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2011. PMID: 21272714. Registry ID: NCT00310570. cards.headline: Mendoza 2022 (mallet finger, wire versus splint): 17 of 19 wired fingers recovered fully; only 7 of 22 splinted fingers completed treatment successfully — non-compliance drove the splint failures
cards.summary: Mendoza 2022 (mallet finger, wire versus splint): 17 of 19 wired fingers recovered fully; only 7 of 22 splinted fingers completed treatment successfully — non-compliance drove the splint failures
cards.people: 41 patients (mean age 43 years) with acute closed mallet finger (Doyle type I), randomised to Kirschner wire fixation (19 patients) or a Stack splint (22 patients), with treatment for about 6 weeks.
cards.result: 17 of the 19 patients treated with a Kirschner wire completed treatment with full recovery. In the Stack splint group only 7 of 22 completed treatment with success and 15 relapsed. The splint failures were driven by non-compliance — patients removing or not wearing the splint as instructed.
cards.watchOut: A single small study (41 patients), and its comparison is not purely wire versus splint: it is wire versus a splint that most patients did not wear properly (only about 61% of splint patients returned at 3 weeks in the full text). Read alongside the O'Brien card — where a well-fitting custom splint had no failures — the lesson may be about achieving continuous immobilisation by any means, not about wires being inherently superior.

cards.headline: Synthesis: for children's reduced finger fractures, taping does the splint's job more comfortably; for mallet finger, continuous immobilisation is what matters — and the splint patients actually wear beats the one they remove
cards.summary: Synthesis: for children's reduced finger fractures, taping does the splint's job more comfortably; for mallet finger, continuous immobilisation is what matters — and the splint patients actually wear beats the one they remove
cards.people: Four sources: a randomised non-inferiority trial in 81 children (Weber 2025), a systematic review of 5 studies in children (Sohail 2026), a multicentre randomised splint trial in 64 mallet-finger patients (O'Brien 2011), and a small randomised wire-versus-splint comparison in 41 mallet-finger patients (Mendoza 2022).
cards.result: Children's displaced extra-articular phalangeal fractures after closed reduction: taping non-inferior to splinting for secondary displacement (3 versus 5 events; Weber 2025), with all fractures healing across the review's studies (Sohail 2026). Mallet finger: final extensor lag did not differ between three splint designs, but failure was 23.8% with Stack and dorsal aluminium splints versus 0% with a custom thermoplastic splint (O'Brien 2011); a Kirschner wire achieved full recovery in 17 of 19 patients versus 7 of 22 completing successfully with a Stack splint, with non-compliance the main driver (Mendoza 2022). PROPOSED SPLIT — equivalence for taping versus splinting in the paediatric fracture tested; for mallet finger, the method that guarantees 6–8 weeks of continuous immobilisation wins, whichever method that is.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. This shelf does not cover thumb fractures (no comparative trial found), fractures involving the joint surface, open fractures, or fractures with rotation or shortening that cannot be corrected closed — those follow surgical judgement, not these cards. Every comparative study carded is small (41–99 participants); the direction of the findings is consistent, but none of them is definitive alone.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weber et al. J Hand Surg Eur Vol. 2025 (PMID: 39487748); Sohail et al. Hand (N Y). 2026 (PMID: 40304136); O'Brien et al. Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation. 2011 (PMID: 21272714); Mendoza Velez et al. Plast Surg (Oakv). 2022 (PMID: 35572082).

shelves.title: Broken leg (tibial shaft fracture): reamed versus unreamed nailing — no overall difference in the 1,319-patient SPRINT trial, with closed fractures favouring reamed nailing and open fractures trending the other way
shelves.question: I've broken my leg — for a tibial shaft fracture fixed with a nail down the centre of the bone, should the surgeon ream the canal before inserting the nail, or use an unreamed nail?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Double-Blind Method · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Fracture Fixation, Intramedullary/methods · Fracture Healing · Fractures, Ununited/etiology · Fractures, Ununited/pathology · Fractures, Ununited/surgery · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Reoperation · Tibial Fractures/etiology · Tibial Fractures/pathology · Tibial Fractures/surgery · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer differs for closed and open fractures. SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers one question within 'broken leg' — for an adult tibial shaft fracture treated with an intramedullary nail, should the medullary canal be reamed before the nail is inserted? In the SPRINT trial (PMID: 19047701; 1,319 adults, the dominant study in this field), the overall composite of major events (re-operation and related endpoints) did not differ significantly: 105 events with reamed versus 114 with unreamed nailing (relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.71–1.15). The split is in the subgroups: in CLOSED fractures, events occurred in 45 of 416 (11%) reamed versus 68 of 410 (17%) unreamed patients (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.96; p=0.03) — a relative reduction of about a third, an absolute difference of about 6 percentage points, driven largely by dynamization procedures. In OPEN fractures the trend ran the other way: 60 of 206 (29%) reamed versus 46 of 194 (24%) unreamed (relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 0.91–1.78; p=0.16), not significant. The Cochrane review (Duan 2012, PMID: 22258982) found insufficient evidence overall, with moderate-quality evidence of no clear difference in major re-operations, though reamed nailing clearly reduced implant failure (relative risk 0.42). The SPRINT economic analysis (Briel 2011, PMID: 21669369) found near-identical costs and quality-adjusted life years for closed fractures. BOUNDARY: rhBMP-2 for open tibial fractures is homed on Shelf #3731 and is not re-carded here; femoral fractures and non-nailing treatments (plates, external fixation, casting) are outside this shelf's declared scope. PROPOSED SPLIT: no overall winner; reamed nailing favoured for closed tibial shaft fractures, no advantage — and a possible disadvantage — shown for open fractures.

cards.headline: SPRINT 2008 (1,319 patients): no overall difference in major events (relative risk 0.90) — but closed fractures favoured reamed nailing (11% versus 17% events) and open fractures trended the other way
cards.summary: SPRINT 2008 (1,319 patients): no overall difference in major events (relative risk 0.90) — but closed fractures favoured reamed nailing (11% versus 17% events) and open fractures trended the other way
cards.people: 1,319 adults with a tibial shaft fracture treated at multiple centres in a blinded randomised trial of reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing; 1,226 patients (93%) completed 1 year of follow-up (622 reamed, 604 unreamed).
cards.result: The primary composite outcome (major events including re-operation for nonunion and related procedures) occurred in 105 reamed versus 114 unreamed patients — relative risk 0.90 (95% CI 0.71–1.15), not significant. In closed fractures, events occurred in 45 of 416 (11%) reamed versus 68 of 410 (17%) unreamed patients (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.47–0.96; p=0.03); the difference was largely accounted for by dynamization procedures. In open fractures, events occurred in 60 of 206 (29%) reamed versus 46 of 194 (24%) unreamed patients (relative risk 1.27, 95% CI 0.91–1.78; p=0.16). Overall, 57 patients (4.6%) required implant exchange or bone grafting for nonunion.
cards.watchOut: The closed-versus-open split is a subgroup finding: the overall trial was null, and the closed-fracture advantage rests substantially on dynamization — a minor, often planned secondary procedure — rather than on nonunion surgery itself. Subgroup effects in a null trial are hypothesis-grading evidence, not proof; the open-fracture trend toward harm (relative risk 1.27) was not significant either. Both directions should be read as 'favoured' and 'not favoured', not as settled.
cards.source: SPRINT Investigators (Bhandari M et al.). Study to Prospectively Evaluate Reamed Intramedullary Nails in Patients with Tibial Fractures (SPRINT): reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, American Volume. 2008. PMID: 19047701. Registry ID: NCT00038129. cards.headline: Duan 2012 (Cochrane): insufficient evidence overall; moderate-quality evidence of no clear difference in major re-operations — but implant failure was clearly lower with reamed nails (relative risk 0.42)
cards.summary: Duan 2012 (Cochrane): insufficient evidence overall; moderate-quality evidence of no clear difference in major re-operations — but implant failure was clearly lower with reamed nails (relative risk 0.42)
cards.people: 11 trials (9 randomised, 2 quasi-randomised) with 2,093 participants and 2,123 tibial fractures, comparing reamed with unreamed intramedullary nailing and other nailing comparisons; the evidence is dominated by the SPRINT trial (1,319 of the participants).
cards.result: For reamed versus unreamed nailing (6 trials), major re-operations occurred in 66 of 789 versus 72 of 756 patients (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21) — no significant difference. There were no significant differences in nonunion, pain, deep infection, malunion or compartment syndrome. Implant failure was significantly less common with reamed nails: 35 of 789 versus 79 of 756 (relative risk 0.42, 95% CI 0.28–0.61). The reviewers concluded there was insufficient evidence overall, with moderate-quality evidence of no clear difference in major re-operations, and that reamed nailing may reduce nonunion-related re-operations in closed rather than open fractures.
cards.watchOut: This review is not independent of the SPRINT card above — SPRINT supplies most of its weight, so the two cards agreeing is largely the same data read twice. The smaller constituent trials were older and at higher risk of bias. The one clearly significant pooled finding, fewer implant failures with reamed nails, did not translate into fewer major re-operations overall.
cards.source: Duan et al. Intramedullary nailing for tibial shaft fractures: reamed versus unreamed nailing (Cochrane review). Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 22258982. Registry ID: none in the record (systematic review; review identifier CD008241). cards.headline: Briel 2011 (SPRINT economic analysis): for closed fractures, reamed and unreamed nailing cost almost exactly the same (difference 51 Canadian dollars) with no quality-of-life advantage either way
cards.summary: Briel 2011 (SPRINT economic analysis): for closed fractures, reamed and unreamed nailing cost almost exactly the same (difference 51 Canadian dollars) with no quality-of-life advantage either way
cards.type: Cost-utility analysis alongside a randomised trial (Briel 2011, SPRINT)
cards.people: Cost-utility analysis alongside the SPRINT trial: quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) calculated from Health Utilities Index 3 questionnaires over the first 12 months after nailing for SPRINT patients, with cost data from a convenience sample of 235 SPRINT patients; costs in 2008 Canadian dollars, from an Ontario governmental perspective.
cards.result: In closed fractures, reamed nailing gave 0.64 QALYs per patient versus 0.65 for unreamed (incremental effect −0.017 QALYs, 95% CI −0.058 to 0.021) at an incremental cost of 51 Canadian dollars per patient (95% CI −2,298 to 2,400). In open fractures, QALYs were 0.59 in both groups (incremental effect −0.0002, 95% CI −0.062 to 0.060) and reamed nailing cost 2,546 Canadian dollars more per patient (95% CI −1,773 to 6,864). The authors concluded there were small differences in both cost and effectiveness, with large uncertainty, between reamed and unreamed nailing.
cards.watchOut: Costs are 2008 Canadian dollars from one provincial payer's perspective, and the cost sample was a 235-patient convenience subset of the trial — the dollar figures do not transfer to other systems or years. The card's value is narrower: within the trial that found the clinical split, choosing the reamed technique for a closed fracture did not cost more, so the closed-fracture preference is not bought at a price.
cards.source: Briel M, Sprague S, Heels-Ansdell D, Guyatt G, Bhandari M, Blackhouse G, Sanders D, Schemitsch E, Swiontkowski M, Tornetta P 3rd, Walter SD, Goeree R; SPRINT Investigators. Economic evaluation of reamed versus unreamed intramedullary nailing in patients with closed and open tibial fractures: results from the study to prospectively evaluate reamed intramedullary nails in patients with tibial fractures (SPRINT). Value in Health. 2011. PMID: 21669369. Registry ID: NCT00038129. cards.headline: Synthesis: no overall winner — reamed nailing is favoured for closed tibial shaft fractures (relative risk 0.67 for major events) and not favoured for open fractures (relative risk 1.27, not significant)
cards.summary: Synthesis: no overall winner — reamed nailing is favoured for closed tibial shaft fractures (relative risk 0.67 for major events) and not favoured for open fractures (relative risk 1.27, not significant)
cards.people: Three sources: the SPRINT randomised trial (1,319 adults; PMID: 19047701), the Cochrane review of 11 trials and 2,093 participants (Duan 2012), and the SPRINT cost-utility analysis (Briel 2011).
cards.result: Overall major-event rates did not differ significantly between reamed and unreamed nailing in SPRINT (105 versus 114 events; relative risk 0.90, 95% CI 0.71–1.15) or in the Cochrane pooling of major re-operations (relative risk 0.88, 95% CI 0.64–1.21). The consistent signal is the interaction with fracture type: closed fractures did better with reaming (11% versus 17% events; relative risk 0.67; absolute difference about 6 percentage points), open fractures trended worse (29% versus 24%; relative risk 1.27, not significant), and reamed nails failed mechanically far less often (relative risk 0.42 for implant failure). Costs and QALYs were near-identical for closed fractures. PROPOSED SPLIT — reamed for closed tibial shaft fractures; no demonstrated advantage, and a possible disadvantage, for open fractures.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope is declared and narrow: adult tibial shaft fractures treated with an intramedullary nail. This shelf says nothing about femoral fractures, plate fixation, external fixation, or non-operative care, and nothing about rhBMP-2 in open tibial fractures (Shelf #3731). The closed/open split comes from subgroup analyses of one dominant trial plus a review dominated by that same trial — consistent, but not independently replicated at SPRINT's scale.
cards.source: Synthesis of SPRINT Investigators. The Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery, American Volume. 2008 (PMID: 19047701); Duan et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 22258982); Briel M et al. Value in Health. 2011 (PMID: 21669369).

shelves.title: Broken nose: closed reduction under local anaesthetic matched general anaesthetic in the comparative studies, and one cohort reported earlier reduction gave better results
shelves.question: I've broken my nose — does closed reduction work as well under local anaesthetic as under general anaesthetic, and does having it done sooner give a better result?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Airway Resistance · Anesthesia, General · Anesthesia, Local · Female · Fractures, Closed/therapy · Humans · Male · Manipulation, Orthopedic · Middle Aged · Nose/injuries · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the comparative evidence for broken-nose treatment is small and old, and it points to local anaesthesia being an acceptable substitute for general anaesthesia for closed reduction, with a suggestion that earlier reduction gives a better cosmetic result. A small randomised trial (Watson 1988, PMID: 3228992; 29 patients) found no significant differences between local and general anaesthesia in appearance or measured nasal airway after manipulation of a displaced fractured nose, and local anaesthesia was acceptable to all but one patient. A 2023 prospective comparison (Jana 2024, PMID: 38440457; 40 patients) likewise found no significant difference in pain scores between local and general anaesthesia, and 90% of local-anaesthesia patients said they would choose it again. On timing, one prospective cohort (Raghvi 2023, PMID: 37974860; 54 patients) reported better outcomes with reduction within 6 hours than after 2 weeks — but its abstract reports pooled results for all patients rather than per-group numbers, so the size of any timing advantage cannot be extracted. No comparative evidence on splinting after reduction was found that could be carded. PROPOSED POSSIBLE: local-anaesthetic reduction is a reasonable alternative to general anaesthesia for suitable fractures; the timing advantage is plausible but unquantified in the records fetched.

cards.headline: Watson 1988 (randomised trial): no significant difference between local and general anaesthesia for manipulating a fractured nose — in appearance or in measured nasal airway
cards.summary: Watson 1988 (randomised trial): no significant difference between local and general anaesthesia for manipulating a fractured nose — in appearance or in measured nasal airway
cards.people: 29 patients with a displaced fractured nose, randomised to manipulation under local anaesthetic (17 patients) or general anaesthetic (12 patients); nasal appearance was assessed and nasal airway measured by rhinomanometry before and after manipulation.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between the local and general anaesthesia groups in appearance or in nasal airway after manipulation. Bony manipulation itself did not affect the nasal airway. Local anaesthesia was acceptable to all but one of the 17 patients who received it. The authors concluded local anaesthesia is an acceptable method for manipulating a displaced fractured nose.
cards.watchOut: A very small trial — 29 patients, from 1988. 'No significant difference' in 29 patients rules out only very large differences; moderate advantages for either technique would be invisible at this size. It covers simple displaced fractures suitable for closed manipulation, not fractures needing open surgery or septal reconstruction.
cards.source: Watson DJ, Parker AJ, Slack RW, Griffiths MV. Local versus general anaesthesia for manipulation of the fractured nose: a randomised clinical trial. Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci. 1988. PMID: 3228992. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Jana 2024 (prospective comparison, 40 patients): pain scores after closed reduction did not differ significantly between local and general anaesthesia — and 90% of local-anaesthesia patients would choose it again
cards.summary: Jana 2024 (prospective comparison, 40 patients): pain scores after closed reduction did not differ significantly between local and general anaesthesia — and 90% of local-anaesthesia patients would choose it again
cards.people: 40 patients aged 18–60 years with Class 1–2 nasal bone and septal fractures at a hospital in Kolkata, India (2022): 20 underwent closed reduction under local anaesthesia with nerve blocks matched to the nose's nerve supply, and 20 under general anaesthesia.
cards.result: Pain-score differences between the local and general anaesthesia groups were not significant immediately after the operation (p=0.088) or at 6 hours (p=0.385). 18 of the 20 local-anaesthesia patients (90%) said they would choose local anaesthesia again. The authors concluded that, with blocks covering the full nerve supply of the nose, closed reduction under local anaesthesia gives pain control comparable to general anaesthesia.
cards.watchOut: Not randomised — patients were allocated to local or general anaesthesia in a prospective comparison of 20 patients per group, so selection could favour either arm, and 40 patients cannot exclude meaningful differences in cosmetic outcome (the study measured pain, not appearance or later deformity). The PubMed page for this record could not be fetched this session; the numbers above come from the published abstract, and the record's MeSH terms were not captured.

cards.headline: Raghvi 2023 (timing cohort, 54 patients): the authors report early closed reduction (within 6 hours) gave better results than late reduction (after 2 weeks) — but no per-group outcome numbers are reported
cards.summary: Raghvi 2023 (timing cohort, 54 patients): the authors report early closed reduction (within 6 hours) gave better results than late reduction (after 2 weeks) — but no per-group outcome numbers are reported
cards.type: Prospective cohort study of reduction timing (Raghvi 2023)
cards.people: 54 patients with nasal bone fractures attending a hospital ENT department in Chennai, India (August 2021–January 2022), in a prospective cohort comparing early closed reduction (within 6 hours of injury) with late closed reduction (after 2 weeks).
cards.result: Across all 54 patients after closed reduction, some deviation remained in 17 (31.5%), arch irregularity in 12 (22.2%), malalignment in 11 (20.4%), bony irregularity in 24 (44.4%) and bony displacement in 19 (35.2%); olfactory disturbance occurred in 2 (3.7%). Overall results were graded excellent in 27 patients (50%), fair in 16 (29.6%), good in 10 (18.5%) and poor in 1 (1.9%). The authors report that outcomes on deformity measures were better with early than with late reduction, but the abstract does not report the early and late groups' results separately, so the size of any timing advantage cannot be stated from this record.
cards.watchOut: This card is included with its central weakness on its face: the timing comparison — the reason for carding it — is asserted by the authors but not quantified per group in the abstract, so no effect size for early versus late reduction is claimed on this shelf. It is a single-centre, non-randomised cohort of 54 patients; patients reduced early may differ systematically from those who presented late. The PubMed page for this record could not be fetched this session; figures come from the published abstract, and MeSH terms were not captured.

shelves.title: Broken ribs: a serratus anterior plane block added to standard care doubled early pain control and halved 24-hour opioid use in the 210-patient SABRE trial
shelves.question: I've broken my ribs and it hurts to breathe — does a serratus anterior plane block (a regional nerve block into the chest wall) control the pain better than standard painkillers alone?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage · Analgesics, Opioid/therapeutic use · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Nerve Block/methods · Pain Management/methods · Pain Measurement · Rib Fractures/complications
shelves.balance: LIKELY (for early pain relief and opioid sparing) — SCOPE DECLARED: this shelf covers one analgesic technique for rib fractures, the ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block (SAPB), a regional block injected into the chest-wall fascial plane. In the SABRE trial (Partyka 2024, PMID: 38691350; 210 emergency-department patients, median age 71), adding a single SAPB to standard care roughly doubled the proportion achieving the composite pain goal at 4 hours (38 of 92 patients, 41%, versus 18 of 92, 19.6%) and halved median 24-hour opioid use (45 versus 91 milligram morphine equivalents). A smaller randomised trial (Teksen 2021, PMID: 33383266; 60 patients) found significantly lower 24-hour tramadol consumption and lower pain scores at every time point to 24 hours with SAPB, and less chronic pain afterwards (1 versus 9 patients). A third randomised trial (Zengin 2025, PMID: 40082780) compared SAPB head-to-head with intercostal nerve block: both worked, intercostal block was better in the first 4 hours, SAPB was better from 8 to 24 hours and no SAPB patient needed extra analgesia versus 43.3% of intercostal-block patients. No trial showed a difference in pneumonia or death. BOUNDARY: epidural analgesia for traumatic rib fractures is homed on Shelf #1313 and surgical stabilisation of rib fractures on Shelf #1268 — neither is re-carded here. Bruised ribs without fracture were not separately studied in these trials. PROPOSED LIKELY for the narrow claim: SAPB added to standard care improves early pain control and reduces opioid requirement after rib fractures.

cards.headline: SABRE 2024 (210 patients, 8 emergency departments): adding a serratus anterior plane block doubled early pain control (41% versus 19.6% met the pain goal at 4 hours) and halved 24-hour opioid use (45 versus 91 mg morphine equivalents)
cards.summary: SABRE 2024 (210 patients, 8 emergency departments): adding a serratus anterior plane block doubled early pain control (41% versus 19.6% met the pain goal at 4 hours) and halved 24-hour opioid use (45 versus 91 mg morphine equivalents)
cards.type: Multicentre open-label pragmatic randomised trial (SABRE, Partyka 2024)
cards.people: 210 patients aged 16 years and over presenting to 8 emergency departments in New South Wales, Australia with rib fractures (median age 71 years), randomised in an open-label pragmatic trial to a single ultrasound-guided serratus anterior plane block plus standard care (105 patients) or standard care alone (105 patients).
cards.result: The primary composite outcome — pain reduced by at least 2 points AND pain below 4 out of 10 at 4 hours — was met by 38 of 92 patients (41%) in the block group versus 18 of 92 (19.6%) in the control group in the complete-case intention-to-treat analysis; the record reports a relative risk of 0.73 (95% CI 0.60–0.89; P=.001) for this comparison, an absolute difference of about 22 percentage points in the proportions meeting the goal. Median opioid requirement in the first 24 hours was 45 milligram morphine equivalents (IQR 19–118) with the block versus 91 (IQR 34–155) without. Pneumonia occurred in 6 patients (10%) versus 7 (11%), median hospital stay was 4.2 versus 5 days, and 30-day mortality was 1 patient (1%) versus 3 (4%) — all similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Open-label: patients and clinicians knew who received the block, and the primary outcome is a pain score — exactly the kind of endpoint expectation can move. The trial shows better early pain control and less opioid use; it does not show fewer pneumonias, shorter stay, or fewer deaths, and was not powered to. One single-shot block was tested; catheter techniques and repeated blocks are outside this card.
cards.source: Partyka et al. Serratus Anterior Plane Block for rib fractures in the emergency department (the SABRE trial). JAMA Surgery. 2024. PMID: 38691350. Registry ID: ACTRN12621000040864 (ANZCTR). cards.headline: Teksen 2021 (60 patients): serratus plane block cut 24-hour tramadol use (p=0.02) and pain scores at every time point, and chronic pain afterwards was reported by 1 block patient versus 9 controls
cards.summary: Teksen 2021 (60 patients): serratus plane block cut 24-hour tramadol use (p=0.02) and pain scores at every time point, and chronic pain afterwards was reported by 1 block patient versus 9 controls
cards.people: 60 patients with rib fractures and a pain score (numerical rating scale) of at least 4, randomised to a serratus anterior plane block or control; both groups had patient-controlled analgesia available.
cards.result: Total 24-hour tramadol consumption was significantly lower in the block group (p=0.02; the abstract does not print the absolute amounts, so none are claimed here). Pain scores were lower with the block at 30 minutes and at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12 and 24 hours (p<0.001 through 4 hours; p=0.002; p=0.026 at the later points, as printed). At follow-up, chronic pain was reported by 9 control patients (4 at rest, 5 on effort) versus 1 block patient (on effort) (p=0.006).
cards.watchOut: 60 patients, single centre. The headline opioid figure cannot be quantified from the abstract — only its significance (p=0.02) — so this card supports direction, not size. cards.headline: Zengin 2025 (block versus block): intercostal nerve block relieved pain better in the first 4 hours; serratus plane block was better from 8 to 24 hours, and 0% of its patients needed extra analgesia versus 43.3% with intercostal block
cards.summary: Zengin 2025 (block versus block): intercostal nerve block relieved pain better in the first 4 hours; serratus plane block was better from 8 to 24 hours, and 0% of its patients needed extra analgesia versus 43.3% with intercostal block
cards.type: Randomised head-to-head trial of two regional blocks (Zengin 2025)
cards.people: Patients aged 18–65 years with unilateral isolated rib fractures (up to 6 ribs), randomised to superficial serratus anterior plane block (20 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine) or intercostal nerve block (3 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine per fractured rib). The abstract does not state the total number randomised (N not documented).
cards.result: Both blocks were effective. Intercostal block produced better pain-score (VAS) reduction in the first 4 hours, particularly for fractures of the 10th–11th ribs; the serratus plane block was better after 8 hours through 24 hours (p<0.05). Additional analgesia was required by 0% of the serratus-block group versus 43.3% of the intercostal-block group (p<0.001). No complications occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: This trial compares two active blocks — it cannot say whether either beats no block (the SABRE and Teksen cards carry that comparison). The total sample size is not stated in the abstract fetched this session and is printed on this card as not documented rather than guessed. Younger patients (18–65) with isolated unilateral fractures only; SABRE's older, broader population is the better guide for the typical elderly rib-fracture patient.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a serratus anterior plane block added to standard care improves early pain control and roughly halves first-day opioid use after rib fractures; no effect on pneumonia or survival has been shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: a serratus anterior plane block added to standard care improves early pain control and roughly halves first-day opioid use after rib fractures; no effect on pneumonia or survival has been shown
cards.people: Three randomised trials: SABRE (210 emergency-department patients; Partyka 2024), a single-centre trial versus standard care with patient-controlled analgesia (60 patients; Teksen 2021), and a head-to-head block comparison (sample size not stated in the abstract; Zengin 2025).
cards.result: Versus standard care: the composite early-pain goal was met by 41% versus 19.6% of patients (SABRE), median 24-hour opioid use was 45 versus 91 milligram morphine equivalents (SABRE), and 24-hour tramadol consumption was significantly lower with the block (Teksen 2021, p=0.02, amounts not reported). Versus another active block: serratus block lasted longer (better pain scores 8–24 hours; 0% versus 43.3% needing extra analgesia) while intercostal block acted better in the first 4 hours (Zengin 2025). Pneumonia and mortality did not differ in SABRE. PROPOSED LIKELY — for early pain relief and opioid sparing only, on two randomised trials against standard care.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope is declared: serratus anterior plane block only. Epidural analgesia (Shelf #1313), erector spinae and other blocks (not carded here), and surgical rib fixation (Shelf #1268) are separate questions with their own shelves. The largest trial was open-label with a pain-score primary outcome; the stamp LIKELY applies to pain and opioid use in the first 24 hours, not to pneumonia, length of stay, or survival, where no benefit has been shown.
cards.source: Synthesis of Partyka et al. JAMA Surgery. 2024 (PMID: 38691350); Tekşen et al. The American Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2021 (PMID: 33383266); Zengin et al. BMC Anesthesiology. 2025 (PMID: 40082780).

shelves.title: Earlier antibiotics in suspected sepsis: every carded study is observational — delay is associated with higher mortality (about 4–12% relative per hour), steepest in septic shock, and no trial calibrates a fixed door-to-antibiotic target
shelves.question: In emergency-department patients with suspected sepsis, does earlier empirical antibiotic administration reduce mortality, and how strong is the evidence behind fixed door-to-antibiotic targets?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Anti-Bacterial Agents/administration & dosage/therapeutic use · Emergency Service, Hospital · Sepsis/drug therapy/mortality · Spain · Time Factors · Time-to-Treatment · Observational Studies as Topic
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded record is a cohort study or a review of cohort studies; there is no randomised trial of antibiotic timing. The direction is consistent. Rodríguez 2025 (PMID: 39898946; 7 emergency-department cohort studies, 118,349 patients, no meta-analysis performed) found per-hour delay carried an adjusted odds ratio of 1.09 for hospital mortality in its high-quality studies. Kumar 2006 (PMID: 16625125; 2,731 patients with septic shock) found survival of 79.9% when effective antibiotics began within the first hour of hypotension, falling an average of 7.6% per hour over the next 6 hours. Seymour 2017 (PMID: 28528569; 49,331 patients under New York's mandated protocol) found a much shallower gradient — odds ratio 1.04 per hour to antibiotics. The evidence supports prompt treatment, fastest for the sickest; it does not calibrate a precise fixed door-to-antibiotic hour, because timing is confounded by how obviously ill the patient looks. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.

cards.headline: Rodríguez 2025: a systematic review of 7 emergency-department cohort studies (118,349 patients) found mortality tended to rise with each hour of antibiotic delay — but pooled no meta-analysis and graded only 3 studies high quality
cards.summary: Rodríguez 2025: a systematic review of 7 emergency-department cohort studies (118,349 patients) found mortality tended to rise with each hour of antibiotic delay — but pooled no meta-analysis and graded only 3 studies high quality
cards.type: Systematic review of observational cohort studies (Rodríguez 2025)
cards.people: 7 observational cohort studies comprising 118,349 adults attended in emergency departments for serious infection or sepsis, of whom 74,141 (62.6%) received early antibiotic treatment; studies published 2010–2023, reviewed to PRISMA with Newcastle-Ottawa quality scoring (3 high quality, 3 moderate, 1 low).
cards.result: The review compared early (within 3 hours of triage) versus deferred (3–6 hours) empirical antibiotics narratively, with no meta-analysis. In the high-quality studies: hospital and 30-day mortality tended to increase when antibiotics were given more than 6 hours after triage versus within 1 hour (hazard ratio 2.25, 95% CI 0.91 to 5.59; p = 0.08); each hour of delay after triage carried an adjusted odds ratio of 1.09 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.13) for hospital mortality; and each additional hour of delay was associated with a 10% relative increase (95% CI 5% to 14%) in the probability of 360-day mortality. The authors recommend starting antibiotics preferably within 3 hours of triage in serious infection without septic shock.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is observational: patients who get antibiotics fastest differ systematically (clearer presentations, more obvious severity), and no pooled estimate exists — the review's own numbers are per-study hazard and odds ratios, several with confidence intervals crossing 1.
cards.source: Rodríguez MR et al. Early empirical antibiotherapy in patients attended for suspected sepsis in emergency departments: a systematic review. Emergencias. 2025. PMID: 39898946. cards.headline: Kumar 2006: in septic shock, survival was 79.9% when effective antibiotics began within the first hour of hypotension, falling by an average of 7.6% with each further hour of delay over the next 6 hours
cards.summary: Kumar 2006: in septic shock, survival was 79.9% when effective antibiotics began within the first hour of hypotension, falling by an average of 7.6% with each further hour of delay over the next 6 hours
cards.people: 2,731 adults with septic shock in 14 intensive care units in Canada and the United States (1989–2004), studied retrospectively; 2,154 (78.9%) received effective antimicrobial therapy only after the onset of recurrent or persistent hypotension.
cards.result: Administration of an antimicrobial effective against the isolated or suspected pathogens within the first hour of documented hypotension was associated with a survival rate of 79.9%. Each hour of delay over the ensuing 6 hours was associated with an average decrease in survival of 7.6%, and delay carried an adjusted odds ratio for in-hospital mortality of 1.119 per hour (95% CI 1.103 to 1.136). Median time to effective therapy was 6 hours; only 50% of patients received effective therapy within 6 hours of hypotension onset.
cards.watchOut: This is septic shock with documented hypotension — the sickest end of sepsis — in data from 1989–2004. Its steep per-hour gradient is routinely quoted for all suspected sepsis, a much broader and less ill population than the one studied.
cards.source: Kumar A et al. Duration of hypotension before initiation of effective antimicrobial therapy is the critical determinant of survival in human septic shock. Critical Care Medicine. 2006. cards.headline: Seymour 2017: across 49,331 New York sepsis patients under a mandated protocol, each hour to antibiotics carried an odds ratio of 1.04 for in-hospital mortality — a far shallower gradient than Kumar's
cards.summary: Seymour 2017: across 49,331 New York sepsis patients under a mandated protocol, each hour to antibiotics carried an odds ratio of 1.04 for in-hospital mortality — a far shallower gradient than Kumar's
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study of a mandated sepsis protocol (Seymour 2017)
cards.people: 49,331 patients with sepsis and septic shock reported to the New York State Department of Health (2014–2016) at 149 hospitals, all with a sepsis protocol initiated within 6 hours of emergency-department arrival and the 3-hour bundle completed within 12 hours; 40,696 (82.5%) completed the bundle within 3 hours.
cards.result: Longer time to completion of the 3-hour bundle was associated with higher risk-adjusted in-hospital mortality (odds ratio 1.04 per hour, 95% CI 1.02 to 1.05), as was longer time to administration of antibiotics (odds ratio 1.04 per hour, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.06). Time to completion of the initial intravenous fluid bolus was not associated with mortality (odds ratio 1.01 per hour, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.02). Median time to antibiotics was 0.95 hours.
cards.watchOut: Risk adjustment cannot remove the core bias: clinicians treat the obviously septic fastest, and protocol-era data compress the timing range (median under 1 hour), which shrinks the observable gradient. An odds ratio of 1.04 per hour is an association, not a measured effect of a fixed door-to-antibiotic target.
cards.source: Seymour CW et al. Time to Treatment and Mortality during Mandated Emergency Care for Sepsis. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28528569. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: earlier antibiotics are consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data — steepest in septic shock, shallow in protocol-era all-sepsis cohorts — and no randomised timing trial exists (observational only)
cards.summary: Synthesis: earlier antibiotics are consistently associated with lower mortality in observational data — steepest in septic shock, shallow in protocol-era all-sepsis cohorts — and no randomised timing trial exists (observational only)
cards.people: The carded evidence: one 2025 systematic review of 7 emergency-department cohort studies (118,349 patients), one retrospective septic-shock cohort (2,731 patients), and one mandated-protocol cohort (49,331 patients). No randomised trial of antibiotic timing is carded, because none exists in this evidence set.
cards.result: All three records associate delay with higher mortality: per-hour odds ratios of 1.09 for hospital mortality in the review's high-quality studies (Rodríguez 2025), an adjusted odds ratio of 1.119 per hour in septic shock with survival falling 7.6% per hour over 6 hours (Kumar 2006), and an odds ratio of 1.04 per hour in the New York mandate cohort (Seymour 2017). The gradient flattens as the population broadens from shock to all sepsis and as baseline speed improves — which is why fixed door-to-antibiotic targets rest on weaker ground than 'treat promptly, fastest for the sickest'. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Observational timing studies can justify urgency; they cannot calibrate an exact hour threshold, because the patients treated latest are systematically different in ways no adjustment fully captures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Rodríguez MR et al. Emergencias. 2025 (PMID: 39898946); Kumar A et al. Critical Care Medicine. 2006 (PMID: 16625125); Seymour CW et al. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28528569).

shelves.title: Preoperative statin loading before cardiac surgery: no reduction in clinical events in pooled randomised evidence (the treatment made no difference), with a possible increase in acute kidney injury — small trials show only biomarker and strain benefits
shelves.question: Does preoperative statin loading reduce events before cardiac surgery?
shelves.mesh: Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Humans · Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA Reductase Inhibitors · Perioperative Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence says no for clinical events. The anchor is a meta-analysis of randomised trials in cardiac surgery (Putzu 2016, PMID: 27919293; 23 RCTs, 5,102 patients): in trials at low risk of bias, statin therapy in the days before surgery made no difference to postoperative atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infections or mortality (the treatment made no difference), and was associated with more acute kidney injury (23.82% vs 19.86%; OR 1.26, 95% CI 1.05 to 1.52). Individual loading trials agree on events while differing on biomarkers: a randomised trial of 60 mg rosuvastatin loading before off-pump bypass (Youn 2011, PMID: 22263153; N = 142) found 30-day major adverse cardiac events in 1.4% vs 5.6% (P = 0.37, not significant) with lower postoperative enzyme release, and a 2024 valve-replacement trial (Prajapathi, PMID: 38681712) found better strain recovery and lower biomarker release with 40 mg rosuvastatin started 7 days before surgery, without clinical-event power. The definitive large single trial of perioperative rosuvastatin (STICS) is homed on shelf #1316 and is not re-carded here; its presence inside the Putzu meta-analysis is part of why the pooled answer is null. PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — preoperative statin loading made no difference to clinical events in randomised evidence and may increase acute kidney injury.

cards.headline: Putzu 2016: across 23 randomised trials (5,102 patients), statin therapy before cardiac surgery made no difference to atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infection or mortality — and was associated with more acute kidney injury (OR 1.26)
cards.summary: Putzu 2016: across 23 randomised trials (5,102 patients), statin therapy before cardiac surgery made no difference to atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infection or mortality — and was associated with more acute kidney injury (OR 1.26)
cards.people: Adults undergoing cardiac surgery in 23 randomised controlled trials of preoperative statin therapy versus placebo or no treatment, totalling 5,102 patients; the primary analysis was restricted to trials at low risk of bias (search to 1 November 2016).
cards.result: In low-risk-of-bias trials there was no difference in postoperative atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infections, or mortality (the treatment made no difference). Acute kidney injury was more frequent with statins: 314 of 1,318 (23.82%) versus 262 of 1,319 (19.86%); OR 1.26 (95% CI 1.05 to 1.52), P = 0.01, supported by trial sequential analysis. On sensitivity analysis, statin therapy was associated with a slight increase in hospital mortality, and analyses including high or unclear risk-of-bias trials likewise showed no benefit on any outcome. The authors conclude there is no evidence that statin therapy in the days prior to cardiac surgery is beneficial.
cards.watchOut: A pooled null across many small trials plus one large trial (STICS, homed on shelf #1316) is stronger than any single small positive trial on this shelf: biomarker improvements in the small trials did not translate into fewer clinical events in the pooled randomised data.
cards.source: Putzu A et al. Perioperative statin therapy in cardiac surgery: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Critical Care. 2016. PMID: 27919293. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Youn 2011: 60 mg rosuvastatin loading before off-pump bypass did not significantly reduce 30-day major adverse cardiac events (1.4% vs 5.6%, P = 0.37) in 142 patients, though enzyme release was lower
cards.summary: Youn 2011: 60 mg rosuvastatin loading before off-pump bypass did not significantly reduce 30-day major adverse cardiac events (1.4% vs 5.6%, P = 0.37) in 142 patients, though enzyme release was lower
cards.people: 142 patients with stable angina scheduled for off-pump coronary artery bypass grafting, randomised to pretreatment with 60 mg rosuvastatin (n = 71) or no pretreatment (n = 71).
cards.result: Major adverse cardiac events within 30 days occurred in 1 patient (1.4%) in the rosuvastatin group and 4 patients (5.6%) in the control group (P = 0.37, not significant). Mean maximum creatine kinase-MB after surgery was lower with rosuvastatin (10.7 ± 9.75 vs 14.6 ± 12.9 ng/mL, P = 0.04), as was mean maximum troponin T (0.18 ± 0.16 vs 0.39 ± 0.70 ng/mL, P = 0.02). The authors conclude high-dose rosuvastatin loading did not significantly reduce 30-day events but reduced myocardial ischaemia markers after off-pump bypass.
cards.watchOut: With 5 events in total, this trial could not detect or exclude a clinically important event difference; its significant findings are laboratory markers, not events.
cards.source: Youn YN et al. Impact of High-Dose Statin Pretreatment in Patients with Stable Angina during Off-Pump Coronary Artery Bypass. The Korean Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2011. PMID: 22263153. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Prajapathi 2024: rosuvastatin 40 mg started 7 days before valve replacement lessened the fall in ventricular strain and lowered biomarker release — surrogate outcomes only, participant N not documented in the record
cards.summary: Prajapathi 2024: rosuvastatin 40 mg started 7 days before valve replacement lessened the fall in ventricular strain and lowered biomarker release — surrogate outcomes only, participant N not documented in the record
cards.people: Patients undergoing valve replacement for rheumatic mitral valve disease, randomised to statin-loaded (rosuvastatin 40 mg initiated 7 days prior to surgery) or non-loaded groups; participant N not documented in the record.
cards.result: The percentage decline in strain at 48 hours was significantly lower in the statin-loaded group (global longitudinal strain 35.8% vs 38.8%, global circumferential strain 34% vs 44.1%, global radial strain 45.7% vs 52.6%; P < 0.001), strain values at 30 days were higher in the loaded group, troponin I, creatine kinase-MB and NT-proBNP at 8, 24 and 48 hours were lower in the loaded group, and hospital and intensive care stays were shorter. No clinical-event comparison (death, infarction, atrial fibrillation) is reported in the record. The authors describe preoperative high-dose rosuvastatin as cardioprotective on these measures.
cards.watchOut: Strain and biomarker benefits without event outcomes are exactly the pattern the pooled randomised analysis (Putzu 2016) shows does not carry through to fewer events; this trial's participant number is not documented in its record, so it is weighted accordingly.
cards.source: Prajapathi S et al. Does high dose statin pretreatment affect global strains in patients undergoing valve replacement. Indian Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2024. PMID: 38681712. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Synthesis: preoperative statin loading improves enzyme and imaging surrogates in small trials, but pooled randomised evidence shows no reduction in clinical events and a possible increase in acute kidney injury
cards.summary: Synthesis: preoperative statin loading improves enzyme and imaging surrogates in small trials, but pooled randomised evidence shows no reduction in clinical events and a possible increase in acute kidney injury
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 23 randomised cardiac-surgery trials (5,102 patients), one randomised off-pump bypass loading trial (N = 142), and one randomised valve-replacement trial (N not documented in the record). Total documented participants exceed 5,200, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled low-bias randomised data show no difference in atrial fibrillation, myocardial infarction, stroke, infection or mortality, with acute kidney injury at 23.82% vs 19.86% (OR 1.26) (Putzu 2016). The bypass loading trial's event difference (1.4% vs 5.6%) was not significant (Youn 2011), and the valve trial reports only strain and biomarker outcomes (Prajapathi 2024). PROPOSED MAYBE (benefit) unproven — the treatment made no difference to clinical events.
cards.watchOut: Continuing a chronic statin through surgery is a different question from giving a new loading dose to a statin-naive patient; this shelf answers only the loading question, and the large STICS trial is read at its home on shelf #1316.
cards.source: Synthesis of Putzu A et al. Critical Care. 2016 (PMID: 27919293); Youn YN et al. Korean Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2011 (PMID: 22263153); Prajapathi S et al. Indian Journal of Thoracic and Cardiovascular Surgery. 2024 (PMID: 38681712).

shelves.title: Stopping GLP-1 drugs before endoscopy (observational only): users have more retained gastric contents and holding is associated with less retention — but no study shows holding prevents aspiration, and gastroparesis patients were excluded from the evidence
shelves.question: Should adults with gastroparesis stop GLP-1 receptor agonists before endoscopy or surgery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Diabetes Mellitus, Type 2 · Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal · Gastrointestinal Contents · Glucagon-Like Peptide-1 Receptor Agonists · Pneumonia, Aspiration · Respiratory Aspiration of Gastric Contents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face. No randomised trial has tested holding versus continuing a GLP-1 receptor agonist before endoscopy or surgery, and no carded study enrolled patients because they had diagnosed gastroparesis — the largest cohort (Wu 2024, PMID: 38485835) explicitly excluded known gastroparesis, so this shelf answers the holding question for GLP-1 users coming to endoscopy, with gastroparesis patients the plausibly highest-risk group the evidence does not directly measure. What the observational evidence does show is consistent on the intermediate outcome and null on the feared one: across 23 observational studies and 262,018 patients, GLP-1 use was associated with about 4.5-fold higher odds of residual gastric contents and of prematurely terminated endoscopy, but no difference in aspiration pneumonia (OR 0.96) (Baig 2025, PMID: 39694296). Holding the drug the way anaesthesia guidance advises was associated with less retention in the one multicentre study that classified holding (4.4% vs 12.7%), with no aspiration events in either group and no significant difference in intubation or aborted procedures (Phan 2025, PMID: 39016372); glycaemic control predicted retention at least as strongly as the drug itself. For surgery under general anaesthesia there is no direct comparative evidence in the carded records at all. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: holding a GLP-1 receptor agonist before elective endoscopy probably reduces retained gastric contents and abandoned procedures, but a reduction in aspiration itself has never been shown, and patients with gastroparesis were excluded from the very studies used to judge their risk.

cards.headline: Baig 2025: across 23 observational studies and 262,018 patients, GLP-1 receptor agonist users had 4.5-fold higher odds of residual gastric contents and of premature endoscopy termination — but no higher risk of aspiration pneumonia (OR 0.96)
cards.summary: Baig 2025: across 23 observational studies and 262,018 patients, GLP-1 receptor agonist users had 4.5-fold higher odds of residual gastric contents and of premature endoscopy termination — but no higher risk of aspiration pneumonia (OR 0.96)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Baig 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024556732) of 23 double-arm observational studies comprising 262,018 adult patients undergoing EGD or endoscopy, comparing GLP-1 receptor agonist users with non-users; studies with a sample size under 20 and single-arm studies were excluded.
cards.result: GLP-1 receptor agonist users had a statistically significant increase in the risk of residual gastric contents (odds ratio 4.54, 95% CI 3.30–6.24) and premature endoscopy termination (OR 4.54, 95% CI 3.05–6.75). There was no significant difference in the risk of aspiration pneumonia (OR 0.96, 95% CI 0.53–1.75; P = .90). Residual contents were significantly less frequent when EGD and colonoscopy were done the same day versus EGD alone (OR 0.28, 95% CI 0.22–0.36). All pooled estimates are relative (odds) measures from observational studies; the record reports no pooled absolute event rates.
cards.watchOut: Every included study is observational: GLP-1 users differ from non-users in diabetes, weight and gastric motility, so the retention association is not proof the drug caused it — and the outcome that matters most, aspiration pneumonia, showed no difference.
cards.source: Baig MU et al. Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist use and the risk of residual gastric contents and aspiration in patients undergoing GI endoscopy: a systematic review and a meta-analysis. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2025. PMID: 39694296. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wu 2024: visible gastric contents in 19% of fasting GLP-1 users versus 5% of controls (adjusted OR 5.8) — in a cohort that excluded patients with known gastroparesis
cards.summary: Wu 2024: visible gastric contents in 19% of fasting GLP-1 users versus 5% of controls (adjusted OR 5.8) — in a cohort that excluded patients with known gastroparesis
cards.people: Historical cohort of esophagogastroduodenoscopies performed 2019–2023 at one institution: 90 procedures in patients taking a GLP-1 receptor agonist at the time of the procedure versus 102 procedures in patients who started a GLP-1 agonist within 1,000 days after their EGD (controls). Emergent procedures without fasting, combined EGD/colonoscopy, known gastroparesis and previous gastric surgery were excluded.
cards.result: Visible gastric content was documented in 17 of 90 procedures in the GLP-1 group (19%) and 5 of 102 in the control group (5%), a confounder-adjusted odds ratio of 5.8 (95% CI 1.7–19.3; P = 0.004) — a relative measure; the absolute rates are 19% versus 5% as printed here. There were five instances of emergent endotracheal intubation in the GLP-1 group versus one in controls, and one case of pulmonary aspiration versus none.
cards.watchOut: The patients this shelf is asked about — those with diagnosed gastroparesis — were excluded from this cohort, and the control group is unusual (future GLP-1 starters); one aspiration event in 192 procedures cannot settle the aspiration question either way.
cards.source: Wu F et al. Association of glucagon-like peptide receptor 1 agonist therapy with the presence of gastric contents in fasting patients undergoing endoscopy under anesthesia care: a historical cohort study. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. 2024. PMID: 38485835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Phan 2025: holding the GLP-1 drug as anaesthesia guidance advises was associated with less retention (4.4% vs 12.7%) — but no aspiration occurred in 815 patients and intubation and aborted-procedure rates did not differ significantly
cards.summary: Phan 2025: holding the GLP-1 drug as anaesthesia guidance advises was associated with less retention (4.4% vs 12.7%) — but no aspiration occurred in 815 patients and intubation and aborted-procedure rates did not differ significantly
cards.people: Multicentre cross-sectional study of 815 patients on confirmed GLP-1 receptor agonists undergoing endoscopy from 2021 to 2023; whether the drug had been held preoperatively was classified retrospectively against American Society of Anesthesiologists guidance (406 patients, 49.8%, held per guidance).
cards.result: Seventy patients (8.7%) had retained gastric contents, 65 of them (93%) with type 2 diabetes; only 1 (1.4%) required unplanned intubation and none had aspiration events. Patients whose GLP-1 drug was held per guidance were less likely to have retained contents (4.4% vs 12.7%, P < 0.001), with no significant differences in intubation (0% vs 2%, P = 0.53) or aborting the procedure for gastric retention (28% vs 18%, P = 0.40). On multivariable analysis, the likelihood of food retention rose 36% (95% CI 1.15–1.60) for every 1% increase in haemoglobin A1c, after adjusting for drug type and holding.
cards.watchOut: Holding was not randomised — clinicians chose whom to hold, and the retained-contents group was overwhelmingly diabetic, so poor glycaemic control (itself a cause of slow gastric emptying) is entangled with the drug effect throughout this literature.
cards.source: Phan J et al. Glucagon-Like Peptide Receptor Agonists Use Before Endoscopy Is Associated With Low Retained Gastric Contents: A Multicenter Cross-Sectional Analysis. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2025. PMID: 39016372. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: holding probably empties the stomach more often, but no study shows it prevents aspiration — and the gastroparesis population itself has never been directly studied
cards.summary: Synthesis: holding probably empties the stomach more often, but no study shows it prevents aspiration — and the gastroparesis population itself has never been directly studied
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 23 observational studies (262,018 patients), one single-centre historical cohort (90 GLP-1 procedures vs 102 controls, gastroparesis excluded) and one multicentre cross-sectional study of 815 GLP-1 users classified by whether the drug was held. Total carded participants exceed 260,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the limitation is design (all observational) and population (gastroparesis excluded), not size.
cards.result: Residual gastric contents were consistently more frequent in GLP-1 users (pooled OR 4.54; 19% vs 5% in the cohort study) and less frequent when the drug was held per anaesthesia guidance (4.4% vs 12.7%), yet aspiration pneumonia showed no difference in the meta-analysis (OR 0.96) and no aspiration events occurred in the 815-patient holding study. No carded record addresses surgery under general anaesthesia directly, and none enrolled patients for diagnosed gastroparesis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: A retained-contents finding is a surrogate: endoscopies get abandoned for it, but the chain from retention to aspiration to harm is asserted, not demonstrated, in every carded record — individualised decisions (dose timing, glycaemic control, procedure urgency) remain the honest reading.
cards.source: Synthesis of Baig MU et al. Gastrointestinal Endoscopy. 2025 (PMID: 39694296); Wu F et al. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. 2024 (PMID: 38485835); Phan J et al. American Journal of Gastroenterology. 2025 (PMID: 39016372).
