shelves.title: Chewing gum after abdominal surgery (SPLIT): pooled small trials say bowel function returns about half a day sooner, but the largest trial inside enhanced-recovery care found no difference at all
shelves.question: Does chewing gum after abdominal surgery speed return of bowel function?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Chewing Gum · Gastrointestinal Motility · Humans · Ileus · Length of Stay · Postoperative Complications · Postoperative Period · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Recovery of Function · Time Factors
shelves.balance: SPLIT (small trials and their meta-analysis: benefit; the largest trial, run inside enhanced-recovery care: the treatment made no difference). The Cochrane review of 81 studies and 9,072 participants found chewing gum shortened time to first flatus by 10.4 hours, time to bowel movement by 12.7 hours and hospital stay by 0.7 days — but categorised many studies at high or unclear risk of bias. The largest single trial (Atkinson 2016, 402 patients analysed, all sites using enhanced recovery programmes) found identical median stays of 7 days in both groups and no difference in bowel function. Smaller colorectal trials split both ways (Byrne 2018: first bowel motion 40 vs 90 hours, but flatus and stay not significantly different; Hsu 2022, n = 60: flatus about 14 hours earlier). The likely reconciliation is that gum helps where baseline care leaves a long ileus, and adds little inside modern enhanced-recovery pathways. PROPOSED SPLIT (meta-analysis of mostly small trials: benefit; largest enhanced-recovery trial: no difference).

cards.headline: Cochrane 2015: across 81 studies and 9,072 participants, chewing gum cut time to first flatus by 10.4 hours and time to bowel movement by 12.7 hours — with many studies at high or unclear risk of bias
cards.summary: Cochrane 2015: across 81 studies and 9,072 participants, chewing gum cut time to first flatus by 10.4 hours and time to bowel movement by 12.7 hours — with many studies at high or unclear risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane, Short 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review of 81 randomised controlled trials recruiting 9,072 participants having abdominal surgery, split into colorectal surgery, caesarean section and other surgery subgroups; chewing gum after surgery versus control.
cards.result: Chewing gum reduced time to first flatus overall by 10.4 hours (95% CI −11.9 to −8.9): 12.5 hours in colorectal surgery, 7.9 hours in caesarean section and 10.6 hours in other surgery. Time to bowel movement fell by 12.7 hours (95% CI −14.5 to −10.9), length of hospital stay by 0.7 days (95% CI −0.8 to −0.5), and time to bowel sounds by 5.0 hours (95% CI −6.4 to −3.7). There was statistical evidence of heterogeneity in all analyses, and the reviewers categorised many studies at high or unclear risk of bias on the domains assessed.
cards.watchOut: The pooled benefit rests on many small trials, most predating or sitting outside enhanced-recovery programmes, with high or unclear bias risk — exactly the setting in which meta-analytic effects tend to shrink when a large rigorous trial is done.
cards.source: Short V et al. Chewing gum for postoperative recovery of gastrointestinal function. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 25914904. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Atkinson 2016: in the largest trial (402 patients, enhanced recovery at all sites), chewing gum made no difference — median hospital stay was 7 days in both groups
cards.summary: Atkinson 2016: in the largest trial (402 patients, enhanced recovery at all sites), chewing gum made no difference — median hospital stay was 7 days in both groups
cards.people: 412 patients undergoing colorectal resection in five UK hospitals, randomised to standard postoperative care with or without sugar-free chewing gum (at least 10 minutes, four times a day on days 1–5); data from 402 patients (199 allocated to gum) were analysed; about 40% in both groups had laparoscopic surgery and all sites used enhanced recovery programmes.
cards.result: Median (interquartile range) length of stay was 7 (5–11) days in both groups (P = 0.962); the hazard ratio for discharge with gum was 0.94 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.15; P = 0.557) — the treatment made no difference. Quality of life at 6 and 12 weeks was worse in the gum group, and complications graded III or above (16 vs 6) and deaths (11 vs 0) were numerically more frequent with gum, although none was classed as related to gum. The authors conclude chewing gum did not alter the return of bowel function or length of stay after colorectal resection.
cards.watchOut: The excess severe complications and deaths were not attributed to gum and the trial was not powered for them, but they remove any 'it can only help' assumption; the setting (universal enhanced recovery) may also be exactly where gum has nothing left to add.
cards.source: Atkinson C et al. Randomized clinical trial of postoperative chewing gum versus standard care after colorectal resection. British Journal of Surgery. 2016. PMID: 27146793. cards.headline: Byrne 2018: first bowel motion came much earlier with gum (median 40 vs 90 hours), but time to first flatus and hospital stay were not significantly different — in 158 patients
cards.summary: Byrne 2018: first bowel motion came much earlier with gum (median 40 vs 90 hours), but time to first flatus and hospital stay were not significantly different — in 158 patients
cards.people: 158 patients (82 chewing gum, 76 no gum) undergoing elective open or laparoscopic bowel surgery, randomised to sugar-free chewing gum or no gum after bowel resection (162 randomised, 4 excluded).
cards.result: Median time to first bowel motion was lower with gum (40.0 h) than without (90.0 h) (P = 0.002). There was no difference in length of stay (5.8 vs 6.1 days; P = 0.403) or in median time to first flatus (42.0 vs 58.0 h; P = 0.076). Intra-operative complications (9% vs 9%) and early postoperative complications (44% vs 55%) did not differ significantly. Total morphine-equivalent use over 7 days was lower with gum, driven by days 2–7, with no difference at 24 hours.
cards.watchOut: The headline bowel-motion difference is a median split in a modest sample with the other two primary outcomes null — a pattern consistent with a real but small effect, or with chance across multiple outcomes.
cards.source: Byrne CM et al. Gum chewing aids bowel function return and analgesic requirements after bowel surgery: a randomized controlled trial. Colorectal Disease. 2018. PMID: 29053219. cards.headline: Hsu 2022: in 60 patients after open colon resection, gum shortened time to first flatus (39.1 vs 52.9 hours) and defecation (54.6 vs 78.0 hours), but only flatus survived adjustment
cards.summary: Hsu 2022: in 60 patients after open colon resection, gum shortened time to first flatus (39.1 vs 52.9 hours) and defecation (54.6 vs 78.0 hours), but only flatus survived adjustment
cards.people: 60 patients with colorectal cancer who had undergone open abdominal colon resection (30 intervention, 30 control); the intervention group chewed xylitol gum for 15 minutes three times daily from the first postoperative day until first flatus and defecation, and both groups received standard care with early walking encouraged. Single-study N = 60, printed here.
cards.result: Time to first flatus was 39.13 ± 15.66 hours with gum versus 52.92 ± 21.97 hours in controls, and time to defecation 54.55 ± 18.90 versus 77.98 ± 34.59 hours — both significantly shorter unadjusted. After controlling for age and surgical duration, only time to first flatus remained significantly shorter in the gum group. The authors recommend gum chewing as an inexpensive, noninvasive intervention in middle-aged and older patients after open abdominal colorectal surgery.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre 60-patient trial in open surgery without enhanced-recovery framing — the setting most favourable to gum — and its defecation result did not survive adjustment for age and surgical duration. (The article title's 'Trail' is as printed in the record.)
cards.source: Hsu YC et al. Effects of Gum Chewing on Recovery From Postoperative Ileus: A Randomized Clinical Trail. Journal of Nursing Research. 2022. PMID: 35951432. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Chewing Gum · Flatulence · Ileus · Postoperative Complications · Xylitol

cards.headline: Synthesis: gum chewing probably speeds bowel recovery where ileus is long, but the largest enhanced-recovery trial found no difference in stay or bowel function — the evidence genuinely splits by setting
cards.summary: Synthesis: gum chewing probably speeds bowel recovery where ileus is long, but the largest enhanced-recovery trial found no difference in stay or bowel function — the evidence genuinely splits by setting
cards.people: The carded evidence: a Cochrane meta-analysis of 81 trials (9,072 participants), one 402-patient multicentre enhanced-recovery trial, and two smaller colorectal trials (158 and 60 patients). The smaller trials are inside the Cochrane total, so numbers are not additive; the evidence base is far over 30 participants and no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled across mostly small trials, gum shortened first flatus by 10.4 hours, bowel movement by 12.7 hours and stay by 0.7 days (Cochrane 2015). Against that, the biggest and most modern trial found identical 7-day median stays and no bowel-function benefit (Atkinson 2016), while Byrne 2018 and Hsu 2022 found earlier bowel motion/flatus without shorter stays. PROPOSED SPLIT (small trials and meta-analysis: benefit; largest enhanced-recovery trial: the treatment made no difference).
cards.watchOut: Setting is the story: gum is a sham-feeding stimulus whose value depends on how much ileus the rest of the pathway leaves behind — extrapolating the pooled estimate into a modern enhanced-recovery unit overstates what the largest trial found.
cards.source: Synthesis of Short V et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015 (PMID: 25914904); Atkinson C et al. British Journal of Surgery. 2016 (PMID: 27146793); Byrne CM et al. Colorectal Disease. 2018 (PMID: 29053219); Hsu YC et al. Journal of Nursing Research. 2022 (PMID: 35951432).

shelves.title: Antibiotic prophylaxis timing: earlier within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference to surgical site infection — the randomised trial and meta-analysis agree; only after-incision or >120-minute-early dosing raises risk
shelves.question: Does giving antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision reduce surgical site infection compared with earlier timing?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Anti-Infective Agents · Cefuroxime · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Humans · Male · Metronidazole · Middle Aged · Risk Factors · Surgical Wound Infection · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY — earlier timing inside the window made no difference. The question behind the familiar 'within 60 minutes' rule is whether minutes matter inside that window, and the best evidence says they do not. In the only large randomised trial (Weber 2017, PMID: 28385346; 5,175 patients analysed), single-shot cefuroxime given a median of 42 minutes before incision in the anaesthesia room did not reduce 30-day surgical site infection compared with a median of 16 minutes before incision in the operating room (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.72–1.21). The WHO-commissioned meta-analysis (de Jonge 2017, PMID: 28723736; 54,552 patients) likewise found no difference between administration 120–60 and 60–0 minutes before incision; risk rose only when prophylaxis was given after incision (OR 1.89) or more than 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26). A 222,439-patient Swiss cohort (Sommerstein 2023, PMID: 37289455) found administration closer to incision associated with slightly lower adjusted odds of infection, but that is observational timing data, subject to confounding by workflow, and it supports staying within 60 minutes rather than any benefit from the early part of the window; the Dutch TAPAS cohort (PMID: 31663971) found no conclusive difference between 60–30 and 30–0 minutes (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.57–1.19). PROPOSED LIKELY — giving prophylaxis earlier within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference to surgical site infection (the treatment made no difference within the window); what matters is giving it before incision and not more than about 120 minutes ahead.

cards.headline: Weber 2017: in the phase 3 randomised trial, cefuroxime given a median of 42 minutes before incision did not reduce surgical site infection versus a median of 16 minutes (OR 0.93) — timing inside the window made no difference
cards.summary: Weber 2017: in the phase 3 randomised trial, cefuroxime given a median of 42 minutes before incision did not reduce surgical site infection versus a median of 16 minutes (OR 0.93) — timing inside the window made no difference
cards.people: 5,580 general-surgery adult inpatients (age 18 or older) at two Swiss hospitals (Basel and Aarau) were randomised to single-shot intravenous cefuroxime 1.5 g (plus metronidazole 500 mg in colorectal surgery) early in the anaesthesia room or late in the operating room; 5,175 patients (2,589 early, 2,586 late) were analysed. Median administration time was 42 minutes before incision (IQR 30–55) in the early group and 16 minutes (IQR 10–25) in the late group.
cards.result: Early administration did not significantly reduce the risk of surgical site infection within 30 days compared with late administration (odds ratio 0.93, 95% CI 0.72–1.21, P = 0.601). The overall SSI rate was 5.1% (234 of 4,596 patients with 30-day follow-up). The authors conclude their findings do not support any narrowing of the 60-minute window for a cephalosporin with a short half-life.
cards.watchOut: One drug (cefuroxime, short half-life) and one country's general-surgery population: the null applies to timing within the hour for this agent, not to agents with long half-lives or to giving prophylaxis after incision, which other evidence shows is harmful.
cards.source: Weber WP et al. Timing of surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis: a phase 3 randomised controlled trial. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2017. PMID: 28385346. Registry ID: NCT01790529. cards.headline: de Jonge 2017: across 54,552 patients, prophylaxis at 120–60 minutes carried the same infection risk as at 60–0 minutes — risk rose only after incision (OR 1.89) or more than 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26)
cards.summary: de Jonge 2017: across 54,552 patients, prophylaxis at 120–60 minutes carried the same infection risk as at 60–0 minutes — risk rose only after incision (OR 1.89) or more than 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis prepared for the World Health Organization guideline for surgical site infection prevention: 14 papers with 54,552 patients receiving preoperative surgical antibiotic prophylaxis, comparing different administration timing intervals, with adjusted odds ratios pooled in a random-effects model.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in surgical site infection when prophylaxis was administered 120–60 minutes prior to incision compared with 60–0 minutes prior to incision, and studies investigating different intervals within the last 60 minutes reported contradictory results. The risk of surgical site infection almost doubled when prophylaxis was administered after the first incision (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.05–3.40) and was 5 times higher when administered more than 120 minutes prior to incision (OR 5.26, 95% CI 3.29–8.39). The authors state the broadly accepted recommendation to administer prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision could not be substantiated as superior to the wider 120-minute frame.
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies are observational timing comparisons, so the interval estimates carry confounding risk; the consistent finding is the absence of a gradient inside two hours, not proof that every minute is equivalent for every drug.
cards.source: de Jonge SW et al. Timing of preoperative antibiotic prophylaxis in 54,552 patients and the risk of surgical site infection: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2017. cards.headline: Sommerstein 2023: in 222,439 Swiss operations, cefuroxime given 0–30 minutes before incision was associated with lower adjusted odds of infection than at 61–120 minutes (aOR 0.85) — observational data pointing the opposite way from 'earlier is better'
cards.summary: Sommerstein 2023: in 222,439 Swiss operations, cefuroxime given 0–30 minutes before incision was associated with lower adjusted odds of infection than at 61–120 minutes (aOR 0.85) — observational data pointing the opposite way from 'earlier is better'
cards.people: Cohort study of adult patients undergoing 1 of 11 major surgical procedures with cefuroxime prophylaxis, documented by the Swissnoso surgical site infection surveillance system at 158 Swiss hospitals, January 2009 to December 2020: 222,439 patients fulfilled inclusion criteria (median age 65.7 years); prophylaxis was given 61–120 minutes before incision in 27,207 (12.2%), 31–60 minutes in 118,004 (53.1%) and 0–30 minutes in 77,228 (34.7%).
cards.result: Surgical site infection was identified in 5,355 patients (2.4%). Administration at 0–30 minutes was associated with a lower infection rate (adjusted odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.78–0.93, P < .001), as was administration at 31–60 minutes (aOR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84–0.98, P = .01), compared with administration at 61–120 minutes. Administration 10–25 minutes before incision was likewise associated with lower odds than 30–55 minutes (aOR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82–0.97). The authors conclude cefuroxime prophylaxis should be administered within 60 minutes prior to incision.
cards.watchOut: Timing in routine care is not random: cases given antibiotics very early may differ (longer set-up, more complex surgery), so the adjusted association cannot overturn the randomised trial's null — it reinforces 'within 60 minutes, before incision', not a race to give it earlier.
cards.source: Sommerstein R et al. Timing of Cefuroxime Surgical Antimicrobial Prophylaxis and Its Association With Surgical Site Infections. JAMA network open. 2023. PMID: 37289455. cards.headline: de Jonge 2021 (TAPAS): within the 60-minute window, 60–30 versus 30–0 minutes showed no conclusive difference in infection risk (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.57–1.19)
cards.summary: de Jonge 2021 (TAPAS): within the 60-minute window, 60–30 versus 30–0 minutes showed no conclusive difference in infection risk (OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.57–1.19)
cards.people: Observational cohort (TAPAS) at a Dutch tertiary referral centre: consecutive patients with an indication for surgical antibiotic prophylaxis undergoing general, orthopaedic or gynaecological surgery over 2 years; 3,001 surgical procedures, with prophylaxis administered within 60 minutes before incision in 87% of procedures; only antibiotics with short infusion time were used.
cards.result: 161 surgical site infections were detected. Multivariable logistic regression indicated no conclusive evidence of a difference in infection risk after prophylaxis administration 60–30 minutes versus 30–0 minutes before incision (odds ratio 0.82, 95% confidence interval 0.57–1.19). The authors could not reproduce the differences in risk reported in earlier studies and identified no clearly superior timing interval within the 60 minutes before incision.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre cohort with 161 events cannot exclude modest effects, and its confidence interval includes a small benefit either way; it is carded as concordant support for the trial and meta-analysis, not as standalone proof.
cards.source: de Jonge SW et al. Timing of Preoperative Antibiotic Prophylaxis and Surgical Site Infection: TAPAS, An Observational Cohort Study. Annals of surgery. 2021. PMID: 31663971. cards.headline: Synthesis: within the hour before incision, earlier is not better — the randomised trial, the WHO meta-analysis and two large cohorts all fail to find a timing gradient; harm appears only after incision or beyond about 120 minutes
cards.summary: Synthesis: within the hour before incision, earlier is not better — the randomised trial, the WHO meta-analysis and two large cohorts all fail to find a timing gradient; harm appears only after incision or beyond about 120 minutes
cards.people: The carded evidence: one phase 3 randomised trial (5,175 analysed), one systematic review and meta-analysis (54,552 patients), and two observational cohorts (222,439 and 3,001 procedures). Total carded participants exceed 280,000, so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Randomised early (median 42 min) versus late (median 16 min) cefuroxime prophylaxis gave an odds ratio of 0.93 for surgical site infection (Weber 2017). Pooled data show no difference between the 120–60 and 60–0 minute intervals, with risk rising after incision (OR 1.89) or beyond 120 minutes before it (OR 5.26) (de Jonge 2017). The largest cohort associates administration closer to incision with slightly lower adjusted odds (Sommerstein 2023), and TAPAS finds no difference between the two halves of the hour (de Jonge 2021). PROPOSED LIKELY — earlier timing within the 60 minutes before incision made no difference (the treatment made no difference within the window).
cards.watchOut: Almost all timing evidence concerns short-half-life cephalosporins given as a single shot; vancomycin and fluoroquinolones need longer infusion lead times for pharmacological reasons this shelf does not address.
cards.source: Synthesis of Weber WP et al. The Lancet. Infectious diseases. 2017 (PMID: 28385346); de Jonge SW et al. Medicine. 2017 (PMID: 28723736); Sommerstein R et al. JAMA network open. 2023 (PMID: 37289455); de Jonge SW et al. Annals of surgery. 2021 (PMID: 31663971).

shelves.title: Multicomponent delirium prevention after surgery: postoperative delirium fell in both surgical trials of Elder Life Programs (2.6% vs 19.4% and 6.6% vs 15.1%), with shorter hospital stays
shelves.question: In older adults after surgery, does a multicomponent delirium prevention program reduce postoperative delirium?
shelves.mesh: Activities of Daily Living · Aged · China · Cognition · Delirium · Female · Hospitalization · Hospitals · Humans · Incidence · Male · Postoperative Complications · Retrospective Studies · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — two concordant cluster-randomised trials in surgical patients, backed by the program's wider meta-analysis, support a real reduction in postoperative delirium. The tailored, family-involved Elder Life Program cut delirium from 19.4% to 2.6% (relative risk 0.14, relative; number needed to treat 5.9; Wang 2020), and the modified three-protocol program cut it from 15.1% to 6.6% after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.44, relative; Chen 2017), with shorter hospital stays in both. Across hospital care the program's meta-analytic odds ratio for delirium is 0.47 (relative; Hshieh 2018). The caution card matters: in the broad elective-surgery literature the multicomponent effect reaches significance only in sensitivity analyses excluding high-bias studies, and no pooled effect size is printed for it (Janssen 2019). The founding trial of the original program in hospitalised medical patients is homed on live shelf #340; this shelf cards the postoperative trials and reviews. Both surgical trials are single-centre and cluster-randomised with high control rates, so absolute benefit elsewhere scales with the local baseline. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a multicomponent delirium prevention program reduces postoperative delirium in older adults after surgery.

cards.headline: Wang 2020 (t-HELP): postoperative delirium occurred in 2.6% with the tailored, family-involved Elder Life Program versus 19.4% with usual care (relative risk 0.14, relative; number needed to treat 5.9)
cards.summary: Wang 2020 (t-HELP): postoperative delirium occurred in 2.6% with the tailored, family-involved Elder Life Program versus 19.4% with usual care (relative risk 0.14, relative; number needed to treat 5.9)
cards.people: Two-arm, single-blind, cluster randomised trial on 6 surgical floors (gastric, colorectal, pancreatic, biliary, thoracic and thyroid) of a hospital in Chengdu, China: 281 older patients after noncardiac surgery (mean age 74.7 years) randomised by nursing unit to the tailored, family-involved Hospital Elder Life Program (n = 152) or usual care (n = 129). The program tailored protocols to each patient's risk-factor profile, with family members and paid caregivers delivering many interventions alongside nurses.
cards.result: Postoperative delirium occurred in 4 participants (2.6%) in the intervention group and 25 (19.4%) in the control group (relative risk 0.14 [95% CI 0.05–0.38], a relative measure; number needed to treat 5.9 [95% CI 4.2–11.1]). The intervention group showed less decline in physical function (activities of daily living and instrumental activities) and cognitive function at discharge, and a shorter mean length of stay (12.15 versus 16.41 days; P < .001).
cards.watchOut: One centre, six clusters, and an unusually high control-group delirium rate (19.4%) inflate the relative effect; family-and-paid-caregiver delivery reflects its setting and may not transfer to wards without that caregiving structure.
cards.source: Wang YY et al. Effect of the Tailored, Family-Involved Hospital Elder Life Program on Postoperative Delirium and Function in Older Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA internal medicine. 2020. PMID: 31633738. Registry ID: ChiCTR-POR-15006944. cards.headline: Chen 2017 (mHELP): postoperative delirium occurred in 6.6% with the modified Elder Life Program versus 15.1% with usual care after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.44, relative), and stay was 2 days shorter
cards.summary: Chen 2017 (mHELP): postoperative delirium occurred in 6.6% with the modified Elder Life Program versus 15.1% with usual care after abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.44, relative), and stay was 2 days shorter
cards.people: Cluster randomised trial (randomised by room) at a 2,000-bed medical centre in Taipei, Taiwan: 377 patients aged 65 or older undergoing elective gastrectomy, pancreaticoduodenectomy or colectomy with expected stay over 6 days, assigned to the modified Hospital Elder Life Program (n = 197; mean age 74.3 years) or usual care (n = 180). A program nurse delivered three daily protocols — orienting communication, oral and nutritional assistance, and early mobilisation — from ward arrival to discharge; delirium was assessed daily by two nurses masked to allocation.
cards.result: Postoperative delirium occurred in 13 of 196 (6.6%) program participants versus 27 of 179 (15.1%) controls (relative risk 0.44 [95% CI 0.23–0.83], a relative measure; P = .008) — described by the authors as a 56% relative reduction in the odds of delirium. Median length of stay was shorter in the program group (12.0 versus 14.0 days; P = .04). The program was delivered for a median of 7 days.
cards.watchOut: A three-protocol 'modified' program in one Taiwanese centre's abdominal-surgery population: it shows a lean bundle can work, but cluster-by-room allocation and a single health system limit how far the effect size travels.
cards.source: Chen CC et al. Effect of a Modified Hospital Elder Life Program on Delirium and Length of Hospital Stay in Patients Undergoing Abdominal Surgery: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial. cards.headline: Hshieh 2018: across 14 studies, Elder Life Programs reduced delirium incidence (odds ratio 0.47, relative) and falls (odds ratio 0.58, relative) — in mixed hospital populations, not surgical patients alone
cards.summary: Hshieh 2018: across 14 studies, Elder Life Programs reduced delirium incidence (odds ratio 0.47, relative) and falls (odds ratio 0.58, relative) — in mixed hospital populations, not surgical patients alone
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the Hospital Elder Life Program from 1999 to 2017: 44 articles included overall, 14 in the meta-analysis of effectiveness, spanning hospitalised older patients (medical and surgical). Program costs, adherence, adaptations and sustainability were reviewed in the remaining articles.
cards.result: Fourteen studies demonstrated significant reductions in delirium incidence (odds ratio 0.47 [95% CI 0.37–0.59], a relative measure). The rate of falls was reduced by 42% (relative) among intervention patients in three comparative studies (odds ratio 0.58 [95% CI 0.35–0.95]). Nine cost studies found savings of $1,600–$3,800 per patient in hospital costs and over $16,000 per person-year in long-term care costs in the year after delirium. Programs generally adhered to or appropriately adapted the model.
cards.watchOut: The pooled population mixes medical and surgical inpatients and many studies were not randomised, so this card supports the program family rather than pricing its postoperative effect; the two surgical trials on this shelf carry that estimate.
cards.source: Hshieh TT et al. Hospital Elder Life Program: Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Effectiveness. The American journal of geriatric psychiatry : official journal of the American Association for Geriatric Psychiatry. 2018. PMID: 30076080. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Janssen 2019: in elective-surgery trials, multicomponent interventions significantly reduced postoperative delirium only in sensitivity analyses excluding high-bias studies — the record gives no pooled effect size for them, printed plainly
cards.summary: Janssen 2019: in elective-surgery trials, multicomponent interventions significantly reduced postoperative delirium only in sensitivity analyses excluding high-bias studies — the record gives no pooled effect size for them, printed plainly
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions to prevent postoperative delirium in elderly patients undergoing elective surgery (search March 2018): 31 randomised trials and 4 before-and-after studies. Acute admissions, planned intensive-care admissions and cardiac surgery were excluded.
cards.result: In 19 studies the intervention decreased delirium incidence; severity was reduced in 3 of 9 studies reporting it and duration in 3 of 6. Pooled analysis showed a significant reduction for dexmedetomidine treatment and for bispectral-index-guided anaesthesia. Based on sensitivity analyses leaving out studies at high risk of bias, multicomponent interventions and antipsychotics could also significantly reduce delirium incidence — the record reports this conclusion without a pooled risk ratio for multicomponent interventions, printed here plainly. The authors note the studies are heterogeneous and high-quality studies are scarce.
cards.watchOut: The least convenient card on the shelf, kept deliberately: the broad postoperative literature is weaker than the two Elder Life trials suggest, and the multicomponent pooled claim survives only after high-bias studies are removed.
cards.source: Janssen TL et al. Prevention of postoperative delirium in elderly patients planned for elective surgery: systematic review and meta-analysis. Clinical interventions in aging. 2019. cards.headline: Synthesis: multicomponent delirium-prevention programs cut postoperative delirium in both carded surgical trials (2.6% versus 19.4% and 6.6% versus 15.1%) and across the wider Elder Life literature (odds ratio 0.47, relative)
cards.summary: Synthesis: multicomponent delirium-prevention programs cut postoperative delirium in both carded surgical trials (2.6% versus 19.4% and 6.6% versus 15.1%) and across the wider Elder Life literature (odds ratio 0.47, relative)
cards.people: The carded evidence: two cluster-randomised postoperative trials of Elder Life Program variants (281 and 377 patients), a meta-analysis of the program across hospital care (14 studies), and a systematic review of postoperative prevention trials (31 randomised trials and 4 before-and-after studies). Review populations overlap the trials, so totals are not summed; the two surgical trials alone total 658 patients, and no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Postoperative delirium fell from 19.4% to 2.6% with the tailored family-involved program (relative risk 0.14, relative; Wang 2020) and from 15.1% to 6.6% with the modified program (relative risk 0.44, relative; Chen 2017), with shorter stays in both. The program meta-analysis gives an odds ratio of 0.47 (relative) for delirium incidence (Hshieh 2018), while the broad postoperative review finds the multicomponent effect significant only in sensitivity analyses (Janssen 2019). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit): a multicomponent delirium prevention program reduces postoperative delirium in older adults.
cards.watchOut: Both surgical trials are single-centre cluster trials from East Asian hospitals with high control-group delirium rates; absolute benefit elsewhere will scale with the local baseline rate, and the founding medical-ward trial of the original program is homed on live shelf #340 rather than re-carded here.

shelves.title: Preoperative BNP improves risk prediction (observational only): pooled OR 19.3 for 30-day events and 58% net reclassification over the RCRI — prediction proven, BNP-guided care untested
shelves.question: Does a preoperative BNP test improve risk prediction before major surgery?
shelves.mesh: Cardiovascular Diseases · Humans · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain · Peptide Fragments · Predictive Value of Tests · Preoperative Care · Risk Assessment · Risk Factors · Surgical Procedures, Operative
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only, printed on the face: every carded study is a prognostic cohort or a meta-analysis of cohorts; no trial has tested BNP-guided management. The association is strong and independent: pooled across 9 studies (3,281 patients), an elevated preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP carried an odds ratio of 19.3 (95% CI 8.5 to 43.7) for 30-day cardiovascular events (Karthikeyan 2009). The added value over clinical scoring is directly measured in the individual-patient meta-analysis (850 vascular patients): BNP above its optimal cut point (116 pg/mL) independently predicted cardiac death or nonfatal MI (OR 7.9, 95% CI 4.7 to 13.3), and adding it to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index improved reclassification in all risk groups (net reclassification improvement 58%; 84% in the intermediate-risk group) (Rodseth 2011). Biccard 2012 adds that, once BNP strata are known, RCRI factors add nothing further (BNP intermediate OR 5.1; high-risk OR 25). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only: yes, a preoperative BNP improves risk prediction beyond clinical scores, on consistent cohort evidence; whether acting on it improves outcomes is untested.

cards.headline: Karthikeyan 2009 [evidence type: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies]: elevated preoperative BNP/NT-proBNP independently predicted 30-day cardiovascular events, pooled OR 19.3
cards.summary: Karthikeyan 2009 [evidence type: systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies]: elevated preoperative BNP/NT-proBNP independently predicted 30-day cardiovascular events, pooled OR 19.3
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies (Karthikeyan 2009)
cards.people: 9 observational studies totalling 3,281 patients undergoing noncardiac surgery, of whom 314 had one or more perioperative cardiovascular complications; an average of 24.8% of patients had an elevated BNP. All studies assessed the independent prognostic value of preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP.
cards.result: All studies showed a statistically significant association between an elevated preoperative BNP level and cardiovascular outcomes. Pooled from 7 studies, the odds ratio was 19.3 (95% CI 8.5 to 43.7; I² = 58%). For studies counting only death, cardiovascular death or myocardial infarction the OR was 44.2 (95% CI 7.6 to 257.0); for studies including other outcomes, 14.7 (95% CI 5.7 to 38.2). The authors conclude an elevated preoperative BNP or NT-proBNP is a powerful, independent predictor of cardiovascular events in the first 30 days after noncardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios of this size in prognostic meta-analyses shrink with adjustment quality and threshold choice (I² = 58–89%): BNP predicts risk powerfully, but the pooled OR overstates what any single cut point delivers in one hospital.
cards.source: Karthikeyan G et al. cards.headline: Rodseth 2011 [evidence type: individual patient data meta-analysis of cohorts]: BNP added to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index improved reclassification — NRI 58% overall, 84% in intermediate-risk patients
cards.summary: Rodseth 2011 [evidence type: individual patient data meta-analysis of cohorts]: BNP added to the Revised Cardiac Risk Index improved reclassification — NRI 58% overall, 84% in intermediate-risk patients
cards.type: Individual patient data meta-analysis of observational cohorts (Rodseth 2011)
cards.people: Individual patient data from 6 datasets in vascular surgery: 5 BNP datasets (n = 632) and 1 NT-proBNP dataset (n = 218) — 850 patients total. Primary endpoint: cardiac death and nonfatal myocardial infarction within 30 days of vascular surgery.
cards.result: A natriuretic peptide level above the optimal cut point independently predicted the primary endpoint (OR 7.9, 95% CI 4.7 to 13.3). BNP cut points: 30 pg/mL for screening (95% sensitivity, 44% specificity), 116 pg/mL optimal (66% sensitivity, 82% specificity), 372 pg/mL diagnostic (32% sensitivity, 95% specificity). After RCRI stratification, reclassification using the optimal cut point significantly improved risk prediction in all groups (net reclassification improvement 58%, P < 0.000001), particularly the intermediate-risk group (NRI 84%, P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Vascular surgery only, and reclassification gains are largest where the clinical score is weakest (intermediate risk): this shows BNP refines a prediction, not that any decision changed by it prevents an event.

cards.headline: Biccard 2012 [evidence type: cohort analysis, n = 850]: once BNP strata were known, no RCRI risk factor independently predicted events — BNP intermediate OR 5.1, high-risk OR 25
cards.summary: Biccard 2012 [evidence type: cohort analysis, n = 850]: once BNP strata were known, no RCRI risk factor independently predicted events — BNP intermediate OR 5.1, high-risk OR 25
cards.people: 850 vascular surgical patients initially risk-stratified using preoperative B-type natriuretic peptides, then reclassified by number of Revised Cardiac Risk Index risk factors; outcome major adverse cardiac events.
cards.result: Reclassification with RCRI risk-factor count worsened BNP-based stratification (P < 0.05 for >0, >2, >3 and >4 risk factors; P = 0.23 for >1). No RCRI risk factor was an independent predictor of major adverse cardiac events when evaluated with preoperative BNP. The only independent predictor was BNP stratification itself (OR 5.1, 95% CI 1.8–15 for the intermediate class; OR 25, 95% CI 8.7–70 for the high-risk class). The authors conclude RCRI clinical risk factors cannot improve a BNP-based stratification model.
cards.watchOut: Same 850-patient vascular dataset family as the Rodseth IPD analysis — the two cards are not fully independent confirmations, and neither extends beyond vascular surgery populations.
cards.source: Biccard BM et al. The influence of clinical risk factors on pre-operative B-type natriuretic peptide risk stratification of vascular surgical patients. Anaesthesia. 2012. cards.headline: Synthesis: BNP consistently and independently predicts perioperative cardiac events and measurably improves on the RCRI — all on observational evidence, with no trial of BNP-guided care
cards.summary: Synthesis: BNP consistently and independently predicts perioperative cardiac events and measurably improves on the RCRI — all on observational evidence, with no trial of BNP-guided care
cards.people: The carded evidence, all observational by design: a meta-analysis of 9 cohort studies (3,281 patients), an individual patient data meta-analysis (850 vascular patients), and a cohort re-analysis of the same 850 patients. Total unique patients ≈ 4,131, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Elevated preoperative BNP/NT-proBNP: pooled OR 19.3 for 30-day cardiovascular events (Karthikeyan 2009). Above the optimal 116 pg/mL cut point: OR 7.9 for cardiac death or nonfatal MI, with net reclassification improvement of 58% over the RCRI (84% in intermediate risk) (Rodseth 2011). RCRI factors added nothing once BNP was known (Biccard 2012). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational only.
cards.watchOut: Prediction is not intervention: no carded study randomised patients to BNP-guided management, so improved prediction has no proven line to fewer infarctions or deaths.

shelves.title: Preoperative oral supplements before major surgery: complications roughly halved in pooled GI-cancer trials (relative risk 0.53) — major-complication benefit unproven
shelves.question: In adults undergoing major surgery, does preoperative oral nutritional supplementation reduce complications in malnourished patients versus no supplementation?
shelves.mesh: Developing Countries · Dietary Supplements · Digestive System Surgical Procedures · Gastrointestinal Neoplasms · Humans · Malnutrition · Postoperative Complications
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit). The strongest carded synthesis is in gastrointestinal cancer surgery in low- and middle-income countries (Knight 2022: 7 randomised trials, 891 patients), where preoperative oral nutritional supplementation roughly halved complications — relative risk 0.53 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.60) for all postoperative surgical complications, 0.52 for infection, and 0.35 for all-cause mortality, with an absolute risk reduction of 0.14 (number needed to treat 7) for all complications. The individual trials are consistent in direction but smaller and softer: Smedley 2004 (179 randomised, lower gastrointestinal surgery) found significantly fewer minor complications with supplements before and after surgery but no difference in major complications; Kabata 2015 (102 patients) found significantly more serious complications in the unsupplemented control group — in patients who were NOT malnourished at entry, printed on its card. No carded trial isolates preoperative-only supplementation in strictly malnourished patients across major surgery generally, so the malnourished-specific claim rests mainly on the Knight meta-analysis population. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative oral supplementation reduces postoperative complications, with the clearest numbers in gastrointestinal cancer surgery; the effect on major complications is unproven.

cards.headline: Knight 2022: preoperative oral supplementation halved complications in gastrointestinal cancer surgery — relative risk 0.53 for all complications, 0.35 for mortality (7 trials, 891 patients)
cards.summary: Knight 2022: preoperative oral supplementation halved complications in gastrointestinal cancer surgery — relative risk 0.53 for all complications, 0.35 for mortality (7 trials, 891 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Knight 2022)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 randomised controlled trials (891 patients: 446 supplementation, 445 control) of preoperative oral nutrition supplementation in gastrointestinal cancer surgery in low- and middle-income countries, searched to March 2022. Malnutrition is the review's framing risk factor; trial-level malnutrition entry criteria vary and are not uniformly reported in the record.
cards.result: Preoperative oral supplementation reduced all-cause postoperative surgical complications (relative risk 0.53, 95% CI 0.46–0.60, P < 0.001, I² = 0%), infection (relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.40–0.67) and all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.35, 95% CI 0.26–0.47). Absolute risk reduction was 0.14 for all complications (number needed to treat 7) and 0.13 for infectious complications (NNT 8). The authors call for additional higher-quality research, particularly in African populations.
cards.watchOut: Effects this large (I² = 0% across small trials in one world region) usually shrink in larger, blinded trials; the setting is gastrointestinal cancer surgery in low- and middle-income countries, not major surgery everywhere.
cards.source: Knight SR et al. The impact of preoperative oral nutrition supplementation on outcomes in patients undergoing gastrointestinal surgery for cancer in low- and middle-income countries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Scientific Reports. 2022. PMID: 35864290. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Smedley 2004: supplements before and after lower gastrointestinal surgery cut minor complications and weight loss, but major complications did not differ (179 randomised, 152 analysed)
cards.summary: Smedley 2004: supplements before and after lower gastrointestinal surgery cut minor complications and weight loss, but major complications did not differ (179 randomised, 152 analysed)
cards.people: 179 patients undergoing lower gastrointestinal tract surgery in three centres, randomised to no supplements (CC, 44 analysed), supplements before and after surgery (SS, 32), postoperative supplements only (CS, 35), or preoperative supplements only (SC, 41); 152 analysed after 27 withdrawals. Preoperative supplements ran from the decision to operate until the day before surgery.
cards.result: Mean energy intake from preoperative supplements was 536–542 kcal/day. There was significantly less postoperative weight loss in the SS group than in the CC and CS groups (P < 0.050), and significantly fewer minor complications in the SS and CS groups than the CC group (P < 0.050). There were no differences in major complications, anthropometrics or quality of life. Mean overall costs were greatest in the unsupplemented group, without reaching significance. The record reports significance levels rather than complication counts — printed as such here.
cards.watchOut: The winning arms combine preoperative with postoperative supplementation, and enrolment was not restricted to malnourished patients — this trial supports perioperative supplementation generally, not the preoperative-only, malnourished-only claim on this shelf.
cards.source: Smedley F et al. Randomized clinical trial of the effects of preoperative and postoperative oral nutritional supplements on clinical course and cost of care. British Journal of Surgery. 2004. PMID: 15286958. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kabata 2015: 14 days of preoperative supplementation cut serious complications versus everyday diet (P < 0.001) — in 102 cancer patients who were not malnourished at entry
cards.summary: Kabata 2015: 14 days of preoperative supplementation cut serious complications versus everyday diet (P < 0.001) — in 102 cancer patients who were not malnourished at entry
cards.people: 102 patients qualifying for gastrointestinal cancer surgery without clinical signs of malnutrition, randomised (54 intervention, 48 control, as analysed) to 14 days of preoperative nutritional supplementation or their everyday diet, then followed 30 days for postoperative complications. Prospective, open-label randomised trial.
cards.result: In the postoperative period, control patients suffered a significantly higher number of serious complications than supplemented patients (P < 0.001). All measured laboratory parameters (albumin, total protein, transferrin, total lymphocyte count) declined significantly in controls (P < 0.001), while they were stable (albumin, total protein) or rose (transferrin, lymphocyte count) in the supplemented group. The record reports P values rather than complication counts — printed as such here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, 102 patients, and deliberately NOT malnourished patients: it shows supplementation can help even the well-nourished, which supports the direction of this shelf's answer but is not evidence about the malnourished population the question names.
cards.source: Kabata P et al. Preoperative nutritional support in cancer patients with no clinical signs of malnutrition--prospective randomized controlled trial. Supportive Care in Cancer. 2015. cards.headline: Synthesis: supplementation before surgery reduces complications in the pooled gastrointestinal-cancer trials (relative risk 0.53), with individual trials agreeing on minor/serious complications but not on major ones
cards.summary: Synthesis: supplementation before surgery reduces complications in the pooled gastrointestinal-cancer trials (relative risk 0.53), with individual trials agreeing on minor/serious complications but not on major ones
cards.people: The carded evidence: one meta-analysis of 7 randomised trials (891 patients), and two individual randomised trials (179 and 102 randomised patients). Populations overlap in kind (gastrointestinal surgery) but the meta-analysis's trials are distinct from the two individually carded trials as far as the records show. Total carded participants exceed 1,100, so no small-N labelling applies.
cards.result: Pooled: complications relative risk 0.53, infection 0.52, mortality 0.35, absolute risk reduction 0.14 (NNT 7) (Knight 2022). Individually: fewer minor complications and less weight loss with perioperative supplements, no difference in major complications (Smedley 2004); fewer serious complications with 14 days of preoperative supplementation, in non-malnourished patients (Kabata 2015). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: No carded trial tests preoperative-only oral supplementation in patients selected for malnutrition across major surgery in general — the shelf generalises from gastrointestinal (mostly cancer) surgery, and says so.

shelves.title: Buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam in the community (partial completion of #3878, children in the ED): the one out-of-hospital trial and the pooled data favour the buccal route — POSSIBLE benefit, and easier to give
shelves.question: Should buccal midazolam be preferred over rectal diazepam for prolonged seizures in the community?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Buccal · Administration, Rectal · Adolescent · Adult · Anti-Anxiety Agents · Anticonvulsants · Blood Pressure · Child · Child, Preschool · Diazepam · Epilepsy, Complex Partial · Epilepsy, Generalized · Epilepsy, Tonic-Clonic · Female · Humans · Incidence · Male · Midazolam · Oxygen · Seizures · Status Epilepticus · Time Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #3878, which covers buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam in children in the emergency department (the McIntyre 2005 trial and the McTague 2018 Cochrane review are carded there and are not re-carded here). The uncovered slice is the community — seizures treated where they happen, by carers or nurses, before hospital. The only randomised trial conducted entirely outside hospital is Scott 1999 (PMID: 10030327), run at a residential school: buccal midazolam stopped 75% of seizures versus 59% for rectal diazepam, a difference that was not significant (p = 0.16) in 42 young people, with no clinically important cardiorespiratory events and universal staff acceptance of the buccal route. The pooled evidence, which mixes community and hospital trials, favours buccal midazolam on the specific pairing: a relative risk of 1.54 for seizure cessation in one meta-analysis (McMullan 2010, PMID: 20624136), while a second, larger meta-analysis found the advantage only on the odds scale (odds ratio 1.78; relative risk 1.15, not significant) (Brigo 2015, PMID: 25817929). Administration is also faster with non-intravenous midazolam. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — buccal midazolam should be preferred in the community: at least as effective as rectal diazepam, probably somewhat more effective, quicker and more socially acceptable to give, on one small out-of-hospital trial plus pooled analyses.

cards.headline: Scott 1999: at a residential school — the community setting — buccal midazolam stopped 75% of prolonged seizures versus 59% for rectal diazepam (p = 0.16, not significant), with no important cardiorespiratory events
cards.summary: Scott 1999: at a residential school — the community setting — buccal midazolam stopped 75% of prolonged seizures versus 59% for rectal diazepam (p = 0.16, not significant), with no important cardiorespiratory events
cards.people: 42 young people with severe epilepsy enrolled at a residential school with on-site medical facilities; continuous seizures of more than 5 minutes' duration were randomly treated with buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam — buccal midazolam was used to treat 40 seizures in 14 students and rectal diazepam 39 seizures in 14 students (79 seizures in total). If the seizure did not stop within 10 minutes, additional medication chosen by the attending physician was given.
cards.result: Midazolam stopped 30 (75%) of 40 seizures and diazepam 23 (59%) of 39 (p = 0.16). The median time from arrival of the nurse to administration of medication was 2 minutes, and time from administration to end of seizure did not differ significantly between the two treatments. No clinically important adverse cardiorespiratory events were identified in the two groups. Buccal midazolam was universally acceptable to the nursing and care staff, and the authors conclude it is at least as effective as rectal diazepam and may become the preferred treatment for long seizures that occur outside hospital because administration via the mouth is more socially acceptable and convenient.
cards.watchOut: The unit of randomisation is the seizure, not the child — 79 seizures in 42 young people at one residential school — and the headline difference is not statistically significant; this trial shows feasibility and acceptability in the community more firmly than superiority.
cards.source: Scott RC et al. Buccal midazolam and rectal diazepam for treatment of prolonged seizures in childhood and adolescence: a randomised trial. Lancet (London, England). 1999. PMID: 10030327. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: McMullan 2010: buccal midazolam was superior to rectal diazepam for seizure cessation (relative risk 1.54), and midazolam was given 2.46 minutes faster than diazepam
cards.summary: McMullan 2010: buccal midazolam was superior to rectal diazepam for seizure cessation (relative risk 1.54), and midazolam was given 2.46 minutes faster than diazepam
cards.people: Meta-analysis of quasi-experimental or randomised controlled trials comparing midazolam and diazepam as first-line treatment for status epilepticus in children and adults, meeting CONSORT-based quality measures: six studies with 774 subjects were included, with administration routes stratified as non-intravenous (buccal, intranasal, intramuscular, rectal) or intravenous.
cards.result: For seizure cessation, midazolam by any route was superior to diazepam by any route (relative risk 1.52, 95% CI 1.27 to 1.82), and buccal midazolam specifically was superior to rectal diazepam in achieving seizure control (relative risk 1.54, 95% CI 1.29 to 1.85) — both relative measures; the record does not print the absolute cessation rates behind them. Midazolam was administered faster than diazepam (mean difference 2.46 minutes, 95% CI 1.52 to 3.39), and respiratory complications requiring intervention were similar regardless of route (relative risk 1.49, 95% CI 0.25 to 8.72).
cards.watchOut: Only six studies, mostly hospital-based, underlie the buccal-versus-rectal estimate — it pools the community trial above with emergency-department trials, so it supports the community preference indirectly rather than measuring it in the community alone.
cards.source: McMullan J et al. Midazolam versus diazepam for the treatment of status epilepticus in children and young adults: a meta-analysis. Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine. 2010. PMID: 20624136. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Brigo 2015: in 19 studies, buccal midazolam beat rectal diazepam on the odds scale (odds ratio 1.78) but not the relative-risk scale (1.15, not significant) — and non-intravenous midazolam was given about 3.6 minutes sooner
cards.summary: Brigo 2015: in 19 studies, buccal midazolam beat rectal diazepam on the odds scale (odds ratio 1.78) but not the relative-risk scale (1.15, not significant) — and non-intravenous midazolam was given about 3.6 minutes sooner
cards.people: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials comparing non-intravenous midazolam with intravenous or rectal diazepam in patients of all ages with early status epilepticus (seizures lasting more than 5 minutes or seizures at arrival in the emergency department): 19 studies with 1,933 seizures in 1,602 patients, of whom 1,573 were younger than 16 years.
cards.result: For seizure cessation, non-intravenous midazolam was as effective as diazepam by any route (1,933 seizures; relative risk 1.03, 95% CI 0.98 to 1.08), with no difference in adverse effects. In the specific buccal midazolam versus rectal diazepam comparison (769 seizures), midazolam was more effective when results were expressed as an odds ratio (1.78, 95% CI 1.11 to 2.85) but not as a relative risk (1.15, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.54). The time interval between arrival and drug administration was significantly shorter with non-intravenous midazolam (348 seizures; mean difference −3.56 minutes, 95% CI −5.00 to −2.11). The authors note buccal midazolam is socially more acceptable and easier to administer, and might have higher efficacy than rectal diazepam in seizure control.
cards.watchOut: The buccal-versus-rectal superiority claim depends on which effect measure is used — significant as an odds ratio, not as a relative risk — and most included seizures were treated in or at hospital, not in the community.
cards.source: Brigo F et al. Nonintravenous midazolam versus intravenous or rectal diazepam for the treatment of early status epilepticus: A systematic review with meta-analysis. Epilepsy & behavior : E&B. 2015. PMID: 25817929. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: for community use, buccal midazolam is at least as effective as rectal diazepam, probably a little more effective, faster to give and more acceptable — the preference rests on the whole pattern, not on any single significant trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: for community use, buccal midazolam is at least as effective as rectal diazepam, probably a little more effective, faster to give and more acceptable — the preference rests on the whole pattern, not on any single significant trial
cards.people: The carded evidence: one randomised trial conducted entirely outside hospital (42 young people, 79 seizures; Scott 1999) and two meta-analyses of the midazolam-versus-diazepam literature (6 studies, 774 subjects; McMullan 2010 — and 19 studies, 1,933 seizures in 1,602 patients; Brigo 2015). Participant totals exceed the small-N threshold, so no small-N stamp labelling applies; the community trial's own small size is printed on its face.
cards.result: In the community trial, buccal midazolam stopped 75% of seizures versus 59% for rectal diazepam (p = 0.16). Pooled buccal-versus-rectal estimates were a relative risk of 1.54 (McMullan 2010) and an odds ratio of 1.78 with a non-significant relative risk of 1.15 (Brigo 2015); non-intravenous midazolam was administered about 2.5 to 3.6 minutes faster, with similar respiratory complications. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — preferred for prolonged seizures in the community.
cards.watchOut: Home shelf #3878 holds the emergency-department evidence (McIntyre 2005 and the Cochrane review); this shelf's community claim leans on one small residential-school trial from 1999 plus pooled analyses dominated by hospital-treated seizures.
cards.source: Synthesis of Scott RC et al. Lancet (London, England). 1999 (PMID: 10030327); McMullan J et al. Academic emergency medicine. 2010 (PMID: 20624136); Brigo F et al. Epilepsy & behavior : E&B. 2015 (PMID: 25817929).

shelves.title: Preoperative iron beyond abdominal surgery: transfusion fell modestly in cardiac surgery (61.1% vs 68.2% in ITACS) and across pooled major-surgery trials — but not at hip-fracture operation, and not in the abdomen
shelves.question: Does preoperative anemia treatment with iron reduce transfusion after major surgery?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Double-Blind Method · Cardiac Surgical Procedures · Female · Erythrocyte Transfusion · Male · Aged · Iron · Middle Aged · Anemia · Administration, Intravenous · Preoperative Care
shelves.balance: PARTIAL completion of live shelf #1126, which covers preoperative intravenous iron before major open ABDOMINAL surgery (PREVENTT, null); this shelf covers the other major-surgery settings — cardiac surgery and hip-fracture surgery — and does not re-card PREVENTT. The picture outside the abdomen is more favourable but smaller in effect than guidelines once assumed. ITACS (Myles 2026; 955 anaemic adults before elective cardiac surgery, 1,000 mg intravenous iron versus placebo) reduced red-cell transfusion (61.1% versus 68.2%; relative risk 0.90; 95% CI 0.82 to 0.99; relative measure — an absolute reduction of 7.1 percentage points) and added a median 1.0 day alive and at home at 90 days, with no difference in major complications. The small INITIATE trial (Kong 2022; 156 cardiac-surgery patients) found lower transfusion odds with intravenous iron PLUS an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent versus oral iron (adjusted odds ratio 0.33) — a combination intervention, so the iron-only contribution cannot be separated. In hip-fracture surgery, IRON NOF (O'Loughlin 2023; 143 anaemic patients, terminated early) found no significant difference in transfusion (26% versus 37%; P = 0.15; the treatment made no difference on its primary outcome), though haemoglobin at 6 weeks was higher on iron. The cross-surgery meta-analysis (Elhenawy 2021; 10 trials, 1,039 participants) found preoperative intravenous iron reduced transfusion (relative risk 0.84; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.99; relative measure — a 16% relative reduction) at moderate certainty. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative iron treatment probably reduces transfusion modestly after major surgery outside the abdomen — shown best in cardiac surgery — a smaller and less certain effect than the abdominal-surgery null on #1126 might suggest is impossible, and than enthusiasts claim.

cards.headline: Myles 2026 (ITACS): before cardiac surgery, intravenous iron cut red-cell transfusion — 61.1% versus 68.2% (relative risk 0.90) — and added 1.0 day alive and at home in 955 anaemic patients
cards.summary: Myles 2026 (ITACS): before cardiac surgery, intravenous iron cut red-cell transfusion — 61.1% versus 68.2% (relative risk 0.90) — and added 1.0 day alive and at home in 955 anaemic patients
cards.people: 955 adults with anaemia undergoing elective cardiac surgery at 33 hospitals in 10 countries (enrolled July 2016 to December 2023), randomised double-blind to intravenous iron 1,000 mg or placebo 1–26 weeks before surgery; 921 patients were assessed for the primary outcome of days alive and at home up to 90 days after surgery. Patients on dialysis or with haemoglobinopathy or iron-storage disorders were excluded.
cards.result: Median days alive and at home to 90 days were 81.1 (interquartile range 74.8 to 83.7) on intravenous iron versus 80.0 (69.5 to 83.6) on placebo (adjusted median difference 1.0 day; 95.4% CI 0.0 to 2.1; P = 0.041). Red-cell transfusions were given to 262 patients (61.1%) in the iron group and 302 (68.2%) in the placebo group (relative risk 0.90; 95% CI 0.82 to 0.99; P = 0.027; relative measure) — an absolute reduction of 7.1 percentage points. No differences were observed for major complications or length of hospital stay. The authors conclude intravenous iron is an effective component of patient blood management in this setting.
cards.watchOut: The relative transfusion reduction (10% relative) is modest and the primary outcome's confidence interval touches 0.0 days; this is a real but small benefit, and ITACS appears on home shelf #1126 only as a fenced pointer with no figures taken — it is carded as evidence here for the first time, on the cardiac-surgery slice.
cards.source: Myles PS et al. Intravenous iron to treat anaemia before cardiac surgery (ITACS): international, double blind, placebo controlled randomised trial. BMJ. 2026. PMID: 42618081. Registry ID: NCT02632760. cards.headline: Kong 2022 (INITIATE): intravenous iron plus darbepoetin beat oral iron on transfusion in cardiac surgery (adjusted odds ratio 0.33) — a combination intervention in 156 patients
cards.summary: Kong 2022 (INITIATE): intravenous iron plus darbepoetin beat oral iron on transfusion in cardiac surgery (adjusted odds ratio 0.33) — a combination intervention in 156 patients
cards.people: 156 elective cardiac-surgery patients with haemoglobin 100–130 g/L (10.0–13.0 g/dL) and iron deficiency (ferritin under 100 μg/L or transferrin saturation under 30%), randomised open-label at a single centre to intravenous ferric derisomaltose 1,000 mg plus darbepoetin 200 μg subcutaneously, or oral ferrous sulfate 600 mg daily; the primary outcome was transfusion of at least one unit of allogeneic red cells during surgery and within 5 days.
cards.result: The odds of red-cell transfusion were lower in the intervention group (adjusted odds ratio 0.33; 95% CI 0.15 to 0.75; P = 0.008; relative measure). The only significant secondary difference was the rise in haemoglobin between randomisation and surgery: 9.5 g/L (0.95 g/dL) greater in the intervention group (95% CI 6.8 to 12.2; P < 0.001). The record reports no absolute transfusion rates in its abstract.
cards.watchOut: The intervention bundles an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent with iron, so none of the transfusion effect can be attributed to iron alone; it is carded as supporting, not anchor, evidence.
cards.source: Kong R et al. cards.headline: O'Loughlin 2023 (IRON NOF): in anaemic hip-fracture patients, intravenous iron at operation did not significantly reduce transfusion — 26% versus 37% (P = 0.15) — in a trial terminated early at 143 patients
cards.summary: O'Loughlin 2023 (IRON NOF): in anaemic hip-fracture patients, intravenous iron at operation did not significantly reduce transfusion — 26% versus 37% (P = 0.15) — in a trial terminated early at 143 patients
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, terminated early (O'Loughlin 2023, IRON NOF)
cards.people: 143 patients over 60 years old with preoperative anaemia undergoing surgery for femoral neck or subtrochanteric fracture at seven Australian hospitals, randomised double-blind to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1,000 mg or placebo (saline) at operation; the primary endpoint was blood transfusion use. The trial was terminated early because of jurisdictional changes to transfusion practice and consent requirements.
cards.result: Blood transfusion occurred in 18 of 70 patients (26%) on intravenous iron versus 27 of 73 (37%) on placebo (odds ratio for transfusion if receiving placebo 1.70; 95% CI 0.83 to 3.47; P = 0.15) — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome, and there was no overall difference in units transfused (odds ratio 1.52; 95% CI 0.77 to 3.00; P = 0.22). Haemoglobin at 6 weeks was higher on iron (116 g/L versus 108 g/L; 11.6 versus 10.8 g/dL; P = 0.01). Length of stay, rehabilitation duration and 6-month mortality did not differ. In younger patients without major bleeding, placebo was associated with more units transfused (incidence rate ratio 3.88; 95% CI 1.16 to 13.0) — a subgroup finding in an underpowered trial.
cards.watchOut: Iron given at the time of fracture surgery has almost no time to raise haemoglobin before transfusion decisions are made — the null may be about timing (a single dose at operation) rather than about preoperative treatment, and early termination left the trial underpowered for its 11-percentage-point observed difference.

randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, terminated early (o'loughlin 2023, iron nof) 143 patients over 60 years old with preoperative anaemia undergoing surgery for femoral neck or subtrochanteric fracture at seven australian hospitals, randomised double-blind to intravenous ferric carboxymaltose 1,000 mg or placebo (saline) at operation; the primary endpoint was blood transfusion use. the trial was terminated early because of jurisdictional changes to transfusion practice and consent requirements. blood transfusion occurred in 18 of 70 patients (26%) on intravenous iron versus 27 of 73 (37%) on placebo (odds ratio for transfusion if receiving placebo 1.70; 95% ci 0.83 to 3.47; p = 0.15) — the treatment made no difference on the primary outcome, and there was no overall difference in units transfused (odds ratio 1.52; 95% ci 0.77 to 3.00; p = 0.22). haemoglobin at 6 weeks was higher on iron (116 g/l versus 108 g/l; 11.6 versus 10.8 g/dl; p = 0.01). length of stay, rehabilitation duration and 6-month mortality did not differ. in younger patients without major bleeding, placebo was associated with more units transfused (incidence rate ratio 3.88; 95% ci 1.16 to 13.0) — a subgroup finding in an underpowered trial. iron given at the time of fracture surgery has almost no time to raise haemoglobin before transfusion decisions are made — the null may be about timing (a single dose at operation) rather than about preoperative treatment, and early termination left the trial underpowered for its 11-percentage-point observed difference. o'loughlin e et al. iron nof trial: iv iron for anaemic patients with femoral fracture. bja open. 2023. pmid: 37638076. registry id: actrn12612000448842 (stated in the record's abstract). mesh: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Elhenawy 2021: across major surgery, preoperative intravenous iron reduced transfusion — relative risk 0.84 (a 16% relative reduction) — in 10 trials and 1,039 participants, at moderate certainty
cards.summary: Elhenawy 2021: across major surgery, preoperative intravenous iron reduced transfusion — relative risk 0.84 (a 16% relative reduction) — in 10 trials and 1,039 participants, at moderate certainty
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 randomised controlled trials (1,039 participants) of preoperative intravenous iron supplementation to correct anaemia before major surgery, compared with placebo or oral iron; certainty was rated moderate because of high risk of bias in some studies in one or two domains.
cards.result: Preoperative intravenous iron significantly decreased allogeneic blood transfusion (relative risk 0.84; 95% CI 0.71 to 0.99; P = 0.04; relative measure — a 16% relative reduction). Haemoglobin was higher after iron preoperatively (mean difference 7.15 g/L; 0.72 g/dL; 95% CI 2.26 to 12.04; P = 0.004) and at follow-up beyond 4 weeks postoperatively (mean difference 6.46 g/L). Iron was not associated with increased non-serious (relative risk 1.13; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.65) or serious adverse effects (relative risk 0.96; 95% CI 0.44 to 2.10). The authors call for further full-scale trials with robust methodology. The record reports no pooled absolute transfusion rates.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis predates ITACS, the largest trial, and pools small trials at high risk of bias; its pooled estimate is consistent with ITACS's modest effect rather than with the large reductions sometimes claimed for preoperative iron.
cards.source: Elhenawy AM et al. Role of preoperative intravenous iron therapy to correct anemia before major surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Systematic Reviews. 2021. PMID: 33485392. cards.headline: Synthesis: outside abdominal surgery, preoperative iron modestly reduces transfusion — proven in cardiac surgery (61.1% versus 68.2%), unproven when given at hip-fracture operation, and pooled at a 16% relative reduction across major surgery
cards.summary: Synthesis: outside abdominal surgery, preoperative iron modestly reduces transfusion — proven in cardiac surgery (61.1% versus 68.2%), unproven when given at hip-fracture operation, and pooled at a 16% relative reduction across major surgery
cards.people: The carded evidence: one large double-blind cardiac-surgery trial (955 patients), one small combination-therapy cardiac trial (156 patients), one early-terminated hip-fracture trial (143 patients), and one cross-surgery meta-analysis (10 trials, 1,039 participants, predating the large trial). Total carded participants exceed 2,200 (the meta-analysis's trials are additional to the individually carded trials above as published before them), so no small-N stamp labelling applies.
cards.result: Cardiac surgery: transfusion 61.1% versus 68.2% (relative risk 0.90) with iron alone (ITACS), and transfusion odds ratio 0.33 for iron plus an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent versus oral iron (INITIATE). Hip-fracture surgery: 26% versus 37%, not significant, trial terminated early (IRON NOF). All major surgery pooled: relative risk 0.84. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Contrast with home shelf #1126 is real and should not be smoothed over: the same intervention was null in major abdominal surgery (PREVENTT) — setting, timing and dose schedule differ, and this shelf's positive stamp applies to the cardiac-led evidence, not to surgery in general.

shelves.title: Perioperative pregabalin (PARTIAL completion of #1249, which homes gabapentin): small pooled reductions in pain and opioid use, more sedation, dizziness and visual disturbance — and the largest synthesis calls the pain effect clinically unimportant
shelves.question: Does perioperative pregabalin reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/drug therapy · Analgesics/therapeutic use · Chronic Pain/drug therapy · Humans · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Pregabalin · gamma-Aminobutyric Acid/analogs & derivatives,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: SPLIT (clinical significance) — this pack is a PARTIAL completion: live shelf #1249 already answers the perioperative question for gabapentin; this shelf asks it for pregabalin specifically, including its harms. The pregabalin-specific syntheses agree on direction and size: across 55 studies (Mishriky 2015), pregabalin lowered 24-hour pain at rest (mean difference −0.38) and on movement (−0.47) and opioid consumption by 8.27 mg morphine equivalents, with less nausea/vomiting and pruritus but more sedation (relative risk 1.46), dizziness (relative risk 1.33) and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52); a second pregabalin-specific synthesis (Eipe 2015, 43 studies) found a 16% relative reduction in analgesic consumption, concentrated in surgeries with pronociceptive pain mechanisms. The split is over meaning, not arithmetic: the largest synthesis (Verret 2020, 281 gabapentinoid trials, 24,682 participants) found pain reductions of 3–10 points on a 100-point scale — at or below the 10-point minimally important difference at every time point, consistent for pregabalin and gabapentin alike — no effect on subacute or chronic pain, and more dizziness and visual disturbance, and concluded routine perioperative use is not supported. The earliest synthesis (Tiippana 2007) pooled gabapentin and pregabalin together and is not carded here because its effects cannot be separated by drug. PROPOSED SPLIT (clinical significance): statistically real, clinically small average benefit, bought with consistently more sedation-type harms.

cards.headline: Mishriky 2015: across 55 studies, perioperative pregabalin cut 24-hour opioid use by 8.27 mg morphine equivalents and pain by ~0.4 points — while raising sedation (relative risk 1.46) and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52)
cards.summary: Mishriky 2015: across 55 studies, perioperative pregabalin cut 24-hour opioid use by 8.27 mg morphine equivalents and pain by ~0.4 points — while raising sedation (relative risk 1.46) and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 55 studies (Mishriky 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 55 studies of perioperative pregabalin versus placebo for postoperative pain, with subgroup and meta-regression analyses by dose (≤75 mg, 100–150 mg, 300 mg) and by single versus repeated dosing.
cards.result: With all doses and regimens combined, pregabalin significantly reduced pain scores at rest (mean difference −0.38, 95% CI −0.57 to −0.20) and during movement (−0.47, 95% CI −0.76 to −0.18) and opioid consumption at 24 hours (−8.27 mg morphine equivalents, 95% CI −10.08 to −6.47) versus placebo. Postoperative nausea and vomiting (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.48–0.80) and pruritus (relative risk 0.49, 95% CI 0.34–0.70) were less common on pregabalin; sedation (relative risk 1.46, 95% CI 1.08–1.98), dizziness (relative risk 1.33, 95% CI 1.07–1.64) and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52, 95% CI 2.05–6.04) were more common. All tested doses spared opioids at 24 hours; data were insufficient for persistent-pain conclusions.
cards.watchOut: The pooled pain differences (under half a point) are averages across very different operations and doses; statistical significance here is not the same as a difference an individual patient would notice — the question the Verret card below takes up directly.
cards.source: Mishriky BM et al. Impact of pregabalin on acute and persistent postoperative pain: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British journal of anaesthesia. 2015. PMID: 25209095. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Eipe 2015: across 43 studies, pregabalin reduced analgesic consumption by 16% (relative) — benefit largely confined to pronociceptive-pain surgery; per 1,000 patients, 41 more were sedated and 10 more had blurred vision
cards.summary: Eipe 2015: across 43 studies, pregabalin reduced analgesic consumption by 16% (relative) — benefit largely confined to pronociceptive-pain surgery; per 1,000 patients, 41 more were sedated and 10 more had blurred vision
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies (Eipe 2015)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 43 studies of perioperative pregabalin versus control for acute postoperative pain, analysed by surgical pain model, with GRADE ratings of evidence quality; 1,423 records were screened.
cards.result: Perioperative pregabalin produced a 16% relative reduction in analgesic consumption (95% CI 9% to 21%; moderate-quality evidence, 24 trials) and a small reduction in pain magnitude in surgeries associated with pronociceptive pain. Per 1,000 patients treated, 10 more experienced blurred vision (95% CI 5 to 20 more; moderate-quality evidence, 17 trials) and 41 more experienced sedation (95% CI 13 to 77 more, 17 trials). The number needed to treat to prevent one case of postoperative nausea and vomiting was 11 (95% CI 7–28, 25 trials). Evidence was inadequate for enhanced-recovery outcomes and serious harms.
cards.watchOut: The 16% figure is a relative reduction in analgesic consumption, printed as relative; the same review stresses that benefit was largely restricted to particular surgical pain models, so the average overstates what to expect after an average operation.
cards.source: Eipe N et al. Perioperative use of pregabalin for acute pain-a systematic review and meta-analysis. Pain. 2015. PMID: 25830925. Registry ID: none in the record.
