cards.headline: Verret 2020: across 281 gabapentinoid trials (24,682 participants), pain reductions of 3–10 points on a 100-point scale never cleared the 10-point clinically important threshold — consistent for pregabalin and gabapentin
cards.summary: Verret 2020: across 281 gabapentinoid trials (24,682 participants), pain reductions of 3–10 points on a 100-point scale never cleared the 10-point clinically important threshold — consistent for pregabalin and gabapentin
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 281 randomised trials (Verret 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 281 randomised trials (24,682 participants) of perioperative gabapentinoids (gabapentin or pregabalin) versus control in adults undergoing surgery; clinical significance was judged against established minimally important differences (10 points on a 100-point pain scale).
cards.result: Gabapentinoids lowered postoperative pain intensity at 6 hours (mean difference −10, 95% CI −12 to −9), 12 hours (−9, 95% CI −10 to −7), 24 hours (−7, 95% CI −8 to −6) and 48 hours (−3, 95% CI −5 to −1), but the effect was not clinically significant at any time point, ranging at or below the minimally important difference, and results were consistent regardless of the type of drug (gabapentin or pregabalin). There was no effect on pain at 72 hours, on subacute or chronic pain; gabapentinoids lowered postoperative nausea and vomiting but increased dizziness and visual disturbance. The authors concluded the results do not support routine use of pregabalin or gabapentin for postoperative pain in adults.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis pools gabapentin with pregabalin, so it cannot by itself size pregabalin's effect — its pregabalin relevance is the stated consistency across drug type; it is carded as the benefit–harm counterweight to the pregabalin-specific syntheses, and the gabapentin-only home question sits on shelf #1249.
cards.source: Verret M et al. Perioperative Use of Gabapentinoids for the Management of Postoperative Acute Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. Anesthesiology. 2020. PMID: 32667154. cards.headline: Synthesis: the pooled numbers agree — small pain and opioid reductions, more sedation-type harms; the disagreement is whether the average benefit matters clinically
cards.summary: Synthesis: the pooled numbers agree — small pain and opioid reductions, more sedation-type harms; the disagreement is whether the average benefit matters clinically
cards.people: The carded evidence: two pregabalin-specific meta-analyses (55 and 43 studies) and one 281-trial gabapentinoid meta-analysis (24,682 participants) whose results were consistent by drug type.
cards.result: Pregabalin versus placebo at 24 hours: pain lower by ~0.4 points and opioid consumption lower by 8.27 mg morphine equivalents (Mishriky); analgesic consumption lower by 16% relative (Eipe); against that, pain differences at or below the minimally important difference at every time point in the largest synthesis (Verret), with sedation (relative risk 1.46), dizziness and visual disturbance (relative risk 3.52) consistently increased and nausea/vomiting reduced. PROPOSED SPLIT (clinical significance): a statistically consistent, clinically small average benefit with a consistent harm cost. The gabapentin version of this question is homed on shelf #1249 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Do not quote the opioid-sparing figures without the harm figures: on this evidence the sedation, dizziness and visual-disturbance increases are as consistent as the analgesic decreases.

shelves.title: Tranexamic acid in noncardiac surgery: composite bleeding 9.1% versus 11.7% on placebo in POISE-3 (9,535 patients) — bleeding benefit clear; formal cardiovascular noninferiority was not established in POISE-3 itself
shelves.question: In adults undergoing noncardiac surgery, does tranexamic acid reduce major bleeding without increasing thrombosis versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Antifibrinolytic Agents/adverse effects,therapeutic use · Canada · Hemorrhage/etiology,prevention & control · Humans · Surgical Procedures, Operative · Thrombosis/chemically induced,drug therapy · Tranexamic Acid/adverse effects,therapeutic use
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit for bleeding), with the safety wording kept exact. POISE-3 (9,535 patients at cardiovascular risk undergoing noncardiac surgery; tranexamic acid 1 g at the start and end of surgery) reduced the composite of life-threatening, major or critical-organ bleeding from 11.7% to 9.1% (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; absolute difference −2.6 percentage points). On safety, the composite cardiovascular outcome was 14.2% versus 13.9% (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.14) — a small difference, but the trial's own noninferiority test failed: the upper confidence bound (1.14) crossed the prespecified 1.125 margin, so noninferiority was not established, and this shelf does not claim it was. The wider randomised base is reassuring on thrombosis: Tsan 2023 pooled 191 trials (40,621 patients) and found thromboembolic events in 4.5% on tranexamic acid versus 4.9% on control (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11) with transfusion roughly halved (9.9% vs 19.4%), while noting trial sequential analysis reached only 64.6% of the required information size; Houston 2020 (69 trials in high-transfusion-risk noncardiac surgery, excluding hip/knee arthroplasty) likewise found fewer transfusions (relative risk 0.59, low-certainty) and no differences in thrombotic outcomes. This is the noncardiac-surgery question only: tranexamic acid in coronary surgery is live shelf #1246 (ATACAS), and its other indication homes (live #138 family, #1601, #1619) are separate questions. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit for bleeding): fewer major bleeds, no thrombotic increase demonstrated across the pooled trials, one formal noninferiority miss in the largest trial printed on the face.

cards.headline: Devereaux 2022 (POISE-3): bleeding composite 9.1% on tranexamic acid versus 11.7% on placebo; cardiovascular composite 14.2% versus 13.9% — noninferiority not established
cards.summary: Devereaux 2022 (POISE-3): bleeding composite 9.1% on tranexamic acid versus 11.7% on placebo; cardiovascular composite 14.2% versus 13.9% — noninferiority not established
cards.people: 9,535 patients undergoing noncardiac surgery (at increased cardiovascular risk, expected to stay at least one night) randomised to tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous bolus or placebo at the start and end of surgery, in a partial factorial design with a blood-pressure strategy comparison reported separately. Efficacy was assessed in 4,757 (tranexamic acid) and 4,778 (placebo) patients; the safety composite in 4,581 and 4,601.
cards.result: A composite bleeding outcome event (life-threatening bleeding, major bleeding, or bleeding into a critical organ at 30 days) occurred in 433 of 4,757 patients (9.1%) on tranexamic acid versus 561 of 4,778 (11.7%) on placebo (hazard ratio 0.76, 95% CI 0.67 to 0.87; absolute difference −2.6 percentage points, 95% CI −3.8 to −1.4; P < 0.001 for superiority). The composite cardiovascular outcome (myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery, nonhemorrhagic stroke, peripheral arterial thrombosis, or symptomatic proximal venous thromboembolism) occurred in 649 of 4,581 (14.2%) versus 639 of 4,601 (13.9%) (hazard ratio 1.02, 95% CI 0.92 to 1.14; absolute difference 0.3 points). The upper boundary of the one-sided 97.5% CI (1.14) exceeded the 1.125 noninferiority margin, so — in the authors' words — the noninferiority of tranexamic acid was not established.
cards.watchOut: Read the safety result exactly: a near-identical event rate is not the same as proven noninferiority, and POISE-3 missed its own margin. The cardiovascular composite is dominated by myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (largely troponin-detected), not by venous thromboembolism alone.

cards.headline: Tsan 2023 (191 trials, 40,621 patients): no difference in thromboembolic events (4.5% vs 4.9%; relative risk 1.02) and transfusion roughly halved (9.9% vs 19.4%)
cards.summary: Tsan 2023 (191 trials, 40,621 patients): no difference in thromboembolic events (4.5% vs 4.9%; relative risk 1.02) and transfusion roughly halved (9.9% vs 19.4%)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 191 randomised trials (Tsan 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review, meta-analysis and trial sequential analysis of 191 randomised trials of prophylactic intravenous tranexamic acid versus placebo or no treatment in non-cardiac surgery; 40,621 patients in total, 37,512 in the primary thromboembolism analysis.
cards.result: The composite peri-operative cardiovascular thromboembolic outcome (deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, myocardial ischaemia/infarction or cerebral ischaemia/infarction) occurred in 4.5% on tranexamic acid versus 4.9% on control (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.11, p = 0.65, I² 0%) — no difference between groups, robust in low-risk-of-bias sensitivity analyses. Transfusion was less frequent on tranexamic acid (9.9% vs 19.4%; relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.51). There was no association with seizure rate or 30-day mortality. Trial sequential analysis achieved only 64.6% of the required information size, so the authors state the evidence is not yet sufficient for a firm conclusion on thromboembolism.
cards.watchOut: Most pooled trials are far smaller than POISE-3 and many did not screen systematically for thrombosis; the pooled null and POISE-3's missed noninferiority margin are both printed because both are true.

cards.headline: Houston 2020 (69 trials, 6,157 patients, high-transfusion-risk noncardiac surgery): transfused patients relatively fewer on tranexamic acid (relative risk 0.59), no thrombotic differences identified
cards.summary: Houston 2020 (69 trials, 6,157 patients, high-transfusion-risk noncardiac surgery): transfused patients relatively fewer on tranexamic acid (relative risk 0.59), no thrombotic differences identified
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 69 randomised trials (Houston 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 69 randomised trials (6,157 patients) of intraoperative intravenous tranexamic acid in adult non-cardiac, non-hip/knee-arthroplasty surgery at high risk of transfusion (comparator-arm transfusion rate at least 5%), searched to June 2019 — the pre-POISE-3 base.
cards.result: Tranexamic acid reduced the proportion of patients transfused (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.72; low-certainty evidence) and the volume transfused (mean difference −0.51 red-cell units). It was not associated with differences in deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, all-cause mortality, length of stay, re-operation for haemorrhage, myocardial infarction, stroke or seizure. The authors caution that thrombotic estimates were limited by lack of systematic screening and short follow-up.
cards.watchOut: Low-certainty evidence by GRADE, and the hip/knee arthroplasty literature — where tranexamic acid is standard — is deliberately excluded, so this card speaks to the broader, less settled noncardiac field.
cards.source: Houston BL et al. Efficacy and Safety of Tranexamic Acid in Major Non-Cardiac Surgeries at High Risk for Transfusion: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. cards.people: Adults undergoing noncardiac surgery: 9,535 patients in POISE-3 and 40,621 across the pooled randomised trials.
cards.result: Bleeding and transfusion fall consistently (POISE-3 absolute bleeding difference −2.6 percentage points; pooled transfusion relative risk 0.46–0.59). Thrombotic event rates are near-identical wherever measured, but the largest trial missed its prespecified cardiovascular noninferiority margin — the honest summary is 'no increase shown', not 'proven equally safe'.
cards.watchOut: Doses and surgical populations vary across the pooled trials; POISE-3 used two 1 g boluses in patients aged 45 or older at cardiovascular risk, and its numbers are the ones to quote for that regimen.

shelves.title: ERAS pathways in gynaecologic surgery: median stay 2 days shorter in both randomised trials (7 vs 9 days in PROFAST; 2 vs 4 days in the Italian trial) — the pooled complication benefit rests mainly on cohort data
shelves.question: In adults undergoing gynaecologic surgery, does an ERAS pathway shorten hospital stay and reduce complications versus conventional care?
shelves.mesh: Adenocarcinoma/epidemiology,pathology,surgery · Adult · Aged · Cytoreduction Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Disease Progression · Enhanced Recovery After Surgery · Feasibility Studies · Female · Gynecologic Surgical Procedures/adverse effects,methods,statistics & numerical data · Humans · Implementation Science · Length of Stay/statistics & numerical data · Middle Aged · Morbidity · Mortality · Ovarian Neoplasms/epidemiology,pathology,surgery · Patient Readmission/statistics & numerical data · Perioperative Care/methods,statistics & numerical data · Peritoneal Neoplasms/epidemiology,secondary,surgery · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology,etiology · Reoperation/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), graded exactly as the assignment requires: the randomised legs support shorter stay; the complication leg is largely observational and is labelled as such. PROFAST (99 women having cytoreductive surgery for advanced ovarian cancer, ERAS protocol compliance 92%) found median stay 7 versus 9 days (p = 0.0099) and fewer readmissions (6% vs 20%) with no difference in complications or mortality. The Italian randomised trial (168 women, benign and malignant disease, protocol adherence 84.8%) found median stay 2 versus 4 days (P < .001) and a lower complication rate. The Bisch 2021 meta-analysis (31 studies, 6,703 patients — only 5 randomised, 26 cohorts) pooled a 1.6-day shorter stay and relatively fewer complications (odds ratio 0.68) and readmissions (odds ratio 0.80) with no mortality difference; because that base is mostly cohort data, its complication figure is observational evidence and cannot lift the stamp. Programme naming: no branded or single proprietary programme was tested — each publication describes an ERAS pathway built from the ERAS Society gynaecologic/gynaecologic-oncology perioperative elements (preoperative education and carbohydrate loading, opioid-sparing analgesia, early feeding and mobilisation, as itemised in the trials), and this pack names it that way rather than inventing a brand. ERAS in colorectal surgery is a different shelf (live #869); liver ERAS is pack #6221. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): stay is shorter on randomised evidence; fewer complications are suggested, mainly by cohorts.

cards.headline: Sánchez-Iglesias 2020 (PROFAST): ERAS cut median stay from 9 to 7 days and readmission from 20% to 6% in advanced ovarian cancer cytoreduction — complications unchanged
cards.summary: Sánchez-Iglesias 2020 (PROFAST): ERAS cut median stay from 9 to 7 days and readmission from 20% to 6% in advanced ovarian cancer cytoreduction — complications unchanged
cards.people: Randomised trial at a Barcelona gynaecologic oncology reference hospital: 110 women recruited for surgery for suspected or diagnosed advanced ovarian cancer, 99 in the primary analysis (50 ERAS protocol, 49 conventional management), all undergoing cytoreductive surgery of medium/high complexity (mean Aletti score 7.4). Overall compliance with the ERAS protocol — the pathway as published in the trial, built from ERAS Society gynaecologic-oncology elements — was 92%.
cards.result: Median length of stay was 2 days shorter on ERAS (7 vs 9 days, p = 0.0099) and readmission was lower (6% vs 20%, p = 0.0334). There were no significant differences in intraoperative or postoperative complications, severe (Clavien-Dindo IIIB–IV) complications, the Comprehensive Complication Index, reoperation, or mortality within 30 days — on complications and mortality the pathway made no difference in this trial.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial of 99 analysed patients in high-complexity cancer surgery; the readmission difference rests on small counts (6% vs 20%), and the trial cannot exclude moderate complication effects in either direction.
cards.source: Sánchez-Iglesias JL et al. PROFAST: A randomised trial implementing enhanced recovery after surgery for highcomplexity advanced ovarian cancer surgery. European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990). 2020. PMID: 32688208. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02172638. cards.headline: Ferrari 2020 (Italian randomised trial): ERAS halved median stay (2 vs 4 days) across benign and malignant gynaecologic surgery, with fewer postoperative complications
cards.summary: Ferrari 2020 (Italian randomised trial): ERAS halved median stay (2 vs 4 days) across benign and malignant gynaecologic surgery, with fewer postoperative complications
cards.people: Randomised trial in Italy: 168 women analysed (83 ERAS protocol, 85 standard perioperative care) undergoing gynaecologic surgery for benign disease (42.9%), endometrial cancer (28.6%) or ovarian cancer (28.6%), by varied surgical access. Mean adherence to the ERAS protocol items — the pathway as published in the trial — was 84.8%.
cards.result: Length of stay was shorter on ERAS (median 2 days, IQR 2–3, vs 4 days, IQR 4–7; P < .001), confirmed in prespecified subgroups by surgical access and disease type. A decreased rate of postoperative complications was noted in the ERAS group (the record does not print the two complication percentages), as were earlier times to bowel movement, flatus, drinking, eating and walking, and better patient satisfaction on the QoR-15 recovery questionnaire.
cards.watchOut: The record reports the complication advantage qualitatively without arm percentages, so this pack prints no invented rates. Discharge timing in ERAS trials is partly a protocol target itself, which can inflate the stay contrast.

cards.headline: Bisch 2021 (meta-analysis, mostly cohorts — observational leg): stay 1.6 days shorter, complications relatively fewer (odds ratio 0.68), readmissions fewer (odds ratio 0.80), mortality unchanged
cards.summary: Bisch 2021 (meta-analysis, mostly cohorts — observational leg): stay 1.6 days shorter, complications relatively fewer (odds ratio 0.68), readmissions fewer (odds ratio 0.80), mortality unchanged
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — predominantly cohort studies, observational leg (Bisch 2021)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis in gynaecologic oncology: 31 studies with 6,703 patients — 5 randomised trials and 26 cohort studies. Length-of-stay meta-analysis covered 27 studies (6,345 patients); complications 21 studies (4,974 patients).
cards.result: ERAS was associated with a 1.6-day shorter length of stay (95% CI 1.2 to 2.1), relatively fewer complications (odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.55 to 0.83 — a relative measure), fewer readmissions (odds ratio 0.80, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.99) and mean cost savings of $2,129, with no difference in 30-day mortality (odds ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.6). Effects did not vary by number of ERAS elements or reported compliance.
cards.watchOut: Labelled observational: 26 of 31 studies are cohorts, in which ERAS-era patients are compared with earlier conventional-care patients — secular improvements in care can masquerade as pathway effects. This card corroborates the randomised stay finding; it does not independently prove the complication benefit.
cards.source: Bisch SP et al. Outcomes of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in gynecologic oncology - A systematic review and meta-analysis. Gynecologic oncology. 2021. PMID: 33388155. cards.headline: Synthesis: ERAS shortens stay after gynaecologic surgery on randomised evidence — POSSIBLE (benefit); the complication claim rests mainly on cohorts
cards.summary: Synthesis: ERAS shortens stay after gynaecologic surgery on randomised evidence — POSSIBLE (benefit); the complication claim rests mainly on cohorts
cards.people: Women undergoing gynaecologic surgery: 267 patients in the two randomised trials and 6,703 across the (mostly cohort) meta-analysis.
cards.result: Stay: consistently about 2 days shorter in both trials and 1.6 days shorter pooled. Complications: unchanged in the larger randomised trial, lower in the smaller one and in the cohort-heavy pool. Readmissions were not increased anywhere and were lower in PROFAST. The mixed randomised picture plus the observational weight caps the stamp at POSSIBLE.

shelves.title: ERAS pathways in liver surgery: discharge 3 days sooner in the one early randomised trial (4 vs 7 days) and fewer medical complications (7% vs 27%); pooled stay 2.2 days shorter across mostly cohort studies
shelves.question: In adults undergoing liver surgery, does an ERAS pathway shorten hospital stay and reduce complications versus conventional care?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Early Ambulation · Female · Fluid Therapy · Hepatectomy/methods · Humans · Length of Stay · Liver Neoplasms/rehabilitation,surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Pain/etiology · Patient Satisfaction · Perioperative Care/methods · Physical Therapy Modalities · Quality of Life · Recovery of Function · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), with the non-randomised weight of the base printed on the face. The randomised anchor is Jones 2013 (91 patients, open liver resection): the enhanced recovery programme — preoperative education and carbohydrate loading, goal-directed fluid therapy, early mobilisation and physiotherapy, as published in the trial — cut time to medically fit for discharge (3 vs 6 days) and actual stay (4 vs 7 days), and reduced medical complications (7% vs 27%) without changing surgical complications, readmissions or mortality. The syntheses agree on stay but rest mostly on cohorts: Noba 2020 pooled 6 randomised trials and 21 cohort studies (3,739 patients) — stay 2.22 days shorter, complications relatively fewer (relative risk 0.71), costs lower, no mortality or readmission increase — and Ahmed 2016 pooled 3 trials and 5 cohorts (810 patients) with the same direction. Premise correction, stated plainly: the slate named a 'Melloul programme' for this row — in the fetched records, Melloul's liver contribution is authorship of the ERAS Society liver-surgery guideline (2016), not a trial; no Melloul randomised trial of liver ERAS was found, so the pack is built on Jones and the syntheses instead. Programme naming: the tested intervention is the enhanced recovery programme as itemised in each publication (ERAS Society liver elements); no branded programme is named in the publications carded. Colorectal ERAS is live shelf #869 and gynaecologic ERAS is pack #6220 — different operations, different shelves. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a consistent stay advantage with a plausible complication advantage, on one small trial plus largely observational pooling.

cards.headline: Jones 2013 (randomised trial): enhanced recovery cut stay from 7 to 4 days and medical complications from 27% to 7% after open liver resection
cards.summary: Jones 2013 (randomised trial): enhanced recovery cut stay from 7 to 4 days and medical complications from 27% to 7% after open liver resection
cards.people: Randomised trial of 91 consecutive patients scheduled for open liver resection: 46 enhanced recovery programme (ERP) and 45 standard care. ERP elements as published: greater preoperative education, preoperative oral carbohydrate loading, postoperative goal-directed fluid therapy, early mobilisation and physiotherapy; both groups received standardised anaesthesia with epidural analgesia.
cards.result: Median time until medically fit for discharge was 3 days on ERP versus 6 days on standard care (P < 0.001), and median length of stay was 4 versus 7 days (P < 0.001). Medical complications were fewer on ERP (7% vs 27%, P = 0.020), while surgical complications (15% vs 11%, P = 0.612), readmissions (4% vs 0%, P = 0.153) and mortality (2% in both groups) did not differ — on those outcomes the programme made no difference. Quality of life over 28 days was better on ERP (P = 0.002); patient satisfaction did not differ.
cards.watchOut: One small single-setting trial (91 patients) from 2013 in open resection; the medical-complication contrast (7% vs 27%) rests on few events, and laparoscopic-era practice may narrow the stay gap.
cards.source: Jones C et al. Randomized clinical trial on enhanced recovery versus standard care following open liver resection. The British journal of surgery. 2013. PMID: 23696477. cards.headline: Noba 2020 (meta-analysis, mostly cohorts — observational leg): stay 2.22 days shorter and complications relatively fewer (relative risk 0.71) with ERAS in liver surgery
cards.summary: Noba 2020 (meta-analysis, mostly cohorts — observational leg): stay 2.22 days shorter and complications relatively fewer (relative risk 0.71) with ERAS in liver surgery
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — predominantly cohort studies, observational leg (Noba 2020)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials and cohort studies (2008–2019) of ERAS versus standard care in liver surgery: 6 randomised trials and 21 cohort studies, 3,739 patients (1,777 ERAS, 1,962 standard care).
cards.result: Length of stay was 2.22 days shorter with ERAS (mean difference −2.22, 95% CI −2.77 to −1.68; p < 0.00001). Fewer ERAS patients experienced complications (relative risk 0.71, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.77 — a relative measure). Hospital costs were significantly lower (standardised mean difference −0.98). The authors conclude ERAS is safe and feasible in hepatectomy without increasing mortality or readmission, while noting the evidence base remains weak and compliance reporting poor.
cards.watchOut: Labelled observational in weight: 21 of 27 studies are cohorts comparing ERAS-era with earlier patients. The authors themselves call the liver-surgery evidence weak; this card corroborates direction, it does not carry the stamp alone.

cards.headline: Ahmed 2016 (fast-track meta-analysis): shorter stay and faster functional recovery with fast-track programmes in liver resection, no increase in morbidity, readmission or mortality
cards.summary: Ahmed 2016 (fast-track meta-analysis): shorter stay and faster functional recovery with fast-track programmes in liver resection, no increase in morbidity, readmission or mortality
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — mixed trials and cohorts (Ahmed 2016)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis (studies 2008–2015) of fast-track (enhanced recovery) programmes versus traditional care in elective liver resection: 3 randomised trials and 5 cohort studies, 394 fast-track and 416 traditional-care patients, with subgroup analyses by open and laparoscopic approach.
cards.result: Length of stay was markedly shortened in the fast-track group in both open and laparoscopic approaches (P < 0.00001), with accelerated functional recovery (P = 0.0008) and lower hospital costs, and no increase in readmission, morbidity or mortality. The fast-track group also had shorter operative time, fewer intensive-care admissions and earlier bowel opening and normal diet. The authors call for specific fast-track guidelines for liver resection and more randomised trials.
cards.watchOut: The record reports pooled significance levels without printing the pooled day-count for stay, so none is invented here. 'Fast track' and 'ERAS' name the same family of pathways in this literature.
cards.source: Ahmed EA et al. Fast track program in liver resection: a PRISMA-compliant systematic review and meta-analysis. Medicine. 2016. PMID: 27428206. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Synthesis: ERAS shortens stay after liver surgery — POSSIBLE (benefit) on one small trial plus mainly observational pooling
cards.people: Adults undergoing liver resection: 91 patients in the randomised trial, 3,739 across the larger meta-analysis and 810 across the earlier one (overlapping bases).
cards.result: Stay falls by roughly 2–3 days in every analysis; medical complications fell in the trial and complications overall fell in the pools; mortality and readmission rose nowhere. shelves.title: Stopping alcohol before surgery: one month of abstinence cut complications from 74% to 31% in one 42-patient trial — but the whole randomised base is only about 210 patients, and a later trial found no complication difference
shelves.question: In adults who drink heavily and are having surgery, does stopping alcohol for about 4 weeks before surgery reduce postoperative complications?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Alcoholism/complications · Colonic Diseases/surgery · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Care · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Preoperative Care · Prognosis · Rectal Diseases/surgery · Temperance
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on a small and mixed base that this shelf prints on its face. The direct answer to the 'about 4 weeks before surgery' question is a single trial: Tønnesen 1999 randomised 42 asymptomatic heavy drinkers (at least 60 g ethanol/day) having colorectal surgery to one month of preoperative abstinence — supported and verified with disulfiram, the programme as published — or continued drinking; complications requiring treatment occurred in 31% versus 74% (P = 0.02), with less postoperative myocardial ischaemia (23% vs 85%) and fewer arrhythmias and hypoxaemic episodes. The Egholm Cochrane synthesis (2018 update; 3 randomised trials, 140 participants drinking 3–40 units/day, all testing intensive programmes with pharmacological withdrawal support, education and relapse prophylaxis) pooled complications at 20 of 61 on intervention versus 33 of 61 on control (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.96; moderate-quality evidence), with more successful quitters (41 of 70 vs 5 of 70) and no demonstrated mortality or length-of-stay difference. Against that, the newest trial — Egholm 2022, 70 ankle-fracture patients on the manual-based Gold Standard Program (GSP-A) started on the day of surgery — achieved far more complete abstinence (18 of 35 vs 5 of 35) yet found complications, quality of life and costs similar between groups: the treatment made no difference to complications there. Premise notes: the slate cited an 'Egholm synthesis 2016' — the fetched synthesis is Egholm's Cochrane review in its 2018 update (first published 2012); and no separate Tønnesen 2002 abstinence trial record was found — the 1999 trial is the Tønnesen anchor inside the Cochrane pool. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): biologically coherent and positive in the one trial that tested the exact preoperative month, but far too small a base for LIKELY, and timing may matter — the null trial started at surgery, not a month before.

cards.headline: Tønnesen 1999: one month of preoperative abstinence cut complications requiring treatment from 74% to 31% in 42 heavy drinkers having colorectal surgery
cards.summary: Tønnesen 1999: one month of preoperative abstinence cut complications requiring treatment from 74% to 31% in 42 heavy drinkers having colorectal surgery
cards.people: Randomised trial in Copenhagen: 42 alcohol misusers without symptoms or liver disease, drinking the equivalent of at least 60 g ethanol/day, admitted for elective colorectal surgery. The intervention was withdrawal from alcohol for 1 month before operation, controlled with disulfiram (the programme as published), versus continuous drinking.
cards.result: Postoperative complications requiring treatment within the first month occurred in 31% of the abstinence group versus 74% of continuous drinkers (P = 0.02). Postoperative myocardial ischaemia (23% vs 85%) and arrhythmias (33% vs 86%) on the second postoperative day, and nightly hypoxaemic episodes (4 vs 18 on the second night), all occurred significantly less often with abstinence; delayed-type hypersensitivity responses were better before surgery and surgical stress responses were lower. The authors propose reduced preclinical organ dysfunction and a smaller stress response as the mechanism.
cards.watchOut: Only 42 patients, unblinded by design (abstinence cannot be blinded), and from the pre-registration era — the record carries no registry ID. The effect size is large and the trial is the entire direct evidence for the exact 4-week preoperative question; treat the percentages as fragile.
cards.source: Tonnesen H et al. Effect of preoperative abstinence on poor postoperative outcome in alcohol misusers: randomised controlled trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 1999. PMID: 10323814. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Egholm 2018 (Cochrane): across 3 small trials (140 participants), intensive alcohol cessation interventions were associated with relatively fewer complications (relative risk 0.62) and far more quitters
cards.summary: Egholm 2018 (Cochrane): across 3 small trials (140 participants), intensive alcohol cessation interventions were associated with relatively fewer complications (relative risk 0.62) and far more quitters
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (2018 update of a 2012 review): 3 randomised trials, 140 participants drinking 3 to 40 alcoholic units/day (1 unit = 12 g ethanol) undergoing elective or acute surgery. All interventions were intensive — pharmacological strategies for withdrawal symptoms, patient education and relapse prophylaxis. Complications were analysable in 122 participants who underwent surgery.
cards.result: Any postoperative complication requiring treatment: 20 of 61 participants on intervention versus 33 of 61 on control (relative risk 0.62, 95% CI 0.40 to 0.96; moderate-quality evidence). Mortality was low and not significantly different (1 of 61 vs 3 of 61; relative risk 0.47, 95% CI 0.07 to 2.96; low-quality evidence). Successful quitting at the end of the programme: 41 of 70 versus 5 of 70 (relative risk 8.22, 95% CI 1.67 to 40.44). No study found a significant length-of-stay difference. One further study was ongoing at the time of the review.
cards.watchOut: The pool is three small trials with differing interventions and outcome measures, and Tønnesen 1999 (carded above) is inside it — the synthesis corroborates the single trial; it is not three independent confirmations of the 4-week regimen.
cards.source: Egholm JW et al. Perioperative alcohol cessation intervention for postoperative complications. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 30408162. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Egholm 2022: the Gold Standard Program (GSP-A) after ankle fracture surgery produced more abstinence (18/35 vs 5/35) but no difference in complications, quality of life or costs
cards.summary: Egholm 2022: the Gold Standard Program (GSP-A) after ankle fracture surgery produced more abstinence (18/35 vs 5/35) but no difference in complications, quality of life or costs
cards.people: Randomised trial of 70 patients having acute ankle fracture surgery who drank at least 21 drinks/week (1 drink = 12 g ethanol), randomised on the day of operation to the manual-based 6-week intensive Gold Standard Program for alcohol (GSP-A — 5 personal meetings, patient education, motivational and pharmacological support including withdrawal prophylaxis, B vitamins and low-dose disulfiram; the programme as named in the publication) or treatment as usual.
cards.result: Complete alcohol cessation postoperatively was higher on GSP-A (18 of 35 vs 5 of 35; number needed to treat 3, p ≤ 0.001), but complications in the short term (12 of 35 vs 14 of 33) and long term (16 of 35 vs 18 of 33), SF-36 quality-of-life scores and hospital costs were similar between groups — the treatment made no difference to complications in this trial. Low-risk consumption in the long term also did not differ (10 of 35 vs 7 of 33, p = 0.5).
cards.watchOut: Crucially different timing: this programme started on the day of surgery for an acute fracture, so there was no preoperative abstinence month — its null result does not directly test this shelf's question, and is carded precisely to keep the shelf honest about the mixed base.
cards.source: Egholm JWM et al. Minor effect of patient education for alcohol cessation intervention on outcomes after acute fracture surgery: a randomized trial of 70 patients. Acta orthopaedica. 2022. PMID: 35417027. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a preoperative month of abstinence probably reduces complications — POSSIBLE (benefit) on about 210 randomised patients in total
cards.summary: Synthesis: a preoperative month of abstinence probably reduces complications — POSSIBLE (benefit) on about 210 randomised patients in total
cards.people: Adults drinking heavily and undergoing surgery: 42 patients in the preoperative-abstinence trial, 140 across the Cochrane pool (which includes that trial) and 70 in the postoperative-start fracture trial.
cards.result: The only trial of the exact intervention (abstinence for about 4 weeks before elective surgery) was strongly positive; the pooled intensive-intervention estimate is positive (relative risk 0.62); the one trial that started the programme at surgery was null for complications despite achieving abstinence. Mortality and length of stay were unchanged everywhere they were measured.

shelves.title: Apnoeic oxygenation at intubation (THRIVE, ENDAO): SPLIT — safe apnoea time clearly prolonged, emergency desaturation benefit shown in pooled data but not in the largest ED trial
shelves.question: In adults having emergency intubation, does apnoeic oxygenation by high-flow nasal oxygen (THRIVE-style) or standard nasal cannula prolong safe apnoea time and reduce desaturation versus standard preoxygenation alone?
shelves.mesh: Administration, Intranasal/methods · Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Airway Management/methods · Apnea/physiopathology · Carbon Dioxide/metabolism · Continuous Positive Airway Pressure/methods · Female · Humans · Insufflation/methods · Intubation, Intratracheal/methods · Larynx/surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Neuromuscular Blockade/methods · Oxygen/administration & dosage · Steam · Time Factors · Trachea/surgery
shelves.balance: SPLIT — apnoeic oxygenation clearly prolongs safe apnoea time in controlled/elective settings, but the largest emergency-department randomised trial found no desaturation benefit. THRIVE (Patel 2015, PMID: 25388828 — uncontrolled physiological series, labelled) kept 25 difficult-airway patients apnoeic for a median 14 minutes with no desaturation below 90%. In obese patients having elective surgery, nasal-cannula apnoeic oxygenation lengthened safe apnoeic duration by a median 103 seconds (Moon 2019, PMID: 31317460). A meta-analysis of emergency intubation (Pavlov 2017, PMID: 28647137; 8 studies, 1,953 patients) found hypoxaemia in 19.1% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 27.6% with usual care — a 30% relative risk reduction. But the ENDAO randomised trial (Caputo 2017, PMID: 28791755; 200 patients) found lowest mean saturation 92% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 93% with usual care (p=0.11). The split is named on the stamp: physiology and pooled data favour it; the biggest single emergency RCT does not. Cross-point: preoxygenation before the apnoeic period (PREOXI/FELLOW) is homed on Shelf #758 — this shelf is only about oxygen during apnoea itself.

cards.headline: Patel 2015 (THRIVE, uncontrolled series, 25 difficult-airway patients): median apnoea time 14 minutes with transnasal high-flow humidified oxygen, and no patient desaturated below 90%
cards.summary: Patel 2015 (THRIVE, uncontrolled series, 25 difficult-airway patients): median apnoea time 14 minutes with transnasal high-flow humidified oxygen, and no patient desaturated below 90%
cards.type: Uncontrolled physiological case series (Patel 2015, THRIVE) — no comparator
cards.people: 25 patients with difficult airways (median Mallampati grade 3; 12 obese, 9 stridulous) undergoing general anaesthesia for hypopharyngeal or laryngotracheal surgery, given continuous transnasal high-flow humidified oxygen for pre-oxygenation and throughout apnoea until a definitive airway was secured, with jaw thrust maintaining airway patency. No control group — labelled as an uncontrolled physiological series.
cards.result: Median (IQR [range]) apnoea time was 14 (9–19 [5–65]) minutes. No patient experienced arterial desaturation below 90%. Mean post-apnoea end-tidal (and in four patients arterial) carbon dioxide was 7.8 kPa, and the rate of rise of end-tidal carbon dioxide was 0.15 kPa per minute — much slower than in classical apnoea, which the authors attribute to flow-dependent deadspace flushing as well as apnoeic oxygenation.
cards.watchOut: Twenty-five selected patients, expert hands, jaw thrust throughout, and no comparator: this proves the physiology can work, not that it improves outcomes in an unselected emergency intubation. Carbon dioxide still rose — THRIVE buys oxygenation time, not ventilation.
cards.source: Patel A et al. Transnasal Humidified Rapid-Insufflation Ventilatory Exchange (THRIVE): a physiological method of increasing apnoea time in patients with difficult airways. Anaesthesia. 2015. PMID: 25388828. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Caputo 2017 (ENDAO, emergency-department RCT, 200 patients): apnoeic oxygenation did not prevent desaturation — lowest mean oxygen saturation 92% vs 93% with usual care (p=0.11) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Caputo 2017 (ENDAO, emergency-department RCT, 200 patients): apnoeic oxygenation did not prevent desaturation — lowest mean oxygen saturation 92% vs 93% with usual care (p=0.11) (the treatment made no difference)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in the emergency department (Caputo 2017, ENDAO)
cards.people: 206 patients enrolled (200 allocated) requiring rapid sequence intubation in an academic urban Level I trauma centre emergency department, randomised to apnoeic oxygenation (n=100) or usual care (n=100); patients in cardiac or traumatic arrest, or without preoxygenation, were excluded. Saturations were recorded in real time by monitors, with a blinded observer recording times.
cards.result: There was no difference in lowest mean oxygen saturation between the groups: 92% (95% CI 91 to 93) with apnoeic oxygenation vs 93% (92 to 94) with usual care (p=0.11). The authors conclude that apnoeic oxygenation during rapid sequence intubation did not prevent desaturation in this study population.
cards.watchOut: Usual-care patients in this trial desaturated less than in many series (lowest mean 93%), leaving little room to show benefit; apnoea times in routine rapid sequence intubation are short. A null here does not erase the physiological effect — it questions its size in already well-preoxygenated ED patients.
cards.source: Caputo N et al. Emergency Department use of Apneic Oxygenation Versus Usual Care During Rapid Sequence Intubation: A Randomized Controlled Trial (The ENDAO Trial). Academic Emergency Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28791755. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Moon 2019 (RCT in obese elective patients, 135 patients): nasal-cannula apnoeic oxygenation lengthened safe apnoeic duration by a median 103 seconds and raised the lowest saturation by 3.8%
cards.summary: Moon 2019 (RCT in obese elective patients, 135 patients): nasal-cannula apnoeic oxygenation lengthened safe apnoeic duration by a median 103 seconds and raised the lowest saturation by 3.8%
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, controlled trial in elective obese patients (Moon 2019)
cards.people: 135 obese patients undergoing non-emergent surgery under general anaesthesia, randomised to control or to apnoeic oxygenation (oxygen vs air comparisons) via a nasopharyngeal airway and standard nasal cannula during a simulated prolonged laryngoscopy; safe apnoeic period was defined from the start of laryngoscopy until SpO2 reached 95%.
cards.result: The oxygen group had a median safe apnoeic duration 103 seconds longer than the control group, and the lowest mean SpO2 during induction was 3.8% higher in the oxygen group. After intubation, mean end-tidal carbon dioxide was 3.0 mmHg higher in the oxygen group than in controls.
cards.watchOut: Elective, simulated prolonged laryngoscopy in a controlled operating room — the endpoint is a physiological margin (time to 95%), not prevented harm, and obese elective patients are not crashing emergency-department patients.
cards.source: Moon TS et al. Apneic Oxygenation During Prolonged Laryngoscopy in Obese Patients: a Randomized, Double-Blinded, Controlled Trial of Nasal Cannula Oxygen Administration. cards.headline: Pavlov 2017 (meta-analysis, emergency intubation, 8 studies, 1,953 patients): hypoxaemia 19.1% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 27.6% with usual care — a 30% relative risk reduction
cards.summary: Pavlov 2017 (meta-analysis, emergency intubation, 8 studies, 1,953 patients): hypoxaemia 19.1% with apnoeic oxygenation vs 27.6% with usual care — a 30% relative risk reduction
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of eight studies of apnoeic oxygenation during emergency endotracheal intubation in critical care settings (emergency department, ICU and retrieval), pooled with a random-effects model on intention-to-treat allocation where available.
cards.result: The pooled absolute risk of clinically significant hypoxaemia was 19.1% in the apnoeic oxygenation group vs 27.6% in the usual care group, with no heterogeneity across studies (I²=0%; p=0.42). Apnoeic oxygenation reduced the relative risk of hypoxaemia by 30% (relative risk about 0.70, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.82) — a relative measure; the absolute difference was 8.5 percentage points. There was a trend toward lower mortality (relative risk of death 0.77, 95% CI 0.59 to 1.02, not significant).
cards.watchOut: The pooled studies mix randomised and observational designs and predate ENDAO's full weight in the literature; a pooled relative benefit built partly on observational data is exactly what a large null RCT then tests. Read alongside the ENDAO card, not instead of it.
cards.source: Pavlov I et al. Apneic oxygenation reduces the incidence of hypoxemia during emergency intubation: A systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Emergency Medicine. 2017. PMID: 28647137. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Waheed 2025 (three-arm emergency-department RCT, 88 patients): high-flow nasal cannula gave the highest median saturation and less desaturation and hypotension than low-flow or standard care, but standard care had the highest first-pass success (93%)
cards.summary: Waheed 2025 (three-arm emergency-department RCT, 88 patients): high-flow nasal cannula gave the highest median saturation and less desaturation and hypotension than low-flow or standard care, but standard care had the highest first-pass success (93%)
cards.type: Three-arm randomised controlled trial in the emergency department (Waheed 2025)
cards.people: 88 adult patients requiring intubation in a tertiary-care emergency department, randomised to apnoeic oxygenation by high-flow nasal cannula (20 L/min), low-flow nasal cannula (10 L/min) or standard care without oxygen delivery, all with head elevation; primary outcomes were lowest oxygen saturation 3 minutes post-intubation and first-pass success.
cards.result: The high-flow group had the highest median SpO2 and less variability than the other groups, and a significantly shorter apnoea duration than the low-flow group. The low-flow group had a higher prevalence of post-intubation hypotension (46%) and oxygen desaturation (57%). The standard-care group had the highest first-attempt success rate (93%). The authors conclude high-flow nasal cannula with head-elevated positioning reduces post-intubation desaturation and hypotension compared with low-flow and standard care.
cards.watchOut: Only 88 patients across three arms, and the record reports several key contrasts without full numbers — treat it as supportive and hypothesis-level, not as a verdict on high-flow vs low-flow.
cards.source: Waheed S et al. Randomized controlled trial to assess the effectiveness of apnoeic oxygenation in adults using a low-flow or high-flow nasal cannula with head side elevation during endotracheal intubation in the emergency department. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — apnoeic oxygenation prolongs safe apnoea time physiologically and pooled emergency data favour it, but the largest emergency-department RCT (ENDAO) found no desaturation benefit
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — apnoeic oxygenation prolongs safe apnoea time physiologically and pooled emergency data favour it, but the largest emergency-department RCT (ENDAO) found no desaturation benefit
cards.people: THRIVE uncontrolled series, 25 patients (Patel 2015); ENDAO ED RCT, 200 allocated (Caputo 2017); obese elective RCT, 135 patients (Moon 2019); emergency-intubation meta-analysis, 8 studies, 1,953 patients (Pavlov 2017); three-arm ED RCT, 88 patients (Waheed 2025).
cards.result: Physiology: median 14 minutes of apnoea without desaturation below 90% on THRIVE; +103 seconds of safe apnoeic duration with nasal-cannula oxygen in obese elective patients. Emergency outcomes: pooled hypoxaemia 19.1% vs 27.6% (30% relative risk reduction, Pavlov) vs ENDAO's null on lowest mean saturation (92% vs 93%, p=0.11). PROPOSED SPLIT — the split is setting and endpoint: safe-apnoea-time gains in controlled settings are consistent; translation into fewer desaturations during real emergency intubation is shown in pooled (partly observational) data but not in the largest single ED trial.
cards.watchOut: Tier C — the developer's personal verdict. Scope: oxygen delivered during the apnoeic period of intubation. Preoxygenation strategy before apnoea (including non-invasive ventilation preoxygenation, PREOXI) and laryngoscopy technique are homed on Shelf #758; the FELLOW apnoeic-oxygenation trial is carded there and is therefore not re-carded here (one-home rule).

shelves.title: Liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel) versus plain bupivacaine: the Cochrane synthesis found no difference, and the pooled advantage is 0.37 pain points — 'small but not clinically relevant'
shelves.question: In adults having surgery, does liposomal bupivacaine (wound infiltration or perineural) reduce postoperative pain and opioid use versus plain bupivacaine or placebo?
shelves.mesh: Anesthetics, Local/administration & dosage*, adverse effects · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee · Bupivacaine/administration & dosage*, adverse effects · Humans · Liposomes · Mammaplasty · Pain Measurement · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy* · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: Graded against the Cochrane synthesis, as commissioned, not the most favourable single trial. For infiltration (Hamilton 2017, 9 studies, 1,377 participants), liposomal bupivacaine beat placebo on cumulative 72-hour pain in one study (very low quality) and showed no difference versus plain bupivacaine hydrochloride in two studies (very low quality). For peripheral nerve block (Hamilton 2016), three of seven trials never published results and the four reported studies (299 participants) did not report pain scores at set time points. The largest pooled comparison (Dinges 2021, 23 RCTs, 1,867 patients) found pain 0.37 points lower at 24 hours and a morphine-equivalent ratio of 0.85 versus plain bupivacaine — statistically significant but, in the authors' own words, small and not clinically relevant. A 100-patient placebo trial of the named product — Exparel (Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc, Parsippany, NJ, as published) — found no difference at any time point. PROPOSED UNLIKELY (benefit beyond plain bupivacaine). Current marketed versions may differ from the tested product.

cards.headline: Hamilton 2017 (Cochrane, infiltration, 9 studies, 1,377 participants): lower pain than placebo in one study, no difference versus plain bupivacaine hydrochloride — very low quality evidence
cards.summary: Hamilton 2017 (Cochrane, infiltration, 9 studies, 1,377 participants): lower pain than placebo in one study, no difference versus plain bupivacaine hydrochloride — very low quality evidence
cards.people: Nine randomised, double-blind, placebo- or active-controlled studies (1,377 participants aged 18 or over undergoing elective surgery at any site) of liposomal bupivacaine infiltration at the surgical site; five parallel-arm studies (965 participants) were analysable — two placebo-controlled and three using plain bupivacaine hydrochloride infiltration as control. The tested product is the liposomal bupivacaine formulation marketed as Exparel (named in the trial record carded below).
cards.result: Three studies (551 participants) reported cumulative pain intensity over 72 hours. Compared with placebo, liposomal bupivacaine was associated with a lower cumulative pain score from 0 to 72 hours in one study (very low quality evidence). Compared with plain bupivacaine hydrochloride, two studies showed no difference for this outcome (very low quality evidence); the reviewers did not meta-analyse because the surgical populations differed (breast augmentation versus knee arthroplasty). No serious adverse events were reported as associated with liposomal bupivacaine, and no study reported withdrawals due to drug-related adverse events (moderate quality evidence). Most studies were at unclear risk of bias; two were at high risk of selective reporting and four at high risk of bias due to small size.
cards.watchOut: The headline comparison for practice — liposomal versus plain bupivacaine — rests on two studies the reviewers would not pool, graded very low quality. 'No difference' here means no demonstrated difference on very low quality evidence, in either direction.

cards.headline: Hamilton 2016 (Cochrane, peripheral nerve block, 7 studies): three completed studies never published results; the four reported studies (299 participants) did not report pain scores at any set time point
cards.summary: Hamilton 2016 (Cochrane, peripheral nerve block, 7 studies): three completed studies never published results; the four reported studies (299 participants) did not report pain scores at any set time point
cards.people: Seven randomised, double-blind, placebo- or active-controlled studies of a single dose of liposomal bupivacaine as a peripheral nerve block in adults undergoing elective surgery; three were recorded as completed or terminated with no published results, leaving four studies (299 participants): two transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block studies, one dorsal penile nerve block and one ankle block (a phase II dose study with pooled data that could not be used).
cards.result: The studies did not report the review's primary outcome (cumulative pain score 0–72 hours) or mean pain scores at 12, 24, 48, 72 or 96 hours. One study reported no difference in mean pain score over the first, second and third postoperative 24-hour periods for liposomal bupivacaine TAP block versus no TAP block. Two laparoscopic-surgery TAP studies reported opposing findings for cumulative postoperative opioid dose. The reviewers concluded there were insufficient data for a clinically meaningful meta-analysis.
cards.watchOut: Three of seven nerve-block trials completed but unpublished is a reporting-bias warning in itself: the perineural evidence base a clinician can actually read is four small studies that mostly did not measure the outcomes the review asked for.

cards.headline: Dinges 2021 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 1,867 patients): pain 0.37 points lower at 24 hours and opioid ratio 0.85 versus plain bupivacaine — statistically significant, explicitly not clinically relevant
cards.summary: Dinges 2021 (meta-analysis, 23 RCTs, 1,867 patients): pain 0.37 points lower at 24 hours and opioid ratio 0.85 versus plain bupivacaine — statistically significant, explicitly not clinically relevant
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (Dinges 2021)
cards.people: 23 randomised controlled trials including 1,867 patients comparing liposomal bupivacaine with bupivacaine hydrochloride (local or peripheral regional single-injection), searched to May 2020; primary endpoints were mean pain score difference and relative morphine-equivalent consumption (ratio of means) at 24 and 72 hours.
cards.result: At 24 hours the mean pain score difference favoured liposomal bupivacaine at −0.37 (95% CI −0.56 to −0.19) and the relative morphine-equivalent consumption was 0.85 (0.82 to 0.89) — a relative measure; the record gives the ratio, not absolute milligram amounts. At 72 hours the pain difference was not significant (−0.25, 95% CI −0.71 to 0.20) and the morphine-equivalent ratio was 0.85 (0.77 to 0.95). The authors conclude the beneficial effect on pain scores and opioid consumption was small but not clinically relevant, despite statistical significance, and was stable across application modalities.
cards.watchOut: A 0.37-point difference on a 0–10 pain scale is below any usual threshold for a difference a patient can feel; statistical significance at this sample size should not be read as a reason to pay the liposomal product's premium over plain bupivacaine.

cards.headline: Jones 2018 (placebo RCT, 100 patients): liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel, Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc) made no difference to vaginal pain or opioid use after posterior vaginal surgery (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Jones 2018 (placebo RCT, 100 patients): liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel, Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc) made no difference to vaginal pain or opioid use after posterior vaginal surgery (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 100 patients randomised double-blind at a single US centre to 20 mL extended-release liposomal bupivacaine (Exparel) (Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc, Parsippany, NJ) (n = 49) or 20 mL saline placebo (n = 51), injected at the end of surgery involving the posterior vaginal wall or muscularis; pain measured on the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale on days 1, 3 and 7, with morphine-equivalent narcotic use.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in vaginal pain scores between liposomal bupivacaine and placebo on day 1 (median 1 [IQR 0–3] in both groups, P = .59), day 3 (median 2 [0–3] vs 1 [0–3], P = .20) or day 7 (median 3 [1–4] vs 1.5 [0–3], P = .06), and cumulative day 1–7 pain scores were also not significant (median 6 [1–10] vs 4 [1–8], P = .14).
cards.watchOut: One operation type at one centre, and day-7 scores numerically favoured placebo — but it is a clean, adequately sized placebo test of the named marketed product, and it found nothing. Individual positive trials in other operations should be read against the Cochrane verdict, not the other way round.

American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2018. PMID: 30273586. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: graded against the Cochrane synthesis, liposomal bupivacaine has not beaten plain bupivacaine in any clinically relevant way
cards.summary: Synthesis: graded against the Cochrane synthesis, liposomal bupivacaine has not beaten plain bupivacaine in any clinically relevant way
cards.people: Two Cochrane reviews (infiltration: 9 studies, 1,377 participants; nerve block: 7 studies, 299 reported participants), a 23-RCT meta-analysis (1,867 patients) and a 100-patient placebo trial of the named product, Exparel (Pacira Pharmaceuticals Inc).
cards.result: Versus plain bupivacaine hydrochloride: no difference in cumulative 72-hour pain in the Cochrane infiltration review (very low quality), and a pooled 24-hour pain advantage of −0.37 points with a morphine-equivalent ratio of 0.85 in the Dinges meta-analysis, judged by its own authors small and not clinically relevant. Versus placebo: inconsistent — one positive study in the Cochrane review, a null 100-patient trial. PROPOSED UNLIKELY (benefit beyond plain bupivacaine).
cards.watchOut: This shelf grades the product against the Cochrane synthesis, as commissioned — not against the most favourable single trial. A clinician choosing between liposomal and plain bupivacaine is choosing on cost and convenience, not on demonstrated analgesic superiority.

shelves.title: Epidural blood patch for post-dural-puncture headache: headache at day 7 in 16% versus 86% on conservative care in the one RCT; 75% complete relief in a 504-patient series, with early patching and large-bore needles predicting failure
shelves.question: In adults with post-dural-puncture headache that has failed conservative treatment, does an epidural blood patch relieve headache versus continued conservative care, and does timing or volume change success?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Back Pain/etiology, therapy · Blood Patch, Epidural* · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Post-Dural Puncture Headache/therapy* · Single-Blind Method · Spinal Puncture* · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: The randomised evidence is one small observer-blind trial (van Kooten 2008, 40 analysed): headache persisted at 24 hours in 58% after blood patch versus 90% on conservative treatment (relative risk 0.64), and at day 7 in 16% versus 86% (relative risk 0.18), with remaining headaches mild after patching. The large prospective Safa-Tisseront series (504 patients with incapacitating headache) found 75% complete relief, 18% incomplete relief and 7% failure; failure was independently predicted by large-bore needle puncture (OR 5.96) and by patching less than 4 days after puncture (OR 2.63). On volume, the Paech randomised trial in 121 obstetric patients found complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26% with 15, 20 and 30 mL, supporting an attempt at 20 mL. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — a large and consistent effect, capped because the versus-conservative randomised base is a single small trial. The Cochrane blood-patch review was not carded: its update record is marked WITHDRAWN in PubMed.

cards.headline: van Kooten 2008 (RCT, 42 randomised, 40 analysed): epidural blood patch versus conservative treatment — headache at day 7 in 16% versus 86% (relative risk 0.18)
cards.summary: van Kooten 2008 (RCT, 42 randomised, 40 analysed): epidural blood patch versus conservative treatment — headache at day 7 in 16% versus 86% (relative risk 0.18)
cards.people: 42 patients presenting with post-dural-puncture headache lasting 24 hours to 1 week, randomised to epidural blood patch (n = 19) or conservative treatment (n = 23); two patients allocated to conservative treatment refused participation directly after randomisation and were excluded, leaving 40 analysed. Primary endpoint was any headache at 24 hours; secondary endpoints were presence and severity of headache at 1 week. Observer-blind, with stratified Mantel-Haenszel adjustment for confounders.
cards.result: At 24 hours, headache was present in 11 of 19 (58%) blood-patch patients versus 19 of 21 analysed (90%) conservative patients (relative risk 0.64, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.96). At day 7, headache was present in 3 (16%) blood-patch patients versus 18 (86%) conservative patients (relative risk 0.18, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.53) — an 82% relative risk reduction, 70 percentage points absolute. Headache was mild in all three remaining blood-patch patients, while 10 of the 18 unrecovered conservative patients had moderate or severe headache. Adjustment for confounders did not affect the results.
cards.watchOut: The only randomised trial of therapeutic blood patch versus conservative care, and it is small: 40 analysed patients, two post-randomisation exclusions in the conservative arm, and patients could not be blinded to a blood patch. The effect is large enough that small-trial fragility is unlikely to erase it, but the exact size (RR 0.18) should not be treated as precise.
cards.source: van Kooten F et al. Epidural blood patch in post dural puncture headache: a randomised, observer-blind, controlled clinical trial. Journal of neurology, neurosurgery, and psychiatry. 2008. PMID: 17635971. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Safa-Tisseront 2001 (prospective series, 504 patients): complete relief in 75%, incomplete relief in 18%, failure in 7% — failure predicted by large-bore needle and patching within 4 days
cards.summary: Safa-Tisseront 2001 (prospective series, 504 patients): complete relief in 75%, incomplete relief in 18%, failure in 7% — failure predicted by large-bore needle and patching within 4 days
cards.people: 504 consecutive patients treated with epidural blood patch for incapacitating post-dural-puncture headache at one hospital, 1988–2000, classified prospectively as complete relief (disappearance of all symptoms), incomplete relief (improved enough to perform normal daily activity) or failure (persistence of severe symptoms); logistic regression identified predictors of failure, including needle diameter, delay from puncture to patch, and injected blood volume.
cards.result: Complete relief occurred in 377 patients (75%), incomplete relief in 93 (18%) and failure in 34 (7%) — so 93% achieved complete or incomplete relief. In multivariate analysis, only two factors independently predicted failure: the diameter of the needle that punctured the dura (OR 5.96, 95% CI 2.63 to 13.47; P < 0.001) and a delay to blood patch of less than 4 days (OR 2.63, 95% CI 1.06 to 6.51; P = 0.037). The authors conclude epidural blood patch is effective for severe post-dural-puncture headache and less effective after large-bore needle puncture.
cards.watchOut: No untreated comparison group — some of these headaches would have resolved with time, so 75% complete relief is an upper bound on the patch's own effect. The timing finding (patching before 4 days predicts failure) is associational: patients patched earliest may be those with the largest leaks and worst headaches.
cards.source: Safa-Tisseront V et al. Effectiveness of epidural blood patch in the management of post-dural puncture headache. Anesthesiology. 2001. PMID: 11506102. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Paech 2011 (volume RCT, 121 obstetric patients): 15, 20 or 30 mL of blood — complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26%; the authors support attempting 20 mL
cards.summary: Paech 2011 (volume RCT, 121 obstetric patients): 15, 20 or 30 mL of blood — complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26%; the authors support attempting 20 mL
cards.people: 121 obstetric patients requiring epidural blood patch after unintentional dural puncture during epidural catheter insertion, randomised multinational and multicentre, blinded, to 15, 20 or 30 mL of autologous blood, stratified by patch timing and centre, and followed for 5 days; primary endpoint was a composite of permanent or partial relief of headache. Median volumes actually administered were 15, 20 and 30 mL, with 98%, 81% and 54% of the respective groups receiving the allocated volume.
cards.result: Permanent or partial relief occurred in 61% (15 mL), 73% (20 mL) and 67% (30 mL) of patients; complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26% respectively. The 0–48 hour headache-score area under the curve was highest in the 15 mL group. Low back pain during or after the patch was similar among groups and of low intensity, though the 15 mL group had the highest post-procedural back-pain scores. No serious morbidity was reported. The authors conclude the optimum volume remains undetermined but support attempting to administer 20 mL.
cards.watchOut: Obstetric patients after epidural-catheter dural puncture only — the volume answer may not transfer to spinal-needle or diagnostic-puncture headaches. Only 54% of the 30 mL group could receive the allocated volume, so the high-volume arm partly tested 'as much as tolerated', not 30 mL.
cards.source: Paech MJ et al. The volume of blood for epidural blood patch in obstetrics: a randomized, blinded clinical trial. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2011. PMID: 21596867. randomised blinded volume trial (paech 2011) 121 obstetric patients requiring epidural blood patch after unintentional dural puncture during epidural catheter insertion, randomised multinational and multicentre, blinded, to 15, 20 or 30 ml of autologous blood, stratified by patch timing and centre, and followed for 5 days; primary endpoint was a composite of permanent or partial relief of headache. median volumes actually administered were 15, 20 and 30 ml, with 98%, 81% and 54% of the respective groups receiving the allocated volume. permanent or partial relief occurred in 61% (15 ml), 73% (20 ml) and 67% (30 ml) of patients; complete relief in 10%, 32% and 26% respectively. the 0–48 hour headache-score area under the curve was highest in the 15 ml group. low back pain during or after the patch was similar among groups and of low intensity, though the 15 ml group had the highest post-procedural back-pain scores. no serious morbidity was reported. the authors conclude the optimum volume remains undetermined but support attempting to administer 20 ml. obstetric patients after epidural-catheter dural puncture only — the volume answer may not transfer to spinal-needle or diagnostic-puncture headaches. only 54% of the 30 ml group could receive the allocated volume, so the high-volume arm partly tested 'as much as tolerated', not 30 ml. paech mj et al. the volume of blood for epidural blood patch in obstetrics: a randomized, blinded clinical trial. anesthesia and analgesia. 2011. pmid: 21596867. registry id: none in the record. mesh: adult · anesthesia, epidural/adverse effects · blood patch, epidural/methods, standards* · female · humans · obstetrics/methods, standards* · post-dural puncture headache/etiology*, therapy* · single-blind method · spinal puncture/adverse effects*

cards.headline: Synthesis: a large, consistent effect in one small RCT and a 504-patient series — blood patch works for established post-dural-puncture headache; timing and volume modify success
cards.summary: Synthesis: a large, consistent effect in one small RCT and a 504-patient series — blood patch works for established post-dural-puncture headache; timing and volume modify success
cards.people: One randomised trial versus conservative treatment (40 analysed), one 504-patient prospective series, and one 121-patient randomised volume trial in obstetric patients.
cards.result: Versus conservative care: headache at day 7 in 16% versus 86% (relative risk 0.18). In practice: 75% complete and 18% incomplete relief in the large series, with failure predicted by large-bore needle (OR 5.96) and patching within 4 days (OR 2.63); 20 mL is the supported target volume. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — capped because the versus-conservative randomised base is a single small trial.
cards.watchOut: The Cochrane review of blood patching (Boonmak & Boonmak) was not carded: its 2013 update record is marked WITHDRAWN in PubMed, so this shelf rests on the primary trial and series instead. Prophylactic patching (before headache) is a different question and is not answered here.
cards.source: Synthesis of van Kooten F et al. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 2008 (PMID: 17635971); Safa-Tisseront V et al. Anesthesiology. 2001 (PMID: 11506102); Paech MJ et al. Anesthesia and Analgesia. 2011 (PMID: 21596867).

shelves.question: In women having mastectomy or breast-conserving surgery, does a pectoral nerve (PECS I/II) block reduce postoperative pain and opioid use versus placebo, no block, or paravertebral block?

shelves.balance: PARTIAL shelf — the PECS slice only, verified against its homes before building: pack #3011 asks the erector spinae plane block question for the same operation and pack #1240 asks paravertebral-versus-general anaesthesia for cancer recurrence; neither homes PECS, and no study carded on those packs is re-carded here. On the PECS evidence itself: Bashandy & Abbas (120 women) found lower pain scores and less morphine in the first 12 hours adding PECS I + II to general anaesthesia versus general anaesthesia alone; Kulhari (40 women) found PECS II gave longer analgesia (294.5 vs 197.5 minutes) and less 24-hour morphine (3.90 vs 5.30 mg) than a single-level paravertebral block. The Meißner meta-analysis (24 RCTs, 1,565 patients) tempers both: resting pain is reduced versus no treatment (mean difference −1.14, moderate quality), but the effect is uncertain versus sham block (−0.83, 95% CI −1.80 to 0.14, very low quality) and versus paravertebral block (−0.18, very low quality). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Bashandy & Abbas 2015 (RCT, 120 women): PECS I + II blocks with general anaesthesia versus general anaesthesia alone — lower pain scores, less morphine in the first 12 hours, less intraoperative fentanyl
cards.summary: Bashandy & Abbas 2015 (RCT, 120 women): PECS I + II blocks with general anaesthesia versus general anaesthesia alone — lower pain scores, less morphine in the first 12 hours, less intraoperative fentanyl
cards.people: 120 adult women scheduled for elective unilateral modified radical mastectomy under general anaesthesia, randomised to general anaesthesia plus pectoral nerves (PECS) I and II blocks (n = 60) or general anaesthesia alone (n = 60); outcomes included visual analogue pain scores, intraoperative fentanyl, postoperative morphine consumption, nausea/vomiting, sedation, and recovery and hospital stay.
cards.result: Pain scores were statistically significantly lower in the PECS group than in controls, postoperative morphine consumption was lower in the PECS group in the first 12 hours after surgery, and intraoperative fentanyl consumption was significantly lower. Postanaesthesia care unit nausea and vomiting and sedation scores were lower with PECS, and recovery-unit and hospital stays were shorter. The abstract reports significance without the group mean pain or morphine values, so no absolute amounts are quoted here.
cards.watchOut: The control is general anaesthesia alone — no sham block — so expectation and unblinded assessment can inflate the benefit, exactly the pattern the meta-analysis below shows (effects shrink against sham). Significance without published group values in the abstract limits what can be verified from the record.
cards.source: Bashandy GM et al. Pectoral nerves I and II blocks in multimodal analgesia for breast cancer surgery: a randomized clinical trial. Regional anesthesia and pain medicine. 2015. PMID: 25376971. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Kulhari 2016 (RCT, 40 women): PECS II versus thoracic paravertebral block — longer analgesia (294.5 vs 197.5 minutes) and less 24-hour morphine (3.90 vs 5.30 mg) with PECS II
cards.summary: Kulhari 2016 (RCT, 40 women): PECS II versus thoracic paravertebral block — longer analgesia (294.5 vs 197.5 minutes) and less 24-hour morphine (3.90 vs 5.30 mg) with PECS II
cards.people: 40 adult women undergoing radical mastectomy, randomised to ultrasound-guided PECS II block (n = 20) or thoracic paravertebral block (n = 20), both with ropivacaine 0.5% 25 mL before induction of anaesthesia, with patient-controlled morphine after surgery; registered as CTRI/2014/06/004692, as reported in the record.
cards.result: Duration of analgesia was significantly longer with PECS II than with paravertebral block (mean 294.5 [SD 52.76] vs 197.5 [31.35] minutes; P < 0.0001), and 24-hour morphine consumption was lower (mean 3.90 [0.79] vs 5.30 [0.98] mg; P < 0.0001). Pain scores were lower in the PECS II group in the initial 2 hours (median 2 [IQR 2–2.5] vs 4 [3–4]; P < 0.0001). Seventeen PECS II patients had T2 dermatomal spread versus four paravertebral patients (P < 0.001). No block-related complication was recorded in either group.
cards.watchOut: Forty patients at one centre, and the paravertebral comparator was a single-level block — the comparison does not cover continuous or multilevel paravertebral techniques, which rank higher in the wider network evidence homed on pack #3011.
cards.source: Kulhari S et al. Efficacy of pectoral nerve block versus thoracic paravertebral block for postoperative analgesia after radical mastectomy: a randomized controlled trial. British journal of anaesthesia. 2016. PMID: 27543533. Registry ID: CTRI/2014/06/004692 (from the record). cards.headline: Meißner 2021 (meta-analysis, 24 RCTs, 1,565 patients): PECS reduces resting pain versus no treatment (mean difference −1.14, moderate quality) — but the effect is uncertain versus sham block and versus paravertebral block (very low quality)
cards.summary: Meißner 2021 (meta-analysis, 24 RCTs, 1,565 patients): PECS reduces resting pain versus no treatment (mean difference −1.14, moderate quality) — but the effect is uncertain versus sham block and versus paravertebral block (very low quality)
cards.people: 24 randomised trials with 1,565 patients comparing pectoral nerve (PECS) blocks with no treatment, sham treatment or other regional anaesthetic techniques in women undergoing breast surgery under general anaesthesia, searched to December 2019; risk of bias assessed, evidence quality graded. Protocol registered as CRD42019126733, as reported in the record.
cards.result: Versus no treatment, PECS might reduce pain at rest (mean difference −1.14, 95% CI −2.1 to −0.18; moderate quality evidence), with an uncertain effect on pain during movement at 24 hours (mean difference −1.79, 95% CI −3.5 to −0.08; very low quality). Versus sham block, the effect on resting pain at 24 hours was uncertain (mean difference −0.83, 95% CI −1.80 to 0.14; very low quality), and versus paravertebral block likewise (mean difference −0.18, 95% CI −1.0 to 0.65; very low quality); PECS may have no effect on movement pain at 24 hours versus paravertebral block (mean difference −0.56, 95% CI −1.53 to 0.41; low quality). Block-related complications were generally poorly reported.
cards.watchOut: The gradient across comparators is the story: clear against nothing, uncertain against a sham injection, and indistinguishable from paravertebral block. Most of the underlying evidence is low or very low quality, and harms were poorly reported across the 24 trials.
cards.source: Meißner M et al. Pectoral nerve blocks for breast surgery: A meta-analysis. European journal of anaesthesiology. 2021. PMID: 33259450. Registry ID: none in the record.
