cards.headline: Synthesis: PECS blocks beat no block and match paravertebral block in a small head-to-head trial — the sham-controlled benefit is unproven
cards.summary: Synthesis: PECS blocks beat no block and match paravertebral block in a small head-to-head trial — the sham-controlled benefit is unproven
cards.people: Two randomised trials (120 women versus general anaesthesia alone; 40 women versus paravertebral block) and a 24-trial meta-analysis (1,565 patients). This shelf covers the PECS technique only; the erector spinae block question for the same operation is homed on pack #3011 and the paravertebral-versus-general-anaesthesia recurrence question on pack #1240.
cards.result: Versus no block: lower pain scores and less early morphine (Bashandy & Abbas), pooled resting-pain difference −1.14 on moderate-quality evidence (Meißner). Versus paravertebral: longer analgesia and less morphine in one 40-patient trial (Kulhari), but a pooled difference of −0.18 (very low quality) across trials. Versus sham: uncertain. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Homed evidence is cross-pointed, not duplicated: pack #3011 (erector spinae plane block for breast cancer surgery) and pack #1240 (paravertebral versus general anaesthesia for recurrence) ask different questions, and none of their carded studies is re-carded here. Within this shelf, 'PECS works' should always be read with its comparator: nothing, sham, or paravertebral.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bashandy GMN & Abbas DN. Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine. 2015 (PMID: 25376971); Kulhari S et al. British Journal of Anaesthesia. 2016 (PMID: 27543533); Meißner M et al. European Journal of Anaesthesiology. 2021 (PMID: 33259450).

shelves.title: HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26: catheter-directed fibrinolysis cut the 7-day composite in intermediate-high-risk pulmonary embolism (4.0% vs 10.3%; 0.7% vs 6.8%) — driven by decompensation, not mortality
shelves.question: In adults with intermediate-high-risk acute pulmonary embolism, does ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis plus anticoagulation, compared with anticoagulation alone, reduce early death, decompensation and major bleeding?
shelves.balance: Standalone pack cross-pointed to live shelf #237 (thrombolysis and catheter treatment for intermediate-risk PE), which cards PEITHO, MOPETT, TOPCOAT, ULTIMA and PEERLESS; neither 2026 trial is carded there and none of #237's PMIDs is re-used here. Two 2026 randomised trials of catheter-directed fibrinolysis versus anticoagulation alone now agree on the composite: HI-PEITHO (n=544, ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed alteplase, funded by Boston Scientific) 4.0% vs 10.3% at 7 days (relative risk 0.39, relative) (PMID 41910345); PRAGUE-26 (n=558, catheter-directed alteplase) 0.7% vs 6.8% (relative risk 0.10, relative) (PMID 42678032). STATED PLAINLY, as the slate requires: both composites are driven by decompensation/collapse and rescue events, not by mortality — deaths were few and not significantly different in either trial. An RCT-only meta-analysis (6 trials, 886 patients) found the same pattern on earlier, smaller trials: less early deterioration (relative risk 0.36, relative), no mortality difference (PMID 42844669). Major bleeding was not significantly increased in either 2026 trial, though PRAGUE-26 recorded 2 intracranial haemorrhages on lysis vs none on anticoagulation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): concordant randomised evidence for preventing early decompensation; a mortality benefit is not shown.

cards.headline: HI-PEITHO (2026): ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis cut the 7-day composite to 4.0% vs 10.3% (relative risk 0.39)
cards.summary: HI-PEITHO (2026): ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed fibrinolysis cut the 7-day composite to 4.0% vs 10.3% (relative risk 0.39)
cards.people: 544 patients with acute intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism (RV/LV diameter ratio at least 1.0, elevated troponin, plus at least two indicators of cardiorespiratory distress), randomised to ultrasound-facilitated, catheter-directed fibrinolysis with alteplase plus anticoagulation (n=273) or anticoagulation alone (n=271). Multinational, adaptive design, blinded outcome adjudication; funded by Boston Scientific.
cards.result: Primary composite (PE-related death, cardiorespiratory decompensation or collapse, or symptomatic PE recurrence within 7 days): 11 patients (4.0%) vs 28 (10.3%) — relative risk 0.39 (95% CI 0.20 to 0.77, P=0.005), a relative measure; the effect was driven primarily by fewer decompensation/collapse events. Major bleeding within 7 days: 4.1% vs 2.2% (P=0.32); within 30 days 4.1% vs 3.0% (P=0.64). No intracranial haemorrhage occurred in either group.
cards.watchOut: The composite is driven by decompensation/rescue events, not mortality — the trial does not show that catheter lysis saves lives. Industry-funded (Boston Scientific); the fetched record does not name the proprietary catheter system, so none is named here. Eligibility required distress indicators on top of intermediate-risk status, so results do not cover all intermediate-risk PE.
cards.source: Ultrasound-Facilitated, Catheter-Directed Fibrinolysis for Acute Pulmonary Embolism (HI-PEITHO). The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026. PMID: 41910345. Registry ID: NCT04790370. cards.headline: PRAGUE-26 (Kroupa 2026): catheter-directed thrombolysis cut the 7-day composite to 0.7% vs 6.8% (relative risk 0.10)
cards.summary: PRAGUE-26 (Kroupa 2026): catheter-directed thrombolysis cut the 7-day composite to 0.7% vs 6.8% (relative risk 0.10)
cards.people: 558 patients with intermediate-high-risk acute pulmonary embolism (haemodynamically stable, simplified PESI at least 1, right-ventricular dysfunction plus elevated troponin or natriuretic peptide), randomised to catheter-directed thrombolysis with alteplase plus anticoagulation (n=280) or anticoagulation alone (n=278). Multicentre, open-label; funded by the Ministry of Health of the Czech Republic and others.
cards.result: Primary composite (death from any cause, PE recurrence, or cardiorespiratory decompensation/collapse within 7 days): 2 patients (0.7%) vs 19 (6.8%) — relative risk 0.10 (95% CI 0.02 to 0.44, P<0.001), a relative measure, driven mainly by less decompensation/collapse. Clinically relevant bleeding by day 7: 4.6% vs 5.0% (P=0.85); major bleeding 1.4% vs 2.2% (P=0.54); intracranial haemorrhage 2 patients (0.7%) vs none. One thrombolysis patient died within 30 days; 4 standard-care patients died within 7 days.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, and again the composite is decompensation-driven: 2 vs 19 events is a small absolute count, and the mortality numbers (1 vs 4 deaths, on different time windows as reported) do not establish a survival benefit. The 2 intracranial haemorrhages on lysis vs 0 on anticoagulation belong on the face beside the benefit.
cards.source: Kroupa J et al. PRAGUE-26: Catheter-Directed Thrombolysis in Intermediate-High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026. PMID: 42678032. Registry ID: NCT05493163. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: RCT meta-analysis 2026: across 6 randomised trials (886 patients), catheter lysis cut early deterioration (relative risk 0.36) with no mortality difference
cards.summary: RCT meta-analysis 2026: across 6 randomised trials (886 patients), catheter lysis cut early deterioration (relative risk 0.36) with no mortality difference
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (2026)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised trials of catheter-directed thrombolysis plus anticoagulation vs anticoagulation alone in acute intermediate-risk pulmonary embolism: 6 RCTs, 886 patients. Its 886-patient total shows it cannot contain both 2026 trials in full — it pools the earlier, smaller randomised record.
cards.result: Catheter-directed thrombolysis reduced the RV/LV ratio more than anticoagulation alone (mean difference −0.11, 95% CI −0.21 to −0.00, P<0.05) and reduced early cardiorespiratory deterioration (risk ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.68, P<0.001 — a relative measure). Major bleeding (risk ratio 1.52, 95% CI 0.71 to 3.24, P=0.28) and intracranial haemorrhage did not differ significantly, but any bleeding and access-site complications were significantly more frequent (P=0.02 for both). Mortality did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Pooled from small trials with surrogate-heavy endpoints (RV/LV ratio) — the same decompensation-not-mortality pattern as the two large trials. It is carded as the pre-2026 randomised context, not as independent confirmation of HI-PEITHO or PRAGUE-26.

cards.headline: Synthesis: catheter-directed fibrinolysis prevents early decompensation in intermediate-high-risk PE — a mortality benefit remains unshown
cards.summary: Synthesis: catheter-directed fibrinolysis prevents early decompensation in intermediate-high-risk PE — a mortality benefit remains unshown
cards.people: HI-PEITHO (544 patients), PRAGUE-26 (558 patients), and an RCT-only meta-analysis of the earlier record (6 trials, 886 patients). Cross-point: live shelf #237 holds PEITHO, MOPETT, TOPCOAT, ULTIMA and PEERLESS; none of its PMIDs is used here.
cards.result: 7-day composites: 4.0% vs 10.3% (relative risk 0.39, relative) and 0.7% vs 6.8% (relative risk 0.10, relative), both driven by decompensation/collapse rather than death. Major bleeding was not significantly increased in either trial (4.1% vs 2.2% at 7 days in HI-PEITHO; 1.4% vs 2.2% in PRAGUE-26), with 2 intracranial haemorrhages on lysis in PRAGUE-26 vs none on anticoagulation. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — for preventing early decompensation; the treatment has not been shown to save lives in this group.
cards.watchOut: Premise verified against live #237 before building: its five cards are PEITHO, MOPETT, TOPCOAT, ULTIMA and PEERLESS — neither 2026 trial is carded there, so this slice is genuinely uncovered. Both 2026 composites lean on clinician-recognised decompensation in trials where one (PRAGUE-26) was open-label; adjudication was blinded in HI-PEITHO.
cards.source: Synthesis of HI-PEITHO. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026 (PMID: 41910345); Kroupa J et al. PRAGUE-26. The New England Journal of Medicine. 2026 (PMID: 42678032); AlTuwayhir AK et al. Cardiology in Review. 2026 (PMID: 42844669).

shelves.title: Low-dose intravenous amisulpride for PONV: complete response 57.7% versus 46.6% added to standard prophylaxis in high-risk patients, and 41.7% versus 28.5% as rescue at the 10 mg dose after failed prophylaxis
shelves.question: In adults at risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting, does low-dose intravenous amisulpride prevent PONV — and rescue established PONV after failed prophylaxis — versus placebo or ondansetron?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) — a concordant multi-trial randomised programme, all placebo-controlled (no head-to-head ondansetron trial was carded; the comparisons are amisulpride added to, or after, standard antiemetics). The formulation was developed as APD421 (named in the dose-finding record); the fetched records name no manufacturer. Dose-finding (Kranke 2013, 215 patients) identified 5 mg as the effective dose: PONV incidence 40% on 5 mg versus 69% on placebo. Two concurrent phase 3 prophylaxis trials of 5 mg alone (Gan 2017, 689 randomised) were individually mixed — complete response 46.9% versus 33.8% (P=0.026) in the US study and 57.4% versus 46.6% (P=0.070) in the European study. The largest prophylaxis trial (Kranke 2018, 1,147 high-risk patients, amisulpride 5 mg ADDED to a standard non-dopaminergic antiemetic) was clearly positive: complete response 57.7% versus 46.6% (difference 11.1 points, 95% CI 5.3–16.8; P<0.001), with less emesis, nausea and rescue use. Rescue after failed prophylaxis (Habib 2019) worked at 10 mg (complete response 41.7% versus 28.5%; P=0.006) but not significantly at 5 mg (33.8%). Safety across trials showed no excess QT prolongation, extrapyramidal effects or sedation versus placebo.

cards.headline: Kranke 2013 (dose-finding, 215 patients): PONV incidence 40% on APD421 (amisulpride) 5 mg versus 69% on placebo — 5 mg was the optimal dose
cards.summary: Kranke 2013 (dose-finding, 215 patients): PONV incidence 40% on APD421 (amisulpride) 5 mg versus 69% on placebo — 5 mg was the optimal dose
cards.people: 215 adult surgical patients with ≥2 Apfel PONV risk factors undergoing surgery ≥1 hour under standard inhalation anaesthesia, randomised to a single intravenous dose at induction of placebo or APD421 (the intravenous amisulpride formulation named in the record) at 1, 5 or 20 mg. Primary endpoint: PONV (vomiting/retching or rescue antiemetic) within 24 hours.
cards.result: PONV occurred in 37 of 54 patients (69%) on placebo, 28 of 58 (48%) on 1 mg (P=0.048), 20 of 50 (40%) on 5 mg (P=0.006) and 30 of 53 (57%) on 20 mg (not significant) — a non-monotonic dose response with 5 mg best; 5 mg also significantly improved vomiting, rescue use and nausea rates. Safety was similar to placebo at all doses, with no significant CNS or cardiac side effects.
cards.watchOut: The 20 mg arm losing significance is a reminder that this is a low-dose antiemetic use, unrelated to antipsychotic dosing; the trial sized the dose, and the phase 3 programme below tested it. Ninety-two percent of participants were female, matching the PONV-risk population but limiting generalisation to low-risk men.
cards.source: Kranke P et al. I.V. APD421 (amisulpride) prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre trial. British journal of anaesthesia. 2013. PMID: 23872464. Registry ID: NCT01510704. cards.headline: Gan 2017 (two concurrent phase 3 trials, 689 patients): 5 mg amisulpride alone — complete response 46.9% versus 33.8% (P=0.026) in the US study, 57.4% versus 46.6% (P=0.070) in the European study
cards.summary: Gan 2017 (two concurrent phase 3 trials, 689 patients): 5 mg amisulpride alone — complete response 46.9% versus 33.8% (P=0.026) in the US study, 57.4% versus 46.6% (P=0.070) in the European study
cards.type: Two concurrent randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials reported together (Gan 2017)
cards.people: 689 adult inpatients undergoing elective surgery under general anaesthesia with at least two Apfel risk factors, randomised across two essentially identical US and European studies to a single 5 mg intravenous amisulpride dose or placebo at induction; 626 were evaluable per protocol. Primary endpoint: complete response (no vomiting/retching and no rescue) over 24 hours.
cards.result: US study: complete response 46.9% (95% CI 39.0–54.9) on amisulpride versus 33.8% (26.2–42.0) on placebo (P=0.026). European study: 57.4% (49.2–65.3) versus 46.6% (38.8–54.6) (P=0.070) — same direction, not significant. Nausea was less frequent on amisulpride in both. Safety profiles did not differ clinically, including QT prolongation, extrapyramidal effects and sedation. A post-hoc pooled analysis supported superiority.
cards.watchOut: One of two sister trials missed significance and the pooled claim rests on a post-hoc change to the analysis plan, as the authors state — this card is the programme's weak joint, and it is why the shelf's weight sits on the larger add-on trial below rather than on amisulpride as sole prophylaxis.

cards.headline: Kranke 2018 (1,147 high-risk patients): amisulpride 5 mg added to a standard antiemetic raised complete response from 46.6% to 57.7% (difference 11.1 points; P<0.001)
cards.summary: Kranke 2018 (1,147 high-risk patients): amisulpride 5 mg added to a standard antiemetic raised complete response from 46.6% to 57.7% (difference 11.1 points; P<0.001)
cards.people: 1,147 adult surgical patients with three or four PONV risk factors undergoing elective surgery under inhalational general anaesthesia, randomised to intravenous amisulpride 5 mg or placebo at induction, each IN ADDITION TO one standard non-dopaminergic antiemetic (most commonly ondansetron or dexamethasone). Primary endpoint: complete response (no emesis or rescue) in the 24 hours after wound closure.
cards.result: Complete response occurred in 330 of 572 patients (57.7%) on amisulpride versus 268 of 575 (46.6%) on placebo (difference 11.1 percentage points, 95% CI 5.3–16.8; P<0.001). Emesis (13.8% versus 20.0%, P=0.003), any nausea (50.0% versus 58.3%, P=0.002), significant nausea (37.1% versus 47.7%, P<0.001) and rescue use (40.9% versus 49.4%, P=0.002) were all lower with amisulpride. Adverse events and ECG/laboratory abnormalities were no more frequent than with placebo.
cards.watchOut: The tested strategy is amisulpride as an add-on to another antiemetic class in high-risk patients — not amisulpride instead of ondansetron, for which no carded head-to-head trial exists. Absolute gain is about 11 points (number needed to treat ≈ 9), not the larger figures a relative framing would suggest.

cards.headline: Habib 2019 (rescue after failed prophylaxis): complete response 41.7% on amisulpride 10 mg versus 28.5% on placebo (P=0.006); the 5 mg dose did not reach significance (33.8%)
cards.summary: Habib 2019 (rescue after failed prophylaxis): complete response 41.7% on amisulpride 10 mg versus 28.5% on placebo (P=0.006); the 5 mg dose did not reach significance (33.8%)
cards.type: Randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 rescue trial (Habib 2019)
cards.people: 2,285 adults undergoing surgery under general inhalational anaesthesia with standard antiemetic prophylaxis were enrolled at 23 sites; the 702 who developed PONV within 24 hours despite prophylaxis were randomised to a single dose of amisulpride 5 mg (237), amisulpride 10 mg (230) or placebo (235). Primary endpoint: complete response (no emesis or rescue) for 24 hours after study drug, excluding emesis in the first 30 minutes.
cards.result: Complete response: 41.7% (96/230) on 10 mg amisulpride versus 28.5% (67/235) on placebo — difference 13.2 points (95% CI 4.6–21.8; odds ratio 1.80; P=0.006). The 5 mg dose gave 33.8% (80/237), a 5.2-point difference that was not significant (P=0.109). Adverse-event rates were comparable across groups with no clinically relevant toxicities.
cards.watchOut: Dose matters and the doses differ by indication on this shelf: 5 mg for prophylaxis, 10 mg for rescue — quoting the rescue result for the 5 mg dose (or vice versa) misstates the programme. Rescue success even on drug was only 41.7%, so most established PONV still needs further treatment.

Anesthesiology. 2019. PMID: 30475232. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: a complete low-dose programme — dose found, prophylaxis shown as add-on, rescue shown at double the prophylaxis dose
cards.summary: Synthesis: a complete low-dose programme — dose found, prophylaxis shown as add-on, rescue shown at double the prophylaxis dose
cards.people: The carded evidence: one dose-finding trial (215 patients), two concurrent single-agent phase 3 prophylaxis trials (689 randomised), one add-on prophylaxis trial (1,147 patients) and one rescue trial (702 randomised after failed prophylaxis). All comparisons are against placebo.
cards.result: Complete response gains: +13.1 points (US phase 3, significant) and +10.8 points (European phase 3, not significant) for 5 mg alone; +11.1 points (P<0.001) for 5 mg added to standard prophylaxis; +13.2 points (P=0.006) for 10 mg rescue. shelves.title: Lung-protective ventilation bundle in major abdominal surgery: major complications 10.5% versus 27.5% in IMPROVE (relative risk 0.40) — the bundle, not the PEEP level, is the slice the PEEP shelf does not cover
shelves.question: In adults having major abdominal surgery, does a lung-protective ventilation strategy (low tidal volume with PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres, as a bundle) reduce postoperative pulmonary complications versus conventional ventilation?
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — the bundle claim rests mainly on one large trial, which caps the stamp. This pack is the PARTIAL companion to live Shelf #1959, which homes the PEEP-LEVEL question (PROVHILO and iPROVE: high or individualised PEEP versus low PEEP, both null) — neither of those reports is re-carded here, and their null result is part of this shelf's logic: within low-tidal-volume ventilation, pushing PEEP higher added nothing, so the benefit below is attributed to the bundle as tested, not to PEEP escalation. In IMPROVE (Futier 2013, 400 patients at intermediate-to-high risk), the full bundle — low tidal volume with PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres — versus nonprotective ventilation (high tidal volume, no PEEP) cut the composite of major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications at 7 days from 27.5% to 10.5% (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.24–0.68), noninvasive ventilation or intubation for respiratory failure from 17.0% to 5.0%, and hospital stay by 2.45 days. A small single-centre trial (Severgnini 2013, 56 patients) found better pulmonary function and infection scores with a protective bundle but was not powered on clinical complications. The individual-patient meta-analysis (Serpa Neto 2014, 3,365 patients) found protective ventilation reduced postoperative lung injury but did NOT improve mortality (adjusted hazard ratio for death with lung injury 0.71, 95% CI 0.41–1.22, independent of strategy). Because IMPROVE changed tidal volume, PEEP and recruitment together against a now-dated control, which component carries the benefit cannot be separated from these cards.

cards.headline: IMPROVE 2013 (400 patients): major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications 10.5% on the lung-protective bundle versus 27.5% on nonprotective ventilation (relative risk 0.40)
cards.summary: IMPROVE 2013 (400 patients): major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications 10.5% on the lung-protective bundle versus 27.5% on nonprotective ventilation (relative risk 0.40)
cards.people: 400 adults at intermediate-to-high risk of pulmonary complications undergoing major abdominal surgery, randomised to lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volume with PEEP and recruitment manoeuvres, as a bundle) or nonprotective ventilation (conventional higher tidal volume without PEEP). Primary outcome: composite of major pulmonary and extrapulmonary complications within 7 days, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: The primary outcome occurred in 21 of 200 patients (10.5%) on lung-protective ventilation versus 55 of 200 (27.5%) on nonprotective ventilation (relative risk 0.40, 95% CI 0.24–0.68; P=0.001) — an absolute reduction of 17 percentage points alongside the relative figure. Noninvasive ventilation or intubation for acute respiratory failure was needed by 5.0% versus 17.0% (relative risk 0.29, 95% CI 0.14–0.61; P=0.001), and hospital stay was shorter by a mean of 2.45 days (95% CI −4.17 to −0.72; P=0.006).
cards.watchOut: A bundle-versus-dated-control comparison: tidal volume, PEEP and recruitment all changed together, and the control (high tidal volume, zero PEEP) is no longer standard care — the trial cannot say how much of the gain modern low-tidal-volume practice already captures, nor which component matters. Live Shelf #1959 shows PEEP escalation within protective ventilation was null, which argues the tidal-volume component may carry much of the effect.
cards.source: Futier E et al. A trial of intraoperative low-tidal-volume ventilation in abdominal surgery. The New England journal of medicine. 2013. PMID: 23902482. Registry ID: NCT01282996. cards.headline: Severgnini 2013 (56 patients): protective bundle (7 mL/kg, PEEP 10, recruitment) improved pulmonary function and infection scores to day 5 — a physiology-sized trial, not a complications trial
cards.summary: Severgnini 2013 (56 patients): protective bundle (7 mL/kg, PEEP 10, recruitment) improved pulmonary function and infection scores to day 5 — a physiology-sized trial, not a complications trial
cards.people: 56 patients undergoing elective open abdominal surgery lasting over 2 hours, assigned to standard ventilation (tidal volume 9 mL/kg ideal body weight, zero PEEP) or a protective strategy (7 mL/kg, PEEP 10 cmH2O and recruitment manoeuvres). Primary outcome was a modified Clinical Pulmonary Infection Score, with gas exchange and pulmonary function tests to day 5.
cards.result: The protective group showed better pulmonary function tests up to day 5, fewer chest X-ray alterations to day 3, higher arterial oxygenation on air at days 1 and 3 (77.1 versus 64.9 mmHg, P=0.0006; 80.5 versus 69.7 mmHg, P=0.0002) but not day 5 (P=0.44), and lower infection scores at days 1 and 3. The proportion still in hospital at day 28 did not differ (7% versus 15%, P=0.42).
cards.watchOut: Fifty-six patients, open-label, surrogate primary outcome: this card supports biological coherence for the bundle, nothing more. Its null length-of-stay result contrasts with IMPROVE's — small trials disagreeing with large ones on secondary outcomes is expected noise, printed here rather than hidden.
cards.source: Severgnini P et al. Protective mechanical ventilation during general anesthesia for open abdominal surgery improves postoperative pulmonary function. Anesthesiology. 2013. PMID: 23542800. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Serpa Neto 2014 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 3,365 patients): protective ventilation reduced postoperative lung injury but did not improve mortality; lung injury carried 20.3% versus 1.4% in-hospital mortality
cards.summary: Serpa Neto 2014 (individual-patient meta-analysis, 3,365 patients): protective ventilation reduced postoperative lung injury but did not improve mortality; lung injury carried 20.3% versus 1.4% in-hospital mortality
cards.type: Systematic review and individual-patient-data meta-analysis (Serpa Neto 2014)
cards.people: 12 investigations in 3,365 adults undergoing abdominal or thoracic surgery, comparing lung-protective with conventional ventilation in randomised trials and observational studies (searched to April 2014); outcomes were postoperative lung injury incidence, morbidity and in-hospital mortality.
cards.result: Postoperative lung injury incidence was similar after abdominal and thoracic surgery (3.4% versus 4.3%, p=0.198). Patients who developed lung injury had far longer ICU (8.0 versus 1.1 days) and hospital (20.9 versus 14.7 days) stays and higher in-hospital mortality (20.3% versus 1.4%; attributable mortality 19%, and 12.2% for abdominal surgery). Lung-protective strategies reduced the incidence of postoperative lung injury, but the risk of death was independent of ventilation strategy (adjusted hazard ratio 0.71, 95% CI 0.41–1.22).
cards.watchOut: This card bounds the claim: fewer lung injuries and complications, no demonstrated mortality benefit. It pools abdominal with thoracic surgery and randomised with observational data, so it corroborates direction rather than providing a clean abdominal-surgery effect size.
cards.source: Serpa Neto A et al. cards.headline: Synthesis: the bundle works against a conventional-ventilation comparator in one large trial; mortality benefit unshown, and the PEEP component alone was null on the home shelf
cards.summary: Synthesis: the bundle works against a conventional-ventilation comparator in one large trial; mortality benefit unshown, and the PEEP component alone was null on the home shelf
cards.people: The carded evidence: one multicentre bundle trial (IMPROVE, 400 patients), one small physiology trial (56 patients) and one individual-patient meta-analysis (3,365 patients). The PEEP-level trials (PROVHILO, iPROVE) are homed on live Shelf #1959 and are not re-carded here.
cards.result: Major complications 10.5% versus 27.5% (relative risk 0.40; absolute −17 points) and respiratory-failure support 5.0% versus 17.0% in IMPROVE; better early pulmonary function in Severgnini; less postoperative lung injury but no mortality difference in the meta-analysis. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): a single large trial carries the bundle claim, its control arm predates current practice, and the active component is unresolved — with the tidal-volume element the leading candidate given #1959's PEEP nulls.
cards.watchOut: Do not combine this shelf's bundle claim with #1959 into 'more PEEP is better' — the evidence points the other way: low tidal volume with modest PEEP is the defensible reading of both shelves together. Emergency and thoracic surgery are outside IMPROVE's population.
cards.source: Synthesis of Futier E et al. N Engl J Med. 2013 (PMID: 23902482); Severgnini P et al. Anesthesiology. 2013 (PMID: 23542800); Serpa Neto A et al. shelves.title: Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring: residual paralysis in recovery falls sharply when a number guides reversal — but the largest observational study found no fewer postoperative pulmonary complications in monitored patients
shelves.question: In adults having major surgery under general anaesthesia with neuromuscular blockade, does quantitative (objective) neuromuscular monitoring, with reversal guided by it, reduce residual paralysis and postoperative pulmonary complications versus qualitative (peripheral-nerve-stimulator / clinical) assessment?
shelves.balance: SPLIT by outcome. For residual paralysis itself the evidence is concordant and favourable: in the one randomised trial (Murphy 2008, 185 patients), residual blockade on arrival in recovery (train-of-four ratio ≤0.9) occurred in 4.5% with intraoperative acceleromyography versus 30.0% with qualitative monitoring (P<0.0001), with fewer hypoxaemic and airway-obstruction events in transit; a 2024 prospective cohort (Thilen, 200 patients) using a quantitative-monitoring-guided reversal protocol recorded 0% residual paralysis at extubation. But for the harder outcome — postoperative pulmonary complications — the largest dataset points the other way: POPULAR (22,803 patients, prospective observational) found neuromuscular monitoring was NOT associated with fewer pulmonary complications (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49, an association in the direction of more complications, most plausibly confounding by indication), and neither reversal nor extubation at a train-of-four ratio ≥0.9 was associated with better pulmonary outcomes. Residual paralysis is clearly measurable and clearly linked to critical respiratory events in recovery (Murphy case-control: mean train-of-four ratio 0.62 in patients with critical respiratory events versus 0.98 in matched controls); whether monitoring-driven care reduces lung complications at population level is unproven. PROPOSED SPLIT (residual paralysis reduced; pulmonary-complication benefit unproven).

cards.headline: Murphy 2008 (randomised trial, 185 patients): intraoperative acceleromyography versus qualitative train-of-four — residual blockade in recovery 4.5% versus 30.0%, with fewer desaturation and airway-obstruction events
cards.summary: Murphy 2008 (randomised trial, 185 patients): intraoperative acceleromyography versus qualitative train-of-four — residual blockade in recovery 4.5% versus 30.0%, with fewer desaturation and airway-obstruction events
cards.people: 185 patients randomised to intraoperative quantitative acceleromyographic monitoring or conventional qualitative train-of-four monitoring, with standardised anaesthetic management; the qualitative group was extubated when standard criteria were met and no fade was seen, the acceleromyography group additionally required a train-of-four ratio >0.80; train-of-four ratios of both groups were measured with acceleromyography on arrival in the recovery unit.
cards.result: Residual neuromuscular blockade in recovery (train-of-four ratio ≤0.9) was less frequent with acceleromyography: 4.5% versus 30.0% (P<0.0001). During transport to recovery, no acceleromyography patient desaturated below 90% or developed airway obstruction, versus 21.1% and 11.1% respectively in the qualitative group (P<0.002). The incidence, severity and duration of hypoxaemic events in the first 30 minutes of recovery admission were all lower with acceleromyography (all P<0.0001).
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial from 2008, and its extubation threshold in the monitored arm was a train-of-four ratio >0.80 — below the ≥0.9 standard now recommended — so the contrast tested is 'some number versus none', not modern protocolised monitoring. Outcomes are early recovery events, not pulmonary complications over the following days.
cards.source: Murphy GS et al. Intraoperative acceleromyographic monitoring reduces the risk of residual neuromuscular blockade and adverse respiratory events in the postanesthesia care unit. Anesthesiology. 2008. PMID: 18719436. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Murphy 2008 (case-control within a 7,459-patient recovery cohort): patients with critical respiratory events had mean train-of-four ratio 0.62, and 73.8% had ratios <0.70 — matched controls averaged 0.98, none <0.70
cards.summary: Murphy 2008 (case-control within a 7,459-patient recovery cohort): patients with critical respiratory events had mean train-of-four ratio 0.62, and 73.8% had ratios <0.70 — matched controls averaged 0.98, none <0.70
cards.people: Over one year, 7,459 patients received a general anaesthetic at one centre; 61 developed a predefined critical respiratory event in the first 15 minutes of recovery admission, and 42 of these cases were matched by age, sex and surgical procedure with control patients who had no event; train-of-four ratios were quantified immediately with acceleromyography.
cards.result: The most common critical respiratory events were severe hypoxaemia (52.4% of matched cases) and upper airway obstruction (35.7%). Mean train-of-four ratio was 0.62 (SD 0.20) in cases versus 0.98 (SD 0.07) in controls (difference -0.36, 95% CI -0.43 to -0.30; P<0.0001); 73.8% of cases had ratios <0.70 and no control patient did. No preoperative or intraoperative variable differed significantly between cases and controls.
cards.watchOut: Observational and associational: it shows residual paralysis travels with critical respiratory events, not that monitoring prevents them. Only 42 of 61 cases could be matched, and monitoring practice during the anaesthetics themselves was not the study's exposure.
cards.source: Murphy GS et al. Residual neuromuscular blockade and critical respiratory events in the postanesthesia care unit. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2008. PMID: 18635478. cards.headline: POPULAR 2019 (prospective observational, 22,803 patients, 28 European countries): neuromuscular monitoring was NOT associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49)
cards.summary: POPULAR 2019 (prospective observational, 22,803 patients, 28 European countries): neuromuscular monitoring was NOT associated with fewer postoperative pulmonary complications (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49)
cards.people: 22,803 adults receiving general anaesthesia for any in-hospital procedure except cardiac surgery at 211 hospitals in 28 European countries, with prospective data collection and a postoperative examination within 3 days; the outcome was postoperative pulmonary complications up to day 28, analysed with adjustment for surgical factors and preoperative physical status.
cards.result: Use of neuromuscular blocking agents was associated with more postoperative pulmonary complications (1,658 of 21,694 patients, 7.6%; adjusted odds ratio 1.86, 95% CI 1.53-2.26). Use of neuromuscular monitoring was not associated with a decreased risk (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49), nor was reversal-agent administration (1.23, 1.07-1.41), choice of sugammadex over neostigmine (1.03, 0.85-1.25), or extubation at a train-of-four ratio ≥0.9 (1.03, 0.82-1.31).
cards.watchOut: Observational: sicker patients and bigger operations are both more likely to be monitored and more likely to develop lung complications, so the adjusted association in the 'harm' direction is most plausibly residual confounding by indication — but the study equally gives no support to the claim that monitoring, as actually practised across Europe, reduced pulmonary complications. Only 2.3% of patients were anaesthetised without a blocking agent, limiting that contrast.
cards.source: Kirmeier E et al. Post-anaesthesia pulmonary complications after use of muscle relaxants (POPULAR): a multicentre, prospective observational study. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2019. PMID: 30224322. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01865513. cards.headline: Thilen 2024 (prospective cohort, 200 patients): a quantitative-monitoring-guided reversal protocol — neostigmine for train-of-four ratio 0.40-0.89, sugammadex for deeper block — recorded 0% residual paralysis at extubation
cards.summary: Thilen 2024 (prospective cohort, 200 patients): a quantitative-monitoring-guided reversal protocol — neostigmine for train-of-four ratio 0.40-0.89, sugammadex for deeper block — recorded 0% residual paralysis at extubation
cards.people: 200 patients having elective surgery with rocuronium at one institution, managed under a protocol that added electromyography-based quantitative monitoring to existing local reversal recommendations: neostigmine if the train-of-four ratio was 0.40-0.89, sugammadex for deeper blockade, and confirmation of a ratio ≥0.9 before extubation; 189 patients completed the study.
cards.result: Residual paralysis (train-of-four ratio <0.9 at extubation) occurred in 0% of patients (95% CI 0-1.9). Of those completing the study, 66 (35%) were reversed with neostigmine, 90 (48%) with sugammadex and 33 (17%) recovered spontaneously. Total reversal-drug acquisition cost was US $11,358 ($60 per patient), versus a projected $19,312 ($103 per patient) had sugammadex been used for everyone.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre before-protocol cohort with no concurrent control arm: the 0% figure shows what a monitored protocol can achieve in motivated hands, not a randomised contrast with qualitative care. The exposure bundles the monitor, the reversal-choice rule and the extubation threshold together.
cards.source: Thilen SR et al. Management of Muscle Relaxation With Rocuronium and Reversal With Neostigmine or Sugammadex Guided by Quantitative Neuromuscular Monitoring. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2024. PMID: 37171989. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03958201. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — monitoring reliably abolishes measurable residual paralysis; a pulmonary-complication benefit has never been shown
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — monitoring reliably abolishes measurable residual paralysis; a pulmonary-complication benefit has never been shown
cards.people: One randomised trial (185 patients), one case-control study nested in 7,459 recoveries, one prospective protocol cohort (200 patients) and one 22,803-patient prospective observational study.
cards.result: Residual blockade in recovery: 4.5% versus 30.0% in the randomised trial, and 0% under a modern quantitative protocol. Critical respiratory events in recovery are strongly associated with residual paralysis (mean train-of-four ratio 0.62 versus 0.98). Postoperative pulmonary complications: no association with monitoring in POPULAR (adjusted odds ratio 1.31, 95% CI 1.15-1.49). PROPOSED SPLIT (residual paralysis reduced; pulmonary benefit unproven), Tier C.
cards.watchOut: This row was graded GAP-E at slate stage because no large randomised trial of monitoring itself exists; the one randomised trial is small and single-centre, and the pulmonary-outcome evidence is observational only and labelled as such.
cards.source: Synthesis of Murphy GS et al. Anesthesiology. 2008 (PMID: 18719436); Murphy GS et al. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2008 (PMID: 18635478); Kirmeier E et al. The Lancet. Respiratory medicine. 2019 (PMID: 30224322); Thilen SR et al. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2024 (PMID: 37171989).

shelves.title: Extended thromboprophylaxis after cancer surgery: four weeks of low-molecular-weight heparin roughly halves venographic clots versus one week (12.0% to 4.8% in ENOXACAN II; 16.3% to 7.3% in FAME), with no increase in bleeding
shelves.question: In adults undergoing major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery, does extended pharmacological thromboprophylaxis (low-molecular-weight heparin for ~4 weeks) reduce symptomatic venous thromboembolism versus in-hospital-only prophylaxis, at what bleeding cost?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit). Two randomised trials from two programmes point the same way. ENOXACAN II (Bergqvist 2002, double-blind, 332 patients in the intention-to-treat efficacy analysis after abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery): venographic venous thromboembolism at days 25-31 was 12.0% on one week of enoxaparin followed by placebo versus 4.8% on four weeks of enoxaparin (P=0.02), a difference that persisted at three months (13.8% versus 5.5%, P=0.01), with no significant difference in bleeding. FAME (Rasmussen 2006, open-label assessor-blinded, 427 randomised after major abdominal surgery, 343 evaluable): cumulative venous thromboembolism fell from 16.3% with 7 days of dalteparin to 7.3% with 28 days — a 55% relative risk reduction (95% CI 15-76; P=0.012), number needed to treat 12 — again with no increase in bleeding. The Cochrane synthesis of four trials found objectively confirmed venous thromboembolism in 14.3% of controls versus 6.1% with prolonged prophylaxis (Peto odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.63), symptomatic venous thromboembolism 1.7% versus 0.2% (odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.06-0.80), and bleeding 3.7% versus 4.1% (not significant). The honest caveat: most events prevented are venogram-detected, largely asymptomatic clots; the symptomatic benefit is real in the pooled data but rests on small absolute numbers (1.7% to 0.2%). PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Bergqvist 2002 — ENOXACAN II (double-blind randomised trial, 332 patients analysed): enoxaparin for 4 weeks versus 1 week after abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery — venographic thrombosis 4.8% versus 12.0% (P=0.02)
cards.summary: Bergqvist 2002 — ENOXACAN II (double-blind randomised trial, 332 patients analysed): enoxaparin for 4 weeks versus 1 week after abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery — venographic thrombosis 4.8% versus 12.0% (P=0.02)
cards.people: Patients undergoing planned curative open surgery for abdominal or pelvic cancer received enoxaparin 40 mg daily for 6-10 days and were then randomised to enoxaparin or placebo for a further 21 days, with bilateral venography at days 25-31; the intention-to-treat efficacy analysis included 332 patients, and patients were followed for three months.
cards.result: Venous thromboembolism at the end of the double-blind phase: 12.0% in the placebo (one-week) group versus 4.8% in the enoxaparin (four-week) group (P=0.02) — an absolute reduction of 7.2 percentage points. At three months the rates were 13.8% versus 5.5% (P=0.01). Three patients in the enoxaparin group and six in the placebo group died within three months. There were no significant differences in bleeding or other complications during the double-blind or follow-up periods.
cards.watchOut: The primary endpoint is venographically demonstrated thrombosis, most of it asymptomatic — the trial was not powered for symptomatic events or death (deaths were 3 versus 6, a comparison it cannot settle). Verified at build from the primary journal report, as the slate cited this programme by name only (coordinator note U2).
cards.source: Bergqvist D et al. Duration of prophylaxis against venous thromboembolism with enoxaparin after surgery for cancer. The New England journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 11919306. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Rasmussen 2006 — FAME (randomised open-label trial, 427 randomised, 343 evaluable): dalteparin 28 days versus 7 days after major abdominal surgery — venous thromboembolism 7.3% versus 16.3%, a 55% relative risk reduction, number needed to treat 12
cards.summary: Rasmussen 2006 — FAME (randomised open-label trial, 427 randomised, 343 evaluable): dalteparin 28 days versus 7 days after major abdominal surgery — venous thromboembolism 7.3% versus 16.3%, a 55% relative risk reduction, number needed to treat 12
cards.people: 590 patients were recruited for major abdominal surgery, of whom 427 were randomised and received at least one day of study medication and 343 reached an evaluable endpoint; the comparison was dalteparin 5000 IU once daily for 28 days versus 7 days, with the primary endpoint objectively verified venous thromboembolism between days 7 and 28 and bilateral venography at day 28 for all patients.
cards.result: Cumulative venous thromboembolism incidence was 16.3% (29 of 178) with short-term prophylaxis versus 7.3% (12 of 165) with prolonged prophylaxis — a 55% relative risk reduction (95% CI 15-76; P=0.012), an absolute reduction of 9.0 percentage points, number needed to treat 12 (95% CI 7-44). Bleeding events were not increased with prolonged treatment.
cards.watchOut: Open-label (though assessor-blinded), and the population is major abdominal surgery rather than cancer surgery exclusively — the cancer-specific anchor is ENOXACAN II. A fifth of randomised patients (427 to 343) did not reach an evaluable endpoint, mainly the day-28 venogram. Verified at build from the primary journal report, as the slate cited this programme by name only (coordinator note U2).
cards.source: Rasmussen MS et al. cards.headline: Rasmussen 2009 (Cochrane review, 4 trials): prolonged low-molecular-weight heparin after abdominal/pelvic surgery — overall venous thromboembolism 6.1% versus 14.3%, symptomatic events 0.2% versus 1.7%, bleeding 4.1% versus 3.7% (not significant)
cards.summary: Rasmussen 2009 (Cochrane review, 4 trials): prolonged low-molecular-weight heparin after abdominal/pelvic surgery — overall venous thromboembolism 6.1% versus 14.3%, symptomatic events 0.2% versus 1.7%, bleeding 4.1% versus 3.7% (not significant)
cards.people: Four eligible controlled trials of prolonged thromboprophylaxis with low-molecular-weight heparin (at least one month) versus in-hospital-only prophylaxis or placebo after major abdominal or pelvic surgery, with venous thromboembolism (deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) confirmed by objective means; studies reporting clinical diagnosis alone were excluded.
cards.result: Overall venous thromboembolism: 14.3% (95% CI 11.2-17.8) in controls versus 6.1% (95% CI 4.0-8.7) with prolonged prophylaxis (Peto odds ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.26-0.63; P<0.0005). Symptomatic venous thromboembolism: 1.7% versus 0.2% (Peto odds ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.06-0.80; P=0.02). Bleeding: 3.7% versus 4.1% (Peto odds ratio 1.11, 95% CI 0.62-1.97; P=0.73). No significant heterogeneity was detected.
cards.watchOut: The pooled base is the same small trial family as the two cards above plus two further trials — the review confirms consistency rather than adding a large independent population, and the symptomatic-event estimate rests on few events, hence its wide confidence interval (0.06-0.80).
cards.source: Rasmussen MS et al. Prolonged thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin for abdominal or pelvic surgery. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2009. PMID: 19160234. cards.headline: Synthesis: LIKELY (benefit) — extending prophylaxis to ~4 weeks prevents late clots, including symptomatic ones, at no measured bleeding cost
cards.summary: Synthesis: LIKELY (benefit) — extending prophylaxis to ~4 weeks prevents late clots, including symptomatic ones, at no measured bleeding cost
cards.people: Two randomised trials (ENOXACAN II, 332 patients with abdominal/pelvic cancer; FAME, 427 randomised after major abdominal surgery) and a Cochrane review of four trials.
cards.result: Venographic/objectively confirmed venous thromboembolism roughly halved in every source (4.8% vs 12.0%; 7.3% vs 16.3%; pooled 6.1% vs 14.3%); pooled symptomatic events fell from 1.7% to 0.2%; bleeding did not increase significantly in any source. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit).
cards.watchOut: The endpoint mix is dominated by imaging-detected asymptomatic thrombosis; the claim a patient cares about — fewer symptomatic clots — is supported by the pooled analysis but with few events. Both primary reports were located and verified at build (slate note U2): ENOXACAN II is PMID 11919306 and FAME is PMID 16881934.

shelves.title: Intercostal cryoanalgesia: SPLIT — after Nuss repair it halves the stay (3 vs 5 days) and cuts opioids, but after thoracotomy two randomised trials found more neuropathic-type pain weeks to months later
shelves.question: In children and adults undergoing Nuss repair of pectus excavatum or thoracotomy, does intercostal cryoanalgesia (cryoablation of intercostal nerves at surgery) reduce postoperative pain, opioid use and length of stay versus epidural or systemic analgesia?
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by operation and by time horizon. For the Nuss procedure, the single randomised trial (Graves 2019; 20 patients — a very small trial, N printed here and on the cards) found intercostal cryoablation beat thoracic epidural on the outcomes that drive Nuss recovery: median stay 3 versus 5 days (P=0.0001) and a mean 416 mg less oral morphine equivalent per patient (52-82% less on postoperative days 1-3), with equal pain scores and no neuropathic pain signal at up to one year — at the cost of 46.5 minutes longer operating time. For thoracotomy, acute results are favourable or neutral (Sepsas 2013, 50 patients: significantly better pain scores and less morphine with cryoanalgesia added to intravenous patient-controlled analgesia; Ju 2008, 107 patients: acute pain scores equal to epidural), but the chronic-pain data point the other way: Ju found allodynia-like pain significantly more frequent after cryoanalgesia at 6 and 12 months, with more moderate-to-severe chronic pain interfering with daily life, and Mustola 2011 (42 patients) found more neuropathic-type pain at 8 weeks when cryoanalgesia was added to epidural. PROPOSED SPLIT (acute benefit, chiefly Nuss; chronic neuropathic-pain concern after thoracotomy).

cards.headline: Graves 2019 (randomised trial, N = 20 — very small): Nuss cryoablation versus thoracic epidural — median stay 3 versus 5 days, 416 mg less oral morphine equivalent, equal pain scores, longer operating time (+46.5 min)
cards.summary: Graves 2019 (randomised trial, N = 20 — very small): Nuss cryoablation versus thoracic epidural — median stay 3 versus 5 days, 416 mg less oral morphine equivalent, equal pain scores, longer operating time (+46.5 min)
cards.people: 20 consecutive patients aged 13 or over undergoing the Nuss procedure for pectus excavatum at a single children's hospital, randomised evenly (10 per group) by closed envelope to intraoperative intercostal nerve cryoablation or thoracic epidural analgesia; primary outcome was postoperative length of stay. The record names no cryoablation system or manufacturer.
cards.result: Median length of stay was 3 days with cryoablation versus 5 days with epidural (P=0.0001). Cryoablation patients required a mean of 416 mg less oral morphine equivalent per patient (P=0.0001), using 52-82% fewer milligrams on postoperative days 1-3 (P<0.01 each day). Mean operating-room time was 46.5 minutes longer with cryoablation (P=0.0001). Pain scores did not differ at any point up to one year, there was no increased incidence of neuropathic pain in the cryoablation group, and no complications occurred in that group (the epidural group had one symptomatic pneumothorax and one urinary retention).
cards.watchOut: N = 20 in total — the smallest randomised base a shelf in this library can rest on, from one centre and one surgical team; effects this large in a trial this small should be read as promising, not settled. The comparator is epidural analgesia specifically, not modern multimodal or block-based care.
cards.source: Graves CE et al. Intraoperative intercostal nerve cryoablation During the Nuss procedure reduces length of stay and opioid requirement: A randomized clinical trial. Journal of pediatric surgery. 2019. PMID: 30935731. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Sepsas 2013 (randomised trial, 50 patients): thoracotomy cryoanalgesia plus intravenous patient-controlled analgesia versus patient-controlled analgesia alone — significantly better pain scores and less morphine over the first days
cards.summary: Sepsas 2013 (randomised trial, 50 patients): thoracotomy cryoanalgesia plus intravenous patient-controlled analgesia versus patient-controlled analgesia alone — significantly better pain scores and less morphine over the first days
cards.people: 50 patients undergoing thoracotomy, randomised to intravenous patient-controlled analgesia alone (n=25) or with intercostal cryoanalgesia added (n=25), with pain intensity on a verbal analogue scale at rest and coughing, analgesic consumption, blood gases and respiratory function assessed over four postoperative days and to the second postoperative month.
cards.result: The cryoanalgesia group had statistically significant improvement in postoperative pain scores (P=10(-4) as printed in the record), reduced consumption of morphine (P=10(-4)) and other analgesics, better blood-gas pH values, and higher forced expiratory volume and vital capacity values at the first and second postoperative months; nausea, numbness, epigastric distension and back pain were also less frequent at several later time points.
cards.watchOut: A small single-centre trial reporting many outcomes at many time points without a single prespecified primary figure in the record — the abstract gives P values rather than the size of the pain-score or morphine differences, so the magnitude of the acute benefit cannot be stated from the verified source. Follow-up for chronic pain was only two months.
cards.source: Sepsas E et al. The role of intercostal cryoanalgesia in post-thoracotomy analgesia. Interactive cardiovascular and thoracic surgery. 2013. PMID: 23424242. cards.headline: Ju 2008 (randomised trial, 107 patients): thoracotomy cryoanalgesia versus epidural — acute pain equal, but allodynia-like pain significantly more common after cryoanalgesia at 6 and 12 months
cards.summary: Ju 2008 (randomised trial, 107 patients): thoracotomy cryoanalgesia versus epidural — acute pain equal, but allodynia-like pain significantly more common after cryoanalgesia at 6 and 12 months
cards.people: 107 adults undergoing thoracotomy, allocated randomly to thoracic epidural bupivacaine and morphine or intercostal nerve cryoanalgesia; acute pain scores and opioid side effects were assessed for three days, and chronic pain incidence, severity and allodynia-like pain at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months.
cards.result: There was no significant difference in numerical rating scale pain scores at rest or on motion over the three postoperative days, and patient satisfaction was similar; side effects, especially mild pruritus, were more frequent with epidural. Chronic pain incidence was high in both groups (42.1-72.1%) and did not differ significantly overall, but allodynia-like pain was reported more often in the cryoanalgesia group at every month assessed, significantly so at the sixth and twelfth months (P<0.05), and more cryoanalgesia patients rated their chronic pain moderate or severe and interfering with daily life (P<0.05). The authors conclude cryoanalgesia may be a factor that increases neuropathic pain.
cards.watchOut: The largest thoracotomy cryoanalgesia trial carded here, and the one with the longest follow-up — its chronic-pain signal cannot be waved away by the shorter studies. Chronic-pain ascertainment was by report at clinic time points, and the trial predates modern definitions of chronic post-surgical pain.
cards.source: Ju H et al. Comparison of epidural analgesia and intercostal nerve cryoanalgesia for post-thoracotomy pain control. European journal of pain (London, England). 2008. PMID: 17870625. cards.headline: Mustola 2011 (randomised trial, 42 patients): epidural plus cryoanalgesia versus epidural alone after thoracotomy — more neuropathic-type pain at 8 weeks with cryoanalgesia (P<0.05); no difference by 6 months
cards.summary: Mustola 2011 (randomised trial, 42 patients): epidural plus cryoanalgesia versus epidural alone after thoracotomy — more neuropathic-type pain at 8 weeks with cryoanalgesia (P<0.05); no difference by 6 months
cards.people: 42 elective posterolateral thoracotomy patients randomised to thoracic epidural analgesia combined with cryoanalgesia of three intercostal nerves (at, above and below the incision) or epidural alone, with cryoanalgesia blinded to patients and investigating anaesthetists; epidural ropivacaine with fentanyl ran for three days, and pain was reviewed at a pain clinic at 8 weeks and 6 months.
cards.result: The cryoanalgesia group had more neuropathic-type pain than the epidural-alone group 8 weeks after operation (P<0.05) and more pain during normal daily activities at 8 weeks (P<0.05). After 6 months there were no statistically significant differences between the groups. The authors conclude intercostal cryoanalgesia seems to increase the incidence of long-term pain after thoracotomy.
cards.watchOut: Small (42 patients) and its harm signal is at 8 weeks rather than the 6-12 month horizon of Ju 2008 — but two independent randomised trials finding more neuropathic-type pain after cryoanalgesia is a pattern, not an accident. Neither trial used the Nuss population, where the one randomised trial found no such signal.
cards.source: Mustola ST et al. Efficacy of thoracic epidural analgesia with or without intercostal nerve cryoanalgesia for postthoracotomy pain. The Annals of thoracic surgery. 2011. PMID: 21353017. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT — the acute win is real, the chronic-pain question is operation-specific and unresolved for thoracotomy
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT — the acute win is real, the chronic-pain question is operation-specific and unresolved for thoracotomy
cards.people: Four randomised trials: Nuss cryoablation versus epidural (20 patients), thoracotomy cryoanalgesia added to systemic analgesia (50), cryoanalgesia versus epidural (107), and epidural with versus without cryoanalgesia (42).
cards.result: Acute outcomes favour or equal cryoanalgesia in every trial (stay 3 vs 5 days and far fewer opioids in the Nuss trial; better pain scores and less morphine in one thoracotomy trial; equal acute pain in another). Chronic neuropathic-type pain was more frequent after cryoanalgesia in both thoracotomy trials that measured it beyond a few weeks. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: No trial names a cryoablation device or manufacturer in its record, so no product can be named on this shelf; devices and freeze protocols differ between centres and eras, and current systems may not behave like the 2008-2013 thoracotomy equipment. The Nuss randomised base is a single trial of 20 patients.

shelves.title: Perioperative probiotics and synbiotics in GI surgery: postoperative infections roughly halved in the trial literature (relative risk 0.56 across 34 trials) — but every trial used a different preparation, so no single product carries the claim
shelves.question: In adults having elective gastrointestinal surgery, do perioperative probiotics or synbiotics reduce postoperative infectious complications (surgical-site infection, pneumonia, anastomotic leak sepsis) versus placebo or standard care?
shelves.balance: LIKELY (benefit) for the class question, with a binding product caveat. The largest synthesis (Chowdhury 2020; 34 randomised trials, 2,723 participants in elective abdominal surgery) found perioperative probiotics or synbiotics reduced postoperative infectious complications with a relative risk of 0.56 (95% CI 0.46-0.69), with synbiotics stronger (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.33-0.66) than probiotics alone (relative risk 0.65, 95% CI 0.53-0.80), no mortality difference (relative risk 0.98) and no significant adverse events. The individual trials agree in direction: Rayes 2005 (66 liver-transplant recipients) found bacterial infections in 3% with a four-strain lactic-acid-bacteria plus four-fibre synbiotic versus 48% with fibres alone; Kanazawa 2005 (44 completing patients, biliary-cancer hepatectomy) found infectious complications in 19% versus 52%; Sugawara 2006 (81 completing patients) found adding preoperative synbiotics cut infections from 30.0% to 12.1% versus postoperative-only synbiotics. The caveat is structural: preparations differ by maker and strain in every trial, several records name organisms but no brand, and where a trial names no product this shelf says so — current commercial products may differ in safety and effectiveness from what was tested. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit), class-level only.

cards.headline: Chowdhury 2020 (meta-analysis, 34 randomised trials, 2,723 participants): probiotics/synbiotics cut postoperative infections — relative risk 0.56 overall, 0.46 for synbiotics, 0.65 for probiotics alone; mortality unchanged
cards.summary: Chowdhury 2020 (meta-analysis, 34 randomised trials, 2,723 participants): probiotics/synbiotics cut postoperative infections — relative risk 0.56 overall, 0.46 for synbiotics, 0.65 for probiotics alone; mortality unchanged
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Chowdhury 2020)
cards.people: 34 randomised controlled trials in adults undergoing elective colorectal, upper gastrointestinal, transplant or hepatopancreaticobiliary surgery; 1,354 patients received probiotic or synbiotic preparations and 1,369 received placebo or standard care; the primary outcome was postoperative infectious complications.
cards.result: Perioperative probiotics or synbiotics significantly reduced infectious complications (relative risk 0.56; 95% CI 0.46-0.69; P<0.00001; I²=42%) — a 44% relative reduction; the record reports the pooled relative effect without a single pooled absolute control rate. Synbiotics had the larger effect (relative risk 0.46; 95% CI 0.33-0.66; n=1,399) versus probiotics alone (relative risk 0.65; 95% CI 0.53-0.80; n=1,324). Synbiotics also shortened total hospital stay (weighted mean difference -3.89 days; 95% CI -6.60 to -1.18). There were no significant differences in mortality (relative risk 0.98; 95% CI 0.54-1.80) or noninfectious complications, and preparations were well tolerated with no significant adverse events reported.
cards.watchOut: A relative-risk headline pooled across dozens of different strains, doses, operations and control conditions (placebo or standard care): it establishes that something in this family helps, not which preparation, dose or duration. Heterogeneity was moderate overall (I²=42%) and high in the synbiotic length-of-stay analysis (I²=91%).
cards.source: Chowdhury AH et al. Perioperative Probiotics or Synbiotics in Adults Undergoing Elective Abdominal Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Annals of surgery. 2020. PMID: 31469748. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Rayes 2005 (randomised double-blind trial, 66 liver-transplant recipients): four lactic-acid bacteria plus four fibres — bacterial infections 3% versus 48% with fibres alone
cards.summary: Rayes 2005 (randomised double-blind trial, 66 liver-transplant recipients): four lactic-acid bacteria plus four fibres — bacterial infections 3% versus 48% with fibres alone
cards.people: 66 liver-transplant recipients receiving early enteral nutrition from the day before surgery for 14 days, randomised to a composition of four lactic acid bacteria and four fibres (synbiotic group) or the four fibres only (control); outcomes included 30-day infection rate, hospital stay, antibiotic duration and noninfectious complications. The record describes the composition by its components and names no brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: Postoperative bacterial infections occurred in 3% of the synbiotic group versus 48% of the fibres-only group — a significant reduction, with mainly mild or moderate infections in both groups — and the duration of antibiotic therapy was significantly shorter with the synbiotic. Fibres and bacteria were well tolerated.
cards.watchOut: A strikingly large effect (3% versus 48%) from a single centre in 66 immunocompromised transplant patients, against a fibres-only control rather than placebo: exactly the setting where a pooled class effect (relative risk 0.56) is more believable than any single trial's number. The tested composition is described, not branded, in the record — it cannot be matched to a named commercial product from this source, and current products may differ.

cards.headline: Kanazawa 2005 (randomised trial, 54 randomised, 44 completing; biliary-cancer hepatectomy): synbiotic enteral feeding — infectious complications 19% (4/21) versus 52% (12/23)
cards.summary: Kanazawa 2005 (randomised trial, 54 randomised, 44 completing; biliary-cancer hepatectomy): synbiotic enteral feeding — infectious complications 19% (4/21) versus 52% (12/23)
cards.people: 54 patients with biliary cancer undergoing high-risk hepatectomy, randomly allocated to postoperative enteral feeding including synbiotics or enteral feeding only; 44 patients completed the trial (21 synbiotics, 23 controls). The record's MeSH identifies the organisms studied (Bifidobacterium and Lacticaseibacillus casei) but names no brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: Infectious complications occurred in 19% (4 of 21) of the synbiotics group versus 52% (12 of 23) of controls (P<0.05). Beneficial bacteria increased after surgery in the synbiotics group and decreased in controls, harmful microorganisms moved in the opposite direction, and total organic acid concentrations rose with synbiotics and fell without. All patients survived surgery (mortality 0%). Gut-barrier measures (lactulose/mannitol ratio and serum diamine oxidase) did not differ between groups.
cards.watchOut: Ten of 54 randomised patients did not complete the trial, and the proposed mechanism (barrier protection) was not confirmed by the trial's own barrier measurements — the infection difference stands, the explanation does not. Single-centre, high-risk hepatectomy population.
cards.source: Kanazawa H et al. Synbiotics reduce postoperative infectious complications: a randomized controlled trial in biliary cancer patients undergoing hepatectomy. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2005. PMID: 15711820. Registry ID: none in the record (pre-registration-era trial). cards.headline: Sugawara 2006 (randomised trial, 101 randomised, 81 completing; biliary-cancer resection): preoperative plus postoperative synbiotics versus postoperative only — infections 12.1% (5/41) versus 30.0% (12/40)
cards.summary: Sugawara 2006 (randomised trial, 101 randomised, 81 completing; biliary-cancer resection): preoperative plus postoperative synbiotics versus postoperative only — infections 12.1% (5/41) versus 30.0% (12/40)
cards.people: 101 patients with biliary cancer involving the hepatic hilus randomised before high-risk hepatectomy to enteral feeding with synbiotics given postoperatively only (group A) or preoperatively plus postoperatively (group B); 81 patients completed the trial. The record's MeSH identifies Bifidobacterium and Lacticaseibacillus casei among the organisms studied and names no brand or manufacturer.
cards.result: Postoperative infectious complications occurred in 30.0% (12 of 40) in group A versus 12.1% (5 of 41) in group B (P<0.05). Preoperative synbiotics increased natural-killer cell activity and lymphocyte counts and lowered interleukin-6 before surgery, and postoperative interleukin-6, white-cell counts and C-reactive protein were significantly lower in group B.
cards.watchOut: This trial's contrast is timing, not synbiotic versus none — both groups received synbiotics, so it shows starting before surgery adds benefit on top of postoperative use; it is not independent proof of the synbiotic-versus-control effect. Twenty of 101 randomised patients did not complete the trial.

shelves.title: Thermoregulation under anaesthesia (physiology): the interthreshold range widens from ~0.5 °C awake to 2.3 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 °C at 0.8 MAC desflurane — volatile agents and propofol push the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds down by degrees while barely moving the sweating threshold, which is why surgical patients cool
shelves.question: In healthy humans under general anaesthesia, how wide does the thermoregulatory interthreshold range become — by how much do volatile anaesthetics and propofol lower the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds while barely moving the sweating threshold, in the volunteer threshold studies?
shelves.balance: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED — graded, per this row's flag, as physiology measured under a drug intervention in volunteers, not resting physiology: the subjects were healthy volunteers given anaesthetics, a patient-adjacent preparation, and every card says so. Textbook framing (Guyton & Hall, body-temperature regulation, as extended by the anaesthesia-physiology literature): awake, sweating, vasoconstriction and shivering switch on within a narrow interthreshold range of core temperatures. The volunteer threshold programme (Sessler and colleagues) measures how anaesthetics tear that range open from the cold side. Desflurane raised the sweating threshold linearly (37.1 → 37.6 → 38.1 °C at 0, 0.5 and 0.8 MAC) but cut the vasoconstriction threshold by ~3 °C at 0.8 MAC, widening the interthreshold range from 0.5 ± 0.3 °C to 2.3 ± 0.7 and 4.6 ± 2.0 °C (Annadata 1995; N = 9). Propofol did the same intravenously: vasoconstriction threshold fell linearly with concentration (slope −0.6 ± 0.1 °C per µg/ml) and shivering similarly (−0.7 ± 0.1), while sweating moved only slightly (+0.1 ± 0.1) (Matsukawa 1995; N = 5). An independent propofol study using an epidural-based model found the interthreshold range was 0.51 ± 0.46 °C on epidural alone and grew by 0.49 ± 0.31 °C per µg/ml of propofol (Leslie 1994; N = 6). The vasoconstriction-to-shivering gap stays ~1–1.5 °C, so patients rarely shiver under anaesthesia simply because vasoconstriction alone usually cannot hold core temperature above the shivering threshold once the range has widened — they cool passively through the dead zone first. The awake counterpart — thresholds, circadian and acclimation shifts without drugs — is pack #6263, cross-pointed here and not duplicated. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (physiology measured under a drug intervention, per the row's grading note).

cards.headline: Annadata 1995 (desflurane): the interthreshold range widened from 0.5 ± 0.3 °C awake to 2.3 ± 0.7 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 ± 2.0 °C at 0.8 MAC — sweating threshold rose ~1 °C while the vasoconstriction threshold fell ~3 °C (N = 9 volunteers)
cards.summary: Annadata 1995 (desflurane): the interthreshold range widened from 0.5 ± 0.3 °C awake to 2.3 ± 0.7 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 ± 2.0 °C at 0.8 MAC — sweating threshold rose ~1 °C while the vasoconstriction threshold fell ~3 °C (N = 9 volunteers)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (volunteer anaesthetic-threshold study, Sessler programme)
cards.people: 9 healthy volunteers each studied on 3 randomly ordered days — control (no anaesthesia), end-tidal desflurane 0.5 MAC (3.5%) and 0.8 MAC (5.6%) — warmed until sweating, then cooled until vasoconstriction and shivering, with skin-temperature changes compensated arithmetically and thresholds expressed as core temperatures at a designated skin temperature of 34 °C. Small volunteer study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Desflurane linearly increased the sweating threshold from 37.1 ± 0.3 °C (control) to 37.6 ± 0.4 °C at 0.5 MAC and 38.1 ± 0.3 °C at 0.8 MAC. It significantly but nonlinearly reduced the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds — the vasoconstriction threshold fell by approximately 3 °C at 0.8 MAC. The sweating-to-vasoconstriction (interthreshold) range therefore increased from 0.5 ± 0.3 °C to 2.3 ± 0.7 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 ± 2.0 °C at 0.8 MAC, while the vasoconstriction-to-shivering range stayed between 1.1 and 1.5 °C on all three days. The authors note shivering was readily induced in volunteers although it is rare in surgical patients, because vasoconstriction usually prevents the further 1–1.5 °C fall the shivering threshold requires.
cards.watchOut: Volunteers under anaesthesia without surgery — physiology measured under a drug intervention, per this shelf's grading: surgical patients add redistribution, exposure and fluids. The vasoconstriction dose-response was nonlinear (less fall than expected at 0.5 MAC), so the range should not be interpolated linearly between MAC levels.
cards.source: Annadata R et al. Desflurane slightly increases the sweating threshold but produces marked, nonlinear decreases in the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds. Anesthesiology. 1995. PMID: 8533913. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Matsukawa 1995 (propofol): vasoconstriction threshold fell linearly at −0.6 °C per µg/ml and shivering at −0.7 °C per µg/ml, while the sweating threshold rose only +0.1 °C per µg/ml (N = 5 volunteers)
cards.summary: Matsukawa 1995 (propofol): vasoconstriction threshold fell linearly at −0.6 °C per µg/ml and shivering at −0.7 °C per µg/ml, while the sweating threshold rose only +0.1 °C per µg/ml (N = 5 volunteers)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (volunteer propofol-threshold study, Sessler programme)
cards.people: 5 healthy volunteers each studied on 4 days — control and target blood propofol concentrations of 2, 4 and 8 µg/ml — heated to provoke sweating, then cooled to elicit vasoconstriction and shivering, with thresholds mathematically compensated to a designated skin temperature of 35.7 °C using the established cutaneous contributions (10% for sweating, 20% for vasoconstriction and shivering). Very small volunteer study — N printed here on the face.
cards.result: Propofol significantly decreased the core temperature triggering vasoconstriction (slope −0.6 ± 0.1 °C·µg⁻¹·ml⁻¹; r² = 0.98 ± 0.02) and shivering (slope −0.7 ± 0.1 °C·µg⁻¹·ml⁻¹; r² = 0.95 ± 0.05), while increasing the sweating threshold only slightly (slope +0.1 ± 0.1 °C·µg⁻¹·ml⁻¹; r² = 0.46 ± 0.39). Because the shivering and vasoconstriction thresholds fall together, the vasoconstriction-to-shivering range increases only slightly during propofol anaesthesia — the widening is almost all in the sweating-to-vasoconstriction interthreshold range. The concentration-response slopes for sweating and vasoconstriction were virtually identical to those from the group's earlier established model, validating the method.
cards.watchOut: N = 5 men, each his own control across four days: the linearity (r² ≈ 0.95–0.98) is what carries the slopes, and the sweating slope's weak fit (r² = 0.46) is printed — propofol's warm-side effect is small and imprecisely estimated.
cards.source: Matsukawa T et al. Propofol linearly reduces the vasoconstriction and shivering thresholds. Anesthesiology. 1995. PMID: 7741292. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.summary: Leslie 1994 (propofol, epidural model): the interthreshold range was 0.51 ± 0.46 °C on epidural anaesthesia alone and grew by 0.49 ± 0.31 °C for each µg/ml of propofol (N = 6 volunteers)
cards.type: Primary human physiology study (volunteer propofol-threshold study, epidural model)
cards.people: 6 healthy male volunteers studied on 3 randomly ordered days — no propofol, target blood propofol 2 µg/ml, and 4 µg/ml — with epidural anaesthesia (approximately T11, 2% 2-chloroprocaine; one volunteer received bupivacaine) confining thermal manipulation to the legs while upper-body skin temperature was held constant; sweating threshold was tympanic temperature at sustained evaporative loss > 40 g·m⁻²·h⁻¹ and vasoconstriction threshold at sustained fingertip flow < 0.25 ml/min.
cards.result: Increasing propofol concentration produced a linear decrease in the vasoconstriction threshold (slope −0.53 ± 0.34 °C·µg⁻¹·ml⁻¹; R² = 0.98 ± 0.04) but had little effect on the sweating threshold. The interthreshold range was 0.51 ± 0.46 °C during epidural anaesthesia alone and increased significantly, by 0.49 ± 0.31 °C·µg⁻¹·ml⁻¹, during propofol administration. The authors conclude that, like volatile anaesthetics, propofol reduces the vasoconstriction threshold and increases the interthreshold range, differing in leaving the sweating threshold unchanged — an independent model and research group session replicating the Matsukawa pattern.
cards.watchOut: The preparation includes an epidural block, which itself alters lower-body thermoregulatory traffic — the record's own baseline (0.51 °C on epidural alone) is therefore the honest comparator, and the propofol increment is measured against it, not against the fully awake state.
cards.source: Leslie K et al. Propofol causes a dose-dependent decrease in the thermoregulatory threshold for vasoconstriction but has little effect on sweating. Anesthesiology. 1994. PMID: 8053585. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: anaesthetics widen the thermoregulatory dead zone roughly tenfold, almost entirely from the cold side — sweating moves ~1 °C at most while vasoconstriction falls ~3 °C — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (measured under a drug intervention)
cards.summary: Synthesis: anaesthetics widen the thermoregulatory dead zone roughly tenfold, almost entirely from the cold side — sweating moves ~1 °C at most while vasoconstriction falls ~3 °C — PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED (measured under a drug intervention)
cards.people: Carded human data: 9 + 5 + 6 healthy volunteers (20 in total), each studied repeatedly across anaesthetic concentrations, in the Sessler-programme threshold studies.
cards.result: Awake or on epidural alone, the interthreshold range is ~0.5 °C. Desflurane widens it to 2.3 °C at 0.5 MAC and 4.6 °C at 0.8 MAC; propofol widens it linearly at ~0.5 °C per µg/ml. The mechanism is asymmetric: the sweating threshold rises slightly (desflurane +1.0 °C at 0.8 MAC; propofol ~+0.1 °C per µg/ml), while the vasoconstriction threshold falls steeply (~3 °C at 0.8 MAC desflurane; −0.53 to −0.6 °C per µg/ml propofol) and the shivering threshold falls with it (−0.7 °C per µg/ml), leaving the vasoconstriction-to-shivering gap at ~1–1.5 °C. A patient in the widened range has no autonomic defence engaged — the physiological reason surgical patients drift cold. All three studies are small volunteer experiments under anaesthesia (a patient-adjacent population, graded as physiology under drug intervention per the row's note); their concordance across two drug classes and two laboratory models is what supports ESTABLISHED. The awake threshold system is pack #6263; this shelf cards none of its references. PROPOSED STAMP: PHYSIOLOGY — ESTABLISHED.
cards.watchOut: Thresholds are core temperatures compensated to a designated skin temperature; at different skin temperatures the absolute thresholds shift (skin contributes ~10–20% of the drive), and neuraxial anaesthesia, opioids and age move them further — none of those modifiers is carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of Annadata R et al. Anesthesiology. 1995 (PMID: 8533913); Matsukawa T et al. Anesthesiology. 1995 (PMID: 7741292); Leslie K et al. Anesthesiology. 1994 (PMID: 8053585). Textbook framing: Guyton & Hall (body-temperature regulation) as extended by the anaesthesia-physiology literature — framing, not evidence cards.
