shelves.title: Droperidol at low antiemetic doses prevents postoperative nausea and vomiting as well as ondansetron — with a boxed warning written for higher doses
shelves.question: In adults at risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting, does droperidol — alone and within combination prophylaxis — prevent PONV versus placebo or ondansetron, and what is the QT/sedation cost at antiemetic doses?
shelves.mesh: Adolescent · Adult · Aged · Ambulatory Surgical Procedures · Anesthesia, Intravenous · Anesthetics, Inhalation/administration & dosage · Anesthetics, Intravenous/administration & dosage · Antiemetics/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Barbiturates/administration & dosage · Double-Blind Method · Droperidol/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Elective Surgical Procedures · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Headache/chemically induced · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Male · Middle Aged · Nausea/prevention & control · Ondansetron/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Patient Satisfaction · Placebos · Postoperative Complications · Premedication · Risk Factors · Vomiting/prevention & control
shelves.balance: The boxed-warning context belongs on the face, stated plainly: droperidol carries an FDA boxed warning about QT prolongation and torsades de pointes, issued in an era of much larger (including antipsychotic) doses, and it sharply reduced antiemetic use. The low-dose evidence is a separate question and is stated separately: at 0.625–1.25 mg, droperidol prevented PONV as well as ondansetron in adults (Fortney's 2,061-patient programme and the Domino meta-analysis), did not prolong QTc beyond saline in a placebo-controlled study, produced only a transient QTc rise at 1.25 mg in a second randomised QT study, and had no attributed torsades or death in a 20,122-patient retrospective cohort (observational evidence, labelled as such). This shelf asks the droperidol-as-antiemetic question only: the live shelf on combination prophylaxis and aprepitant for PONV already covers droperidol as one component of the IMPACT factorial trial, and droperidol's emergency-department sedation use is a different shelf — neither is duplicated here. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) at low antiemetic doses.

cards.headline: Fortney 1998 (two identical RCTs, N = 2,061): droperidol 1.25 mg beat ondansetron for complete response in the first 2 hours (69% vs 62%); both droperidol doses beat placebo
cards.summary: Fortney 1998 (two identical RCTs, N = 2,061): droperidol 1.25 mg beat ondansetron for complete response in the first 2 hours (69% vs 62%); both droperidol doses beat placebo
cards.people: 2,061 adult surgical outpatients at high risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) in two identical randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies, given intravenous ondansetron 4 mg, droperidol 0.625 mg, droperidol 1.25 mg or placebo 20 minutes before induction.
cards.result: Complete response (no emesis or rescue antiemetic) at 0–2 hours was 46% with placebo, 62% with ondansetron, 63% with droperidol 0.625 mg and 69% with droperidol 1.25 mg (droperidol 1.25 mg superior to ondansetron, P < 0.05). Over 0–24 hours the antiemetic groups did not differ from each other and all remained superior to placebo; the proportion without nausea over 24 hours was greater with droperidol 1.25 mg (43%) than with ondansetron or droperidol 0.625 mg (29% each). Headache was more common with ondansetron than with either droperidol dose.
cards.watchOut: 1990s ambulatory anaesthesia (barbiturate induction, nitrous oxide/isoflurane/enflurane maintenance) — absolute PONV rates may not transfer to modern practice, though the head-to-head comparison stands.
cards.source: Fortney JT et al. A comparison of the efficacy, safety, and patient satisfaction of ondansetron versus droperidol as antiemetics for elective outpatient surgical procedures. S3A-409 and S3A-410 Study Groups. Anesthesia and analgesia. 1998. PMID: 9539593. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Domino 1999 (meta-analysis, 54 RCTs): droperidol and ondansetron were equally effective against vomiting in adults, and both beat metoclopramide
cards.summary: Domino 1999 (meta-analysis, 54 RCTs): droperidol and ondansetron were equally effective against vomiting in adults, and both beat metoclopramide
cards.people: A meta-analysis of 54 double-blind randomised trials of prophylactic ondansetron, droperidol and/or metoclopramide during general anaesthesia (adults and children).
cards.result: Against vomiting, droperidol (pooled odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.85; P < 0.001) and ondansetron (OR 0.43, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.61) were each more effective than metoclopramide. In adults, ondansetron and droperidol were equally effective (pooled OR 0.87; P = 0.45); ondansetron was more effective than droperidol only in children. The overall risk of adverse effects did not differ among the drugs.
cards.watchOut: Odds ratios are relative measures; the abstract gives no pooled absolute vomiting rates, so no absolute benefit is claimed here. The trials predate the boxed warning and modern combination prophylaxis.
cards.source: Domino KB et al. Comparative efficacy and safety of ondansetron, droperidol, and metoclopramide for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting: a meta-analysis. Anesthesia and analgesia. 1999. PMID: 10357347. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: White 2005 (placebo-controlled QT study, N = 120): low-dose droperidol did not prolong QTc more than saline during or after anaesthesia (the treatment made no difference to QTc versus saline)
cards.summary: White 2005 (placebo-controlled QT study, N = 120): low-dose droperidol did not prolong QTc more than saline during or after anaesthesia (the treatment made no difference to QTc versus saline)
cards.people: 120 outpatients having otolaryngologic procedures under a standardised general anaesthetic, randomised to saline or droperidol 0.625 mg or 1.25 mg intravenously, with electrocardiographic QTc measurement during a 10-minute observation period and, in 60 further patients, 12-lead electrocardiograms up to 2 hours after surgery.
cards.result: Droperidol 0.625 mg and 1.25 mg prolonged the QT interval by an average of 15 ± 40 ms and 22 ± 41 ms at 3–6 minutes, not significantly different from saline (12 ± 35 ms); there was no droperidol-induced QTc prolongation after surgery and no ectopic beats were observed on any recording. General anaesthesia itself was associated with a 14–16 ms QTc prolongation in the early postoperative period.
cards.watchOut: A surrogate endpoint (QTc) in 120 relatively low-risk patients — it cannot exclude a rare torsades event, which is exactly the event the boxed warning concerns.
cards.source: White PF et al. Effect of low-dose droperidol on the QT interval during and after general anesthesia: a placebo-controlled study. Anesthesiology. 2005. PMID: 15915020. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nuttall 2013 (retrospective cohort, 20,122 patients given droperidol): no case of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or death was attributed to low-dose droperidol — observational evidence, labelled as such
cards.summary: Nuttall 2013 (retrospective cohort, 20,122 patients given droperidol): no case of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or death was attributed to low-dose droperidol — observational evidence, labelled as such
cards.people: 20,122 surgical patients who received 35,536 doses of droperidol (low dose, 0.625 mg) in the 3 years after droperidol returned to one institution's formulary, cross-matched against electrocardiogram and adverse-outcome databases; 858 charts were reviewed in detail. Observational evidence — no randomised comparison.
cards.result: Twelve patients had ventricular tachycardia (4) or death (8) documented within 48 hours of droperidol, but no patient developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or death due to droperidol administration (n = 0): the deaths were in patients on palliative care and the tachycardia cases had pre-existing cardiac conditions. Among 523 patients with a documented QTc > 440 ms before droperidol, none developed ventricular tachycardia or death as a direct result of the drug.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and single-institution: absence of an attributed event in 20,122 patients bounds but does not abolish a rare risk, and attribution was by chart review.
cards.source: Nuttall GA et al. Does low-dose droperidol increase the risk of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia or death in the surgical patient? Anesthesiology. 2013. PMID: 23291623. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Tracz 2015 (double-blind RCT, N = 75): droperidol 1.25 mg caused only a transient QTc rise at 10 minutes; no patient exceeded 500 ms and transmural dispersion did not change
cards.summary: Tracz 2015 (double-blind RCT, N = 75): droperidol 1.25 mg caused only a transient QTc rise at 10 minutes; no patient exceeded 500 ms and transmural dispersion did not change
cards.people: 75 patients randomly allocated to droperidol 0.625 mg, droperidol 1.25 mg or ondansetron 8 mg for PONV prophylaxis, with QTc calculated by both Bazett and Framingham corrections and transmural dispersion of repolarisation measured.
cards.result: Transient QT prolongation followed droperidol 1.25 mg at 10 minutes only; the 0.625 mg and ondansetron groups showed no QTc change. By Bazett correction, QTc exceeded 480 ms in two patients on droperidol 1.25 mg and one on ondansetron; no patient exceeded 500 ms, and by Framingham correction none exceeded 480 ms. There were no significant differences in transmural dispersion within or between groups.
cards.watchOut: The authors restrict their reassurance to men without cardiovascular disorders and a low pro-QTc score — it does not extend to patients with cardiac disease or other QT-prolonging drugs.
cards.source: Tracz K et al. Small doses of droperidol do not present relevant torsadogenic actions: a double-blind, ondansetron-controlled study. British journal of clinical pharmacology. 2015. PMID: 25293524. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: low-dose droperidol prevents PONV as well as ondansetron in adults, and the low-dose QT signal is small and transient — against a boxed warning written for a different dose era
cards.summary: Synthesis: low-dose droperidol prevents PONV as well as ondansetron in adults, and the low-dose QT signal is small and transient — against a boxed warning written for a different dose era
cards.people: Two large placebo-controlled trials (2,061 patients), a 54-trial meta-analysis, two small randomised QT studies (120 and 75 patients) and one large retrospective safety cohort (20,122 patients).
cards.result: Efficacy: droperidol 0.625–1.25 mg beat placebo and matched ondansetron in adults. QT: no QTc prolongation beyond saline in the placebo-controlled study, a transient 10-minute rise at 1.25 mg in the ondansetron-controlled study, and no attributed torsades or death in 20,122 exposed patients. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) for PONV prevention at these doses, with the boxed-warning context carried on the face (see balance).
cards.watchOut: Sedation and extrapyramidal effects at antiemetic doses are not quantified by the carded QT-focused safety reports; where sedation matters, that gap belongs in the clinical decision.
cards.source: Synthesis of Fortney JT et al. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1998; Domino KB et al. Anesthesia & Analgesia. 1999; White PF et al. Anesthesiology. 2005; Nuttall GA et al. Anesthesiology. 2013; Tracz K et al. British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology. 2015.

shelves.title: Preoperative botulinum toxin for large ventral hernia: series report closure in over 90%, matched comparisons show no added benefit
shelves.question: In adults with large incisional/ventral hernias with loss of domain, does preoperative botulinum toxin A injection of the lateral abdominal wall muscles (± progressive pneumoperitoneum) increase fascial-closure rates and reduce component-separation need and recurrence versus repair without chemical component separation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Abdominal Wall/surgery · Herniorrhaphy/adverse effects,methods · Botulinum Toxins, Type A · Surgical Mesh · Hernia, Ventral/surgery · Recurrence
shelves.balance: No randomised trial was found for this question — the whole base is observational and is labelled as such on every card. The split is real: consecutive programmes (Bueno-Lledó's 100 loss-of-domain cases with toxin plus pneumoperitoneum, Deerenberg's 108 reconstructions) report fascial closure in 91–97%, and a prospective comparison achieved closure in all toxin patients; but the 2025 propensity-matched meta-analysis (851 patients) found the treatment made no difference to closure, recurrence or component-separation need, and its trial sequential analysis says the matched evidence is still too small to settle the question. Product and protocol discipline: doses and timing vary widely (an average 243 units in one programme; toxin given ~38 days ahead combined with pneumoperitoneum in another), and the botulinum toxin product/brand is not named in the carded records — so no single pooled closure-rate claim is made. PROPOSED SPLIT (observational).

cards.headline: Bueno-Lledó 2020 (prospective comparative study, N = 80): fascial closure was achieved in all 40 botulinum-toxin patients, and skin necrosis occurred only with component separation (12.5%)
cards.summary: Bueno-Lledó 2020 (prospective comparative study, N = 80): fascial closure was achieved in all 40 botulinum-toxin patients, and skin necrosis occurred only with component separation (12.5%)
cards.people: 80 consecutive patients with large midline incisional hernias (transverse diameters 11–17 cm, all W3) at one tertiary centre: 40 given preoperative botulinum toxin A followed by open Rives repair, compared prospectively with 40 who underwent open (modified anterior) component separation. Non-randomised comparative evidence.
cards.result: Complete fascial closure was possible in all patients in the botulinum toxin group. No complications occurred during botulinum toxin administration. Surgical-site complications were most frequent in the component-separation group, especially skin necrosis (12.5%, P = .020). At a median 19.6 months of follow-up, two hernia recurrences were reported, both in the component-separation group.
cards.watchOut: Non-randomised and single-centre: the toxin group may have been selected as more favourable candidates, and the record does not name the botulinum toxin product or brand.
cards.source: Bueno-Lledó J et al. Botulinum toxin to avoid component separation in midline large hernias. Langenbeck's archives of surgery. 2020. PMID: 32576404. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Bueno-Lledó 2020 (loss-of-domain series, N = 100): botulinum toxin plus progressive pneumoperitoneum cut the hernia-volume ratio by 15% and allowed complete fascial closure in 97%
cards.summary: Bueno-Lledó 2020 (loss-of-domain series, N = 100): botulinum toxin plus progressive pneumoperitoneum cut the hernia-volume ratio by 15% and allowed complete fascial closure in 97%
cards.people: 100 consecutive patients with loss-of-domain hernias treated with combined preoperative botulinum toxin type A and progressive pneumoperitoneum, analysed retrospectively from 753 ventral incisional hernia operations (2010–2018). Single-arm series — no control group.
cards.result: Botulinum toxin was given a mean 38.2 days before surgery and the median insufflated pneumoperitoneum volume was 8,600 mL. The combination significantly reduced the hernia-volume/abdominal-cavity-volume ratio by an average of 15% on CT (p = 0.001). Complete fascial closure was possible in 97% (mesh bridging in 3 cases), anterior component separation and transversus abdominis release were the most frequent repair techniques, and 8 recurrences (8%) were reported over a mean 34.5 months of follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The toxin and pneumoperitoneum effects cannot be separated in a combined, uncontrolled series; the 97% closure figure has no untreated comparator.
cards.source: Bueno-Lledó J et al. Preoperative Botulinum Toxin and Progressive Pneumoperitoneum in Loss of Domain Hernias-Our First 100 Cases. Frontiers in surgery. 2020. PMID: 32181259. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: not captured from the record this session

cards.headline: Deerenberg 2021 (prospective cohort, N = 108): fascial closure in 91% of massive loss-of-domain reconstructions after botulinum toxin — but 57% still needed component separation and 40% had a complication
cards.summary: Deerenberg 2021 (prospective cohort, N = 108): fascial closure in 91% of massive loss-of-domain reconstructions after botulinum toxin — but 57% still needed component separation and 40% had a complication
cards.people: 108 patients at one institution given preoperative botulinum toxin A (average 243 units, mean 32.5 days before surgery) before abdominal wall reconstruction for midline or flank hernias; hernias were massive (mean defect width 15.3 cm) with significant loss of domain (mean 46% of visceral volume outside the abdominal cavity). Single-arm prospective cohort.
cards.result: Fascial closure was achieved in 91%, with 57% requiring component separation techniques and mesh used in 98%. No complications followed the toxin injection itself. Postoperative complications occurred in 40% (surgical-site occurrences 19%, surgical-site infection 12%, respiratory failure requiring intubation 7%, mesh infection 2%, no fascial dehiscence), and recurrence was identified in 7 patients after a mean 14 months.
cards.watchOut: No control group, and the toxin product/brand is not named in the record — protocols (dose, timing, injection sites) vary widely between programmes and are not interchangeable.
cards.source: Deerenberg EB et al. The Effects of Preoperative Botulinum Toxin A Injection on Abdominal Wall Reconstruction. The Journal of surgical research. 2021. PMID: 33360691. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Dias 2023 (systematic review of observational studies): lateral abdominal muscles advanced by an average of 4.11 cm after preoperative botulinum toxin, with low reported infection and recurrence rates
cards.summary: Dias 2023 (systematic review of observational studies): lateral abdominal muscles advanced by an average of 4.11 cm after preoperative botulinum toxin, with low reported infection and recurrence rates
cards.type: Systematic review/meta-analysis of observational studies (Dias 2023) — observational
cards.people: A PRISMA systematic review of observational studies of preoperative botulinum toxin application for ventral hernia repair, including loss-of-domain cases.
cards.result: The review found advance of the lateral abdominal musculature by an average of 4.11 cm, with low heterogeneity, and low rates of surgical-site infection, surgical-site occurrences and recurrence across the included series. The authors conclude the muscle lengthening can help improve morbidity and recurrence outcomes.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis of uncontrolled series inherits their selection bias: patients offered toxin prehabilitation are chosen because closure looks achievable.

cards.headline: Florencio de Mesquita 2025 (propensity-matched meta-analysis, 6 studies, 851 patients): botulinum toxin made no significant difference to fascial closure, recurrence or component-separation need (the treatment made no difference on the matched comparisons)
cards.summary: Florencio de Mesquita 2025 (propensity-matched meta-analysis, 6 studies, 851 patients): botulinum toxin made no significant difference to fascial closure, recurrence or component-separation need (the treatment made no difference on the matched comparisons)
cards.type: Meta-analysis of propensity-matched observational studies (2025) — observational
cards.people: Six propensity-score matched studies (851 patients) comparing preoperative botulinum toxin A plus abdominal wall reconstruction with standard reconstruction alone for complex hernias; mean age 60.5 years, mean BMI 31.8 kg/m2. Comparative observational evidence, pooled.
cards.result: There were no significant differences in fascial closure rate (odds ratio 1.54, 95% CI 0.78 to 3.05; p = 0.21), hernia recurrence (OR 0.81, 95% CI 0.33 to 2.01; p = 0.65), component separation (OR 1.50, 95% CI 0.54 to 4.14; p = 0.4), surgical-site infection/occurrences, hospital stay or operation time. Trial sequential analysis indicated none of the outcomes had reached the sample size needed for a definitive conclusion.
cards.watchOut: Propensity matching adjusts only for measured differences; unmeasured selection (surgeon judgement about who can close) remains, in both directions.
cards.source: Florencio de Mesquita C et al. Preoperative botulinum toxin for complex abdominal wall reconstruction: a meta-analysis of propensity-score matched studies with trial sequential analysis. Hernia. 2025. PMID: 39966195. cards.headline: Synthesis: the series say closure becomes possible; the matched comparisons say the toxin itself has not been shown to add it — a genuine split, on observational evidence only
cards.summary: Synthesis: the series say closure becomes possible; the matched comparisons say the toxin itself has not been shown to add it — a genuine split, on observational evidence only
cards.people: No randomised trial exists in this base: one prospective comparative study (80 patients), two large single-arm programmes (100 and 108 patients), an observational systematic review, and a propensity-matched meta-analysis (851 patients).
cards.result: Uncontrolled programmes report 91–97% fascial closure and ~4.11 cm of lateral muscle advance; the one prospective head-to-head comparison achieved closure in all toxin patients with fewer wound complications than component separation. Against that, the propensity-matched pooling found no significant difference in closure, recurrence or component-separation need, with trial sequential analysis saying the question is not yet answerable. PROPOSED SPLIT, observational throughout.
cards.watchOut: Doses and protocols vary widely across programmes (the carded reports range from an average 243 units to combined toxin-plus-pneumoperitoneum protocols, given roughly 4–6 weeks pre-operatively), and the botulinum toxin product/brand is not named in the carded records — do not pool these into a single closure-rate claim.
cards.source: Synthesis of Bueno-Lledó J et al. Langenbeck's Archives of Surgery. 2020; Bueno-Lledó J et al. Frontiers in Surgery. 2020; Deerenberg EB et al. Journal of Surgical Research. 2021; Dias ERM et al. Hernia. 2023; Florencio de Mesquita C et al. Hernia. 2025.

shelves.title: Intravenous paracetamol relieves postoperative pain versus placebo — but randomised trials found no advantage over the oral form
shelves.question: In adults having major surgery, does intravenous paracetamol (acetaminophen) reduce postoperative pain and opioid consumption versus placebo — and does it add anything over oral paracetamol or NSAIDs where those can be given?
shelves.mesh: Acetaminophen/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Adult · Analgesics/administration & dosage · Child · Humans · Injections, Intravenous · Postoperative Pain/drug therapy · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Time Factors
shelves.balance: The two halves of this question have different answers, and both are on the face. Versus placebo, intravenous paracetamol works modestly: 37% versus 16% achieve at least 50% pain relief over 4 hours after a single dose (NNT 4.0), opioid use falls by 30% relative over 4 hours (labelled relative; it did not reduce opioid adverse events), and repeated 1 g doses beat placebo over 24 hours in orthopaedic surgery. Versus active comparators in the Cochrane review, differences were neither statistically nor clinically significant — and against the oral form specifically, a 486-patient equivalence trial and a 120-patient trial both found the intravenous route made no difference to pain or opioid use beyond, in one trial, the first 4 hours. So the intravenous form's real indication is the patient who cannot take oral medication. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo, qualified as in the stamp.

cards.headline: Tzortzopoulou 2011 (Cochrane review, 36 studies, 3,896 participants): a single intravenous dose gave at least 50% pain relief to 37% versus 16% on placebo (NNT 4.0), and cut opioid use by 30% relative over 4 hours
cards.summary: Tzortzopoulou 2011 (Cochrane review, 36 studies, 3,896 participants): a single intravenous dose gave at least 50% pain relief to 37% versus 16% on placebo (NNT 4.0), and cut opioid use by 30% relative over 4 hours
cards.people: 36 randomised, double-blind, placebo- or active-controlled single-dose trials (3,896 participants, adults and children) of intravenous paracetamol or its prodrug propacetamol for acute postoperative pain.
cards.result: At least 50% pain relief over 4 hours was experienced by 37% of participants on intravenous propacetamol/paracetamol versus 16% on placebo (number needed to treat 4.0, 95% CI 3.5 to 4.8); over 6 hours the NNT was 5.3. Opioid requirement was 30% less over 4 hours than placebo (a relative reduction; the review's absolute morphine amounts are not stated in the record) — but this did not translate into fewer opioid-induced adverse events. Comparisons with active comparators (opioids or NSAIDs) were not statistically or clinically significant. Adverse events matched placebo, except pain on infusion with propacetamol (23% vs 1%).
cards.watchOut: Single-dose trials, many with propacetamol (the prodrug) rather than paracetamol itself, and a 4–6 hour horizon — they do not answer multi-day or repeated-dose questions.
cards.source: Tzortzopoulou A et al. Single dose intravenous propacetamol or intravenous paracetamol for postoperative pain. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2011. PMID: 21975764. cochrane systematic review (tzortzopoulou 2011) 36 randomised, double-blind, placebo- or active-controlled single-dose trials (3,896 participants, adults and children) of intravenous paracetamol or its prodrug propacetamol for acute postoperative pain. at least 50% pain relief over 4 hours was experienced by 37% of participants on intravenous propacetamol/paracetamol versus 16% on placebo (number needed to treat 4.0, 95% ci 3.5 to 4.8); over 6 hours the nnt was 5.3. opioid requirement was 30% less over 4 hours than placebo (a relative reduction; the review's absolute morphine amounts are not stated in the record) — but this did not translate into fewer opioid-induced adverse events. comparisons with active comparators (opioids or nsaids) were not statistically or clinically significant. adverse events matched placebo, except pain on infusion with propacetamol (23% vs 1%). single-dose trials, many with propacetamol (the prodrug) rather than paracetamol itself, and a 4–6 hour horizon — they do not answer multi-day or repeated-dose questions. tzortzopoulou a et al. single dose intravenous propacetamol or intravenous paracetamol for postoperative pain. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2011. pmid: 21975764. registry id: none in the record. mesh: acetaminophen/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · adult · analgesics/administration & dosage · child · humans · injections, intravenous · postoperative pain/drug therapy · randomized controlled trials as topic · time factors

cards.headline: Sinatra 2005 (repeated-dose RCT, N = 151): intravenous paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours relieved pain from 15 minutes and significantly reduced 24-hour morphine consumption versus placebo
cards.summary: Sinatra 2005 (repeated-dose RCT, N = 151): intravenous paracetamol 1 g every 6 hours relieved pain from 15 minutes and significantly reduced 24-hour morphine consumption versus placebo
cards.people: 151 patients with moderate-to-severe pain after major orthopaedic surgery, randomised to intravenous acetaminophen (paracetamol) 1 g, propacetamol 2 g or placebo every 6 hours over 24 hours, with intravenous patient-controlled morphine rescue available.
cards.result: Both active groups differed significantly from placebo on pain relief from 15 minutes to 6 hours (P < 0.05), and median time to morphine rescue was 3 hours (intravenous paracetamol) and 2.6 hours (propacetamol) versus 0.8 hours (placebo). Intravenous paracetamol and propacetamol significantly reduced morphine consumption over the 24-hour period versus placebo (the record does not state the absolute milligram difference).
cards.watchOut: One operation type (major orthopaedic surgery) and a 24-hour window; the tested intravenous product is named in the record only generically as intravenous acetaminophen injection.

cards.headline: Hickman 2018 (equivalence RCT, N = 486): preoperative oral paracetamol was equivalent to intraoperative intravenous paracetamol for 24-hour opioid use and pain after hip/knee replacement (the intravenous route made no difference)
cards.summary: Hickman 2018 (equivalence RCT, N = 486): preoperative oral paracetamol was equivalent to intraoperative intravenous paracetamol for 24-hour opioid use and pain after hip/knee replacement (the intravenous route made no difference)
cards.people: 486 adults undergoing total hip or knee arthroplasty in a single-centre randomised placebo-controlled equivalence trial: oral paracetamol 1 g (two 500-mg capsules) before surgery with an intravenous placebo infusion, versus oral placebo capsules followed by intravenous paracetamol 1,000 mg intraoperatively.
cards.result: Postoperative opioid use in morphine milligram equivalents was equivalent between the oral and intravenous groups (the mean difference in median values lay within the prespecified equivalence margin), with no significant differences in mean pain scores over 24 hours. Intravenous paracetamol was also not superior for postoperative nausea and vomiting, time to ambulation, time to first as-needed pain medication, recovery-room stay or total hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: Equivalence within a prespecified margin in arthroplasty patients who could swallow a preoperative capsule — it says nothing about patients who cannot take oral medication, where the intravenous route is the only option.
cards.source: Hickman SR et al. Randomized trial of oral versus intravenous acetaminophen for postoperative pain control. American journal of health-system pharmacy. 2018. PMID: 29523533. cards.headline: Politi 2017 (RCT, N = 120): intravenous and oral paracetamol (1 g every 6 hours) did not differ in 24-hour narcotic use (3.71 vs 3.48 hydromorphone equivalents, P = .76) or pain, except in the first 4 hours
cards.summary: Politi 2017 (RCT, N = 120): intravenous and oral paracetamol (1 g every 6 hours) did not differ in 24-hour narcotic use (3.71 vs 3.48 hydromorphone equivalents, P = .76) or pain, except in the first 4 hours
cards.people: 120 patients undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty by one surgeon, randomised to intravenous (63) or oral (57) paracetamol 1 g preoperatively then every 6 hours for 24 hours, on top of a standard multimodal perioperative regimen.
cards.result: 24-hour average hydromorphone equivalents were 3.71 (intravenous) versus 3.48 (oral) (P = .76), with no significant difference at any individual 4-hour interval. Average 24-hour pain scores were 3.00 versus 3.40 (P = .06); the only significant interval was the first 0–4 hours, favouring intravenous (P = .03). The authors conclude the intravenous form may help immediately after surgery but, after that, provides no significant benefit over the much less expensive oral form.
cards.watchOut: Single surgeon, single centre, arthroplasty only — and both arms received paracetamol, so this card answers route, not whether paracetamol itself works.
cards.source: Politi JR et al. Randomized Prospective Trial Comparing the Use of Intravenous versus Oral Acetaminophen in Total Joint Arthroplasty. The Journal of arthroplasty. 2017. PMID: 27839957. cards.headline: Synthesis: intravenous paracetamol works against placebo for a few hours per dose — and two randomised trials found the oral route just as good where it can be used
cards.summary: Synthesis: intravenous paracetamol works against placebo for a few hours per dose — and two randomised trials found the oral route just as good where it can be used
cards.people: A Cochrane single-dose review (36 studies, 3,896 participants), a repeated-dose placebo-controlled trial (151 patients), and two randomised intravenous-versus-oral trials (486 and 120 patients, both arthroplasty).
cards.result: Versus placebo: about 37% versus 16% achieve at least 50% pain relief over 4 hours (NNT 4.0), with opioid sparing that did not reduce opioid adverse events. Versus oral: equivalence in the larger trial and no significant difference in the smaller — the intravenous route's advantage is confined to patients who cannot take oral medication and, in one trial, the first 4 postoperative hours. PROPOSED LIKELY (benefit) versus placebo, with the no-added-benefit-over-oral finding carried in the stamp.
cards.watchOut: Effect sizes are modest, as the slate flag required stating: the absolute gain is roughly one extra patient in five achieving half pain relief for about four hours per dose — present it as such, not as a strong analgesic.
cards.source: Synthesis of Tzortzopoulou A et al. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2011; Sinatra RS et al. Anesthesiology. 2005; Hickman SR et al. American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy. 2018; Politi JR et al. The Journal of Arthroplasty. 2017.

shelves.title: Perioperative intravenous magnesium: opioid sparing of about 6–8 mg and small pain-score gains, on highly heterogeneous trials
shelves.question: In adults having surgery under general or regional anaesthesia, does perioperative intravenous magnesium sulfate reduce postoperative pain, opioid use and shivering versus placebo?
shelves.mesh: Acute Pain/prevention & control · Analgesics, Opioid/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Bradycardia/chemically induced,epidemiology · Endpoint Determination · Female · Humans · Infusions, Intravenous · Injections, Intravenous · Magnesium Sulfate/administration & dosage,adverse effects,therapeutic use · Male · Morphine/administration & dosage,therapeutic use · Pain Measurement/drug effects · Postoperative Pain/prevention & control · Perioperative Care · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: Two meta-analyses, thirteen years apart, point the same way — 24-hour morphine down by 7.6 mg (24.4% relative, labelled as such) in the 2013 pooling and by 6.28 mg morphine equivalents in the 2026 pooling, with pain scores lower by roughly half to one point on a 0–10 scale — but heterogeneity is very high (I² up to 96%) and certainty low-to-moderate, which caps the stamp at POSSIBLE. Dosing and timing vary across trials (the carded individual trials used 50 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg/hour). The slate question also asked about shivering: none of the carded reports measured shivering, so this shelf makes no shivering claim rather than borrowing one. This is the analgesia question only — it is explicitly distinct from the magnesium-for-cisplatin-nephroprotection question in an earlier slate. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).

cards.headline: Albrecht 2013 (meta-analysis, 25 trials): perioperative intravenous magnesium cut 24-hour morphine consumption by 24.4% relative (7.6 mg absolute) and lowered pain scores by 4.2/100 at rest and 9.2/100 on movement
cards.summary: Albrecht 2013 (meta-analysis, 25 trials): perioperative intravenous magnesium cut 24-hour morphine consumption by 24.4% relative (7.6 mg absolute) and lowered pain scores by 4.2/100 at rest and 9.2/100 on movement
cards.people: 25 randomised trials comparing perioperative intravenous magnesium sulfate with placebo across surgical populations, with bolus and/or continuous-infusion regimens.
cards.result: Cumulative intravenous morphine consumption at 24 hours was reduced by a mean difference of 7.6 mg (95% CI −9.5 to −5.8 mg; p < 0.00001) — a 24.4% relative reduction, printed with its absolute difference. Numeric pain scores at 24 hours were reduced by 4.2 points (95% CI −6.3 to −2.1) at rest and 9.2 points (95% CI −16.1 to −2.3) on movement, out of 100. No serious adverse effects were reported in the included trials.
cards.watchOut: Pain-score gains of 4–9 points on a 100-point scale are small; dosing and timing were heterogeneous across the 25 trials, so no single regimen is endorsed by this pooling.
cards.source: Albrecht E et al. Peri-operative intravenous administration of magnesium sulphate and postoperative pain: a meta-analysis. Anaesthesia. 2013. PMID: 23121612. cards.headline: Tomaszek 2026 (meta-analysis, 22–24 RCTs, 1,750 participants): magnesium reduced early pain (−0.90/10) and 24-hour pain (−0.59/10) and opioid use (−6.28 mg morphine equivalents), with very high heterogeneity
cards.summary: Tomaszek 2026 (meta-analysis, 22–24 RCTs, 1,750 participants): magnesium reduced early pain (−0.90/10) and 24-hour pain (−0.59/10) and opioid use (−6.28 mg morphine equivalents), with very high heterogeneity
cards.people: Randomised trials published 2015–2026 comparing intravenous magnesium sulfate with placebo in adults under general anaesthesia: 24 trials in the qualitative synthesis, 22 (23 comparisons, 1,750 participants) in the quantitative meta-analysis, with GRADE certainty assessed.
cards.result: Magnesium reduced early postoperative pain (mean difference −0.90 on a 0–10 scale, 95% CI −1.33 to −0.47) and pain at 24 hours (−0.59, 95% CI −1.00 to −0.18), but not at 12 hours (−0.52, 95% CI −1.15 to 0.11). Opioid consumption fell by 6.28 mg morphine equivalents (95% CI −8.94 to −3.61) and time to first rescue analgesia lengthened by 85.61 minutes. Heterogeneity was substantial (I² 66–96%) and certainty ranged from very low to moderate, highest for pain at 24 hours.
cards.watchOut: With I² up to 96%, the pooled averages describe a direction, not a dependable size — individual regimens and operations differ too much for the mean difference to be quoted as an expectation.
cards.source: Tomaszek L et al. Effect of Intravenous Magnesium on Postoperative Pain and Analgesic Outcomes in Patients Undergoing General Anesthesia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. cards.headline: Benevides 2021 (double-blind RCT, N = 86, spinal anaesthesia): magnesium infusion lowered pain scores at 6 hours at rest and on movement, but tramadol consumption did not differ significantly (the treatment made no difference to opioid use in this trial)
cards.summary: Benevides 2021 (double-blind RCT, N = 86, spinal anaesthesia): magnesium infusion lowered pain scores at 6 hours at rest and on movement, but tramadol consumption did not differ significantly (the treatment made no difference to opioid use in this trial)
cards.people: 86 patients having abdominal hysterectomy under spinal anaesthesia with intrathecal morphine, randomised to magnesium sulfate 50 mg/kg over 15 minutes then 15 mg/kg/hour until the end of surgery, or the same volume of saline; both groups also received dipyrone, ketoprofen and dexamethasone.
cards.result: Serum magnesium was higher in the magnesium group at the end of surgery and 1 hour after (p = 0.000). Pain scores were reduced in the magnesium group at 6 hours, at rest and on movement (p < 0.05). Tramadol consumption did not differ significantly (15.5 ± 36.6 mg vs 29.2 ± 67.8 mg, p = 0.53), and haemodynamics, pruritus, nausea and vomiting were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: A spinal-anaesthesia population already receiving intrathecal morphine and two non-opioid analgesics — a hard background against which to show opioid sparing, and not the general-anaesthesia setting of the meta-analyses.
cards.source: Benevides ML et al. Intravenous magnesium sulfate for postoperative analgesia after abdominal hysterectomy under spinal anesthesia: a randomized, double-blind trial. Brazilian journal of anesthesiology. 2021. PMID: 33762190. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ryu 2016 (RCT, N = 84, laparoscopic gastrectomy): magnesium infusion improved surgical-space scores and lowered 24-hour pain, while using less rocuronium
cards.summary: Ryu 2016 (RCT, N = 84, laparoscopic gastrectomy): magnesium infusion improved surgical-space scores and lowered 24-hour pain, while using less rocuronium
cards.people: 84 patients having elective laparoscopic gastrectomy, randomised to saline or magnesium sulfate (50 mg/kg loading over 10 minutes, then 15 mg/kg/hour) while moderate neuromuscular blockade was maintained with rocuronium.
cards.result: Surgical rating scores were higher with magnesium: an optimal score of 5 was achieved in 40.5% of the magnesium group versus 2.7% of controls (P < 0.0001), despite less rocuronium being required (24.2 vs 27.5 mg/hour, P = 0.017). Postoperative pain at the operation site was less severe in the magnesium group at 24 hours (P = 0.009). Recovery profiles and adverse events were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Pain was a secondary outcome in a trial designed around surgical-space conditions and neuromuscular blockade — its pain finding supports, but does not by itself establish, the analgesic claim.
cards.source: Ryu JH et al. Prospective, randomized and controlled trial on magnesium sulfate administration during laparoscopic gastrectomy: effects on surgical space conditions and recovery profiles. BMC anesthesiology. 2016. cards.headline: Synthesis: two meta-analyses a decade apart agree magnesium spares opioid and trims pain scores slightly — with heterogeneity too high to promise a size, and the shivering limb unproven in the carded base
cards.summary: Synthesis: two meta-analyses a decade apart agree magnesium spares opioid and trims pain scores slightly — with heterogeneity too high to promise a size, and the shivering limb unproven in the carded base
cards.people: Two meta-analyses of randomised trials (25 trials; and 22–24 trials with 1,750 participants) and two individual randomised trials (86 and 84 patients).
cards.result: Opioid consumption fell by about 6–8 mg morphine equivalents at 24 hours in both poolings, and pain scores by roughly half a point to one point on a 0–10 scale, with substantial heterogeneity and low-to-moderate certainty. One carded trial found no opioid sparing against a rich multimodal background. On shivering — part of the slate question — none of the carded reports measured it, so no shivering claim is made on this shelf. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) for pain and opioid sparing. This shelf is distinct from the cisplatin-nephroprotection magnesium question taken in an earlier slate — a different question, not duplicated here.
cards.watchOut: Magnesium potentiates neuromuscular blockade (the gastrectomy trial needed less rocuronium) — a dosing/safety interaction for anaesthetists, separate from analgesia.
cards.source: Synthesis of Albrecht E et al. Anaesthesia. 2013; Tomaszek L et al. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2026; Benevides ML et al. Brazilian Journal of Anesthesiology. 2021; Ryu JH et al. BMC Anesthesiology. 2016.

shelves.title: Wound-edge protectors: meta-analyses claim a third fewer infections, the large ROSSINI trial found none
shelves.question: In adults having open or laparoscopic abdominal (and other clean-contaminated) surgery, does a wound-edge protector reduce surgical-site infection versus no protector, and do dual-ring devices outperform single-ring devices?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Aged · Confidence Intervals · Humans · Length of Stay · Middle Aged · Odds Ratio · Plastics · Quality of Life · Single-Blind Method · Surgical Drapes · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control
shelves.balance: This is the natural SPLIT the slate predicted. Three syntheses of mostly small, older trials — all at considerable risk of bias in one review's assessment — pool to relative risk ratios of 0.55–0.65 for surgical-site infection, with dual-ring devices looking better than single-ring in subgroup analyses (0.29–0.31 vs 0.71–0.83), a contrast one synthesis explicitly warns may reflect poorer double-ring data. The ROSSINI trial, the large multicentre randomised trial with blinded outcome assessment, found 24.7% versus 25.4% — the treatment made no difference. Devices are named by design only: the carded records do not give brands. PROPOSED SPLIT.

cards.headline: Pinkney 2013 — ROSSINI (multicentre RCT, 760 patients): wound-edge protection made no difference to surgical-site infection — 24.7% with the device versus 25.4% without (the treatment made no difference)
cards.summary: Pinkney 2013 — ROSSINI (multicentre RCT, 760 patients): wound-edge protection made no difference to surgical-site infection — 24.7% with the device versus 25.4% without (the treatment made no difference)
cards.people: 760 patients undergoing laparotomy at 21 UK hospitals, randomised to standard care or a wound-edge protection device during surgery; surgical-site infection within 30 days was assessed by blinded clinicians and patient self-report. 735 patients were analysed for the primary outcome.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection occurred in 91 of 369 patients (24.7%) in the device group and 93 of 366 (25.4%) in the control group (odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.69 to 1.36; P = 0.85). The lack of benefit was consistent across clinician and patient assessments and all secondary outcomes, including quality of life and hospital stay.
cards.watchOut: The largest and most rigorous trial in this base, and it is null — it outweighs the smaller positive trials in the meta-analyses below. The record does not name the specific device brand used.
cards.source: Pinkney TD et al. Impact of wound edge protection devices on surgical site infection after laparotomy: multicentre randomised controlled trial (ROSSINI Trial). BMJ. 2013. cards.headline: Gheorghe 2012 (systematic review, 12 studies, 1,933 patients): pooled risk ratio 0.60 favoured wound-edge protection — but every included study was at considerable risk of bias
cards.summary: Gheorghe 2012 (systematic review, 12 studies, 1,933 patients): pooled risk ratio 0.60 favoured wound-edge protection — but every included study was at considerable risk of bias
cards.people: Twelve studies reporting primary data (1,933 patients) on wound-edge protection devices versus standard care in open abdominal surgery, reviewed to Cochrane principles.
cards.result: An exploratory meta-analysis gave a pooled risk ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.41 to 0.86) for surgical-site infection — a 40% relative reduction — with no significant heterogeneity or publication bias detected. However, the quality assessment found all included studies at considerable risk of bias, and the authors called for a large, good-quality randomised trial (the call ROSSINI then answered, with a null result).
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative effect from small, biased trials is exactly the pattern that a large rigorous trial often overturns — read this card together with ROSSINI, not instead of it.

cards.headline: Edwards 2012 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 1,008 patients): wound protectors reduced infection in gastrointestinal/biliary surgery (risk ratio 0.55), driven by dual-ring devices (0.31) rather than single-ring (0.83, not significant)
cards.summary: Edwards 2012 (meta-analysis, 6 RCTs, 1,008 patients): wound protectors reduced infection in gastrointestinal/biliary surgery (risk ratio 0.55), driven by dual-ring devices (0.31) rather than single-ring (0.83, not significant)
cards.people: Six randomised trials (1,008 patients) of impervious wound-edge protectors in gastrointestinal and biliary tract surgery.
cards.result: Wound protector use was associated with a significantly lower surgical-site infection rate (risk ratio 0.55, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.98; P = 0.04) — a relative measure; the record does not give a single pooled absolute rate. By device design, dual-ring protectors showed a stronger effect (RR 0.31, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.67; P = 0.003) than single-ring protectors (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.83; P = 0.64, not significant). Publication year significantly influenced the pooled result.
cards.watchOut: Only six small trials, and the dual-ring/single-ring contrast is a between-trial subgroup comparison — device type is confounded with trial era and quality.
cards.source: Edwards JP et al. Wound protectors reduce surgical site infection: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. International journal of surgery. 2012. PMID: 22584694. cards.headline: Mihaljevic 2015 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 16 RCTs, 3,695 patients): protectors reduced infection overall (risk ratio 0.65), with double-ring devices at 0.29 versus single-ring at 0.71 — a subgroup the authors flag may reflect poorer double-ring data quality
cards.summary: Mihaljevic 2015 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 16 RCTs, 3,695 patients): protectors reduced infection overall (risk ratio 0.65), with double-ring devices at 0.29 versus single-ring at 0.71 — a subgroup the authors flag may reflect poorer double-ring data quality
cards.people: 16 randomised trials (3,695 patients, 1972–2014) of wound-edge protectors in patients undergoing laparotomy, with critical appraisal that found methodological flaws, predominantly in the older trials.
cards.result: Wound-edge protectors significantly reduced surgical-site infection (risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.83; p = 0.0007; I² = 52%), with a similar effect in colorectal surgery (RR 0.65). Double-ring devices showed a greater protective effect (RR 0.29, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.55) than single-ring devices (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.54 to 0.92) — but the authors note this might largely be due to the lower quality of the available double-ring data. Effects were larger in contaminated cases (RR 0.44) than clean-contaminated (RR 0.72), and for superficial infections (RR 0.45).
cards.watchOut: This pooling includes the era of trials ROSSINI was designed to supersede; whether ROSSINI's own data are inside the 16 trials matters and the record's trial list is not reproduced here — the split with ROSSINI is therefore presented, not resolved.
cards.source: Mihaljevic AL et al. Wound edge protectors in open abdominal surgery to reduce surgical site infections: a systematic review and meta-analysis. PloS one. 2015. PMID: 25816365. cards.headline: Synthesis: meta-analyses of small trials say protectors cut infections by about a third relative; the one large rigorous trial found 24.7% versus 25.4% — a textbook split
cards.summary: Synthesis: meta-analyses of small trials say protectors cut infections by about a third relative; the one large rigorous trial found 24.7% versus 25.4% — a textbook split
cards.people: One large multicentre RCT (760 patients) and three meta-analyses/systematic reviews (1,008–3,695 patients) dominated by smaller, older trials at considerable risk of bias.
cards.result: The pooled relative effects favour protectors (risk ratios 0.55–0.65 overall; double-ring subgroups 0.29–0.31 versus single-ring 0.71–0.83), while ROSSINI — the largest, blinded-outcome trial — found no difference at all. Whether dual-ring devices genuinely outperform single-ring devices is suggested by two subgroup analyses and undermined by the data-quality caveat in one of them. PROPOSED SPLIT.
cards.watchOut: Tested devices are identified in the carded records only by design (single-ring versus dual-ring impervious protectors), not by brand — no brand claim is made on this shelf.
cards.source: Synthesis of Pinkney TD et al. BMJ. 2013 (ROSSINI); Gheorghe A et al. Annals of Surgery. 2012; Edwards JP et al. International Journal of Surgery. 2012; Mihaljevic AL et al. PLoS One. 2015.

shelves.title: Training the breathing muscles before bypass surgery: pulmonary complications halved in high-risk patients — in one centre's trial programme
shelves.question: In adults at high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications undergoing coronary-artery bypass (or other major cardiac) surgery, does preoperative inspiratory muscle training reduce postoperative pulmonary complications and length of stay versus sham / usual preoperative care?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Breathing Exercises · Coronary Artery Bypass · Cough/etiology,prevention & control · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Male · Pleural Effusion/etiology,prevention & control · Pneumonia/etiology,prevention & control · Pneumothorax/etiology,prevention & control · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Preoperative Care · Respiratory Function Tests · Respiratory Tract Diseases/etiology,prevention & control · Risk Assessment · Single-Blind Method
shelves.balance: One programme dominates this evidence, and it is positive. In the Hulzebos randomised trial (279 high-risk CABG patients), preoperative inspiratory muscle training cut postoperative pulmonary complications from 35.0% to 18.0% (odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.92) and pneumonia from 16.1% to 6.5% (odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84), and shortened median postoperative stay from 8 to 7 days (P = .02). The same programme's pilot (26 patients) found significantly less atelectasis and good feasibility, and its secondary quality-of-life analysis (235 patients) confirmed the pneumonia and stay benefits while finding no quality-of-life improvement. The Cochrane review of preoperative physical therapy for elective cardiac surgery (8 trials, 856 patients) points the same way — atelectasis relative risk 0.52 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.87) and pneumonia relative risk 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.83), both relative measures — but it pools mixed physical-therapy programmes, not inspiratory muscle training alone. This is the preoperative prehabilitation question only: inspiratory muscle training for COPD and for weaning from prolonged ventilation are different questions, homed on their own shelves in this library, and none of their evidence is re-carded here. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit): preoperative inspiratory muscle training probably prevents pulmonary complications in high-risk CABG patients — resting largely on one centre's trial programme.

cards.headline: Hulzebos 2006 (randomised trial, N = 279, high-risk CABG): pulmonary complications 18.0% vs 35.0% (odds ratio 0.52) and pneumonia 6.5% vs 16.1% (odds ratio 0.40) with preoperative inspiratory muscle training
cards.summary: Hulzebos 2006 (randomised trial, N = 279, high-risk CABG): pulmonary complications 18.0% vs 35.0% (odds ratio 0.52) and pneumonia 6.5% vs 16.1% (odds ratio 0.40) with preoperative inspiratory muscle training
cards.people: 279 patients at high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications scheduled for elective coronary artery bypass graft surgery at University Medical Center Utrecht (of 655 referred, 299 met high-risk criteria), randomly assigned single-blind to preoperative inspiratory muscle training (140 patients) or usual care (139 patients); both groups received the same postoperative physical therapy, with follow-up to hospital discharge.
cards.result: Postoperative pulmonary complications occurred in 25 of 139 analysed patients (18.0%) in the training group versus 48 of 137 (35.0%) in the usual-care group (odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.92). Pneumonia occurred in 9 of 139 (6.5%) versus 22 of 137 (16.1%) (odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84). Median duration of postoperative hospitalisation was 7 days (range 5-41) in the training group versus 8 days (range 6-70) in the usual-care group (P = .02). The authors conclude preoperative inspiratory muscle training reduced pulmonary complications and hospital stay in high-risk CABG patients.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, single-blind, and restricted to patients pre-selected as high risk — the absolute gains (17 percentage points fewer complications) belong to that high-risk population and will shrink in unselected CABG patients; usual-care controls received no sham training, so attention effects are not excluded.
cards.source: Hulzebos EH et al. cards.headline: Hulzebos 2006 pilot (randomised pilot, N = 26): training was feasible and well liked, atelectasis was significantly less frequent, and stay was 2 days shorter (not significant)
cards.summary: Hulzebos 2006 pilot (randomised pilot, N = 26): training was feasible and well liked, atelectasis was significantly less frequent, and stay was 2 days shorter (not significant)
cards.people: 26 patients at high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications scheduled for coronary artery bypass graft surgery at the same Utrecht centre, randomly assigned to 2-4 weeks of preoperative inspiratory muscle training plus usual care (14 patients) or usual care alone (12 patients); primary outcomes were feasibility — adverse events, patient satisfaction and motivation — with pulmonary complications and hospital stay as secondary outcomes.
cards.result: Feasibility was good and no adverse events were observed; treatment satisfaction scored 7.9 (± 0.7) and motivation 8.2 (± 1.0) on 10-point scales. Postoperative atelectasis occurred in significantly fewer patients in the intervention group than the control group (P = 0.05). Length of hospital stay was 7.93 (± 1.94) days in the intervention group versus 9.92 (± 5.78) days in the control group (P = 0.24). The authors conclude preoperative training was well tolerated and prevented atelectasis, and that a larger trial was warranted — the trial carded above.

cards.headline: Valkenet 2017 (secondary analysis of the Hulzebos trial, 235 patients): pneumonia and stay benefits confirmed, but quality of life did not improve
cards.summary: Valkenet 2017 (secondary analysis of the Hulzebos trial, 235 patients): pneumonia and stay benefits confirmed, but quality of life did not improve
cards.type: Secondary analysis of a randomised trial (Valkenet 2017)
cards.people: Complementary secondary analysis of the published Hulzebos randomised trial (same registration, ISRCTN17691887), using data from 235 patients awaiting coronary artery bypass graft surgery at the Dutch university hospital who completed at least one quality-of-life questionnaire; the intervention group followed a home-based preoperative inspiratory muscle training programme and quality of life was measured at five time points.
cards.result: In line with the initial trial, pneumonia incidence and length of hospital stay were decreased significantly in the intervention group. Quality of life improved significantly after surgery compared with baseline in all patients, but no significant differences in quality of life were observed over time between the intervention and usual-care groups. The authors conclude the decreases in pneumonia and stay did not act as a mediator of improved quality of life.
cards.watchOut: The same trial programme and substantially the same patients as the main Hulzebos card — it adds the quality-of-life null, it does not add an independent replication; quality-of-life follow-up is limited to patients who returned questionnaires.
cards.source: Valkenet K et al. cards.headline: Hulzebos 2012 (Cochrane review, 8 trials, 856 patients): preoperative physical therapy reduced atelectasis (relative risk 0.52) and pneumonia (relative risk 0.45) in elective cardiac surgery
cards.summary: Hulzebos 2012 (Cochrane review, 8 trials, 856 patients): preoperative physical therapy reduced atelectasis (relative risk 0.52) and pneumonia (relative risk 0.45) in elective cardiac surgery
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised and quasi-randomised trials of preoperative physical therapy with an exercise component versus no or sham therapy in adults undergoing elective cardiac surgery: eight trials with 856 patients, of which five used inspiratory muscle training and three used mixed interventions (aerobic or breathing exercises); only one study used sham training in controls.
cards.result: Patients receiving preoperative physical therapy had a reduced risk of postoperative atelectasis (four studies, 379 participants; relative risk 0.52, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.87; P = 0.01) and pneumonia (five studies, 448 participants; relative risk 0.45, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.83; P = 0.01) — relative measures — but not of pneumothorax or mechanical ventilation over 48 hours, and all-cause postoperative death did not differ (relative risk 0.66, 95% CI 0.02 to 18.48). Postoperative hospital stay was significantly shorter (three studies, 347 participants; mean difference -3.21 days, 95% CI -5.73 to -0.69). No adverse events were detected in the three studies reporting them. The reviewers conclude evidence from small trials suggests preoperative physical therapy reduces pulmonary complications and stay in elective cardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: The review pools inspiratory muscle training with mixed exercise programmes and includes the Hulzebos trial itself, so it corroborates the direction of effect without being independent of the anchor programme; most component trials are small.
cards.source: Hulzebos EH et al. Preoperative physical therapy for elective cardiac surgery patients. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012. PMID: 23152283. cards.headline: Synthesis: one strong trial programme plus a concordant Cochrane review — preoperative inspiratory muscle training halves pulmonary complications in high-risk CABG patients, without improving quality of life
cards.summary: Synthesis: one strong trial programme plus a concordant Cochrane review — preoperative inspiratory muscle training halves pulmonary complications in high-risk CABG patients, without improving quality of life
cards.people: One main randomised trial (279 patients), its pilot (26 patients) and its secondary quality-of-life analysis (235 patients, same programme), plus a Cochrane review of eight preoperative physical-therapy trials (856 patients) that includes the anchor trial.
cards.result: Pulmonary complications 18.0% versus 35.0% (odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.30 to 0.92); pneumonia 6.5% versus 16.1% (odds ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.19 to 0.84); median stay 7 versus 8 days. Cochrane pooled relative risks: atelectasis 0.52 (95% CI 0.32 to 0.87), pneumonia 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.83). Quality of life: no between-group difference. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit).
cards.watchOut: Independent replication outside the Utrecht programme, and extension beyond CABG to other major surgery, remain the open questions; nothing carded here supports low-risk patients, in whom absolute gains would be far smaller.
cards.source: Synthesis of Hulzebos EH et al. JAMA. 2006 (PMID: 17047215); Hulzebos EH et al. Clinical Rehabilitation. 2006 (PMID: 17065538); Valkenet K et al. Physiotherapy. 2017 (PMID: 27569662); Hulzebos EH et al. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2012 (PMID: 23152283).

shelves.title: Showering with chlorhexidine before surgery: the skin gets cleaner, the wound-infection rate does not clearly fall
shelves.question: In adults undergoing elective surgery, does preoperative whole-body bathing/showering with chlorhexidine (wash or impregnated cloths, as tested) at home before admission reduce surgical-site infection versus plain soap / no antiseptic bathing?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Infective Agents, Local/administration & dosage · Baths/methods · Chlorhexidine/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · Disinfection/methods · Female · Humans · Male · Preoperative Care/methods · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Soaps/administration & dosage · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control
shelves.balance: SPLIT, and the split is comparator and era. Against placebo detergent, the largest trial (Lynch/Byrne 1992, 3,482 patients) found wound infection rates essentially identical (inpatient 5.79% versus 5.75%; outpatient 8.54% versus 9.38%) and chlorhexidine not cost-effective, and the Cochrane review (Webster & Osborne 2015; 7 trials, 10,157 participants) pooled chlorhexidine versus placebo to a relative risk of 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04) — no clear benefit — and versus bar soap to 1.02 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.84). Against weaker comparators the older trials look better: Hayek 1987 (1,989 patients) found overall infection of 9.0% on chlorhexidine versus 12.8% on bar soap and 11.7% on placebo, and Wihlborg 1987 (1,530 operations) reported a significant reduction with chlorhexidine showering versus local washing or no washing. Chlorhexidine unquestionably reduces skin bacterial counts (Garibaldi 1988) — the gap between cleaner skin and fewer infections is the story of this literature. The Cochrane verdict is presented here as it stands: equivocal, with no clear evidence of benefit over other wash products. This shelf asks the at-home, whole-population preoperative bathing question only: universal ICU decolonisation and intraoperative skin preparation are different questions, homed on their own shelves in this library (live shelves #587 and #656), and none of their trials is re-carded here. PROPOSED SPLIT: bathing with chlorhexidine before surgery has not been shown to beat placebo or soap in the largest trials, whatever it does to skin flora.

cards.headline: Hayek 1987 (placebo-controlled trial, N = 1,989): wound infection 9.0% with chlorhexidine versus 12.8% with bar soap and 11.7% with placebo
cards.summary: Hayek 1987 (placebo-controlled trial, N = 1,989): wound infection 9.0% with chlorhexidine versus 12.8% with bar soap and 11.7% with placebo
cards.people: 1,989 patients who bathed or showered twice in the 24 hours before operation with chlorhexidine detergent, placebo, or conventional bar soap, in a placebo-controlled trial of preoperative whole-body washing; outcomes were postoperative wound infection rates overall and in clean surgery, including Staphylococcus aureus infection.
cards.result: The overall infection rate was 9.0% with chlorhexidine, against 12.8% in the bar soap group and 11.7% in the placebo group. In the clean surgery group, infection rates were 7.2% (chlorhexidine) against 10.2% (bar soap) and 10.0% (placebo). The Staphylococcus aureus infection rate in the clean group was 3% for chlorhexidine against 6% for bar soap.
cards.watchOut: A 1980s trial from an era of higher baseline infection rates and different perioperative care (no modern antibiotic-prophylaxis standards); its placebo arm is a detergent placebo, and the record reports rates without confidence intervals, so precision cannot be judged from the record.
cards.source: Hayek LJ et al. A placebo-controlled trial of the effect of two preoperative baths or showers with chlorhexidine detergent on postoperative wound infection rates. The Journal of Hospital Infection. 1987. PMID: 2889770. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lynch 1992 (randomised trial, N = 3,482): wound infection essentially identical with chlorhexidine versus placebo detergent (inpatient 5.79% vs 5.75%) — and chlorhexidine cost more
cards.summary: Lynch 1992 (randomised trial, N = 3,482): wound infection essentially identical with chlorhexidine versus placebo detergent (inpatient 5.79% vs 5.75%) — and chlorhexidine cost more
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial with cost-effectiveness analysis (Lynch 1992)
cards.people: 3,482 general surgical patients who showered three times before elective clean or potentially contaminated surgery with a chlorhexidine detergent (1,744 patients) or a placebo detergent (1,738 patients), with wound infections counted both in hospital and after discharge, and a cost-effectiveness analysis.
cards.result: Patients showering with chlorhexidine had a significant reduction in skin flora compared with placebo. Wound infection rates were similar in the two groups: 5.79% versus 5.75% for inpatient infections and 8.54% versus 9.38% for outpatient infections — most infections occurred outside hospital (312 outpatient versus 201 inpatient). Average hospital costs were higher in the chlorhexidine group for both non-infected patients (847.95 pounds versus 804.60 pounds) and infected patients (1,459.70 pounds versus 1,414.22 pounds). A matched vascular-surgery comparison showed no significant difference. The authors conclude preoperative whole-body disinfection with chlorhexidine detergent is not a cost-effective treatment for reducing wound infection.
cards.watchOut: Three preoperative showers is a more intensive regimen than the single home shower many services advise, so this null cannot be dismissed as under-dosing; it is the largest placebo-controlled trial in the Cochrane pool and anchors the null side of the split.
cards.source: Lynch W et al. Cost-effectiveness analysis of the use of chlorhexidine detergent in preoperative whole-body disinfection in wound infection prophylaxis. The Journal of Hospital Infection. 1992. PMID: 1353510. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Wihlborg 1987 (controlled trial, 1,530 operations): overall wound infection 3.4%, significantly reduced in patients who showered with chlorhexidine soap
cards.summary: Wihlborg 1987 (controlled trial, 1,530 operations): overall wound infection 3.4%, significantly reduced in patients who showered with chlorhexidine soap
cards.people: 1,530 operations for biliary tract disease, inguinal hernia and breast cancer in a controlled clinical study comparing preoperative whole-body disinfection with chlorhexidine soap against local washing and no washing at all, with postoperative wound infection in clean surgery as the outcome.
cards.result: The overall infection rate was 3.4%. Among patients who had a preoperative shower with chlorhexidine, the wound infection rate was significantly reduced compared with the local-washing and no-washing comparators, as reported by the author. The record does not print the arm-specific infection rates, so the size of the reduction cannot be stated from the record this session (arm rates: N not documented in the record).
cards.watchOut: The comparators here are local washing or no washing — the weakest comparators in this literature — and without arm-specific rates in the record the claim of significance cannot be weighed; this card is the positive pole of the split, not its centre of gravity.
cards.source: Wihlborg O et al. The effect of washing with chlorhexidine soap on wound infection rate in general surgery. A controlled clinical study. Annales Chirurgiae et Gynaecologiae. 1987. cards.headline: Webster & Osborne 2015 (Cochrane review, 7 trials, 10,157 participants): no clear evidence of benefit — relative risk 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04) versus placebo, 1.02 versus bar soap
cards.summary: Webster & Osborne 2015 (Cochrane review, 7 trials, 10,157 participants): no clear evidence of benefit — relative risk 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04) versus placebo, 1.02 versus bar soap
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review (fifth update) of randomised controlled trials comparing antiseptic full-body preoperative bathing or showering with non-antiseptic preparations in people undergoing surgery: seven trials with 10,157 participants; the antiseptic in all trials was 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (Hibiscrub/Riohex, as published). Three trials (7,791 participants) compared chlorhexidine with placebo, three (1,443) compared bar soap with chlorhexidine, and three (1,192) compared chlorhexidine bathing with no washing.
cards.result: Bathing with chlorhexidine compared with placebo did not significantly reduce surgical site infection (relative risk 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.04); restricting to high-quality trials gave a relative risk of 0.95 (95% CI 0.82 to 1.10). Against bar soap there was no difference (relative risk 1.02, 95% CI 0.57 to 1.84). Against no washing, one large study found a significant difference favouring chlorhexidine (relative risk 0.36, 95% CI 0.17 to 0.79) while the smaller studies found no difference. The reviewers conclude the review provides no clear evidence of benefit for preoperative showering or bathing with chlorhexidine over other wash products to reduce surgical site infection. All pooled figures are relative risks, printed with their confidence intervals.
cards.watchOut: The review is the governing synthesis for this shelf and its verdict is equivocal by design: the placebo-controlled pool is dominated by the large null trial carded here, while the favourable no-washing comparison rests on one large study — newer chlorhexidine-impregnated cloth studies are mostly observational and do not overturn it.
cards.source: Webster J et al. Preoperative bathing or showering with skin antiseptics to prevent surgical site infection. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2015. PMID: 25927093. the antiseptic in all trials was 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (hibiscrub/riohex, as published). three trials (7,791 participants) compared chlorhexidine with placebo, three (1,443) compared bar soap with chlorhexidine, and three (1,192) compared chlorhexidine bathing with no washing. bathing with chlorhexidine compared with placebo did not significantly reduce surgical site infection (relative risk 0.91, 95% ci 0.80 to 1.04); restricting to high-quality trials gave a relative risk of 0.95 (95% ci 0.82 to 1.10). against bar soap there was no difference (relative risk 1.02, 95% ci 0.57 to 1.84). against no washing, one large study found a significant difference favouring chlorhexidine (relative risk 0.36, 95% ci 0.17 to 0.79) while the smaller studies found no difference. the reviewers conclude the review provides no clear evidence of benefit for preoperative showering or bathing with chlorhexidine over other wash products to reduce surgical site infection. all pooled figures are relative risks, printed with their confidence intervals. the review is the governing synthesis for this shelf and its verdict is equivocal by design: the placebo-controlled pool is dominated by the large null trial carded here, while the favourable no-washing comparison rests on one large study — newer chlorhexidine-impregnated cloth studies are mostly observational and do not overturn it. webster j et al. preoperative bathing or showering with skin antiseptics to prevent surgical site infection. the cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. pmid: 25927093. registry id: none in the record. mesh: anti-infective agents, local/administration & dosage · baths/methods · chlorhexidine/administration & dosage,analogs & derivatives · disinfection/methods · female · humans · male · preoperative care/methods · randomized controlled trials as topic · soaps/administration & dosage · surgical wound infection/prevention & control

cards.headline: Synthesis: chlorhexidine bathing cleans the skin but has not been shown to prevent wound infection better than placebo or soap in the largest trials — benefit appears only against not washing
cards.summary: Synthesis: chlorhexidine bathing cleans the skin but has not been shown to prevent wound infection better than placebo or soap in the largest trials — benefit appears only against not washing
cards.people: Three primary trials and reports carded here (1,989; 3,482 and 1,530 patients/operations) plus the Cochrane review of seven trials (10,157 participants) that pools them with the rest of the randomised base.
cards.result: Versus placebo: pooled relative risk 0.91 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.04), and 5.79% versus 5.75% inpatient infection in the largest trial. Versus bar soap: pooled relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.57 to 1.84), against 9.0% versus 12.8% in the oldest placebo-controlled trial. Versus no washing: one large study at relative risk 0.36 (95% CI 0.17 to 0.79). Skin colonisation and intraoperative wound contamination are consistently lower with chlorhexidine, without a corresponding proven infection benefit. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the comparator split.
cards.watchOut: Almost all primary trials predate modern prophylaxis, screening and decolonisation practice; whether chlorhexidine cloths (a different, leave-on exposure) prevent infection is a thinner, largely observational literature and is not settled by this shelf.
