shelves.title: TAR versus anterior component separation for large incisional hernias: less wound trouble in the cohort evidence, no proven recurrence gain — and almost no randomised data
shelves.question: In adults with complex/large incisional hernias, does posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (TAR) reduce recurrence and wound morbidity versus anterior component separation (with or without mesh), and how do open and robotic TAR compare?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Abdominal Muscles/surgery · Incisional Hernia/etiology,surgery · Hernia, Ventral/surgery,complications · Surgical Wound Infection/etiology,complications · Seroma/epidemiology,etiology · Herniorrhaphy/adverse effects,methods · Hematoma · Surgical Mesh/adverse effects · Recurrence
shelves.balance: Evidence-question (GAP-E) framing: this comparison rests overwhelmingly on cohort studies pooled in systematic reviews, not on randomised trials — one small randomised study (43 patients) verified at build is the exception, and it is carded and labelled as such. The cohort syntheses agree that posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (TAR) carries less wound morbidity than anterior component separation: overall wound complications odds ratio 2.58 favouring TAR (Mohamedahmed 2025; 8 studies, 2,293 patients), surgical site infection odds ratio 1.32, seroma odds ratio 1.93 and haematoma odds ratio 1.81 in the earlier synthesis (Oprea 2023; 19 studies, 3,412 patients) — odds ratios comparing anterior with posterior separation, printed as relative measures. Recurrence does not clearly favour TAR: 4.27% after anterior separation versus 6.11% after posterior separation in Oprea 2023, and no significant recurrence difference in Mohamedahmed 2025. Open TAR alone, pooled across 22 cohort studies (4,910 patients), shows 6% recurrence but 34% overall morbidity. The small randomised study (Demetrashvili 2025) found surgical site occurrences in 19% on TAR versus 50% on anterior separation (P = 0.033), with no significant differences in infection, recurrence or quality of life. Hybrid robotic TAR versus open TAR (propensity-matched cohorts) shortened stay (3 versus 5 days) with fewer surgical site occurrences (5% versus 15%). Pooled cohort rates must not be read as randomised effects. PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled: TAR probably reduces wound morbidity compared with anterior separation, with no proven recurrence advantage.

cards.headline: Oprea 2023 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 19 studies, 3,412 patients — cohort base): anterior separation carried more wound morbidity; recurrence was 4.27% (anterior) vs 6.11% (posterior)
cards.summary: Oprea 2023 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 19 studies, 3,412 patients — cohort base): anterior separation carried more wound morbidity; recurrence was 4.27% (anterior) vs 6.11% (posterior)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (Oprea 2023)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies reporting outcomes of anterior component separation (ACS; 1,709 patients) versus posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (PCSTAR; 1,703 patients) for complex incisional hernias, published before December 2021, with hernia recurrence after a minimum 1-year follow-up as a principal outcome. The included studies are comparative cohorts, not randomised trials.
cards.result: Pooled hernia recurrence was 5.15% overall (odds ratio 0.68, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9; P = 0.0175), with recurrence rates of 4.27% after ACS versus 6.11% after PCSTAR as printed in the record. Pooled surgical site infection was 10.6% (odds ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.65; P = 0.0119), seroma 9.75% (odds ratio 1.93, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.44; P = 0.0001) and haematoma 3.83% (odds ratio 1.81, 95% CI 1.26 to 2.61; P = 0.0012), with ACS associated with increased wound morbidity, seroma and haematoma. The authors conclude PCSTAR was superior for wound morbidity, surgical site infection, seroma and haematoma, and that the procedure should be further evaluated in head-to-head randomised trials. All comparative figures are odds ratios (relative measures) pooled from cohort studies.
cards.watchOut: Cohort pooling: technique choice is confounded by defect size, contamination, surgeon preference and era, and mesh types and positions differ between the pooled series — the wound-morbidity gradient is consistent, but its size cannot be read as the causal effect of the technique.
cards.source: Oprea V et al. Hernia. 2023. PMID: 36729336. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mohamedahmed 2025 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 8 studies, 2,293 patients): wound complications odds ratio 2.58 and infection odds ratio 1.72 favouring posterior separation; recurrence, operating time and stay did not differ
cards.summary: Mohamedahmed 2025 (systematic review/meta-analysis, 8 studies, 2,293 patients): wound complications odds ratio 2.58 and infection odds ratio 1.72 favouring posterior separation; recurrence, operating time and stay did not differ
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, predominantly observational (Mohamedahmed 2025)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies published 1990 to June 2025 comparing anterior component separation (ACS; 1,573 patients) with posterior component separation with transversus abdominis release (PCSTAR; 720 patients) for large incisional hernias: eight studies comprising three randomised controlled trials and five observational studies by the review's own classification, with risk of bias assessed by Cochrane and MINORS tools.
cards.result: The PCSTAR group had a lower rate of overall wound complications (odds ratio 2.58, P = 0.004, comparing ACS with PCSTAR) and surgical site infections (odds ratio 1.72, P = 0.05). No significant differences were observed for haematoma (odds ratio 0.87, P = 0.51), seroma (odds ratio 1.77, P = 0.11), recurrence (odds ratio 1.81, P = 0.31), operative time (mean difference -6.57, P = 0.77) or length of stay (mean difference -0.67, P = 0.16). Randomised studies showed low risk of bias in most domains and non-randomised studies moderate quality, per the review. The authors conclude both techniques are comparable overall, PCSTAR seems associated with fewer wound complications and infections, and further adequately powered randomised trials are required. Figures are odds ratios (relative measures).
cards.watchOut: Only eight studies and three small randomised trials by the review's classification — the randomised reports inside this pool could not be individually verified from the review record this session, so this shelf does not present the pool as randomised evidence; the one randomised study carded separately here is Demetrashvili 2025.

cards.headline: Demetrashvili 2025 (randomised controlled study, N = 43 — the one randomised report verified at build): surgical site occurrences 19% with TAR vs 50% with anterior separation (P = 0.033); no difference in recurrence or quality of life
cards.summary: Demetrashvili 2025 (randomised controlled study, N = 43 — the one randomised report verified at build): surgical site occurrences 19% with TAR vs 50% with anterior separation (P = 0.033); no difference in recurrence or quality of life
cards.people: 43 adults undergoing elective open component separation for midline large ventral hernia between December 2016 and July 2022, analysed in an anterior component separation group (22 patients) and a transversus abdominis release group (21 patients) in a study published as a randomised controlled study; outcomes included hospital stay, surgical site occurrences (SSO), recurrence and quality of life by the Carolinas Comfort Scale.
cards.result: Surgical site occurrences were significantly less frequent in the TAR group (4 of 21; 19%) than in the anterior separation group (11 of 22; 50%) (odds ratio 1.87, 95% CI 1.07 to 3.24, as printed in the record; P = 0.033). Seroma was the most frequent occurrence, ranging from 9.5% (TAR) to 40.9% (anterior) (P = 0.018). There was no significant difference between groups in surgical site infection, haematoma, wound dehiscence, skin necrosis, hernia recurrence or quality of life. The authors conclude TAR was associated with significantly fewer surgical site occurrences, with comparable recurrence and quality of life.
cards.watchOut: 43 patients at one centre over five and a half years — a randomised label on a very small base; a handful of events moving arms would erase the significance, and recurrence follow-up in a study this size cannot settle durability.

cards.headline: Sadava 2024 (systematic review of open TAR alone, 22 studies, 4,910 patients — cohorts): pooled recurrence 6%, overall morbidity 34%, infection 11%, mortality 1%
cards.summary: Sadava 2024 (systematic review of open TAR alone, 22 studies, 4,910 patients — cohorts): pooled recurrence 6%, overall morbidity 34%, infection 11%, mortality 1%
cards.type: Systematic review and proportional meta-analysis of cohort studies (Sadava 2024)
cards.people: Systematic review and proportional meta-analysis of open transversus abdominis release (open TAR) for incisional hernia repair: 22 studies with 4,910 patients; mean hernia defect 394 cm² (range 140-622) and mean mesh area 1,065 cm² (range 557-2,206); mean follow-up 19.7 months (range 1-32).
cards.result: Weighted pooled proportions were: recurrence 6% (95% CI 3 to 10%), overall morbidity 34% (95% CI 26 to 43%), surgical site occurrences 22% (95% CI 16 to 29%), surgical site infection 11% (95% CI 8 to 16%), surgical site occurrences requiring procedural intervention 4% (95% CI 3 to 7%), major morbidity 6% (95% CI 4 to 10%) and mortality 1% (95% CI 1 to 2%). A significant improvement in quality of life after open TAR was reported among the included studies. The authors conclude open TAR is effective for complex ventral hernias with a low recurrence rate and improved quality of life, while emphasising that the relatively high morbidity requires better patient selection and optimisation.
cards.watchOut: Single-arm pooling with no comparator: these are the outcomes of patients selected for open TAR (large defects, mean 394 cm²), useful as benchmarks for consent, not as evidence that TAR beats any alternative.

cards.headline: Abdu 2021 (propensity-matched cohort, 95 hybrid robotic vs 285 open TAR): stay 3 vs 5 days (P < 0.001) and surgical site occurrences 5% vs 15% (P = 0.015) with the hybrid robotic approach
cards.summary: Abdu 2021 (propensity-matched cohort, 95 hybrid robotic vs 285 open TAR): stay 3 vs 5 days (P < 0.001) and surgical site occurrences 5% vs 15% (P = 0.015) with the hybrid robotic approach
cards.people: Patients undergoing transversus abdominis release recorded in the AHSQC database: 95 patients receiving hybrid robotic TAR propensity-matched with a contemporary cohort of 285 patients receiving open TAR; outcomes were hospital length of stay and 30-day outcomes.
cards.result: Median length of stay was significantly shorter in the hybrid robotic cohort (3 versus 5 days, P < 0.001). Surgical site occurrences were also lower with hybrid robotic TAR (5% versus 15%, P = 0.015). Readmission rates did not differ (6% versus 8%, P = 0.65). The authors conclude hybrid robotic TAR shows improved length of stay and fewer surgical-site occurrences than open TAR, and that further studies are needed on the reasons for the shorter stay and on long-term outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Registry cohorts with propensity matching cannot remove selection by defect complexity or surgeon, 30 days is too short for recurrence, and 'hybrid robotic' is not the fully robotic technique — long-term and cost comparisons are outside this record.
cards.source: Abdu R et al. Hybrid robotic transversus abdominis release versus open: propensity-matched analysis of 30-day outcomes. Hernia. 2021. PMID: 32607651. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: cohort evidence consistently favours TAR over anterior separation for wound morbidity, not for recurrence — with a single small randomised study pointing the same way
cards.summary: Synthesis: cohort evidence consistently favours TAR over anterior separation for wound morbidity, not for recurrence — with a single small randomised study pointing the same way
cards.people: Two comparative syntheses (3,412 and 2,293 patients, predominantly cohorts), one small randomised study (43 patients), one single-arm TAR synthesis (4,910 patients) and one propensity-matched robotic-versus-open cohort (380 patients). No large randomised trial of TAR versus anterior separation is carded.
cards.result: Wound complications: odds ratio 2.58 favouring posterior separation (Mohamedahmed 2025); infection odds ratio 1.32, seroma 1.93, haematoma 1.81 (Oprea 2023) — relative measures from cohorts. Randomised: surgical site occurrences 19% versus 50% (Demetrashvili 2025, N = 43). Recurrence: 4.27% anterior versus 6.11% posterior (Oprea 2023); no significant difference (Mohamedahmed 2025). Open TAR benchmarks: recurrence 6%, morbidity 34% (Sadava 2024). PROPOSED POSSIBLE (benefit) — observational evidence, labelled.
cards.watchOut: Until an adequately powered randomised trial reports, technique selection remains confounded in every pooled number on this shelf; contaminated fields, loss of domain and emergency repair are barely represented in the carded base.

shelves.title: Biological mesh after extralevator APR (BIOPEX): no better wound healing — but far fewer perineal hernias at five years, in the only trial there is
shelves.question: In patients undergoing extralevator abdominoperineal resection for rectal cancer, does biological mesh closure of the pelvic floor reduce perineal wound complications and later perineal hernia versus primary perineal wound closure?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Acellular Dermis · Aged · Animals · Female · Hernia/prevention & control · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Pelvic Floor/surgery · Perineum/physiology,surgery · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Prospective Studies · Quality of Life · Radiotherapy, Adjuvant · Rectal Neoplasms/radiotherapy,surgery · Single-Blind Method · Surgical Mesh · Surgical Wound Infection/prevention & control · Swine · Wound Healing
shelves.balance: Single-programme flag, stated plainly: every card on this shelf is one trial — BIOPEX, a Dutch multicentre randomised trial of 104 patients — reported at three horizons (the protocol paper, the primary results and the 5-year results). The reports are not three independent trials. On its primary endpoint the trial was negative: uncomplicated perineal wound healing at 30 days was 66% (33 of 50) after primary closure versus 63% (30 of 48) after biological mesh closure (relative risk 1.056, 95% CI 0.7854 to 1.4197; P = 0.7177) — the mesh made no difference to wound healing (the treatment made no difference). The hernia signal is the interesting half: freedom from perineal hernia at 1 year was 73% after primary closure versus 87% after mesh closure (P = 0.0316), and at 5 years the actuarial symptomatic perineal hernia rate was 7% (95% CI 0 to 30) after mesh versus 30% (95% CI 10 to 49) after primary closure (P = 0.006), with hernia repair in 2% versus 13% (P = 0.062). Quality of life, functional outcomes, recurrence and survival did not differ at 5 years. The mesh tested was a non-cross-linked porcine acellular dermal mesh; the trial record does not give a brand name, so none is claimed here. PROPOSED SPLIT: no wound-healing benefit, a real-looking late hernia benefit — from a single trial programme of 104 patients, which caps confidence.

cards.headline: Musters 2014 (BIOPEX protocol paper — design only, no results): a multicentre randomised trial of biological mesh versus primary closure after extralevator APR, planned N = 104
cards.summary: Musters 2014 (BIOPEX protocol paper — design only, no results): a multicentre randomised trial of biological mesh versus primary closure after extralevator APR, planned N = 104
cards.people: Study protocol for the BIOPEX multicentre randomised controlled trial: patients with primary rectal cancer scheduled for extralevator abdominoperineal resection after neoadjuvant (chemo)radiotherapy, randomised between primary perineal wound closure and pelvic floor reconstruction with a biological mesh derived from porcine dermis, followed for 1 year with patients and outcome assessors blinded to treatment. This card documents the programme's design and registration; it reports no outcome data.
cards.result: The primary endpoint is the percentage of uncomplicated perineal wound healing, defined as a Southampton wound score of less than II on day 30. Secondary endpoints are hospital stay, incidence of perineal hernia, quality of life and costs. Planned sample size was 104 patients. The authors describe BIOPEX as the first randomised multicentre study of biological mesh for perineal closure after extralevator resection with neoadjuvant radiotherapy.
cards.watchOut: A protocol paper carded for programme provenance only — it must never be counted as outcome evidence; the shelf's outcome evidence is the two results reports that follow.

cards.headline: Musters 2017 (BIOPEX primary results, N = 104): uncomplicated wound healing 66% primary closure vs 63% mesh (P = 0.72) — no difference — but 1-year freedom from perineal hernia 73% vs 87% (P = 0.0316)
cards.summary: Musters 2017 (BIOPEX primary results, N = 104): uncomplicated wound healing 66% primary closure vs 63% mesh (P = 0.72) — no difference — but 1-year freedom from perineal hernia 73% vs 87% (P = 0.0316)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, primary report (BIOPEX, Musters 2017)
cards.people: 104 patients undergoing extralevator abdominoperineal resection with preoperative radiotherapy for rectal cancer, randomly assigned to primary perineal closure (54 patients) or biological mesh closure of the pelvic floor (50 patients) with a non-cross-linked porcine acellular dermal mesh (brand name not given in the record) sutured to the pelvic floor remnants, followed by the same layered perineal closure in both arms; the randomisation outcome was concealed from patients and the perineal wound assessor, with follow-up for 1 year.
cards.result: Uncomplicated perineal wound healing at 30 days (Southampton wound score less than 2) was 66% (33 of 50; 3 not evaluable) after primary closure and 63% (30 of 48) after biological mesh closure (relative risk 1.056, 95% CI 0.7854 to 1.4197; P = 0.7177) — no significant difference. Freedom from perineal hernia at 1 year was 73% (95% CI 60.93 to 85.07) after primary closure versus 87% (95% CI 77.49 to 96.51) after mesh closure (P = 0.0316). The authors conclude perineal wound healing was not improved by biological mesh, and that the significantly lower 1-year perineal hernia rate is a promising secondary finding needing longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: The hernia finding is a secondary endpoint in a trial that was negative on its primary endpoint, with wide confidence intervals around the 1-year freedom-from-hernia estimates — hypothesis-strengthening, not proof; all patients had preoperative radiotherapy, so results may not transfer to non-irradiated resections.
cards.source: Musters GD et al. Biological Mesh Closure of the Pelvic Floor After Extralevator Abdominoperineal Resection for Rectal Cancer: A Multicenter Randomized Controlled Trial (the BIOPEX-study). Annals of Surgery. 2017. PMID: 27768621. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Blok 2022 (BIOPEX 5-year results, same 104 patients): symptomatic perineal hernia 7% after mesh vs 30% after primary closure (P = 0.006); no differences in wound problems, quality of life or survival
cards.summary: Blok 2022 (BIOPEX 5-year results, same 104 patients): symptomatic perineal hernia 7% after mesh vs 30% after primary closure (P = 0.006); no differences in wound problems, quality of life or survival
cards.type: Long-term (5-year) follow-up report of a randomised trial (BIOPEX, Blok 2022)
cards.people: Post-hoc secondary analysis of the BIOPEX randomised trial population — biological mesh closure (50 patients; 2 dropouts) versus primary perineal closure (54 patients; 1 dropout) after extralevator abdominoperineal resection and preoperative radiotherapy for rectal cancer — followed for 5 years, with symptomatic perineal hernia as the primary focus and actuarial probabilities by Kaplan-Meier.
cards.result: Actuarial 5-year symptomatic perineal hernia rates were 7% (95% CI 0 to 30) after biological mesh closure versus 30% (95% CI 10 to 49) after primary closure (P = 0.006). One patient (2%) in the mesh group underwent elective perineal hernia repair, compared with 7 patients (13%) in the primary closure group (P = 0.062). Reoperations for small bowel obstruction were necessary in 1 of 48 patients (2%) versus 5 of 53 (9%) (P = 0.208). No significant differences were found for chronic perineal wound problems, locoregional recurrence, overall survival, or the main domains of quality of life and functional outcome. The authors conclude the symptomatic perineal hernia rate at 5 years was significantly lower after biological mesh closure, without quality-of-life or functional benefit.
cards.watchOut: A post-hoc secondary analysis of the same 104 patients — the 5-year hernia percentages rest on small event counts (the mesh arm's confidence interval runs from 0% to 30%), and deaths and recurrences over 5 years in a rectal-cancer population shrink the at-risk denominator.
cards.source: Blok RD et al. Cumulative 5-year Results of a Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Biological Mesh With Primary Perineal Wound Closure After Extralevator Abdominoperineal Resection (BIOPEX-study). Annals of Surgery. 2022. PMID: 33534231. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — biological mesh did not improve perineal wound healing, but symptomatic perineal hernia at 5 years was 7% versus 30%
cards.summary: Synthesis: one trial, three reports — biological mesh did not improve perineal wound healing, but symptomatic perineal hernia at 5 years was 7% versus 30%
cards.people: A single randomised trial programme (BIOPEX, 104 patients) documented by its protocol paper (2014), its primary results report (2017) and its 5-year follow-up report (2022). Total evidence base: 104 randomised patients — printed in the stamp, per the single-programme flag.
cards.result: Primary endpoint (30-day uncomplicated wound healing): 66% primary closure versus 63% mesh (relative risk 1.056, 95% CI 0.7854 to 1.4197; P = 0.7177) — the treatment made no difference. Perineal hernia: freedom from hernia at 1 year 73% versus 87% (P = 0.0316); symptomatic hernia at 5 years 7% versus 30% (P = 0.006); hernia repair 2% versus 13% (P = 0.062). No differences in chronic wound problems, quality of life, function, recurrence or survival. PROPOSED SPLIT, naming the wound-versus-hernia split.
cards.watchOut: There is no second trial: a confirmatory randomised trial (or the flap-closure trial this group designed next) could move either half of this split, and cost-effectiveness of an expensive biological mesh for a hernia benefit alone is not addressed by any carded report.
cards.source: Synthesis of Musters GD et al. BMC Surgery. 2014 (PMID: 25163547); Musters GD et al. Annals of Surgery. 2017 (PMID: 27768621); Blok RD et al. Annals of Surgery. 2022 (PMID: 33534231).

shelves.title: Robotic versus laparoscopic hernia repair
shelves.question: In adults undergoing minimally invasive inguinal or ventral hernia repair, does robotic repair improve pain, recovery, recurrence or complications versus laparoscopic repair, and at what cost in operating time and resource use?
shelves.mesh: Hernia, Inguinal/surgery · Hernia, Ventral/surgery · Herniorrhaphy/methods · Laparoscopy · Robotic Surgical Procedures · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the two limbs answer differently over time. Inguinal: the RIVAL randomised programme (102 patients, follow-on to 2 years) found no difference in pain, quality of life, wound events or recurrence (1 recurrence per arm at 2 years), while robotic repair took a median 75.5 versus 40.5 minutes and cost a median $3258 versus $1421. Ventral: the Houston blinded randomised trial (124 patients) found no difference in its primary outcome — days in hospital within 90 days (relative rate 0.90, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.19) — or in early complications, again with longer operating time (141 vs 77 minutes) and higher cost (adjusted difference $2767); its 2-year follow-on reported recurrence 4% robotic versus 13% laparoscopic (relative risk 0.3, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.39; not significant) and reoperation 0% versus 11% (P=0.019), which the authors themselves label hypothesis-generating. So: early outcomes and costs consistently favour laparoscopy or neutrality; a possible late durability advantage for robotic ventral repair is unconfirmed. A robotic-versus-open protocol exists with no results yet, so the open comparison is unanswered.

cards.headline: RIVAL 2020 (inguinal): robotic repair gave no pain, quality-of-life or wound advantage over laparoscopic repair, at longer operating time and higher cost
cards.summary: RIVAL 2020 (inguinal): robotic repair gave no pain, quality-of-life or wound advantage over laparoscopic repair, at longer operating time and higher cost
cards.type: Multicentre, single-blinded, randomised pilot trial (inguinal hernia)
cards.people: 102 patients analysed (of 113 enrolled) with unilateral primary or recurrent inguinal hernia at 6 academic sites: laparoscopic transabdominal preperitoneal repair 54 (mean age 57.2 years, 88.9% male) versus robotic transabdominal preperitoneal repair 48 (mean age 56.1 years, 91.6% male); 30-day follow-up.
cards.result: No differences at preoperative, 1-week or 30-day points in wound events, readmissions, pain (visual analogue scale) or quality of life (SF-36). Robotic repair took longer (median operative time 75.5 vs 40.5 minutes; P<.001), cost more (median $3258 vs $1421; P<.001) and gave surgeons higher frustration scores (NASA Task Load Index 32.7 vs 20.1; P=.004), with no ergonomic advantage.
cards.watchOut: A pilot trial with no single primary outcome and only 30 days of follow-up — it can rule in 'no early benefit', not settle recurrence; several hernia trials in this field are device-maker-supported, and the record does not state the funder on its face.
cards.source: Prabhu AS et al. Robotic Inguinal vs Transabdominal Laparoscopic Inguinal Hernia Repair: The RIVAL Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Surg. 2020. PMID: 32186683. Registry ID: ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT02816658 , from the record's databank fields. cards.headline: RIVAL 1–2-year follow-up: pain, quality of life and recurrence remained the same after robotic and laparoscopic inguinal repair (1 recurrence in each arm at 2 years)
cards.summary: RIVAL 1–2-year follow-up: pain, quality of life and recurrence remained the same after robotic and laparoscopic inguinal repair (1 recurrence in each arm at 2 years)
cards.type: Randomised trial long-term follow-up report (inguinal hernia) — same programme as the RIVAL primary report, not an independent trial
cards.people: Of the 102 RIVAL patients, 83 (81%) completed 1-year follow-up (45 laparoscopic, 38 robotic) and 77 (75%) completed 2-year follow-up (43 laparoscopic, 34 robotic).
cards.result: At 1 and 2 years pain was similar in both groups, no patient in either arm had neuropathic pain, health-related quality of life and physical activity were similar, and no long-term wound morbidity occurred. At 2 years hernia recurrence was 1 laparoscopic versus 1 robotic (P=1.0).
cards.watchOut: A quarter of patients were lost by 2 years and recurrence counts of one per arm cannot distinguish the approaches; this is a follow-on report of the same trial, not a second trial.
cards.source: Miller BT et al. Laparoscopic versus robotic inguinal hernia repair: 1- and 2-year outcomes from the RIVAL trial. Surg Endosc. 2023. PMID: 35578051. cards.headline: Olavarria 2020 (ventral): robotic repair did not reduce days in hospital within 90 days versus laparoscopic repair, and cost more with longer operating time
cards.summary: Olavarria 2020 (ventral): robotic repair did not reduce days in hospital within 90 days versus laparoscopic repair, and cost more with longer operating time
cards.type: Pragmatic, multicentre, blinded randomised trial (ventral hernia)
cards.people: 124 patients deemed appropriate candidates for elective minimally invasive ventral hernia repair at Houston hernia clinics, randomised to robotic repair (65) or laparoscopic repair (59); 90-day follow-up completed in 123 (99%).
cards.result: No difference in the primary outcome, days in hospital within 90 days (median 0 vs 0 days; relative rate 0.90, 95% CI 0.37 to 2.19; P=0.82), nor in emergency visits, wound complications, recurrence or reoperation. Robotic repair took longer (141 vs 77 minutes; mean difference 62.89 minutes, 95% CI 45.75 to 80.01) and cost more ($15,865 vs $12,955; adjusted absolute difference $2767, 95% CI $910 to $4626; P=0.004). Two enterotomies occurred with robotic repair versus none with laparoscopic repair, and median 1-month abdominal-wall quality-of-life improvement was 3 points robotic versus 15 laparoscopic.
cards.watchOut: A single-region pragmatic trial of intraperitoneal onlay mesh repair; the quality-of-life gap at 1 month and the two enterotomies are secondary signals in a 124-patient trial, not settled harms.

cards.type: Randomised trial 2-year follow-up report (ventral hernia) — same programme as the Olavarria primary report, not an independent trial
cards.people: Of 124 randomised patients, 101 completed 2-year follow-up (54 of 65 robotic, 83%; 47 of 59 laparoscopic, 80%).
cards.result: No differences in surgical-site infection or surgical-site occurrence. Hernia recurrence occurred in 2 patients (4%) after robotic repair versus 6 (13%) after laparoscopic repair (relative risk 0.3, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.39; P=0.12 — not significant). cards.headline: Synthesis: no early benefit in either limb; the only pro-robotic signal is a late, fragile one in a single ventral trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: no early benefit in either limb; the only pro-robotic signal is a late, fragile one in a single ventral trial
cards.people: Two randomised programmes: RIVAL (102 patients, inguinal, with 1–2-year follow-on) and the Houston ventral trial (124 patients, with 2-year follow-on). A robotic-versus-open ventral protocol (the Robovent trial) has been published as a protocol with no results in its record, so it contributes no evidence here.
cards.result: Inguinal limb: no difference in pain, quality of life, wound events or 2-year recurrence, with robotic repair slower and more expensive. Ventral limb: no difference in the primary outcome (hospital days within 90 days) or in early complications, again slower and more expensive; at 2 years recurrence and reoperation numerically favoured robotic repair without a significant recurrence difference. Across both limbs the consistent, replicated findings are longer operating time and higher cost for the robot.
cards.watchOut: Do not read the 2-year ventral signal as established benefit: it comes from one trial, few events and incomplete follow-up. Equally, these trials enrolled straightforward elective cases operated on by experienced minimally invasive surgeons — they do not answer complex or large hernias.
cards.source: Synthesis of the cards above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Preoperative hair removal: razor shaving raises surgical-site infection risk versus clipping (relative risk 1.64) and versus no removal (1.82); clip on the day of surgery instead
shelves.question: In adults undergoing elective surgery, does preoperative hair removal method matter for surgical-site infection — clipping or depilatory cream versus shaving with a razor, and any removal versus no removal — and does timing (day before vs day of surgery) change the risk?
shelves.mesh: Hair Removal · Humans · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: LIKELY. The randomised record — three primary trials carded here (1,013, 253 and 200 patients) inside a Cochrane review of 25 trials and 8,919 participants — says the razor is the harmful method: shaving probably increases surgical-site infection versus clipping (relative risk 1.64, a relative measure; 7 studies, 3,723 participants) and versus no removal at all (relative risk 1.82; about 17 more infections per 1,000 patients in absolute terms), and razors also caused more skin injury (relative risk 1.74). Clipping versus no removal showed little difference (relative risk 0.95), and depilatory cream was statistically indistinguishable from shaving in its 253-patient head-to-head trial and from no removal in the review. Timing mattered in the largest primary trial: clipping on the morning of surgery had the fewest infections. The classic trials predate modern surgical-site infection surveillance definitions — stated here as the row directs — so their absolute rates, not their direction, are the dated part.

cards.headline: Alexander 1983 RCT (n=1,013): morning-of-surgery clipping had significantly fewer wound infections than shaving (night before or morning); the authors calculated shaving should be abandoned
cards.summary: Alexander 1983 RCT (n=1,013): morning-of-surgery clipping had significantly fewer wound infections than shaving (night before or morning); the authors calculated shaving should be abandoned
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial, shaving vs clipping, night before vs morning of surgery
cards.people: 1,013 patients undergoing elective operations at a single hospital, prospectively randomised to razor shaving or electric clipping, performed either the night before or the morning of operation.
cards.result: The morning clipping method was associated with significantly fewer wound infections than the other methods, both at discharge and at 30-day follow-up, with the greatest benefit in clean wounds. The authors estimated that replacing shaving with morning clipping would save approximately $270,000 per 1,000 patients treated (1983 prices) and concluded that preoperative shaving is deleterious and the practice should be abandoned. The record's abstract does not print the per-group infection percentages, so none are given here.
cards.watchOut: A 1983 single-hospital trial: surgical-site infection surveillance definitions and perioperative care (antibiotic prophylaxis, skin antisepsis) have changed substantially since, so its absolute rates do not transfer to modern practice — its direction (razor worse than clippers) is what the later syntheses confirm.
cards.source: Alexander JW et al. The influence of hair-removal methods on wound infections. Archives of surgery. 1983. PMID: 6824435. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Hair Removal · Humans · Preoperative Care · Prospective Studies · Surgical Wound Infection

cards.headline: Balthazar 1982 RCT (n=200): wound infections 2% after razor shaving versus 1% after clipping in inguinal hernia repair; skin cuts in 7% shaved versus 4% clipped
cards.summary: Balthazar 1982 RCT (n=200): wound infections 2% after razor shaving versus 1% after clipping in inguinal hernia repair; skin cuts in 7% shaved versus 4% clipped
cards.type: Randomised prospective trial, razor shaving vs electric clipping immediately before operation
cards.people: 200 patients having elective inguinal hernia repair under a strict protocol, randomised to routine razor shaving or electrical clipping immediately before operation.
cards.result: Unsatisfactory skin preparation (gross cuts in the skin during hair removal) occurred in 7% of the shaved group and 4% of the clipped group. Two subcutaneous wound infections occurred in the shaved group (2%) and one in the clipped group (1%). The authors concluded that clipping immediately before operation is safe, well tolerated, and does not increase postoperative wound infection risk.
cards.watchOut: A small 1982 hernia-only trial with only three infections in total — it cannot on its own distinguish the methods; it is carded as part of the primary randomised base the Cochrane review aggregates.

cards.headline: Thur de Koos 1983 RCT (n=253): shaving versus depilatory cream — no statistical difference in wound infection; the cream allowed removal the day before and suited hard-to-shave areas
cards.summary: Thur de Koos 1983 RCT (n=253): shaving versus depilatory cream — no statistical difference in wound infection; the cream allowed removal the day before and suited hard-to-shave areas
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial, razor shaving vs chemical depilatory cream
cards.people: 253 patients undergoing preoperative skin preparation, randomised to shaving or chemical depilation, with wound infection as the outcome.
cards.result: No statistical difference in wound infection was found between shaving and depilatory cream. Depilation saved time by allowing hair removal the day before surgery and offered an advantage in areas difficult to shave, or where diagnostic procedures and operations were scheduled in the same area in close succession. The record's abstract does not print the per-group infection percentages, so none are given here.
cards.watchOut: A 1983 trial with abstract-level reporting only; depilatory creams can cause skin reactions in some patients, which this abstract does not quantify.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Tanner 2021): 25 trials, 8,919 participants — razor shaving probably increases surgical-site infection versus clipping (relative risk 1.64, a relative measure) and versus no removal (relative risk 1.82); clipping versus no removal: little difference (relative risk 0.95)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Tanner 2021): 25 trials, 8,919 participants — razor shaving probably increases surgical-site infection versus clipping (relative risk 1.64, a relative measure) and versus no removal (relative risk 1.82); clipping versus no removal: little difference (relative risk 0.95)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 19 randomised and 6 quasi-randomised trials (second update)
cards.people: 25 trials with 8,919 participants undergoing surgery, comparing hair removal methods (razor shaving, clipping, depilatory cream), timing and setting, and removal versus no removal, with surgical-site infection as the outcome.
cards.result: Shaving with a razor versus clipping (7 studies, 3,723 participants): risk of surgical-site infection probably increased with the razor — relative risk 1.64 (95% CI 1.16 to 2.33), a relative measure; skin injury was also probably increased with razors (relative risk 1.74). Shaving versus no removal (7 studies, 1,706 participants): relative risk 1.82 (95% CI 1.05 to 3.14), representing 17 more infections per 1,000 patients in absolute terms. Clipping versus no removal (3 studies, 1,733 participants): relative risk 0.95 (95% CI 0.65 to 1.39) — little difference. Depilatory cream versus no removal (1 trial, 267 participants): relative risk 1.02 with wide confidence intervals. Certainty was moderate for the razor comparisons and low for clipping/cream versus no removal.
cards.watchOut: The underlying trials are old and small by modern standards and predate current infection surveillance definitions; the review's certainty ratings (moderate at best) are printed on this card rather than upgraded.

cards.headline: Synthesis: razors are the problem, not hair removal itself — clipping and depilatory cream carry similar, lower infection risk, and clipping is no worse than leaving hair in place
cards.summary: Synthesis: razors are the problem, not hair removal itself — clipping and depilatory cream carry similar, lower infection risk, and clipping is no worse than leaving hair in place
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The primary trials and the Cochrane aggregate agree: shaving with a razor raises surgical-site infection risk relative to clipping (relative risk 1.64) and relative to no removal (relative risk 1.82, about 17 more infections per 1,000 patients), while clipping versus no removal shows little difference (relative risk 0.95) and depilatory cream performed no differently from shaving in its head-to-head trial or from no removal in the review. Where timing was tested, clipping on the morning of surgery performed best. The practical reading: if hair must be removed, clip (or use depilatory cream) rather than shave — and do not shave the night before.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Surgical hand antisepsis: alcohol rubbing equalled scrubbing on infections (2.44% vs 2.48% in 4,387 patients); the rest of the evidence is hand bacterial counts, a surrogate
shelves.question: In surgical teams, does alcohol-based hand rubbing achieve surgical-site infection rates and hand bacterial counts equivalent to traditional aqueous antiseptic hand scrubbing for surgical hand antisepsis?
shelves.mesh: Anti-Infective Agents, Local · Antisepsis · Colony Count, Microbial · General Surgery · Hand · Hand Disinfection · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE. On the patient outcome, the base is essentially one trial: Parienti 2002 (4,387 patients) found 30-day surgical-site infection of 2.44% with alcohol hand-rubbing versus 2.48% with traditional antiseptic scrubbing (difference 0.04%, 95% CI −0.88% to 0.96%) — (the treatment made no difference) — with better antisepsis-duration compliance (44% vs 28%) and less skin dryness/irritation with rubbing. The Cochrane review (14 trials) found no clear infection difference in any comparison and graded the evidence low to very low quality. Everything else measures hand bacterial counts — a surrogate, labelled as such on its cards: alcohol-based protocols matched or beat aqueous scrubs on counts (240-staff and 23-nurse trials). Colony-count equivalence is NOT surgical-site infection equivalence, and this shelf does not present it as such.

cards.headline: Parienti 2002 RCT (4,387 patients): surgical-site infection 2.44% with alcohol hand-rubbing versus 2.48% with traditional antiseptic scrubbing — equivalent, with better compliance and skin tolerance for rubbing
cards.summary: Parienti 2002 RCT (4,387 patients): surgical-site infection 2.44% with alcohol hand-rubbing versus 2.48% with traditional antiseptic scrubbing — equivalent, with better compliance and skin tolerance for rubbing
cards.type: Multicentre randomised equivalence trial, alcohol hand-rubbing vs traditional antiseptic hand-scrubbing; outcome measured in patients
cards.people: 4,387 consecutive patients undergoing clean and clean-contaminated surgery in six French surgical services (2000–2001); services alternated monthly between a hand-rubbing protocol (75% aqueous alcoholic solution with propanol-1, propanol-2 and mecetronium etilsulfate, preceded by a 1-minute non-antiseptic wash before the day's first procedure) and traditional scrubbing with 4% povidone-iodine or 4% chlorhexidine gluconate preparations.
cards.result: Thirty-day surgical-site infection rates were 55 of 2,252 (2.44%) with hand-rubbing and 53 of 2,135 (2.48%) with hand-scrubbing — a difference of 0.04% (95% CI −0.88% to 0.96%): (the treatment made no difference) to infection rates, meeting the trial's equivalence aim. Compliance with the recommended antisepsis duration was better with rubbing (44% vs 28%; P=.008), and rubbing caused less skin dryness and irritation.
cards.watchOut: The only large trial with a patient infection outcome — the rest of this shelf's base measures hand bacterial counts, a surrogate. cards.headline: Tsai 2017 RCT (240 surgical staff): waterless alcohol hand rub and chlorhexidine scrub both left fewer hand bacteria than povidone-iodine scrub immediately after disinfection — a bacterial-count (surrogate) endpoint, not infections
cards.summary: Tsai 2017 RCT (240 surgical staff): waterless alcohol hand rub and chlorhexidine scrub both left fewer hand bacteria than povidone-iodine scrub immediately after disinfection — a bacterial-count (surrogate) endpoint, not infections
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of three antisepsis methods; endpoint colony-forming units on hands (surrogate endpoint, labelled as such)
cards.people: 240 surgical staff at a Taipei hospital, 80 per method: conventional 10% povidone-iodine scrub, conventional 4% chlorhexidine scrub, or waterless hand rub (1% chlorhexidine gluconate with 61% ethyl alcohol). Colony-forming units were counted by hand imprinting before and after disinfection and after surgery.
cards.result: After disinfection, mean colony-forming unit counts were 0.5 (chlorhexidine scrub) and 1.4 (waterless rub) versus 4.3 (povidone-iodine scrub) — both significantly lower (P<0.01 and P<0.05 respectively). After surgery, no significant difference between the groups remained. The antiseptic method was the only significant predictor of post-disinfection counts in the authors' regression (P=.0036).
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE ENDPOINT: hand bacterial counts immediately after disinfection are not surgical-site infections, and the between-method difference had disappeared by the end of surgery. This card supports antiseptic potency, not patient-level equivalence.
cards.source: Tsai JC et al. Antiseptic Effect of Conventional Povidone-Iodine Scrub, Chlorhexidine Scrub, and Waterless Hand Rub in a Surgical Setting. Infection control and hospital epidemiology. 2017. PMID: 27995837. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Pereira 1997 RCT (23 theatre nurses): alcohol-based protocols matched the best detergent scrub on hand bacterial counts over a working week, with less skin drying reported — a bacterial-count (surrogate) endpoint
cards.summary: Pereira 1997 RCT (23 theatre nurses): alcohol-based protocols matched the best detergent scrub on hand bacterial counts over a working week, with less skin drying reported — a bacterial-count (surrogate) endpoint
cards.type: Randomised-order crossover evaluation of five surgical handwashing protocols; endpoint microbial counts and skin condition (surrogate endpoint, labelled as such)
cards.people: 23 operating theatre nurses, each completing all five protocols in randomised order with a week of normal work between protocols: chlorhexidine 4% scrubs of two durations, a povidone-iodine/triclosan scrub, and two protocols adding an alcohol-based antiseptic step (isopropanol 70% with chlorhexidine 0.5%, or ethanol 70% with chlorhexidine 0.5%).
cards.result: The alcohol-based protocols and the longest chlorhexidine scrub were generally associated with the lowest post-scrub colony-forming unit counts. After a week of exclusive use, the alcohol-based protocols gave significantly lower counts than the detergent-only comparators in two of three post-scrub samples (P=0.003 and P=0.035). Skin-condition differences were mostly not statistically significant, but many subjects reported the alcohol protocols as less drying.
cards.watchOut: SURROGATE ENDPOINT in 23 volunteers: hand bacterial counts, not patient infections. A small crossover volunteer study — it shows alcohol protocols are at least as antiseptic as scrubbing, nothing about infection rates.
cards.source: Pereira LJ et al. An evaluation of five protocols for surgical handwashing in relation to skin condition and microbial counts. The Journal of hospital infection. 1997. PMID: 9172045. cards.headline: Cochrane review (Tanner 2016): 14 trials — four reported surgical-site infection and none showed a clear difference between methods; chlorhexidine scrubs reduced hand bacterial counts versus povidone-iodine, on low- to very-low-quality evidence
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Tanner 2016): 14 trials — four reported surgical-site infection and none showed a clear difference between methods; chlorhexidine scrubs reduced hand bacterial counts versus povidone-iodine, on low- to very-low-quality evidence
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of 14 randomised trials of surgical hand antisepsis
cards.people: 14 randomised trials of surgical hand antisepsis methods, durations and solutions: four trials reported surgical-site infection rates (including the 4,387-patient Parienti trial carded here, a 3,317-participant basic-hygiene versus alcohol-rub trial, a 500-participant alcohol versus aqueous trial, and a 100-participant trial); ten reported hand colony-forming units only.
cards.result: For surgical-site infection there was no clear evidence of a difference in any comparison: basic hand hygiene versus alcohol rub plus hydrogen peroxide, relative risk 0.97 (95% CI 0.77 to 1.23); alcohol-only rub versus aqueous scrub, relative risk 0.56 (95% CI 0.23 to 1.34); alcohol rubs with additional active ingredients versus aqueous scrubs, relative risk 1.02 (95% CI 0.70 to 1.48) — all relative measures with confidence intervals spanning no difference. For bacterial counts, chlorhexidine gluconate scrubs reduced colony-forming units versus povidone-iodine scrubs in three studies, and alcohol rubs with additional antiseptic ingredients reduced counts versus aqueous scrubs in three comparisons — all low- or very-low-quality evidence. The review's conclusion: there is no firm evidence that one type of hand antisepsis is better than another in reducing surgical-site infections.
cards.watchOut: The review itself grades almost all of this evidence low or very low quality; colony-count findings must not be read as infection findings — the review says their clinical relevance is unclear.
cards.source: Tanner J et al. Surgical hand antisepsis to reduce surgical site infection. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2016. PMID: 26799160. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: alcohol hand-rubbing matched traditional scrubbing on the one outcome that matters — patient infections, in the single large equivalence trial — while the wider trial base only shows bacterial-count equivalence and must not be upgraded into infection equivalence
cards.summary: Synthesis: alcohol hand-rubbing matched traditional scrubbing on the one outcome that matters — patient infections, in the single large equivalence trial — while the wider trial base only shows bacterial-count equivalence and must not be upgraded into infection equivalence
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The patient-outcome evidence is one equivalence trial (4,387 patients: infection 2.44% rubbing vs 2.48% scrubbing) inside a Cochrane review whose other infection-outcome trials were smaller and imprecise, all consistent with no difference. The bacterial-count trials (240 staff; 23 nurses) show alcohol-based protocols are at least as antiseptic as aqueous scrubs and kinder to skin, with better protocol compliance in Parienti — but counts are a surrogate, and this shelf labels them so on every card, as the commissioning row requires.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis DURATION: a single preoperative dose matched multiple/prolonged doses at every tested site (gastric, bypass, colorectal, caesarean, orthopaedic)
shelves.question: In adults undergoing surgery, does a single preoperative dose of antibiotic prophylaxis prevent surgical-site infection as effectively as multiple-dose or prolonged postoperative prophylaxis — answered per surgical site (gastric, colorectal, coronary bypass, orthopaedic, caesarean) — and what is saved in adverse effects and resistance pressure? (DURATION only: prophylaxis TIMING is homed at pack #5749.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anti-Bacterial Agents · Antibiotic Prophylaxis · Drug Therapy, Combination · Female · Follow-Up Studies · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Stomach Neoplasms · Surgical Wound Infection · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no difference) — carded PER SURGICAL SITE, never as one pooled claim, and cross-pointing the separate TIMING question (when the dose is given) to pack #5749, which is not re-carded here. At every site with a direct randomised comparison, a single preoperative dose prevented surgical-site infection as well as multiple or prolonged doses: gastric cancer surgery (SSI 9.5% single vs 8.6% multiple, n=486 analysed), coronary bypass (sternal infection 14% vs 13% and donor-site 38% vs 39% as reported in 1994, 844 evaluable), elective colorectal surgery (overall infection 16.7% vs 13.3%, small n=93 — its N is printed on its card), and caesarean section (wound infection 6.6% vs 7.4%, n=162; clinical endometritis was actually lower with the single dose, 0.0% vs 6.1%). The orthopaedic syntheses agree: 14 implant RCTs (9,691 procedures) gave infection 2% vs 2% (odds ratio 0.92, relative) and 7 closed-fracture trials (3,808 patients) a risk ratio of 1.24 with a wide interval — both rated low/very-low quality. The 1998 all-surgery systematic review likewise found no clear advantage either way (combined odds ratio ~1.05). Extra doses therefore buy antibiotic exposure, cost and resistance pressure without a demonstrated infection benefit at any tested site; the older trials predate modern SSI surveillance and resistance ecology, which is stated on the face.

cards.headline: Gastric surgery RCT (Mohri 2007): single-dose vs multiple-dose prophylaxis in gastric cancer surgery — surgical-site infection 9.5% vs 8.6% (486 analysed of 501 randomised)
cards.summary: Gastric surgery RCT (Mohri 2007): single-dose vs multiple-dose prophylaxis in gastric cancer surgery — surgical-site infection 9.5% vs 8.6% (486 analysed of 501 randomised)
cards.type: Multicentre randomised trial, single-dose vs multiple-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis — GASTRIC site
cards.people: 501 patients undergoing elective surgery for gastric cancer at ten centres (2001–2004) were randomised to a single dose or a multiple-dose regimen of antimicrobial prophylaxis; 243 patients in each group were included in the final intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: The surgical-site infection rate was 9.5% (23 of 243) with a single dose and 8.6% (21 of 243) with multiple doses — a difference of 0.9 percentage points (95% CI −4.3 to 5.9). Antimicrobial prophylaxis had no major adverse effects in either group. The authors concluded the incidence of surgical-site infection in elective gastric cancer surgery was similar with both regimens.
cards.watchOut: A cancer-surgery population at one site (stomach) in 2001–2004: the result answers the gastric question, and its confidence interval (−4.3 to +5.9 points) cannot exclude a small difference in either direction.
cards.source: Mohri Y et al. Randomized clinical trial of single- versus multiple-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis in gastric cancer surgery. The British journal of surgery. 2007. PMID: 17514671. cards.headline: Coronary bypass RCT (Nooyen 1994): single-dose cefuroxime vs a 3-day course — sternal wound infection 14% vs 13% and donor-site infection 38% vs 39% as reported (844 evaluable of 1,016 randomised)
cards.summary: Coronary bypass RCT (Nooyen 1994): single-dose cefuroxime vs a 3-day course — sternal wound infection 14% vs 13% and donor-site infection 38% vs 39% as reported (844 evaluable of 1,016 randomised)
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial, single-dose vs 3-day cefuroxime — CORONARY BYPASS site
cards.people: 1,016 consecutive coronary artery bypass grafting patients were prospectively randomised to a single intravenous dose of cefuroxime 20 mg/kg at induction of anaesthesia (group A) or the same dose followed by 750 mg three times daily for three consecutive days (group B); 844 patients were evaluable (419 vs 425) after 9 early deaths (0.9%, none from infection) and 163 exclusions. Risk factors were comparable between groups.
cards.result: No significant differences in wound infection were observed: sternal site infection was 14% in the single-dose group versus 13% in the three-day group, and donor site infection occurred in 38% versus 39%, as reported in the record. The authors concluded that in coronary artery bypass grafting a single dose of cefuroxime is as effective as a three-day course in preventing wound infection.
cards.watchOut: A 1994 trial: the reported infection rates (especially 38–39% at the donor site) reflect that era's definitions and surveillance and are far above modern bypass-series rates — the between-group comparison, not the absolute rates, is the usable content. 163 randomised patients were not evaluable.
cards.source: Nooyen SM et al. Prospective randomised comparison of single-dose versus multiple-dose cefuroxime for prophylaxis in coronary artery bypass grafting. European journal of clinical microbiology & infectious diseases : official publication of the European Society of Clinical Microbiology. 1994. PMID: 7889965. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Colorectal surgery RCT (Ahn 2013) — SMALL N=93, printed on the face: single-dose vs three-dose cephalosporin + metronidazole — overall postoperative infection 16.7% vs 13.3%, no significant difference
cards.summary: Colorectal surgery RCT (Ahn 2013) — SMALL N=93, printed on the face: single-dose vs three-dose cephalosporin + metronidazole — overall postoperative infection 16.7% vs 13.3%, no significant difference
cards.type: Randomised trial, single-dose vs three-dose prophylaxis — COLORECTAL site (small, N=93)
cards.people: 93 patients undergoing elective colorectal surgery (2009–2010) were enrolled: the single-dose group (n=48) received one preoperative intravenous dose and the three-dose group (n=45) one preoperative plus two postoperative doses of a second-generation cephalosporin and metronidazole.
cards.result: The overall postoperative infection rate did not differ between groups (16.7% single-dose vs 13.3% three-dose; P=0.653), nor did incisional surgical-site infection (6.3%, 3 of 48, vs 4.4%, 2 of 45; P=0.700) or organ/space infection (4.2% vs 6.7%; P=0.593). The number of antibiotic doses was not an independent risk factor for surgical-site infection in multivariable analysis. The authors state single-dose prophylaxis was equivalent in this study but that further study is needed because of the small number of participants.
cards.watchOut: SMALL N=93: with 93 patients this trial can only exclude very large differences, and its authors say so. It is carded as the colorectal site's direct comparison, labelled small, and is not load-bearing on its own — the site pattern matters because it matches the larger trials at other sites.
cards.source: Ahn BK et al. Single-dose antibiotic prophylaxis is effective enough in colorectal surgery. ANZ journal of surgery. 2013. PMID: 22946966. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Caesarean section RCT (Igwemadu 2022): single-dose vs multiple-dose ceftriaxone + metronidazole — wound infection 6.6% vs 7.4%; clinical endometritis 0.0% vs 6.1% (lower with the single dose)
cards.summary: Caesarean section RCT (Igwemadu 2022): single-dose vs multiple-dose ceftriaxone + metronidazole — wound infection 6.6% vs 7.4%; clinical endometritis 0.0% vs 6.1% (lower with the single dose)
cards.type: Open-label randomised trial, single-dose vs multiple-dose prophylaxis — CAESAREAN site
cards.people: 162 consenting patients admitted for caesarean section (elective or emergency) at a Nigerian federal medical centre were randomised open-label: both arms received intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g and metronidazole 500 mg 30–60 minutes before incision; the multiple-dose arm additionally received parenteral doses for 48 hours and then oral cefuroxime and metronidazole for 5 days. Patients were monitored for 2 weeks for wound infection, febrile morbidity and clinical endometritis.
cards.result: There was no statistical difference in wound infection (6.6% single-dose vs 7.4% multiple-dose; P=.882) or febrile morbidity (11.8% vs 11.1%; P=.807). Clinical endometritis was significantly less frequent in the single-dose arm (0.0% vs 6.1%; P=.028). The authors conclude single-dose prophylaxis is as effective as multiple doses for preventing post-caesarean infections and that adopting it in low-risk patients would reduce cost, workload and antibiotic resistance pressure.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-centre, 2-week follow-up, and the endometritis difference rests on a handful of events in the multiple-dose arm — read it as 'no advantage to prolonging', not as proof that extra doses cause endometritis.
cards.source: Igwemadu GT et al. Single-dose versus multiple-dose antibiotics prophylaxis for preventing caesarean section postpartum infections: A randomized controlled trial. Women's health (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35670414. Registry ID: PACTR2020044658330781. cards.headline: Orthopaedic meta-analysis (Ryan 2019): 14 RCTs, 9,691 implant procedures — infection 2% with a single dose vs 2% with multiple doses (odds ratio 0.92, relative); evidence quality rated very low
cards.summary: Orthopaedic meta-analysis (Ryan 2019): 14 RCTs, 9,691 implant procedures — infection 2% with a single dose vs 2% with multiple doses (odds ratio 0.92, relative); evidence quality rated very low
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials, single vs multiple doses — ORTHOPAEDIC (implant) site
cards.people: Fourteen randomised trials (1980–2017) of single-dose preoperative antibiotics versus pre- plus postoperative prophylaxis in orthopaedic procedures where implants were placed — seven arthroplasty, one spine and six general orthopaedic trials (two of hip fracture fixation) — pooled in a random-effects meta-analysis.
cards.result: There was no difference in infection risk between single- and multiple-dose groups: 83 infections in 4,263 single-dose procedures (2%) versus 101 in 5,428 multiple-dose procedures (2%); odds ratio 0.92 (95% CI 0.56 to 1.51; P=0.740 — a relative measure, printed with the absolute rates), with moderate heterogeneity (I²=36%). Bias was largely uncertain (high risk in four studies) and the GRADE quality of evidence was very low, downgraded for risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision. The authors note the finding is consistent with the CDC single-dose recommendation but that a sufficiently powered randomised study is still needed.
cards.watchOut: Very-low-quality pooled evidence by the authors' own GRADE rating: 'no difference found' in underpowered, heterogeneous older trials is weaker than a modern noninferiority trial would be. The closed-fracture meta-analysis (Slobogean 2008; 7 trials, 3,808 patients; risk ratio 1.24, 95% CI 0.60 to 2.60 for single vs multiple doses — relative, interval spanning no difference widely) points the same inconclusive-but-null way and is summarised here rather than carded separately.
cards.source: Ryan SP et al. Is There a Difference in Infection Risk Between Single and Multiple Doses of Prophylactic Antibiotics? A Meta-analysis. Clinical orthopaedics and related research. 2019. PMID: 30811357. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: All-surgery systematic review (McDonald 1998): 25 years of randomised trials — combined odds ratio ~1.05, no clear advantage to multiple-dose over single-dose prophylaxis in any subgroup
cards.summary: All-surgery systematic review (McDonald 1998): 25 years of randomised trials — combined odds ratio ~1.05, no clear advantage to multiple-dose over single-dose prophylaxis in any subgroup
cards.type: Systematic review of randomised trials, single vs multiple doses — ALL MAJOR SURGERY (cross-site synthesis, not a site claim)
cards.people: Prospective randomised trials of single- versus multiple-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis for major surgery, identified from MEDLINE and other searches, restricted to trials using the same antimicrobial in each treatment arm and published in English; subgroup analyses covered antimicrobial class, blinded wound assessment, multiple-dose duration (>24 h vs ≤24 h) and surgery type (obstetric/gynaecological vs other).
cards.result: The combined odds ratio for surgical-site infection was 1.06 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.25) by fixed-effects and 1.04 (95% CI 0.86 to 1.25) by random-effects modelling (relative measures; an odds ratio near 1.0 with an interval straddling 1.0 indicates no clear advantage of either regimen, per the review's own framing). No subgroup analysis showed a statistically significant difference. The authors recommended continued use of single-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis for major surgery, with further studies in neglected disciplines.
cards.watchOut: A 1998 review of still older trials, and one included vascular-surgery study had challenged the single-dose principle at the time — the review is carded as the cross-site frame only; this shelf's claims rest on the per-site cards above, not on pooling unlike operations.
cards.source: McDonald M et al. Single- versus multiple-dose antimicrobial prophylaxis for major surgery: a systematic review. The Australian and New Zealand journal of surgery. 1998. PMID: 9623456. cards.headline: Synthesis: at every surgical site with a direct comparison — gastric, coronary bypass, colorectal (small n=93), caesarean, orthopaedic implants — a single preoperative dose matched multiple/prolonged doses for surgical-site infection
cards.summary: Synthesis: at every surgical site with a direct comparison — gastric, coronary bypass, colorectal (small n=93), caesarean, orthopaedic implants — a single preoperative dose matched multiple/prolonged doses for surgical-site infection
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf, organised by surgical site as the commissioning row requires.
cards.result: Gastric cancer surgery: SSI 9.5% vs 8.6% (n=486 analysed). Coronary bypass (1994): sternal 14% vs 13%, donor site 38% vs 39% as reported (844 evaluable). Colorectal: overall infection 16.7% vs 13.3% in a small trial (N=93, printed on its card). Caesarean: wound infection 6.6% vs 7.4% (n=162), endometritis 0.0% vs 6.1%. Orthopaedic implants: pooled infection 2% vs 2% across 14 RCTs (odds ratio 0.92, relative; very-low GRADE), with the closed-fracture meta-analysis (risk ratio 1.24, wide interval) summarised on that card. The 1998 all-surgery review found the same null (combined odds ratio ~1.05). No site showed a demonstrated benefit from prolonging prophylaxis beyond the operation; the savings from a single dose are antibiotic exposure, cost and resistance pressure. This shelf answers DURATION only — the TIMING question (prophylaxis within 60 minutes before incision versus earlier) is homed at pack #5749, whose trials are not re-carded here. Older trials predate modern SSI surveillance and resistance ecology, so absolute rates on the older cards should not be read as today's rates.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each site's limits; this synthesis adds no new data and does not pool the sites into a single effect estimate.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Shortened preoperative fasting vs nil-by-mouth-from-midnight: no increase in gastric volume or acidity in 4 verified primary RCTs or the Cochrane review (surrogates); less thirst with drinking
shelves.question: In adults having elective surgery under general anaesthesia, does a shortened preoperative fast — clear fluids permitted up to about 2 hours before anaesthesia — cause more regurgitation/aspiration or larger, more acidic gastric contents than the traditional nil-by-mouth-from-midnight policy, and does it reduce thirst and preoperative discomfort? (Gastric volume and pH are surrogates for aspiration risk throughout.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Anesthesia, General · Drinking · Fasting · Gastroesophageal Reflux · Humans · Intraoperative Complications · Pneumonia, Aspiration · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: SPLIT — (no difference) on the gastric-contents safety surrogate, (benefit) on preoperative comfort. Four primary randomised trials verified individually from their own records from inside the Cochrane review's programme (Brady 2003: 22 trials, 38 comparisons), plus the review itself, agree: permitting clear fluids 2–3 hours before anaesthesia did NOT increase residual gastric volume or lower gastric pH versus an overnight/standard fast — Hutchinson 1988 (n=300 inpatients: volumes 24.5, 23.7 and 23.2 mL across coffee, orange-juice and fasted groups; pH ~2.0 in all), Phillips 1993 (n=100: residual volume 22 vs 19 mL, pH 2.64 vs 2.26, for free clear fluids until premedication vs a 6-hour fast), McGrady 1988 (n=50: water 100 mL 2 hours preoperatively — gastric residue non-significantly lower, pH identical) and Maltby 1986 (n=140: 150 mL water 2.5 hours preoperatively gave LOWER gastric volume than a sip-only regimen, 17.6 vs 26.7 mL, in the placebo-tablet groups). Gastric volume and pH are SURROGATES, labelled as such on every card: aspiration itself is too rare for any of these trials to power, and the Cochrane review found few trials reporting aspiration/regurgitation at all and almost none in high-risk patients. On comfort, Phillips found less preoperative thirst with drinking, and the review concluded a shortened fluid fast carries no evidence of increased aspiration risk. This shelf is about fasting-DURATION policy for ordinary fluids and food — the proprietary carbohydrate-drink question is homed at live #1956 and is not re-carded here.

cards.headline: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Hutchinson 1988): 150 mL coffee or orange juice 2–3 hours before surgery vs overnight fast in 300 inpatients — residual gastric volume and pH did not differ (SURROGATE endpoints)
cards.summary: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Hutchinson 1988): 150 mL coffee or orange juice 2–3 hours before surgery vs overnight fast in 300 inpatients — residual gastric volume and pH did not differ (SURROGATE endpoints)
cards.type: Randomised trial of preoperative fluid timing (primary report inside the Brady 2003 Cochrane programme) — gastric volume/pH SURROGATES
cards.people: 300 elective surgical inpatients (ASA physical status I–II) randomly assigned to six groups; this Part I report covers the three placebo-tablet groups: 150 mL coffee (group 1), 150 mL orange juice (group 2) taken between 2 and 3 hours before the scheduled surgery time, or continued overnight fast (group 3). No opiate or belladonna premedication was given; residual gastric fluid was suctioned via nasogastric tube immediately after induction of anaesthesia.
cards.result: Residual gastric fluid volumes did not differ significantly among the groups (coffee 24.5 ± 21.6 mL; orange juice 23.7 ± 18.4 mL; overnight fast 23.2 ± 17.3 mL; P>0.1), and neither did pH (2.18 ± 1.58; 1.95 ± 1.24; 1.95 ± 1.62; P>0.1). SURROGATE endpoints: gastric volume and pH stand in for aspiration risk, which this trial did not measure.
cards.watchOut: Coffee and orange juice are not 'clear fluids' in the modern guideline sense, and the population was low-risk ASA I–II elective inpatients — the trial says nothing about patients at increased aspiration risk. The ranitidine groups of the same study are reported in its Part II paper and are not carded here.
cards.source: Hutchinson A et al. Gastric fluid volume and pH in elective inpatients. Part I: Coffee or orange juice versus overnight fast. Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie. 1988. PMID: 3349549. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Phillips 1993): free clear fluids until premedication vs a 6-hour fast in 100 elective patients — gastric volume 22 vs 19 mL and pH 2.64 vs 2.26 (SURROGATES), with less preoperative thirst in the drinking group
cards.summary: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Phillips 1993): free clear fluids until premedication vs a 6-hour fast in 100 elective patients — gastric volume 22 vs 19 mL and pH 2.64 vs 2.26 (SURROGATES), with less preoperative thirst in the drinking group
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial of preoperative drinking vs fasting (primary report inside the Brady 2003 Cochrane programme) — gastric volume/pH SURROGATES plus thirst
cards.people: 100 elective surgical patients randomly allocated to free clear fluids up to the time of oral premedication (mean intake 388 mL in the 6 hours before surgery) or conventional fasting for 6 hours. Residual gastric volume and pH were measured after induction of anaesthesia.
cards.result: Preoperative drinking did not affect mean (SD) residual gastric volume (22 (21) mL in the drinking group vs 19 (16) mL in the fasted group) or pH (2.64 (1.57) vs 2.26 (1.45)). The drinking group experienced less preoperative thirst. No problems with aspiration or regurgitation were encountered in either group — an observation, not a powered safety result, in 100 patients. The authors conclude that allowing elective patients to drink clear fluids until 2 hours before anaesthesia may enhance comfort without compromising safety. SURROGATE endpoints (volume/pH) as on every card of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The control was a 6-hour fast, not literally nil-by-mouth-from-midnight for every patient, and 100 patients cannot detect a difference in aspiration, an event orders of magnitude rarer than this sample.
cards.source: Phillips S et al. Preoperative drinking does not affect gastric contents. British journal of anaesthesia. 1993. PMID: 8431336. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.type: Randomised trial of preoperative water vs fasting (primary report inside the Brady 2003 Cochrane programme) — gastric volume/pH SURROGATES
cards.people: 50 patients investigated before elective surgery: one group was given 100 mL of water 2 hours before operation and the other was fasted as usual. Volume and pH of gastric contents were measured immediately after induction of anaesthesia.
cards.result: The mean gastric residue was less in the patients given water, but the difference was not statistically significant, and there was no difference in gastric pH between the two groups. SURROGATE endpoints (volume/pH), as on every card of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: The smallest primary on this shelf (n=50) and its record reports the direction and significance of the volume difference without the group means — it is carded for its verified null on pH and non-significant volume result, and is not load-bearing alone.

cards.headline: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Maltby 1986): 150 mL water ~2.5 hours preoperatively vs a sip-only regimen in 140 outpatients — gastric volume was LOWER with the drink (17.6 vs 26.7 mL) in the placebo-tablet groups (SURROGATES)
cards.summary: Primary RCT inside the Cochrane review (Maltby 1986): 150 mL water ~2.5 hours preoperatively vs a sip-only regimen in 140 outpatients — gastric volume was LOWER with the drink (17.6 vs 26.7 mL) in the placebo-tablet groups (SURROGATES)
cards.type: Randomised factorial trial of preoperative fluid (and ranitidine) (primary report inside the Brady 2003 Cochrane programme) — gastric volume/pH SURROGATES
cards.people: 140 unpremedicated ambulatory outpatients presenting for first-trimester therapeutic abortion, randomly assigned to four groups in a factorial design: at an average of 2.5 hours preoperatively all received oral ranitidine 150 mg or a placebo tablet with a bromosulphthalein marker in 10 mL water, followed by either 150 mL water or no further fluid. Gastric volume, pH and emptying were measured intraoperatively. The fluid comparison on this card is between the two placebo-tablet groups, isolating the drink from the ranitidine effect.
cards.result: Gastric volume was significantly less in patients given 150 mL water (17.6 ± 14.5 mL) than in those given only the marker sip (26.7 ± 18.9 mL; P<0.02), and was lower still in the ranitidine groups (8.3 ± 7.3 and 9.5 ± 7.7 mL; P<0.001). Mean pH was significantly higher only in the ranitidine groups (5.52 ± 1.79 and 5.03 ± 1.79) than in the placebo groups (1.75 ± 0.94 with water; 1.92 ± 1.27 without) — the drink itself did not change pH. The combined at-risk pattern (residual volume ≥25 mL with pH <2.5) occurred in 46% of the sip-only placebo group, 23% of the water placebo group and no ranitidine patient. There was no correlation between gastric volume or pH and the ingestion-to-surgery interval in patients given water. SURROGATE endpoints, as on every card of this shelf.
cards.watchOut: A specific population — pregnant patients having first-trimester abortion under anaesthesia — and a factorial design in which ranitidine, not the drink, drove the pH and volume extremes; only the placebo-tablet fluid comparison is used for this shelf's question. A companion factorial trial from the same group (Sutherland 1987, n=100 daycare patients; water 20.6 vs 29.9 mL in the placebo groups) found the same direction and is summarised here rather than carded separately.
cards.source: Maltby JR et al. Preoperative oral fluids: is a five-hour fast justified prior to elective surgery?. Anesthesia and analgesia. 1986. PMID: 3767008. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Cochrane systematic review (Brady 2003): 22 trials, 38 randomised comparisons — no evidence that a shortened fluid fast increased aspiration, regurgitation or related morbidity versus nil-by-mouth-from-midnight; water before surgery lowered gastric volumes
cards.summary: Cochrane systematic review (Brady 2003): 22 trials, 38 randomised comparisons — no evidence that a shortened fluid fast increased aspiration, regurgitation or related morbidity versus nil-by-mouth-from-midnight; water before surgery lowered gastric volumes
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of the randomised preoperative-fasting programme (the review from which this shelf's primary cards are drawn)
cards.people: Randomised controlled trials comparing different preoperative fasting regimens in adults (38 comparisons within 22 trials), searched to August 2003. Most participants were 'healthy' adults not considered at increased risk of regurgitation or aspiration; fluids evaluated included water, coffee, fruit juice, clear fluids and other drinks including isotonic and carbohydrate drinks.
cards.result: There was no evidence that the volume or pH of gastric contents differed significantly between groups permitted a shortened preoperative fluid fast and groups on a standard fast, and no indication that the volume of fluid permitted (low or high) changed outcomes versus a standard fast. Participants given a drink of water preoperatively had a significantly lower volume of gastric contents than standard-fast groups, though the difference was modest and clinically insignificant. Few trials reported the incidence of aspiration or regurgitation or related morbidity, relying instead on intraoperative gastric volume and pH — the surrogate limitation that applies to this whole shelf. Few trials studied populations at increased aspiration risk. The reviewers concluded there was no evidence a shortened fluid fast increases aspiration risk and encouraged clinicians to adjust remaining nil-by-mouth-from-midnight policies for patients not considered at risk.
cards.watchOut: The review is a 2003 snapshot (literature to August 2003) of small, mostly low-risk-population trials with surrogate outcomes — it is carded as the programme's frame; the shelf's claims rest on the individually verified primary cards above.
cards.source: Brady M et al. Preoperative fasting for adults to prevent perioperative complications. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2003. PMID: 14584013. Registry ID: none in the record.
