cards.headline: Synthesis: shortened clear-fluid fasting did not worsen gastric volume or pH in any verified primary trial and reduced thirst — but every trial measured surrogates, and aspiration-risk patients were barely studied
cards.summary: Synthesis: shortened clear-fluid fasting did not worsen gastric volume or pH in any verified primary trial and reduced thirst — but every trial measured surrogates, and aspiration-risk patients were barely studied
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf (four primary randomised trials verified individually from their own records, plus the Cochrane review of the programme).
cards.result: Hutchinson 1988 (n=300): gastric volume 24.5/23.7/23.2 mL and pH ~2.0 across coffee, orange-juice and overnight-fast groups. Phillips 1993 (n=100): volume 22 vs 19 mL, pH 2.64 vs 2.26, less thirst with drinking. McGrady 1988 (n=50): water 2 hours preoperatively — residue non-significantly lower, pH unchanged. Maltby 1986 (n=140): 150 mL water lowered gastric volume versus a sip-only regimen (17.6 vs 26.7 mL) without changing pH. The Cochrane review (22 trials) found the same pattern overall and no evidence of increased aspiration, regurgitation or related morbidity with a shortened fluid fast. The stop-condition for this row is met: four primaries (≥3 required) verify individually, each with ≥10 participants. The boundary of the claim is equally clear: gastric volume and pH are surrogates, aspiration is too rare for these trials to measure, high-risk patients were largely excluded, and the food limb of modern policy (a light meal to ~6 hours) rests on this fluid evidence plus guideline extrapolation rather than on large food trials. The carbohydrate-drink intervention question is homed at live #1956 and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Donor-site dressings for split-thickness skin grafts: SPLIT by class — hydrogel unsupported, povidone-iodine foam fastest in one RCT, polyurethane vs alginate a comfort/workload trade-off
shelves.question: In patients with split-thickness skin-graft donor sites, which dressing class — hydrogel, hydrocellular foam, polyurethane film, calcium alginate, petrolatum / povidone-iodine gauze — heals the donor site fastest with least pain, infection and dressing-change burden, and does the answer differ in burns versus elective grafting?
shelves.mesh: Child · Humans · Hydrogels · Skin Transplantation · Ointments · Bandages, Hydrocolloid · Wound Infection · Alginates
shelves.balance: SPLIT by dressing class and endpoint — there is no single winner. A Cochrane review found only two hydrogel trials (162 participants) and insufficient evidence for hydrogel, with amorphous hydrogel possibly SLOWER to heal than alginate or acetate gauze (low certainty). A 3-arm RCT (67 adults, 73 donor sites) found the hydrocolloid Aquacel and the film Mediskin I re-epithelialised faster than the foam Allevyn, with less pain on dressing change for Aquacel. A small burns-unit RCT (n=36) found no healing or pain difference between polyurethane (Allevyn) and calcium alginate (Kaltostat) but more dressing changes and cost with polyurethane, while a meta-analysis of the same comparison (4 RCTs, 127 subjects) found no pain difference and better patient comfort with polyurethane. A Korean phase 4 RCT (n=106) found povidone-iodine foam (Betafoam) epithelialised fastest (12.74 days vs 16.61 hydrocellular foam vs 15.06 petrolatum gauze) with no infections in any arm. Healing-time definitions differ by trial and are carded as published, never pooled. Tested products and companies are named on each card where the publication gives them.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Younis 2023): only two hydrogel trials (162 participants) — insufficient evidence; amorphous hydrogel may heal SLOWER than alginate or gauze (low certainty)
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Younis 2023): only two hydrogel trials (162 participants) — insufficient evidence; amorphous hydrogel may heal SLOWER than alginate or gauze (low certainty)
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, hydrogel dressings for split-thickness skin-graft donor sites
cards.people: Two randomised trials of hydrogel dressings for split-thickness skin-graft donor sites (162 participants): a 3-arm children's-hospital study (101 participants) comparing the hydrogel Sorbact with Algisite (alginate) and Cuticerin (acetate gauze with water-repellent ointment), and a 61-participant study in three surgery departments comparing an octenidine-containing hydrogel with an identical non-antimicrobial hydrogel. Both studies were at high risk of attrition bias.
cards.result: Amorphous hydrogel dressings may increase time to wound healing compared with alginate (mean difference 1.67 days; 95% CI 0.56 to 2.78; 1 study, 69 participants; low-certainty evidence) or Cuticerin (MD 1.67 days; 95% CI 0.55 to 2.79; 1 study, 68 participants; low-certainty evidence). Effects on donor-site pain and wound complications (scarring, itching) are uncertain (very low certainty); no adverse events were reported in any group, and neither study reported quality of life or wound infection. For octenidine hydrogel versus plain hydrogel, the effect on healing time (MD 0.40; 95% CI 0.28 to 0.52; 1 study, 41 participants) and infection is uncertain (very low certainty). The authors conclude there is insufficient evidence to determine the effect of hydrogel dressings and call for adequately powered RCTs.
cards.watchOut: The hydrogel evidence is two small trials, one in children; product names are as published in the review (manufacturers not given in the record for these products). Low/very-low certainty throughout.
cards.source: Younis AS et al. Hydrogel dressings for donor sites of split-thickness skin grafts. The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. 2023. PMID: 37584338. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Three-arm RCT (Karlsson 2014): Aquacel (hydrocolloid) and Mediskin I (film) re-epithelialised faster than Allevyn (foam); Aquacel least painful to change (67 adults, 73 donor sites)
cards.summary: Three-arm RCT (Karlsson 2014): Aquacel (hydrocolloid) and Mediskin I (film) re-epithelialised faster than Allevyn (foam); Aquacel least painful to change (67 adults, 73 donor sites)
cards.type: Prospective randomised 3-arm trial, hydrocolloid vs foam vs film dressings for skin-graft donor sites (products and companies as published)
cards.people: 67 adults with 73 split-thickness skin-graft donor sites (thigh, not reharvested, 30–400 cm²) at a hand/plastic surgery department with a burn unit, randomised to Aquacel (ConvaTec, Skillman, New Jersey), Allevyn (Smith & Nephew, St Petersburg, Florida) or Mediskin I (Mölnlycke Health Care AB, Gothenburg, Sweden), assessed on postoperative days 3, 14 and 21 for healing, infection, pain, impact on everyday life, ease of use and cost.
cards.result: Re-epithelialisation was significantly faster with Aquacel or Mediskin I than with Allevyn. Infections did not differ significantly between groups. Patients wearing Aquacel reported significantly less pain on dressing change and less impact on everyday life than those wearing Allevyn, and Aquacel was significantly easier for caregivers to use than Allevyn or Mediskin I. Treatment cost differed significantly, Mediskin I being the most expensive. The authors support Aquacel for donor sites on healing time, discomfort, ease of use and low unit cost.
cards.watchOut: The unit of analysis mixes patients (67) and donor sites (73); healing was assessed at fixed days rather than as a continuous time-to-event, and the trial is from a single centre with a burn unit.
cards.source: Karlsson M et al. Dressing the split-thickness skin graft donor site: a randomized clinical trial. Advances in Skin & Wound Care. 2014. PMID: 24343389. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Burns-unit RCT (Higgins 2012): polyurethane (Allevyn) vs calcium alginate (Kaltostat) — no difference in healing or pain, but more dressing changes and cost with polyurethane (n=36)
cards.summary: Burns-unit RCT (Higgins 2012): polyurethane (Allevyn) vs calcium alginate (Kaltostat) — no difference in healing or pain, but more dressing changes and cost with polyurethane (n=36)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, polyurethane vs calcium alginate dressings for skin-graft donor sites (product names as published; companies not given in the record)
cards.people: 36 patients randomised to Allevyn (polyurethane) or Kaltostat (calcium alginate) for donor-site management after split-skin graft surgery in a burns unit (August 2009 to April 2010). Primary outcomes were pain intensity and adverse events; secondary outcomes included time to wound healing, ease of application/removal and satisfaction.
cards.result: There were no significant differences between groups in time to wound healing, pain intensity, length of stay, or staff and patient satisfaction. Time to first dressing change was earlier with Allevyn (5.5 vs 8.11 days; P=0.014); excessive exudate led to significantly more dressing changes before day 10 with Allevyn, and the total number of dressing changes was also greater (P=0.007). The authors conclude Allevyn was associated with increased nursing time and product cost, and that Kaltostat remains the dressing of choice for initial donor-site dressing in their burns unit.
cards.watchOut: Small (n=36), single burns unit, and its 'dressing of choice' conclusion is a local cost/workload judgement, not a healing advantage — contrast the meta-analysis card below, which found better patient comfort with polyurethane.
cards.source: Higgins L et al. Split-thickness skin graft donor site management: a randomized controlled trial comparing polyurethane with calcium alginate dressings. International Wound Journal. 2012. PMID: 22051247. Registry ID: none in the record. randomised controlled trial, polyurethane vs calcium alginate dressings for skin-graft donor sites (product names as published; companies not given in the record) 36 patients randomised to allevyn (polyurethane) or kaltostat (calcium alginate) for donor-site management after split-skin graft surgery in a burns unit (august 2009 to april 2010). primary outcomes were pain intensity and adverse events; secondary outcomes included time to wound healing, ease of application/removal and satisfaction. there were no significant differences between groups in time to wound healing, pain intensity, length of stay, or staff and patient satisfaction. time to first dressing change was earlier with allevyn (5.5 vs 8.11 days; p=0.014); excessive exudate led to significantly more dressing changes before day 10 with allevyn, and the total number of dressing changes was also greater (p=0.007). the authors conclude allevyn was associated with increased nursing time and product cost, and that kaltostat remains the dressing of choice for initial donor-site dressing in their burns unit. small (n=36), single burns unit, and its 'dressing of choice' conclusion is a local cost/workload judgement, not a healing advantage — contrast the meta-analysis card below, which found better patient comfort with polyurethane. higgins l et al. split-thickness skin graft donor site management: a randomized controlled trial comparing polyurethane with calcium alginate dressings. international wound journal. 2012. pmid: 22051247. registry id: none in the record. mesh: alginates · bandages · burns · female · glucuronic acid · hexuronic acids · humans · length of stay · male · pain measurement · patient satisfaction · polyurethanes · plastic surgery procedures · skin transplantation · wound healing

cards.headline: Korean phase 4 RCT (Pak 2019): povidone-iodine foam (Betafoam) epithelialised fastest — 12.74 days vs 16.61 (hydrocellular foam) vs 15.06 (petrolatum gauze); no infections (n=106)
cards.summary: Korean phase 4 RCT (Pak 2019): povidone-iodine foam (Betafoam) epithelialised fastest — 12.74 days vs 16.61 (hydrocellular foam) vs 15.06 (petrolatum gauze); no infections (n=106)
cards.type: Prospective randomised phase 4 multicentre trial, povidone-iodine foam vs hydrocellular foam vs petrolatum gauze for skin-graft donor sites (product names as published; companies not given in the record)
cards.people: 106 consenting adults (≥19 years) scheduled for split-thickness skin grafting at eight Korean sites, randomised 1:1:1 to povidone-iodine foam dressing (Betafoam), hydrocellular foam dressing (Allevyn) or petrolatum gauze, for up to 28 days after donor-site harvest (March 2016 to April 2017). Outcomes were time to complete epithelialisation, complete epithelialisation at day 14, and wound infection.
cards.result: Epithelialisation time was shortest with povidone-iodine foam (12.74 ± 3.51 days) versus hydrocellular foam (16.61 ± 4.45 days; P=0.0003) and petrolatum gauze (15.06 ± 4.26 days; P=0.0205). At day 14, complete epithelialisation was 83.87% with povidone-iodine foam versus 36.36% (hydrocellular foam; P=0.0001) and 55.88% (petrolatum gauze; P=0.0146) — absolute rates, printed all. There were no wound infections in any group, and adverse-event rates were comparable (P=0.1940).
cards.watchOut: The record's publication types do not include 'Randomized Controlled Trial' though the abstract describes 1:1:1 randomisation; with zero infections in all arms the trial says nothing about infection prevention, and its epithelialisation assessment may not match other trials' healing definitions.
cards.source: Pak CS et al. Comparison of the efficacy and safety of povidone-iodine foam dressing (Betafoam), hydrocellular foam dressing (Allevyn), and petrolatum gauze for split-thickness skin graft donor site dressing. International Wound Journal. 2019. PMID: 30479060. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Alsaif 2021): polyurethane vs calcium alginate — no difference in pain or adverse effects; patient comfort favoured polyurethane (4 RCTs, 127 subjects)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Alsaif 2021): polyurethane vs calcium alginate — no difference in pain or adverse effects; patient comfort favoured polyurethane (4 RCTs, 127 subjects)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis, polyurethane vs calcium alginate dressings for skin-graft donor sites
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials and observational studies comparing polyurethane with calcium alginate dressings for split-thickness skin-graft donor sites: four RCTs enrolling 127 subjects were identified for the quantitative comparison.
cards.result: There was no significant difference between polyurethane and calcium alginate in pain intensity on day 1 (mean difference 0.13; P=0.80) or day 5 (MD 0.20; P=0.38), ease of application (odds ratio 3.08; P=0.47), or adverse effects (excessive exudate, infection, haematoma). Patient comfort significantly favoured polyurethane (OR 44.11; P<0.00001) — an implausibly large odds ratio from very small studies, printed as published. The authors judge polyurethane more favourable for comfort, healing and cosmetic outcomes while noting comparable pain and adverse-effect profiles, and call for cost-effectiveness studies.
cards.watchOut: Only 127 subjects across four RCTs — this synthesis largely re-presents the small primary trials (including the Higgins trial carded above), so it is not independent confirmation; the comfort odds ratio of 44.11 signals very sparse data. Its PubMed record carries no MeSH terms.
cards.source: Alsaif A et al. Polyurethane Versus Calcium Alginate Dressings for Split-Thickness Skin Graft Donor Site: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Cureus. 2021. PMID: 34987912. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Synthesis: donor-site dressing choice is SPLIT by class and endpoint — hydrogel unsupported (possibly slower), povidone-iodine foam fastest in one RCT, hydrocolloid/film faster than foam in another, polyurethane vs alginate a comfort-and-workload trade-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: donor-site dressing choice is SPLIT by class and endpoint — hydrogel unsupported (possibly slower), povidone-iodine foam fastest in one RCT, hydrocolloid/film faster than foam in another, polyurethane vs alginate a comfort-and-workload trade-off
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: No dressing class wins across endpoints. Hydrogel: insufficient evidence (Cochrane, 2 trials, 162 participants), with low-certainty evidence of slower healing than alginate or gauze. Speed of epithelialisation: povidone-iodine foam beat hydrocellular foam and petrolatum gauze in a 106-patient RCT (12.74 vs 16.61 vs 15.06 days), and a hydrocolloid (Aquacel) and a film (Mediskin I) beat a foam (Allevyn) in a 73-site RCT. Polyurethane versus calcium alginate: no healing or pain difference in the primary RCT (n=36) or the meta-analysis (127 subjects), with polyurethane costing more dressing changes in the trial but scoring better on patient comfort in the synthesis. Infection rates were low and did not differ in any carded report. The graft site itself is a different wound and a different shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Healing-time definitions differ between trials and have not been pooled.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Prophylactic incisional NPWT beyond fracture & caesarean (PARTIAL of live #651): groin RCTs support it (SSI OR 0.35, relative); laparotomy unsettled — RCT-only synthesis null (RR 0.56, CI crosses 1)
shelves.question: In adults with primarily closed surgical incisions other than lower-limb fracture and caesarean incisions — closed laparotomy (general / colorectal), vascular groin incisions, orthopaedic and breast incisions — does prophylactic incisional negative-pressure wound therapy reduce surgical-site infection and wound complications versus a standard dressing? (The fracture and caesarean question is asked at live #651.)
shelves.mesh: Humans · Models, Statistical · Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy · Postoperative Complications · Seroma · Surgical Wound Dehiscence · Surgical Wound Infection · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: SPLIT by incision site and by study design — carded per site, never as one pooled closed-incision claim. This shelf is the PARTIAL slice beyond live #651, which asks only the lower-limb fracture and caesarean question. GROIN (arterial surgery): a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs (1,049 incisions) found SSI reduced (OR 0.35, relative), and two primary RCTs carded here agree in direction, one significant (major wound complications 8.5% vs 25% in high-risk patients) and one not (30-day SSI 11% vs 19%, underpowered). LAPAROTOMY: syntheses disagree — a JAMA Surgery meta-analysis including non-randomised studies found SSI lower (OR 0.25, relative), while the RCT-only meta-analysis found no significant difference (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.03), and the one primary laparotomy RCT carded here (n=50) was significant only on a one-sided test. ALL CLOSED INCISIONS (2016): infection RR 0.54 (relative), moderate-quality evidence with heterogeneity. Three retracted syntheses in this literature were fenced and NOT carded (see the synthesis card).

cards.headline: All-closed-incisions meta-analysis (Hyldig 2016): NPWT reduced wound infection (RR 0.54, relative) and seroma (RR 0.48, relative) across 10 RCTs — moderate-quality, heterogeneous evidence
cards.summary: All-closed-incisions meta-analysis (Hyldig 2016): NPWT reduced wound infection (RR 0.54, relative) and seroma (RR 0.48, relative) across 10 RCTs — moderate-quality, heterogeneous evidence
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, incisional NPWT vs standard dressings on closed incisions (all sites)
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of negative-pressure wound therapy versus standard dressings on closed surgical incisions: 10 studies reporting 1,311 incisions in 1,089 patients, across mixed surgical sites (the fracture and caesarean slices of this literature are homed at live #651; this shelf's question is the other incisions).
cards.result: NPWT was associated with a significant reduction in wound infection (relative risk 0.54; 95% CI 0.33 to 0.89) and seroma formation (RR 0.48; 95% CI 0.27 to 0.84) versus standard care — relative measures; the reduction in wound dehiscence was not significant. Numbers needed to treat were 3 (seroma), 17 (dehiscence) and 25 (infection). Methodological heterogeneity led to downgrading the quality of evidence to moderate for infection and seroma and low for dehiscence, and the authors state no general recommendations can be made yet.
cards.watchOut: A pooled all-sites estimate from 2016 with heterogeneity the authors themselves flag — it is carded as background; the site-specific cards below govern the laparotomy and groin answers, and this pooled figure must not be quoted as the answer for any single incision type.
cards.source: Hyldig N et al. Meta-analysis of negative-pressure wound therapy for closed surgical incisions. The British Journal of Surgery. 2016. PMID: 26994715. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laparotomy meta-analysis (Sahebally 2018, JAMA Surgery): SSI lower with NPWT (pooled OR 0.25, relative) — but only 3 of 9 studies were randomised
cards.summary: Laparotomy meta-analysis (Sahebally 2018, JAMA Surgery): SSI lower with NPWT (pooled OR 0.25, relative) — but only 3 of 9 studies were randomised
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (randomised and non-randomised studies), prophylactic NPWT for closed laparotomy incisions in general/colorectal surgery
cards.people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of prophylactic NPWT for closed laparotomy incisions in general and colorectal surgery (elective and emergency): 9 unique studies (3 randomised trials, 2 prospective and 4 retrospective studies) capturing 1,266 patients, with 1,187 patients (1,189 incisions) in the final analysis. Significant clinical and methodologic heterogeneity existed among studies.
cards.result: On random-effects analysis, NPWT was associated with a significantly lower SSI rate than standard dressings (pooled odds ratio 0.25; 95% CI 0.12 to 0.52; P<.001) — a relative measure. There was no difference in seroma (OR 0.38; 95% CI 0.12 to 1.23; P=.11) or wound dehiscence (OR 2.03; 95% CI 0.61 to 6.78; P=.25). In a sensitivity analysis restricted to colorectal procedures, NPWT significantly reduced SSI (OR 0.16; 95% CI 0.07 to 0.36).
cards.watchOut: Two-thirds of its studies are non-randomised, so the striking OR 0.25 is vulnerable to selection bias — compare the RCT-only synthesis on the next card, which does not confirm it.
cards.source: Sahebally SM et al. Negative Pressure Wound Therapy for Closed Laparotomy Incisions in General and Colorectal Surgery: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis. JAMA Surgery. 2018. PMID: 30267040. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laparotomy RCT-only meta-analysis (Kuper 2020): NO significant SSI difference (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.03) across 5 RCTs, 792 patients — routine use not supported
cards.summary: Laparotomy RCT-only meta-analysis (Kuper 2020): NO significant SSI difference (RR 0.56; 95% CI 0.30 to 1.03) across 5 RCTs, 792 patients — routine use not supported
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised trials only, prophylactic NPWT for closed laparotomy incisions
cards.people: A meta-analysis restricted to English-language randomised controlled trials comparing prophylactic NPWT with standard dressings on primarily closed laparotomy incisions after open abdominal surgery (searches to December 31, 2018): 5 RCTs totalling 792 patients, analysed with a random-effects model. Statistical heterogeneity was significant (I²=67.4%; P=0.015).
cards.result: There was no significant difference in surgical-site infection risk between NPWT and standard dressings: relative risk 0.56 (95% CI 0.30 to 1.03; P=0.064) — a relative measure whose confidence interval crosses 1. The authors conclude the adoption of NPWT for routine SSI prophylaxis following laparotomy is currently not supported and should be used primarily in the context of a clinical trial.
cards.watchOut: The point estimate favours NPWT but is not significant and heterogeneity is high; this RCT-only result and the JAMA Surgery result above differ mainly in which study designs were admitted — that design difference is the lesson of the laparotomy slice.
cards.source: Kuper TM et al. Prophylactic Negative Pressure Wound Therapy for Closed Laparotomy Incisions: A Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Annals of Surgery. 2020. PMID: 31860549. cards.headline: Primary laparotomy RCT — P.I.C.O. trial (O'Leary 2017): 30-day SSI 8.3% vs 32.0%, significant only one-sided (P=0.043 one-sided; P=0.074 two-sided), in 50 patients
cards.summary: Primary laparotomy RCT — P.I.C.O. trial (O'Leary 2017): 30-day SSI 8.3% vs 32.0%, significant only one-sided (P=0.043 one-sided; P=0.074 two-sided), in 50 patients
cards.type: Primary randomised controlled open-label trial (P.I.C.O.), prophylactic negative-pressure dressing vs standard dressing on closed laparotomy wounds — one of the RCTs inside the laparotomy syntheses above
cards.people: 50 patients undergoing open abdominal surgery randomised to a prophylactic negative-pressure dressing (n=25) or standard dressing (n=25) on the closed laparotomy wound, in a randomised, controlled, open-label trial analysed per protocol. Primary endpoint was SSI incidence at 30 days; secondary endpoints included SSI at 4 days, length of stay, cosmetic outcome and patient satisfaction.
cards.result: SSI at 30 days was 8.3% with the negative-pressure dressing versus 32.0% with standard dressing (P=0.043 one-sided; P=0.074 two-sided) — absolute rates, printed both, with the test sidedness stated because the conclusion depends on it. There was no difference in SSI at 4 days (4.1% vs 8.0%). Length of stay was significantly shorter with the negative-pressure dressing (6.1 vs 14.7 days; P=0.019 two-sided); cosmetic outcome and patient satisfaction did not differ. Standard dressing was the only significant predictor of SSI in their analysis.
cards.watchOut: Only 50 patients, per-protocol analysis, and its headline significance is one-sided only (two-sided P=0.074) — carded so the laparotomy slice rests on a primary trial as well as syntheses, with its fragility on the face.
cards.source: O'Leary DP et al. Prophylactic Negative Pressure Dressing Use in Closed Laparotomy Wounds Following Abdominal Operations: A Randomized, Controlled, Open-label Trial: The P.I.C.O. Trial. cards.headline: Groin-incision meta-analysis (Svensson-Björk 2019): incisional NPWT reduced SSI after arterial surgery (OR 0.35, relative) across 7 RCTs, 1,049 incisions — moderate-quality evidence
cards.summary: Groin-incision meta-analysis (Svensson-Björk 2019): incisional NPWT reduced SSI after arterial surgery (OR 0.35, relative) across 7 RCTs, 1,049 incisions — moderate-quality evidence
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, incisional NPWT for closed groin incisions in arterial surgery
cards.people: A systematic review with meta-analysis of randomised trials of incisional NPWT on closed groin incisions after arterial surgery, with an a priori published protocol (PROSPERO CRD42018090298): 7 RCTs including 1,049 incisions. Heterogeneity was low (I²=0%); the quality of evidence was graded moderate; two studies had multiple risk-of-bias domains rated high.
cards.result: Meta-analysis showed a reduction in surgical-site infection with incisional NPWT (odds ratio 0.35; 95% CI 0.24 to 0.50; P<0.001) — a relative measure. A subgroup meta-analysis of three studies of lower-limb revascularisation procedures only (363 incisions) showed a similar reduction (OR 0.37; 95% CI 0.22 to 0.63). The authors note the risk of bias and the need for a high-quality RCT with cost-effectiveness analysis.
cards.watchOut: RCT-only and low-heterogeneity — the strongest synthesis design on this shelf — but two included studies carried multiple high risk-of-bias ratings, and absolute SSI rates are not given in the record, so the size of the absolute benefit cannot be printed from this record alone; the two primary groin RCTs below supply absolute rates.

cards.headline: Primary groin RCT (Lee 2017): 30-day SSI 11% with NPWT vs 19% with standard dressing — NOT significant (P=.24); the trial was underpowered (102 high-risk patients)
cards.summary: Primary groin RCT (Lee 2017): 30-day SSI 11% with NPWT vs 19% with standard dressing — NOT significant (P=.24); the trial was underpowered (102 high-risk patients)
cards.type: Primary single-centre randomised trial, NPWT vs standard dressing on closed high-risk groin wounds in lower-extremity revascularisation — one of the RCTs inside the groin synthesis above
cards.people: 102 patients at high risk for SSI (previous femoral artery surgical exposure 29%, BMI >30 kg/m² 39%, or ischaemic tissue loss 32%) undergoing lower-extremity revascularisation with primarily closed groin wounds at a single academic centre, randomised to NPWT or standard dressing. Procedures included femoral-to-distal bypass (57%), femoral endarterectomy (18%) and femoral-to-femoral crossover (17%).
cards.result: The primary outcome, 30-day groin SSI, was 11% in the NPWT group versus 19% in the standard-dressing group (P=.24 — not significant; absolute rates printed both). Mean hospital stay was significantly shorter with NPWT (6.4 vs 8.9 days; P=.01). There was no difference in readmission or reoperation for SSI, or mortality. The authors state the infection rate was lower than expected, leaving the study underpowered to detect a difference at the prespecified level.
cards.watchOut: Null on its primary outcome and underpowered by its authors' own account — carded because a shelf built only on the pooled groin estimate would hide that one of its primary trials did not reach significance.

cards.headline: Primary groin RCT (Kwon 2018): negative-pressure therapy (Prevena, Acelity) cut major wound complications in high-risk groin incisions (8.5% vs 25%; P<.001) — 119 incisions
cards.summary: Primary groin RCT (Kwon 2018): negative-pressure therapy (Prevena, Acelity) cut major wound complications in high-risk groin incisions (8.5% vs 25%; P<.001) — 119 incisions
cards.type: Primary single-institution randomised trial, negative-pressure therapy (named product as published) vs standard gauze on closed high-risk vascular groin incisions — one of the RCTs inside the groin synthesis above
cards.people: 119 femoral incisions closed primarily after elective vascular surgery (inflow and outflow procedures) at a single institution, in incisions categorised as high risk for wound complications (BMI >30 kg/m², pannus, reoperation, prosthetic graft, poor nutrition, immunosuppression, or HbA1c >8%), randomised 1:1 to standard gauze (n=60) or negative-pressure therapy with the Prevena system (Acelity, San Antonio, Tex) (n=59); a further 21 low-risk incisions served as controls. Follow-up was 30 days for wound complications, length of stay, reoperation, readmission and variable hospital costs.
cards.result: Major wound complications were 8.5% with negative-pressure therapy versus 25% in high-risk controls (P<.001) — absolute rates, printed both — including five of the six infections in the therapy group versus all 12 infections in 60 control incisions, as reported. Reoperation (8.5%; P<.05) and readmission (6.8%; P<.04) were also reduced, but length of stay was not (10.6 days in both high-risk groups). Average variable cost was lower with therapy ($30,492 vs $36,537; saving $6,045 per patient; P=.11 — not significant). Low-risk controls had a 4.8% major-complication rate. The authors recommend negative-pressure therapy for groin incisions at high risk of wound complications.
cards.watchOut: Single institution, incisions (not patients) as the unit, and the population is selected high-risk incisions — the 25% control complication rate is what makes the absolute benefit large, and it should not be extrapolated to low-risk groin incisions (4.8% in this study's own low-risk controls).
cards.source: Kwon J et al. A randomized clinical trial evaluating negative pressure therapy to decrease vascular groin incision complications. Journal of Vascular Surgery. 2018. PMID: 30126781. cards.headline: Synthesis: beyond fracture and caesarean — groin incisions have the most consistent RCT support for incisional NPWT; laparotomy is unsettled (positive mixed-design synthesis, null RCT-only synthesis); retracted syntheses in this literature were fenced and not carded
cards.summary: Synthesis: beyond fracture and caesarean — groin incisions have the most consistent RCT support for incisional NPWT; laparotomy is unsettled (positive mixed-design synthesis, null RCT-only synthesis); retracted syntheses in this literature were fenced and not carded
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Carded per incision site, never pooled. GROIN: 7 RCTs pooled to OR 0.35 (relative) for SSI, with one primary RCT significant on major wound complications in high-risk incisions (8.5% vs 25%) and one null on 30-day SSI (11% vs 19%, underpowered). LAPAROTOMY: a mixed-design synthesis found OR 0.25 (relative) while the RCT-only synthesis found RR 0.56 with a confidence interval crossing 1, and the carded primary RCT (n=50) reached significance only one-sided. shelves.title: Barbed vs conventional sutures: closure 4–16 minutes faster and cheaper in arthroplasty and spine syntheses, complications split by layer — full-layer barbed closure raised complications to 19.7%
shelves.question: In adults having wound closure with sutures — total knee and hip arthroplasty, spine surgery and other fields as tested — do knotless barbed sutures shorten closure and operating time versus conventional sutures, and do they differ in wound complications, dehiscence and cost?
shelves.mesh: Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/instrumentation,methods · Equipment Design · Humans · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Sutures · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Hip/adverse effects,methods · Arthroplasty, Replacement, Knee/adverse effects,methods · Female · Male · Postoperative Complications · Suture Techniques/instrumentation · Treatment Outcome · Length of Stay · Operative Time · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology · Spine/surgery · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology · Suture Techniques · Wound Healing/physiology · Costs and Cost Analysis · Single-Blind Method · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Knee Joint/surgery · Osteoarthritis, Knee/surgery · Range of Motion, Articular · Suture Techniques/economics · Blood Loss, Surgical · California · Disability Evaluation · Health Care Costs · Joint Capsule/surgery · Surgical Wound/complications · Suture Techniques/adverse effects · Prospective Studies
shelves.balance: SPLIT. The time benefit is consistent everywhere it was randomised: the TKA synthesis (6 RCTs, 826 knees) found closure 4.41 minutes faster with barbed suture, the hip/knee synthesis (4 level-I trials, 588 patients) found 6.3 minutes faster, and the spine synthesis (7 studies, 8,645 patients) found closure 16.36 minutes and operating time 20.13 minutes shorter. Cost follows time in most reports (synthesis cost difference −282.61 in the units reported; $298 per case in the hip/knee synthesis; $324 vs $419 in the largest TKA RCT). Wound complications are where the record splits: the syntheses find no significant difference, and two TKA RCTs found fewer complications with barbed suture, but a 582-patient three-arm TKA RCT found full-layer barbed closure RAISED incision complications to 19.7% versus 7.2% for capsule-only barbed and 9.3% for traditional capsule closure, and an early TJA RCT reported more frequent and severe wound complications with barbed suture. The defensible reading is layer-specific: barbed suture for the capsule/deep layer saves time without a complication penalty in the randomised record; full-layer (including skin) barbed closure is the limb with a harm signal. Stop-condition check: at least three primary RCTs from inside the syntheses are carded per field for arthroplasty (Gililland 2014, Chan 2017, Sah 2015, Feng 2020) and one primary spine RCT from inside the spine synthesis (Shi 2022) — the spine primary base is one RCT, stated on the face. The retracted TKA synthesis PMID 37519132 is NOT carded, per the row fence. Tested products are named where the publication gives them (Stratafix in Chan 2017); where the record names no brand, the card says so.

cards.headline: TKA synthesis (Li 2020): barbed vs traditional suture in primary total knee arthroplasty — closure 4.41 minutes faster and cheaper, no significant rise in complications across 6 RCTs (826 knees)
cards.summary: TKA synthesis (Li 2020): barbed vs traditional suture in primary total knee arthroplasty — closure 4.41 minutes faster and cheaper, no significant rise in complications across 6 RCTs (826 knees)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (barbed vs traditional suture, primary TKA)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of barbed versus conventional suture for incision closure after primary total knee arthroplasty; 6 RCTs totalling 826 knees were included.
cards.result: Barbed suture shortened wound closure time (mean difference −4.41 minutes, 95% CI −5.11 to −3.72; P<.00001), reduced total wound-closure cost (mean difference −282.61, 95% CI −445.36 to −119.85; P=.0007, currency as reported in the source trials) and reduced needle-stick injury (risk ratio 0.14, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.78; P=.02). Complications did not differ significantly (risk ratio 0.80; P=.38) and neither did suture breakage (risk ratio 4.58, 95% CI 0.16 to 128.29; P=.37), range of motion at 6 weeks and 3 months, or Knee Society Score at 6 weeks. The authors concluded barbed suture is fast, low-cost, safe and effective in TKA while calling for more literature and longer follow-up.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis card: its numbers pool the primary RCTs carded separately below and must not be counted as independent of them. The complication confidence interval printed in the record is internally inconsistent with its P value, so this card reports the risk ratio and P value as printed and claims no more.

cards.headline: Hip and knee synthesis (Borzio 2016): 4 level-I trials, 588 patients — barbed closure 6.3 minutes faster, $298 saved per case, minor and major complication odds not significantly different
cards.summary: Hip and knee synthesis (Borzio 2016): 4 level-I trials, 588 patients — barbed closure 6.3 minutes faster, $298 saved per case, minor and major complication odds not significantly different
cards.type: Meta-analysis of level-I trials (barbed vs conventional suture, total hip and knee arthroplasty)
cards.people: Meta-analysis of all level-I trials of bidirectional barbed suture in total joint arthroplasty: 4 studies, 588 randomised patients — barbed closure 290 joint replacements (268 knees, 22 hips) versus conventional closure 298 (279 knees, 19 hips).
cards.result: Wound closure with barbed suture was 6.3 minutes faster than conventional closure (P<0.05). Odds of a minor complication were nearly identical (odds ratio 1.04, P=0.95) and odds of a major complication were not significantly different (odds ratio 2.94, P=0.27). Mean overall saving, counting the higher suture price, was USD 298 per case across hip and knee arthroplasty.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 trials and only 41 hips in total: this synthesis is really a knee-arthroplasty synthesis with a small hip limb, and the major-complication odds ratio of 2.94, though non-significant, is imprecise and points the wrong way — the primary hip RCTs are carded on the companion hip records, not here.

cards.headline: Spine synthesis (Sarhan 2024): barbed vs conventional closure in spine surgery — operating time 20.13 minutes and closure time 16.36 minutes shorter; complications, infection, stay and reintervention not significantly different (7 studies, 8,645 patients)
cards.summary: Spine synthesis (Sarhan 2024): barbed vs conventional closure in spine surgery — operating time 20.13 minutes and closure time 16.36 minutes shorter; complications, infection, stay and reintervention not significantly different (7 studies, 8,645 patients)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (barbed vs conventional suture, spine surgery)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of barbed versus conventional sutures for wound closure in spine surgery: 7 eligible studies totalling 8,645 patients (search to 5 May 2024).
cards.result: Barbed sutures gave shorter operative time (mean difference −20.13 minutes, 95% CI −28.47 to −11.78; P<0.001) and shorter wound closure time (mean difference −16.36 minutes, 95% CI −20.9 to −11.82; P<0.001). Overall postoperative wound complications (risk ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.60 to 1.14; P=0.25), postoperative infection (risk ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.33 to 1.06; P=0.08), length of stay (mean difference −0.26 days, 95% CI −0.75 to 0.22; P=0.28) and reintervention (risk ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.48 to 2.05; P=0.98) did not differ significantly. The authors called for high-quality RCTs with long-term follow-up and cost-effectiveness assessment.
cards.watchOut: The 7 included studies are NOT all randomised — the record does not restrict eligibility to RCTs, and the large patient total is carried by non-randomised series. The only primary spine RCT carded on this shelf is Shi 2022 below; do not read the pooled time saving as RCT-grade for spine.
cards.source: Sarhan K et al. Barbed sutures versus conventional sutures for wound closure in spine surgeries: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Neurosurgical review. 2024. PMID: 39384652. cards.headline: Primary TKA RCT (Gililland 2014): barbed running vs knotted interrupted closure in 411 randomised patients — closure 9.8 vs 14.5 minutes, total closure cost $324 vs $419, early complications similar
cards.summary: Primary TKA RCT (Gililland 2014): barbed running vs knotted interrupted closure in 411 randomised patients — closure 9.8 vs 14.5 minutes, total closure cost $324 vs $419, early complications similar
cards.type: Primary multicentre RCT (barbed running vs knotted interrupted closure, primary TKA) — inside the syntheses above
cards.people: Multicentre prospective randomised trial: 411 patients undergoing primary total knee arthroplasty randomised to barbed running closure (n=191) or knotted interrupted suture closure (n=203) as analysed. This trial sits inside the TKA syntheses carded above. The record names no barbed product brand.
cards.result: Closure time was shorter with barbed suture (9.8 vs 14.5 minutes; P<0.001) and total closure cost was lower ($324 vs $419; P<0.001), counting suture and operating-room time costs. Early complications and outcomes were similar between groups.
cards.watchOut: Early complications only: a 411-patient trial cannot exclude differences in uncommon events such as deep infection, and no product brand is named in the record, so the result cannot be tied to one manufacturer's barbed suture.
cards.source: Gililland JM et al. Barbed versus standard sutures for closure in total knee arthroplasty: a multicenter prospective randomized trial. The Journal of arthroplasty. 2014. PMID: 24973931. cards.headline: Primary TKA RCT (Chan 2017): bidirectional barbed Stratafix vs Vicryl in 109 knees — arthrotomy closure 325 vs 491 seconds, fewer leak tests (2 vs 10) and fewer wound complications (2 vs 11), saving USD 48.7 per case locally
cards.summary: Primary TKA RCT (Chan 2017): bidirectional barbed Stratafix vs Vicryl in 109 knees — arthrotomy closure 325 vs 491 seconds, fewer leak tests (2 vs 10) and fewer wound complications (2 vs 11), saving USD 48.7 per case locally
cards.type: Primary RCT (bidirectional barbed Stratafix vs Vicryl, primary TKA) — inside the syntheses above; tested product named
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 109 knees in primary total knee arthroplasty: bidirectional barbed suture (Stratafix, Ethicon Inc) versus traditional synthetic absorbable suture (Vicryl, Ethicon Inc) for arthrotomy and subcutaneous closure; follow-up to 3 months. This trial sits inside the TKA syntheses carded above.
cards.result: Closure was significantly faster with barbed suture (arthrotomy 325 vs 491 seconds; subcutaneous 306 vs 381 seconds; P<.05). The traditional group had significantly more positive leak tests (10 vs 2; P<.05) and more wound complications (11 vs 2; P<.05). Range of motion and Knee Society Score did not differ. Counting suture material and operating-time cost, barbed suture saved on average USD 48.7 per TKA at the authors' institute.
cards.watchOut: Single-centre and small (109 knees): the complication advantage (2 vs 11) rests on few events, and the cost saving is an institute-specific figure that depends on local operating-room time pricing.
cards.source: Chan VWK et al. Does Barbed Suture Lower Cost and Improve Outcome in Total Knee Arthroplasty? A Randomized Controlled Trial. The Journal of arthroplasty. 2017. PMID: 28089469. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary bilateral TKA RCT (Sah 2015): within-patient randomised comparison in 50 patients — barbed closure 11.4 vs 16.1 minutes and $175 cheaper per case, no difference in scores, range of motion or wound appearance at 1 year
cards.summary: Primary bilateral TKA RCT (Sah 2015): within-patient randomised comparison in 50 patients — barbed closure 11.4 vs 16.1 minutes and $175 cheaper per case, no difference in scores, range of motion or wound appearance at 1 year
cards.type: Primary within-patient RCT (bidirectional barbed vs standard suture, simultaneous bilateral TKA) — inside the syntheses above
cards.people: Prospective randomised within-patient controlled trial: 50 consecutive patients having simultaneous bilateral total knee arthroplasties under one anaesthetic, one knee closed with running knotless bidirectional barbed suture and the other with standard interrupted and running sutures, randomly assigned by side; follow-up to 1 year. This trial sits inside the TKA syntheses carded above. The record names no barbed product brand.
cards.result: Mean wound closure time was 4.7 minutes less with barbed suture (11.4 ± 2.2 vs 16.1 ± 2.2 minutes; P<0.001); overall tourniquet time did not differ. There were no needle disengagements or suture breakages with barbed closure, versus 5 premature needle disengagements and 3 breakages with standard closure (P<0.005). No wound dehiscence or arthrotomy disruption occurred with either technique. One-year range of motion (126.7° vs 125.6°) and Knee Society knee scores (92.8 vs 93.3) did not differ. Counting material against time saved, barbed closure saved a mean USD 175 per case.
cards.watchOut: Fifty patients, however elegant the within-patient design: as the author states, larger numbers are needed to compare uncommon complications, and none were observed in this small series — absence here is not proof of safety.
cards.source: Sah AP et al. Is There an Advantage to Knotless Barbed Suture in TKA Wound Closure? A Randomized Trial in Simultaneous Bilateral TKAs. Clinical orthopaedics and related research. 2015. PMID: 25631171. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary TKA RCT (Feng 2020): the layer matters — full-layer barbed closure RAISED incision complications to 19.7%, while capsule-only barbed closure (7.2%) matched traditional capsule closure (9.3%); both barbed strategies were faster (582 patients, three arms)
cards.summary: Primary TKA RCT (Feng 2020): the layer matters — full-layer barbed closure RAISED incision complications to 19.7%, while capsule-only barbed closure (7.2%) matched traditional capsule closure (9.3%); both barbed strategies were faster (582 patients, three arms)
cards.type: Primary three-arm RCT (full-layer barbed vs capsule-only barbed vs traditional capsule closure, TKA)
cards.people: Single-centre randomised controlled trial, December 2017 to April 2019: 582 patients having total knee arthroplasty assigned to full-layer barbed suture (group A, n=193), barbed suture for the joint capsule only (group B, n=195), or traditional absorbable suture for the joint capsule (group C, n=194); primary endpoint incision complications within 3 months.
cards.result: Incision complications were significantly higher with full-layer barbed closure: 19.7% in group A versus 7.2% in group B and 9.3% in group C (P<0.0125); capsule-only barbed and traditional capsule closure did not differ. Closure time was shorter in both barbed groups (13.5 ± 2.0 minutes in A and 16.1 ± 1.9 minutes in B) than with traditional closure (25.0 ± 2.0 minutes; P<0.001). The authors concluded full-thickness bidirectional barbed closure is not recommended, while capsule barbed closure is effective and time-saving.
cards.watchOut: This is the shelf's principal harm signal and it is layer-specific: it condemns barbed suture carried through every layer including skin, not capsule closure. Single-centre; the record states registration at ClinicalTrials.gov with the ChiCTR number printed in the source line.
cards.source: Feng S et al. Are There Lower Complication Rates with Bidirectional Barbed Suture in Total Knee Arthroplasty Incision Closure? A Randomized Clinical Trial. Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research. 2020. PMID: 32753571. Registry ID: ChiCTR-IPR-17013677. cards.headline: Primary spine RCT (Shi 2022): knotless barbed vs conventional closure in posterior long-segment lumbar surgery (181 patients) — operating-room and closure times shorter and wound complications (dehiscence and infection) fewer, with no difference in stay, readmission or cost
cards.summary: Primary spine RCT (Shi 2022): knotless barbed vs conventional closure in posterior long-segment lumbar surgery (181 patients) — operating-room and closure times shorter and wound complications (dehiscence and infection) fewer, with no difference in stay, readmission or cost
cards.type: Primary RCT (knotless barbed vs conventional closure, posterior long-segment lumbar surgery) — inside the spine synthesis above
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trial: 181 patients undergoing posterior long-segment lumbar surgery assigned to barbed suture wound closure (n=91) or conventional suture closure (n=90). This trial sits inside the spine synthesis carded above. The record names no barbed product brand.
cards.result: The barbed group had significantly lower operating-room time (P=0.036), wound closure time (P<0.001), average wound closure time (P<0.001) and wound complication rates for dehiscence and infection combined (P=0.031). Incision length (P=0.086), length of stay (P=0.174), 90-day readmission (P=0.232) and costs (P=0.205) did not differ significantly. The fetched record prints P values without the group time or complication numbers, and this card claims none.
cards.watchOut: The spine field's only carded primary RCT: one trial of 181 patients in long-segment lumbar surgery cannot carry the whole spine question, and its abstract reports significance without the underlying numbers.

cards.headline: Synthesis: barbed suture reliably buys closure time in every randomised field tested, at no pooled complication cost for deep/capsular closure — but full-layer barbed closure raised complications in the largest three-arm TKA trial, so the answer is layer-specific, not blanket
cards.summary: Synthesis: barbed suture reliably buys closure time in every randomised field tested, at no pooled complication cost for deep/capsular closure — but full-layer barbed closure raised complications in the largest three-arm TKA trial, so the answer is layer-specific, not blanket
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: 3 syntheses (TKA 6 RCTs / 826 knees; hip+knee 4 level-I trials / 588 patients; spine 7 studies / 8,645 patients) and 5 primary RCTs (411, 109, 50 within-patient, 582 and 181 patients).
cards.result: Closure time falls by roughly 4–6 minutes in arthroplasty syntheses and by about 16 minutes for closure (20 minutes operating time) in the spine synthesis, and cost falls with time in most reports. Pooled complications do not differ in any synthesis. Against that, Feng 2020 (n=582) found full-layer barbed closure caused significantly more incision complications (19.7%) than capsule-only barbed (7.2%) or traditional capsule closure (9.3%), while Chan 2017 found fewer complications with barbed closure (2 vs 11) — a genuine split at primary-trial level, resolved most plausibly by layer: capsule/deep barbed closure is the supported use. The retracted TKA synthesis PMID 37519132 was not carded, per the commissioning row's fence. No randomised evidence here addresses dehiscence as a stand-alone powered endpoint.
cards.watchOut: Synthesis and primary cards overlap by design (the primaries sit inside the syntheses): never add their patient totals together as if independent.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Early postoperative showering (FLOOR-RISK): no infection increase in any randomised report — Cochrane's only trial 8.5% vs 8.8% (RR 0.96, CI 0.62–1.48), 7-RCT meta-analysis null — but the base is thin
shelves.question: After surgery, does early bathing or showering (within about 48 hours, wound uncovered or as tested) increase wound infection or dehiscence versus keeping the wound dry and covered until suture removal or a later time point — and how do pain, comfort and satisfaction compare?

shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, stated on the face: this shelf rests on a thin primary base — the Cochrane review found exactly ONE eligible randomised trial (857 patients having minor skin excision), and the primary randomised reports carded here total four (857; 444; 32; 51 patients) plus a 2020 meta-analysis pooling 7 RCTs (1,881 patients for infection). Within that base, no report finds early showering increases infection: the Cochrane trial found surgical site infection in 8.5% with bathing from 12 hours versus 8.8% with bathing delayed at least 48 hours (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48 — wide, so a clinically important effect either way is not excluded); the 2020 meta-analysis of showering on or before postoperative day 2 versus later found no difference in infection or complications; the largest primary RCT (444 patients, showering from 48 hours) found 1.8% versus 2.7% infection; and the small sternotomy RCT (51 patients) found FEWER sternal infections with showering at 48–72 hours (7.7% vs 32.0%) alongside less pain and higher comfort and satisfaction (patient-reported outcomes). Comfort and satisfaction favour early showering wherever measured. PROPOSED STAMP: MAYBE (weak evidence) — no infection increase is shown, but the base is too thin and the confidence intervals too wide to call the question settled.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (Toon 2015): only ONE randomised trial exists for early vs delayed postoperative bathing — 857 minor skin excision patients, infection 8.5% (bathing from 12 hours) vs 8.8% (delayed at least 48 hours), risk ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.48); evidence inconclusive
cards.summary: Cochrane review (Toon 2015): only ONE randomised trial exists for early vs delayed postoperative bathing — 857 minor skin excision patients, infection 8.5% (bathing from 12 hours) vs 8.8% (delayed at least 48 hours), risk ratio 0.96 (95% CI 0.62 to 1.48); evidence inconclusive
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review (early vs delayed postoperative bathing/showering) — one included RCT
cards.people: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials of early (within 48 hours) versus delayed (over 48 hours) postoperative bathing or showering in patients with closed surgical wounds. Only one trial was identified: 857 patients undergoing minor skin excision in primary care, wounds sutured, randomised to dressing removal after 12 hours with normal bathing resumed (n=415) or dressing retained at least 48 hours (n=442).
cards.result: The single included trial, at high risk of bias, reported only surgical site infection: 8.5% in the early bathing group versus 8.8% in the delayed group (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48) — no statistically significant difference, but the confidence interval is wide enough that a clinically significant increase or decrease in infection from early bathing cannot be ruled out. The reviewers concluded there is no conclusive randomised evidence on the benefits or harms of early versus delayed showering or bathing and recommended further trials.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK at the root of this shelf: the entire Cochrane-eligible randomised base in 2015 was one high-risk-of-bias trial in minor skin excision — its 8–9% infection rates do not transfer to major surgery, and its confidence interval excludes neither harm nor benefit.
cards.source: Toon CD et al. Early versus delayed post-operative bathing or showering to prevent wound complications. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2015. PMID: 26204454. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Copeland-Halperin 2020): 7 RCTs, 1,881 patients — showering on or before postoperative day 2 vs later showed no difference in infection (P=0.45) or complications (P=0.36)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Copeland-Halperin 2020): 7 RCTs, 1,881 patients — showering on or before postoperative day 2 vs later showed no difference in infection (P=0.45) or complications (P=0.36)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (postoperative showering timing)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to randomised controlled trials of postoperative showering timing: 7 RCTs (1,881 patients; 605 showered on or before postoperative day 2) in the infection analysis and 5 RCTs (958 patients; 477 early) in the complications analysis, across surgical specialties and closure methods.
cards.result: There was no difference in infection rate (P=0.45) or complication rate (P=0.36) between patients allowed to shower within the first 48 hours postoperatively and those prohibited from showering until postoperative day 3 to beyond one week. The authors concluded the published literature demonstrates no increase in overall wound infections or complications with earlier showering, while noting additional randomised studies are needed to determine ideal timing.
cards.watchOut: A pooled null across mixed specialties, closure methods and drain policies: it averages away any procedure-specific risk, and its primary trials include the small reports carded separately below — do not count the totals twice.
cards.source: Copeland-Halperin LR et al. Does the timing of postoperative showering impact infection rates? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of plastic, reconstructive & aesthetic surgery : JPRAS. 2020. PMID: 32307234. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary RCT (Hsieh 2016): showering from 48 hours after clean or clean-contaminated surgery (444 randomised) — infection 1.8% vs 2.7% keeping the wound dry (P=0.751), pain comparable, satisfaction higher and wound-care costs lower with showering
cards.summary: Primary RCT (Hsieh 2016): showering from 48 hours after clean or clean-contaminated surgery (444 randomised) — infection 1.8% vs 2.7% keeping the wound dry (P=0.751), pain comparable, satisfaction higher and wound-care costs lower with showering
cards.type: Primary RCT (showering from 48 hours vs keeping wound dry, clean/clean-contaminated surgery) — inside the 2020 synthesis above
cards.people: Prospective randomised controlled trial, May 2013 to March 2014: 444 patients undergoing thyroid, lung, inguinal hernia, or face and extremity surgery with clean or clean-contaminated wounds, randomised to showering (n=222) or keeping the wound dry (n=222) for wound care starting 48 hours after surgery; 220 per group analysed after 2 losses per group. This trial sits inside the 2020 synthesis carded above.
cards.result: Superficial surgical site infection occurred in 4 of 220 shower patients (1.8%) versus 6 of 220 non-shower patients (2.7%; P=0.751). Postoperative pain scores were comparable. Patients in the shower group were more satisfied with their wound care (a patient-reported outcome) and their wound-care costs were lower. The authors concluded clean and clean-contaminated wounds can be safely showered 48 hours after surgery.
cards.watchOut: Ten infections in total: the trial is powered to exclude only very large infection increases, and its operations (thyroid, lung, hernia, face/extremity) do not include sternotomy, joint replacement or contaminated wounds.
cards.source: Hsieh PY et al. Postoperative Showering for Clean and Clean-contaminated Wounds: A Prospective, Randomized Controlled Trial. Annals of surgery. 2016. PMID: 26655923. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Primary RCT (Gök 2022): showering at 48–72 hours after CABG via median sternotomy (N=51, printed on the face) — sternal wound infection 7.7% vs 32.0% without showering (P=0.038), with less pain and higher comfort and satisfaction
cards.summary: Primary RCT (Gök 2022): showering at 48–72 hours after CABG via median sternotomy (N=51, printed on the face) — sternal wound infection 7.7% vs 32.0% without showering (P=0.038), with less pain and higher comfort and satisfaction
cards.type: Primary RCT (showering 48–72 hours vs delayed showering, CABG median sternotomy) — counts as one primary report per the commissioning row
cards.people: Randomised controlled clinical trial: 51 patients after coronary artery bypass graft surgery through median sternotomy, allocated to showering in the first 48–72 hours (n=26) or no showering until chest-tube suture removal, showering the next day (n=25). N=51 is small and this card is not load-bearing for the shelf's infection conclusion.
cards.result: Sternal wound infection was significantly lower in the shower group (2 of 26, 7.7%) than in the non-shower group (8 of 25, 32.0%; P=0.038); logistic regression gave an adjusted odds ratio of 0.177 (95% CI 0.033 to 0.940; P=0.042) for early showering. Pain severity was significantly lower in the shower group, and comfort and satisfaction scores — patient-reported outcomes — were significantly higher (P<0.05).
cards.watchOut: N=51 with 10 infections total: a 32% control-group sternal infection rate is far above typical sternotomy series, so the apparent protective effect is fragile and likely inflated; read it as 'no harm signal in sternotomy', not as proof showering prevents sternal infection.
cards.source: Gök F et al. The effects of showering in 48-72 h after coronary artery bypass graft surgery through median sternotomy on wound infection, pain, comfort, and satisfaction: randomized controlled trial. European journal of cardiovascular nursing. 2022. PMID: 33871023. Registry ID: NCT04250961. cards.headline: Primary RCT (Yu 2016): showering at 2 days vs 2 weeks after total knee arthroplasty (N=32, printed on the face) — no difference in bacterial recolonisation of the incision and no infections in either group; patients preferred early showering
cards.summary: Primary RCT (Yu 2016): showering at 2 days vs 2 weeks after total knee arthroplasty (N=32, printed on the face) — no difference in bacterial recolonisation of the incision and no infections in either group; patients preferred early showering
cards.type: Primary RCT (showering at 2 days vs 2 weeks after TKA; bacterial colonisation endpoint) — inside the 2020 synthesis above
cards.people: Randomised controlled trial of 32 total knee arthroplasty patients: 16 allowed to shower at 2 days postoperatively and 16 asked to wait until 2 weeks. Skin swabs adjacent to the incision were cultured preoperatively, after closure, at dressing removal and at 2 weeks, with a contralateral-knee control swab; a patient-preference survey was also carried out. N=32 is very small and this card addresses colonisation, not clinical infection.
cards.result: No difference was found between groups in rate of bacterial colonisation or bacterial type, and no patient in either group developed infection. Patients overwhelmingly preferred early showering (reported across survey items, P=.28–.99). The authors concluded there is no difference in surgical-site bacterial recolonisation between early and delayed showering after primary TKA.
cards.watchOut: A colonisation-endpoint study of 32 patients with zero infections: it can say early showering does not change skin flora at the incision, and nothing quantitative about prosthetic joint infection risk.
cards.source: Yu AL et al. Wound Hygiene Practices After Total Knee Arthroplasty: Does It Matter? The Journal of arthroplasty. 2016. PMID: 27129759. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — across one Cochrane trial (857), one 444-patient RCT, two very small RCTs (51 and 32) and a 7-RCT meta-analysis (1,881 patients), early showering (from 12 hours to 48–72 hours, as tested) has never been shown to increase wound infection, and comfort/satisfaction favour it — but confidence intervals remain wide and no large trial in major surgery exists
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — across one Cochrane trial (857), one 444-patient RCT, two very small RCTs (51 and 32) and a 7-RCT meta-analysis (1,881 patients), early showering (from 12 hours to 48–72 hours, as tested) has never been shown to increase wound infection, and comfort/satisfaction favour it — but confidence intervals remain wide and no large trial in major surgery exists
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The stop-condition for this row is met: at least three primary randomised reports from inside the Cochrane review and the 2020 synthesis combined are carded (Hsieh 2016, n=444; Yu 2016, n=32; plus the Cochrane review's own included trial, 857 patients, reported on the Cochrane card), and the sternotomy RCT (Gök 2022, n=51) counts as the additional primary report the row specifies. Every point estimate for infection sits at or below the delayed-showering rate, yet the Cochrane interval (risk ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.62 to 1.48) cannot exclude a substantial increase, and the only sternotomy trial is implausibly positive for its size. The honest statement is: no evidence of harm from early showering as tested, consistent patient-reported comfort and satisfaction gains, and a base too thin for certainty — which is why the stamp is MAYBE (weak evidence) rather than a settled no-difference.
cards.watchOut: Protocols differed (uncovered showering from 12 hours after minor excision; from 48 hours in the larger trials; sternotomy at 48–72 hours): this shelf answers 'early as tested', not every showering protocol, drain situation or contaminated wound.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Antimicrobial dressings on closed incisions: silver RR 0.78 (22% relative reduction) and DACC RR 0.49 pooled — primary trials mixed, mupirocin null
shelves.question: In patients with primarily closed surgical incisions, do antimicrobial dressings — silver, dialkylcarbamoyl chloride (DACC), PHMB, chlorhexidine or mupirocin-impregnated — reduce surgical-site infection versus a standard inert dressing, and does the answer differ by antimicrobial class and by surgical field?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Surgical Wound Infection · Bandages · Anti-Infective Agents · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Anti-Bacterial Agents
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) — synthesis-anchored, carded per class and never as one pooled claim. The 2026 synthesis of 35 RCTs (8,718 participants) found silver dressings at relative risk 0.78 — a 22% RELATIVE reduction, moderate-certainty — and DACC dressings at relative risk 0.49 (a 51% relative reduction, 3 studies, moderate-certainty), while mupirocin dressings were not associated with benefit. The primary trials carded from inside the synthesis keep the claim at POSSIBLE: for silver, one large positive trial (gastrointestinal, 6.8% vs 11.4%) against three non-significant trials (caesarean 4.6% vs 4.2%; colorectal 15.5% vs 20.4%; breast 6.6% vs 12.9%); for DACC, two sequential single-centre caesarean trials (1.8% vs 5.2% significant; pilot 2.8% vs 9.8% not) plus their costing — below the ≥3-independent-trial threshold for a DACC class claim, stated on the face.

cards.summary: Synthesis of 35 RCTs (Yusuf 2026): silver dressings gave a relative risk of 0.78 for surgical-site infection — a 22% RELATIVE reduction, moderate-certainty; DACC dressings gave relative risk 0.49 (3 studies); mupirocin dressings were NOT associated with benefit (relative risk 0.62, interval wide, very low certainty)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 35 RCTs (the synthesis anchoring this shelf; the primary trials below are carded from inside it, per class, as the row's builder condition requires)
cards.people: 35 randomised trials with 8,718 participants, in patients with closed incisional wounds after elective or emergency surgery, comparing antimicrobial dressings with any other inert dressing. Pairwise meta-analyses were performed for silver (21 studies, 5,504 participants), dialkylcarbamoyl chloride (DACC) (3 studies, 892 participants) and mupirocin (3 studies, 1,320 participants). The primary outcome was surgical-site infection within 30 days (90 days if a prosthesis was used).
cards.result: Silver dressings: relative risk 0.78 (95% CI 0.62 to 0.97; I²=43%; moderate-certainty evidence) — that is a 22% relative risk reduction, printed as relative, as the standing wording rule and the row both require; the synthesis abstract gives no pooled absolute infection rates, so none are printed here. DACC dressings: relative risk 0.49 (0.29 to 0.83; I²=0%; moderate-certainty) — a 51% relative reduction on only 3 studies. Mupirocin dressings: relative risk 0.62 (0.15 to 2.63; I²=67%; very low-certainty) — not associated with prevention. Evidence for other agents was insufficient. The authors conclude silver and DACC dressings probably reduce surgical-site infection in closed surgical wounds, with residual uncertainty for other antimicrobial dressings.
cards.watchOut: A pooled relative risk is not a pooled claim that 'antimicrobial dressings work': the classes differ, the mupirocin limb is null, and the primary silver trials carded below are mixed — one large positive trial and three non-significant ones. That tension is the shelf's balance and is kept on the face.
cards.source: Yusuf SM et al. Antimicrobial dressings for the prevention of surgical-site infection: systematic review and meta-analysis. The British journal of surgery. 2026. PMID: 41677813. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Surgical Wound Infection · Bandages · Anti-Infective Agents · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Anti-Bacterial Agents

cards.headline: Silver — Kosugi 2024 (gastrointestinal surgery): ionic silver Hydrofiber dressing (Aquacel Ag, as named in the report) reduced superficial SSI versus film dressing — 6.8% vs 11.4% (P=0.019), the largest silver trial carded here
cards.summary: Silver — Kosugi 2024 (gastrointestinal surgery): ionic silver Hydrofiber dressing (Aquacel Ag, as named in the report) reduced superficial SSI versus film dressing — 6.8% vs 11.4% (P=0.019), the largest silver trial carded here
cards.type: Randomised trial — silver class, gastrointestinal surgery (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above)
cards.people: 865 patients undergoing elective gastrointestinal surgery (427 ionic silver dressing, 438 film dressing) qualified for the primary-endpoint analysis in this randomised trial; the benefit was concentrated in lower gastrointestinal surgery, with no significant difference in upper gastrointestinal surgery.
cards.result: Superficial surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in 6.8% of the silver-dressing group versus 11.4% of the film-dressing group (absolute rates; P=0.019). In lower gastrointestinal surgery the difference was significant (P=0.042); in upper gastrointestinal surgery it was not. On multivariable analysis the ionic silver dressing was an independent factor for reducing superficial SSI (odds ratio 0.602, 95% CI 0.367 to 0.986; P=0.044) — an odds ratio, a relative-type measure, printed beside the absolute rates.
cards.watchOut: Product naming: the report names the tested product as Aquacel Ag Hydrofiber dressing; it does not name a company in its PubMed record, so none is printed — per the standing rule, name exactly what the publication gives and say plainly where it does not. Single trial, one surgical field.
cards.source: Kosugi C et al. A Randomized Trial of Ionic Silver Dressing to Reduce Surgical Site Infection After Gastrointestinal Surgery. Annals of surgery open : perspectives of surgical history, education, and clinical approaches. 2024. PMID: 38883952. Registry ID: UMIN000043081 (named in the report; no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry in the record). MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Silver — Connery 2019 (caesarean delivery): silver nylon dressing did NOT reduce superficial SSI versus identical-appearing gauze — 4.6% vs 4.2% (P=0.96), a null trial
cards.summary: Silver — Connery 2019 (caesarean delivery): silver nylon dressing did NOT reduce superficial SSI versus identical-appearing gauze — 4.6% vs 4.2% (P=0.96), a null trial
cards.type: Blinded randomised trial — silver class, caesarean delivery (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above)
cards.people: 657 women undergoing scheduled or unscheduled caesarean delivery at a single site, randomised to a silver nylon dressing or an identical-appearing gauze dressing (blinded trial; women with vertical skin incisions were excluded). Wounds were assessed at 1 and 6 weeks; mean body mass index was about 36 in both groups.
cards.result: Superficial surgical-site infection within 6 weeks occurred in 4.6% of the silver nylon group versus 4.2% of the gauze group (P=0.96) — absolute rates, essentially identical. Rates at 1 week were 1.2% versus 0.9%. After adjustment, current smoking, body mass index ≥40 and longer surgery — not dressing type — were associated with superficial infection.
cards.watchOut: A well-blinded null in the field where the DACC trials below were positive: dressing class, product and surgical field all matter, and a silver result in one field does not transfer to another.
cards.source: Connery SA et al. Effect of using silver nylon dressings to prevent superficial surgical site infection after cesarean delivery: a randomized clinical trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2019. PMID: 30849351. Registry ID: NCT01697748. cards.headline: Silver — Biffi 2012 (colorectal cancer surgery): ionic silver dressing (Aquacel Ag Hydrofiber, as named in the report) did NOT significantly reduce SSI versus a common dressing — 15.5% vs 20.4% (P=0.451)
cards.summary: Silver — Biffi 2012 (colorectal cancer surgery): ionic silver dressing (Aquacel Ag Hydrofiber, as named in the report) did NOT significantly reduce SSI versus a common dressing — 15.5% vs 20.4% (P=0.451)
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial — silver class, colorectal surgery (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above)
cards.people: 112 adults undergoing elective colorectal cancer surgery at two university-affiliated hospitals (58 experimental, 54 control) qualified for the primary-endpoint analysis of this randomised double-blind trial; the experimental dressing was covered with a common dressing to preserve blinding.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection within 30 days occurred in 15.5% of the ionic-silver group versus 20.4% of controls (absolute rates) — a difference that was not statistically significant (P=0.451), overall or by infection grade. The authors state the trial did not confirm the superiority suggested by their earlier preliminary study.
cards.watchOut: Only 112 patients: underpowered for the observed difference, so this is 'not shown', not 'shown not to work' — but it cannot be counted as a positive trial either.
cards.source: Biffi R et al. Surgical site infections following colorectal cancer surgery: a randomized prospective trial comparing common and advanced antimicrobial dressing containing ionic silver. cards.headline: Silver — Struik 2018 (breast cancer surgery): silver carboxymethylcellulose dressing (AQUACEL Ag Surgical, as named in the report) did NOT significantly reduce SSI versus standard gauze — 6.6% vs 12.9% (relative risk 0.51, interval crossing 1; P=0.112) — but improved satisfaction and reduced dressing changes and wound costs
cards.summary: Silver — Struik 2018 (breast cancer surgery): silver carboxymethylcellulose dressing (AQUACEL Ag Surgical, as named in the report) did NOT significantly reduce SSI versus standard gauze — 6.6% vs 12.9% (relative risk 0.51, interval crossing 1; P=0.112) — but improved satisfaction and reduced dressing changes and wound costs
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — silver class, breast surgery (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above)
cards.people: 230 women aged 18 or older undergoing breast-conserving or ablative surgery for breast cancer at a single centre (106 silver dressing, 124 standard gauze), analysed for surgical-site infection by CDC criteria.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection occurred in 7 patients (6.6%) in the silver group and 16 (12.9%) in controls — relative risk 0.51 (95% CI 0.22 to 1.20), a relative measure beside the absolute rates; P=0.112 (adjusted odds ratio 0.49, P=0.135), so not significant. The silver group had better patient satisfaction (median 8 vs 7), fewer dressing changes within 48 hours and lower mean wound-related treatment costs in both costing models. An unplanned exploratory subgroup of breast-conserving surgery patients (1.8% vs 10.8%) is not printed as a finding — it was unplanned and non-significant after adjustment.
cards.watchOut: A non-significant infection result with real secondary benefits (satisfaction, fewer changes, lower wound costs): the shelf does not let the secondary benefits upgrade the infection claim.
cards.source: Struik GM et al. A randomized controlled trial on the effect of a silver carboxymethylcellulose dressing on surgical site infections after breast cancer surgery. PloS one. 2018. PMID: 29791437. Registry ID: NTR5840 (named in the report; no ClinicalTrials.gov databank entry in the record).
