cards.headline: DACC — Stanirowski 2016 (caesarean section, main trial): DACC-impregnated dressing reduced SSI versus standard dressing — 1.8% vs 5.2% (P=0.04), in 543 women
cards.summary: DACC — Stanirowski 2016 (caesarean section, main trial): DACC-impregnated dressing reduced SSI versus standard dressing — 1.8% vs 5.2% (P=0.04), in 543 women
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial — DACC class, caesarean section (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above; the main DACC trial)
cards.people: 543 women undergoing elective or emergency caesarean section at a single tertiary centre (about 1,300 deliveries a year), randomised after skin closure to a dialkylcarbamoyl chloride (DACC)-impregnated dressing or a standard surgical dressing. DACC binds bacteria by a purely physical mechanism, per the programme's reports.
cards.result: Surgical-site infection rates were 1.8% with the DACC dressing versus 5.2% with the standard dressing (absolute rates; P=0.04). Total costs of prophylaxis and treatment were lower in the DACC group (1,065 versus 5,775 euros in the patients who developed infection, per the report's costing). Independent risk factors for infection included higher pre-pregnancy body mass index, smoking in pregnancy, and standard-dressing application (adjusted odds ratio 2.94, 95% CI 1.1 to 9.3) — a relative-type measure beside the absolute rates.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, single surgical field, one research group: the DACC evidence carded here is two sequential caesarean trials from the same centre plus a costing of this trial — NOT the ≥3 independent RCTs per class that the row's builder condition asks for before a class claim, so this shelf makes no ≥3-trial DACC class claim and says so on the face.
cards.source: Stanirowski PJ et al. Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating Dialkylcarbamoyl Chloride Impregnated Dressings for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infections in Adult Women Undergoing Cesarean Section. Surgical infections. 2016. PMID: 26891115. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: DACC — Stanirowski 2016 pilot (caesarean section): SSI 2.8% with DACC versus 9.8% with standard dressing in 142 women — a non-significant trend (P=0.08)
cards.summary: DACC — Stanirowski 2016 pilot (caesarean section): SSI 2.8% with DACC versus 9.8% with standard dressing in 142 women — a non-significant trend (P=0.08)
cards.type: Randomised pilot trial — DACC class, caesarean section (a primary trial from inside the synthesis above; the pilot preceding the main trial)
cards.people: 142 women after planned or emergency caesarean section at the same tertiary centre as the main trial above, in an earlier single-blinded randomised pilot (December 2013 to March 2014, before the main trial's June 2014 start), assessed for superficial and deep surgical-site infection over the first 14 days.
cards.result: Superficial and deep surgical-site infection occurred in 2.8% of the DACC group versus 9.8% of the standard-dressing group (absolute rates; P=0.08 — not significant). Patients with infections in the standard-dressing group required systemic antibiotic therapy significantly more often (P=0.03). Pre-pregnancy body mass index was the only significant risk factor in the pilot's regression model.
cards.watchOut: A pilot, printed with its N: it is a trend that the main trial then tested, not independent confirmation of it — same centre, same group, sequential enrolment.
cards.source: Stanirowski PJ et al. Dialkylcarbamoyl chloride-impregnated dressing for the prevention of surgical site infection in women undergoing cesarean section: a pilot study. Archives of medical science : AMS. 2016. PMID: 27695495. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: DACC — cost-effectiveness companion (Stanirowski 2019): a costing OF the main DACC trial above, not a new trial — applying UK NHS unit costs, prophylaxis-plus-treatment cost £24.69 per patient with the bacterial-binding dressing versus £48.97 with standard care
cards.summary: DACC — cost-effectiveness companion (Stanirowski 2019): a costing OF the main DACC trial above, not a new trial — applying UK NHS unit costs, prophylaxis-plus-treatment cost £24.69 per patient with the bacterial-binding dressing versus £48.97 with standard care
cards.type: Cost-effectiveness analysis of the main DACC trial above (a companion report OF that trial — not independent clinical evidence)
cards.people: The same 543-woman caesarean trial as the main DACC card above (272 bacterial-binding [DACC] dressing, 271 standard care), with resource use recorded to 14 days and UK NHS unit costs applied to generalise the Polish trial's results to the NHS.
cards.result: Infection rates in the underlying trial were 5 of 272 (1.8%) versus 14 of 271 (5.2%), P=0.04 (absolute rates, as on the main card). The bacterial-binding group had six fewer outpatient visits and 33 fewer hospital bed-days. Applying UK unit costs at 2017 prices, prophylaxis and treatment cost £48.97 per patient under standard care versus £24.69 with the bacterial-binding dressing (a difference of £24.27 per patient); an alternative single-episode-cost approach gave a saving of £119 per patient.
cards.watchOut: A costing inherits every limit of the single trial it costs: single-centre, caesarean-only, one group. It answers 'what would this result cost or save', not 'does it work elsewhere'.
cards.source: Stanirowski PJ et al. Cost-effectiveness of a bacterial-binding dressing to prevent surgical site infection following caesarean section. Journal of wound care. 2019. PMID: 30975057. cards.headline: Synthesis: pooled, silver and DACC dressings probably reduce surgical-site infection on closed incisions (relative risks 0.78 and 0.49 — 22% and 51% RELATIVE reductions, moderate certainty) and mupirocin does not — but the primary silver trials carded here are one positive and three non-significant, and the DACC trials are two sequential caesarean trials from one centre
cards.summary: Synthesis: pooled, silver and DACC dressings probably reduce surgical-site infection on closed incisions (relative risks 0.78 and 0.49 — 22% and 51% RELATIVE reductions, moderate certainty) and mupirocin does not — but the primary silver trials carded here are one positive and three non-significant, and the DACC trials are two sequential caesarean trials from one centre
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the 35-trial synthesis (8,718 participants), four primary silver trials (865, 657, 230 and 112 patients) and the DACC programme (543-patient main trial, 142-patient pilot, and a costing of the main trial).
cards.result: By class, never pooled into one claim: silver — pooled relative risk 0.78 (a 22% relative reduction, moderate certainty) across 21 trials, yet of the four primary trials carded here only the 865-patient gastrointestinal trial was significant (6.8% vs 11.4%); the caesarean (4.6% vs 4.2%), colorectal (15.5% vs 20.4%) and breast (6.6% vs 12.9%) trials were not. DACC — pooled relative risk 0.49 across 3 studies in the synthesis; individually verified here are two sequential single-centre caesarean trials (1.8% vs 5.2%, significant; pilot 2.8% vs 9.8%, not significant) plus their costing, which is below the ≥3-independent-trial threshold for a class claim, and the shelf says so. Mupirocin — not associated with benefit (relative risk 0.62, very low certainty). Cross-point only, in prose: live #1281 asks silver dressings for venous leg ulcers (an open chronic wound) and live #651 homes incisional negative-pressure therapy — different questions, not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: Absolute pooled infection rates are not given in the synthesis abstract and are not invented here; every relative effect on this shelf is labelled relative with the trial-level absolute rates beside it.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Postoperative coffee/caffeine for bowel recovery: SPLIT — coffee works in gynaecological trials, null as coffee in colorectal, caffeine capsules positive on one endpoint only
shelves.question: After abdominal or pelvic surgery (colorectal, gynaecological and other abdominal fields as tested), does postoperative coffee or caffeine speed recovery of bowel function — time to first flatus, first bowel motion and tolerance of diet — and shorten ileus and hospital stay versus water, tea or no drink?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Coffee · Time Factors · Caffeine · Colectomy · Ileus · Postoperative Complications · Colorectal Neoplasms
shelves.balance: SPLIT — by surgical field and by agent, with coffee and isolated-caffeine arms kept separate throughout, as the row directs. In gynaecological surgery, coffee sped bowel recovery in both trials (flatus 19 vs 25 hours laparoscopic and 30.2 vs 40.2 hours after open staging surgery; ileus 2.0% vs 14.9% in the laparoscopic trial). In colorectal surgery, the one three-arm trial found NO effect of caffeinated coffee, decaffeinated coffee or warm water on time to first bowel movement (2.86 / 2.58 / 2.94 days, P=0.53), while isolated caffeine capsules shortened time to first stool by 18 hours on one endpoint only (flatus, diet tolerance and stay not significant), a direction the colorectal synthesis supports for bowel movement and food intake but not flatus or stay. No carded trial showed a shorter hospital stay. Whether caffeine is the active agent is unresolved — the trials disagree, and that disagreement is the balance.

cards.headline: Three-arm colorectal trial (Nasseri 2023): neither caffeinated coffee NOR decaffeinated coffee sped bowel recovery after minimally invasive colorectal surgery — time to first bowel movement 2.86 days (caffeinated), 2.58 (decaffeinated) and 2.94 (warm water), P=0.53, a null result
cards.summary: Three-arm colorectal trial (Nasseri 2023): neither caffeinated coffee NOR decaffeinated coffee sped bowel recovery after minimally invasive colorectal surgery — time to first bowel movement 2.86 days (caffeinated), 2.58 (decaffeinated) and 2.94 (warm water), P=0.53, a null result
cards.type: Three-arm randomised controlled trial (caffeinated coffee vs decaffeinated coffee vs warm water), minimally invasive colorectal surgery
cards.people: 99 patients undergoing elective robotic or laparoscopic small or large bowel operations at a single tertiary centre, randomised to warm water (31), decaffeinated coffee (31) or caffeinated coffee (37) — a 4-ounce cup three times daily from postoperative day 1. This three-arm design is the one trial carded here that can separate coffee from caffeine, and its arms are kept separate, as the row directs.
cards.result: Mean time to first bowel movement was 2.94 days (SD 1.4) on warm water, 2.58 (1.2) on decaffeinated coffee and 2.86 (1.3) on caffeinated coffee (P=0.53 — no significant difference). No significant differences were observed in postoperative morbidity, and multivariable regression found no significant association between any intervention and time to first bowel movement or length of hospital stay. The authors conclude coffee, caffeinated or decaffeinated, does not expedite return of bowel function after minimally invasive operation.
cards.watchOut: A null in the field where the positive gynaecological coffee trials below were done, and the only carded trial with a decaffeinated arm: if caffeine were the active agent, the caffeinated arm should have separated from decaffeinated — it did not, in either direction.
cards.source: Nasseri Y et al. Does coffee affect bowel recovery following minimally invasive colorectal operations? A three-armed randomized controlled trial. International journal of colorectal disease. 2023. PMID: 37470901. Registry ID: NCT02639728. cards.headline: Isolated-caffeine trial (Parnasa 2021, double-blind): caffeine capsules 100 mg three times daily brought first stool 18 hours earlier than placebo after elective colorectal resection (P=0.012) — but first flatus, diet tolerance and hospital stay did NOT reach significance
cards.summary: Isolated-caffeine trial (Parnasa 2021, double-blind): caffeine capsules 100 mg three times daily brought first stool 18 hours earlier than placebo after elective colorectal resection (P=0.012) — but first flatus, diet tolerance and hospital stay did NOT reach significance
cards.type: Prospective double-blind randomised trial of isolated caffeine (capsules) vs placebo, elective colorectal resection
cards.people: 70 patients scheduled for elective laparoscopic colectomy were randomised to oral caffeine 100 mg three times daily or placebo after the procedure; after exclusions, 30 caffeine and 28 placebo patients were analysed (median age 56 years). This card is the isolated-caffeine limb, kept separate from the coffee cards, as the row directs.
cards.result: First passage of stool occurred 18 hours earlier in the caffeine group than in the placebo group (P=0.012). The other endpoints — time to first flatus, time to tolerate a solid low-residue diet, and length of hospital stay — did not reach statistical significance. No caffeine-related adverse events were observed. The authors conclude caffeine is safe and significantly shortens time to first bowel movement, and may thus potentially shorten hospital stay — a potential the trial itself did not demonstrate.
cards.watchOut: 58 analysed patients and one significant endpoint out of four: a promising single-endpoint result, not a demonstrated shortening of ileus or stay. Note the contrast with the three-arm trial above, where caffeinated coffee as a drink did nothing.
cards.source: Parnasa SY et al. Does caffeine enhance bowel recovery after elective colorectal resection? A prospective double-blinded randomized clinical trial. Techniques in coloproctology. 2021. cards.headline: Coffee after laparoscopic gynaecological surgery (Gungorduk 2020): coffee shortened time to first flatus (median 19 vs 25 hours), first defecation (30 vs 38 hours) and time to tolerate food (2 vs 3 days), and ileus was 2.0% vs 14.9%
cards.summary: Coffee after laparoscopic gynaecological surgery (Gungorduk 2020): coffee shortened time to first flatus (median 19 vs 25 hours), first defecation (30 vs 38 hours) and time to tolerate food (2 vs 3 days), and ileus was 2.0% vs 14.9%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of coffee vs warm water, laparoscopic gynaecological surgery
cards.people: 96 patients after laparoscopic gynaecological surgery (total hysterectomy and bilateral salpingectomy in all, with salpingo-oophorectomy and lymphadenectomy as indicated), allocated to 3 cups of coffee (49) or warm water (47) at 6, 12 and 18 hours after the operation. The primary endpoint was time to first passage of flatus.
cards.result: Median time to flatus was 19 hours (range 13–35) with coffee versus 25 (15–42) with warm water (hazard ratio 1.9, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.9; P=0.0009); median time to defecation 30 (22–54) versus 38 (26–65) hours (hazard ratio 2.4, 1.5 to 3.8; P<0.0001); and mean time to tolerate food 2 versus 3 days (hazard ratio 1.5, 1.02 to 2.3; P=0.002) — hazard ratios are relative measures beside the absolute times. Postoperative ileus occurred in 1 coffee patient (2.0%) versus 7 control patients (14.9%), P=0.02. No adverse events were attributed to coffee.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded (coffee versus water cannot be blinded) with time-to-event endpoints reported by patients and staff who knew the allocation — a real risk of bias in exactly the direction of the result, to be weighed against the trial below, which found the same direction after much bigger surgery.
cards.source: Gungorduk K et al. Coffee consumption for recovery of intestinal function after laparoscopic gynecological surgery: A randomized controlled trial. International journal of surgery (London, England). 2020. PMID: 32853783. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Coffee after complete staging surgery for gynaecological cancer (Güngördük 2017): coffee shortened mean time to flatus (30.2 vs 40.2 hours), defecation (43.1 vs 58.5 hours) and tolerance of food (3.4 vs 4.7 days), all P<0.001; mild ileus symptoms 10.3% vs 30.4%
cards.summary: Coffee after complete staging surgery for gynaecological cancer (Güngördük 2017): coffee shortened mean time to flatus (30.2 vs 40.2 hours), defecation (43.1 vs 58.5 hours) and tolerance of food (3.4 vs 4.7 days), all P<0.001; mild ileus symptoms 10.3% vs 30.4%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial of coffee vs no coffee, open gynaecological-cancer staging surgery
cards.people: 114 patients undergoing complete staging surgery for endometrial, ovarian, cervical or tubal cancer — total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy with systematic pelvic and para-aortic lymphadenectomy in all — allocated preoperatively to coffee three times daily (58) or routine postoperative care without coffee (56). The primary outcome was time to first passage of flatus.
cards.result: Mean time to flatus was 30.2 hours (SD 8.0) with coffee versus 40.2 (12.1) without (P<0.001); mean time to defecation 43.1 (9.4) versus 58.5 (17.0) hours (P<0.001); and mean time to tolerate food 3.4 (1.2) versus 4.7 (1.6) days (P<0.001) — absolute times in both groups, printed in pairs. Mild ileus symptoms occurred in 6 coffee patients (10.3%) versus 17 controls (30.4%), P=0.01. Coffee was well tolerated and accepted, with no intervention-related side effects observed.
cards.watchOut: The control was routine care with no drink, not a matched warm-water control, and the trial was single-blind at most — so attention and expectation effects cannot be separated from a coffee effect. The effect sizes (about 10 hours to flatus, 15 hours to defecation) are nonetheless the largest carded here.
cards.source: Güngördük K et al. Effects of coffee consumption on gut recovery after surgery of gynecological cancer patients: a randomized controlled trial. American journal of obstetrics and gynecology. 2017. PMID: 27780709. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Colorectal caffeine synthesis (Vaghiri 2024): across 8 studies and 610 patients, caffeine significantly reduced time to first bowel movement (standardised mean difference −0.39) and to first solid food intake (−0.41) in elective laparoscopic colorectal surgery — but NOT time to first flatus, hospital stay, or morbidity
cards.summary: Colorectal caffeine synthesis (Vaghiri 2024): across 8 studies and 610 patients, caffeine significantly reduced time to first bowel movement (standardised mean difference −0.39) and to first solid food intake (−0.41) in elective laparoscopic colorectal surgery — but NOT time to first flatus, hospital stay, or morbidity
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised and non-randomised studies, colorectal surgery (synthesis — its included trials overlap the primary trials carded above and it is not independent evidence)
cards.people: Six randomised and two non-randomised studies with 610 patients in total, comparing caffeinated versus non-caffeinated drinks after colorectal surgery, searched to September 2023. Outcomes were bowel movement resumption, time to first flatus and solid food intake, and length of hospital stay, with postoperative morbidity as a secondary analysis.
cards.result: Caffeine intake significantly reduced time to first bowel movement (standardised mean difference −0.39, 95% CI −0.66 to −0.12; P=0.005) and time to first solid food intake (−0.41, −0.79 to −0.04; P=0.03) — standardised mean differences are relative-type, scale-free measures, and the synthesis gives no pooled absolute times, so none are printed here. Time to first flatus, length of hospital stay and the secondary morbidity outcomes did not differ significantly. The authors conclude caffeine may be a reasonable strategy after elective colorectal surgery but call for larger randomised trials with homogeneous protocols, especially on dosage form (caffeine versus coffee).
cards.watchOut: The synthesis pools coffee drinks and caffeine preparations together — exactly the distinction the primary trials disagree about — and includes non-randomised studies. Read it as a summary of the colorectal limb, not as a verdict on coffee itself.
cards.source: Vaghiri S et al. Caffeine intake enhances bowel recovery after colorectal surgery: a meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized studies. Updates in surgery. 2024. PMID: 38700642. cards.headline: Synthesis: SPLIT by field and by agent — coffee clearly sped bowel recovery in two gynaecological trials, did nothing as caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee in the one three-arm colorectal trial, and isolated caffeine shortened time to first stool on one endpoint in one small colorectal trial
cards.summary: Synthesis: SPLIT by field and by agent — coffee clearly sped bowel recovery in two gynaecological trials, did nothing as caffeinated or decaffeinated coffee in the one three-arm colorectal trial, and isolated caffeine shortened time to first stool on one endpoint in one small colorectal trial
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three randomised coffee trials (99 colorectal three-arm; 96 laparoscopic gynaecological; 114 gynaecological-cancer staging), one randomised isolated-caffeine trial (58 analysed) and one colorectal synthesis (8 studies, 610 patients, overlapping the trials above).
cards.result: Gynaecological coffee: time to flatus about 6–10 hours shorter, defecation about 8–15 hours shorter, food tolerance about 1–1.3 days sooner, and ileus 2.0% vs 14.9% in the laparoscopic trial. Colorectal coffee: null on every endpoint in the three-arm trial, for both caffeinated and decaffeinated coffee versus warm water. Isolated caffeine (capsules, colorectal): first stool 18 hours earlier, with flatus, diet tolerance and stay not significant; the colorectal synthesis agrees in direction for bowel movement and food intake only (standardised mean differences −0.39 and −0.41), not for flatus or stay. Whether caffeine is the active agent is therefore unresolved — the trials disagree, and that disagreement is this shelf's balance, as the row directs. Cross-point only, in prose: chewing gum and alvimopan for postoperative ileus are homed at live #1129 / pack #5690, and pack #2435 asks coffee and cardiac ectopy in non-surgical adults — different questions, not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: No carded trial was blinded for coffee versus a drink control except the caffeine-capsule trial, and none showed a shorter hospital stay: the demonstrated benefit, where it exists, is faster bowel function, not faster discharge.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Small bites fascial closure (STITCH): hernia 13% vs 21% at 1 year and 34% vs 49% at 13 years; 7-trial pooled relative risk 0.46
shelves.question: In adults having elective midline laparotomy, does fascial closure with the small-bites technique (5 mm x 5 mm bites of slowly absorbable continuous suture, suture-length-to-wound-length ratio at least 4:1) reduce incisional hernia, burst abdomen and wound infection versus conventional large-bites closure?
shelves.mesh: Abdominal Wound Closure Techniques/adverse effects · Aged · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Laparotomy/adverse effects/methods · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Suture Techniques · Treatment Outcome · Incisional Hernia/prevention & control · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic
shelves.balance: LIKELY benefit. Four distinct randomised trials plus a 7-trial synthesis point the same way on hernia, with one small null factorial trial in high-risk patients as the exception. STITCH (560 randomised, elective midline laparotomy): incisional hernia at 1 year 13% with small bites versus 21% with large bites (adjusted odds ratio 0.52), and its 13-year follow-up report found cumulative hernia incidence 34% versus 49% (hazard ratio 0.61). Millbourn (691 randomised) found infection and herniation less common with small stitches, without printing event percentages in its record. ESTOIH's 5-year report (362 in the analysis) found hernia 9.14% versus 13.90%, not significant. The 2025 synthesis of 7 RCTs / 2,299 patients gives a relative risk of 0.46 for incisional hernia — a 54% relative risk reduction — and 0.73 for surgical-site infection (a 27% relative risk reduction). Coelho's 107-patient 2x2 factorial trial in overweight/obese high-risk patients found no difference in 1-year major complications (18% vs 19%). Follow-up length and hernia ascertainment differ by trial and are carded as published, never pooled. PROPOSED STAMP: LIKELY (benefit).

cards.headline: Millbourn 2011 RCT (691 randomised): infection and incisional hernia were less common with small stitches than with large stitches in midline incisions; a very high suture-length to wound-length ratio added no harm
cards.summary: Millbourn 2011 RCT (691 randomised): infection and incisional hernia were less common with small stitches than with large stitches in midline incisions; a very high suture-length to wound-length ratio added no harm
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, small stitches vs large stitches for midline incision closure
cards.people: 691 patients operated on through a midline incision, randomised to closure with small stitches (321 patients; stitches placed 5-8 mm from the wound edge and less than 5 mm apart) or large stitches (370 patients; placed more than 1 cm from the wound edge).
cards.result: Surgical site infection and incisional hernia were less common with small stitches (the fetched record states the direction without printing the event percentages, and this card claims no percentages). With small stitches, no risk factors for infection or herniation were identified; with large stitches, wound contamination and diabetes were independent risk factors for infection, and long operation time and surgical site infection were risk factors for herniation. A very high suture-length to wound-length ratio did not affect complication rates, and raising the ratio well above 4 had no adverse effect.
cards.watchOut: The record prints no hernia or infection percentages for this trial, so none are claimed here; the trial predates STITCH and used 5-8 mm stitch placement rather than the standardised 5 mm x 5 mm STITCH definition.
cards.source: Millbourn D et al. Risk factors for wound complications in midline abdominal incisions related to the size of stitches. Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery. 2011. PMID: 21279664. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: STITCH RCT (Deerenberg 2015, 560 randomised): small bites cut 1-year incisional hernia from 21% to 13% versus large bites (adjusted odds ratio 0.52), with no significant difference in adverse events
cards.summary: STITCH RCT (Deerenberg 2015, 560 randomised): small bites cut 1-year incisional hernia from 21% to 13% versus large bites (adjusted odds ratio 0.52), with no significant difference in adverse events
cards.type: Double-blind multicentre randomised controlled trial (STITCH), small bites vs large bites fascial closure
cards.people: 560 adults scheduled for elective abdominal surgery with midline laparotomy at ten hospitals in the Netherlands, randomised to small tissue bites of 5 mm every 5 mm (276 patients) or large bites of 1 cm every 1 cm (284 patients); 545 (97%) completed follow-up and were included in the primary outcome analysis. Patients and investigators were masked to allocation.
cards.result: At 1 year, incisional hernia occurred in 35 of 268 patients (13%) in the small bites group versus 57 of 277 (21%) in the large bites group (covariate-adjusted odds ratio 0.52, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.87; P=0.0131) — an absolute difference of 8 percentage points. Small bites closures used more stitches (mean 45 [SD 12] vs 25 [10]), achieved a higher suture-length to wound-length ratio (5.0 [1.5] vs 4.3 [1.4]) and took longer (14 [6] vs 10 [4] minutes). Rates of adverse events did not differ significantly between groups.
cards.watchOut: Elective midline laparotomy only, in Dutch surgical and gynaecological departments; the trial's own 2011 protocol report (PMID 21871072, same registration NCT01132209) is the design paper for this same trial and is not carded as a separate trial. Hernia was assessed at 1 year; longer-term results are the separate follow-up card below.
cards.source: Deerenberg EB et al. Small bites versus large bites for closure of abdominal midline incisions (STITCH): a double-blind, multicentre, randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2015. PMID: 26188742. Registry ID: NCT01132209. cards.headline: STITCH 13-year follow-up (van den Berg 2026): cumulative incisional hernia 34% after small bites versus 49% after large bites (hazard ratio 0.61) — a long-term report OF the STITCH trial above, not a new trial
cards.summary: STITCH 13-year follow-up (van den Berg 2026): cumulative incisional hernia 34% after small bites versus 49% after large bites (hazard ratio 0.61) — a long-term report OF the STITCH trial above, not a new trial
cards.type: Long-term (13-year) follow-up report of the STITCH randomised trial (same programme and registration as the STITCH card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The STITCH cohort: 559 patients undergoing elective midline laparotomy at 10 Dutch centres (275 randomised to small bites, 284 to large bites as reported in this follow-up record); median time to censoring 8 years (IQR 2-13). Small bites were continuous 5 mm x 5 mm polydioxanone 2-0 on a 31-mm needle; large bites 10 mm x 10 mm looped polydioxanone on a 48-mm needle (the tested products as published).
cards.result: At 13 years, cumulative incidence of incisional hernia (clinical and radiologic) was 34% in the small-bites group and 49% in the large-bites group (hazard ratio 0.61, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.86). Hernias wider than 20 mm occurred in 17% versus 34% (hazard ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60), and hernias were smaller after small bites (mean 25 mm vs 43 mm; P=.02). Hernia repair rates were similar, and patients with an incisional hernia reported significantly lower quality of life.
cards.watchOut: Same trial as the 2015 STITCH card: do not count this as a second STITCH-sized trial. Only 170 patients were alive without hernia at final follow-up and imaging was incomplete (122 of those 170 had additional ultrasound), so late cumulative incidences rest on time-to-event methods with competing risks.
cards.source: van den Berg R et al. Small Bites vs Large Bites for Closure of Abdominal Midline Incisions: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA surgery. 2026. PMID: 41920572. Registry ID: NCT01132209. cards.headline: ESTOIH 5-year RCT report (Fortelny 2025, 362 analysed): incisional hernia 9.14% with short bites versus 13.90% with large bites at 5 years — direction favoured short bites but the difference was not significant
cards.summary: ESTOIH 5-year RCT report (Fortelny 2025, 362 analysed): incisional hernia 9.14% with short bites versus 13.90% with large bites at 5 years — direction favoured short bites but the difference was not significant
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised controlled trial, 5-year report (ESTOIH), short bite vs large bite with poly-4-hydroxybutyrate suture
cards.people: 362 patients in the 5-year intention-to-treat analysis of the ESTOIH prospective multicentre double-blind randomised trial of primary elective midline closure (175 short-bite, 187 large-bite), closed with an ultra-long-term absorbable elastic monofilament suture (Monomax, based on poly-4-hydroxybutyrate — the tested product as published).
cards.result: Incisional hernia at 5 years was 9.14% in the short-bite group versus 13.90% in the large-bite group; the between-group difference was not significant (odds ratio 1.60 as printed, 95% CI 0.82 to 3.10; P=0.155). Hernia rates rose between 3 and 5 years in both groups (short bite 7.58% to 9.14%; large bite 10.45% to 13.90%), and the large-bite rate was higher at every time point. The authors conclude the short-bite technique with this suture may achieve a very low long-term hernia rate.
cards.watchOut: A 5-year report of one trial (its 1- and 3-year results were published separately and are not re-carded); the suture material (poly-4-hydroxybutyrate) differs from STITCH's polydioxanone, so technique and material are confounded across trials; the 5-year comparison is not statistically significant.
cards.source: Fortelny RH et al. 5-year clinical outcome of the ESTOIH trial comparing the short-bite versus large-bite technique for elective midline abdominal closure. Hernia : the journal of hernias and abdominal wall surgery. 2025. PMID: 40879826. Registry ID: NCT01965249. cards.headline: Coelho 2023 factorial RCT (107 randomised, high-risk patients): small bites did not reduce 1-year major complications versus large bites (18% vs 19%)
cards.summary: Coelho 2023 factorial RCT (107 randomised, high-risk patients): small bites did not reduce 1-year major complications versus large bites (18% vs 19%)
cards.type: Multispecialty 2x2 factorial randomised controlled trial, small bites vs large bites (crossed with biologic mesh vs no mesh)
cards.people: 107 high-risk patients (overweight, obese or current smokers; 16% smokers, 31% overweight, 55% obese) undergoing abdominal operation with a midline incision of 5 cm or more, randomised in a 2x2 factorial design to sublay biologic mesh or no mesh and to small bites (55 patients; 0.5 x 0.5 cm) or large bites (52 patients; 1 x 1 cm) fascial closure.
cards.result: At 1 year there were no differences in the primary composite of major complications (ventral incisional hernia, surgical site infection, reoperation and death): mesh versus no mesh 21% versus 16% (P=0.62); small bites versus large bites 18% versus 19% (P=1.00). The authors concluded biologic mesh and small bites appeared to have no benefit in this population and that further randomised trials are needed among high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: Small (107 patients), powered for a 20-percentage-point difference in a composite outcome — it cannot exclude the hernia-specific benefit seen in STITCH; the population (overweight/obese high-risk, mixed abdominal operations) differs from STITCH's elective midline population.
cards.source: Coelho R et al. Hernia Prevention Using Biologic Mesh and/or Small Bites: A Multispecialty 2 x 2 Factorial Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of the American College of Surgeons. 2023. PMID: 37458369. Registry ID: NCT03148496. cards.headline: Synthesis of the randomised trials (Alrashidi 2025): 7 RCTs, 2,299 patients — small bites gave a relative risk of 0.46 for incisional hernia and 0.73 for surgical-site infection versus large bites
cards.summary: Synthesis of the randomised trials (Alrashidi 2025): 7 RCTs, 2,299 patients — small bites gave a relative risk of 0.46 for incisional hernia and 0.73 for surgical-site infection versus large bites
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis of randomised trials
cards.people: Seven randomised controlled trials encompassing 2,299 patients undergoing closure of midline abdominal incisions, pooled in a systematic review and meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis (searches to 15 December 2024).
cards.result: Compared with large bites, small bites were associated with a reduced incidence of ventral incisional hernia (relative risk 0.46, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.60 — a 54% relative risk reduction) and of surgical site infection (relative risk 0.73, 95% CI 0.58 to 0.92 — a 27% relative risk reduction), and with a shorter hospital stay (mean difference -1.03 days, 95% CI -1.72 to -0.33). There was no significant difference in all-cause mortality (relative risk 0.70, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.06), anastomotic leak or ileus. The pooled relative risks are relative measures; the absolute hernia rates in the largest trial were 13% versus 21% at 1 year (STITCH card above).
cards.watchOut: The pooled trials differ in suture material, population risk and hernia ascertainment/follow-up (1 to 5 years as carded above); the pooled relative risk should be read beside the per-trial absolute rates, not as a single universal effect.

cards.result: Four distinct randomised trials are carded: Millbourn 2011 (691 randomised; direction favoured small stitches, percentages not printed in its record), STITCH 2015 (560 randomised; hernia 13% vs 21% at 1 year, adjusted odds ratio 0.52) with its labelled 13-year follow-up report (cumulative 34% vs 49%, hazard ratio 0.61), ESTOIH at 5 years (362 analysed; 9.14% vs 13.90%, not significant) and Coelho 2023 (107 high-risk patients; no difference in 1-year major complications, 18% vs 19%). The 2025 synthesis of 7 RCTs / 2,299 patients gives relative risk 0.46 for hernia (a 54% relative risk reduction) and 0.73 for surgical-site infection (a 27% relative risk reduction). The STITCH protocol report (PMID 21871072) is the design paper for STITCH itself and is deliberately not counted as a separate trial. No empty-abstract record was carded on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Glove and instrument change before abdominal closure (ChEETAh, single programme): SSI 16.0% vs 18.9% in 13,301 LMIC patients (adjusted risk ratio 0.87)
shelves.question: In patients having abdominal surgery in low- and middle-income settings, does a routine change of sterile gloves and separate sterile instruments immediately before abdominal wound closure reduce surgical-site infection versus continuing with the gloves and instruments used for the operation?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Adult · Child · Developing Countries · Surgical Wound Infection/epidemiology/prevention & control · Abdominal Wound Closure Techniques · Pragmatic Clinical Trials as Topic · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Cost-Effectiveness Analysis
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, single programme — stated on the face: the entire randomised base is ONE trial programme (ChEETAh), and the three reports carded here are reports OF that programme (the trial, its protocol and its cost-effectiveness analysis), labelled as such, exactly as single-programme shelves are labelled elsewhere in this library. In that one pragmatic cluster-randomised trial (81 hospitals, seven low- and middle-income countries, 13,301 patients), routine glove and instrument change before abdominal closure reduced 30-day surgical-site infection from 18.9% to 16.0% (adjusted risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.95 — a 13% relative risk reduction, an absolute reduction of 2.9 percentage points), and the model-based cost-effectiveness analysis found similar costs ($259.92 vs $261.10 per patient). The setting — LMIC abdominal surgery with a high baseline SSI rate — is part of the claim and is not generalised to high-income settings on this shelf. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE (benefit), single-programme.

cards.headline: ChEETAh cluster RCT (2022, 13,301 patients, 81 hospitals, 7 LMICs): routine glove and instrument change before closure cut 30-day SSI from 18.9% to 16.0% (adjusted risk ratio 0.87)
cards.summary: ChEETAh cluster RCT (2022, 13,301 patients, 81 hospitals, 7 LMICs): routine glove and instrument change before closure cut 30-day SSI from 18.9% to 16.0% (adjusted risk ratio 0.87)
cards.type: Pragmatic multicentre cluster-randomised trial (ChEETAh), routine glove and instrument change vs current practice — the single randomised trial of this programme
cards.people: 13,301 consecutive adults and children undergoing emergency or elective abdominal surgery (excluding caesarean section) for a clean-contaminated, contaminated or dirty operation in 81 hospital clusters in seven low-income and middle-income countries (Benin, Ghana, India, Mexico, Nigeria, Rwanda, South Africa); 7,157 patients in 42 current-practice clusters and 6,144 in 39 intervention clusters. The intervention was routine change of gloves and instruments before wound closure for the whole scrub team.
cards.result: Glove and instrument change took place in 6,044 of 6,144 intervention patients (98.3%) versus 58 of 7,157 (0.8%) under current practice. The 30-day surgical-site infection rate (CDC criteria, intention-to-treat) was 931 of 5,789 (16.0%) in the intervention group versus 1,280 of 6,768 (18.9%) under current practice (adjusted risk ratio 0.87, 95% CI 0.79 to 0.95; P=0.0032) — a 13% relative risk reduction and an absolute reduction of 2.9 percentage points. There was no evidence of heterogeneity across prespecified subgroups. No specific serious-adverse-event data were collected.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: this is the ONLY randomised trial of this intervention — every other card on this shelf is a report of this same programme. Cluster-randomised and unmasked to site investigators and outcome assessors (patients were masked); conducted only in low- and middle-income settings with a high baseline SSI rate (18.9%), so the absolute benefit does not transfer directly to low-baseline settings.
cards.source: NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery et al. Lancet (London, England). 2022. PMID: 36328045. Registry ID: NCT03700749. cards.headline: Programme report — protocol (2022): the published ChEETAh design — a pragmatic cluster trial powered to detect a fall in 30-day SSI from 16% to 12%, planning 12,800 participants from 64 clusters (a report OF the ChEETAh programme, not a separate trial)
cards.summary: Programme report — protocol (2022): the published ChEETAh design — a pragmatic cluster trial powered to detect a fall in 30-day SSI from 16% to 12%, planning 12,800 participants from 64 clusters (a report OF the ChEETAh programme, not a separate trial)
cards.type: Programme report: published study protocol for the ChEETAh cluster-randomised trial (same programme as the trial card above — not independent evidence)
cards.people: The ChEETAh programme: hospitals (clusters) in low- and middle-income countries where glove and instrument change was not routine; eligible patients were adults and children undergoing emergency or elective clean-contaminated, contaminated or dirty abdominal surgery. A 12-month internal pilot planned 12 clusters and approximately 600 participants.
cards.result: The protocol specifies the intervention (before closing the abdominal wall, surgeons and the scrub nurse change gloves and use separate sterile instruments, versus no change under standard practice), the primary outcome (SSI within 30 days by CDC criteria) and secondary outcomes (SSI before discharge, readmission, reoperation, length of stay, return to normal activities and death to 30 days). The main trial was powered to detect a minimum reduction from 16% to 12%, recruiting 12,800 participants from 64 clusters. The completed trial (card above) exceeded this, randomising 81 clusters and 13,301 patients.
cards.watchOut: A design/protocol report: it carries no outcome data and must not be counted as a second trial. Its registration number (NCT03980652) differs from the main trial report's (NCT03700749) as printed in the two records.

cards.headline: Programme report — cost-effectiveness (2024): modelled cost of glove/instrument change was essentially the same as current practice ($259.92 vs $261.10) with fewer SSIs (17.6% vs 19.7%) — a model-based analysis OF the ChEETAh trial, not a new trial
cards.summary: Programme report — cost-effectiveness (2024): modelled cost of glove/instrument change was essentially the same as current practice ($259.92 vs $261.10) with fewer SSIs (17.6% vs 19.7%) — a model-based analysis OF the ChEETAh trial, not a new trial
cards.type: Programme report: model-based cost-effectiveness analysis of the ChEETAh trial (same programme as the trial card above — not independent comparative evidence)
cards.people: A decision-analytic model using clinical data from the ChEETAh trial (seven LMICs) and SSI cost data from the KIWI study; base-case resource use and unit costs from India, with secondary analyses using Mexico and Ghana data. Costs are 2021 US dollars from a health-care provider perspective.
cards.result: In the base case, the average cost of the intervention was $259.92 compared with $261.10 for current practice (cost difference -$1.18, 95% CI -4.08 to 1.33). An estimated 17.6% of intervention patients had an SSI compared with 19.7% under current practice (modelled absolute risk reduction 2.10%). At all cost-effectiveness thresholds assumed ($0 to $14,000), the intervention had a higher likelihood of being cost-effective than current practice; results were similar using Mexico and Ghana costing data.
cards.watchOut: Modelled, not observed, costs and effects: the modelled SSI rates (17.6% vs 19.7%) differ slightly from the trial's observed rates (16.0% vs 18.9%) because the model pools outcomes with single-country (India) costing. It adds economic, not clinical, evidence.
cards.source: NIHR Global Health Research Unit on Global Surgery et al. shelves.title: Early vs later postoperative catheter removal: fewer infections and shorter stays with early removal, but retention noninferiority unproven in the rectal synthesis — a field-by-field split
shelves.question: After surgery, does early removal of the indwelling urinary catheter (immediately, on the day of surgery, or on postoperative day 1, as tested by field) versus standard later removal change urinary retention and re-catheterisation, urinary tract infection and length of stay — and does the answer differ between rectal / pelvic colorectal surgery, gynaecological and pelvic-floor surgery, and upper gastrointestinal surgery?
shelves.mesh: Acute Disease · Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Antagonists · Adult · Colorectal Surgery · Device Removal · Female · Humans · Incidence · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Outcome Assessment, Health Care · Postoperative Period · Prazosin · Prospective Studies · Urinary Catheters · Urinary Retention · Urinary Tract Infections
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the retention–infection trade-off stays unresolved on the face, exactly where the trials leave it. Earlier removal consistently reduces urinary infection and shortens stay where measured: after pelvic colorectal surgery, day-1 removal (with an oral α-antagonist, part of that trial's intervention) was noninferior for retention (8.5% vs 9.9%) with infection 0% vs 11.3% and a day shorter in hospital; after radical gastrectomy, immediate removal was noninferior to early removal for retention (4.4% vs 3.4%; difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −4.6 to 6.6, within the 10% margin) with better comfort. But the rectal-surgery synthesis (4 trials, 409 patients) could NOT establish noninferiority for retention (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19) even while confirming the infection advantage (risk difference −11 percentage points). The gynaecological/pelvic-floor trials are small (57 women in the day-of-surgery voiding-trial study) and mixed on their primary reads. The answer differs by surgical field, so the cards are kept per field and never pooled into one 'remove early' claim.

cards.headline: Gastrectomy RCT (Wei 2025): immediate catheter removal after radical gastrectomy under ERAS was noninferior to early removal for urinary retention (4.4% vs 3.4%; difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −4.6 to 6.6) and more comfortable
cards.summary: Gastrectomy RCT (Wei 2025): immediate catheter removal after radical gastrectomy under ERAS was noninferior to early removal for urinary retention (4.4% vs 3.4%; difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −4.6 to 6.6) and more comfortable
cards.type: Single-centre non-inferiority randomised trial, immediate vs early catheter removal after radical gastrectomy under ERAS (China)
cards.people: Patients undergoing radical gastrectomy under ERAS protocols at a university-affiliated hospital in China, randomised 1:1 to immediate removal or early removal of the urinary catheter; data were analysed for 92 patients (immediate) and 89 (early) of 248 assessed for eligibility, in a non-inferiority trial with a 10% margin for postoperative urinary retention.
cards.result: Postoperative urinary retention occurred in 4.4% (immediate) versus 3.4% (early) (P=0.733; difference 1.0 percentage point, 95% CI −4.6 to 6.6) — within the prespecified 10% non-inferiority margin. Patient comfort was significantly higher with immediate removal (Kolcaba General Comfort Questionnaire score 74.9 (SD 7.6) vs 72.5 (SD 8.0); P=0.041). The authors note successful immediate removal probably relies on multimodal analgesia and goal-directed fluid therapy within ERAS.
cards.watchOut: Unblinded, single-centre, and framed by its authors as a feasibility result inside a full ERAS protocol — the comparison is immediate versus early removal (both early by older standards), not early versus late.
cards.source: Wei C et al. Immediate versus early urinary catheter removal after gastrectomy under enhanced recovery after surgery protocols: randomized clinical trial. BJS open. 2025. PMID: 40827509. Registry ID: NCT06718114. cards.headline: Pelvic colorectal RCT (Patel 2018): day-1 removal (with prazosin) was noninferior to day-3 removal for retention (8.5% vs 9.9%), with infection 0% vs 11.3% and a shorter stay
cards.summary: Pelvic colorectal RCT (Patel 2018): day-1 removal (with prazosin) was noninferior to day-3 removal for retention (8.5% vs 9.9%), with infection 0% vs 11.3% and a shorter stay
cards.type: Prospective randomised noninferiority trial, day-1 (with α-antagonist co-therapy) vs day-3 catheter removal after pelvic colorectal surgery
cards.people: 142 patients undergoing colorectal surgery below the peritoneal reflection (66% ileal pouch–anal anastomosis, 18% low anterior resection; mean age 44.8 years, 54% men), randomised 1:1 to catheter removal on postoperative day 1 or day 3; patients in the early arm received the α-antagonist prazosin 1 mg orally 6 hours before removal — the α-blocker is part of the tested intervention.
cards.result: Overall urinary retention was 9.2% (13/142), with no difference between early (6/71, 8.5%) and standard (7/71, 9.9%) removal (relative risk 0.86, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.42); the risk difference was −1.4 percentage points (95% CI −8.3 to 11.1), confirming noninferiority as analysed by the authors. Symptomatic infection was significantly lower with early removal (0% vs 11.3%; P=0.01), and length of stay was shorter (median 4 days, IQR 3–6, vs 5 days, IQR 4–7; P=0.03).
cards.watchOut: The early-removal package included prazosin — the result is for removal-plus-α-blockade, not removal timing alone; patients and investigators were unblinded, and the population (mean age ~45, mostly pouch surgery) is younger than typical rectal-cancer cohorts.
cards.source: Patel DN et al. Early Urinary Catheter Removal Following Pelvic Colorectal Surgery: A Prospective, Randomized, Noninferiority Trial. Diseases of the colon and rectum. 2018. PMID: 30192326. Registry ID: NCT01923129. cards.headline: Pelvic-floor RCT (Carter-Brooks 2018): a day-of-surgery voiding trial did not prolong catheter use after prolapse surgery — intention-to-treat time to void 15.9 vs 28.4 hours (P=0.081, not significant); per-protocol difference significant
cards.summary: Pelvic-floor RCT (Carter-Brooks 2018): a day-of-surgery voiding trial did not prolong catheter use after prolapse surgery — intention-to-treat time to void 15.9 vs 28.4 hours (P=0.081, not significant); per-protocol difference significant
cards.type: Randomised parallel-arm trial, day-of-surgery vs postoperative-day-1 voiding trial after pelvic floor reconstructive surgery
cards.people: 57 women undergoing major pelvic floor reconstructive surgery (obliterative and apical suspension procedures for pelvic organ prolapse; mean age 65, 77.2% stage III prolapse), randomised 1:1 to a retrograde voiding trial 4 hours postoperatively on the day of surgery or at 6 am on postoperative day 1.
cards.result: In the intention-to-treat analysis (n=57) there was no significant difference in time to spontaneous void (15.9 ± 3.8 vs 28.4 ± 3.1 hours; P=0.081). In the adjusted analysis, an early voiding trial decreased time to spontaneous void (adjusted beta −2.00 hours; P=0.031) after controlling for vaginal packing and stage IV prolapse; in the per-protocol analysis (4 crossovers excluded), spontaneous void occurred 17 hours faster with the early trial (14.6 ± 3.7 vs 31.8 ± 2.9 hours; P=0.022). Early-trial patients ambulated sooner and more often (P=0.02).
cards.watchOut: A small trial (57 women) whose headline intention-to-treat read is not significant — the favourable numbers come from adjusted and per-protocol analyses and must be labelled as such; it tests voiding-trial timing, a narrower intervention than catheter-removal day.
cards.source: Carter-Brooks CM et al. Early catheter removal after pelvic floor reconstructive surgery: a randomized trial. International urogynecology journal. 2018. PMID: 29600401. cards.headline: Anterior prolapse RCT (Chansriniyom 2023): catheter removal at 24 hours was comparable to day-3 removal for postoperative urinary retention, with shorter hospitalisation
cards.summary: Anterior prolapse RCT (Chansriniyom 2023): catheter removal at 24 hours was comparable to day-3 removal for postoperative urinary retention, with shorter hospitalisation
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, 24-hour vs day-3 catheter removal after anterior compartment prolapse surgery
cards.people: Women undergoing anterior compartment prolapse surgery (anterior colporrhaphy and colpocleisis) at a university hospital in 2020–21, randomised to early transurethral catheter removal (24 hours postoperatively) or conventional removal on postoperative day 3; the calculated sample size was 68 patients (34 per group). Postoperative urinary retention was diagnosed when the second void's residual volume exceeded 150 mL.
cards.result: As reported by the authors, early catheter removal was comparable in postoperative urinary retention rate to conventional removal, with shorter hospitalisation in the early group, and there was no rehospitalisation owing to urinary retention. (The PubMed record reports this comparison qualitatively, without the per-group retention rates — no rates are printed here rather than reconstructed.) Secondary outcomes assessed included urinary tract infection, asymptomatic bacteriuria, time to ambulation, time to spontaneous voiding and patient satisfaction.
cards.watchOut: The record's abstract does not print the numerical retention rates, so this card carries the authors' qualitative conclusion only; it is a small single-centre trial in one prolapse operation and should not be pooled with the colorectal or gastric fields.
cards.source: Chansriniyom N et al. Rate of Postoperative Urinary Retention after Anterior Compartment Prolapse Surgery: A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Early versus Conventional Transurethral Catheter Removal. Journal of clinical medicine. 2023. PMID: 37240539. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Rectal-surgery synthesis (Castelo 2020): early removal was superior for urinary tract infection (risk difference −11 percentage points) but noninferiority for urinary retention was NOT established (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19)
cards.summary: Rectal-surgery synthesis (Castelo 2020): early removal was superior for urinary tract infection (risk difference −11 percentage points) but noninferiority for urinary retention was NOT established (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials, early vs late catheter removal after rectal surgery
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials of early (up to postoperative day 2) versus late (after day 2) catheter removal after rectal surgery: four trials, 409 patients (literature searched to February 2019).
cards.result: For acute urinary retention there was insufficient evidence to conclude noninferiority of early removal (risk difference 9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to 19; P for noninferiority = 0.31, against a 15-percentage-point margin taken from an included trial). For urinary tract infection, early removal was superior (risk difference −11 percentage points, 95% CI −17 to −4; P=0.001). Length-of-stay results were mixed, and there were insufficient data for subgroup analyses.
cards.watchOut: Only four trials and 409 patients, and its 'early' definition (up to day 2) pools different removal days; its failure to establish retention noninferiority is the counterweight to the individual positive trials and is kept unresolved on this shelf's face.
cards.source: Castelo M et al. Early urinary catheter removal after rectal surgery: systematic review and meta-analysis. BJS open. 2020. PMID: 32379937. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: earlier removal buys fewer infections and shorter stays in every field tested, but retention noninferiority is proven only trial-by-trial — the rectal synthesis could not establish it
cards.summary: Synthesis: earlier removal buys fewer infections and shorter stays in every field tested, but retention noninferiority is proven only trial-by-trial — the rectal synthesis could not establish it
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across upper gastrointestinal (gastrectomy), pelvic colorectal and gynaecological/pelvic-floor surgery, earlier catheter removal did not significantly increase retention in the individual randomised trials — day-1 removal with an α-antagonist was noninferior after pelvic colorectal surgery, and immediate removal was noninferior after gastrectomy — while urinary infection was consistently lower (0% vs 11.3% in the colorectal trial; risk difference −11 percentage points in the rectal synthesis) and stay shorter. The pooled rectal evidence nonetheless failed to establish noninferiority for retention (risk difference +9 percentage points, 90% CI −1 to +19). The trade-off is therefore field- and protocol-specific, not a universal 'remove on day 1' rule.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each field's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: BIS-guided protocols for preventing intraoperative awareness: SPLIT by comparator — beats routine care (B-Aware, 2 vs 11 cases), no better than end-tidal-agent alerts (B-Unaware, BAG-RECALL)
shelves.question: In adults at high risk of intraoperative awareness having general anaesthesia, does a bispectral-index (BIS)-guided protocol — BIS-guided care versus routine care, or a BIS-alert protocol versus an end-tidal anaesthetic concentration (ETAC)-alert protocol — reduce confirmed awareness with explicit recall versus the comparator?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesia Recovery Period · Anesthesia, General · Awareness · Double-Blind Method · Electroencephalography · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Monitoring, Intraoperative · Patient Satisfaction · Postoperative Complications · Risk Factors · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the answer turns entirely on the comparator, and the cards are kept per comparator, never pooled. Against ROUTINE CARE, BIS guidance worked: B-Aware (2,463 high-risk patients) found confirmed awareness in 2 patients on BIS-guided care versus 11 on routine care (P=0.022) — an 82% relative risk reduction (95% CI 17 to 98), with absolute rates of roughly 0.16% versus 0.89% and a number needed to treat of 138. Against an active END-TIDAL anaesthetic concentration (ETAC) alert protocol, BIS guidance did not work: B-Unaware (2,000 patients) found definite awareness in 2 patients in each group, and BAG-RECALL (6,041 patients) found definite awareness in 7 of 2,861 (0.24%) on BIS-alert versus 2 of 2,852 (0.07%) on ETAC-alert — superiority of BIS not demonstrated, with numerically MORE awareness on BIS. The Cochrane synthesis matches the split exactly: BIS beats clinical signs (Peto odds ratio 0.36, relative; low-certainty) but does not differ from ETAC (Peto odds ratio 1.13, relative; low-certainty). Awareness is rare, so absolute event counts are printed beside every relative measure on this shelf. This shelf is distinct from live #1123 (anaesthetic DEPTH targets — BIS 50 vs 35 — for mortality, and EEG guidance for delirium; BALANCED and ENGAGES are homed there and are not re-carded here); cross-point in prose only.

cards.headline: B-Aware RCT (Myles 2004): BIS-guided anaesthesia reduced confirmed awareness versus routine care in high-risk patients — 2 vs 11 cases (P=0.022), an 82% relative risk reduction (95% CI 17 to 98); absolute rates ~0.16% vs ~0.89%, NNT 138
cards.summary: B-Aware RCT (Myles 2004): BIS-guided anaesthesia reduced confirmed awareness versus routine care in high-risk patients — 2 vs 11 cases (P=0.022), an 82% relative risk reduction (95% CI 17 to 98); absolute rates ~0.16% vs ~0.89%, NNT 138
cards.type: Prospective randomised double-blind multicentre trial (B-Aware), BIS-guided anaesthesia vs routine care, high-risk patients
cards.people: 2,463 adults at high risk of awareness undergoing relaxant general anaesthesia, randomised to BIS-guided anaesthesia (1,225) or routine care (1,238) in a prospective double-blind multicentre trial; awareness was assessed by a blinded observer at 2–6 hours, 24–36 hours and 30 days, with every report adjudicated by a blinded independent committee.
cards.result: There were 2 reports of confirmed awareness in the BIS-guided group versus 11 in the routine care group (P=0.022). BIS-guided anaesthesia reduced the risk of awareness by 82% (95% CI 17 to 98) — a relative measure; in absolute terms that is 2 of 1,225 (0.16%) versus 11 of 1,238 (0.89%). The authors calculated a number needed to treat of 138 and, at US$16 per BIS use, a cost of about US$2,200 to prevent one case of awareness in high-risk patients. Awareness affects 0.1–0.2% of all surgical patients, per the report.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is routine care without any structured depth/alert protocol — the trial shows BIS beats unaided practice, not that BIS beats another alert system; with only 13 confirmed events in total, the relative reduction's confidence interval is very wide (17 to 98%).
cards.source: Myles PS et al. Bispectral index monitoring to prevent awareness during anaesthesia: the B-Aware randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2004. PMID: 15172773. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: B-Unaware RCT (Avidan 2008): a BIS protocol (target 40–60) was NOT better than an end-tidal-agent protocol (0.7–1.3 MAC) — definite awareness in 2 patients in each group of ~1,000 assessed
cards.summary: B-Unaware RCT (Avidan 2008): a BIS protocol (target 40–60) was NOT better than an end-tidal-agent protocol (0.7–1.3 MAC) — definite awareness in 2 patients in each group of ~1,000 assessed
cards.type: Randomised trial (B-Unaware), BIS-guided protocol vs ETAG-guided protocol, high-risk patients
cards.people: 2,000 patients at high risk of awareness, randomised to BIS-guided anaesthesia (target BIS 40 to 60) or end-tidal anaesthetic gas (ETAG)-guided anaesthesia (target 0.7 to 1.3 MAC); 967 (BIS) and 974 (ETAG) patients were assessed for awareness at up to 24 hours, 24–72 hours and 30 days after extubation.
cards.result: Two cases of definite anaesthesia awareness occurred in EACH group (absolute difference 0%; 95% CI −0.56 to 0.57 percentage points). Awareness occurred even when BIS values and ETAG concentrations were within target ranges (BIS above 60 in one definite case; ETAG below 0.7 MAC in three). Mean time-averaged ETAG concentration was nearly identical between groups (0.81 vs 0.82 MAC; P=0.10), so the BIS protocol did not reduce volatile-agent administration either. The authors concluded their findings do not support routine BIS monitoring as standard practice.
cards.watchOut: Only 4 definite events in ~1,941 assessed patients — the trial cannot exclude small differences, but its point result directly contradicts any claim that BIS guidance is superior to a disciplined end-tidal-agent protocol; the comparator, not the monitor, is the difference from B-Aware.

randomised trial (b-unaware), bis-guided protocol vs etag-guided protocol, high-risk patients 2,000 patients at high risk of awareness, randomised to bis-guided anaesthesia (target bis 40 to 60) or end-tidal anaesthetic gas (etag)-guided anaesthesia (target 0.7 to 1.3 mac); 967 (bis) and 974 (etag) patients were assessed for awareness at up to 24 hours, 24–72 hours and 30 days after extubation. two cases of definite anaesthesia awareness occurred in each group (absolute difference 0%; 95% ci −0.56 to 0.57 percentage points). awareness occurred even when bis values and etag concentrations were within target ranges (bis above 60 in one definite case; etag below 0.7 mac in three). mean time-averaged etag concentration was nearly identical between groups (0.81 vs 0.82 mac; p=0.10), so the bis protocol did not reduce volatile-agent administration either. the authors concluded their findings do not support routine bis monitoring as standard practice. only 4 definite events in ~1,941 assessed patients — the trial cannot exclude small differences, but its point result directly contradicts any claim that bis guidance is superior to a disciplined end-tidal-agent protocol; the comparator, not the monitor, is the difference from b-aware. avidan ms et al. anesthesia awareness and the bispectral index. the new england journal of medicine. 2008. pmid: 18337600. registry id: nct00281489. mesh: adult · aged · algorithms · anesthesia, general · anesthetics, general · awareness · breath tests · electroencephalography · female · humans · intraoperative period · male · middle aged · monitoring, intraoperative · prospective studies · risk · signal processing, computer-assisted · surveys and questionnaires

cards.headline: BAG-RECALL RCT (Avidan 2011): BIS-alert protocol was NOT superior to ETAC-alert protocol — definite awareness 7/2,861 (0.24%) on BIS versus 2/2,852 (0.07%) on ETAC; definite-or-possible awareness 0.66% vs 0.28%
cards.summary: BAG-RECALL RCT (Avidan 2011): BIS-alert protocol was NOT superior to ETAC-alert protocol — definite awareness 7/2,861 (0.24%) on BIS versus 2/2,852 (0.07%) on ETAC; definite-or-possible awareness 0.66% vs 0.28%
cards.type: Prospective randomised evaluator-blinded trial (BAG-RECALL), BIS-alert protocol vs ETAC-alert protocol, high-risk patients
cards.people: 6,041 patients at high risk for awareness at three medical centres, randomised to BIS-guided anaesthesia with an audible alert if BIS was below 40 or above 60, or ETAC-guided anaesthesia with an audible alert if ETAC was below 0.7 or above 1.3 MAC; both protocols included structured education and checklists, and outcome assessors were blinded.
cards.result: Definite intraoperative awareness occurred in 7 of 2,861 patients (0.24%) in the BIS group versus 2 of 2,852 (0.07%) in the ETAC group (difference 0.17 percentage points, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.38; P=0.98 for superiority) — superiority of the BIS protocol was NOT demonstrated. Definite-or-possible awareness occurred in 19 patients (0.66%) on BIS versus 8 (0.28%) on ETAC (difference 0.38 percentage points, 95% CI 0.03 to 0.74). There was no difference in the amount of anaesthesia administered or in major postoperative adverse outcomes.
cards.watchOut: The largest trial of the three points numerically AGAINST the BIS protocol; because both arms had active alerts plus education and checklists, the trial tests the alert source (brain monitor vs agent concentration), not monitoring versus nothing.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Lewis 2019): BIS may reduce awareness versus clinical signs (Peto odds ratio 0.36, relative; 27 studies, 9,765 participants) but shows no difference versus ETAG (Peto odds ratio 1.13, relative; 5 studies, 26,572 participants) — low-certainty evidence throughout
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Lewis 2019): BIS may reduce awareness versus clinical signs (Peto odds ratio 0.36, relative; 27 studies, 9,765 participants) but shows no difference versus ETAG (Peto odds ratio 1.13, relative; 5 studies, 26,572 participants) — low-certainty evidence throughout
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, BIS guidance vs clinical signs and vs ETAG guidance
cards.people: Systematic review of 52 randomised and quasi-randomised studies with 41,331 adults having general anaesthesia for any surgery, comparing BIS-guided anaesthesia with clinical signs or with end-tidal anaesthetic gas guidance (search to 26 March 2019); BIS targets across studies were within 40 to 60.
cards.result: Versus clinical signs, BIS-guided anaesthesia may reduce intraoperative awareness (Peto odds ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.60 — a relative measure; 27 studies, 9,765 participants; awareness incidence 3 per 1,000 with BIS versus 9 per 1,000 with clinical signs), and improved early recovery times (eye opening faster by 1.78 minutes; PACU discharge faster by 6.86 minutes). Versus ETAG, there was no evidence of a difference in awareness (Peto odds ratio 1.13, 95% CI 0.56 to 2.26; 5 studies, 26,572 participants; incidence 1 per 1,000 in both groups). All outcomes were graded low-certainty, chiefly because awareness is so infrequent that estimates remain imprecise and anaesthetists could not be blinded.
cards.watchOut: A synthesis whose two comparison limbs point in opposite directions — quoting only the clinical-signs limb (odds ratio 0.36) without the ETAG limb (1.13) would misstate the evidence; certainty is low for every outcome.

cards.headline: Synthesis: BIS guidance prevents awareness compared with routine care/clinical signs, but not compared with a disciplined end-tidal-agent alert protocol — the comparator decides the answer
cards.summary: Synthesis: BIS guidance prevents awareness compared with routine care/clinical signs, but not compared with a disciplined end-tidal-agent alert protocol — the comparator decides the answer
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: B-Aware showed BIS-guided care reduced confirmed awareness versus routine care (2 vs 11 cases; 82% relative risk reduction, absolute rates ~0.16% vs ~0.89%). B-Unaware (2 definite cases in each arm) and BAG-RECALL (definite awareness 0.24% on BIS-alert vs 0.07% on ETAC-alert) showed no superiority of a BIS protocol over an end-tidal-agent protocol, and the Cochrane review reproduces exactly that split (odds ratio 0.36 vs clinical signs; 1.13 vs ETAG; both relative, both low-certainty). Awareness is rare in every arm, so the practical question is which alert discipline a service runs, not whether BIS is 'effective' in the abstract.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Distinct from live #1123, which asks about anaesthetic depth targets and delirium, not awareness prevention.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Active warming/prewarming vs unwarmed care: wound infection 19%→6% (colorectal) and 14%→5% (clean surgery) — the unwarmed-comparator slice presupposed by PROTECT (live #1125)
shelves.question: In adults having surgery, does active perioperative warming — maintaining intraoperative normothermia, or preoperative warming (prewarming) before induction — versus unwarmed / routine thermal care permitting mild hypothermia reduce surgical-site infection and wound complications, and how much inadvertent perioperative hypothermia does each warming strategy prevent?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Body Temperature · Colonic Diseases · Double-Blind Method · Female · Humans · Hypothermia · Incidence · Intestine, Large · Intraoperative Care · Length of Stay · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Care · Risk Factors · Smoking · Surgical Wound Infection
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit) for the unwarmed-comparator question, with the era boundary printed on the face. Against care that permitted mild hypothermia, warming clearly reduced wound infection: intraoperative normothermia in colorectal surgery (final core temperature 36.6 °C vs 34.7 °C) cut wound infection from 19% (18/96) to 6% (6/104) and shortened hospitalisation by 2.6 days (Kurz 1996), and preoperative warming before clean surgery cut wound infection from 14% (19/139) to 5% (13/277) (Melling 2001). The Cochrane synthesis of active body-surface warming versus control found surgical-site infection reduced (risk ratio 0.36, a relative measure; 3 trials, 589 participants, low-quality evidence). Prewarming also reduces intraoperative hypothermia exposure even when everyone is warmed during surgery (Lau 2018), and resistive-fabric warming matched forced-air warming on temperature in elderly hemiarthroplasty (Kümin 2021). The boundary: Kurz and Melling are pre-modern-ERAS trials whose control arms reached temperatures no current routine permits, and the modern PROTECT trial (live #1125) found no cardiac-composite benefit from aggressive warming to ≥37 °C over routine management targeting 35.5 °C — both arms warmed. This shelf is the warming-versus-unwarmed / infection slice that live #1125 presupposes; it does not re-ask PROTECT's question. Where a publication names a warming product it is named on its card (BairPaws forced-air system, 3M, in Lau 2018), per the product-naming rule.

cards.headline: Kurz 1996 (Study of Wound Infection and Temperature Group): intraoperative normothermia (36.6 °C) versus routine care permitting hypothermia (34.7 °C) cut colorectal wound infection from 19% to 6% (P=0.009) and shortened hospitalisation by 2.6 days
cards.summary: Kurz 1996 (Study of Wound Infection and Temperature Group): intraoperative normothermia (36.6 °C) versus routine care permitting hypothermia (34.7 °C) cut colorectal wound infection from 19% to 6% (P=0.009) and shortened hospitalisation by 2.6 days
cards.type: Randomised double-blind trial, additional intraoperative warming (normothermia) vs routine thermal care, colorectal surgery
cards.people: 200 patients undergoing colorectal surgery, randomised to routine intraoperative thermal care (hypothermia group) or additional warming (normothermia group); anaesthetic care was standardised, all patients received cefamandole and metronidazole, and wound assessment was double-blind (infection = culture-positive pus).
cards.result: Mean final intraoperative core temperature was 34.7 ± 0.6 °C in the hypothermia group versus 36.6 ± 0.5 °C in the normothermia group (P<0.001). Surgical-wound infections occurred in 18 of 96 patients (19%) assigned to hypothermia versus 6 of 104 (6%) assigned to normothermia (P=0.009) — absolute rates. Sutures were removed one day later in the hypothermia group (P=0.002), and hospitalisation was prolonged by 2.6 days (about 20%; P=0.01).
cards.watchOut: A 1996 trial whose control arm was allowed to reach 34.7 °C — a depth of hypothermia modern routine care (which warms everyone) does not permit; the effect size belongs to that contrast and must not be applied to comparisons between two warmed strategies.
cards.source: Kurz A et al. Perioperative normothermia to reduce the incidence of surgical-wound infection and shorten hospitalization. Study of Wound Infection and Temperature Group. The New England journal of medicine. 1996. PMID: 8606715. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Melling 2001: preoperative warming for at least 30 minutes (local or systemic) before clean surgery cut wound infection from 14% (19/139) unwarmed to 5% (13/277) warmed (P=0.001)
cards.summary: Melling 2001: preoperative warming for at least 30 minutes (local or systemic) before clean surgery cut wound infection from 14% (19/139) unwarmed to 5% (13/277) warmed (P=0.001)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, preoperative local or systemic warming vs no warming, clean (breast/varicose-vein/hernia) surgery
cards.people: 421 patients having clean surgery (breast, varicose vein or hernia), randomised to a non-warmed (standard) group or to local or systemic preoperative warming applied for at least 30 minutes before surgery; outcomes were assessed masked at 2 and 6 weeks, analysed by intention to treat.
cards.result: Wound infections occurred in 19 of 139 non-warmed patients (14%) versus 13 of 277 warmed patients (5%) (P=0.001) — absolute rates, with the two warming methods (local and systemic) combined as published. Wound scores were also significantly lower in warmed patients (P=0.007). There was no significant difference in haematomas or seromas, but the non-warmed group was prescribed significantly more postoperative antibiotics (P=0.002). The authors note the warming therapies, applied per manufacturers' guidelines, have no known side-effects.
cards.watchOut: Short, clean operations in 2001 — the unwarmed control and the 14% baseline infection rate are of their era; the trial combines two different warming methods into one warmed group, so it supports prewarming as a strategy, not any single device.
cards.source: Melling AC et al. Effects of preoperative warming on the incidence of wound infection after clean surgery: a randomised controlled trial. Lancet (London, England). 2001. PMID: 11567703. cards.headline: Lau 2018: at least 30 minutes of preoperative forced-air warming reduced intraoperative hypothermia exposure even though all patients were warmed intraoperatively (median hypothermia magnitude 0.00 vs 0.05 °C·hr⁻¹; P=0.005); no difference in surgical-site infection or other secondary outcomes
cards.summary: Lau 2018: at least 30 minutes of preoperative forced-air warming reduced intraoperative hypothermia exposure even though all patients were warmed intraoperatively (median hypothermia magnitude 0.00 vs 0.05 °C·hr⁻¹; P=0.005); no difference in surgical-site infection or other secondary outcomes
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, preoperative forced-air warming (BairPaws, 3M) vs warmed blankets on request, with intraoperative warming in both arms
cards.people: 200 adults having elective non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia (101 control, 99 pre-warmed), randomised to preoperative warming with a BairPaws forced-air warming system (3M) for at least 30 minutes or to warmed blankets on request; all patients received intraoperative forced-air warming, and temperature was measured with the SpotOn system. Randomisation was stratified by scheduled surgical duration.
cards.result: The primary outcome — magnitude of intraoperative hypothermia (area under the time–temperature curve below 36 °C) — was lower in pre-warmed patients (median 0.00, IQR 0.00–0.12 °C·hr⁻¹) than controls (median 0.05, IQR 0.00–0.36 °C·hr⁻¹) (median difference −0.01 °C·hr⁻¹, 95% CI −0.04 to 0.00; P=0.005). There were no between-group differences in surgical-site infections, packed red-cell requirements or 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption. Redistribution hypothermia still occurred despite pre- and intraoperative warming.
cards.watchOut: A temperature-endpoint trial: it shows prewarming reduces hypothermia exposure on top of intraoperative warming, but it was not powered for, and found no difference in, infection — the infection claim rests on Kurz, Melling and the Cochrane synthesis, not on this card.
