cards.headline: Kümin 2021: resistive-fabric warming was a viable alternative to forced-air warming for preventing inadvertent perioperative hypothermia in elderly hemiarthroplasty (257 patients with continuous zero-flux thermometry; no difference in hypothermia proportions at <36.5 °C or <36.0 °C)
cards.summary: Kümin 2021: resistive-fabric warming was a viable alternative to forced-air warming for preventing inadvertent perioperative hypothermia in elderly hemiarthroplasty (257 patients with continuous zero-flux thermometry; no difference in hypothermia proportions at <36.5 °C or <36.0 °C)
cards.type: Temperature-recorded randomised subset analysis, resistive-fabric warming vs forced-air warming, elderly hemiarthroplasty
cards.people: 257 elderly patients randomised to forced-air warming or resistive-fabric warming within a prior randomised trial of patient warming after hemiarthroplasty (predominantly under regional rather than general anaesthesia), with core temperature recorded in detail by constant zero-flux thermometry; regression models compared warming groups with temperature-related covariates.
cards.result: Patients in the resistive-fabric group were 0.08 °C cooler on the modelled comparison and had a cumulative hypothermia score 1.87 lower than the forced-air group, as published; there was no difference between groups in the proportion of hypothermic patients at either the <36.5 °C or the <36.0 °C threshold. The authors conclude resistive-fabric warming is a viable alternative to forced-air warming for preventing inadvertent perioperative hypothermia during hemiarthroplasty.
cards.watchOut: A device-versus-device temperature comparison (both arms actively warmed) in a subset of a larger trial — it answers 'which warming method', not 'warming versus none', and reports temperature, not infection outcomes.

cards.headline: Cochrane synthesis (Madrid 2016): active body-surface warming versus control reduced surgical-site infection (risk ratio 0.36, relative; 3 trials, 589 participants, low-quality evidence), shivering and blood loss, with no mortality benefit
cards.summary: Cochrane synthesis (Madrid 2016): active body-surface warming versus control reduced surgical-site infection (risk ratio 0.36, relative; 3 trials, 589 participants, low-quality evidence), shivering and blood loss, with no mortality benefit
cards.type: Cochrane systematic review of randomised trials, active body-surface warming systems vs control and vs each other
cards.people: Systematic review of 67 randomised trials with 5,438 adults having surgery (79 comparisons): 45 trials compared active body-surface warming systems against control, 18 compared two warming systems, and 10 compared administration techniques; forced-air warming was by far the most studied intervention.
cards.result: Active warming versus control reduced surgical-site infection (risk ratio 0.36, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.66 — a relative measure; 3 RCTs, 589 participants, low-quality evidence). One low-risk-of-bias study found fewer major cardiovascular complications with forced-air warming in high-cardiovascular-risk patients (risk ratio 0.22, 95% CI 0.05 to 1.00; 1 RCT, 300 participants, 12 events). There was no beneficial effect on mortality. Warming also reduced measured blood loss (mean difference −46.17 mL, 95% CI −82.74 to −9.59) without reducing transfusion, and reduced shivering (risk ratio 0.39, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.54, relative). Adverse-effect data were limited (thermal burns the most relevant); nothing suggested a significant risk from warming systems.
cards.watchOut: The infection estimate rests on only 3 trials and 589 participants at low quality, and most included trials were open-label with unclear bias — the direction is consistent with the two classic trials, but the pooled relative effect should not be read as precise.

cards.headline: Synthesis: warming versus unwarmed care prevents wound infection (19%→6% colorectal; 14%→5% clean surgery; Cochrane risk ratio 0.36, relative) — a claim bounded by its era, since modern routine care warms everyone and PROTECT (live #1125) found no extra benefit from aggressive warming
cards.summary: Synthesis: warming versus unwarmed care prevents wound infection (19%→6% colorectal; 14%→5% clean surgery; Cochrane risk ratio 0.36, relative) — a claim bounded by its era, since modern routine care warms everyone and PROTECT (live #1125) found no extra benefit from aggressive warming
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Where the comparator permitted hypothermia, active warming or prewarming roughly halved or better the wound-infection rate (Kurz 1996: 6% vs 19%; Melling 2001: 5% vs 14%; Cochrane risk ratio 0.36, relative, low-quality evidence), and prewarming measurably reduces intraoperative hypothermia exposure even on top of intraoperative warming (Lau 2018), with resistive-fabric and forced-air systems performing comparably on temperature (Kümin 2021). The modern boundary stands beside the claim: those control arms reached temperatures current practice avoids, and aggressive warming beyond routine warmed management did not improve PROTECT's cardiac composite (live #1125) — this shelf answers warming versus unwarmed care, not how warm is warm enough among warmed strategies.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. This is the unwarmed-comparator slice presupposed by live #1125 (PROTECT), whose own question and cards are not re-carded here.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Multimodal prehabilitation in non-colorectal major surgery: fewer complications in high-risk abdominal (relative risk 0.5), lung-resection (34% vs 55%) and sarcopenic hepatectomy (13.3% vs 50%) trials — the slice outside live #936
shelves.question: In adults having major surgery OTHER than colorectal resection — elective major abdominal surgery in high-risk patients, lung resection, and major hepatectomy in patients with sarcopenia — does multimodal prehabilitation (structured exercise, nutrition, respiratory-muscle training and psychosocial components, as tested) reduce postoperative complications and shorten hospital stay versus usual care or postoperative rehabilitation?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen · Aged · Digestive System Surgical Procedures · Elective Surgical Procedures · Exercise Therapy · Female · Humans · Male · Postoperative Complications · Precision Medicine · Preoperative Care · Retrospective Studies · Risk Factors · Treatment Outcome
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), carded per surgical field and per programme — never as a general 'prehabilitation works' claim, because every trial selected its population differently. High-risk elective major abdominal surgery (Barberan-Garcia 2018; analysed 125): personalised prehabilitation roughly halved the proportion of patients with postoperative complications (relative risk 0.5, a relative measure). Lung resection in physiologically high-risk patients (Brat 2025; 122 completed): multimodal prehabilitation with high-intensity respiratory-muscle training reduced postoperative pulmonary complications (34% vs 55%) and shortened stay (7 vs 9 days). Major hepatectomy in sarcopenia (PREHEP, Berardi 2025; 60 analysed): 6-week exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation reduced overall morbidity (13.3% vs 50%; absolute risk reduction 36.7 percentage points, number needed to treat 3), with all major complications in the control group. The BMJ network/component meta-analysis (186 trials, 15,684 participants) supports exercise and nutrition as the active components, but at mostly very-low certainty — component-level claims rest on that synthesis, not on any single trial. This shelf is the non-colorectal slice: frail patients awaiting colorectal resection are homed at live #936 (whose PREHAB colorectal trial is not re-carded here), and prehabilitation before hip/knee arthroplasty is homed at pack #3746; both are cross-pointed in prose only.

cards.headline: Barberan-Garcia 2018: personalised prehabilitation in high-risk patients having elective major abdominal surgery reduced the proportion with postoperative complications (relative risk 0.5, relative; P=0.001) and increased aerobic capacity
cards.summary: Barberan-Garcia 2018: personalised prehabilitation in high-risk patients having elective major abdominal surgery reduced the proportion with postoperative complications (relative risk 0.5, relative; P=0.001) and increased aerobic capacity
cards.type: Randomised blinded controlled trial, personalised prehabilitation vs standard care, high-risk elective major abdominal surgery
cards.people: Patients at high risk for elective major abdominal surgery (age over 70 years and/or ASA score III/IV), randomised 1:1 to standard care (71) or standard care plus personalised prehabilitation (73) — motivational interview, high-intensity endurance training and promotion of physical activity; after 19 exclusions for changes in the surgical plan, 63 controls and 62 intervention patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis.
cards.result: Prehabilitation enhanced aerobic capacity (endurance time change +135% (SD 218); P<0.001). The intervention reduced the number of patients with postoperative complications by 51% (relative risk 0.5, 95% CI 0.3 to 0.8; P=0.001 — a relative measure) and reduced the complication rate per patient (0.5 (SD 1.0) vs 1.4 (SD 1.6); P=0.001) compared with controls.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre trial with 125 analysed patients and a per-patient complication count as a key read; 'high-risk' here means age/ASA selection, which differs from the frailty selection at live #936 and the sarcopenia selection in PREHEP — the populations must not be merged.
cards.source: Barberan-Garcia A et al. Personalised Prehabilitation in High-risk Patients Undergoing Elective Major Abdominal Surgery: A Randomized Blinded Controlled Trial. Annals of surgery. 2018. cards.headline: Brat 2025: multimodal prehabilitation with high-intensity respiratory-muscle training before lung resection reduced postoperative pulmonary complications (34% vs 55%; P=0.029) and shortened stay (7 vs 9 days) in physiologically high-risk patients
cards.summary: Brat 2025: multimodal prehabilitation with high-intensity respiratory-muscle training before lung resection reduced postoperative pulmonary complications (34% vs 55%; P=0.029) and shortened stay (7 vs 9 days) in physiologically high-risk patients
cards.type: Multicentre randomised controlled trial, multimodal prehabilitation (respiratory-muscle training, smoking cessation, nutrition, psychological support) vs usual care, lung resection in CPET-defined high-risk patients
cards.people: Patients undergoing lung resection selected as high-risk for postoperative pulmonary complications by a VE/VCO2 slope of at least 33 on cardiopulmonary exercise testing, randomised at multiple centres to usual care or a 14-day multimodal prehabilitation programme (high-intensity respiratory-muscle training, smoking cessation, nutritional and psychological support); 122 patients completed the study (58 prehabilitation, 64 usual care).
cards.result: Postoperative pulmonary complications (pneumonia, atelectasis, respiratory failure needing mechanical ventilation, ARDS, prolonged air leak) occurred in 20 of 58 patients (34%) with prehabilitation versus 35 of 64 (55%) with usual care (odds ratio 2.29 as published for the comparison, 95% CI 1.10 to 4.77; P=0.029 — absolute rates 34% vs 55%). Hospital stay was shorter after prehabilitation (7 days, IQR 6–9, vs 9 days, IQR 7–11; P=0.038). Mean VE/VCO2 slope improved from 39 (SD 8) to 36 (SD 9) after prehabilitation (P=0.01), and patient-reported quality of life improved.
cards.watchOut: The population is a narrow physiological slice (VE/VCO2 slope ≥33) and the programme is short (14 days) and respiratory-muscle-centred — neither the population nor the programme transfers directly to other surgical fields; the published odds ratio is oriented to the usual-care group's higher odds and is read here beside the absolute rates.

cards.headline: PREHEP (Berardi 2025): 6-week exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation in sarcopenic patients having major hepatectomy reduced 90-day morbidity (13.3% vs 50%; absolute risk reduction 36.7 percentage points, NNT 3); all major complications occurred in the control group
cards.summary: PREHEP (Berardi 2025): 6-week exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation in sarcopenic patients having major hepatectomy reduced 90-day morbidity (13.3% vs 50%; absolute risk reduction 36.7 percentage points, NNT 3); all major complications occurred in the control group
cards.type: Single-centre open-label randomised trial (PREHEP), 6-week exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation vs standard care, major hepatectomy in sarcopenia
cards.people: 70 adults with radiologically and functionally confirmed sarcopenia scheduled for major liver resection and requiring future liver remnant hypertrophy, randomised 1:1 at a single Italian tertiary centre to a 6-week structured prehabilitation programme (daily walking, supervised biweekly in-hospital exercise, branched-chain amino acid and immune nutritional supplementation) during the wait for remnant hypertrophy, or standard care; 60 patients (30 per arm) were included in the final analysis, most after portal vein embolisation and right hepatectomy.
cards.result: Overall 90-day postoperative morbidity (Clavien-Dindo) was significantly lower with prehabilitation: 4 of 30 patients (13.3%) versus 15 of 30 (50%) (odds ratio 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.55; P=.004), an absolute risk reduction of 36.7 percentage points and a number needed to treat of 3. All major complications occurred in the control group (6 of 30, 20%; P=.02). Muscle mass and strength improved significantly only in the prehabilitation arm.
cards.watchOut: A small (60 analysed), single-centre, open-label trial in a highly selected sarcopenic population with an unusually long built-in preoperative window (remnant hypertrophy) — the very large effect (NNT 3) needs multicentre confirmation before it is generalised beyond this setting.

cards.headline: BMJ network/component synthesis (McIsaac 2025): across 186 prehabilitation trials (15,684 participants), isolated exercise (odds ratio 0.50, relative), isolated nutrition (0.62) and exercise+nutrition+psychosocial (0.64) most likely reduced complications — at very-low certainty; exercise and nutrition are the components that carry the effect
cards.summary: BMJ network/component synthesis (McIsaac 2025): across 186 prehabilitation trials (15,684 participants), isolated exercise (odds ratio 0.50, relative), isolated nutrition (0.62) and exercise+nutrition+psychosocial (0.64) most likely reduced complications — at very-low certainty; exercise and nutrition are the components that carry the effect
cards.type: Systematic review with network and component network meta-analyses of prehabilitation randomised trials across major surgery
cards.people: Systematic review with network and component network meta-analyses of 186 unique randomised trials with 15,684 adults preparing for major surgery, comparing prehabilitation interventions and components (exercise, nutrition, cognitive, psychosocial) against usual care; certainty assessed with the CINeMA approach.
cards.result: For postoperative complications, the treatments most likely to beat usual care were isolated exercise (odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.39 to 0.64 — a relative measure; very-low certainty), isolated nutritional prehabilitation (0.62, 0.50 to 0.77; very-low certainty) and combined exercise, nutrition plus psychosocial prehabilitation (0.64, 0.45 to 0.92; very-low certainty). Length of stay was most reduced by combined exercise and psychosocial (−2.44 days; very-low certainty) and combined exercise and nutrition (−1.22 days; moderate certainty). In the component analysis, exercise and nutrition were the individual components most likely to improve all critical outcomes. Certainty was generally low to very low (trial bias and imprecision), though exercise and nutrition results were robust when high-risk-of-bias trials were excluded.
cards.watchOut: This synthesis spans ALL major surgery including the colorectal population homed at live #936 — it is carded here for component-level inference only, and its very-low certainty grades mean it supports, but cannot substitute for, the field-specific trials carded above.

cards.result: Three randomised trials in three differently selected non-colorectal populations each found fewer postoperative complications with multimodal prehabilitation: personalised prehabilitation in high-risk major abdominal surgery (relative risk 0.5, relative), respiratory-muscle-centred prehabilitation before lung resection (pulmonary complications 34% vs 55%), and exercise-and-nutrition prehabilitation in sarcopenic major hepatectomy (morbidity 13.3% vs 50%). The BMJ component network analysis attributes the benefit mainly to the exercise and nutrition components, at low-to-very-low certainty. Frail colorectal patients (live #936) and arthroplasty patients (pack #3746) are separate questions, homed elsewhere and not re-carded here.

shelves.title: DASI before major non-cardiac surgery (METS programme reports): subjective assessment had 19.2% sensitivity for inability to reach 4 METs; DASI — threshold 34 — was the only bedside measure predicting 30-day death or MI
shelves.question: Before major non-cardiac surgery, how well do bedside measures of functional capacity — the Duke Activity Status Index (DASI) questionnaire and clinicians' subjective assessment in metabolic equivalents — predict 30-day death, myocardial infarction / myocardial injury and complications, and how do they compare with cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak oxygen consumption) and NT-proBNP?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Exercise Test · Exercise Tolerance · Female · Health Status · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Natriuretic Peptide, Brain/blood · Peptide Fragments/blood · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Prospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Sensitivity and Specificity · Health Status Indicators · Self Report · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE — the DASI questionnaire carries prognostic information, clinicians' subjective assessment does not. All three reports are reports OF one programme, labelled as such on the face: the METS international cohort (1,401 patients; 30-day death or myocardial infarction in 28, 2%), its nested DASI analysis (1,546 participants), and a pooled analysis of METS with the FIT After Surgery cohort (3,485 patients). In METS, subjective assessment had only 19.2% sensitivity (95% CI 14.2 to 25) for identifying inability to attain 4 METs on cardiopulmonary exercise testing, and only DASI scores were associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction (adjusted odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99, per DASI point). The nested analysis located a threshold at a DASI score of 34. The pooled analysis found DASI added prognostic information beyond age, the Revised Cardiac Risk Index and natriuretic peptide (likelihood ratio test p=0.009 for the primary outcome), but final-model discrimination stayed modest (c-index 0.70-0.71) with limited net clinical benefit. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no report shows that raising a DASI score changes outcomes. PROPOSED STAMP: POSSIBLE.

cards.headline: METS cohort (Wijeysundera 2018): subjective assessment missed most patients unable to reach 4 METs on CPET (sensitivity 19.2%); only DASI predicted 30-day death or myocardial infarction — a report OF the METS programme
cards.summary: METS cohort (Wijeysundera 2018): subjective assessment missed most patients unable to reach 4 METs on CPET (sensitivity 19.2%); only DASI predicted 30-day death or myocardial infarction — a report OF the METS programme
cards.type: Programme report: international prospective cohort study (the METS study — primary report of the programme)
cards.people: 1,401 adults aged at least 40 years at elevated cardiac risk, scheduled for major elective non-cardiac surgery at 25 hospitals in Canada, the UK, Australia and New Zealand; all had subjective assessment, the DASI questionnaire, cardiopulmonary exercise testing (peak oxygen consumption) and NT-proBNP measurement.
cards.result: 28 of 1,401 patients (2%) died or had a myocardial infarction within 30 days. Subjective assessment had 19.2% sensitivity (95% CI 14.2 to 25) and 94.7% specificity (95% CI 93.2 to 95.9) for identifying inability to attain four metabolic equivalents during CPET. Only DASI scores were associated with the primary outcome (adjusted odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.99, per DASI point; p=0.03); CPET peak oxygen consumption and NT-proBNP were not, as published. The authors concluded subjectively assessed functional capacity should not be used for preoperative risk evaluation and that a measure such as DASI could be considered instead.
cards.watchOut: Programme report, labelled: this is the primary METS cohort, and the next two cards are further reports of the same programme (one nested in it, one pooling it with one other cohort) — they are not three independent cohorts. Only 28 primary-outcome events occurred, so the prognostic estimates rest on a small absolute event count, printed here.
cards.source: Wijeysundera DN et al. Assessment of functional capacity before major non-cardiac surgery: an international, prospective cohort study. Lancet (London, England). 2018. PMID: 30070222. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Nested METS analysis (Wijeysundera 2020): a DASI score of 34 is the threshold — above it each point lowered odds of 30-day death or myocardial injury, below it each point lost raised odds — a report OF the METS programme
cards.summary: Nested METS analysis (Wijeysundera 2020): a DASI score of 34 is the threshold — above it each point lowered odds of 30-day death or myocardial injury, below it each point lost raised odds — a report OF the METS programme
cards.type: Programme report: nested cohort analysis OF the METS study (same programme as the card above — not an independent cohort)
cards.people: 1,546 participants aged at least 40 years at elevated cardiac risk who had inpatient noncardiac surgery, in a nested cohort analysis of the METS study; outcomes were 30-day death or myocardial injury (primary), 30-day death or myocardial infarction, in-hospital moderate-to-severe complications, and 1-year death or new disability.
cards.result: DASI associations were non-linear around a score of 34. Above 34, each 1-point increase was associated with reduced odds of 30-day death or myocardial injury (odds ratio 0.97, 95% CI 0.96 to 0.99) and of 1-year death or new disability (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.92 to 0.99). Below 34, each 1-point decrease was associated with increased odds of 30-day death or myocardial infarction (odds ratio 1.05, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.09) and of moderate-to-severe complications (odds ratio 1.03, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.05). A DASI score of 34 was identified as the threshold for identifying patients at risk.
cards.watchOut: Programme report, labelled: the participants are the METS cohort re-analysed (1,546 in this analysis), so this card refines the threshold from the primary report rather than confirming it in new patients.

cards.headline: Pooled METS + FIT After Surgery analysis (Wijeysundera 2026): DASI added prognostic information beyond age, RCRI and natriuretic peptide, but discrimination stayed modest (c-index 0.70-0.71) — a programme report pooling METS with one further cohort
cards.summary: Pooled METS + FIT After Surgery analysis (Wijeysundera 2026): DASI added prognostic information beyond age, RCRI and natriuretic peptide, but discrimination stayed modest (c-index 0.70-0.71) — a programme report pooling METS with one further cohort
cards.type: Programme report: international pooled cohort analysis (METS pooled with FIT After Surgery — METS participants overlap the two cards above)
cards.people: 3,485 adults undergoing elective major non-cardiac surgery in a pooled analysis of two prospective cohorts — METS and Functional Improvement Trajectories After Surgery (FIT After Surgery), data collected March 2013 to April 2023; primary outcome was 30-day major cardiac complications (myocardial infarction or non-fatal cardiac arrest) or death, which occurred in 126 patients (3.6%); all-cause major complications occurred in 647 (19%).
cards.result: DASI provided prognostic information beyond age, Revised Cardiac Risk Index and natriuretic peptide concentration for the primary outcome (likelihood ratio test p=0.009) and beyond age, sex and surgery type for major complications (p<0.001). Inclusion of DASI improved prognostic performance across multiple metrics, but overall discrimination of the final models remained modest (c-index 0.70-0.71) with limited net clinical benefit, and predicted risk at a given DASI score varied substantially by age, RCRI and natriuretic peptide — supporting DASI as a continuous prognostic marker rather than a dichotomous screening test.
cards.watchOut: Programme report, labelled: half of the pooled data are the METS participants already carded above, so the three cards are one programme's reports plus one added cohort, not three independent validations. cards.headline: Synthesis: across the METS programme's reports, subjective assessment is unreliable (19.2% sensitivity for inability to reach 4 METs), DASI is the only bedside measure associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction, and its added value in pooled data is real but modest
cards.summary: Synthesis: across the METS programme's reports, subjective assessment is unreliable (19.2% sensitivity for inability to reach 4 METs), DASI is the only bedside measure associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction, and its added value in pooled data is real but modest
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf — one programme (METS), reported three times, with FIT After Surgery added in the pooled report.
cards.result: Subjective functional-capacity assessment should not be used for preoperative risk evaluation: in METS it identified only 19.2% (95% CI 14.2 to 25) of patients unable to attain 4 METs on CPET. DASI scores were associated with 30-day death or myocardial infarction (adjusted odds ratio 0.96 per point), with a threshold at 34 in the nested analysis, and in the pooled METS + FIT After Surgery analysis DASI added prognostic information beyond established predictors (p=0.009) while final discrimination remained modest (c-index 0.70-0.71). CPET peak oxygen consumption and NT-proBNP were not associated with the primary outcome in the primary METS report, as published. Nothing here shows that improving a DASI score improves outcomes — this is prognostic accuracy only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; all three are programme reports of substantially the same patients, labelled as such, and this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Incentive spirometry after abdominal surgery: Cochrane found no benefit vs no therapy or deep breathing (12 trials); small trials beat only other breathing therapies on lung function; the PRIME-AIR bundle including it was null
shelves.question: After upper abdominal or other major surgery, does incentive spirometry — volume- or flow-oriented, as tested — versus no therapy, deep-breathing exercises or other lung-expansion therapy reduce postoperative pulmonary complications, and does a structured perioperative lung-expansion bundle that includes it (PRIME-AIR) beat usual care?
shelves.mesh: Abdomen/surgery · Adult · Bronchial Diseases/prevention & control · Humans · Lung Diseases/prevention & control · Pneumonia/prevention & control · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control · Pulmonary Atelectasis/prevention & control · Randomized Controlled Trials as Topic · Respiratory Insufficiency/prevention & control · Respiratory Therapy/methods · Spirometry/methods · Tracheal Diseases/prevention & control
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) — the device itself is unproven against the comparators that matter. The Cochrane synthesis (12 trials, 1,834 participants; 1,160 in meta-analysis) found NO statistically significant difference between incentive spirometry and no respiratory treatment for clinical complications (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.18), none versus deep-breathing exercises for respiratory failure, and none versus other chest physiotherapy — its conclusion is low-quality evidence of lack of effectiveness, and that uncertainty stays on the face of this shelf. The small head-to-head trials carded here compare one breathing therapy against another (volume spirometry vs diaphragmatic breathing, n=58; spirometry vs EzPAP, n=112, complications 3.6% vs 7.1%, not significant; flow vs volume spirometry, n=50) and show at most better spirometric recovery — they must not be pooled into a 'spirometry works' claim. The one large trial, PRIME-AIR (n=751 analysed), tested a perioperative lung-expansion BUNDLE that included supervised postoperative incentive spirometry and found no reduction in pulmonary-complication severity versus usual care (mean severity 1.60 vs 1.53, P=0.19); a bundle's result cannot be attributed to the spirometer, and it is carded as a bundle limb only.

cards.headline: Cochrane review (do Nascimento Junior 2014; 12 trials, 1,834 participants): no significant difference between incentive spirometry and no treatment, deep breathing or other physiotherapy for postoperative pulmonary complications after upper abdominal surgery — low-quality evidence of lack of effectiveness
cards.summary: Cochrane review (do Nascimento Junior 2014; 12 trials, 1,834 participants): no significant difference between incentive spirometry and no treatment, deep breathing or other physiotherapy for postoperative pulmonary complications after upper abdominal surgery — low-quality evidence of lack of effectiveness
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised trials (Cochrane, updated 2014), incentive spirometry vs no therapy / deep breathing / other physiotherapy
cards.people: 12 randomised trials with 1,834 adults admitted for any type of upper abdominal surgery (including laparoscopic procedures); data from 1,160 patients could be included in the meta-analysis. Four trials (152 patients) compared incentive spirometry with no respiratory treatment, two (194 patients) with deep-breathing exercises, and two (946 patients) with other chest physiotherapy.
cards.result: Versus no respiratory treatment, incentive spirometry did not significantly reduce clinical complications (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.18). Versus deep-breathing exercises, there was no significant difference in respiratory failure (relative risk 0.67, 95% CI 0.04 to 10.50). Versus other chest physiotherapy, there were no significant differences in the risk of developing a pulmonary condition or in the type of complication. The reviewers concluded there is low-quality evidence regarding the lack of effectiveness of incentive spirometry for prevention of postoperative pulmonary complications after upper abdominal surgery, and called for large, well-designed trials. Trial quality was hard to assess (predominantly 'unclear' bias) and compliance with the prescribed therapy was not reported.
cards.watchOut: This is the balance anchor of the shelf and its uncertainty is the headline: 'no significant difference' on low-quality, poorly reported trials is not proof of no effect — but it is the only synthesis of spirometry against no therapy, and no card below overturns it, because none of them uses a no-therapy control.
cards.source: do Nascimento Junior P et al. Incentive spirometry for prevention of postoperative pulmonary complications in upper abdominal surgery. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2014. PMID: 24510642. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Volume incentive spirometry vs diaphragmatic breathing after open abdominal surgery (Zhao 2023, n=58): pulmonary function (FEV1, FVC, PEF) and SpO2 recovered better with volume spirometry — a comparison of two active breathing therapies, not of spirometry against no therapy
cards.summary: Volume incentive spirometry vs diaphragmatic breathing after open abdominal surgery (Zhao 2023, n=58): pulmonary function (FEV1, FVC, PEF) and SpO2 recovered better with volume spirometry — a comparison of two active breathing therapies, not of spirometry against no therapy
cards.type: Single-centre randomised trial, volume incentive spirometry vs diaphragmatic breathing exercises after open abdominal surgery
cards.people: 58 patients after open abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia, randomised to diaphragmatic breathing exercises (n=29) or volume incentive spirometry exercises (n=29); haemodynamics, pulmonary function and blood gases recorded before surgery and on postoperative days 1, 3 and 5.
cards.result: Pulmonary function fell postoperatively in both groups and then recovered. On postoperative days 1, 3 and 5 the volume-spirometry group had significantly higher peak expiratory flow, FEV1, FVC and FEV1/FVC ratio than the diaphragmatic-breathing group, and significantly higher SpO2 on days 3 and 5 (all P<0.05). Base excess and pH were significantly higher in the spirometry group on day 1. The authors concluded volume incentive spirometry might be the better option for improving pulmonary function and blood gases, hence lowering the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications — but complication incidence itself is not reported as a comparative result in the record.
cards.watchOut: 58 patients, surrogate endpoints (spirometry values and blood gases over 5 days), and an active comparator: better FEV1 recovery than diaphragmatic breathing does not show that spirometry prevents pulmonary complications, and the title's complication claim goes beyond the comparative data printed in the abstract.

cards.headline: Incentive spirometry vs EzPAP lung-expansion therapy after upper abdominal surgery (Rowley 2019, n=112): no difference in dorsal ventilation redistribution, length of stay (4 days both) or pulmonary complications (3.6% vs 7.1%, P=0.19)
cards.summary: Incentive spirometry vs EzPAP lung-expansion therapy after upper abdominal surgery (Rowley 2019, n=112): no difference in dorsal ventilation redistribution, length of stay (4 days both) or pulmonary complications (3.6% vs 7.1%, P=0.19)
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial, incentive spirometry vs EzPAP lung-expansion therapy after upper abdominal surgery
cards.people: 112 adults after upper abdominal surgery (enrolled January 2017 to November 2018), allocated to incentive spirometry (n=56) or EzPAP positive-pressure lung-expansion therapy (n=56), each given 3 times a day on postoperative days 1–5; ventilation redistribution was measured by electrical impedance tomography during a session on days 1, 3 and 5.
cards.result: Dorsal end-expiratory lung impedance rose after therapy in both groups, with no significant between-group difference on day 1 (16% vs 12%, P=0.39), day 3 (6% vs 6%, P=0.68) or day 5 (9% vs 6%, P=0.46). Hospital length of stay was 4 days in both groups (P=0.30) and the incidence of postoperative pulmonary complications was similar (3.6% with incentive spirometry vs 7.1% with EzPAP, P=0.19).
cards.watchOut: Another active-comparator trial with a physiological primary endpoint (impedance-measured ventilation redistribution): equivalence with EzPAP says nothing about either therapy versus no therapy, and with 4 vs 8 complication events the trial had no power over the clinical endpoint.
cards.source: Rowley DD et al. A Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Two Lung Expansion Therapies After Upper Abdominal Surgery. Respiratory care. 2019. PMID: 31113857. Registry ID: NCT02892773. cards.headline: Flow vs volume incentive spirometry in open abdominal surgery (Kumar 2016, n=50): pulmonary function was better preserved by days 4–5 with both device types; the volume group improved more on six-minute walk distance by discharge
cards.summary: Flow vs volume incentive spirometry in open abdominal surgery (Kumar 2016, n=50): pulmonary function was better preserved by days 4–5 with both device types; the volume group improved more on six-minute walk distance by discharge
cards.type: Randomised clinical trial, flow-oriented vs volume-oriented incentive spirometry in open abdominal surgery (device-type comparison)
cards.people: 50 patients (37 men, 13 women) undergoing open abdominal surgery at a hospital in Mangalore, India, allocated by block randomisation to flow incentive spirometry or volume incentive spirometry; FVC, FEV1 and peak expiratory flow measured preoperatively and to postoperative day 5, with six-minute walk testing preoperatively and at discharge.
cards.result: Pulmonary function (FVC, FEV1, peak flow) fell significantly on postoperative days 1–3 versus preoperative values in both groups and was better preserved on days 4 and 5 in both the flow and volume groups. Six-minute walk performance improved significantly from the preoperative period to discharge, with a greater statistically significant improvement in distance covered in the volume-incentive group than the flow-incentive group. No adverse events were recorded with either device.
cards.watchOut: This card answers only the device-type question (flow vs volume) — there is no non-spirometry arm at all — and its outcomes are spirometric values and walk distance in 50 patients, not pulmonary complications.

cards.headline: Bundle limb — PRIME-AIR phase 3 trial (Fernandez-Bustamante 2025, n=751 analysed): a perioperative lung-expansion bundle INCLUDING supervised postoperative incentive spirometry did not reduce pulmonary-complication severity versus usual care (mean severity 1.60 vs 1.53, P=0.19) — a bundle result, not spirometry evidence
cards.summary: Bundle limb — PRIME-AIR phase 3 trial (Fernandez-Bustamante 2025, n=751 analysed): a perioperative lung-expansion bundle INCLUDING supervised postoperative incentive spirometry did not reduce pulmonary-complication severity versus usual care (mean severity 1.60 vs 1.53, P=0.19) — a bundle result, not spirometry evidence
cards.type: Bundle limb: multicentre randomised phase 3 trial (PRIME-AIR) of a perioperative lung-expansion bundle (one component is supervised incentive spirometry) vs usual care — NOT a trial of incentive spirometry alone
cards.people: Adults at intermediate or high risk of postoperative pulmonary complications (ARISCAT score ≥26, BMI <35 kg/m²) having elective open abdominal surgery expected to last ≥2 hours, at 17 US academic hospitals; 794 were randomised and 751 formed the modified intention-to-treat population (379 bundle, 372 usual care; mean age 61.8 years). The bundle comprised preoperative education, intraoperative protective ventilation with individualised PEEP, weight- and monitoring-based neuromuscular blockade and reversal, and postoperative supervised incentive spirometry and mobilisation encouragement.
cards.result: By postoperative day 7 the most common pulmonary-complication severity was grade 2 in both groups (56% bundle vs 60% usual care), and mean severity was similar (1.60 [SD 0.94] vs 1.53 [0.93]; mean difference 0.07, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.18; P=0.19), despite high bundle adherence (72–98%) and higher delivered PEEP in the bundle group (7.5 vs 5.6 cmH2O). Serious adverse events occurred in 9% of each group; deaths by 90 days were 6 (2%) in the bundle group and 5 (1%) with usual care.
cards.watchOut: Bundle limb, labelled as such: the bundle combined education, individualised PEEP ventilation, neuromuscular-blockade management, spirometry and mobilisation, so its null result cannot be attributed to — or held against — the spirometer alone. It is carded only because the commissioning row asks the bundle question beside the device question.

cards.headline: Synthesis: against no therapy or deep breathing, incentive spirometry has no demonstrated benefit (Cochrane, 12 trials); the small modern trials compare it with other active breathing therapies on physiological endpoints, and the one large bundle trial that included it was null
cards.summary: Synthesis: against no therapy or deep breathing, incentive spirometry has no demonstrated benefit (Cochrane, 12 trials); the small modern trials compare it with other active breathing therapies on physiological endpoints, and the one large bundle trial that included it was null
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The evidence separates cleanly by comparator. Versus no respiratory treatment, deep-breathing exercises or other physiotherapy, the Cochrane meta-analysis found no significant reduction in pulmonary complications (relative risk 0.59, 95% CI 0.30 to 1.18 versus no treatment) on low-quality evidence. Versus another active therapy, volume spirometry recovered spirometric values faster than diaphragmatic breathing (n=58), spirometry and EzPAP were indistinguishable on ventilation redistribution and complications (n=112), and volume devices beat flow devices on walk distance (n=50). The PRIME-AIR bundle including supervised spirometry did not reduce complication severity in 751 patients. No carded trial shows incentive spirometry preventing pulmonary complications against an untreated control.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Hypotension Prediction Index guidance: less time hypotensive in small trials, but no less AKI (6.1% vs 7.0% in the 917-patient multicentre trial), no fewer complications, no mortality benefit
shelves.question: In adults having surgery under general anaesthesia, does haemodynamic management guided by the Hypotension Prediction Index (HPI) — a machine-learning early-warning algorithm for impending hypotension — versus standard care or conventional goal-directed therapy reduce the depth and duration of intraoperative hypotension and postoperative acute kidney injury?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Female · Aged · Male · Hemodynamics/physiology · Postoperative Complications/prevention & control,epidemiology · Abdomen/surgery · Acute Kidney Injury/epidemiology,prevention & control,etiology · Hypotension/diagnosis,physiopathology,therapy · Middle Aged · Length of Stay
shelves.balance: SPLIT — the index moves the process measure and not the patient outcomes. In two small randomised trials, HPI-guided management (Hypotension Prediction Index, Edwards Lifesciences, USA — a named commercial product, named per card as published) reduced the burden of intraoperative hypotension: time-weighted average MAP below 65 mmHg 0.02 vs 0.37 in a 60-patient trial, and time-weighted area below threshold 0.19 vs 0.66 mmHg when HPI was added to conventional goal-directed therapy in 64 patients — the Sapporo design, which separates the index itself from simply doing more goal-directed therapy, though at the cost of more norepinephrine use. But the one large trial — 917 patients, 28 hospitals, moderate-to-severe AKI as the primary outcome — found no benefit: AKI 6.1% vs 7.0% (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.49), complications 31.9% vs 29.7%, mortality 1.1% vs 0.9%. The 2026 meta-analysis of 8 randomised trials (1,534 patients) agrees: no significant difference in AKI, complications, mortality, length of stay or fluid use, with the hypotension-metric reductions confined to post hoc analyses in unblinded trials at high risk of bias. The related intraoperative blood-pressure STRATEGY trials (INPRESS individualised targets; POISE-3 hypotension-avoidance) are cross-points only — they are carded elsewhere and are not evidence about this device.

cards.headline: Multicentre RCT (Ripollés-Melchor 2025, 28 hospitals, n=917): HPI-guided management did NOT reduce moderate-to-severe AKI (6.1% vs 7.0%; risk ratio 0.89, P=0.66), complications or 30-day mortality versus standard care in abdominal surgery
cards.summary: Multicentre RCT (Ripollés-Melchor 2025, 28 hospitals, n=917): HPI-guided management did NOT reduce moderate-to-severe AKI (6.1% vs 7.0%; risk ratio 0.89, P=0.66), complications or 30-day mortality versus standard care in abdominal surgery
cards.type: Multicentre randomised clinical trial (28 hospitals), HPI-guided haemodynamic management vs standard care in elective abdominal surgery — primary outcome moderate-to-severe AKI
cards.people: 917 patients (aged ≥65, or >18 with ASA physical status >II) having moderate- to high-risk elective abdominal surgery across 28 hospitals (October 2022 to February 2024), in the intention-to-treat analysis; median age 71 (HPI) and 70 (standard care). In the HPI group (Hypotension Prediction Index; Edwards Lifesciences, USA), an index value above 80 triggered fluids and/or vasopressors/inotropes guided by haemodynamic data; the comparator was the wide range of real-world haemodynamic approaches at the participating hospitals.
cards.result: Moderate-to-severe acute kidney injury within 7 days occurred in 6.1% (28 of 459) on HPI guidance versus 7.0% (32 of 458) on standard care (risk ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.54 to 1.49; P=0.66). Overall complications were 31.9% versus 29.7% (risk ratio 1.08, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.37; P=0.52); renal replacement therapy did not differ; median hospital stay was 6 days in both groups; 30-day mortality was 1.1% versus 0.9% (risk ratio 1.35, 95% CI 0.36 to 5.10; P=0.66). The authors concluded HPI-guided therapy did not reduce postoperative AKI or overall complications compared with standard care.
cards.watchOut: This is the only card powered on a patient outcome, and it is null on every one of them; its comparator ('a wide range of real-world approaches') is heterogeneous by design, which cuts both ways — it is the pragmatic question, but it cannot show whether HPI beats a single protocolised alternative.
cards.source: Ripollés-Melchor J et al. Hemodynamic Management Guided by the Hypotension Prediction Index in Abdominal Surgery: A Multicenter Randomized Clinical Trial. Anesthesiology. 2025. PMID: 39746186. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Single-centre RCT (Lai 2024, n=60): HPI guidance cut hypotension severity — time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg 0.02 vs 0.37 (P<0.001) — in long operations under general anaesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring
cards.summary: Single-centre RCT (Lai 2024, n=60): HPI guidance cut hypotension severity — time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg 0.02 vs 0.37 (P<0.001) — in long operations under general anaesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring
cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial, HPI-guided management vs standard care (treatment threshold MAP <65 mmHg) — hypotension-burden endpoints only
cards.people: 60 patients undergoing general anaesthesia with invasive arterial monitoring at a tertiary referral hospital, randomised 1:1 to haemodynamic management with HPI guidance (treatment initiated at HPI >85) or standard care (treatment at MAP <65 mmHg); median age 62 years, 48 of 60 male, median surgery duration 490 minutes.
cards.result: The primary outcome, hypotension severity as time-weighted average MAP below 65 mmHg, was significantly lower with HPI guidance: median 0.02 (IQR 0.003–0.08) versus 0.37 (0.20–0.58), P<0.001, with similar findings for the <60 and <55 mmHg thresholds. Median intraoperative MAP was higher in the intervention group (87.54 vs 77.92 mmHg, P<0.001). The authors state that further investigation is needed to assess the impact of HPI on patient outcomes — this trial reports none.
cards.watchOut: 60 patients, one centre, and a process endpoint: acting earlier on a prediction alert almost mechanically reduces time below the threshold that triggers the control arm's treatment. No kidney, complication or mortality outcome is reported.
cards.source: Lai CJ et al. Hypotension prediction index for prevention of intraoperative hypotension in patients undergoing general anesthesia: a randomized controlled trial. Perioperative medicine (London, England). 2024. PMID: 38879506. Registry ID: NCT04966364. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Sapporo RCT (Yoshikawa 2024, n=64): adding HPI to conventional goal-directed therapy (FloTrac) reduced the time-weighted area below the hypotension threshold (0.19 vs 0.66 mmHg; median difference −0.41, P=0.005) — the design that isolates the index itself — but norepinephrine use rose (40% vs 17%)
cards.summary: Sapporo RCT (Yoshikawa 2024, n=64): adding HPI to conventional goal-directed therapy (FloTrac) reduced the time-weighted area below the hypotension threshold (0.19 vs 0.66 mmHg; median difference −0.41, P=0.005) — the design that isolates the index itself — but norepinephrine use rose (40% vs 17%)
cards.type: Single-centre randomised controlled trial, HPI + conventional goal-directed therapy vs conventional goal-directed therapy alone (FloTrac) in major non-cardiac surgery
cards.people: 64 adults having major non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia at Sapporo Medical University Hospital, randomised to conventional goal-directed therapy alone (FloTrac group) or the combination of the Hypotension Prediction Index and conventional goal-directed therapy (HPI group). To isolate the independent utility of the index, peak arterial-pressure rates and dynamic arterial elastance were not included in the HPI group's treatment algorithm.
cards.result: The time-weighted average of the area below the hypotension threshold was lower in the HPI group: 0.19 mmHg (IQR 0.06–0.80) versus 0.66 mmHg (0.28–1.67), median difference −0.41 mmHg (95% CI −0.69 to −0.10; P=0.005). Norepinephrine was administered to more patients in the HPI group (12 of 30 [40%] vs 5 [17%]; P=0.045). There were no significant differences in fluid or blood-product volumes between the groups.
cards.watchOut: The ambiguity this shelf must keep on its face: even here, where goal-directed therapy is held constant in both arms, the HPI arm achieved less hypotension partly by treating more patients with norepinephrine — earlier/more vasopressor is the mechanism, and whether that trade is net-beneficial is exactly what the patient-outcome trials do not show.
cards.source: Yoshikawa Y et al. Effect of using hypotension prediction index versus conventional goal-directed haemodynamic management to reduce intraoperative hypotension in non-cardiac surgery: A randomised controlled trial. Journal of clinical anesthesia. 2024. PMID: 38039629. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Ripollés-Melchor 2026; 8 trials, 1,534 patients): no significant benefit on AKI (odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.13), complications, mortality or length of stay; hypotension metrics improved only in post hoc analyses of unblinded, high-bias-risk trials
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of the randomised trials (Ripollés-Melchor 2026; 8 trials, 1,534 patients): no significant benefit on AKI (odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.13), complications, mortality or length of stay; hypotension metrics improved only in post hoc analyses of unblinded, high-bias-risk trials
cards.type: Meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials of HPI-guided management in abdominal surgery (PROSPERO CRD42023490654)
cards.people: 8 randomised controlled trials involving 1,534 adults undergoing major abdominal surgery, comparing HPI-guided management with standard care (search of PubMed, EMBASE and Cochrane databases); primary outcomes were postoperative complications, AKI, perioperative mortality and hospital length of stay, with post hoc analyses of intraoperative-hypotension metrics. The small 2025–2026 HPI trials noted at mining are inside this synthesis rather than carded separately.
cards.result: No significant differences were observed for AKI (odds ratio 0.85, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.13), postoperative complications (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.46), mortality (odds ratio 0.96, 95% CI 0.32 to 2.83), length of stay (standardised mean difference −0.15, 95% CI −0.73 to 0.42) or fluid use (standardised mean difference −0.06, 95% CI −0.35 to 0.24) — odds ratios and standardised mean differences are relative/standardised measures, printed beside the null absolute findings of the large trial carded above. Post hoc analyses showed reduced time-weighted average MAP <65 mmHg, area under the threshold and total time below 65 mmHg, but the authors state the clinical relevance remains uncertain given the lack of blinding and high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: The hypotension-metric benefits are explicitly post hoc and come from trials that cannot be blinded (the team sees the alert), so performance and co-intervention bias run in the intervention's favour on exactly those metrics — while the pre-specified patient outcomes are uniformly null.
cards.source: Ripollés-Melchor J et al. Impact of hypotension prediction index-guided management on intraoperative hypotension and postoperative outcomes in abdominal surgery: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials. Anaesthesia, critical care & pain medicine. 2026. PMID: 41175934. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42023490654. cards.headline: Synthesis: HPI guidance reliably reduces measured intraoperative hypotension in small trials and pooled process metrics, and reliably fails — so far — to reduce AKI, complications or death, including in the one 917-patient multicentre trial powered to look
cards.summary: Synthesis: HPI guidance reliably reduces measured intraoperative hypotension in small trials and pooled process metrics, and reliably fails — so far — to reduce AKI, complications or death, including in the one 917-patient multicentre trial powered to look
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The pattern is consistent across the base: process first, outcomes absent. Lai 2024 (n=60) and Yoshikawa 2024 (n=64, HPI added to goal-directed therapy in both arms' lineage) show less time below MAP 65 mmHg with HPI guidance; Ripollés-Melchor 2025 (n=917, 28 hospitals) shows AKI 6.1% vs 7.0%, complications 31.9% vs 29.7% and mortality 1.1% vs 0.9%; and the 8-trial meta-analysis (1,534 patients) finds no significant patient-outcome benefit. This shelf is the prediction-index device slice only: the INPRESS individualised blood-pressure-target trial and the POISE-3 hypotension-avoidance strategy trial ask different (strategy, not device) questions, are carded elsewhere, and are cross-points, not cards here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Preoperative frailty predicts death or new disability: CFS and modified Fried perform alike (adjusted ORs 2.51 and 2.60 at 90 days), CFS is easier to use; cardiac cohort — hospital mortality 9.8% frail vs 1.0% nonfrail
shelves.question: Before major elective surgery in older adults, how well does a bedside frailty assessment — the Clinical Frailty Scale and the (modified) Fried phenotype, as tested — predict death or new disability after surgery, and how do the instruments compare?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Disability Evaluation · Female · Frail Elderly · Geriatric Assessment · Humans · Male · Mortality · Ontario · Patient Discharge · Postoperative Complications/mortality · Postoperative Period · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors · Time Factors
shelves.balance: LIKELY (predictive) — this is a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf, and no card on it implies that modifying a frailty score changes outcomes. In the prospective multicentre Canadian cohort of patients ≥65 having elective noncardiac surgery (702 enrolled, 645 with complete follow-up), frailty by either instrument predicted death or patient-reported new disability at 90 days with near-identical adjusted odds ratios (Clinical Frailty Scale 2.51, 95% CI 1.50 to 4.21; modified Fried Index 2.60, 95% CI 1.57 to 4.31), true- and false-positive rates did not differ significantly, frailty was the only significant predictor in the multivariable analysis, and the CFS was easier and quicker to use with less missing data — the head-to-head comparison is this shelf's core content. The prespecified 1-year follow-up of the SAME programme (labelled as such, not an independent cohort) found frailty associated with the disability trajectory over a year (P<0.0001), including an early increase in disability in more than a third of people with frailty before a net decrease by 365 days. The independent limb is a cardiac-surgery cohort (Alberta, n=529, CFS ≥5 in 9.6%): hospital mortality 9.8% in frail versus 1.0% in nonfrail patients (adjusted hazard ratio 3.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 16.34 — imprecise), with longer intensive-care and hospital stays. Cross-points: frailty as the population for colorectal prehabilitation (live #936) and the DASI/subjective functional-capacity question (Slate 13 row S13-4-05) are different questions and are not carded here.

cards.headline: Prospective multicentre cohort (McIsaac 2020, n=702; 645 complete): Clinical Frailty Scale and modified Fried Index predicted death or new disability at 90 days equally well (adjusted odds ratios 2.51 and 2.60) — and the CFS was easier to use, quicker, and had less missing data
cards.summary: Prospective multicentre cohort (McIsaac 2020, n=702; 645 complete): Clinical Frailty Scale and modified Fried Index predicted death or new disability at 90 days equally well (adjusted odds ratios 2.51 and 2.60) — and the CFS was easier to use, quicker, and had less missing data
cards.type: Prospective multicentre cohort study, head-to-head prognostic comparison of the Clinical Frailty Scale vs the modified Fried Index before elective noncardiac surgery (primary outcome at 90 days)
cards.people: 702 participants aged ≥65 having elective noncardiac surgery in a prospective multicentre (Canadian) cohort, assessed preoperatively with both the modified Fried Index (mFI) and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS); 645 had complete follow-up. The CFS identified 297 (42.3%) with frailty and the mFI 257 (36.6%); 72 (11.1%) died or experienced a new patient-reported disability by 90 days.
cards.result: Frailty was significantly associated with the primary outcome of death or patient-reported new disability at 90 days for both instruments (CFS adjusted odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.50 to 4.21; mFI adjusted odds ratio 2.60, 95% CI 1.57 to 4.31) — odds ratios are relative measures, printed beside the absolute event rate of 11.1% above. True-positive and false-positive rates were not significantly different between the instruments, and frailty was the only significant predictor of death or new disability in the multivariable analysis. Need for institutional discharge, costs and length of stay were significantly increased in individuals with frailty. The CFS was easier to use, required less time and had less missing data; the authors concluded clinicians should consider the CFS over the mFI.
cards.watchOut: Prognostic, not interventional: an adjusted odds ratio of ~2.5 identifies a higher-risk group; it does not show that treating or reversing the frailty state improves outcomes, and the two instruments classified overlapping but different minorities as frail (42.3% vs 36.6%) despite similar average accuracy.
cards.source: McIsaac DI et al. Frailty as a Predictor of Death or New Disability After Surgery: A Prospective Cohort Study. Annals of surgery. 2020. PMID: 30048320. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Programme report — prespecified 1-year follow-up of the same Canadian cohort (McIsaac 2020, BJA; 687 of 702 with 1-year follow-up): frailty changed the disability trajectory over the year (P<0.0001) — more than a third of people with frailty first got worse, then achieved a net decrease in disability by 365 days (a report OF the cohort programme above, not an independent cohort)
cards.summary: Programme report — prespecified 1-year follow-up of the same Canadian cohort (McIsaac 2020, BJA; 687 of 702 with 1-year follow-up): frailty changed the disability trajectory over the year (P<0.0001) — more than a third of people with frailty first got worse, then achieved a net decrease in disability by 365 days (a report OF the cohort programme above, not an independent cohort)
cards.type: Programme report: prespecified 1-year follow-up of the prospective multicentre cohort carded above (same research programme and substantially the same participants — not independent prognostic evidence)
cards.people: The same prospective multicentre cohort programme as the Annals of Surgery card above: patients ≥65 assessed before major elective noncardiac surgery with the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS) and the Fried Phenotype (FP); 1-year follow-up was complete for 687 of 702 participants (97.9%). Disability was measured with the WHO Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 at baseline, 30, 90 and 365 days.
cards.result: Frailty was associated with a significant difference in disability trajectory (P<0.0001). Compared with baseline, people with frailty had LOWER disability scores at 365 days (CFS frailty: −7.3 points, 95% CI −10.2 to −4.5; FP frailty: −5.4 points, 95% CI −8.5 to −2.3), while people without frailty had no significant change (no CFS frailty: +0.8 points, 95% CI −1.7 to 3.2; no FP frailty: +1.1 points, 95% CI −3.5 to 1.3). More than one-third of people with frailty experienced an early increase in disability before achieving a net decrease. The authors conclude that decision-making should integrate the trade-off between early adverse outcomes and longer-term benefit when frailty is present.
cards.watchOut: Labelled programme report: this is the 1-year limb of the same cohort as the 90-day card, so the shelf's noncardiac evidence is ONE cohort programme reported twice, not two cohorts — the independent limb is the cardiac-surgery cohort below. The late net decrease in disability among survivors with frailty is also subject to survivor effects (those who died contribute no 365-day score).
cards.source: McIsaac DI et al. Frailty and long-term postoperative disability trajectories: a prospective multicentre cohort study. British journal of anaesthesia. 2020. PMID: 32778405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Independent cohort — cardiac surgery, Alberta (Montgomery 2021, n=529): preoperative frailty (CFS ≥5) in 9.6%; hospital mortality 9.8% in frail vs 1.0% in nonfrail patients (adjusted hazard ratio 3.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 16.34), with ICU stay 2.2 days and hospital stay 9.3 days longer (median differences)
cards.summary: Independent cohort — cardiac surgery, Alberta (Montgomery 2021, n=529): preoperative frailty (CFS ≥5) in 9.6%; hospital mortality 9.8% in frail vs 1.0% in nonfrail patients (adjusted hazard ratio 3.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 16.34), with ICU stay 2.2 days and hospital stay 9.3 days longer (median differences)
cards.type: Independent prospective cohort study, preoperative Clinical Frailty Scale (≥5 = frail) before nonemergent cardiac surgery — the independent limb of this shelf
cards.people: 529 adults aged ≥50 referred for nonemergent cardiac surgery in Alberta, Canada (November 2011 to March 2014), screened preoperatively for frailty defined as a Clinical Frailty Scale score of 5 or greater; mean age 67 (SD 9) years, 25.9% women. Frailty prevalence was 9.6% (n=51; 95% CI 7.3% to 12.5%); frail patients were older (median 75 vs 67 years), more often female (51.0% vs 23.2%) and had higher EuroSCORE II (mean 8 vs 5).
cards.result: Hospital mortality was 9.8% among frail patients versus 1.0% among nonfrail patients (adjusted hazard ratio 3.84, 95% CI 0.90 to 16.34 — a relative measure whose interval crosses 1, printed beside the absolute rates). Frail patients had a longer median cardiovascular intensive-care stay (median difference 2.2 days, 95% CI 1.60 to 2.79) and hospital stay (median difference 9.3 days, 95% CI 8.2 to 10.3). The authors conclude preoperative frailty has important implications for the postoperative clinical course and resource utilisation of patients undergoing cardiac surgery.
cards.watchOut: Only 51 frail patients and 5 deaths among them drive the mortality contrast, hence the wide interval crossing 1; this cohort used the CFS alone (no Fried head-to-head), in a cardiac-surgery population with a much lower frailty prevalence (9.6%) than the noncardiac cohort (42.3% by CFS) — prevalence, and therefore predictive value, is setting-dependent.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bedside frailty assessment before major elective surgery predicts death or new disability — both instruments perform alike at 90 days (adjusted odds ratios ≈2.5), the CFS is the more feasible instrument, and the independent cardiac cohort points the same way on mortality and stay
cards.summary: Synthesis: bedside frailty assessment before major elective surgery predicts death or new disability — both instruments perform alike at 90 days (adjusted odds ratios ≈2.5), the CFS is the more feasible instrument, and the independent cardiac cohort points the same way on mortality and stay
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: One noncardiac cohort programme (reported at 90 days and at 1 year, labelled as one programme) and one independent cardiac-surgery cohort make up the base. At 90 days, frailty by the Clinical Frailty Scale (adjusted odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.50 to 4.21) or the modified Fried Index (2.60, 95% CI 1.57 to 4.31) predicted death or new disability, with no significant accuracy difference and a clear feasibility advantage for the CFS. At 1 year, frailty marked a worse early trajectory with later net recovery among survivors. In cardiac surgery, CFS-defined frailty (9.6% of 529) accompanied 9.8% versus 1.0% hospital mortality and substantially longer stays, on small frail numbers. Nothing here is treatment evidence: these instruments stratify risk for consent and planning; whether acting on the score changes outcomes is a different question, asked on other shelves.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each cohort's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: ARISCAT score: excellent at derivation (AUROC 0.88–0.90), good in emergency abdominal surgery (0.83), poor in lung resection (0.60) — accuracy is field-dependent
shelves.question: Before surgery, how well does the ARISCAT score (preoperative oxygen saturation, recent respiratory infection, age, preoperative anaemia, incision site, duration and emergency status) predict postoperative pulmonary complications, how does it calibrate and discriminate outside its derivation population — emergency abdominal, lung-resection and other fields — and how does it compare with the other published pulmonary-complication prediction models?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anesthesia · Cohort Studies · Data Collection · Female · Humans · Length of Stay · Logistic Models · Lung Diseases · Male · Middle Aged · Population · Postoperative Complications · Predictive Value of Tests · Prospective Studies · Respiration, Artificial · Risk Factors · Sample Size · Seasons · Spain · Treatment Outcome · Abdomen · Denmark · Lung · Risk Assessment · Retrospective Studies · Respiration Disorders · Models, Statistical
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — field-dependent, and that dependence is the answer. At derivation in a broad surgical population (2,464 patients, 59 hospitals) the ARISCAT score discriminated excellently (AUROC 0.90 development, 0.88 validation). In prospective external validation in major emergency abdominal surgery it held up well (AUC 0.83, observed complications 36.1% vs 24.9% predicted — good discrimination with under-prediction of absolute risk). In lung resection it performed poorly (c-index 0.60), as did every comparator score in that field (LAS VEGAS 0.68, SPORC 0.63, CARDOT 0.64). Across 116 published pulmonary-complication models, the 2025 meta-analysis gives ARISCAT a summary c-statistic of 0.76 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86). The derivation AUROC must never be printed as the score's accuracy in general. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no card claims that computing ARISCAT changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Derivation (Canet 2010): seven preoperative factors predict postoperative pulmonary complications — AUROC 0.90 in the development subsample and 0.88 in the validation subsample (2,464 patients, 59 hospitals)
cards.summary: Derivation (Canet 2010): seven preoperative factors predict postoperative pulmonary complications — AUROC 0.90 in the development subsample and 0.88 in the validation subsample (2,464 patients, 59 hospitals)
cards.type: Prospective multicentre cohort — derivation and internal (split-sample) validation of the ARISCAT score
cards.people: 2,464 patients undergoing surgical procedures under general, neuraxial or regional anaesthesia, randomly selected across 59 hospitals in Catalonia; the cohort was randomly split into a development subsample and a validation subsample. A postoperative pulmonary complication (respiratory infection, respiratory failure, bronchospasm, atelectasis, pleural effusion, pneumothorax or aspiration pneumonitis) occurred in 123 patients (5%).
cards.result: Seven independent risk factors formed the index: low preoperative arterial oxygen saturation, acute respiratory infection in the previous month, age, preoperative anaemia, upper abdominal or intrathoracic surgery, surgical duration of at least 2 hours, and emergency surgery. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.90 (95% CI 0.85 to 0.94) in the development subsample and 0.88 (95% CI 0.84 to 0.93) in the validation subsample. Thirty-day mortality was 19.5% (95% CI 12.5 to 26.5%) in patients with a pulmonary complication versus 0.5% (95% CI 0.2 to 0.8%) without.
cards.watchOut: Internal validation in the derivation population is the score's best case: later cards show discrimination falling to 0.83 in emergency abdominal surgery and 0.60 in lung resection. The derivation cohort's SF-8 quality-of-life companion paper (PMID 20418697, same population) is a different question and is NOT carded here.
cards.source: Canet J et al. Prediction of postoperative pulmonary complications in a population-based surgical cohort. Anesthesiology. 2010. PMID: 21045639. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: External validation in emergency abdominal surgery (Kokotovic 2022): AUC 0.83 with good calibration, but ARISCAT under-predicted absolute risk — observed complications 36.1% vs 24.9% predicted (585 patients, Denmark)
cards.summary: External validation in emergency abdominal surgery (Kokotovic 2022): AUC 0.83 with good calibration, but ARISCAT under-predicted absolute risk — observed complications 36.1% vs 24.9% predicted (585 patients, Denmark)
cards.type: Prospective external validation cohort (major emergency abdominal surgery)
cards.people: 585 patients undergoing major emergency abdominal surgery at a Danish university hospital (median age 70 years; most had emergency laparotomy without bowel resection), prospectively enrolled March 2017 to January 2019; predicted versus observed postoperative pulmonary complications compared under the TRIPOD statement.
cards.result: The observed frequency of postoperative pulmonary complications was 36.1%, against 24.9% predicted by ARISCAT — the score under-predicted absolute risk in this high-risk field. Discrimination was good: AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.79 to 0.86), with a Brier score of 0.19. Calibration was good by the Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit analysis (P > 0.25), with a calibration-plot slope of 0.9546 and intercept 0.1269.
cards.watchOut: Good discrimination with under-predicted absolute risk: a patient's ARISCAT category ranks risk well in this field, but the predicted percentage itself runs low (24.9% predicted vs 36.1% observed).
cards.source: Kokotovic D et al. The ARISCAT score is a promising model to predict postoperative pulmonary complications after major emergency abdominal surgery: an external validation in a Danish cohort. European journal of trauma and emergency surgery : official publication of the European Trauma Society. 2022. PMID: 35050387. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Lung resection (Zorrilla-Vaca 2023): ARISCAT c-index only 0.60 in 2,104 patients — and every comparator score was also poor in this field (LAS VEGAS 0.68, SPORC 0.63, CARDOT 0.64)
cards.summary: Lung resection (Zorrilla-Vaca 2023): ARISCAT c-index only 0.60 in 2,104 patients — and every comparator score was also poor in this field (LAS VEGAS 0.68, SPORC 0.63, CARDOT 0.64)
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre head-to-head validation and comparison of four pulmonary risk scores (lung resection)
cards.people: 2,104 adults undergoing lung resection surgery under one-lung ventilation at a single centre (retrospective historic cohort); 123 patients (5.9%) developed postoperative pulmonary complications. Four scores were compared head-to-head: ARISCAT, LAS VEGAS, SPORC and the thoracic-specific CARDOT score.
cards.result: All scoring systems had poor discriminatory power in lung resection: ARISCAT c-index 0.60 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.65), LAS VEGAS 0.68 (95% CI 0.63 to 0.73), SPORC 0.63 (95% CI 0.59 to 0.68) and CARDOT 0.64 (95% CI 0.58 to 0.70). Adding predicted postoperative FEV1 slightly improved LAS VEGAS (c-index 0.70) and CARDOT (0.68). Calibration analysis showed slight overestimation with ARISCAT (intercept −0.28) and LAS VEGAS (−0.27). The authors concluded none of the scores had adequate discriminatory power after lung resection.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre retrospective cohort in one surgical field: the lesson is field-dependence, not that ARISCAT is a poor score everywhere — its emergency-abdominal performance (card above) was materially better.
cards.source: Zorrilla-Vaca A et al. Performance Comparison of Pulmonary Risk Scoring Systems in Lung Resection. Journal of cardiothoracic and vascular anesthesia. 2023. PMID: 37330329. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Humans · Lung Diseases · Retrospective Studies · Lung · Risk Factors · Respiration Disorders · Postoperative Complications

cards.headline: Synthesis of 116 models (Huang 2025): ARISCAT's pooled c-statistic across cohorts is 0.76 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86) — moderate-to-good, and 90.2% of all pulmonary-complication models carried a high risk of bias
cards.summary: Synthesis of 116 models (Huang 2025): ARISCAT's pooled c-statistic across cohorts is 0.76 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86) — moderate-to-good, and 90.2% of all pulmonary-complication models carried a high risk of bias
cards.type: Systematic review and Bayesian meta-analysis of postoperative pulmonary complication prediction models
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 123 studies covering 116 prediction models for postoperative pulmonary complications (search to June 2024); 14 models (1,004,029 patients) were eligible for meta-analysis of the c-statistic, with bias assessed by PROBAST.
cards.result: Across all models the c-statistic ranged from 0.614 to 0.996 (median 0.80), with half of models self-reporting good (>0.8) discrimination. In meta-analysis, the ARISCAT score's summary c-statistic was 0.76 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.86) — between its derivation values (0.88–0.90) and its lung-resection value (0.60), as the field-dependence on this shelf predicts. Comparators pooled similarly (Xue's model 0.82; CARDOT 0.73). Reliability was limited by a lack of external validation cohorts, and 90.2% of models were assessed at high risk of bias.
cards.watchOut: A pooled c-statistic averages over unlike surgical fields; it does not restore the derivation AUROC as a general accuracy figure, and most models in this literature are at high risk of bias.
cards.source: Huang Z et al. Prediction models for postoperative pulmonary complications: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British journal of anaesthesia. 2025. PMID: 40473567. cards.headline: Synthesis: ARISCAT discriminates excellently at derivation (0.88–0.90), well in emergency abdominal surgery (0.83, with absolute risk under-predicted), and poorly in lung resection (0.60) — quote the score only with its surgical field
cards.summary: Synthesis: ARISCAT discriminates excellently at derivation (0.88–0.90), well in emergency abdominal surgery (0.83, with absolute risk under-predicted), and poorly in lung resection (0.60) — quote the score only with its surgical field
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The four reports agree on one pattern: ARISCAT's discrimination is field-dependent. Derivation and internal validation in a broad Catalan surgical population gave AUROCs of 0.90 and 0.88 (Canet 2010); prospective external validation in Danish major emergency abdominal surgery gave an AUC of 0.83 with good calibration but under-predicted absolute risk (36.1% observed vs 24.9% predicted; Kokotovic 2022); in lung resection the c-index fell to 0.60, with all comparator scores also poor (Zorrilla-Vaca 2023); and the 116-model meta-analysis pools ARISCAT at 0.76 (Huang 2025). No report carded here tests whether acting on an ARISCAT score improves outcomes — this shelf answers the prediction question only.
