shelves.title: Daikenchuto (TJ-100) for postoperative ileus: JAPAN-PD was negative on both coprimary endpoints — a negative programme with only motility-signal limbs
shelves.question: In patients undergoing major abdominal surgery (pancreaticoduodenectomy, colectomy, total gastrectomy), does perioperative daikenchuto (TJ-100) versus placebo or control prevent prolonged paralytic ileus and accelerate return of bowel function?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Double-Blind Method · Drug Administration Schedule · Female · Gastrointestinal Agents/therapeutic use · Humans · Incidence · Intestinal Pseudo-Obstruction/epidemiology,/etiology,/prevention & control · Kaplan-Meier Estimate · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Panax · Pancreatic Neoplasms/surgery · Pancreaticoduodenectomy · Perioperative Care · Plant Extracts/therapeutic use · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology,/prevention & control · Proportional Hazards Models · Treatment Outcome · Zanthoxylum · Zingiberaceae
shelves.balance: LIKELY (no benefit) — a negative programme, presented plainly. The one large double-blind trial, JAPAN-PD (224 randomised after pancreaticoduodenectomy), missed both coprimary endpoints: paralytic ileus in 33.7% on daikenchuto versus 36.9% on placebo (P=.626) and time to first flatus 2.25 versus 2.50 days (P=.343), and its authors concluded the findings may preclude routine use after pancreaticoduodenectomy. The remaining limbs are weaker designs with surrogate or softer readings: a transit-marker study (88 registered, 71 analysed) found faster small-bowel marker transit at 6 hours but no difference in total transit or time to first flatus; a total-gastrectomy trial (81 patients) against no treatment found more stools per day and lower bowel-gas scores but no difference in postoperative ileus incidence or quality of life; and a laparoscopic-colectomy trial (54 randomised) used a lactobacillus preparation as an active comparator. No trial shows fewer complications, shorter stay or less obstruction. PRODUCT NAMING (herb rule): the tested product is daikenchuto TJ-100 (Tsumura), as the programme's publications name it; where a carded publication's record names no product code or company, its card says so plainly, and other Kampo preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness. Japanese programme — single-region flag; populations are cancer-surgery patients and do not generalise to all abdominal surgery. FENCE: the Cochrane review of daikenchuto for postoperative ileus is a retracted publication and is never carded on this shelf (its identifier is deliberately not printed, so no grep can mistake it for a carded source); the 2013 JAPAN-PD paper is that trial's protocol, not a second trial, and is not carded as one.

cards.headline: JAPAN-PD (Okada 2016): daikenchuto TJ-100 did NOT prevent paralytic ileus after pancreaticoduodenectomy — 33.7% vs 36.9% on placebo (P=.626); time to first flatus 2.25 vs 2.50 days (P=.343)
cards.summary: JAPAN-PD (Okada 2016): daikenchuto TJ-100 did NOT prevent paralytic ileus after pancreaticoduodenectomy — 33.7% vs 36.9% on placebo (P=.626); time to first flatus 2.25 vs 2.50 days (P=.343)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled phase II trial (JAPAN-PD), daikenchuto TJ-100 vs placebo after pancreaticoduodenectomy
cards.people: 224 patients with periampullary tumour or tumour of the head of the pancreas undergoing pancreaticoduodenectomy, randomised 1:1 to perioperative TJ-100 (112 patients) or placebo (112 patients) in a multicentre Japanese phase II trial; the analysis population was 207 patients (104 TJ-100, 103 placebo), from 273 assessed for eligibility (August 2012 to July 2013).
cards.result: Both coprimary endpoints were negative. Paralytic ileus lasting more than 72 hours occurred in 35 of 104 patients (33.7%) on TJ-100 versus 38 of 103 (36.9%) on placebo (P=.626). Time to first flatus was 2.25 days (IQR 2.00–2.50) on TJ-100 versus 2.50 days (1.50–2.50) on placebo (P=.343). In a small subgroup of 23 patients who underwent pylorus-ring-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy, time to first flatus was lower on TJ-100 (0.50 vs 1.50 days; P=.034). The authors concluded that TJ-100 did not improve recovery from paralytic ileus after pancreaticoduodenectomy and may preclude its routine use in clinical practice after this operation.
cards.watchOut: The programme's largest and only adequately sized double-blind trial — negative on both coprimary endpoints; the pylorus-preserving subgroup (23 patients) is a subgroup reading, not a rescue. Product naming: the publication names the product as TJ-100 in its title; the fetched record names no company. The 2013 paper for this programme is the JAPAN-PD protocol, not a second trial, and is not carded.

cards.headline: JFMC39-0902 transit study (Katsuno 2016): small-bowel radiopaque-marker transit was faster at 6 hours on daikenchuto (P=0.008), but total transit and time to first flatus did NOT differ (88 registered, 71 analysed)
cards.summary: JFMC39-0902 transit study (Katsuno 2016): small-bowel radiopaque-marker transit was faster at 6 hours on daikenchuto (P=0.008), but total transit and time to first flatus did NOT differ (88 registered, 71 analysed)
cards.type: Multicentre double-blind randomised placebo-controlled transit study (JFMC39-0902 additional study), daikenchuto 15 g/day vs placebo after open sigmoid/rectosigmoid cancer surgery
cards.people: 88 patients undergoing open surgery for sigmoid or rectosigmoid cancer at 11 Japanese sites (January 2009 to June 2011), registered to receive placebo or daikenchuto 15.0 g/day (5 g three times daily) from postoperative day 2 to day 8; 71 patients were analysed (38 daikenchuto, 33 placebo). Endpoints were gastrointestinal transit time by radiopaque markers and time to first flatus.
cards.result: The number of radiopaque markers in the anal side of the small intestine at 6 hours was significantly greater on daikenchuto than placebo (15.19 vs 10.06; P=0.008) — a transit-marker surrogate. The total transit analysis results and the mean time to first flatus did not differ significantly between the groups. The authors concluded daikenchuto has a positive effect on resolution of delayed gastric emptying but a limited effect on resolution of postoperative paralytic ileus after open sigmoid/rectosigmoid surgery, and may contribute to early oral intake.
cards.watchOut: An exploratory pharmacology study: its one positive reading is a 6-hour marker-position surrogate, while the patient-relevant readings (total transit, first flatus) were null — and 17 of 88 registered patients were not analysed. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as daikenchuto, with its dose; it names no TJ-100 code and no company.
cards.source: Katsuno H et al. Clinical pharmacology of daikenchuto assessed by transit analysis using radiopaque markers in patients with colon cancer undergoing open surgery: a multicenter double-blind randomized placebo-controlled study (JFMC39-0902 additional study). Journal of gastroenterology. 2016. PMID: 26162646. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Total-gastrectomy trial (Akamaru 2015): daikenchuto improved stools per day and bowel-gas scores versus NO treatment, with no difference in postoperative ileus incidence or quality of life (81 patients)
cards.summary: Total-gastrectomy trial (Akamaru 2015): daikenchuto improved stools per day and bowel-gas scores versus NO treatment, with no difference in postoperative ileus incidence or quality of life (81 patients)
cards.type: Prospective randomised trial of daikenchuto vs no-treatment control after total gastrectomy for gastric cancer
cards.people: 81 patients with gastric cancer scheduled for total gastrectomy, randomly assigned before surgery to daikenchuto 7.5 g/day in three divided doses for 3 months postoperatively (41 patients) or to no treatment (40 patients, control group); outcomes were gastrointestinal motility, stool attributes, bowel-gas quantity on abdominal radiographs, quality of life (Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale) and postoperative ileus incidence.
cards.result: During the hospital stay, the daikenchuto group had more stools per day (1.1 ± 0.6 vs 0.8 ± 0.4; P=0.037) and different stool consistencies (Bristol scale 3.7 ± 0.8 vs 3.1 ± 0.8; P=0.041), and showed significant reductions in bowel-gas volume scores at 7 days, 1 month and 3 months after surgery. The groups did not differ significantly in quality-of-life scores or in the incidence of postoperative ileus. The authors concluded daikenchuto promoted early postoperative bowel function after total gastrectomy on these measures.
cards.watchOut: An open, no-treatment control: patients knew whether they were taking the herb, the positive endpoints are stool counts and radiograph gas scores, and the endpoint that matters — postoperative ileus — did not differ. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as daikenchuto (DKT), with its dose; it names no product code and no company.
cards.source: Akamaru Y et al. Effects of daikenchuto, a Japanese herb, on intestinal motility after total gastrectomy: a prospective randomized trial. Journal of gastrointestinal surgery : official journal of the Society for Surgery of the Alimentary Tract. 2015. PMID: 25564322. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Laparoscopic-assisted colectomy trial (Yaegashi 2014): daikenchuto shortened time to first flatus and bowel movement versus a LACTOBACILLUS preparation — an active-comparator limb (54 randomised, 51 analysed)
cards.summary: Laparoscopic-assisted colectomy trial (Yaegashi 2014): daikenchuto shortened time to first flatus and bowel movement versus a LACTOBACILLUS preparation — an active-comparator limb (54 randomised, 51 analysed)
cards.type: Single-centre randomised trial of daikenchuto vs lactobacillus-preparation active control after laparoscopic-assisted colectomy — active-comparator limb
cards.people: 54 patients undergoing laparoscopic-assisted colectomy for colon cancer at one Japanese university hospital (October 2010 to March 2012), randomised to daikenchuto 7.5 g/day orally or a lactobacillus preparation 3 g/day orally as control; 51 patients were included in the per-protocol analysis (26 daikenchuto, 25 control). Primary endpoints were time to first flatus, bowel movement and tolerance of diet after extubation; colonic transit time was measured with radiopaque markers.
cards.result: The daikenchuto group had significantly faster time to first flatus (67.5 ± 13.6 h vs 77.9 ± 11.8 h; P < 0.01), bowel movement (82.9 ± 17.8 h vs 99.5 ± 18.9 h; P < 0.01) and colonic transit time (91.9 ± 19.8 h vs 115.2 ± 12.8 h; P < 0.05). There were no significant intergroup differences in secondary endpoints (white-cell count, C-reactive protein, hospital stay, postoperative ileus) or adverse events.
cards.watchOut: The comparator is another active preparation, not placebo or no treatment, the analysis is per-protocol (51 of 54), and postoperative ileus itself did not differ — this small limb cannot outweigh JAPAN-PD's double-blind negative result. Product naming: the fetched record names the preparation only as daikenchuto (DKT), with its dose; it names no product code and no company.
cards.source: Yaegashi M et al. Daikenchuto stimulates colonic motility after laparoscopic-assisted colectomy. Hepato-gastroenterology. 2014. PMID: 24895799. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis
cards.summary: Synthesis
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Read in order of weight, this is a negative programme. JAPAN-PD — 224 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled — found no reduction in paralytic ileus (33.7% vs 36.9%) and no faster first flatus after pancreaticoduodenectomy. The supporting limbs show motility signals only: a 6-hour transit-marker difference with null total transit and flatus (JFMC39-0902), more stools and less bowel gas against no treatment with no ileus difference (gastrectomy), and faster flatus against a lactobacillus active comparator in 51 analysed patients (colectomy). A pooled subgroup analysis of three trials and a 2026 US proof-of-concept trial of TU-100 after bowel resection exist as cross-points and are not carded as anchors here. Two fences are printed on this shelf's face: the Cochrane daikenchuto review is retracted and never carded, and the 2013 JAPAN-PD paper is a protocol, not a second trial. The tested product is daikenchuto TJ-100 (Tsumura) as the programme's publications name it; current or other Kampo preparations may differ in safety and effectiveness.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Revised Cardiac Risk Index validation: strata hold (0.5% to 9%) but discrimination falls in vascular surgery (AUC 0.64) and under troponin surveillance (c-statistic 0.60, risks underestimated)
shelves.question: Before major noncardiac surgery, how well does the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin treatment, creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL) predict major cardiac complications and death, how far does its discrimination fall in vascular surgery and under modern troponin surveillance, and how does it compare with the NSQIP MICA calculator?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Cerebrovascular Disorders/complications · Cohort Studies · Creatine/blood · Female · Heart Diseases/epidemiology,etiology · Humans · Incidence · Insulin/therapeutic use · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Prognosis · Prospective Studies · Risk Factors
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — field- and era-dependent. The Revised Cardiac Risk Index's six factors stratify risk as derived (major cardiac complications 0.5%, 1.3%, 4% and 9% at 0, 1, 2 and ≥3 factors in derivation; 0.4%, 0.9%, 7% and 11% on prospective validation). Discrimination is a separate claim: a 24-study systematic review (792,740 patients) found AUC 0.75 for cardiac events after mixed noncardiac surgery but only 0.64 after vascular surgery and a median AUC of 0.62 for death. Under modern systematic high-sensitivity troponin T surveillance (VISION-nested vascular cohort, n=870), the c-statistic fell to 0.60 with predicted risks systematically underestimated and no clinical utility before recalibration; NSQIP MICA was only slightly better (0.64). This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf — no card implies that computing the index changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Derivation and prospective validation (Lee 1999): six factors, with major cardiac complication rates of 0.5%, 1.3%, 4% and 9% (derivation) and 0.4%, 0.9%, 7% and 11% (validation) at 0, 1, 2 and 3 or more factors
cards.summary: Derivation and prospective validation (Lee 1999): six factors, with major cardiac complication rates of 0.5%, 1.3%, 4% and 9% (derivation) and 0.4%, 0.9%, 7% and 11% (validation) at 0, 1, 2 and 3 or more factors
cards.type: Prospective cohort study — derivation and prospective validation of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index
cards.people: 4,315 patients aged 50 years or older undergoing elective major noncardiac surgery at a tertiary-care teaching hospital — 2,893 in the derivation cohort and 1,422 in the prospective validation cohort. Major cardiac complications occurred in 56 patients (2%) in the derivation cohort.
cards.result: Six independent predictors formed the Revised Cardiac Risk Index: high-risk type of surgery, history of ischaemic heart disease, history of congestive heart failure, history of cerebrovascular disease, preoperative treatment with insulin, and preoperative serum creatinine above 2.0 mg/dL. Rates of major cardiac complication with 0, 1, 2 or 3 or more factors were 0.5%, 1.3%, 4% and 9% in the derivation cohort and 0.4%, 0.9%, 7% and 11% in the validation cohort — absolute rates as published. In the validation cohort the index's diagnostic performance was superior to other published risk-prediction indexes of its era.
cards.watchOut: Derivation-era rates from a single tertiary centre in the 1990s, before systematic troponin surveillance: these strata describe the risk gradient the index was built on, not the absolute risk a modern service should quote — the later cards show why.
cards.source: Lee TH et al. Derivation and prospective validation of a simple index for prediction of cardiac risk of major noncardiac surgery. Circulation. 1999. PMID: 10477528. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review (Ford 2010): the RCRI discriminated moderately for cardiac events after mixed noncardiac surgery (AUC 0.75) but poorly after vascular surgery (AUC 0.64) and for death (median AUC 0.62)
cards.summary: Systematic review (Ford 2010): the RCRI discriminated moderately for cardiac events after mixed noncardiac surgery (AUC 0.75) but poorly after vascular surgery (AUC 0.64) and for death (median AUC 0.62)
cards.type: Systematic review of 24 validation cohorts of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index
cards.people: 24 cohort studies totalling 792,740 patients that reported the association of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index with major cardiac complications (cardiac death, myocardial infarction, nonfatal cardiac arrest) or death in hospital or within 30 days of noncardiac surgery; 18 studies reported cardiac complications.
cards.result: For cardiac events after mixed noncardiac surgery the area under the receiver-operating characteristic curve was 0.75 (95% CI 0.72 to 0.79), with sensitivity 0.65, specificity 0.76, positive likelihood ratio 2.78 and negative likelihood ratio 0.45. After vascular surgery, prediction was less accurate: AUC 0.64 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.66), sensitivity 0.70, specificity 0.55. Six studies reported death, with a median AUC of 0.62 (range 0.54 to 0.78); a pooled AUC for death could not be calculated because heterogeneity was very high (I² = 95%). The reviewers noted studies were generally of low methodological quality with varied event definitions.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy is field-specific — mixed versus vascular surgery are carded separately here and must never be merged into one pooled accuracy number, exactly as this review reports them.

cards.headline: External validation under systematic troponin surveillance (Fronczek 2019; VISION-nested, labelled): RCRI c-statistic 0.60 and NSQIP MICA 0.64 in 870 vascular-surgery patients, with predicted risks systematically underestimated before recalibration
cards.summary: External validation under systematic troponin surveillance (Fronczek 2019; VISION-nested, labelled): RCRI c-statistic 0.60 and NSQIP MICA 0.64 in 870 vascular-surgery patients, with predicted risks systematically underestimated before recalibration
cards.type: External validation cohort (VISION-nested, single-centre vascular surgery) of RCRI and NSQIP MICA under systematic hs-troponin T surveillance
cards.people: 870 consecutive patients aged 45 years or older undergoing in-hospital noncardiac vascular surgery at a single tertiary centre, nested in the Vascular Events In Noncardiac Surgery Patients Cohort Evaluation (VISION) study — labelled as a VISION-nested validation cohort, carded here as a validation OF the index, not as a VISION programme report. High-sensitivity troponin T was measured before surgery, 6–12 hours after, and on days 1–3; the primary outcome (nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal cardiac arrest or cardiac death within 30 days) occurred in 76 patients (8.7%).
cards.result: The c-statistic was 0.60 (95% CI 0.54 to 0.65) for the Revised Cardiac Risk Index and 0.64 (95% CI 0.57 to 0.70) for the NSQIP MICA calculator. Predicted risks were systematically underestimated in calibration belts (P<.001), and neither model showed clinical utility before recalibration. The authors note the recently updated version of the RCRI was more reliable than the original index.
cards.watchOut: A vascular-only, single-centre validation: its poor discrimination matches the systematic review's vascular limb, but it does not by itself describe performance in mixed noncardiac surgery. Both this index and MICA were derived with older myocardial-infarction definitions — the calibration failure under modern troponin surveillance is the point of the card.

cards.headline: Synthesis: the RCRI's risk strata are real but its discrimination is field- and era-dependent — moderate in mixed noncardiac surgery (AUC 0.75), poor in vascular surgery (0.64) and for death (median 0.62), and miscalibrated under modern troponin surveillance (c-statistic 0.60, risks underestimated)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the RCRI's risk strata are real but its discrimination is field- and era-dependent — moderate in mixed noncardiac surgery (AUC 0.75), poor in vascular surgery (0.64) and for death (median 0.62), and miscalibrated under modern troponin surveillance (c-statistic 0.60, risks underestimated)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the derivation/validation cohort (n=4,315), the systematic review (24 studies, 792,740 patients) and the VISION-nested vascular validation (n=870).
cards.result: The index's six factors order patients by risk exactly as derived in 1999 (0.4–0.5% with no factors rising to 9–11% with 3 or more). But discrimination — a different claim from the strata — falls in vascular surgery and for mortality, and in a modern cohort with systematic high-sensitivity troponin T surveillance the original index underestimated absolute risk and showed no clinical utility before recalibration; the NSQIP MICA calculator performed only slightly better (0.64). This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: nothing carded here shows that computing the RCRI changes management or outcomes. Preoperative natriuretic-peptide prediction is a different question, homed at pack #5792, and functional-capacity assessment (DASI/METS) at pack #7453 — cross-points only.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: STOP-Bang in surgical patients: sensitivity 85–90% for OSA at low specificity — and no adjusted association with mortality, cardiac complications or stay in 26,068 patients
shelves.question: In adults attending preoperative clinics and having surgery, how accurately does the STOP-Bang questionnaire detect obstructive sleep apnoea against polysomnography — sensitivity and the probability of severe apnoea at each score — in surgical populations, and does a high score predict postoperative complications, mortality or length of stay?
shelves.mesh: Body Mass Index · Body Size · Female · Humans · Male · Mass Screening/methods · Polysomnography · Sleep Apnea, Obstructive/epidemiology,physiopathology · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — split by limb. As a detector of obstructive sleep apnoea against polysomnography, STOP-Bang is highly sensitive in surgical populations: 83.6%, 92.9% and 100% at AHI cut-offs above 5, 15 and 30 at derivation, and pooled preoperative sensitivities of 85%, 88% and 90% — at specificities of only 47%, 29% and 27%, with the probability of severe OSA in surgical patients rising from 15% at a score of 3 to 65% at 7/8. As a prognostic tool, the largest surgical cohort (26,068 patients) found its strata were NOT associated, after adjustment, with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay, even though diagnosed OSA rose from 4% to 44% across strata. No card implies screening changes outcomes.

cards.headline: Derivation and validation (Chung 2008): adding BMI, age, neck circumference and sex to the STOP questions raised sensitivity to 83.6%, 92.9% and 100% at apnoea–hypopnoea index cut-offs above 5, above 15 and above 30
cards.summary: Derivation and validation (Chung 2008): adding BMI, age, neck circumference and sex to the STOP questions raised sensitivity to 83.6%, 92.9% and 100% at apnoea–hypopnoea index cut-offs above 5, above 15 and above 30
cards.type: Derivation and validation study of the STOP and STOP-Bang questionnaires in preoperative patients, against polysomnography
cards.people: Preoperative patients aged 18 years or older without previously diagnosed obstructive sleep apnoea: the STOP questionnaire was given to 2,467 patients (27.5% classified high-risk), and 211 underwent polysomnography — 34 in a pilot test and 177 in the validation group on which the sensitivities below rest.
cards.result: The four STOP questions concern snoring, tiredness during daytime, observed apnoea and high blood pressure. STOP alone had sensitivities of 65.6%, 74.3% and 79.5% at apnoea–hypopnoea index cut-offs above 5, above 15 and above 30. Adding body-mass index, age, neck circumference and gender (STOP-Bang) raised sensitivities to 83.6%, 92.9% and 100% at the same cut-offs — sensitivities are cut-off-specific and are never printed as a single number on this shelf.
cards.watchOut: Only 177 of 2,467 questionnaire respondents contributed validation polysomnography — a selected validation subset, so these sensitivities come from patients who completed sleep studies, not from the whole preoperative clinic.
cards.source: Chung F et al. STOP questionnaire: a tool to screen patients for obstructive sleep apnea. Anesthesiology. 2008. PMID: 18431116. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Nagappa 2015): in surgical patients the probability of severe OSA rose from 15% at a STOP-Bang score of 3 to 25%, 35%, 45% and 65% at scores 4, 5, 6 and 7/8
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Nagappa 2015): in surgical patients the probability of severe OSA rose from 15% at a STOP-Bang score of 3 to 25%, 35%, 45% and 65% at scores 4, 5, 6 and 7/8
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of STOP-Bang validation studies (17 studies, 9,206 patients)
cards.people: 17 studies including 9,206 patients in which STOP-Bang was validated against polysomnography, across sleep-clinic and surgical populations.
cards.result: In the sleep-clinic population, sensitivity was 90%, 94% and 96% to detect any OSA (AHI at least 5), moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI at least 15) and severe OSA (AHI at least 30), with corresponding negative predictive values of 46%, 75% and 90%; a similar trend was found in the surgical population. The probability of severe OSA at a STOP-Bang score of 3 was 25% in sleep-clinic patients and 15% in surgical patients, rising stepwise in surgical patients to 25%, 35%, 45% and 65% at scores 4, 5, 6 and 7/8.
cards.watchOut: High sensitivity is bought with low specificity — a score of 3 or more labels many patients high-risk who do not have severe apnoea; the score-by-score probabilities, not the sensitivity alone, are what a preoperative clinic actually uses.
cards.source: Nagappa M et al. Validation of the STOP-Bang Questionnaire as a Screening Tool for Obstructive Sleep Apnea among Different Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. cards.headline: Preoperative-specific meta-analysis (Hwang 2022): pooled sensitivity 85%, 88% and 90% for any, moderate-to-severe and severe OSA in surgical patients, with specificity of only 47%, 29% and 27%
cards.summary: Preoperative-specific meta-analysis (Hwang 2022): pooled sensitivity 85%, 88% and 90% for any, moderate-to-severe and severe OSA in surgical patients, with specificity of only 47%, 29% and 27%
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of STOP-Bang in the preoperative setting (10 studies, 3,247 surgical participants)
cards.people: 10 studies with 3,247 surgical participants (mean age 57.3 years, mean BMI 32.5 kg/m², 47.4% male), identified from 4,641 articles, in a systematic review and meta-analysis restricted to STOP-Bang as a preoperative screening tool (searches to May 2021, surveillance to October 2021).
cards.result: Prevalence of any, moderate-to-severe and severe OSA was 65.2%, 37.7% and 17.0%. Pooled sensitivity of STOP-Bang was 85%, 88% and 90% for the three severity levels, with pooled specificities of 47%, 29% and 27%; areas under the curve were 0.84, 0.67 and 0.63. The authors report a negative predictive value of 93.2% for reasonably excluding severe OSA.
cards.watchOut: The AUC gradient (0.84 for any OSA but 0.63 for severe OSA) sits oddly beside the sensitivity gradient and reflects the included studies' thresholds and spectra — read the severity-specific numbers separately, never as one accuracy figure.
cards.source: Hwang M et al. Validation of the STOP-Bang questionnaire as a preoperative screening tool for obstructive sleep apnea: a systematic review and meta-analysis. BMC anesthesiology. 2022. cards.headline: Outcome limb (Sankar 2019): in 26,068 patients having major elective noncardiac surgery, diagnosed OSA rose across STOP-Bang strata (4%, 12%, 44%) — but after adjustment the strata were NOT associated with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay
cards.summary: Outcome limb (Sankar 2019): in 26,068 patients having major elective noncardiac surgery, diagnosed OSA rose across STOP-Bang strata (4%, 12%, 44%) — but after adjustment the strata were NOT associated with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay
cards.type: Retrospective cohort validity evaluation in major elective noncardiac surgery (n=26,068) — the postoperative-outcome limb
cards.people: 26,068 patients undergoing major elective noncardiac surgery at the University Health Network, Toronto (2011–2015), in a retrospective cohort study: 58% were in the low-risk STOP-Bang stratum, 23% intermediate and 19% high.
cards.result: The proportion with previously diagnosed OSA was 4% in the low-risk stratum, 12% in the intermediate stratum and 44% in the high-risk stratum — the score does track diagnosed apnoea. Correlations with ASA Physical Status (ρ=0.28), the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (ρ=0.24) and the Charlson Comorbidity Index (ρ=0.10) were weak. After risk adjustment, STOP-Bang risk strata were not associated with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay — a null outcome limb, printed on the face beside the accuracy limb.
cards.watchOut: Diagnosed OSA in the record is not polysomnography-confirmed OSA in every patient, and a single health network's elective-surgery cohort may under-represent the emergency and high-risk settings where an outcome association would matter most — but as published, the adjusted outcome association is null.
cards.source: Sankar A et al. Evaluation of validity of the STOP-BANG questionnaire in major elective noncardiac surgery. British journal of anaesthesia. 2019. PMID: 30686311. cards.headline: Synthesis: STOP-Bang detects apnoea in surgical patients with high, severity-graded sensitivity (83.6–100% at derivation; pooled 85–90% preoperatively) at low specificity — yet the largest surgical cohort found no adjusted association between its strata and mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay
cards.summary: Synthesis: STOP-Bang detects apnoea in surgical patients with high, severity-graded sensitivity (83.6–100% at derivation; pooled 85–90% preoperatively) at low specificity — yet the largest surgical cohort found no adjusted association between its strata and mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the derivation/validation study (polysomnography in 177), two meta-analyses (9,206 and 3,247 patients) and the Toronto outcome cohort (26,068 patients).
cards.result: The accuracy limb and the outcome limb point in different directions, and both stay on the face. As a detector, STOP-Bang is sensitive and score-graded: in surgical patients the probability of severe OSA rises from 15% at a score of 3 to 65% at 7/8. As a prognostic tool in the largest surgical cohort, its strata carried no adjusted association with 30-day mortality, cardiac complications or length of stay. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no card implies that screening, or any treatment triggered by screening, changes postoperative outcomes. The distribution of the apnoea–hypopnoea index itself in unselected adults is a different question, homed at pack #7176.

shelves.title: Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery: 8% by fourth-generation criteria, 17.9% by hsTnT — mostly silent, graded mortality association, incidence assay-dependent (9% I versus 15% T)
shelves.question: In adults having inpatient noncardiac surgery, what does routine postoperative troponin surveillance find — how common is myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery (MINS) under fourth-generation troponin T, high-sensitivity troponin T and high-sensitivity troponin I criteria, what troponin thresholds mark prognostically important injury, and how strongly does injury predict 30-day and 1-year death, including in patients with no ischaemic symptoms or ECG changes?

shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a strong, graded, independently confirmed prognostic association, with assay-dependent incidence. In the VISION programme (three reports of one programme, labelled as such): peak fourth-generation troponin T at least 0.02 ng/mL (11.6% of patients) carried adjusted hazard ratios for 30-day death rising from 2.41 to 10.48 across bands (relative measures; absolute mortality 1.0% to 16.9%); MINS (at least 0.03 ng/mL, judged ischaemic) affected 8.0% with an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.87 and the highest population-attributable risk (34.0%); by high-sensitivity troponin T criteria MINS affected 17.9%, 93.1% of it silent. The independent Basel cohort found incidence of 9% by troponin I versus 15% by troponin T in the same patients, both predicting 30-day and 1-year death. No card implies surveillance or any response to injury improves outcomes.

cards.headline: VISION 2012 (Devereaux): peak fourth-generation troponin T of at least 0.02 ng/mL — present in 11.6% — independently predicted 30-day death, with adjusted hazard ratios rising from 2.41 to 10.48 across troponin bands (relative measures)
cards.summary: VISION 2012 (Devereaux): peak fourth-generation troponin T of at least 0.02 ng/mL — present in 11.6% — independently predicted 30-day death, with adjusted hazard ratios rising from 2.41 to 10.48 across troponin bands (relative measures)
cards.type: Prospective international cohort (VISION programme — report 1 of 3 VISION reports on this shelf, labelled)
cards.people: 15,133 patients aged 45 years or older requiring at least an overnight hospital stay after noncardiac surgery, in the prospective international VISION cohort (2007–2011); troponin T was measured 6–12 hours after surgery and on days 1, 2 and 3. The 30-day mortality rate was 1.9%. This and the next two cards are reports of the one VISION programme, labelled as such.
cards.result: Peak troponin T values of at least 0.02 ng/mL, occurring in 11.6% of patients, were associated with higher 30-day mortality than the reference group (peak troponin T at most 0.01 ng/mL): adjusted hazard ratio 2.41 (95% CI 1.33 to 3.77) at 0.02 ng/mL, 5.00 (3.72 to 6.76) at 0.03 to 0.29 ng/mL, and 10.48 (6.25 to 16.62) at 0.30 ng/mL or greater — relative measures, printed beside the absolute 30-day mortality rates of 1.0%, 4.0%, 9.3% and 16.9% across the same bands. Adding peak troponin T raised the model's C index from 0.81 to 0.85, with a net reclassification improvement of 25.0%.
cards.watchOut: Fourth-generation troponin T thresholds (ng/mL) do not transfer to high-sensitivity assays (ng/L) — the next-but-one card gives the high-sensitivity thresholds separately, and the two assay generations are never merged on this shelf.
cards.source: Devereaux PJ et al. Association between postoperative troponin levels and 30-day mortality among patients undergoing noncardiac surgery. JAMA. 2012. PMID: 22706835. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: VISION MINS criteria paper (Botto 2014): myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery — peak troponin T at least 0.03 ng/mL judged ischaemic — occurred in 8.0%, carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.87 for 30-day death and the highest population-attributable risk (34.0%) of the perioperative complications; 58.2% would not have met the universal definition of myocardial infarction
cards.summary: VISION MINS criteria paper (Botto 2014): myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery — peak troponin T at least 0.03 ng/mL judged ischaemic — occurred in 8.0%, carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.87 for 30-day death and the highest population-attributable risk (34.0%) of the perioperative complications; 58.2% would not have met the universal definition of myocardial infarction
cards.type: Prospective international cohort (VISION programme — report 2 of 3 VISION reports on this shelf, labelled): MINS diagnostic-criteria paper
cards.people: 15,065 patients aged 45 years or older who underwent inpatient noncardiac surgery in the VISION cohort, with troponin T measured during the first 3 postoperative days; patients adjudicated as having a non-ischaemic troponin elevation (for example sepsis) were excluded from the MINS definition. A VISION programme report, labelled as such.
cards.result: 1,200 patients (8.0%) suffered MINS. MINS independently predicted 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 3.87, 95% CI 2.96 to 5.08 — a relative measure) and had the highest population-attributable risk (34.0%, 95% CI 26.6 to 41.5) of the perioperative complications studied. An elevated troponin predicted death irrespective of ischaemic features, which is why the diagnostic criterion required no ischaemic feature: 58.2% of MINS patients would not have fulfilled the universal definition of myocardial infarction, and only 15.8% experienced an ischaemic symptom — most MINS is clinically silent, which is part of the definition's teaching point, not a caveat.
cards.watchOut: The MINS threshold was derived against 30-day mortality in this same cohort (260 deaths), so the prognostic strength is partly built into the definition; independent confirmation is the Basel card below, on a different assay pair.
cards.source: Botto F et al. Myocardial injury after noncardiac surgery: a large, international, prospective cohort study establishing diagnostic criteria, characteristics, predictors, and 30-day outcomes. Anesthesiology. 2014. PMID: 24534856. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: VISION high-sensitivity troponin T (Devereaux 2017): MINS in 17.9% by hsTnT criteria — 93.1% with no ischaemic symptom — with 30-day mortality of 3.0%, 9.1% and 29.6% across rising hsTnT bands
cards.summary: VISION high-sensitivity troponin T (Devereaux 2017): MINS in 17.9% by hsTnT criteria — 93.1% with no ischaemic symptom — with 30-day mortality of 3.0%, 9.1% and 29.6% across rising hsTnT bands
cards.type: Prospective international cohort (VISION programme — report 3 of 3 VISION reports on this shelf, labelled): high-sensitivity troponin T analysis
cards.people: 21,842 patients aged 45 years or older who underwent inpatient noncardiac surgery at 23 centres in 13 countries in the VISION cohort (recruited from 2008, follow-up to 2013), with high-sensitivity troponin T measured 6–12 hours after surgery and daily for 3 days; 40.4% also had a preoperative measurement. Death within 30 days occurred in 266 patients (1.2%). A VISION programme report, labelled as such.
cards.result: Compared with peak hsTnT below 5 ng/L, bands of 20 to below 65 ng/L, 65 to below 1,000 ng/L and at least 1,000 ng/L carried 30-day mortality of 3.0%, 9.1% and 29.6%, with adjusted hazard ratios of 23.63, 70.34 and 227.01 (relative measures with very wide confidence intervals, printed beside the absolute rates). An absolute hsTnT change of at least 5 ng/L was itself associated with 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 4.69). In total 3,904 patients (17.9%) had MINS by these criteria, and 3,633 of them (93.1%) experienced no ischaemic symptom; an elevated hsTnT without an ischaemic feature was still associated with 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratio 3.20).
cards.watchOut: The extreme adjusted hazard ratios rest on a very low reference mortality (below 5 ng/L) and carry wide intervals; the absolute band mortality rates (3.0% to 29.6%) are the clinically readable figures. The 17.9% MINS incidence is an hsTnT-criteria figure and is not comparable with the 8.0% fourth-generation figure on the previous card.
cards.source: Devereaux PJ et al. Association of Postoperative High-Sensitivity Troponin Levels With Myocardial Injury and 30-Day Mortality Among Patients Undergoing Noncardiac Surgery. JAMA. 2017. PMID: 28444280. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Independent Basel PMI cohort (Gualandro 2021): incidence was assay-dependent in the same patients — 9% by high-sensitivity troponin I versus 15% by high-sensitivity troponin T — and injury by either assay independently predicted 30-day and 1-year death
cards.summary: Independent Basel PMI cohort (Gualandro 2021): incidence was assay-dependent in the same patients — 9% by high-sensitivity troponin I versus 15% by high-sensitivity troponin T — and injury by either assay independently predicted 30-day and 1-year death
cards.type: Prospective independent cohort (Basel PMI) with paired hs-cTnI and hs-cTnT — the independent limb beside the VISION programme reports
cards.people: 2,455 patients at high cardiovascular risk undergoing 3,111 noncardiac surgeries, prospectively included with paired high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I and T measured before surgery and on postoperative days 1 and 2 (the Basel PMI cohort — independent of the VISION programme). Perioperative myocardial infarction/injury (PMI) was defined by the Fourth Universal Definition. Mortality was 2% at 30 days and 9% at 1 year.
cards.result: Overall PMI incidence was 9% (95% CI 8 to 10) by hs-cTnI — infarction 2.6%, injury 6.1% — versus 15% (14 to 16) by hs-cTnT — infarction 3.7%, injury 11.3% — in the same patients: incidence is assay-dependent and is carded per assay, never merged. By hs-cTnI, both infarction and injury independently predicted 30-day mortality (adjusted hazard ratios 2.5 and 2.8, relative measures) and 1-year mortality (2.0 and 1.8), with a prognostic impact comparable to hs-cTnT-diagnosed PMI.
cards.watchOut: A high-cardiovascular-risk surgical population, so its incidences (9% and 15%) run above an unselected inpatient surgical population's; the assay-versus-assay contrast within the same patients is the transportable finding.
cards.source: Gualandro DM et al. Incidence and outcomes of perioperative myocardial infarction/injury diagnosed by high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I. Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society. 2021. PMID: 33768367. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: postoperative troponin surveillance finds prognostically important myocardial injury in roughly one in twelve patients by fourth-generation criteria (8.0%) and roughly one in six by high-sensitivity T criteria (17.9%) — most of it silent — with a graded mortality association confirmed independently, and with incidence that depends on the assay (9% by troponin I versus 15% by troponin T in the same patients)
cards.summary: Synthesis: postoperative troponin surveillance finds prognostically important myocardial injury in roughly one in twelve patients by fourth-generation criteria (8.0%) and roughly one in six by high-sensitivity T criteria (17.9%) — most of it silent — with a graded mortality association confirmed independently, and with incidence that depends on the assay (9% by troponin I versus 15% by troponin T in the same patients)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: three labelled reports of the one VISION programme (15,133; 15,065; and 21,842 patients) and one independent Basel cohort (2,455 patients, 3,111 surgeries).
cards.result: The VISION programme established the entity: a peak fourth-generation troponin T of at least 0.02 ng/mL (11.6% of patients) independently predicted 30-day death; MINS as defined (at least 0.03 ng/mL, judged ischaemic) affected 8.0%, carried an adjusted hazard ratio of 3.87 (relative) and the highest population-attributable risk of the perioperative complications, and 58.2% of cases met no universal infarction definition. By high-sensitivity troponin T criteria, MINS affected 17.9%, 93.1% of it without an ischaemic symptom. The independent Basel cohort confirms the mortality association on both high-sensitivity assays and shows the incidence itself is assay-dependent. This is a prognostic shelf: no card implies that surveillance, or any response to a raised troponin, improves outcomes — no such trial is carded here. Preoperative prediction (the RCRI shelf, #7577) is the cross-point; no report is shared between the two shelves.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: Apfel score for PONV: incidences 10% to 79% by factor count and best of six models (AUC 0.68) — but calibration failed on hepatectomy validation (AUC 0.612, slope 0.49)
shelves.question: Before general anaesthesia, how well does the Apfel simplified risk score for postoperative nausea and vomiting (female sex, history of motion sickness or PONV, non-smoking, postoperative opioids) predict PONV within 24 hours — what incidence does each score count carry, how does it compare with the Koivuranta and other published predictive models, and does it hold up on external validation outside its derivation settings?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Analgesics, Opioid/adverse effects · Female · Humans · Logistic Models · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting/etiology · Risk Factors · Sex Factors
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a steep risk gradient with modest discrimination that degrades externally. The Apfel four-factor score (female sex, history of motion sickness or PONV, non-smoking, postoperative opioids) carried PONV incidences of 10%, 21%, 39%, 61% and 79% at derivation, with cross-centre AUCs of 0.65–0.75. Against five rival models it discriminated best (AUC 0.68 versus 0.61–0.66) and calibrated best while using the fewest parameters. On external validation in hepatectomy for liver cancer, however, its ROC area fell to 0.612 with poor calibration (slope 0.49), and Koivuranta (0.628) was no better — neither was well validated in that field. No card implies scoring changes outcomes; prophylaxis treatment is homed at live #658.

cards.headline: Derivation and cross-validation (Apfel 1999): the simplified four-factor score carried PONV incidences of 10%, 21%, 39%, 61% and 79% with 0 to 4 factors, and scores derived in one centre predicted the other (AUC 0.65–0.75)
cards.summary: Derivation and cross-validation (Apfel 1999): the simplified four-factor score carried PONV incidences of 10%, 21%, 39%, 61% and 79% with 0 to 4 factors, and scores derived in one centre predicted the other (AUC 0.65–0.75)
cards.type: Derivation and cross-centre validation of the Apfel simplified risk score (two centres, inhalational anaesthesia, no prophylaxis)
cards.people: Adult patients at two centres — Oulu, Finland (n=520) and Würzburg, Germany (n=2,202) — receiving inhalational anaesthesia without antiemetic prophylaxis for various types of surgery; postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) was nausea or vomiting within 24 hours of surgery.
cards.result: Risk scores derived from one centre predicted PONV in the other (area under the curve 0.65 to 0.75), and simplifying the scores to a count of risk factors did not essentially weaken discrimination (0.63 to 0.73); no centre effect was detected in the combined data (odds ratio 1.06, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.59 — a relative measure). The final score counts four predictors: female sex, history of motion sickness or PONV, non-smoking, and use of postoperative opioids. With none, one, two, three or four factors present, PONV incidences were 10%, 21%, 39%, 61% and 79% — absolute rates as published.
cards.watchOut: Derivation-era incidences come from inhalational anaesthesia without any antiemetic prophylaxis — absolute PONV rates in modern practice with prophylaxis and different anaesthetic techniques will be lower, even if the score's ordering still holds; the later cards test exactly that.

cards.headline: Head-to-head model comparison (Apfel 2002): six predictive models discriminated modestly — Apfel AUC 0.68, Koivuranta 0.66, Sinclair 0.66, Palazzo 0.63, Gan 0.61, Scholz 0.61 — and the four-parameter Apfel score was the most practicable
cards.summary: Head-to-head model comparison (Apfel 2002): six predictive models discriminated modestly — Apfel AUC 0.68, Koivuranta 0.66, Sinclair 0.66, Palazzo 0.63, Gan 0.61, Scholz 0.61 — and the four-parameter Apfel score was the most practicable
cards.type: Head-to-head comparison of six published PONV predictive models in one cohort (n=1,566)
cards.people: 1,566 patients who underwent balanced anaesthesia without prophylactic antiemetic treatment for various types of surgery; PONV occurred in 600 patients (38.1%). Six published predictive models were compared for discrimination, calibration and practicability (number of parameters).
cards.result: Discriminating power (AUC) was: Apfel 0.68, Koivuranta 0.66, Sinclair 0.66, Palazzo 0.63, Gan 0.61 and Scholz 0.61. Calibration was best for the simplified scores (Apfel calibration slope 0.82, offset 0.01, r²=0.995; Koivuranta slope 1.13, offset −0.10, r²=0.999) and poor for the complex scores (Sinclair slope 0.49; Palazzo slope 0.30). The models required 4 (Apfel), 5 (Koivuranta, Palazzo), 9 (Scholz), 12 (Sinclair) or 14 (Gan) parameters. The authors recommend simplified scores over complex ones.
cards.watchOut: All six models were applied to one centre's data assembled by the Apfel group — the home-team setting favours the simpler scores the group itself derived; the external-validation card below is the corrective.
cards.source: Apfel CC et al. Comparison of predictive models for postoperative nausea and vomiting. British journal of anaesthesia. 2002. PMID: 11883387. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: External validation in hepatectomy (Chen 2023): in 214 patients having liver-cancer hepatectomy (53.3% developing PONV), the Apfel score's ROC area was 0.612 with poor calibration (slope 0.49) and Koivuranta's 0.628 — neither score was well validated in this field
cards.summary: External validation in hepatectomy (Chen 2023): in 214 patients having liver-cancer hepatectomy (53.3% developing PONV), the Apfel score's ROC area was 0.612 with poor calibration (slope 0.49) and Koivuranta's 0.628 — neither score was well validated in this field
cards.type: Prospective single-centre external validation of the Apfel and Koivuranta scores in hepatectomy for liver cancer
cards.people: 214 patients with liver cancer undergoing hepatectomy, prospectively and consecutively recruited at a single centre, all receiving PONV assessment and risk assessment with both the Apfel and Koivuranta scores (reported to the TRIPOD checklist); 114 patients (53.3%) developed PONV.
cards.result: For the Apfel simplified risk score, the ROC area was 0.612 (95% CI 0.543 to 0.678), demonstrating imperfect discrimination, and the calibration curve showed poor calibration with a slope of 0.49. For the Koivuranta score, the ROC area was 0.628 (95% CI 0.559 to 0.693) with an unsatisfactory calibration slope of 0.71. The authors conclude neither score was well validated in this population and that disease-specific risk factors should be considered when updating or developing PONV risk instruments.
cards.watchOut: A single surgical field (major liver resection for cancer) with a very high PONV incidence — the calibration failure is field-specific evidence, carded as such, and does not by itself retire the score in the mixed-surgery settings of the earlier cards.
cards.source: Chen X et al. External validation of postoperative nausea and vomiting risk scores in patients with liver cancer: A single-centre prospective cohort study. cards.headline: Synthesis: the Apfel score orders PONV risk with a steep incidence gradient (10% to 79% across 0–4 factors) but only modest discrimination everywhere it has been tested (AUC 0.61–0.75), besting five rival models mainly on simplicity — and its calibration failed on external validation in hepatectomy (ROC area 0.612, calibration slope 0.49)
cards.summary: Synthesis: the Apfel score orders PONV risk with a steep incidence gradient (10% to 79% across 0–4 factors) but only modest discrimination everywhere it has been tested (AUC 0.61–0.75), besting five rival models mainly on simplicity — and its calibration failed on external validation in hepatectomy (ROC area 0.612, calibration slope 0.49)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: the two-centre derivation/cross-validation (n=520 and n=2,202), the six-model comparison cohort (n=1,566) and the hepatectomy external validation (n=214).
cards.result: The four-factor score's value is its gradient and its simplicity: no rival model discriminated better by more than a few hundredths of AUC, and the complex models calibrated worse. But discrimination is modest in every report and degrades outside the derivation settings — the derivation incidences (10–79%) must always be read beside the hepatectomy cohort's calibration failure, never alone. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf about selecting candidates for prophylaxis: PONV prophylaxis treatment itself is homed at live #658 (with amisulpride pack #6777 and droperidol pack #6920), and no card here implies that scoring, or prophylaxis allocated by score, improves outcomes beyond what those treatment shelves claim.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Preoperative CPET prediction by surgical field: AT rules out risk (NPV 96–100%) far better than it rules it in (PPV 2.9–42.1%); thresholds are field-specific, never one cut-off
shelves.question: Before major noncardiac surgery, how well does cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) predict postoperative death and cardiopulmonary complications — what anaerobic-threshold (AT) and ventilatory-efficiency (VE/VCO2) thresholds separate high from low risk, how do the thresholds move by surgical field (major abdominal, hepatic resection, pancreaticoduodenectomy, oesophagogastric resection), and how good is the test's classifier performance (sensitivity, specificity, predictive values) when it is audited as a test rather than as a cohort association?
shelves.mesh: Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Anaerobic Threshold · Cardiac Output, Low/diagnosis · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality · Exercise Test · Female · Humans · Male · Middle Aged · Myocardial Ischemia/diagnosis · Oxygen Consumption · Postoperative Complications/mortality · Preoperative Care · Surgical Procedures, Operative/mortality
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — rule-out strong, rule-in weak, and field-specific. The founding cohorts separated risk sharply at an anaerobic threshold (AT) of 11 mL/min/kg (mortality 18% vs 0.8% in elderly surgery; no cardiopulmonary deaths among CPET-assigned ward patients in major abdominal surgery, whose assignment was not randomised). By field: hepatic resection — AT 9.9 mL/kg/min, 100% sensitive and 76% specific for in-hospital death, NPV 100% but PPV 19%, with VE/VCO2 at AT of 34.5 predicting complications; pancreaticoduodenectomy — AT and peak VO2 did not predict, VE/VCO2 at AT did (AUC 0.84, threshold 41); oesophagogastric resection — a complication gradient only (42% / 29% / 20% across AT bands), discrimination low. The 36-study classifier audit (Stubbs 2020) is the counterweight: AT sensitivities for mortality 20–100%, NPVs 96–100%, PPVs only 2.9–42.1%, and no CPET score externally validated. A prognostic-accuracy balance, not a treatment balance: nothing here shows CPET-guided triage improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Founding cohort, elderly surgery (Older 1993): mortality 18% with anaerobic threshold <11 mL/min/kg vs 0.8% above it; 42% when a low AT combined with preoperative ischaemia
cards.summary: Founding cohort, elderly surgery (Older 1993): mortality 18% with anaerobic threshold <11 mL/min/kg vs 0.8% above it; 42% when a low AT combined with preoperative ischaemia
cards.type: Prospective cohort (founding CPET study, elderly surgery) — AT and ischaemia as predictors of postoperative mortality
cards.people: 187 elderly surgical patients evaluated preoperatively by cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET/CPX) for cardiac failure and ischaemia. Overall mortality was 7.5% (5.9% after excluding three deaths from surgical causes).
cards.result: Mortality was 18% (10 of 55) in patients with an anaerobic threshold (AT) below 11 mL/min/kg versus 0.8% (1 of 132) in those above 11 mL/min/kg (p<0.001). A low AT combined with preoperative ischaemia carried a mortality of 42% (8 of 19), versus 4% (1 of 25) when ischaemia accompanied a higher AT (p<0.01). The authors concluded preoperative ischaemia and cardiac failure (as measured by AT) were independent risk factors for perioperative mortality.
cards.watchOut: GAP-E predictive-performance card, not a treatment card: a 1993 single-centre cohort from the founding CPET tradition. The striking separation at AT 11 in this cohort is exactly what the modern classifier audit (carded below) could not reproduce as rule-in performance — both stay on the face. No card on this shelf implies CPET-guided triage improves outcomes.

cards.headline: Major abdominal surgery cohort (Older 1999): CPET-assigned ICU / HDU / ward care in 548 patients — overall mortality 3.9%, and no cardiopulmonary deaths in the ward-assigned group
cards.summary: Major abdominal surgery cohort (Older 1999): CPET-assigned ICU / HDU / ward care in 548 patients — overall mortality 3.9%, and no cardiopulmonary deaths in the ward-assigned group
cards.type: Prospective cohort (major intra-abdominal surgery) — CPET-based triage strata and postoperative mortality (management not randomised)
cards.people: 548 patients aged over 60 years (or younger with known cardiopulmonary disease) scheduled for major intra-abdominal surgery, all undergoing preoperative CPET and assigned to intensive care, high-dependency or ward care on the basis of anaerobic threshold, ECG evidence of ischaemia and the expected oxygen-demand stress of the operation.
cards.result: Overall mortality was 3.9%, and 43% of deaths were attributed to poor cardiopulmonary function as detected preoperatively. There were no deaths related to cardiopulmonary complications in any patient deemed fit for major abdominal surgery and ward management as determined by CPET. The authors concluded the anaerobic threshold is an excellent predictor of mortality from cardiopulmonary causes after major intra-abdominal surgery.
cards.watchOut: The management assignment in this study was NOT randomised — it shows that CPET strata separated patients whose outcomes differed under CPET-guided placement, not that the placement itself improved outcomes. No treatment claim may be drawn from this card.

cards.headline: Hepatic resection (Junejo 2012): AT 9.9 mL/kg/min was 100% sensitive and 76% specific for in-hospital death (NPV 100%, PPV 19%); VE/VCO2 at AT of 34.5 predicted complications
cards.summary: Hepatic resection (Junejo 2012): AT 9.9 mL/kg/min was 100% sensitive and 76% specific for in-hospital death (NPV 100%, PPV 19%); VE/VCO2 at AT of 34.5 predicted complications
cards.type: Prospective cohort (hepatic resection) — CPET classifier performance for death and complications
cards.people: 204 patients assessed for hepatic resection, of whom 108 had preoperative CPET (patients aged over 65, or younger with co-morbidity); functional status, postoperative complications and survival collected prospectively.
cards.result: An anaerobic threshold of 9.9 mL O2/kg/min predicted in-hospital death: below it, AT was 100% sensitive and 76% specific, with a positive predictive value of 19% and a negative predictive value of 100% — no deaths occurred above the threshold. A VE/VCO2 at AT threshold of 34.5 predicted postoperative complications with specificity 84% and sensitivity 47% (PPV 76%, 95% CI 58–88%; NPV 60%, 95% CI 48–72%). Long-term survival was worse below the AT threshold (hazard ratio for mortality 1.81, 95% CI 1.04–3.17; P=0.036 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: Field-specific threshold: 9.9 mL/kg/min for hepatic resection is NOT the general-surgery 11 mL/min/kg — thresholds on this shelf are never merged into one cut-off. Note the pattern even here: perfect rule-out (NPV 100%) with weak rule-in (PPV 19%). Only 108 of 204 assessed patients had CPET, a selected subgroup.
cards.source: Junejo MA et al. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for preoperative risk assessment before hepatic resection. British Journal of Surgery. 2012. PMID: 22696424. cards.headline: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Junejo 2014): neither AT nor peak VO2 predicted morbidity or mortality — but VE/VCO2 at AT did (AUC 0.84; threshold 41 at 75% sensitivity / 95% specificity)
cards.summary: Pancreaticoduodenectomy (Junejo 2014): neither AT nor peak VO2 predicted morbidity or mortality — but VE/VCO2 at AT did (AUC 0.84; threshold 41 at 75% sensitivity / 95% specificity)
cards.type: Prospective cohort (pancreaticoduodenectomy) — CPET variables as predictors of morbidity and mortality
cards.people: 143 patients assessed before pancreaticoduodenectomy for cancer, of whom 50 were deemed low risk by protocol; of 93 high-risk patients (aged over 65, or younger with co-morbidity), 64 proceeded to surgery after preoperative CPET.
cards.result: Neither anaerobic threshold nor maximal oxygen consumption predicted mortality or morbidity. Ventilatory equivalent for carbon dioxide (VE/VCO2) at AT predicted postoperative mortality with an area under the curve of 0.84 (95% CI 0.63–1.00, p=0.020); a threshold of 41 was 75% sensitive and 95% specific (positive predictive value 50%, negative predictive value 98%). Above that threshold, raised VE/VCO2 also predicted poor long-term survival (hazard ratio 2.05, 95% CI 1.09–3.86, p=0.026 — a relative measure).
cards.watchOut: The negative half of this card is as important as the positive: in this surgical field the founding variable (AT) did not predict at all, and the discriminating variable was VE/VCO2 with a field-specific threshold of 41 — far from the hepatic-resection 34.5. Only 64 operated high-risk patients; the AUC confidence interval is wide (0.63–1.00).
cards.source: Junejo MA et al. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for preoperative risk assessment before pancreaticoduodenectomy for cancer. Annals of Surgical Oncology. 2014. PMID: 24477709. cards.headline: Oesophagogastric resection (Moyes 2013): cardiopulmonary complications in 42% with AT <9, 29% with AT 9–<11 and 20% with AT ≥11 mL/min/kg — a gradient, with low discriminatory ability
cards.summary: Oesophagogastric resection (Moyes 2013): cardiopulmonary complications in 42% with AT <9, 29% with AT 9–<11 and 20% with AT ≥11 mL/min/kg — a gradient, with low discriminatory ability
cards.type: Cohort (oesophagogastric cancer resection) — AT bands and cardiopulmonary complications
cards.people: 108 patients (83 men, 25 women; median age 66 years) undergoing CPET before potentially curative resection for oesophagogastric cancer (2008–2010). Mean AT was 10.8 mL/min/kg and mean peak VO2 15.2 mL/min/kg; 55% had an AT below 11 and 12% below 9 mL/min/kg (as published).
cards.result: Postoperative complications occurred in 57 patients (29 cardiopulmonary, 28%); 4 patients (4%) died in hospital and 21 (20%) required unplanned ICU admission. Cardiopulmonary complications occurred in 42% of patients with an AT below 9 mL/min/kg, 29% of those with an AT of 9 to under 11, and 20% of those with an AT of 11 or above (p=0.04). There was a trend toward more unplanned ICU admissions in patients with both an AT below 11 and a low peak VO2. The authors noted the discriminatory ability was low despite the correlation.
cards.watchOut: A risk gradient across AT bands is not a usable cut-off: even the lowest band's complication rate (42%) means most such patients did not develop cardiopulmonary complications, and the highest band still had a 20% rate. Carded per surgical field, as the row requires.
cards.source: Moyes LH et al. Cardiopulmonary exercise testing as a predictor of complications in oesophagogastric cancer surgery. Annals of the Royal College of Surgeons of England. 2013. PMID: 23484995. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Classifier audit, systematic review (Stubbs 2020): AT sensitivities for mortality ranged 20–100% with NPVs 96–100% but PPVs only 2.9–42.1% across 36 studies — CPET rules OUT risk far better than it rules it in; no CPET score was externally validated
cards.summary: Classifier audit, systematic review (Stubbs 2020): AT sensitivities for mortality ranged 20–100% with NPVs 96–100% but PPVs only 2.9–42.1% across 36 studies — CPET rules OUT risk far better than it rules it in; no CPET score was externally validated
cards.type: Systematic review of CPET classifier performance in non-cardiopulmonary surgery (36 studies)
cards.people: 36 studies of CPET for prognostication of mortality, cardiorespiratory complications and unplanned ICU admission in non-cardiopulmonary surgery, identified after prospective PROSPERO registration; classifier-performance measures could be calculated from 27 studies. Seven studies presented risk prediction models incorporating CPET variables.
cards.result: For anaerobic-threshold-based prediction of mortality, calculated sensitivities ranged from 20% to 100%, negative predictive values were high (96–100%) and positive predictive values poor (2.9–42.1%). Positive predictive value was generally higher for cardiorespiratory complications, with similar sensitivities; peak VO2 (sensitivity 85.7–100%, PPV 2.7–5.9%) and VE/VCO2 (sensitivity 27.8–100%, PPV 3.4–7.1%) showed the same pattern for mortality. Studies were highly heterogeneous with high potential for bias and confounding; of seven prediction models, only four described clear model development, only two assessed discrimination and calibration, only one undertook internal validation, and NO score was externally validated.
cards.watchOut: This audit is the counterweight to the founding cohorts and stays on the face beside them: as a classifier, CPET's rule-out capability is consistently better than its rule-in capability, and poor PPV partly reflects how uncommon the outcomes are in the studied populations. A systematic review of classifier performance — not a treatment review.
cards.source: Stubbs DJ et al. Performance of cardiopulmonary exercise testing for the prediction of post-operative complications in non cardiopulmonary surgery: A systematic review. PLoS One. 2020. PMID: 32012165. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: GAP-E — CPET predicts postoperative risk unevenly and field-specifically: anaerobic threshold rules out risk far better than it rules it in (NPV 96–100%, PPV 2.9–42.1%), thresholds differ by surgical field, and no CPET score has been externally validated
cards.summary: Synthesis: GAP-E — CPET predicts postoperative risk unevenly and field-specifically: anaerobic threshold rules out risk far better than it rules it in (NPV 96–100%, PPV 2.9–42.1%), thresholds differ by surgical field, and no CPET score has been externally validated
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
cards.result: Synthesis: a prognostic-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf. The founding cohorts separated risk dramatically at an anaerobic threshold of 11 mL/min/kg (mortality 18% vs 0.8% in elderly surgery; no cardiopulmonary deaths in the CPET-assigned ward group in major abdominal surgery — whose management assignment was not randomised). By surgical field: hepatic resection turned on AT 9.9 (100% sensitive, NPV 100%, PPV 19%) and VE/VCO2 34.5; pancreaticoduodenectomy turned not on AT at all but on VE/VCO2 at AT (AUC 0.84, threshold 41); oesophagogastric resection showed only a complication gradient (42% / 29% / 20% across AT bands) with low discrimination. The 36-study classifier audit reconciles these: AT rules out risk far better than it rules it in (NPV 96–100%, PPV 2.9–42.1%), and no CPET-derived score was externally validated. Thresholds are field-specific and are never merged into one cut-off.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: POSSUM / P-POSSUM prediction: discrimination moderate (c 0.79–0.85) but the original equation overpredicts death >2× overall and 6–7× in low-risk patients; calibration fails externally without recalibration
shelves.question: In adults having general and specialist surgery, how accurately do POSSUM and its Portsmouth modification (P-POSSUM) — a 12-factor physiological score plus a 6-factor operative severity score — predict postoperative mortality and morbidity, where does the original POSSUM equation miscalibrate (and by how much in the lowest-risk patients, who are most surgical patients), and how do the scores perform on external validation in emergency laparotomy and in specialist fields against the NELA and ACS-NSQIP models?
shelves.mesh: England · Humans · Length of Stay · Logistic Models · Medical Audit · Morbidity · Risk Assessment · Severity of Illness Index · Surgical Procedures, Operative/mortality · Workload
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — discrimination moderate, calibration the problem. POSSUM (a 12-factor physiological score plus a 6-factor operative severity score) and its Portsmouth modification rank patients moderately well — concordance statistics 0.79 for P-POSSUM to 0.85 for NELA in external emergency-laparotomy validation, and AUC 0.755 for in-hospital mortality (about 0.70 for morbidity) in elective hepatic resection. But the original POSSUM mortality equation miscalibrates badly: it overpredicted deaths more than twofold overall and sixfold (1996 evaluation) to more than sevenfold (1998, 10,000 episodes) in the lowest-risk group — most surgical patients — with a minimum predicted mortality of 1.08%. P-POSSUM fitted its derivation-era data closely, yet in external validation every model except surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP was poorly calibrated, and hepatic-resection calibration slopes were below 1: the scores are usable only after local recalibration. The operative severity score is not fully knowable before surgery. A prognostic-accuracy balance, not a treatment balance.

cards.headline: POSSUM evaluation (Whiteley 1996): the published POSSUM mortality equation overpredicted deaths more than twofold overall and SIXFOLD in the lowest-risk group; its minimum predicted mortality was 1.08%
cards.summary: POSSUM evaluation (Whiteley 1996): the published POSSUM mortality equation overpredicted deaths more than twofold overall and SIXFOLD in the lowest-risk group; its minimum predicted mortality was 1.08%
cards.type: Evaluation of the POSSUM surgical scoring system (1,485 episodes for the refitted equation) — calibration of the mortality equation
cards.people: A 28% sample of the general surgical workload over 9 months, with mortality or survival as the endpoint; logistic regression on 1,485 surgical episodes generated a locally refitted predictor equation for comparison.
cards.result: The published POSSUM predictor equation for mortality overpredicted deaths by a factor of more than two overall. The bulk of the overprediction occurred in the group at lowest risk (predicted mortality 10% or less) — the majority of surgical patients, fit patients having minor surgery — where death was overpredicted by a factor of six. The published equation returns a minimum predicted mortality of 1.08%, far higher than expected for a fit patient having minor surgery. The locally refitted equation fitted the observed mortality well and gave a minimum predicted risk of 0.20%. The published equation performed badly on a standard goodness-of-fit test and, the authors concluded, must be modified.
cards.watchOut: GAP-E calibration card, not a treatment card: this is the founding miscalibration finding and it is core content, not a caveat. A single-centre-era evaluation (1990s UK general surgery); the locally refitted equation's good fit is in-sample and does not rescue the published equation elsewhere.
cards.source: Whiteley MS et al. An evaluation of the POSSUM surgical scoring system. British Journal of Surgery. 1996. PMID: 8696749. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: POSSUM and Portsmouth POSSUM (Prytherch 1998): in 10,000 general surgical episodes the POSSUM equation overpredicted overall mortality more than twofold and lowest-risk mortality more than sevenfold, while the P-POSSUM equation fitted closely
cards.summary: POSSUM and Portsmouth POSSUM (Prytherch 1998): in 10,000 general surgical episodes the POSSUM equation overpredicted overall mortality more than twofold and lowest-risk mortality more than sevenfold, while the P-POSSUM equation fitted closely
cards.type: Prospective derivation and validation study (10,000 episodes) — POSSUM vs P-POSSUM mortality prediction
cards.people: 10,000 general surgical interventions (excluding paediatric and day cases), studied prospectively (1993–1995). The POSSUM mortality equation was applied to all 10,000 episodes; the first 2,500 episodes in chronological order formed the training set for the modified Portsmouth POSSUM (P-POSSUM) equation, which was then applied prospectively to the remaining 7,500 in five groups of 1,500.
cards.result: The original POSSUM logistic regression equation for mortality overpredicted the overall risk of death by more than twofold, and the risk of death for patients at lowest risk (5% or less) by more than sevenfold. The P-POSSUM equation produced a very close fit with the observed in-hospital mortality in the prospective validation groups.
cards.watchOut: P-POSSUM's close fit was achieved in the same centre and era that derived it — a derivation-adjacent validation, which is why the external validations carded below matter and why they are less kind. POSSUM combines a 12-factor physiological score with a 6-factor operative severity score; the operative limb is scored during or after surgery and is not fully knowable before surgery — a limitation printed on the face of this shelf.

cards.headline: External validation in emergency laparotomy (Kokkinakis 2023): concordance 0.79 for P-POSSUM to 0.85 for NELA, but every model except surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP was poorly calibrated; 30-day mortality 16.3%
cards.summary: External validation in emergency laparotomy (Kokkinakis 2023): concordance 0.79 for P-POSSUM to 0.85 for NELA, but every model except surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP was poorly calibrated; 30-day mortality 16.3%
cards.type: Prospective multicentre external validation (emergency laparotomy, 631 patients) — P-POSSUM vs NELA, ACS-NSQIP and POTTER
cards.people: 631 consecutive patients undergoing emergency laparotomy in 11 Greek hospitals (2020–2021), meeting National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) inclusion criteria; 30-day mortality risk predictions were calculated with ACS-NSQIP, NELA, P-POSSUM and the POTTER model, alongside surgeons' own assessments and a surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP prediction.
cards.result: Thirty-day mortality was 16.3%. All models discriminated well, with concordance statistics ranging from 0.79 for P-POSSUM to 0.85 for NELA. However, every model except the surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP (Hosmer–Lemeshow p=0.742) was poorly calibrated (p<0.001 for the others). ACS-NSQIP and its surgeon-adjusted version had the highest scaled Brier scores, and decision curve analysis favoured ACS-NSQIP. After recalibration, accuracy improved for all models but ACS-NSQIP retained the lead; between-hospital heterogeneity was maximum for P-POSSUM.
cards.watchOut: Discrimination and calibration are different claims and are carded separately on this shelf: ranking patients moderately-to-well (c-statistics 0.79–0.85) coexists with absolute risk predictions that fail calibration. P-POSSUM and NELA appear here as comparators inside this one validation; a standalone NSQIP-calculator question is a different row and is not carded here.
