prospective multicentre external validation (emergency laparotomy, 631 patients) — p-possum vs nela, acs-nsqip and potter 631 consecutive patients undergoing emergency laparotomy in 11 greek hospitals (2020–2021), meeting national emergency laparotomy audit (nela) inclusion criteria; 30-day mortality risk predictions were calculated with acs-nsqip, nela, p-possum and the potter model, alongside surgeons' own assessments and a surgeon-adjusted acs-nsqip prediction. thirty-day mortality was 16.3%. all models discriminated well, with concordance statistics ranging from 0.79 for p-possum to 0.85 for nela. however, every model except the surgeon-adjusted acs-nsqip (hosmer–lemeshow p=0.742) was poorly calibrated (p<0.001 for the others). acs-nsqip and its surgeon-adjusted version had the highest scaled brier scores, and decision curve analysis favoured acs-nsqip. after recalibration, accuracy improved for all models but acs-nsqip retained the lead; between-hospital heterogeneity was maximum for p-possum. discrimination and calibration are different claims and are carded separately on this shelf: ranking patients moderately-to-well (c-statistics 0.79–0.85) coexists with absolute risk predictions that fail calibration. p-possum and nela appear here as comparators inside this one validation; a standalone nsqip-calculator question is a different row and is not carded here. kokkinakis s et al. prospective multicenter external validation of postoperative mortality prediction tools in patients undergoing emergency laparotomy. journal of trauma and acute care surgery. 2023. pmid: 36726191. registry id: nct04615520. mesh: humans · laparotomy · prospective studies · postoperative complications · risk assessment · morbidity · retrospective studies · quality improvement · multicenter studies as topic

cards.headline: External validation in elective hepatic resection (Bogovic 2026): POSSUM / P-POSSUM AUC 0.755 for in-hospital mortality and about 0.70 for morbidity, with calibration slopes below 1 — usable only after local recalibration
cards.summary: External validation in elective hepatic resection (Bogovic 2026): POSSUM / P-POSSUM AUC 0.755 for in-hospital mortality and about 0.70 for morbidity, with calibration slopes below 1 — usable only after local recalibration
cards.type: External validation and logistic recalibration of POSSUM / P-POSSUM (elective hepatic resection, 194 patients)
cards.people: 194 consecutive adults with computable predictions (of 200 assessed) undergoing elective hepatic resection at one university hospital (2020–2023), analysed retrospectively; POSSUM and P-POSSUM scores were calculated with the original logistic equations, with bootstrap (1,000 resamples) calibration assessment and logistic recalibration. Clinically relevant morbidity (Clavien–Dindo ≥II) occurred in 75.3%, major morbidity (≥IIIa) in 37.6%, and in-hospital mortality in 7.7% (15/194).
cards.result: Discrimination was fair for morbidity and higher for mortality: AUC 0.696 (95% CI 0.595–0.789) for clinically relevant morbidity, 0.697 (95% CI 0.620–0.764) for major morbidity, and 0.755 (95% CI 0.647–0.851) for in-hospital mortality. Out-of-bag bootstrap calibration slopes were below 1 for every endpoint (morbidity α 0.16, β 0.837, Brier 0.172; major morbidity α −0.051, β 0.907, Brier 0.215; mortality α −0.34, β 0.843, Brier 0.068), supporting local model updating. After recalibration, performance was stable without evidence of overfitting, and decision curve analysis suggested clinical utility across relevant threshold probabilities.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, retrospective, specialist-field validation of 194 patients — it shows the scores can support risk prediction in hepatobiliary surgery only when locally recalibrated and validated first, which is the opposite of using the original equations off the shelf. The 2026 publication date is as recorded in its PubMed record.
cards.source: Bogovic N et al. External validation and logistic recalibration of POSSUM and P-POSSUM for predicting postoperative morbidity and mortality after elective hepatic resection. BMC Surgery. 2026. PMID: 41588405. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: GAP-E — POSSUM discriminates moderately but its original mortality equation miscalibrates badly, overpredicting more than twofold overall and six- to sevenfold in the lowest-risk patients; P-POSSUM fixed the fit at home, but external validations still find poor calibration without local recalibration
cards.summary: Synthesis: GAP-E — POSSUM discriminates moderately but its original mortality equation miscalibrates badly, overpredicting more than twofold overall and six- to sevenfold in the lowest-risk patients; P-POSSUM fixed the fit at home, but external validations still find poor calibration without local recalibration
cards.people: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
cards.result: Synthesis: a prognostic-accuracy / audit shelf, not a treatment shelf, with discrimination and calibration kept separate. The original POSSUM mortality equation overpredicted deaths more than twofold overall and sixfold (Whiteley 1996) to more than sevenfold (Prytherch 1998) in the lowest-risk patients — who are most surgical patients — and cannot predict below a 1.08% minimum mortality. The Portsmouth modification (P-POSSUM), derived on the first 2,500 of 10,000 episodes, fitted the remaining episodes closely. Externally, the picture weakens: in 631 Greek emergency-laparotomy patients, concordance ranged from 0.79 (P-POSSUM) to 0.85 (NELA) yet every model except surgeon-adjusted ACS-NSQIP was poorly calibrated; in 194 elective hepatic resections, AUCs were 0.755 for mortality and about 0.70 for morbidity with calibration slopes below 1, supporting use only after local recalibration. The operative-severity limb is scored during or after surgery and is not fully knowable beforehand.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.

shelves.title: ASA physical status: a single subjective grade predicts mortality only moderately (sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67) — better in low-death-rate settings, and assigned unreliably
shelves.question: Before surgery, how much does the American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status (ASA-PS) classification — a single subjective grade from I (healthy) to V (moribund) — actually predict postoperative mortality and medical complications, how does its accuracy vary with the population's underlying death rate and surgical field (inpatient vs ambulatory), and how reliably do anaesthetists assign the same patient to the same class?
shelves.mesh: Anesthesiology · Effect Modifier, Epidemiologic · Elective Surgical Procedures · Hospital Mortality · Humans · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications · Risk Assessment · Surgical Procedures, Operative · United States · Ambulatory Surgical Procedures · Anesthesiologists · Outpatients · Adult · Comorbidity · Male · Morbidity · Reproducibility of Results · Retrospective Studies · Adolescent · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Female · Health Status · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate, setting-dependent, and unreliably assigned. A single subjective grade (ASA physical status I–V) discriminates postoperative mortality only moderately on pooled evidence (77 studies, 165,705 patients: sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67, summary ROC area 0.736), performing better where underlying death rates are lower. The gradient is real and steep — in 2,089,830 ambulatory cases ASA class associated stepwise with complications (c-statistic 0.70), mortality (0.74) and readmission (0.67), with an odds ratio of 89 for death in ASA IV versus healthy patients against 0.08% absolute mortality — and the grade tracks objective comorbidity (27 of 31 Elixhauser groups), yet an objective-measures model predicted 30-day mortality better than ASA alone. The reliability limb is weak: in a 601-anaesthetist fictitious-case survey agreement was low and accuracy fell with experience. Neither 'ASA works' nor 'ASA is useless' is the finding; a c-statistic near 0.74 for a one-item subjective grade, with low inter-rater agreement, is.

cards.headline: Meta-analysis of 77 studies (165,705 patients): ASA physical status predicts postoperative mortality only moderately — pooled sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67, summary ROC area 0.736 — and better where death rates are lower
cards.summary: Meta-analysis of 77 studies (165,705 patients): ASA physical status predicts postoperative mortality only moderately — pooled sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67, summary ROC area 0.736 — and better where death rates are lower
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of ASA physical status predictive accuracy for postoperative mortality (77 studies)
cards.people: 77 published studies totalling 165,705 surgical patients, pooled with random-effects models and metaregression to test whether ASA physical status accuracy varies across surgical populations with different underlying mortality risks.
cards.result: Pooled performance for postoperative mortality was sensitivity 0.74 (95% CI 0.73 to 0.74), specificity 0.67 (95% CI 0.67 to 0.67) and area under the summary receiver operating curve 0.736 (95% CI 0.725 to 0.747). Metaregression found study death rate and surgical specialty were significant modifiers: ASA physical status was a better predictor of postoperative mortality in settings with lower rather than higher death rates.
cards.watchOut: A pooled accuracy estimate across 77 heterogeneous studies and specialties: the setting-dependence is part of the result, so 0.74 / 0.67 must not be printed as the grade's performance in every surgical population.
cards.source: Koo CY et al. A meta-analysis of the predictive accuracy of postoperative mortality using the American Society of Anesthesiologists' physical status classification system. World journal of surgery. 2015. PMID: 25234196. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Ambulatory surgery, 2,089,830 ACS-NSQIP cases: ASA class associates stepwise with complications (c-statistic 0.70), mortality (0.74) and readmission (0.67); odds ratio 89 for death in ASA IV vs healthy patients
cards.summary: Ambulatory surgery, 2,089,830 ACS-NSQIP cases: ASA class associates stepwise with complications (c-statistic 0.70), mortality (0.74) and readmission (0.67); odds ratio 89 for death in ASA IV vs healthy patients
cards.type: Retrospective registry cohort (ACS-NSQIP ambulatory surgery, 2,089,830 cases)
cards.people: 2,089,830 outpatient (ambulatory) surgical cases from the 2005–2016 ACS-NSQIP Participant Use Data Files; 24,777 patients (1.19%) had a 30-day medical complication and 1,701 (0.08%) died within 30 days; over 30,000 ASA physical status IV patients had outpatient surgery.
cards.result: Multivariable analysis showed a stepwise independent association between ASA class and medical complications (c-statistic 0.70), mortality (c-statistic 0.74) and readmissions (c-statistic 0.67), maintained across surgical procedures and anaesthesia techniques. ASA IV patients had a much greater chance of dying than healthy patients — odds ratio 89 (95% CI 55 to 143; P < 0.001), an odds ratio, not a risk ratio — against a very low absolute outpatient mortality of 0.08% overall.
cards.watchOut: The odds ratio of 89 sits on a 0.08% absolute mortality base in ambulatory surgery and must never be read as an 89-fold absolute risk; discrimination (c-statistic 0.74 for mortality) is the same moderate range as the meta-analysis, in a much larger but lower-risk population.
cards.source: Foley C et al. American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification as a reliable predictor of postoperative medical complications and mortality following ambulatory surgery: an analysis of 2,089,830 ACS-NSQIP outpatient cases. BMC surgery. 2021. PMID: 34020623. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Single-centre cohort (56,820 cases): ASA assignment tracks objective comorbidity — 27 of 31 Elixhauser comorbidities correlate with it — yet a model built from those objective measures predicts 30-day mortality better than ASA alone
cards.summary: Single-centre cohort (56,820 cases): ASA assignment tracks objective comorbidity — 27 of 31 Elixhauser comorbidities correlate with it — yet a model built from those objective measures predicts 30-day mortality better than ASA alone
cards.type: Retrospective single-centre cohort study of ASA assignment versus objective comorbidity measures (56,820 cases)
cards.people: 56,820 adult surgical cases at one medical centre (2 November 2017 to 22 April 2020); a multivariable ordinal logistic regression model related ASA physical status assignment to Elixhauser comorbidity groups, age, sex, body weight and emergency status, and its mortality prediction was compared with ASA or comorbidity indices alone.
cards.result: Twenty-seven Elixhauser comorbidities were independently associated with ASA physical status; older age (adjusted odds ratio 1.39 per 10 years), male sex (1.24), higher body weight (1.08 per 10 kg) and ASA emergency status (2.11) were also independently associated with higher ASA assignments — all odds ratios. The derived objective-measures model was a better predictor of 30-day mortality than models including either single ASA physical status or comorbidity indices in isolation (P < 0.001).
cards.watchOut: Correlation with comorbidity shows the grade captures real illness burden, not that it is assigned identically by different clinicians; and the head-to-head result cuts the other way for prediction — objective measures beat the single subjective grade for 30-day mortality.
cards.source: Li G et al. Reliability of the ASA Physical Status Classification System in Predicting Surgical Morbidity: a Retrospective Analysis. Journal of medical systems. 2021. PMID: 34296341. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Adult · Comorbidity · Humans · Male · Morbidity · Postoperative Complications · Reproducibility of Results · Retrospective Studies

cards.headline: Reliability limb — survey of 601 Italian anaesthetists scoring 8 fictitious patients: inter-observer agreement was low, and assignment accuracy fell as years of experience rose
cards.summary: Reliability limb — survey of 601 Italian anaesthetists scoring 8 fictitious patients: inter-observer agreement was low, and assignment accuracy fell as years of experience rose
cards.type: National survey-based reliability study (fictitious cases, 601 anaesthetists and residents) — agreement evidence, not a patient cohort
cards.people: 601 correctly completed online surveys from Italian anaesthetists and residents of differing experience, each assigning ASA physical status classes to the same 8 fictitious patients; respondents were subdivided into 5 experience classes.
cards.result: The highest mean number of correct answers was obtained by residents, and it decreased progressively with increasing work experience; the lowest value was recorded in the most experienced group (≥20 years of experience). The authors conclude that low inter-reliability and experience-dependence of ASA physical status must be taken into account when evaluating a patient, particularly where wide differences in experience are present.
cards.watchOut: This is a fictitious-case survey, not a patient cohort: it is carded as agreement / reliability evidence only and is never pooled with the outcome cohorts above; 'correct' here means matching the survey's reference assignments for invented patients.
cards.source: De Cassai A et al. Assignment of ASA-physical status relates to anesthesiologists' experience: a survey-based national-study. Korean journal of anesthesiology. 2019. PMID: 30424587. cards.headline: Synthesis: a single subjective grade discriminates moderately (c-statistics / summary ROC ~0.70–0.74) with a steep stepwise gradient, performs better in lower-death-rate settings, tracks objective comorbidity — and is assigned unreliably, with agreement falling as experience rises
cards.summary: Synthesis: a single subjective grade discriminates moderately (c-statistics / summary ROC ~0.70–0.74) with a steep stepwise gradient, performs better in lower-death-rate settings, tracks objective comorbidity — and is assigned unreliably, with agreement falling as experience rises
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Across the four reports carded: the 77-study meta-analysis gives pooled sensitivity 0.74, specificity 0.67 and summary ROC area 0.736 for postoperative mortality, with accuracy better in lower-death-rate settings; the 2,089,830-case ambulatory cohort shows the same moderate discrimination (mortality c-statistic 0.74) with a stepwise gradient and an odds ratio of 89 for death in ASA IV versus healthy patients on a 0.08% absolute mortality base; the 56,820-case cohort shows the grade tracks 27 of 31 Elixhauser comorbidities but is beaten for mortality prediction by a model built from objective measures; and the 601-respondent fictitious-case survey shows low inter-observer agreement that worsens with experience. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf: no card shows that assigning an ASA class changes any outcome.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Cross-point only: the multi-variable POSSUM / P-POSSUM audit scores are a different instrument, carded separately (shelf #7612 territory in this wave's slate — the POSSUM row S17-4-02), and no PMID is shared.

shelves.title: Preoperative Mini-Cog predicting postoperative delirium: pooled odds ratio 3.79 (relative) but sensitivity only 0.50 — and one cohort's association vanishes on adjustment (GAP-E)
shelves.question: Before elective surgery in older adults, how well does a positive Mini-Cog screen (three-item recall plus clock draw; standard cut-off <3) predict postoperative delirium — what are its pooled sensitivity, specificity and odds ratio on modern meta-analysis, how far does the association survive adjustment for age, frailty and ASA grade in individual cohorts, and how stable is the score itself between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery?

shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a real association with coin-flip sensitivity (GAP-E). The first systematic review and meta-analysis of preoperative Mini-Cog for postoperative delirium (16 studies, 4,980 patients) found low scores associated with delirium at a pooled odds ratio of 3.79 — a relative measure, labelled as such — with pooled sensitivity of only 0.50 and specificity 0.80 (standardised-cut-off subgroup odds ratio 3.40). The tension prints in full: in a 319-patient high-risk colorectal cohort the delirium association (univariate odds ratio 3.04) lost significance after adjustment for age, frailty and ASA grade (0.49), while an association with 90-day mortality remained (4.65); and in an 80-patient prospective cohort the score itself was stable between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery (kappa 0.78), with impairment on either occasion strongly associated with PACU delirium. No carded evidence shows screening prevents delirium.

cards.headline: First systematic review and meta-analysis (Yajima 2025): 16 studies, 4,980 patients — low preoperative Mini-Cog scores were associated with postoperative delirium at a pooled odds ratio of 3.79 (a relative measure), with pooled sensitivity of only 0.50 and specificity 0.80; the standardised-cut-off subgroup gave an odds ratio of 3.40
cards.summary: First systematic review and meta-analysis (Yajima 2025): 16 studies, 4,980 patients — low preoperative Mini-Cog scores were associated with postoperative delirium at a pooled odds ratio of 3.79 (a relative measure), with pooled sensitivity of only 0.50 and specificity 0.80; the standardised-cut-off subgroup gave an odds ratio of 3.40
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (preoperative Mini-Cog for postoperative delirium) — the pooled-accuracy card
cards.people: 16 studies involving 4,980 surgical patients (mean / median ages 70 to 80 years; the proportion scoring below the Mini-Cog cut-off ranged from 12.5% to 60.5%), systematically reviewed to May 2024 with quality assessed by QUADAS-2; random-effects pooling of odds ratios, sensitivity and specificity. Mini-Cog: three-item recall plus clock draw; standard cut-off <3.
cards.result: Low Mini-Cog scores were significantly associated with increased postoperative-delirium risk (odds ratio 3.79, 95% CI 2.81 to 5.12; I² = 57%) — an odds ratio, a relative measure, printed as such. The Mini-Cog showed a pooled specificity of 0.80 and a pooled sensitivity of 0.50 for predicting delirium. A sensitivity analysis restricted to studies using the standardised cut-off (<3) and validated delirium-assessment tools gave an odds ratio of 3.40 (95% CI 2.56 to 4.53). Half of the included studies showed a low risk of bias across all QUADAS-2 domains, and funnel-plot and Egger's-test assessment showed no significant publication bias. The authors concluded the Mini-Cog has moderate predictive ability — high specificity but limited sensitivity — and should not be used as the sole predictor.
cards.watchOut: The tension is the content: an odds ratio near 4 (relative) coexists with sensitivity 0.50 — the screen misses half of the patients who go on to become delirious. Heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 57%) and cut-offs and delirium-assessment methods varied across the pooled studies.
cards.source: Yajima S et al. Predictive ability of Mini-Cog for postoperative delirium: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Geriatrics & gerontology international. 2025. PMID: 40343388. cards.headline: Colorectal cohort (Fiamanya 2022): in 319 high-risk elective patients, Mini-Cog impairment predicted delirium univariately (odds ratio 3.04) but lost significance after adjustment (odds ratio 0.49), while remaining associated with 90-day mortality (odds ratio 4.65) — all odds ratios, relative measures
cards.summary: Colorectal cohort (Fiamanya 2022): in 319 high-risk elective patients, Mini-Cog impairment predicted delirium univariately (odds ratio 3.04) but lost significance after adjustment (odds ratio 0.49), while remaining associated with 90-day mortality (odds ratio 4.65) — all odds ratios, relative measures
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (preoperative Mini-Cog and postoperative delirium, elective colorectal surgery) — the adjustment-tension card
cards.people: 319 elective colorectal surgery patients at high risk of mortality by age or comorbidity, screened at a preoperative clinic at The York Hospital (data gathered prospectively, October 2015 to December 2017; analysed retrospectively); 52 patients (16%) were cognitively impaired on the Mini-Cog. Outcomes: postoperative delirium, 90-day mortality, length of stay.
cards.result: Patients with cognitive impairment were more likely to develop postoperative delirium in univariate analysis (odds ratio 3.04, 95% CI 1.15 to 8.03); however, cognitive impairment lost significance when controlled for confounding factors in the multivariable model (odds ratio 0.492, 95% CI 0.177 to 1.368). Cognitive impairment remained significantly associated with 90-day mortality in univariate analysis (odds ratio 4.65, 95% CI 1.36 to 15.9), as did frailty (odds ratio 7.28), ASA grade (odds ratio 5.95) and age. The authors concluded the Mini-Cog is not independently associated with postoperative delirium in this high-risk colorectal cohort, while showing promise as a possible predictor of 90-day mortality.
cards.watchOut: A single-centre, single-specialty cohort of 319 patients: its adjusted null does not overturn the pooled estimate, but it shows the association is not robust to adjustment for age, frailty and ASA grade in at least one well-conducted cohort — both findings print on this shelf.
cards.source: Fiamanya S et al. The association between preoperative Mini-Cog© score and postoperative delirium (POD): a retrospective cohort study. Perioperative medicine (London, England). 2022. PMID: 35443735. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Test-stability cohort (Tiwary 2021): Mini-Cog scores agreed well between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery (weighted kappa 0.78, about 8 days apart) in 80 older patients, and impairment on either occasion was strongly associated with post-anaesthesia-care-unit delirium (odds ratios 12.8 and 29.0, relative, with wide intervals)
cards.summary: Test-stability cohort (Tiwary 2021): Mini-Cog scores agreed well between the preoperative clinic and the day of surgery (weighted kappa 0.78, about 8 days apart) in 80 older patients, and impairment on either occasion was strongly associated with post-anaesthesia-care-unit delirium (odds ratios 12.8 and 29.0, relative, with wide intervals)
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (Mini-Cog agreement between clinic and day of surgery; association with PACU delirium) — measurement-stability evidence, never pooled with the outcome cohorts
cards.people: 80 patients aged 65 to 89 years having elective inpatient surgery under general anaesthesia (of 128 meeting eligibility criteria), each given the Mini-Cog in the preoperative clinic and again on the day of surgery (mean interval 8.4 days, SD 6.9); delirium assessed in the post-anaesthesia care unit (PACU) with the Short Confusion Assessment Method. Ten patients were impaired on the clinic-day test.
cards.result: Clinic-day and surgery-day Mini-Cog scores had high agreement (ordinally weighted kappa 0.78, 95% CI 0.69 to 0.87). Patients with surgery-day scores compatible with cognitive impairment (≤2) had an estimated 12.8 times higher odds of PACU delirium than patients with normal scores (odds ratio 12.8, 95% CI 2.6 to 63.8); clinic-day impairment gave an odds ratio of 29.0, as published. Both scores were described as highly predictive of PACU delirium, and the authors supported using the Mini-Cog on the day of surgery to screen older patients.
cards.watchOut: Only 80 patients and 10 impaired at baseline: the odds ratios are large but their intervals are very wide, and the outcome is PACU (emergence) delirium, not ward postoperative delirium. This card is carded for score stability (kappa 0.78), as commissioned — not as a third accuracy estimate.

cards.headline: Synthesis: a positive preoperative Mini-Cog marks real risk but catches only half of cases — pooled odds ratio 3.79 (relative) with sensitivity 0.50 and specificity 0.80 across 16 studies and 4,980 patients; one high-risk colorectal cohort's delirium association disappeared on adjustment (odds ratio 0.49) while a mortality association remained (4.65); and the score itself is stable between clinic and the day of surgery (kappa 0.78)
cards.summary: Synthesis: a positive preoperative Mini-Cog marks real risk but catches only half of cases — pooled odds ratio 3.79 (relative) with sensitivity 0.50 and specificity 0.80 across 16 studies and 4,980 patients; one high-risk colorectal cohort's delirium association disappeared on adjustment (odds ratio 0.49) while a mortality association remained (4.65); and the score itself is stable between clinic and the day of surgery (kappa 0.78)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: one systematic review and meta-analysis (16 studies, 4,980 patients), one retrospective cohort (319 patients), and one prospective stability cohort (80 patients).
cards.result: Pooled: odds ratio 3.79 (95% CI 2.81 to 5.12 — a relative measure) for postoperative delirium with low Mini-Cog scores; 3.40 in the standardised-cut-off subgroup; pooled sensitivity 0.50, specificity 0.80. Adjusted tension: univariate odds ratio 3.04 falling to 0.49 (non-significant) after adjustment in the colorectal cohort, against a persisting 90-day-mortality association (odds ratio 4.65). Stability: clinic versus day-of-surgery agreement kappa 0.78. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: no carded evidence shows that screening, or any pathway a positive screen triggers, prevents delirium, and no card may imply it. Distinct from the frailty-instrument shelves (a different construct) and from the CAM-ICU / 4AT delirium-detection shelves (detection after delirium is suspected, not preoperative prediction) — cross-points only, no shared reports.
cards.watchOut: Sensitivity 0.50 is the operative limit: a normal Mini-Cog does not clear an older surgical patient of delirium risk.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Scorpion antivenom + prazosin for Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation: resolution within 10 hours in 91–92% vs 23–40% on prazosin alone (4 randomised reports, N = 301; Egyptian mirror trial's mortality difference non-significant)
shelves.question: In children and adults with grade 2–severe Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation and autonomic storm, does adding scorpion antivenom to prazosin — or, in the mirror comparison, adding prazosin to antivenom — versus either agent alone speed resolution of the autonomic syndrome and prevent deterioration? (4 randomised reports, N = 301; comparison and species limbs labelled.)
shelves.mesh: Administration, Oral · Adolescent · Adrenergic alpha-1 Receptor Antagonists · Adult · Animals · Antivenins · Child · Child, Preschool · Drug Combinations · Female · Humans · Immunologic Factors · Infant · Infusions, Intravenous · Male · Prazosin · Scorpion Stings · Scorpion Venoms · Scorpions · Treatment Outcome · Young Adult
shelves.balance: POSSIBLE (benefit), on 4 randomised reports (N = 301 in total) with the comparisons and species limbs labelled and never pooled. Three trials ask whether antivenom added to prazosin helps in Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation: the BMJ trial (70 patients, grade 2) found complete resolution of the clinical syndrome within 10 hours in 91.4% on antivenom plus prazosin versus 22.9% on prazosin alone, with mean recovery 8.0 vs 17.7 hours; the paediatric trial (50 children) found 92% vs 40% clear of autonomic symptoms within 10 hours and deterioration to grade 3–4 in 8% vs 44%; and the three-arm trial (81 patients, severe envenomation) found complete recovery in 4.14 hours on antivenom versus 19.28 hours on prazosin. The fourth trial asks the mirror question — prazosin added to antivenom, in Egypt, where the scorpion species is not M. tamulus (population limb labelled): hospital stay was identical (median 3 days), antivenom consumption was lower on the combination (median 6 vs 9 vials), and mortality was 8% vs 20% — NOT statistically significant, printed as such. All four trials are open-label; three are single-centre Indian studies from one research tradition. Endpoints are time to resolution of a clinical syndrome score — no trial is powered for mortality. Product naming (clarification exception): the tested antivenom is the Indian polyvalent scorpion antivenom as the publications describe it; antivenoms are species- and maker-specific, and these results do not transfer to other regions' antivenoms (the North American Centruroides product homed at live #1257 included). The 2007 Mahad comparison is non-randomised and is never counted here.

cards.headline: BMJ RCT (Bawaskar 2011): antivenom plus prazosin resolved the clinical syndrome within 10 hours in 91.4% versus 22.9% on prazosin alone; mean recovery 8.0 vs 17.7 hours
cards.summary: BMJ RCT (Bawaskar 2011): antivenom plus prazosin resolved the clinical syndrome within 10 hours in 91.4% versus 22.9% on prazosin alone; mean recovery 8.0 vs 17.7 hours
cards.type: Randomised open-label clinical trial, scorpion antivenom + prazosin vs prazosin alone, grade 2 envenomation
cards.people: 70 patients older than 6 months with grade 2 Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation and autonomic storm, without cardiorespiratory or central-nervous-system abnormalities, at a general hospital in Mahad, Maharashtra, India, randomised open-label (35 scorpion antivenom plus prazosin, 35 prazosin alone); analysis was by intention to treat.
cards.result: Complete resolution of the clinical syndrome (sweating, salivation, cool extremities, priapism, hypertension or hypotension, tachycardia) within 10 hours occurred in 32 of 35 patients (91.4%, 95% CI 76.9 to 97.8) on the combination versus 8 of 35 (22.9%, 11.8 to 39.3) on prazosin alone. Mean recovery time was 8.0 hours (95% CI 6.5 to 9.5) versus 17.7 hours (15.4 to 19.9) — a mean difference of −9.7 hours. Fewer prazosin doses were required on the combination (mean 2 vs 4). Deterioration to a higher grade was similar (4 of 35 vs 5 of 35), and hypotension was reported in 12 of 35 (34.3%) versus 19 of 35 (54.3%), a non-significant difference.
cards.watchOut: Open-label and single-centre, with a syndrome-resolution endpoint assessed by unmasked clinicians; grade 2 patients without cardiorespiratory or CNS involvement — the result does not speak to the most severe presentations or to mortality.
cards.source: Bawaskar HS et al. Efficacy and safety of scorpion antivenom plus prazosin compared with prazosin alone for venomous scorpion (Mesobuthus tamulus) sting: randomised open label clinical trial. BMJ (Clinical research ed.). 2011. PMID: 21209062. Registry ID: CTRI/2010/091/000584. cards.headline: Paediatric RCT (Pandi 2014): 50 children — 92% on antivenom plus prazosin were clear of autonomic symptoms within 10 hours versus 40% on prazosin alone; deterioration to grade 3–4 in 8% vs 44%
cards.summary: Paediatric RCT (Pandi 2014): 50 children — 92% on antivenom plus prazosin were clear of autonomic symptoms within 10 hours versus 40% on prazosin alone; deterioration to grade 3–4 in 8% vs 44%
cards.type: Randomised controlled trial in children, scorpion antivenom + prazosin vs prazosin alone
cards.people: 50 children with definite history and/or systemic manifestations of Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation at a tertiary care hospital in south India (February 2012 to July 2013), randomised (25 to intravenous scorpion antivenom as a slow bolus combined with prazosin, 25 to prazosin alone).
cards.result: Children on the combination recovered earlier by a mean of 9.1 hours (95% CI 6.0 to 12.2); 23 of 25 (92%) were clear of autonomic symptoms within 10 hours versus 10 of 25 (40%) on prazosin alone (difference 52 percentage points, 95% CI 29 to 75). Deterioration to clinical grade 3 or 4 occurred in 8% versus 44% (P < 0.01). Mean prazosin dose required was 54 µg/kg versus 130.8 µg/kg (P < 0.01). The antivenom was not associated with severe adverse reactions, and the authors report that its use reduced the incidence of myocardial dysfunction.
cards.watchOut: A 50-child, single-centre trial; the abstract does not describe masking, and the endpoints are symptom resolution and grade deterioration, not mortality or long-term cardiac outcomes.
cards.source: Pandi K et al. Efficacy of scorpion antivenom plus prazosin versus prazosin alone for Mesobuthus tamulus scorpion sting envenomation in children: a randomised controlled trial. cards.headline: Three-arm trial (Natu 2010): 81 patients with severe envenomation assigned to antivenom (n = 28), prazosin (n = 25) or both (n = 28) — complete clinical recovery in 4.14 hours on antivenom versus 19.28 hours on prazosin (P < 0.001)
cards.summary: Three-arm trial (Natu 2010): 81 patients with severe envenomation assigned to antivenom (n = 28), prazosin (n = 25) or both (n = 28) — complete clinical recovery in 4.14 hours on antivenom versus 19.28 hours on prazosin (P < 0.001)
cards.type: Prospective open-label three-arm randomised comparison, antivenom vs prazosin vs both, severe envenomation
cards.people: 81 patients from rural districts of Maharashtra, India, presenting with severe scorpion envenomation, assigned prospectively in an open-label trial to anti-scorpion venom serum (AScVS, intravenous slow bolus 40–100 mL by severity; n = 28), prazosin 1 mg every 3 hours (n = 25), or both (n = 28); severity was graded with a composite clinical scoring system and admission scores were comparable across groups.
cards.result: Complete clinical recovery was noted in 4.14 (SD 1.6) hours in patients given AScVS versus 19.28 (SD 5.03) hours in those given prazosin (P < 0.001). There was no incidence of anaphylactic reaction to AScVS. The fetched abstract reports the antivenom-versus-prazosin recovery contrast; it does not print a separate recovery time for the combined-therapy arm, and none is claimed here.
cards.watchOut: Open-label, single-region, and reported through a locally proposed composite score; the combination arm's own recovery time is not printed in the fetched abstract, so this card supports the antivenom-versus-prazosin limb only.

cards.headline: Egyptian mirror-comparison RCT (Shokry Zaghary 2025): prazosin added to antivenom — hospital stay identical (median 3 days), fewer antivenom vials (median 6 vs 9), and mortality 8% vs 20% NOT statistically significant, printed as such (species limb: not M. tamulus)
cards.summary: Egyptian mirror-comparison RCT (Shokry Zaghary 2025): prazosin added to antivenom — hospital stay identical (median 3 days), fewer antivenom vials (median 6 vs 9), and mortality 8% vs 20% NOT statistically significant, printed as such (species limb: not M. tamulus)
cards.type: Prospective randomised comparative study (mirror comparison), antivenom + prazosin vs antivenom alone, Egypt — species/population limb labelled
cards.people: 100 patients with scorpion stings at Sohag University Hospitals, Egypt (February 2023 to July 2024), randomised prospectively (50 antivenom plus prazosin, 50 antivenom alone); median age 7 years, 54% male, most from rural areas. The scorpion species in this Egyptian population is not Mesobuthus tamulus — a separate population limb from the Indian trials above.
cards.result: Duration of hospital stay did not differ (median 3 days in each group). Antivenom consumption was significantly lower on the combination (median 6 vials vs 9 vials). Overall mortality was 14%: 4 of 50 (8%) on the combination versus 10 of 50 (20%) on antivenom alone — observed more often in the antivenom-alone group but NOT statistically significant, as the authors state. Complications likewise occurred more often on antivenom alone without significant p values.
cards.watchOut: This trial asks the reverse question (prazosin added to antivenom) in a different country and scorpion fauna; its mortality difference (8% vs 20%) is non-significant in 100 patients and must never be quoted without that label.
cards.source: Shokry Zaghary MM et al. A comparative study of using scorpion antivenom versus scorpion antivenom and prazosin drug for scorpion stings management in Sohag University Hospitals. cards.headline: Synthesis: 4 randomised reports, N = 301 — adding antivenom to prazosin consistently and greatly sped syndrome resolution in Indian M. tamulus trials; the mirror Egyptian trial found fewer antivenom vials, identical stay, and a non-significant mortality difference
cards.summary: Synthesis: 4 randomised reports, N = 301 — adding antivenom to prazosin consistently and greatly sped syndrome resolution in Indian M. tamulus trials; the mirror Egyptian trial found fewer antivenom vials, identical stay, and a non-significant mortality difference
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: The three Indian comparisons (n = 70, 50 and 81) agree that antivenom-containing treatment resolves the autonomic syndrome many hours faster than prazosin alone (within-10-hour resolution 91.4% vs 22.9% and 92% vs 40% in the two head-to-head combination trials; recovery 4.14 vs 19.28 hours for antivenom vs prazosin in the three-arm trial), with fewer prazosin doses and, in children, less deterioration to grade 3–4 (8% vs 44%). The Egyptian mirror trial (n = 100) found no difference in hospital stay, lower antivenom consumption with added prazosin, and mortality of 8% vs 20% that was not statistically significant. No trial is powered for mortality, all are open-label, and the tested antivenoms are species- and maker-specific products whose results do not transfer to other regions. The 2007 Mahad comparison is explicitly non-randomised (antivenom given at primary health centres before referral versus prazosin on direct presentation) and is a cross-point only — it is not counted among this shelf's 4 randomised reports. North American Centruroides antivenom versus placebo is a different species, syndrome and question, homed at live #1257.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Varespladib adjunctively for snakebite envenoming (FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 RCTs): BRAVO primary null with point estimate favouring placebo; 2026 post-antivenom trial missed both limb primaries
shelves.question: In patients with snakebite envenoming receiving standard care including antivenom, does varespladib (oral methyl prodrug, or intravenous-then-oral) versus placebo improve early severity scores and functional recovery? FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 randomised trials, both primary-null.
shelves.mesh: Humans · Snake Bites · Male · Female · Double-Blind Method · Adult · Keto Acids · India · Middle Aged · United States · Benzoates · Administration, Oral · Young Adult · Antivenins · Adolescent · Treatment Outcome · Animals · Acetates · Indoles
shelves.balance: MAYBE (weak evidence) (no difference) — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 phase 2 randomised trials, both primary-null, printed on the face. BRAVO (95 randomised in India and the USA) gave oral varespladib methyl twice daily for 1 week added to standard care including antivenom: Snakebite Severity Score improvement to the 6–9-hour average was 1.1 on varespladib versus 1.5 on placebo (difference −0.4, 95% CI −0.8 to 0.1, P = 0.13) — the point estimate favours placebo, printed as reported. Its prespecified subgroup treated within 5 hours of the bite (n = 37) showed clinically important differences, but that is a subgroup reading of a null trial, labelled hypothesis-generating only wherever it appears here, and the later trial does not test it. The 2026 adjunctive trial (140 randomised, 139 analysed) gave intravenous-then-oral varespladib started a mean 7.3 hours after the bite and 3.3 hours after antivenom: the elapid primary (time to recovery of 5-second head-lift) was 27.6 vs 36.2 hours (P = 0.6) and the viper primary (severity-score AUC to day 14) was 660 vs 629 (P = 0.7) — both primaries unmet, the limbs labelled and never pooled. Nothing in either trial supports varespladib instead of, or before, antivenom. The BRAVO protocol paper is carded labelled as a protocol — it is not a results report and is never counted.

cards.headline: BRAVO phase 2 RCT (Gerardo 2024): the primary endpoint was NOT met — severity-score improvement 1.1 on oral varespladib versus 1.5 on placebo (difference −0.4, 95% CI −0.8 to 0.1, P = 0.13), the point estimate favouring placebo
cards.summary: BRAVO phase 2 RCT (Gerardo 2024): the primary endpoint was NOT met — severity-score improvement 1.1 on oral varespladib versus 1.5 on placebo (difference −0.4, 95% CI −0.8 to 0.1, P = 0.13), the point estimate favouring placebo
cards.type: Phase 2 double-blind randomised placebo-controlled trial (BRAVO), oral varespladib methyl + standard care vs placebo + standard care
cards.people: 95 patients with snakebite envenoming randomised (1:1) in emergency departments in India and the USA (August 2021 to November 2022) to oral varespladib methyl or placebo twice daily for 1 week, all receiving standard care including antivenom; the most common bites were Russell's viper (n = 29), copperhead (n = 18) and rattlesnake (n = 14).
cards.result: The primary outcome — change in composite Snakebite Severity Score from baseline to the average at 6 and 9 hours — improved by 1.1 (95% CI 0.7 to 1.6) on varespladib versus 1.5 (95% CI 1.0 to 2.0) on placebo (difference −0.4, 95% CI −0.8 to 0.1, P = 0.13). Key secondary outcomes were not significantly different between groups. In a prespecified subgroup initiating study drug within 5 hours of the bite (n = 37), clinically important differences were observed for illness severity over the first week, patient-reported function on days 3 and 7, and complete recovery — a subgroup reading of a null trial, hypothesis-generating only. No death or treatment-emergent serious adverse event occurred.
cards.watchOut: A null phase 2 trial whose point estimate favours placebo on its primary outcome; the within-5-hours subgroup (n = 37) is prespecified but remains a subgroup of a null trial and is never printed on this shelf as a finding.
cards.source: Gerardo CJ et al. Oral varespladib for the treatment of snakebite envenoming in India and the USA (BRAVO): a phase II randomised clinical trial. BMJ global health. 2024. PMID: 39442939. cards.headline: Adjunctive phase 2 RCT (Gerardo 2026): BOTH limb primaries unmet — elapid head-lift recovery 27.6 vs 36.2 hours (P = 0.6); viper severity-score AUC 660 vs 629 (P = 0.7); treatment began a mean 7.3 hours after the bite and 3.3 hours after antivenom
cards.summary: Adjunctive phase 2 RCT (Gerardo 2026): BOTH limb primaries unmet — elapid head-lift recovery 27.6 vs 36.2 hours (P = 0.6); viper severity-score AUC 660 vs 629 (P = 0.7); treatment began a mean 7.3 hours after the bite and 3.3 hours after antivenom
cards.type: Phase 2 multicentre randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial, IV-then-oral varespladib vs placebo, adjunctive to antivenom (elapid and viper limbs labelled)
cards.people: 140 patients with snakebite envenoming randomised (1:1) in India and the USA (June 2023 to October 2024), 139 analysed (73 varespladib, 66 placebo), to intravenous followed by oral varespladib or placebo, both in addition to standard care including antivenom; the elapid and viper limbs carried separate primary endpoints, labelled here and never pooled.
cards.result: Among elapid-bite patients, mean time to recovery of a 5-second head-lift was 27.6 hours on varespladib versus 36.2 hours on placebo (P = 0.6). Among viper-bite patients, the 3-item Snakebite Severity Score area under the curve to day 14 was 660 on varespladib versus 629 on placebo (P = 0.7). Neither primary endpoint was met. No serious adverse event occurred with varespladib. The authors note that interpretation is limited by heterogeneity in snake species, venom composition, clinical manifestations and antivenom treatments.
cards.watchOut: Late dosing is the design, not an excuse printed after the fact: drug started on average 7.3 hours after the bite and 3.3 hours after antivenom, so this trial tests late adjunctive use only — and it does not test BRAVO's within-5-hours subgroup hypothesis.

cards.headline: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 trials, both primary-null: the near-universal-venom-component rationale for varespladib has now failed its primary endpoint twice, with early oral dosing (BRAVO) and with post-antivenom IV-then-oral dosing (2026)
cards.summary: Synthesis: FLOOR-RISK — exactly 2 phase 2 trials, both primary-null: the near-universal-venom-component rationale for varespladib has now failed its primary endpoint twice, with early oral dosing (BRAVO) and with post-antivenom IV-then-oral dosing (2026)
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: BRAVO (95 randomised): severity-score improvement 1.1 vs 1.5 favouring placebo numerically (difference −0.4, P = 0.13), with a hypothesis-generating prespecified subgroup signal in patients treated within 5 hours (n = 37). The 2026 trial (140 randomised): elapid primary P = 0.6 and viper primary P = 0.7, with treatment begun hours after antivenom. No deaths or varespladib serious adverse events occurred in either trial. Species and setting limbs differ between and within the trials (Russell's viper, copperhead and rattlesnake predominated in BRAVO; the 2026 trial split elapid and viper primaries) and are never pooled. Both trials gave varespladib in addition to standard care including antivenom; nothing in either supports its use before or instead of antivenom.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each trial's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Bedside airway tests predict difficult intubation specifically but not sensitively: upper lip bite class 3 likelihood ratio 14, pooled sensitivities only 0.38–0.52
shelves.question: Before tracheal intubation in adults without obvious airway abnormality, how accurately do the bedside airway examination tests — the modified Mallampati classification, the upper lip bite test, thyromental and hyomental distance, retrognathia and multivariate scores such as Wilson and LEMON — predict difficult laryngoscopy, difficult intubation and difficult mask ventilation, and how far apart are the tests' sensitivities (all of them low) from their specificities (all of them high)?
shelves.mesh: Airway Obstruction/diagnosis · Humans · Intubation, Intratracheal/adverse effects · Jaw/anatomy & histology · Likelihood Functions · Mouth/anatomy & histology · Pharynx/anatomy & histology · Risk Factors · Sensitivity and Specificity · Anesthesia, General · Diagnostic Techniques, Respiratory System · Laryngeal Masks · Laryngoscopy · ROC Curve · Reproducibility of Results · Adult · Airway Management/statistics & numerical data · Intubation, Intratracheal/statistics & numerical data · Laryngoscopy/statistics & numerical data · Physical Examination/methods · Point-of-Care Systems/statistics & numerical data · Treatment Failure · Intubation, Intratracheal/methods · Preoperative Care/methods · Airway Management/methods · Clinical Decision-Making/methods
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — rule-in strong, rule-out weak, and that asymmetry is the whole content. Across four syntheses the bedside tests are consistently specific (0.83–0.98) and consistently insensitive (sensitivities 0.38–0.52 in the 2024 meta-analysis; Cochrane summary sensitivities as low as 0.17–0.24 for some test/outcome pairs): a positive upper lip bite test (class 3) is the strongest single finding (positive likelihood ratio 14, raising difficult-intubation probability from 10% to over 60% in the JAMA review), but no negative bedside test reliably excludes a difficult airway. The four difficulty descriptors — mask ventilation, laryngoscopy, intubation, failed intubation — are different reference standards and are never pooled here. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: nothing carded shows that testing, or any preparation a positive test triggers, improves outcomes. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — high specificity, low sensitivity (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Rational Clinical Examination review (Detsky 2019): upper lip bite class 3 is the best single finding (positive likelihood ratio 14, specificity 0.96) — but no finding reliably excludes difficult intubation
cards.summary: Rational Clinical Examination review (Detsky 2019): upper lip bite class 3 is the best single finding (positive likelihood ratio 14, specificity 0.96) — but no finding reliably excludes difficult intubation
cards.type: Systematic review (Rational Clinical Examination), bivariate random-effects meta-analysis of bedside findings vs difficult intubation
cards.people: 62 high-quality (level 1–3) studies involving 33,559 patients, in which 10% (95% CI 8.2% to 12%) were difficult to intubate; MEDLINE and EMBASE searched 1946/1947 to June 2018.
cards.result: The findings that best predicted difficult intubation were: upper lip bite test class 3 (lower incisors cannot reach the upper lip) — positive likelihood ratio 14 (95% CI 8.9 to 22), specificity 0.96 (95% CI 0.93 to 0.97); shorter hyomental distance (<3–5.5 cm) — positive likelihood ratio 6.4 (95% CI 4.1 to 10), specificity 0.97; retrognathia — positive likelihood ratio 6.0 (95% CI 3.1 to 11), specificity 0.98; and the Wilson score combination — positive likelihood ratio 9.1 (95% CI 5.1 to 16), specificity 0.95. The widely used modified Mallampati score (≥3) had a positive likelihood ratio of only 4.1 (95% CI 3.0 to 5.6; specificity 0.87). An abnormal upper lip bite test raises the probability of difficult intubation from 10% to greater than 60% for the average-risk patient; the authors conclude no clinical finding reliably excludes a difficult intubation. Likelihood ratios are labelled as such, as published.
cards.watchOut: The reference standard here is difficult intubation only, and the 10% base rate drives the post-test probabilities quoted; likelihood ratios from other cards use different reference standards (laryngoscopy, mask ventilation) and must not be interchanged with these.
cards.source: Detsky ME et al. Will This Patient Be Difficult to Intubate?: The Rational Clinical Examination Systematic Review. JAMA. 2019. PMID: 30721300. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Mallampati meta-analysis (Lee 2006): modified test fair for difficult intubation (sROC area 0.83), original test poor (0.58), both poor for difficult mask ventilation — 'not useful screening tests' used alone
cards.summary: Mallampati meta-analysis (Lee 2006): modified test fair for difficult intubation (sROC area 0.83), original test poor (0.58), both poor for difficult mask ventilation — 'not useful screening tests' used alone
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of the original and modified Mallampati tests
cards.people: 42 prospective studies enrolling 34,513 patients undergoing general anaesthesia, in which a preoperative Mallampati test was compared with difficult laryngoscopy, difficult intubation or difficult ventilation as reference tests; definitions of the reference tests varied widely.
cards.result: For predicting difficult laryngoscopy, the two Mallampati versions had areas under the summary ROC curve of 0.89 ± 0.05 and 0.78 ± 0.05 as published. For predicting difficult intubation, the modified Mallampati test had good accuracy (sROC area 0.83 ± 0.03) whereas the original Mallampati test was poor (0.58 ± 0.12). The Mallampati tests were poor at identifying difficult mask ventilation. Publication bias was not detected. The authors conclude that used alone the Mallampati tests have limited accuracy for predicting the difficult airway and are not useful screening tests.
cards.watchOut: The oldest synthesis carded (2006) and confined to one test family; its sROC areas are not sensitivities and must not be read as the proportion of difficult airways detected — the Cochrane and 2024 cards give the per-test sensitivities, which are low.
cards.source: Lee A et al. A systematic review (meta-analysis) of the accuracy of the Mallampati tests to predict the difficult airway. Anesthesia and analgesia. 2006. PMID: 16717341. cards.headline: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review (Roth 2018): every bedside test characterised separately for each of four reference standards — sensitivities 0.17–0.67 against specificities 0.80–0.95
cards.summary: Cochrane diagnostic-accuracy review (Roth 2018): every bedside test characterised separately for each of four reference standards — sensitivities 0.17–0.67 against specificities 0.80–0.95
cards.type: Cochrane diagnostic test accuracy systematic review, per-test and per-reference-standard
cards.people: 133 studies (127 cohort-type, 6 case-control) involving 844,206 participants — adults with no apparent anatomical airway abnormalities having standard laryngoscopy and intubation. Seven prespecified index tests were evaluated (modified Mallampati in 105 studies, thyromental distance 52, mouth opening 34, upper lip bite 30, sternomental distance 18, Mallampati 6, Wilson risk score 6); difficult laryngoscopy was the reference standard in 92 studies, difficult tracheal intubation in 50, difficult face mask ventilation in 7 and failed intubation in 2.
cards.result: For difficult laryngoscopy, summary sensitivity ranged from 0.22 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.33; mouth opening test) to 0.67 (95% CI 0.45 to 0.83; upper lip bite test), and summary specificity from 0.80 (modified Mallampati) to 0.95 (Wilson risk score); the upper lip bite test had the highest sensitivity for difficult laryngoscopy (P < 0.001). For difficult tracheal intubation, summary sensitivity ranged from 0.24 (thyromental distance) to 0.51 (modified Mallampati test, the highest, P < 0.001) and specificity from 0.87 to 0.93. For difficult face mask ventilation only the modified Mallampati test could be summarised: sensitivity 0.17 (95% CI 0.06 to 0.39), specificity 0.90. The authors conclude that all investigated tests had relatively low sensitivities with high variability while specificities were consistently and markedly higher, so standard bedside tests should be interpreted with caution and do not appear to be good screening tests.
cards.watchOut: Failed intubation rested on only 2 studies and difficult face mask ventilation on 7, so those limbs are thin; the review's search was updated in March 2018 but those results were not incorporated, and 27 studies awaited classification.
cards.source: Roth D et al. Airway physical examination tests for detection of difficult airway management in apparently normal adult patients. The Cochrane database of systematic reviews. 2018. PMID: 29761867. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Largest meta-analysis (Wang 2024): modified Mallampati sensitivity 0.39 / specificity 0.86, thyromental distance 0.38 / 0.83, upper lip bite 0.52 / 0.84 — ultrasound distance-to-epiglottis higher at 0.80 / 0.77
cards.summary: Largest meta-analysis (Wang 2024): modified Mallampati sensitivity 0.39 / specificity 0.86, thyromental distance 0.38 / 0.83, upper lip bite 0.52 / 0.84 — ultrasound distance-to-epiglottis higher at 0.80 / 0.77
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 difficult-intubation prediction methods
cards.people: 227 articles representing 526 studies, encompassing 686,089 adult patients without obvious airway abnormalities undergoing all types of surgery; 11 prediction methods across physical examination, multivariate scoring systems and imaging tests; bias assessed with QUADAS-2.
cards.result: Pooled performance for predicting difficult tracheal intubation: modified Mallampati test sensitivity 0.39 and specificity 0.86; thyromental distance sensitivity 0.38 and specificity 0.83; upper lip bite test sensitivity 0.52 and specificity 0.84. Multivariate systems such as LEMON and the Wilson risk score showed moderate sensitivity and specificity. Ultrasound distance from skin to epiglottis showed higher sensitivity (0.80) and specificity (0.77) than the bedside tests. Significant heterogeneity across studies was influenced by sample size and study design. The authors conclude no single preoperative method shows clear superiority and support a combined, multi-modal approach with standardised procedures and clear cut-off values.
cards.watchOut: The ultrasound figure comes from a different (imaging) method family with its own operator dependence; it does not rehabilitate the bedside tests, whose pooled sensitivities here (0.38–0.52) mean roughly half to two-thirds of difficult intubations are missed by any one of them.

cards.headline: Synthesis: bedside airway tests are specific but insensitive in every synthesis — a positive test (especially upper lip bite class 3) usefully raises risk, a negative test barely lowers it, and no test is a rule-out
cards.summary: Synthesis: bedside airway tests are specific but insensitive in every synthesis — a positive test (especially upper lip bite class 3) usefully raises risk, a negative test barely lowers it, and no test is a rule-out
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Four syntheses agree on the asymmetry. The JAMA Rational Clinical Examination review (62 studies, 33,559 patients, 10% difficult to intubate) found the strongest rule-in findings were upper lip bite class 3 (positive likelihood ratio 14, specificity 0.96), short hyomental distance (likelihood ratio 6.4, specificity 0.97), retrognathia (6.0, 0.98) and the Wilson score (9.1, 0.95), with modified Mallampati ≥3 at only 4.1. The Cochrane review, keeping the four reference standards separate, found sensitivities of 0.17–0.67 against specificities of 0.80–0.95. The 2024 meta-analysis (686,089 patients) pooled bedside-test sensitivities at 0.38–0.52. The Mallampati-only meta-analysis reached the same verdict in 2006: limited accuracy used alone, not a useful screening test. shelves.title: Preoperative IVC collapsibility predicts post-induction hypotension moderately: pooled sensitivity 0.68 / specificity 0.78, best at a 40–45% threshold, on a definitionally heterogeneous literature
shelves.question: Before elective surgery under general anaesthesia, how accurately do preoperative inferior-vena-cava ultrasound measures — the collapsibility index and the maximum IVC diameter — predict hypotension after induction, what pooled sensitivity and specificity do they deliver, at what collapsibility thresholds does performance peak, and how much of the literature's spread is definitional (differing hypotension definitions, measurement methods and cut-offs) rather than biological?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Hypotension/etiology · Vena Cava, Inferior/diagnostic imaging · Anesthesia, General/methods · Observational Studies as Topic · Ultrasonography/methods · Predictive Value of Tests · Adult · Anesthesia, General/adverse effects · Anesthesiology · Hypotension/diagnostic imaging,etiology · Hypotension, Controlled · Aged · Aged, 80 and over · Blood Volume · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Prospective Studies · Sensitivity and Specificity · Ultrasonography
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate for general-anaesthesia induction hypotension, on a definitionally heterogeneous literature. The 2024 meta-analysis of 14 prospective observational studies (1,166 patients) pooled IVC collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 (HSROC-AUC 0.80), with performance peaking at a 40–45% collapsibility threshold (HSROC-AUC 0.86). The 2023 systematic review (21 studies, spinal and general anaesthesia carded as separate slices here) could not pool at all: post-spinal collapsibility-index sensitivity ranged 58.8–84.6% and specificity 23.5–93.1%, and the spread was driven by differing hypotension definitions, measurement methods and cut-offs. The single primary study carded (83 analysable patients, standardised propofol induction) shows the pattern in miniature at a ≥50% threshold: high specificity (90.0%) but sensitivity of only 45.5%. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only: nothing carded shows an IVC-guided fluid or vasopressor strategy prevents post-induction hypotension. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — moderate, threshold- and definition-dependent (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Meta-analysis (Dana 2024): pooled IVC collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 for post-induction hypotension (HSROC-AUC 0.80), peaking at a 40–45% threshold (HSROC-AUC 0.86)
cards.summary: Meta-analysis (Dana 2024): pooled IVC collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 for post-induction hypotension (HSROC-AUC 0.80), peaking at a 40–45% threshold (HSROC-AUC 0.86)
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective observational studies (general anaesthesia only)
cards.people: 14 prospective observational studies involving 1,166 adults presenting for elective surgery under general anaesthesia (obstetric and exclusively-obesity populations excluded); MEDLINE, PubMed and Embase searched to March 2023; quality by Newcastle-Ottawa scores, certainty by GRADE. The review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42022316140).
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity of the IVC collapsibility index (IVC-CI) for predicting postinduction hypotension was 0.68 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.79) and pooled specificity 0.78 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.85), with a hierarchical summary ROC area under the curve of 0.80 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.85; high quality of evidence, as graded by the authors). An IVC-CI threshold range of 40–45% had the highest HSROC-AUC, 0.86 (95% CI 0.69 to 0.93). The authors recommend future studies use an IVC-CI threshold of 40–45% (low certainty of evidence for that recommendation) and note it remains unestablished whether ultrasound-guided preoperative optimisation improves outcomes in high-risk patients.
cards.watchOut: All 14 studies are observational and the pooled pair (0.68 / 0.78) still misses about a third of patients who become hypotensive; the 40–45% 'best threshold' rests on subgroup analysis with wide confidence intervals (HSROC-AUC 95% CI 0.69 to 0.93) and low-certainty grading.
cards.source: Dana E et al. Inferior vena cava ultrasound to predict hypotension after general anesthesia induction: a systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies. Canadian journal of anaesthesia = Journal canadien d'anesthesie. 2024. PMID: 38961000. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42022316140. cards.headline: Systematic review (Chowdhury 2023): pooling precluded by heterogeneity — post-spinal collapsibility-index sensitivity ranged 58.8–84.6% and specificity 23.5–93.1% across studies (spinal slice, carded separately)
cards.summary: Systematic review (Chowdhury 2023): pooling precluded by heterogeneity — post-spinal collapsibility-index sensitivity ranged 58.8–84.6% and specificity 23.5–93.1% across studies (spinal slice, carded separately)
cards.type: Systematic review without meta-analysis (spinal and general anaesthesia slices reported separately)
cards.people: 21 studies (4 randomised trials and 17 observational studies) of preoperative IVC ultrasound predicting hypotension after anaesthesia: 15 in spinal anaesthesia and 6 in general anaesthesia, in adult patients.
cards.result: Heterogeneity in patient populations, definitions of post-anaesthesia hypotension, IVC ultrasound assessment methods and cut-off values precluded pooled meta-analysis. For post-spinal hypotension (the spinal slice, not pooled with general anaesthesia here), the maximum and minimum reported sensitivities of the IVC collapsibility index were 84.6% and 58.8%, and the maximum and minimum specificities 93.1% and 23.5%. For hypotension after general anaesthesia induction, reported sensitivity ranged from 45.5% to 86.67% and specificity from 77.27% to 94.29%. The authors conclude the literature is heterogeneous in both methodology and results and that standardisation of the hypotension definition, the ultrasound method and the diameter / collapsibility cut-offs is necessary before clinically relevant conclusions can be drawn.
cards.watchOut: A specificity range whose low end is 23.5% means some primary studies' cut-offs flagged most patients who never became hypotensive; ranges across non-standardised studies describe the literature's inconsistency, not a confidence interval for any single usable cut-off.

cards.headline: Primary prospective study (Szabó 2019): collapsibility index ≥50% — systolic fall 53.8 vs 35.8 mm Hg, but sensitivity only 45.5% against specificity 90.0% (AUC 64.8%)
cards.summary: Primary prospective study (Szabó 2019): collapsibility index ≥50% — systolic fall 53.8 vs 35.8 mm Hg, but sensitivity only 45.5% against specificity 90.0% (AUC 64.8%)
cards.type: Prospective observational study, standardised propofol induction, single primary cohort
cards.people: 102 patients undergoing elective general surgery under general anaesthesia with standardised propofol induction were recruited; 83 were analysable (20 with a collapsing IVC, collapsibility index ≥50%; 63 non-collapsing), after 19 exclusions including 7 for inadequate IVC visualisation. IVC collapsibility was measured under spontaneous breathing; hypotension was defined as systolic pressure <90 mm Hg or a ≥30% drop from baseline.
cards.result: The mean decrease in systolic pressure after induction was 53.8 ± 15.3 mm Hg in the collapsing group versus 35.8 ± 18.1 mm Hg in the non-collapsing group (P = 0.0001); median relative mean arterial pressure change was 34.1% (IQR 23.2–43.0%) versus 24.2% (IQR 17.2–30.2%) (P = 0.0029) — relative changes, labelled as such. ROC analysis gave an AUC of 64.8% (95% CI 52.1–77.5%). At the 50% collapsibility level, sensitivity was only 45.5% (95% CI 28.1–63.7%) but specificity was 90.0% (95% CI 78.2–96.7%), with positive predictive value 75.0% and negative predictive value 71.4%. The authors conclude a preoperative collapsibility index ≥50% predicts postinduction hypotension with high specificity but low sensitivity.
cards.watchOut: Small and single-centre, with 19 of 102 recruited patients excluded (7 because the IVC could not be visualised at all — a real-world failure mode of the test); at this threshold more than half of the patients who became hypotensive were missed.
cards.source: Szabó M et al. Role of inferior vena cava collapsibility index in the prediction of hypotension associated with general anesthesia: an observational study. BMC anesthesiology. 2019. PMID: 31390983. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.result: The general-anaesthesia meta-analysis (Dana 2024; 14 prospective studies, 1,166 patients) pooled collapsibility-index sensitivity 0.68 and specificity 0.78 with HSROC-AUC 0.80, peaking at a 40–45% threshold (HSROC-AUC 0.86). Whether acting on the measurement prevents hypotension is untested in everything carded here.

shelves.title: Preoperative six-minute walk distance predicts postoperative complications: thresholds 325 m (mixed high-risk) vs 450–454 m (cancer resection), and performable when spirometry is contraindicated
shelves.question: Before elective surgery, how well does the preoperative six-minute walk test distance predict postoperative pulmonary complications and other postoperative complications — what thresholds have been derived in thoracic, oesophageal and mixed high-risk cohorts (325 m, 450 m, 454 m), how do their sensitivities and specificities compare, and how does the test perform in patients who cannot perform spirometry at all?

shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — a consistent direction on a small, mostly retrospective base, with thresholds that are cohort property, not constants. Four non-METS reports: a prospective mixed high-risk cohort (N = 78) derived a ≤325 m threshold with 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity for postoperative pulmonary complications, and showed the test could be completed by the 17.9% of patients who had contraindications to spirometry; an oesophageal-cancer cohort (N = 111) derived ≤454 m (sensitivity 71.0%, specificity 54.8%) for Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications; a lung-resection cohort (N = 321, the largest) derived ≤450 m for pneumonia (69.2% / 71.1%); and a small VATS lobectomy cohort (N = 66) found ≤450 m carried an odds ratio of 5.674 for 30-day pulmonary complications, labelled an odds ratio. Three of four cohorts are retrospective and none exceeds 321 patients, which prints on the face. A fifth report — a secondary analysis of the METS cohort (PMID 33442834) — was verified at mining but is deliberately NOT carded on this shelf, per the commissioning row. This is a prognostic-accuracy shelf only. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — consistent, threshold-variable, small-base (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Prospective mixed high-risk cohort (Keeratichananont 2016): patients developing pulmonary complications walked 256 vs 440 m; ≤325 m gave 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity — and all patients with spirometry contraindications completed the walk test
cards.summary: Prospective mixed high-risk cohort (Keeratichananont 2016): patients developing pulmonary complications walked 256 vs 440 m; ≤325 m gave 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity — and all patients with spirometry contraindications completed the walk test
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (mixed thoracic / non-thoracic high-risk surgery); shared cohort with shelf #7688, stated on both
cards.people: 78 high-risk patients scheduled for elective thoracic or non-thoracic surgery under general anaesthesia at Songklanagarind Hospital, Thailand, all indicated for preoperative pulmonary evaluation; preoperative spirometry and 6-minute walk test performed, 30-day postoperative pulmonary complications (PPC) recorded prospectively. PPC developed in 17 cases (21%).
cards.result: Patients developing PPC had a significantly lower preoperative walk distance than patients without PPC (256.0 ± 48.0 m versus 440.0 ± 117.1 m, P < 0.001). A walk distance of ≤325 m was the threshold for predicting PPC, with 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity, and predictive value similar to FEV1 % predicted. On multiple regression, older age, poor general health status, smoking history, low FEV1 % predicted and shorter walk distance were independent factors associated with PPC. The walk test was completed in all cases without complication: 14 cases (17.9%) had contraindications to spirometry and two more could not achieve acceptable spirometry efforts — the test's distinctive claim is that it remains performable in exactly the patients spirometry cannot assess. This same cohort is carded on shelf #7688 for its spirometry limb, stated there and here.
cards.watchOut: Small (N = 78) single-centre prospective cohort: a 100% specificity from 61 non-events is fragile, and the 325 m threshold is far below the 450–454 m thresholds of the cancer-resection cohorts carded below — thresholds travel with the cohort, not with the test.

cards.headline: Oesophageal-cancer cohort (Inoue 2020): ≤454 m predicted Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications with 71.0% sensitivity and only 54.8% specificity
cards.summary: Oesophageal-cancer cohort (Inoue 2020): ≤454 m predicted Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications with 71.0% sensitivity and only 54.8% specificity
cards.people: 111 patients with oesophageal cancer who underwent thoracic surgery followed by postoperative rehabilitation (January 2013 to December 2015), reviewed retrospectively; 42 patients experienced Clavien–Dindo grade ≥II complications. Walk distance correlated with age, serum albumin, haemoglobin and hand grip strength.
cards.result: The walk distance of patients with grade ≥II complications was significantly shorter than that of patients with grade ≤I complications. On ROC analysis, a walk distance of ≤454 m was the threshold for predicting grade ≥II complications, with 71.0% sensitivity and 54.8% specificity. Grade ≥II complications led to delayed ambulation and longer hospital stays. On multiple regression, lower preoperative walk distance and lower % predicted FEV1 were preoperative risk factors for grade ≥II complications.

cards.headline: Lung-resection cohort (Hattori 2018): pneumonia patients walked 425 vs 500 m; ≤450 m gave 69.2% sensitivity and 71.1% specificity for postoperative pneumonia
cards.summary: Lung-resection cohort (Hattori 2018): pneumonia patients walked 425 vs 500 m; ≤450 m gave 69.2% sensitivity and 71.1% specificity for postoperative pneumonia
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (lung resection for malignancy)
cards.people: 321 patients with malignant lung tumours (283 primary lung cancer, 38 metastatic) who underwent lung resection at Nagoya University Hospital (January 2014 to December 2015), reviewed retrospectively; preoperative pulmonary function tests and 6-minute walk test assessed. Pneumonia developed in 13 patients and caused longer hospital stays.
cards.result: The preoperative walk distance of patients with pneumonia was significantly lower than that of patients without pneumonia (425 vs 500 m, P = 0.002). On ROC analysis, a walk distance of ≤450 m was the threshold for predicting postoperative pneumonia, with 69.2% sensitivity and 71.1% specificity. In a logistic model, walk distance ≤450 m, FEV1 <80% predicted, diffusion capacity <80% predicted, serum albumin <3.5 g/dL and operative blood loss ≥200 g were significantly associated with postoperative pneumonia.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and built on only 13 pneumonia events, so the 450 m threshold and its accuracy pair rest on a small numerator despite the largest cohort on this shelf (N = 321); the outcome is pneumonia alone, not the broader pulmonary-complication composite of the other cards.
cards.source: Hattori K et al. Preoperative six-minute walk distance is associated with pneumonia after lung resection. Interactive cardiovascular and thoracic surgery. 2018. PMID: 29049742. cards.headline: VATS lobectomy cohort (Maki 2025): walk distance ≤450 m predicted 30-day pulmonary complications at an odds ratio of 5.674 (95% CI 1.206 to 26.684)
cards.summary: VATS lobectomy cohort (Maki 2025): walk distance ≤450 m predicted 30-day pulmonary complications at an odds ratio of 5.674 (95% CI 1.206 to 26.684)
cards.people: 66 patients who underwent video-assisted thoracic surgery (VATS) lobectomy for non-small-cell lung cancer (January to September 2022), reviewed retrospectively; 11 patients developed postoperative pulmonary complications (pneumonia, atelectasis, lung fistula) and 55 did not.
cards.result: On multivariate logistic regression, a preoperative 6-minute walk distance of ≤450 m was a significant predictor of postoperative pulmonary complications: odds ratio 5.674 (95% CI 1.206 to 26.684; P = 0.028) — an odds ratio, labelled as such, not a relative risk and not a sensitivity/specificity pair, neither of which this report provides. The authors suggest the walk test could serve as a risk-stratification tool before VATS lobectomy.
cards.watchOut: The smallest cohort carded (N = 66, 11 events) and the confidence interval is correspondingly wide (1.206 to 26.684); the odds ratio overstates the relative risk for an outcome occurring in 11 of 66 patients, which is why it is labelled and never converted.
cards.source: Maki N et al. Preoperative Six-Minute Walking Distance as a Predictor of Postoperative Complications in Patients Undergoing Lobectomy for Non-Small-Cell Lung Cancer. cards.headline: Synthesis: shorter preoperative walk distance predicts postoperative complications in all four cohorts, but the derived threshold is 325 m in a mixed high-risk cohort against 450–454 m in cancer-resection cohorts — there is no universal cut-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: shorter preoperative walk distance predicts postoperative complications in all four cohorts, but the derived threshold is 325 m in a mixed high-risk cohort against 450–454 m in cancer-resection cohorts — there is no universal cut-off
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Four independent non-METS reports, total N = 576, three of them retrospective: Keeratichananont 2016 (prospective, N = 78) found ≤325 m predicted pulmonary complications at 77% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with the walk test completed by all 14 patients (17.9%) who had contraindications to spirometry; Inoue 2020 (N = 111) found ≤454 m for grade ≥II complications at 71.0% / 54.8%; Hattori 2018 (N = 321) found ≤450 m for pneumonia at 69.2% / 71.1%; Maki 2025 (N = 66) found ≤450 m carried an odds ratio of 5.674 for 30-day pulmonary complications. A fifth report, a secondary analysis of the METS cohort (PMID 33442834, 2021), was verified at mining but is deliberately not carded here, per the commissioning row's programme-labelling caution; the shelf stands on the four non-METS reports. The six-minute walk REFERENCE-values question (what distance is normal) is a different question, built at pack #7158, and is not re-carded here.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each cohort's surgery type, outcome definition and limits; this synthesis adds no new data. No carded report tests whether acting on a low walk distance (prehabilitation, changed surgical plan) improves outcomes.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
