shelves.title: Stair climbing before lung resection: poor performance carries a pooled relative risk of 2.34 for complications; <12 m vs >22 m strata differ 2-fold in complications and 13-fold in mortality (relative)
shelves.question: Before major lung resection, how well does performance on the symptom-limited stair-climbing test — height climbed, time, desaturation and heart-rate change — predict postoperative cardiopulmonary complications and death, what height thresholds separate risk (about 10–12 m vs more than 22 m), and when should a poor stair-climbing result trigger formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing instead of deciding the question itself?
shelves.mesh: Exercise Test · Heart Rate · Humans · Lung Neoplasms/physiopathology,surgery · Pneumonectomy/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications/etiology · Predictive Value of Tests · Preoperative Period · Stair Climbing · Time Factors · Aged · Analysis of Variance · Cardiovascular Diseases/mortality,physiopathology · Cohort Studies · Cost of Illness · Cost-Benefit Analysis · Exercise Test/methods · Female · Heart Function Tests · Logistic Models · Lung Neoplasms/mortality,surgery · Male · Middle Aged · Multivariate Analysis · Pneumonectomy/adverse effects,economics,methods · Postoperative Complications/mortality,physiopathology · Preoperative Care/methods · Respiratory Function Tests · Retrospective Studies · Risk Assessment · Sensitivity and Specificity · Survival Analysis · Exercise Test/adverse effects,methods · Treatment Outcome · Lung Neoplasms/complications,surgery · Forced Expiratory Volume/physiology · Postoperative Complications/diagnosis,etiology,surgery
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — poor stair-climbing performance is consistently associated with more postoperative complications after lung resection, but the test is not standardised and its thresholds are strata from individual cohorts. The 2020 meta-analysis (13 articles, 2,038 patients; 6 pooled) found poor performance associated with complications at a pooled risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43) — a relative measure, labelled as such — with the complication threshold estimated at a 10 m climb, across studies that used incompatible criteria (height, rise time, desaturation, heart-rate change). The founding prospective cohort (640 lobectomy / pneumonectomy patients) found patients climbing less than 12 m had 2-fold cardiopulmonary complications, 13-fold mortality and 2.5-fold costs compared with patients climbing more than 22 m — relative comparisons between extreme strata in one centre, printed with their strata; the fetched record does not print the strata's absolute rates, and none is claimed. A 2022 cohort in limited-pulmonary-function patients (424 tested) found height achieved and heart-rate change (ΔHR >30 bpm) independently predictive. Both the meta-analysis and the founding cohort position a poor result as a trigger for formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing, not as a decision in itself. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — associated, non-standardised, extreme-strata (see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Boujibar 2020): poor stair-climbing performance associated with postoperative complications at a pooled risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43), threshold estimated at a 10 m climb
cards.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Boujibar 2020): poor stair-climbing performance associated with postoperative complications at a pooled risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43), threshold estimated at a 10 m climb
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (stair-climbing test before thoracic surgery)
cards.people: 13 articles totalling 2,038 lung-resection patients in the systematic review, 6 of them in the meta-analysis; literature to May 2020 across PubMed/MEDLINE, PEDro, Cochrane Library, Embase and CINAHL; risk of bias assessed with the Quality in Prognosis Studies tool. The meta-analysis was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42019121348).
cards.result: The included studies used multiple, incompatible test evaluation criteria: rise time, height climbed, desaturation and heart-rate change. Pooling was possible only for height of rise at a variable threshold: poor performance was associated with postoperative complications at a risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43; I² = 53%, P = 0.06) — a relative measure, labelled as such, with no absolute complication rates pooled. The threshold for occurrence of complications was estimated at a 10 m climb. The authors conclude the stair-climbing test could be used as a first-line functional screening test to predict postoperative morbidity after thoracic surgery, and that patients with a poor result (<10 m) should be referred to formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing.
cards.watchOut: Only 6 of 13 articles could be pooled, and only on the height criterion at a variable threshold; the pooled risk ratio is relative and the record pools no absolute rates, so it cannot say how many extra complications a poor climb means in any given service.
cards.source: Boujibar F et al. Performance at stair-climbing test is associated with postoperative complications after lung resection: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Thorax. 2020. PMID: 32651199. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42019121348. cards.headline: Founding prospective cohort (Brunelli 2008): climbing less than 12 m vs more than 22 m — 2-fold cardiopulmonary complications, 13-fold mortality and 2.5-fold costs (relative comparisons between extreme strata)
cards.summary: Founding prospective cohort (Brunelli 2008): climbing less than 12 m vs more than 22 m — 2-fold cardiopulmonary complications, 13-fold mortality and 2.5-fold costs (relative comparisons between extreme strata)
cards.type: Prospective routine-evaluation cohort (symptom-limited stair climbing before major lung resection)
cards.people: 640 patients who had lobectomy (n = 533) or pneumonectomy (n = 107) for lung cancer (January 2000 to April 2007) and performed a preoperative symptom-limited stair-climbing test as part of routine evaluation; altitude climbed was calculated as number of steps × height of the step in metres, with cut-offs identified by sensitivity/specificity analysis and associations tested by univariate and multivariate regression validated by bootstrap.
cards.result: The altitude reached was reliably associated with increased cardiopulmonary complications (P = 0.04), mortality (P = 0.02) and costs (P < 0.0001). In patients who climbed less than 12 m, cardiopulmonary complications, mortality and costs were 2-fold (P < 0.0001), 13-fold (P < 0.0001) and 2.5-fold higher, respectively, than in patients who climbed more than 22 m — all relative comparisons between the extreme performance strata of this single centre's cohort, labelled as such; the fetched record does not print the absolute complication or mortality rates within each stratum, and this card claims none. The authors recommend the test in all lung resection candidates, with poor performers undergoing formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing with measurement of oxygen consumption.
cards.watchOut: The 13-fold mortality figure compares the worst climbers (<12 m) with the best (>22 m) in one centre and is a relative comparison without absolute stratum rates in the record — it must never be printed as a standalone figure or applied to a patient in the middle range.
cards.source: Brunelli A et al. Performance at symptom-limited stair-climbing test is associated with increased cardiopulmonary complications, mortality, and costs after major lung resection. The Annals of thoracic surgery. 2008. PMID: 18573431. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Limited-pulmonary-function cohort (Xiao 2022): height achieved and heart-rate change (ΔHR) were the independent stair-climbing predictors of cardiopulmonary complications among 424 tested patients
cards.summary: Limited-pulmonary-function cohort (Xiao 2022): height achieved and heart-rate change (ΔHR) were the independent stair-climbing predictors of cardiopulmonary complications among 424 tested patients
cards.type: Retrospective cohort study (stair climbing in lung cancer with limited pulmonary function)
cards.people: 727 hospitalised lung cancer patients with limited pulmonary function were reviewed retrospectively; 424 of them underwent a preoperative stair-climbing test and form the analysed cohort. 89 cardiopulmonary complications occurred in 69 patients, 16.3% of the tested cohort.
cards.result: Postoperative cardiopulmonary complication rates differed significantly between groups stratified by smoking index, % FEV1, % diffusion capacity, stair-climbing results, excision extension and anaesthetic duration (P < 0.05). On multivariate analysis, only height achieved (P < 0.001), change in heart rate (ΔHR; P < 0.001) and excision extension (P = 0.006) were independent risk factors for postoperative cardiopulmonary complications. The authors conclude the stair-climbing test can be used as a preoperative screening method in lung cancer patients with limited pulmonary function, and suggest that for patients who climb less than 6 floors or have ΔHR >30 bpm, sublobar resection should be selected to reduce the complication rate.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective, confined to patients already selected for limited pulmonary function, and 303 of the 727 reviewed patients never performed the test; the 'less than 6 floors / ΔHR >30 bpm' surgical recommendation is the authors' suggestion from this one cohort, not a validated decision rule, and its floor count is not convertible to the metre thresholds of the other cards.

cards.headline: Synthesis: poor stair climbing consistently predicts more complications after lung resection (pooled relative risk 2.34; <12 m vs >22 m strata at 2-fold complications and 13-fold mortality), but criteria and thresholds differ by study and a poor result is a trigger for CPET, not a verdict
cards.summary: Synthesis: poor stair climbing consistently predicts more complications after lung resection (pooled relative risk 2.34; <12 m vs >22 m strata at 2-fold complications and 13-fold mortality), but criteria and thresholds differ by study and a poor result is a trigger for CPET, not a verdict
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf.
cards.result: Boujibar 2020 pooled six studies to a risk ratio of 2.34 (95% CI 1.59 to 3.43) for complications with poor performance — a relative measure — estimating the complication threshold at a 10 m climb, while noting the literature's criteria (height, time, desaturation, heart-rate change) cannot be merged. Brunelli 2008 (640 patients, prospective routine evaluation) supplies the extreme-strata comparisons: <12 m versus >22 m at 2-fold complications, 13-fold mortality and 2.5-fold costs, all relative and without absolute stratum rates in the record. Xiao 2022 (424 tested, limited pulmonary function) adds the heart-rate criterion: height achieved and ΔHR were independent predictors, with ΔHR >30 bpm named in the authors' conclusion. Both the meta-analysis and the founding cohort direct poor performers to formal cardiopulmonary exercise testing (the laboratory test built at pack #7611, cross-point only) rather than deciding operability on the stairs alone.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's criteria, population and limits; this synthesis adds no new data. Height, time, desaturation and heart-rate criteria are never merged into a single 'stair-climbing result'.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Preoperative spirometry does not establishedly predict pulmonary complications: 2002 review null, 2022 review inconclusive (65% for / 35% against), possible exception in upper abdominal surgery with COPD indicators
shelves.question: Before non-thoracic surgery, how well do preoperative pulmonary function tests — spirometry (FEV1, FVC), hypercarbia and blood-gas measures — predict postoperative pulmonary complications, why do the two systematic reviews reach null and inconclusive conclusions respectively, and in which subgroup (upper abdominal surgery, patients with COPD indicators) does the primary literature still argue for testing?
shelves.mesh: Humans · Lung Diseases/etiology · Postoperative Complications · Predictive Value of Tests · Postoperative Complications/diagnosis,etiology · Prospective Studies · Pulmonary Disease, Chronic Obstructive/complications,diagnosis · Respiratory Function Tests/adverse effects · Spirometry/adverse effects · Aged · Anesthesia, General · Cohort Studies · Elective Surgical Procedures/methods · Exercise Test/methods · Female · Male · Middle Aged · Postoperative Complications/epidemiology,physiopathology · Preoperative Care/methods · Regression Analysis · Risk Factors · Sensitivity and Specificity · Spirometry/methods · Thailand
shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED, and the null / inconclusive direction is this shelf's content. The 2002 systematic review of blinded studies (7 studies, 28 predictors) found neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values independently associated with postoperative pulmonary complications after non-thoracic surgery; only anaesthesia duration and postoperative nasogastric tube placement were significant in more than one study. The 2022 systematic review (46 original studies, high risk of bias on QUADAS-2) could reach only a qualitative verdict — inconclusive, with 65% of prospective studies for and 35% against preoperative spirometry — and named one possible-benefit subgroup: upper abdominal surgery in the low-selection-bias studies (3 studies, 959 participants, for; 1 study, 60 participants, against), with spirometry to be considered in patients with COPD indicators scheduling for upper abdominal surgery. The single positive primary report carded (N = 78, FEV1 % predicted an independent predictor alongside walk distance) is small and is shared with the six-minute-walk shelf #7686, stated on both; it is not pooled with the syntheses into a positive summary. Outside that named subgroup, no card presents spirometry as an established preoperative risk tool. PROPOSED STAMP: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — NOT ESTABLISHED (null / inconclusive syntheses; see proposedStamp).

cards.headline: Systematic review of blinded studies (Fisher 2002): neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values were independently associated with postoperative pulmonary complications
cards.summary: Systematic review of blinded studies (Fisher 2002): neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values were independently associated with postoperative pulmonary complications
cards.type: Systematic review of blinded predictor studies (non-thoracic surgery)
cards.people: 7 studies meeting criteria (independent, blinded comparisons of preoperative or operative factors with postoperative pulmonary complications after non-thoracic surgery; MEDLINE 1966–2001 plus manual searches and expert contact). The definition of postoperative pulmonary complications differed among studies and incidence varied from 2% to 19%.
cards.result: Of 28 preoperative or operative predictors evaluated across the 7 studies, 16 were associated significantly with postoperative pulmonary complications, but only 2 — duration of anaesthesia and postoperative nasogastric tube placement — were significant in more than one study. The positive (2.2 to 5.1) and negative (0.2 to 0.8) likelihood ratios for these 16 variables suggest only modest predictive value, likelihood ratios labelled as such. Neither hypercarbia nor reduced spirometry values were independently associated with an increased risk of postoperative pulmonary complications. The authors conclude few studies have rigorously evaluated these variables and that prospective blinded studies are needed.
cards.watchOut: The null is a null of independent association in only 7 rigorously blinded studies from a 1966–2001 literature, with complication definitions varying between studies — it shows spirometry was not shown to add independent prediction, not that lung function is clinically irrelevant.
cards.source: Fisher BW et al. Predicting pulmonary complications after nonthoracic surgery: a systematic review of blinded studies. The American journal of medicine. 2002. PMID: 11893349. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: Humans · Lung Diseases/etiology · Postoperative Complications · Predictive Value of Tests

cards.headline: Systematic review (Dankert 2022): 46 studies, qualitative synthesis inconclusive — 65% of prospective studies for, 35% against preoperative spirometry; possible benefit confined to upper abdominal surgery
cards.summary: Systematic review (Dankert 2022): 46 studies, qualitative synthesis inconclusive — 65% of prospective studies for, 35% against preoperative spirometry; possible benefit confined to upper abdominal surgery
cards.type: Systematic review of diagnostic / prognostic accuracy studies (non-thoracic surgery)
cards.people: 46 original research studies using pulmonary function test findings (spirometry, blood gas analysis) as index tests and postoperative pulmonary complications as the target condition in non-thoracic surgery; framed by PIT criteria and PRISMA-DTA, quality assessed with QUADAS-2, which showed a high risk of bias regarding patient selection, blinding and outcome definitions. The review was registered on PROSPERO (CRD42020215502).
cards.result: Qualitative synthesis of the prospective studies was inconclusive: 65% argue for and 35% against preoperative spirometry, and 43% argue for blood gas analysis. A post-hoc subgroup analysis of prospective studies with low risk of selection bias identified a possible benefit in upper abdominal surgery (three studies with 959 participants argued for and one study with 60 participants against spirometry). The authors conclude that, the literature being inconclusive, it is currently unknown whether pulmonary function tests improve risk assessment before non-thoracic surgery, and that spirometry should be considered in individuals with key indicators for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease scheduling for upper abdominal surgery.
cards.watchOut: A vote count (65% / 35%) is not a pooled effect: with high QUADAS-2 risk of bias and no meta-analytic estimate, 'inconclusive' is the strongest honest verdict, and the upper-abdominal subgroup signal is post-hoc and rests on 3-for / 1-against small studies.
cards.source: Dankert A et al. Pulmonary Function Tests for the Prediction of Postoperative Pulmonary Complications. Deutsches Arzteblatt international. 2022. PMID: 34939921. Registry ID: PROSPERO CRD42020215502. cards.headline: Single positive primary report (Keeratichananont 2016; N = 78, shared with shelf #7686): FEV1 % predicted was an independent predictor of pulmonary complications alongside walk distance — while 17.9% of the cohort could not perform spirometry at all
cards.summary: Single positive primary report (Keeratichananont 2016; N = 78, shared with shelf #7686): FEV1 % predicted was an independent predictor of pulmonary complications alongside walk distance — while 17.9% of the cohort could not perform spirometry at all
cards.type: Prospective cohort study (single positive primary report; shared with shelf #7686, stated on both)
cards.people: 78 high-risk patients scheduled for elective thoracic or non-thoracic surgery under general anaesthesia at Songklanagarind Hospital, Thailand, all indicated for preoperative pulmonary evaluation; 30-day postoperative pulmonary complications developed in 17 cases (21%). SHARED COHORT: this is the same report that anchors shelf #7686 (six-minute walk test), stated there and here.
cards.result: On multiple regression analysis, older age, poor general health status, smoking history, low mean FEV1 % predicted (by spirometry) and shorter 6-minute walk distance were the independent factors associated with postoperative pulmonary complications — so in this small cohort spirometry did carry independent predictive information, against the direction of the two syntheses carded above. At the same time, 14 of the 78 patients (17.9%) had contraindications to spirometry and two more could not achieve acceptable spirometry efforts, so the test was unobtainable in about a fifth of exactly the high-risk patients it was meant to assess (all completed the walk test).
cards.watchOut: One small single-centre cohort (N = 78, 17 events) with several predictors fitted to few events: it cannot overturn two systematic reviews, it is not pooled with them into a positive summary, and its spirometry limb excludes by design the fifth of patients who could not perform the test.
cards.source: Keeratichananont W et al. Value of preoperative 6-minute walk test for predicting postoperative pulmonary complications. Therapeutic advances in respiratory disease. 2016. PMID: 26546478. Registry ID: none in the record. shelves.title: Preoperative Timed-Up-and-Go predicting complications: odds ratio 3.43 for major complications in onco-geriatric surgery (AUC 0.64) and adjusted odds ratio 4.97 at a ≥18.4 s cut-off in spine surgery — but no complication prediction at all in gynaecological laparoscopy at a >12 s frailty cut-off
shelves.question: Before elective surgery, how well does the preoperative Timed-Up-and-Go (TUG) time predict postoperative complications — what thresholds have been derived (about 12 s as a frailty cut-off, 18.4 s in spine surgery), what odds and discrimination does a slow TUG carry in onco-geriatric and spine cohorts, and in which surgical population (gynaecological laparoscopy) did it fail to predict complications at all?

shelves.balance: PREDICTIVE PERFORMANCE — positive in two cohorts, null in a third, and never with a shared threshold. In onco-geriatric surgery (Huisman 2014; 280 patients), high TUG independently predicted major complications at an odds ratio of 3.43 (an odds ratio, as published), but discrimination was weak — AUC 0.64 for TUG against 0.59 for ASA class — even though absolute major-complication risk was 50.0% in the high-TUG group against 25.6% for ASA ≥3. In thoracolumbar spine surgery (Komodikis 2020; 103 patients), slow TUG (unable to perform, or ≥18.4 s) independently predicted high-grade complications at an adjusted odds ratio of 4.97, with a wide interval (95% CI 1.18 to 22.47). In gynaecological cancer surgery (Anastasio 2025; 174 patients, 70.6% laparoscopy), frailty at TUG >12 s predicted transfusion (19.2% vs 4.1%) but there were no differences in major or minor complication rates after laparoscopic surgery, and TUG predicted neither length of stay nor discharge disposition. The >12 s frailty cut-off and the ≥18.4 s spine cut-off are different operationalisations of the same test; no card prints a universal threshold. This is the prediction question — TUG reference values in healthy people are a different shelf (pack #7160).

cards.headline: Onco-geriatric cohort (Huisman 2014): 280 patients aged ≥70 — TUG independently predicted major complications (odds ratio 3.43, 95% CI 1.14 to 10.35, an odds ratio) with AUC 0.64 vs 0.59 for ASA; absolute risk 50.0% in the high-TUG group
cards.summary: Onco-geriatric cohort (Huisman 2014): 280 patients aged ≥70 — TUG independently predicted major complications (odds ratio 3.43, 95% CI 1.14 to 10.35, an odds ratio) with AUC 0.64 vs 0.59 for ASA; absolute risk 50.0% in the high-TUG group
cards.type: Prospective multicentre cohort, preoperative TUG predicting 30-day major complications in onco-geriatric surgery (280 patients)
cards.people: Prospective multicentre cohort of 280 patients aged ≥70 undergoing elective surgery for solid tumours (median age 76; 180, or 64.3%, underwent major surgery); preoperative TUG and ASA classification were recorded and the primary end point was 30-day morbidity; 55 patients (20.1%) experienced major complications.
cards.result: TUG and ASA were independent predictors of major complications (TUG: odds ratio 3.43; 95% CI 1.14 to 10.35 — an odds ratio, printed as published; ASA 1 vs 2: OR 5.91; ASA 1 vs 3&4: OR 12.77). Absolute risks: 50.0% of patients with high TUG and 25.6% of patients with ASA ≥3 experienced major complications. Discrimination was modest for both: AUC for TUG 0.64 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.73, P = 0.001) and for ASA 0.59 (95% CI 0.51 to 0.67, P = 0.04). The authors note TUG identified twice as many at-risk patients as ASA.
cards.watchOut: An odds ratio of 3.43 with an AUC of 0.64 is association without strong discrimination — the test ranks patients only slightly better than ASA's 0.59. The abstract does not print the high-TUG threshold value; no threshold from another cohort may be imported onto this card.
cards.source: Huisman MG et al. "Timed Up & Go": a screening tool for predicting 30-day morbidity in onco-geriatric surgical patients? A multicenter cohort study. PloS one. 2014. PMID: 24475186. cards.headline: Spine cohort (Komodikis 2020): 103 patients — slow TUG (unable to perform or ≥18.4 s) independently predicted high-grade complications at an adjusted odds ratio of 4.97 (95% CI 1.18 to 22.47, an odds ratio)
cards.summary: Spine cohort (Komodikis 2020): 103 patients — slow TUG (unable to perform or ≥18.4 s) independently predicted high-grade complications at an adjusted odds ratio of 4.97 (95% CI 1.18 to 22.47, an odds ratio)
cards.type: Prospective cohort, preoperative TUG predicting adverse outcomes in thoracolumbar spine surgery (103 patients)
cards.people: Prospective cohort of 103 patients (mean age 62.95 ± 10.97 years) undergoing elective thoracolumbar spine surgery at a tertiary hospital, 2017–2018; patients were assigned to the slow-TUG group if unable to perform the test or if performance time was ≥18.4 s, and followed to 6 weeks after surgery.
cards.result: Slow-TUG patients were more often ASA class 3 (74.1% vs 47.4%, P = .02), non-independent (25.9% vs 5.3%, P < .01) and frail (92.3% vs 42.1%, P < .01). TUG was an independent predictor of high-grade complications (adjusted odds ratio 4.97, 95% CI: 1.18 to 22.47 — an odds ratio, printed as published), overall complications (OR 3.77, 95% CI: 1.33 to 11.81), discharge to a skilled-nursing facility (OR 3.2, 95% CI: 1.00 to 10.70), readmission within 6 weeks (OR 9.14, 95% CI: 2.39 to 41.26) and length of stay (adjusted incident rate ratio 1.45, 95% CI: 1.16 to 1.80).
cards.watchOut: The ≥18.4 s cut-off was derived in this 103-patient spine cohort — it is not a general frailty threshold, and the confidence interval (1.18 to 22.47) is wide enough to include a near-null effect. 'Unable to perform' is grouped with slow times; the two are not the same finding.
cards.source: Komodikis G et al. Usefulness of Timed Up and Go (TUG) Test for Prediction of Adverse Outcomes in Patients Undergoing Thoracolumbar Spine Surgery. Neurosurgery. 2020. PMID: 31813977. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Gynaecological cohort (Anastasio 2025) — the null: 174 patients, frailty at TUG >12 s — more transfusions (19.2% vs 4.1%) but NO differences in major or minor complication rates after laparoscopic surgery, and no prediction of length of stay or disposition
cards.summary: Gynaecological cohort (Anastasio 2025) — the null: 174 patients, frailty at TUG >12 s — more transfusions (19.2% vs 4.1%) but NO differences in major or minor complication rates after laparoscopic surgery, and no prediction of length of stay or disposition
cards.type: Retrospective cohort, preoperative TUG (frailty >12 s) and perioperative outcomes in gynaecological cancer surgery (174 patients)
cards.people: Retrospective cohort of 174 patients undergoing surgery with gynaecological oncologists (October 2019 to October 2023) with a preoperative TUG recorded: 39 (22.4%) laparotomy, 123 (70.6%) laparoscopy, 12 (6.9%) other minor surgery; TUG >12 seconds defined frailty; ASA scores and modified frailty index were comparators.
cards.result: Frail patients (TUG >12 s) were older, with higher modified frailty index scores and lower preoperative albumin. There were no differences in major or minor complication rates after laparoscopic surgery between frail and nonfrail patients. ASA and modified frailty index were not associated with transfusion (P > .05). Frail patients were more likely to receive a perioperative blood transfusion in the overall cohort (19.2% vs 4.1%, P = .0034). TUG time did not predict length of stay or postoperative disposition. Slower TUG times were associated with comorbidities, older age and malnutrition.
cards.watchOut: The null is specific: no complication prediction after laparoscopy, the dominant approach in this cohort — it does not refute the open-surgery cohorts, and the transfusion association is not a complication prediction. Retrospective, single-system, and the frailty group is defined by the test being evaluated.
cards.source: Anastasio MK et al. Use of the Frailty "Timed Up and Go" Test to Predict Perioperative Complications in Patients Undergoing Gynecologic Cancer Surgery. Journal of minimally invasive gynecology. 2025. PMID: 40381988. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Synthesis: preoperative TUG predicts complications in onco-geriatric (OR 3.43, AUC 0.64) and spine cohorts (adjusted OR 4.97 at ≥18.4 s) but not in gynaecological laparoscopy at >12 s — two thresholds, three populations, cohorts of 103–280, so the test's prediction is population property, not a cut-off
cards.summary: Synthesis: preoperative TUG predicts complications in onco-geriatric (OR 3.43, AUC 0.64) and spine cohorts (adjusted OR 4.97 at ≥18.4 s) but not in gynaecological laparoscopy at >12 s — two thresholds, three populations, cohorts of 103–280, so the test's prediction is population property, not a cut-off
cards.people: All reports carded on this shelf: two prospective cohorts (280 onco-geriatric patients; 103 spine patients) and one retrospective cohort (174 gynaecological cancer patients). No anchor is shared with the TUG reference-values shelf (pack #7160), which asks the different, normative question.
cards.result: The balance is SPLIT by population and approach: positive associations where surgery was predominantly open and patients older or spine-operated; null for complications where surgery was predominantly laparoscopic. Odds ratios are printed as odds ratios beside the absolute risks where the reports give them (50.0% high-TUG major-complication risk in the onco-geriatric cohort). No universal TUG cut-off for surgical risk exists on this evidence — 12 s and 18.4 s answer to different cohorts.
cards.watchOut: See the individual cards for each report's limits; this synthesis adds no new data.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Glasgow Coma Scale reliability between raters: adequate only in good-quality studies (7 of 52 reviewed), 33.1% exact accuracy on standardised vignettes, and high agreement (kappa/ICC 0.85–0.96) only after 19 hours of training — motor is the least reliable component throughout
shelves.question: At the bedside, how reliable is the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal and motor components and their sum) between raters — what does the systematic review of 52 reliability studies find once study quality is accounted for, how accurate is scoring by mixed emergency providers against expert scoring of standardised cases, and what reliability is achievable after standardised training in a high-volume trauma centre?
shelves.mesh: Databases, Bibliographic · Evidence-Based Medicine · Glasgow Coma Scale/standards/statistics & numerical data · Humans · Observer Variation · Predictive Value of Tests · Reproducibility of Results
shelves.balance: A measurement-reliability shelf, not a prognostic or treatment shelf: no card converts reliability data into claims about GCS-based triage or intubation thresholds. The three anchors genuinely disagree in register, and the training-dependence is the content. The systematic review of 52 studies found good methodological quality in only 7 (13%); in those, kappa was ≥0.6 in 85% and all ICCs indicated excellent reliability, while poor-quality studies showed lower estimates, and component reliability exceeded sum-score reliability. Mixed emergency providers scored standardised video vignettes with only 33.1% exact total-score accuracy (verbal most accurate at 69.2%, motor least at 59.8%, and 9.2% assigning scores that do not exist) — a vignette figure, printed as such. After a 19-hour standardised training programme, triage and resuscitation nurses reached weighted kappa and ICC 0.85–0.96 with 65.3% exact agreement — and agreement fell in traumatic brain injury and ISS ≥16, where the score matters most. The motor component is the least reliable in both primary studies.

cards.headline: GCS reliability systematic review (Reith 2016 — 52 reliability studies): methodological quality was good in only 7 studies (13%), fair in 18 and poor in 27; in the good-quality studies kappa was ≥0.6 in 85% and all ICCs indicated excellent reliability, while poor-quality studies showed lower estimates; component reliability exceeded sum-score reliability, and training/education, level of consciousness and stimulus type influenced reliability
cards.summary: GCS reliability systematic review (Reith 2016 — 52 reliability studies): methodological quality was good in only 7 studies (13%), fair in 18 and poor in 27; in the good-quality studies kappa was ≥0.6 in 85% and all ICCs indicated excellent reliability, while poor-quality studies showed lower estimates; component reliability exceeded sum-score reliability, and training/education, level of consciousness and stimulus type influenced reliability
cards.type: Systematic review of GCS reliability studies (synthesis of 52 studies)
cards.people: Observational studies assessing the reliability of the Glasgow Coma Scale (eye, verbal and motor components and their sum) by a statistical measure, searched in MEDLINE, EMBASE and CINAHL; 52 studies, with methodological quality rated by the COSMIN checklist and reliability estimates synthesised narratively because of heterogeneity. A synthesis — not a primary cohort.
cards.result: Significant heterogeneity was found in the type of reliability estimates used, patients studied, setting and observer characteristics. Methodological quality was good in 7 studies (13%), fair in 18 and poor in 27. In good-quality studies, kappa values were ≥0.6 in 85% and all intraclass correlation coefficients indicated excellent reliability; poor-quality studies showed lower reliability estimates. Reliability for the GCS components was higher than for the sum score. Factors that may influence reliability include education and training, the level of consciousness and the type of stimuli used. The authors conclude that, although reliability was adequate in good-quality studies, further improvement is desirable and a renewed focus on training/education and standardisation is required.
cards.watchOut: Only 13% of the underlying literature is good quality — the reassuring headline ('adequate in good-quality studies') rests on 7 studies, and the other 45 are the literature clinicians actually produced. No card on this shelf converts reliability data into claims about GCS-based triage or intubation thresholds.
cards.source: Reith FC et al. The reliability of the Glasgow Coma Scale: a systematic review. Intensive care medicine. 2016. PMID: 26564211. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: GCS scoring accuracy on standardised video vignettes (Bledsoe 2015 — 217 emergency providers, 2,084 scorings of 10 standardised adult cases against two board-certified neurologists whose own agreement was κ = 1): overall total-score accuracy was only 33.1% (95% CI 30.2–36.0%), verbal the most accurate component (69.2%), motor the least (59.8%), and 9.2% of subjects assigned scores that do not exist in the scale
cards.summary: GCS scoring accuracy on standardised video vignettes (Bledsoe 2015 — 217 emergency providers, 2,084 scorings of 10 standardised adult cases against two board-certified neurologists whose own agreement was κ = 1): overall total-score accuracy was only 33.1% (95% CI 30.2–36.0%), verbal the most accurate component (69.2%), motor the least (59.8%), and 9.2% of subjects assigned scores that do not exist in the scale
cards.type: Prospective video-vignette accuracy study (mixed emergency providers vs expert scoring)
cards.people: 217 emergency providers of various types within a modern EMS system, scoring 10 standardised video vignettes of adults, compared with expert scoring by two board-certified neurologists (inter-rater reliability κ = 1); 2,084 observations of GCS scoring. A vignette study — it measures scoring of filmed cases, not live patients, and prints as such.
cards.result: Overall total GCS scoring accuracy was 33.1% (95% CI 30.2–36.0). The verbal component was the most accurate (69.2%, 67.8–70.4), eye opening second (61.2%, 59.5–62.9) and the motor component the least accurate (59.8%, 58.1–61.5). A small number of subjects (9.2%) assigned GCS scores that do not exist in the GCS scoring system. The authors conclude GCS scoring should not be considered accurate and that a more simplified scoring system should be developed and validated.
cards.watchOut: Filmed vignettes remove the hardest parts of live assessment (eliciting responses, choosing stimuli) and still only a third of total scores were exactly right — but the figure is a vignette figure and must never be quoted as live-patient accuracy. The motor component being least accurate here matches the training study's lowest agreement for motor response.
cards.source: Bledsoe BE et al. Glasgow Coma Scale Scoring is Often Inaccurate. Prehospital and disaster medicine. 2015. PMID: 25489727. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: GCS reliability after standardised training (Zhang 2025 — 875 trauma patients each scored independently by triage and resuscitation nurses, 71 nurses, after a 19-hour standardised training programme in a high-volume Chinese trauma centre): weighted kappa and ICC 0.85–0.96 across components and total, exact total-score agreement 65.3% and 89.8% within 1 point, motor the least consistent component (75.1% agreement), with traumatic brain injury (adjusted OR 0.22) and ISS ≥16 (adjusted OR 0.34) reducing agreement
cards.summary: GCS reliability after standardised training (Zhang 2025 — 875 trauma patients each scored independently by triage and resuscitation nurses, 71 nurses, after a 19-hour standardised training programme in a high-volume Chinese trauma centre): weighted kappa and ICC 0.85–0.96 across components and total, exact total-score agreement 65.3% and 89.8% within 1 point, motor the least consistent component (75.1% agreement), with traumatic brain injury (adjusted OR 0.22) and ISS ≥16 (adjusted OR 0.34) reducing agreement
cards.type: Prospective inter-rater reliability study after standardised training (single high-volume trauma centre)
cards.people: 875 trauma patients and 71 nurses (30 triage, 41 resuscitation) in a high-volume Chinese trauma centre, April–December 2024; each patient received two independent GCS assessments within ≤5 minutes, after all nurses completed a 19-hour standardised GCS training programme; agreement assessed by percentage agreement, weighted Cohen's kappa, ICC and correlation, with multivariable logistic regression for factors associated with consistency. Adjusted odds ratios are relative measures, printed as reported.
cards.result: GCS components and total scores showed high inter-rater reliability (weighted kappa 0.85–0.96; ICC 0.85–0.96). Perfect agreement occurred in 65.3% of total scores, with 89.8% differing by ≤1 point. Verbal response showed the highest component agreement (87.1%), followed by eye opening (86.5%) and motor response (75.1%). Traumatic brain injury (adjusted OR = 0.22, P < 0.001) and injury severity score ≥16 (adjusted OR = 0.34, P < 0.001) were associated with reduced agreement; nurses' experience, education and professional rank did not significantly affect reliability.
cards.watchOut: The high agreement was achieved after 19 hours of standardised training — the training is part of the result, and these figures must not be quoted as the reliability of untrained bedside scoring. Even after training, exact agreement was only 65.3%, and agreement fell precisely in the sickest patients (TBI, ISS ≥16), where the score matters most.
cards.source: Zhang Y et al. Inter-rater Reliability of the Glasgow Coma Scale Between Triage and Resuscitation Nurses After Standardized Training. Journal of nursing management. 2025. cards.headline: Synthesis: GCS reliability is training-dependent and unsettled in ordinary practice — adequate in the 7 good-quality studies of 52 reviewed, only 33.1% exact total-score accuracy on standardised vignettes by mixed emergency providers, and high agreement (weighted kappa / ICC 0.85–0.96, 65.3% exact) only after 19 hours of standardised training; the motor component is the least reliable in both primary studies and the sum score is less reliable than its components

shelves.title: Shock index in adult trauma — FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 syntheses, no third report (~905,000 patients inside them): moderate accuracy for massive transfusion (AUC 0.85) against near-chance mortality discrimination in the larger synthesis (AUC 0.553 vs 0.747 in the smaller)
shelves.question: In adult trauma patients at arrival, how accurately does the shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) predict massive transfusion and death — what pooled sensitivity, specificity and AUC do the trauma syntheses deliver for each outcome, and how does it compare with the Revised Trauma Score and the (post-resuscitation, anatomical) Injury Severity Score as a mortality predictor? (FLOOR-RISK: basis is exactly 2 syntheses, no third report — printed on the face and carried in the stamp line.)
shelves.mesh: Adult · Humans · Blood Transfusion · Emergency Service, Hospital · Patients
shelves.balance: FLOOR-RISK, per the coordinator's ruling: this shelf's basis is exactly 2 syntheses, no third report — printed here, in the title and in the stamp line. Inside them sit 35 studies / 670,728 patients and 12 studies / 234,129 patients (about 905,000 patients in total, with overlapping primary-study sets — a mass statement, not independent patients). The verdict splits by outcome. For massive transfusion (assessed in the larger synthesis only): pooled sensitivity 0.68, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.85, likelihood ratios 4.24 and 0.39. For mortality the syntheses disagree — AUC 0.553 (near chance; sensitivity 0.358, specificity 0.742) in the larger synthesis vs 0.747 in the smaller — and both sit below the Revised Trauma Score (AUC 0.852) and ISS (0.855) for mortality, with RTS and ISS not significantly different in paired studies (P = 0.91). No single shock-index AUC prints without its outcome and synthesis named; cut-offs vary across primary studies and no universal threshold is printed; no card implies shock-index-triggered transfusion pathways improve outcomes.

cards.headline: Shock index synthesis 1 of 2 (Carsetti 2023, Critical Care — 35 studies, 670,728 trauma patients): for massive transfusion, pooled sensitivity 0.68, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.85, positive likelihood ratio 4.24 and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (both labelled as likelihood ratios); for mortality, pooled sensitivity 0.358, specificity 0.742 and AUC 0.553 — the authors conclude the index is not accurate for mortality prediction
cards.summary: Shock index synthesis 1 of 2 (Carsetti 2023, Critical Care — 35 studies, 670,728 trauma patients): for massive transfusion, pooled sensitivity 0.68, specificity 0.84, AUC 0.85, positive likelihood ratio 4.24 and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (both labelled as likelihood ratios); for mortality, pooled sensitivity 0.358, specificity 0.742 and AUC 0.553 — the authors conclude the index is not accurate for mortality prediction
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (synthesis 1 of exactly 2 on this FLOOR-RISK shelf; primary-study sets overlap)
cards.people: Adult trauma patients with shock index (heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure) recorded at arrival in the field or the emergency department, in studies reporting massive transfusion or mortality; systematic search of MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science to March 2022, risk of bias by QUADAS-2. One of exactly 2 syntheses on this FLOOR-RISK shelf — the sets of primary studies overlap between the two syntheses.
cards.result: For massive transfusion the overall sensitivity was 0.68 (95% CI as published 0.57–0.76), specificity 0.84 (0.79–0.88) and AUC 0.85 (0.81–0.88), with positive likelihood ratio 4.24 (3.18–5.65) and negative likelihood ratio 0.39 (0.29–0.52). For mortality the overall sensitivity was 0.358, specificity 0.742 and AUC 0.553, with likelihood ratios 1.39 and 0.87. The authors conclude shock index may have a limited role as the sole tool to predict the need for massive transfusion, and is not accurate to predict mortality, though it may help identify patients at low risk of mortality.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: this shelf rests on exactly 2 syntheses, no third report — printed here, in the title, the balance and the stamp. An AUC of 0.553 for mortality is near chance; no summary may quote the transfusion AUC (0.85) as 'the' shock-index AUC without naming its outcome and synthesis.

cards.people: Adult trauma patients in studies of diagnostic accuracy for in-hospital mortality (the prespecified primary endpoint), searched from inception to May 2026 as published; pooled by bivariate random-effects and hierarchical summary ROC models, with a paired comparison in studies reporting both RTS and ISS. One of exactly 2 syntheses on this FLOOR-RISK shelf — its primary studies overlap the larger synthesis's set. ISS is a post-resuscitation anatomical score, not available at arrival, and prints as such.
cards.result: Pooled sensitivity/specificity were 0.679/0.763 for shock index (5 studies, AUC 0.747), 0.788/0.801 for the Revised Trauma Score (6 studies, AUC 0.852) and 0.788/0.796 for ISS (9 studies, AUC 0.855). In the six studies reporting both RTS and ISS, a paired bivariate comparison found no significant difference in diagnostic accuracy (likelihood-ratio test, P = 0.91; within-study sensitivity OR 1.59, 95% CI 0.82–3.07; specificity OR 0.89, 0.55–1.45 — relative measures, printed as reported). The authors conclude the tools serve different, complementary roles across the trauma timeline rather than competing as predictors.
cards.watchOut: FLOOR-RISK: exactly 2 syntheses, no third report. This synthesis's shock-index mortality AUC (0.747, from only 5 of its 12 studies) disagrees with the larger synthesis's 0.553 — the disagreement prints, and neither figure may be presented as the settled mortality accuracy of the index. Cut-offs vary across primary studies; no universal threshold is printed on this shelf.

shelves.title: Bedside swallow screening after surgery: a structured targeted screen reached 90% sensitivity / 83% specificity after liver transplantation, while the unstructured clinical examination missed silent aspiration in 27% of lung-transplant patients who looked normal at the bedside
shelves.question: After surgery, how well do bedside swallow screens and bedside clinical swallowing examinations detect postoperative dysphagia and aspiration against instrumental evaluation (fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing or videofluoroscopy) — what sensitivity and specificity did a targeted bedside swallow screen achieve after liver transplantation, how discriminative is the patient-reported EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery, and how much aspiration does the unstructured clinical bedside examination miss after lung transplantation, where silent aspiration predominates?
shelves.mesh: Adult · Deglutition · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis · Female · Humans · Liver Transplantation · Male · Middle Aged · Point-of-Care Testing · Postoperative Complications/diagnosis · Prospective Studies · Sensitivity and Specificity · Aged · Deglutition/physiology · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis, etiology, physiopathology · Endoscopy, Digestive System · Follow-Up Studies · Lung Transplantation/adverse effects · Postoperative Complications · Retrospective Studies · Young Adult · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis, etiology, prevention & control · Graft Rejection · Larynx/physiopathology · Postoperative Care/methods · Preoperative Care/methods · Prevalence · Prognosis · Risk Factors · Trachea/physiopathology · Cervical Vertebrae/surgery · China · Deglutition Disorders/diagnosis, epidemiology, etiology · Dysphonia/diagnosis, etiology · Hospitals · Reproducibility of Results · Spinal Fusion · Surveys and Questionnaires
shelves.balance: This is a screening-accuracy shelf, not a treatment shelf: no card may imply screen-guided postoperative feeding pathways improve pneumonia or mortality outcomes — no anchor tests that. The headline is the instrument gradient. At the structured end, a targeted bedside swallow screen (mental status, laryngeal sensation/elevation, progressively larger water volumes — a screen previously validated by the same programme after cardiac surgery, programme-labelled) achieved 90% sensitivity and 83% specificity against FEES in 50 liver-transplant patients screened within 24 hours of extubation, with 40% failing the screen and 90% of failures confirmed dysphagic. In the middle, the patient-reported EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery discriminated only moderately (AUC 0.68; at a cut score of ≥7, sensitivity 72.7%, specificity 64.3%, PPV 51.6%, NPV 81.8%) in a 64-patient prospective study where instrumentally confirmed dysphagia doubled from 15.6% to 34.4% after surgery. At the unstructured end, the clinical bedside examination demonstrably misses silent aspiration after lung transplantation: in 321 referred patients (297 completing evaluation), clinical signs were apparent in 54% but instrumental testing found deep penetration or aspiration in 67%, and 27% had an entirely normal clinical examination yet deep penetration or aspiration; in the earlier 263-recipient series, provocative evaluation was positive in 70.5% of those tested, aspiration occurred in 63.8% of positive evaluations, and 77.6% of aspirations were clinically silent. Both lung-transplant series are retrospective and subject to referral selection (patients referred for evaluation) — printed on their cards. The fifth report's reference standard is another questionnaire (the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory), not an instrumental standard: its AUCs (>0.9 for the HSS-Dysphagia subscale) are never printed beside the FEES-referenced figures without that distinction. The evidence comes from transplant and anterior cervical populations only; no verified screen-validation report in general, cardiac or abdominal surgical populations was carried through — no figure may be generalised across operations. Distinct from the GUSS (stroke/ICU) and Yale Swallow Protocol (general hospital/TBI) shelves: no anchor is shared.

cards.headline: Targeted bedside swallow screen after liver transplantation (2019): sensitivity 90% and specificity 83% for detecting dysphagia against FEES — 40% of 50 patients failed the screen and 90% of failures were confirmed dysphagic
cards.summary: Targeted bedside swallow screen after liver transplantation (2019): sensitivity 90% and specificity 83% for detecting dysphagia against FEES — 40% of 50 patients failed the screen and 90% of failures were confirmed dysphagic
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic study — structured targeted screen vs FEES (liver transplantation)
cards.people: Prospective study of 50 adult liver-transplant patients at one institution over 5 months, screened within 24 hours of extubation and before oral intake with a targeted swallow screen (direct assessment of mental status and laryngeal sensation/elevation on progressively larger water volumes) previously validated by the same programme after cardiac surgery — programme-labelled. Fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing (FEES) was requested for failed screens.
cards.result: Twenty patients (40%) failed the targeted screen and 18 of the 20 (90%) failed the subsequent FEES (overall dysphagia incidence 40%). The screen's sensitivity was 90% and specificity 83% for detecting dysphagia. Patients with dysphagia were older and had significantly longer ICU and hospital stays. The authors conclude a simple bedside screen can efficiently screen these patients and that the findings require further validation.
cards.watchOut: Single centre, N = 50, and the screen's own programme reporting its validation — programme-labelled. FEES was requested for failed screens, so the specificity estimate rests on the screen-negative pathway as reported; do not generalise the 90%/83% pair to other operations.
cards.source: Mukdad L et al. A Targeted Swallow Screen for the Detection of Postoperative Dysphagia in Liver Transplant Patients. Progress in transplantation (Aliso Viejo, Calif.). 2019. cards.headline: EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery (2026): instrumentally confirmed dysphagia doubled from 15.6% to 34.4% after surgery, and EAT-10 discrimination was only moderate (AUC 0.68); at a cut score of ≥7, sensitivity was 72.7%, specificity 64.3%, PPV 51.6% and NPV 81.8%
cards.summary: EAT-10 after anterior cervical spine surgery (2026): instrumentally confirmed dysphagia doubled from 15.6% to 34.4% after surgery, and EAT-10 discrimination was only moderate (AUC 0.68); at a cut score of ≥7, sensitivity was 72.7%, specificity 64.3%, PPV 51.6% and NPV 81.8%
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic study — patient-reported EAT-10 vs FEES (anterior cervical spine surgery)
cards.people: Prospective single-site study of 64 clinically referred adults undergoing otolaryngology-assisted anterior cervical spine surgery (82.8% revision surgery; mean age 57.6 years), completing the patient-reported EAT-10 and FEES before and after surgery; dysphagia defined instrumentally (residue and/or Penetration-Aspiration Scale ≥6). This report's PubMed record carries no MeSH terms ('none in the record' in its source line).
cards.result: EAT-10 scores worsened by an average of 6.0 points after surgery (P < 0.001) and instrumentally confirmed dysphagia doubled from 15.6% to 34.4% (P < 0.01). ROC analysis showed moderate discriminative ability for EAT-10 (AUC 0.68); at a cut score of ≥7, sensitivity was 72.7%, specificity 64.3%, PPV 51.6% and NPV 81.8%. The authors propose EAT-10 as a useful patient-reported adjunct alongside other bedside tools, not a stand-alone screen.
cards.watchOut: A referred, mostly revision-surgery population at one site — the prevalence (34.4% post-operative) and the PPV/NPV pair travel with that setting. AUC 0.68 is moderate: never headline EAT-10 as an accurate screen from this report.
cards.source: Quinn N et al. EAT-10 to Screen Instrumentally Confirmed Dysphagia Following Anterior Cervical Spine Surgery. Laryngoscope investigative otolaryngology. 2026. PMID: 42909303. Registry ID: none in the record. MeSH: none in the record

cards.headline: Clinical bedside examination after lung transplantation (2017): clinical signs of aspiration were apparent in 54%, but instrumental testing found deep laryngeal penetration or aspiration in 67% — and 27% of patients had an entirely normal clinical bedside examination yet deep penetration or aspiration on instrumental testing
cards.summary: Clinical bedside examination after lung transplantation (2017): clinical signs of aspiration were apparent in 54%, but instrumental testing found deep laryngeal penetration or aspiration in 67% — and 27% of patients had an entirely normal clinical bedside examination yet deep penetration or aspiration on instrumental testing
cards.type: Retrospective series — unstructured clinical examination vs instrumental testing (lung transplantation)
cards.people: Retrospective series of 321 lung-transplant patients (April 2009–September 2012) referred for swallowing evaluation, 297 completing it; a speech-language-pathology clinical bedside examination was followed by modified barium swallow or FEES. Referral-selected population — printed here and on the face of this shelf.
cards.result: Clinical signs of aspiration were apparent in 160 patients (54%). Deep laryngeal penetration or aspiration were identified in 198 (67%) during instrumental testing. Eighty-one patients (27%) had an entirely normal clinical examination but were found to have deep penetration or aspiration instrumentally. The authors conclude the clinical bedside examination is not sensitive enough and will fail to identify patients with silent aspiration.
cards.watchOut: Retrospective and referral-selected: these percentages describe referred patients, not all lung-transplant recipients. The finding is a miss-rate demonstration, not a sensitivity/specificity pair — never convert it into one.
cards.source: Baumann B et al. Postoperative Swallowing Assessment After Lung Transplantation. The Annals of thoracic surgery. 2017. PMID: 28483151. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Provocative swallowing evaluation after lung transplantation (2007): positive for penetration or aspiration in 70.5% of those tested; aspiration occurred in 63.8% of positive evaluations, and 77.6% of aspirations were clinically silent
cards.summary: Provocative swallowing evaluation after lung transplantation (2007): positive for penetration or aspiration in 70.5% of those tested; aspiration occurred in 63.8% of positive evaluations, and 77.6% of aspirations were clinically silent
cards.type: Retrospective series — provocative/instrumental evaluation yield and silent aspiration (lung transplantation)
cards.people: Retrospective single-centre series of 263 lung-transplant recipients (2001–2005); provocative swallowing evaluation (mostly fiberoptic endoscopic) was performed in 149 patients, 114 did not receive formal evaluation. Referral-selected — the evaluated group had more pre-operative reflux and post-operative complications than the unevaluated group.
cards.result: Swallowing evaluation was positive for laryngeal penetration or tracheal aspiration in 70.5% (105 of 149). Aspiration occurred in 63.8% (67) of positive evaluations, and 77.6% (52) of aspiration assessments were clinically silent. The unevaluated group had a significantly shorter hospital stay (P = 0.004). The authors conclude prospective evaluation identifies strikingly high rates of dysphagia after lung transplantation, much of it silent.
cards.watchOut: Only 56.7% of recipients were evaluated, and they were the higher-risk group — the 70.5% positivity is a yield in selected patients, not a population prevalence. 'Clinically silent' here means no clinical signs accompanied instrumentally proven aspiration.
cards.source: Atkins BZ et al. Assessing oropharyngeal dysphagia after lung transplantation: altered swallowing mechanisms and increased morbidity. The Journal of heart and lung transplantation : the official publication of the International Society for Heart Transplantation. 2007. PMID: 18022080. Registry ID: none in the record. cards.headline: Questionnaire-vs-questionnaire comparison after anterior cervical spine surgery (2022): the HSS-Dysphagia subscale reached AUCs >0.9 — against the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory, ANOTHER QUESTIONNAIRE, not an instrumental standard; the Bazaz scale was least accurate
cards.summary: Questionnaire-vs-questionnaire comparison after anterior cervical spine surgery (2022): the HSS-Dysphagia subscale reached AUCs >0.9 — against the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory, ANOTHER QUESTIONNAIRE, not an instrumental standard; the Bazaz scale was least accurate
cards.type: Prospective diagnostic study — patient-reported instruments vs a questionnaire reference standard (anterior cervical spine surgery)
cards.people: Prospective diagnostic study in a Chinese population: 150 consecutive patients after anterior cervical spine surgery evaluated with the Bazaz scale, Dysphagia Short Questionnaire (DSQ) and HSS-Dysphagia and Dysphonia Inventory (HSS-DDI), with the MD Anderson Dysphagia Inventory (MDADI) as the reference criterion; 132 completed all surveys.
cards.result: All surveys correlated significantly with each other. The HSS-DDI and its dysphagia subscale showed near-perfect reliability (Cronbach α 0.969 and 0.957). Against the MDADI reference, both HSS-DDI and the HSS-Dysphagia subscale had greater accuracy (AUCs >0.9) for detecting mild and moderate/severe dysphagia; the Bazaz scale was considered less accurate than the other scales.
cards.watchOut: BINDING: the reference standard is a questionnaire, not FEES or videofluoroscopy. These AUCs are never printed beside the FEES-referenced figures on this shelf without that distinction, and they measure agreement with another symptom inventory, not detection of aspiration.
cards.source: Liang G et al. Comparison of Bazaz scale, Dysphagia Short Questionnaire, and Hospital for Special Surgery-Dysphagia and Dysphonia Inventory for Assessing Dysphagia Symptoms After Anterior Cervical Spine Surgery in Chinese Population. cards.headline: Synthesis: after surgery, structure is what performs — a targeted screen hit 90%/83% in one small series, a symptom questionnaire managed AUC 0.68, and the unstructured clinical examination misses silent aspiration outright
cards.summary: Synthesis: after surgery, structure is what performs — a targeted screen hit 90%/83% in one small series, a symptom questionnaire managed AUC 0.68, and the unstructured clinical examination misses silent aspiration outright
cards.people: Five postoperative reports: one prospective screen validation (liver transplant, N = 50), one prospective questionnaire-vs-FEES study (cervical spine, N = 64), two retrospective lung-transplant series (321 referred; 263 recipients, 149 evaluated) and one questionnaire-vs-questionnaire study (132 completers). Populations are transplant and anterior cervical only.
cards.result: The gradient is the finding: structured targeted screen 90% sensitivity / 83% specificity (single centre, programme's own validation); EAT-10 moderate discrimination (AUC 0.68); unstructured clinical examination with a demonstrated silent-aspiration miss (27% normal examination despite instrumental penetration/aspiration; 77.6% of aspirations silent). No anchor tests whether screening changes pneumonia, feeding or mortality outcomes.
cards.watchOut: Screening accuracy only — no outcome claim. Referral selection in both lung-transplant series and the questionnaire reference standard in the fifth report stay printed wherever their figures are used.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.

shelves.title: Alvarado score for suspected appendicitis: a strong rule-out at a cut-off of 5 (sensitivity 99%) and a weak rule-in at 7 (specificity 81% overall, 57% in men) — well calibrated in men, over-predicting in women, and not the most accurate score in the 2025 adult meta-analysis
shelves.question: In patients with suspected acute appendicitis, how accurately does the Alvarado score (migration of pain, anorexia, nausea/vomiting, right-lower-quadrant tenderness, rebound, fever, leucocytosis and neutrophil shift; 10 points) separate appendicitis from other causes of abdominal pain — what sensitivity does the score achieve at the rule-out cut-off of 5, how poorly does it rule in at 7, what stratum-specific likelihood ratios does the prospective-studies review derive for adults, and how does the score compare with the RIPASA score in the 2025 adult meta-analysis?
shelves.mesh: Appendicitis/diagnosis · Humans · Predictive Value of Tests · Severity of Illness Index · Adult · Appendicitis/classification, diagnosis · Child · Diagnosis, Differential · Appendicitis/diagnosis, surgery · Acute Disease · Sensitivity and Specificity
shelves.balance: This shelf rests on 3 syntheses whose primary-study sets overlap — the count prints as 3 syntheses. It is a diagnostic-accuracy shelf, not a management shelf: no card may imply Alvarado-guided imaging or observation pathways improve outcomes. The asymmetry is the content. Rule-out: at cut-point 5, sensitivity was 99% overall (96% men, 99% women, 99% children) in the 42-study systematic review. Rule-in: at cut-point 7, specificity was only 81% overall — 57% in men, 73% in women, 76% in children. Calibration splits by sex: the score was well calibrated in men across all risk strata but over-predicted the probability of appendicitis in women across all strata (and in children in the intermediate and high groups) — printed beside the headline 99% wherever that figure appears. The prospective-studies review (26 cohort studies avoiding verification bias) gives adult stratum likelihood ratios, labelled as likelihood ratios: 0.03 at <4 points, 0.42 at 4–6 and 3.4 at ≥7; and 0.01 / 0.98 / 6.7 across the <5 / 5–8 / ≥9 bands — with pretest probability differing systematically between the child (~33%) and adult (~66%) study sets, printed with those ratios. The 2025 adult meta-analysis (40 studies) found the RIPASA score most accurate (sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.913, diagnostic odds ratio labelled as such in the source), significantly exceeding the Alvarado and modified Alvarado scores: the Alvarado score is the most studied but not the most accurate, and the shelf says so.

cards.headline: Systematic review (2011, 42 studies): at cut-point 5 the score ruled out appendicitis with sensitivity 99% overall (96% in men, 99% in women and in children), while at cut-point 7, the recommended rule-in threshold, specificity was only 81% overall and 57% in men, 73% in women and 76% in children; the score was well calibrated in men but over-predicted appendicitis probability in women across all risk strata
cards.summary: Systematic review (2011, 42 studies): at cut-point 5 the score ruled out appendicitis with sensitivity 99% overall (96% in men, 99% in women and in children), while at cut-point 7, the recommended rule-in threshold, specificity was only 81% overall and 57% in men, 73% in women and 76% in children; the score was well calibrated in men but over-predicted appendicitis probability in women across all risk strata
cards.type: Systematic review — Alvarado score discrimination and calibration (synthesis; overlapping primary studies)
cards.people: Systematic review of 42 validation studies of the Alvarado score in suspected appendicitis, analysing discrimination at cut-points 5 and 7 and calibration across low (1–4), intermediate (5–6) and high (7–10) risk strata, in men, women and children.
cards.result: At cut-point 5 the score was good at ruling out admission for appendicitis (sensitivity 99% overall; 96% men, 99% women, 99% children). At cut-point 7 it performed poorly at ruling in (specificity overall 81%; men 57%, women 73%, children 76%). Calibration was good in men across all strata (relative risks 1.06, 1.09 and 1.02 across low/intermediate/high), but the score over-predicted appendicitis probability in women across all risk strata and in children in the intermediate and high groups. The reviewers conclude the score is a useful rule-out at 5 for all groups.
cards.watchOut: The sex asymmetry prints beside the headline 99%: a rule-in specificity of 57% in men at cut 7 means most score-positive men in these studies did not have appendicitis confirmed at that threshold's operating point — never quote 'cut 7 = operate' from this review.

systematic review — alvarado score discrimination and calibration (synthesis; overlapping primary studies) systematic review of 42 validation studies of the alvarado score in suspected appendicitis, analysing discrimination at cut-points 5 and 7 and calibration across low (1–4), intermediate (5–6) and high (7–10) risk strata, in men, women and children. at cut-point 5 the score was good at ruling out admission for appendicitis (sensitivity 99% overall; 96% men, 99% women, 99% children). at cut-point 7 it performed poorly at ruling in (specificity overall 81%; men 57%, women 73%, children 76%). calibration was good in men across all strata (relative risks 1.06, 1.09 and 1.02 across low/intermediate/high), but the score over-predicted appendicitis probability in women across all risk strata and in children in the intermediate and high groups. the reviewers conclude the score is a useful rule-out at 5 for all groups. the sex asymmetry prints beside the headline 99%: a rule-in specificity of 57% in men at cut 7 means most score-positive men in these studies did not have appendicitis confirmed at that threshold's operating point — never quote 'cut 7 = operate' from this review. ohle r et al. the alvarado score for predicting acute appendicitis: a systematic review. bmc medicine. 2011. pmid: 22204638. registry id: none in the record. mesh: appendicitis/diagnosis · humans · predictive value of tests · severity of illness index

cards.headline: Prospective-studies review (2014): for the Alvarado score in adults, the likelihood ratios (labelled as such) were 0.03 at <4 points, 0.42 at 4–6 points and 3.4 at ≥7 points, and 0.01 / 0.98 / 6.7 across the <5 / 5–8 / ≥9 bands — against pretest probabilities of about 66% in adult studies and 33% in child studies

cards.type: Systematic review of prospective cohorts — Alvarado stratum likelihood ratios (synthesis; overlapping primary studies)
cards.people: Systematic review restricted to 26 prospective cohort studies of the Alvarado and Pediatric Appendicitis Scores that avoided verification bias, calculating summary likelihood ratios at all possible cut-offs from the available data.
cards.result: In adults, Alvarado likelihood ratios were 0.03 (<4 points), 0.42 (4–6) and 3.4 (≥7); and 0.01 (<5), 0.98 (5–8) and 6.7 (≥9). In children they were 0.02 / 0.27 / 4.2 and 0.04 / 1.2 / 8.5 across the same bands; for the Pediatric Appendicitis Score, 0.13 / 0.70 / 8.1. Pretest probability of appendicitis was approximately 33% in the child studies and 66% in the adult studies. The authors derive setting-specific rules: in adults with pretest probability ≥60%, a score of 8 or higher rules in; a score below 4 rules out in children at pretest probability up to about 60%.
cards.watchOut: Likelihood ratios print with their population (adult vs child) and the pretest probabilities of the underlying study sets (~66% vs ~33%) — a likelihood ratio quoted without its band and population is not this review's finding.

cards.headline: Adult meta-analysis (2025, 40 studies): the RIPASA score showed the highest accuracy (sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.913, diagnostic odds ratio labelled as such in the source), significantly exceeding the Alvarado and modified Alvarado scores — the Alvarado score is the most studied but not the most accurate
cards.summary: Adult meta-analysis (2025, 40 studies): the RIPASA score showed the highest accuracy (sensitivity 0.93, specificity 0.81, AUC 0.913, diagnostic odds ratio labelled as such in the source), significantly exceeding the Alvarado and modified Alvarado scores — the Alvarado score is the most studied but not the most accurate
cards.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis — clinical scores for appendicitis in adults (synthesis; overlapping primary studies)
cards.people: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 diagnostic-accuracy studies of clinical scores for acute appendicitis in adults, each compared against histopathological findings.
cards.result: The RIPASA score showed superior sensitivity (0.93, 95% CI 0.78–0.98), specificity (0.81, 0.62–0.91) and diagnostic odds ratio (45.3, 10.9–187.2, labelled as such), with a summary ROC AUC of 0.913; heterogeneity was very high (I² 86–96%). A significant difference was found between RIPASA and both the Alvarado score (P < 0.002) and the modified Alvarado score (P < 0.004) in SROC curves. The authors conclude RIPASA is the most effective scoring system, while the Alvarado score remains the most studied.
cards.watchOut: Adults only, histopathology reference. The very high heterogeneity (I² up to 96%) prints with the RIPASA figures; this card compares scores — it does not supply a new Alvarado pooled pair, and none may be back-computed from it.

cards.headline: Synthesis: use the Alvarado score to rule out at 5, not to rule in at 7 — and know that in adults a comparator score (RIPASA) pooled more accurately in 2025
cards.summary: Synthesis: use the Alvarado score to rule out at 5, not to rule in at 7 — and know that in adults a comparator score (RIPASA) pooled more accurately in 2025
cards.people: Three syntheses with overlapping primary-study sets, counted as syntheses: a 42-study review (discrimination and calibration), a 26-prospective-study review (stratum likelihood ratios) and a 40-study adult meta-analysis (score comparison).
cards.result: Rule-out at cut-point 5: sensitivity 99% overall. Rule-in at cut-point 7: specificity 81% overall, as low as 57% in men. Adult likelihood ratios run from 0.03 (<4 points) to 6.7 (≥9 points). Calibration is good in men and over-predicting in women. RIPASA exceeded Alvarado in adults (AUC 0.913) with very high heterogeneity.
cards.watchOut: Accuracy only — no Alvarado-guided management outcome is tested anywhere in this base, and no card claims one.
cards.source: Synthesis of the reports carded above; no additional source.
